I played Galactic Civilization II and while I did not find it as enjoyable as some people did - too grindy for me - I could see the reasons why people loved it so much. It was fun and had character.
Galactic Civilization III however? I cannot in good conscience recommend it. I gave it a good try and I'm deleting it from my hard drive as we speak for the following reasons:
1. It's an INCOMPLETE re-skinned GalCiv II. It has some new minor tweaks (shipyard for example) but it's mostly just an updated and prettier GalCiv II with some major features missing (espionage, elections, etc)
2. Its claims are unfounded. Largest space game? Try Distant Worlds instead. Unique races? There are one or two tweaks in the technology tree or buildings and that's all there is. It's not like Sword of the Stars with completely different feel for different races.
3. Rather uninspired tech tree. To be fair GalCiv II was the same but advancement in tech tree is nothing more than going from Weapon X to Weapon X + 1. There was nothing in the technology tree that changes the mechanics of the game. In Master of Orion (1!) we go through the same iteration of Weapon X, X+1, X+2 but then at some point we get the fancy schmancy Black Hole Generator. I played the game 20 years ago and I still remember the god damn Black Hole Generator! What can we say about this game 20 years from now? "Ya - Remember that beam+20?? That was cool!!"?
4. Completely unbalanced and boring ground invasion. In my experience a single transport was able to conquer the Drengin homeworld. The ground invasion tech tree? Nope - didn't need that.
5. To be fair there were moments when I had fun with this game. Reminded me of late 90's or early 2000's strategy game. Seeing it's 2016...that unfortunately counts against this game.
6. The straw that breaks the camel's back - the greed for further DLCs and expansions as opposed to fixing the base game. I got this game 6 months after release. I accepted it still had flaws and was hoping there'd be further improvements down the road. Then I saw the news that there's an expansion coming out already. On top of the 3 DLCs already out.

ABZU is a highly visual and musical experience which I really enjoyed. I will say that if you don't have a decently powerful PC, you will experience peformance issues. I have a gtx 1060 and at 1440p I mostly got 60 fps in my playthrough, although there were ocassional dips into the 40's. These dips occured where I would expect them to be... rendering big swarms of fish and trippy geometric ceilings in an endless array of colors can take it's toll. Maybe they could have done some optimizing, but if you have the hardware you can plow through the issues.
The music is top notch, beautifully orchestrated and fits the theme. Each area is visually stunning, I had a great time just sitting back and enjoying the views throughout the game. As for gameplay, it's fairly light. The controls work well enough and there are some collectibles, but ultimately there isn't much challenge in this game, and that was okay for me. Some gamers may not be happy with the lack of challenge, but I found it a nice change of pace, and it was very relaxing.
I purchases ABZU on sale for $10 and thought it was well worth the price. Multiple times I found myself in awe of how fluid and beautiful this game was. And even though it is short, I think it is even worth its full price, considering the amount of work they put into it.

I really did try to like this game.  The whole 'adult-oriented fantasy' genre is right up my alley.  And I was genuinely hoping that this game would live up to its 'hype.'
Unfortunately, there's just too much wrong with this game for me to give it a 'thumbs-up.'  Here's a short list of problems I had, in no particulary order:
---  The game is extremely difficult at first.  Living through the excessively long Prologue should get one an achievement !  And, it doesn't get any easier until one is mostly through the first Chapter.
---  It is far too linear to be an RPG.  I would call this game an Action game with RPG elements (kind of like a medieval Deus Ex).
---  Gameplay is not intuitive at all (at least it wasn't to me).  I looked FOREVER for the one part I needed to trap the huge monster in the beginning.  If you can find it and use it as it is meant to be used (and not throw it away as garbage) you should give yourself a HUGE pat on the back.
---  There are too many 'historical anachronisms' which (for me) break immersion.  For instance, I don't believe modern psychological theory (and terminology) has any place in a game supposedly set in the 14th Century.
I could easily add a couple more items to the list, but I will stop here.
I was disappointed in this game.  Perhaps the next installment will be better.

I Wanna be the Cat is a wonderful game oozing with charm. The game offers a huge amount of variety with the vast amount of rooms, all catering to different difficulties to ensure every player has something they can have fun with, and the promise of future updates with more levels and gamemodes only makes this more exciting.
The single player is a very enjoyable roguelike platforming adventure with whimsical bosses and tricky challenges, always keeping to a high standard of design and polish. A lot of care has been put into the graphics, making the world feel very warm and vibrant, and the added challenges make for many hours of fun with the single-player mode alone.
Where the game hits a real stride is the race mode, allowing up to 8 players to race been a series of maps that are procedurally generated into one another, making for a very comfortable flow whilst you're battling it out with your friends or new opponents. I'd like to see the room-search updated a little as the current state only shows rooms that aren't mid-game, making it tricky to hop into a lobby if you don't even know they exist. Regardless, racing brings a new side to I Wanna be the Guy fangames that hasn't been touched on before, and it's a great deal of fun.
If you're looking for a charming and challenging platformer with a great deal of passion put into it, you'll be right at home with this one.

I give this a tepid recomendation. A lot of Paradox fanboy's are giving this a lot of hype (as other steam reviews will demonstrate), but i don't actually feel this game deserves that much praise. where to start
GOOD
-Customization is wonderful, it is just awesome
-The initial gameplay of explore, colonize, research, fight small skirmishes, and all the other typical 4x systems work enough to make you feel excited and keep you occupied at the beggining of the game.
-it good to be able to micro manage planets and not make it feel like a boring chore *cough* CK2 casltes *cough*
-the way you research is actually fun and engaging
-micro managing fleets, fleet armanents and building defensive structures can actually be really fun.
-MULTIPLAYER IS AWESOME, JUST STELLAR
BAD
-diplomacy....what the hell happened to diplomacy??? green and red opinion modifiers are nothing new, but there is no feeling that these other species are alive. its all about getting that trade bar at "1 green" when trading and that is all that matters with AI. at least with EU4 and CK2 i felt that there were some "people" behind the decisions and not just a literal green modifier that forces them to accept no matter what.
-forming alliances and federations is a hassle since the alliance has to approve wars (you can't go solo when in an alliance) and federations change presidents, causing the AI to take control and do something stupid. federations can also overlap with some species, meaning if i attack species "x" in federation "x" with species "Y" who also happens to be a different federation called "Y" then it calls both federations Y and X into the war even though i am not declaring on species Y. I don't know if this is a bug, but its dumb ethier way.
-battles are non interactive and you can barely see all those minor improvements you painstakingly updgraded and researched for your fleets.
-science ships and construction ships become a hassle in the late game since you have to manually control them, take a lesson from Civilzation and add an explore or auto build button.
-planets become a hassle as you get to the late game, making it clear the UI was clearly not designed for super late game.
-wars take way to long at the late game, i have spent 30 years sieging half this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s planets and destorying his fleets. but he won't surrender because there is no war exhaustion system, at least i don't believe so.
to sum it up. early game-mid game are quite fun, but late game is a micro managing hell that the UI was not designed for, wars are not that interesting due to how stale the battles are, and diplomacy is boring. However, all these problems (not the UI one, but i can live with that) are fixed by the stellar mulitplayer and that was what this game was really designed for considering how Paradox marketed it for. hell the first button on the home screen is multiplayer and not single player. i just wish more time and energy went to the UI and single player.

text: I come from EU4 and CKII (and what I could take of HOI2) so I was super excited for a Paradox sci-fi. The amount of detail present in past games made learning them a slow hours long process but also reflected a lot of work and very serious amountsof substance. This is no different in Stellaris except that you're not spending half your day learning. Every aspect I could have asked for seems to be present so far. Want to genetically modify a steam-age civilization of newly discovered humans? You can. Want exploration and colonization? There's tons. Want to be a fanatically individualist race of fungus people? Of course. Want to edit your own ships? Why not. Orbital bombardment and planetary assaults? You got it, and with amazing graphics too. LORE?! Plenty. So I played this game already almost 20 hours and got 12/25 achievements. Here are my thoughts:
At the moment this game consists of two different modes: 100 lives singleplayer and online racing.
First the singleplayer:
Based on the sentence: 'A cat has nine lives' Nemega added 91 and lets you beat a randomly chosen set of levels in multiple worlds.
Between the levels you can find chests and shops with items which you can buy with ingame currency. Also at a certain point in the world and at the end there are bosses. They are funny parodies of bosses which are popular in the I wanna be the guy fanbase.
There are three difficulties to choose from: Medium, Hard and Impossible.
Medium is the perfect difficulty for beginners. Hard and impossible have harder bosses with added phases and overall more challenging levels.
If you lose all your lives in a run you can buy perks with coins for the following rounds. These consist of useful items, added lives and many more.
Now on to the online racing:
In this mode you can create your own room or join one to play a randomly chosen set of levels in a race. Up to eight players can try to reach the goal first. Even if you don't have any players to race against, you can play it alone and train your movement.
This mode also consists of three difficulties: Easy, Medium and Hard. In each one you need to beat a different amount of levels to finish the race.
I really need to say that this mode is addicting. I think I played this mode four hours straight with a full lobby of people.
Even if this game has still a few bugs, Nemega is trying his best to make this game as enjoyable as possible. He already released three patches, so I don't think this will be a problem.
Overall if you enjoy jump 'n' runs or speedruns and if you are up for a challenge, try it out. I never saw a game like this before and I really enjoy it. You could say this game has endless content with the randomized levels and there will also be a new mode added in the future. This game is worth the price.

Short review:
Compared to Civ:BE since that's the closest analog:  I was looking for a game with more "feel".  I wanted to land on a planet that felt alien, that had many and monstrous aliens.  I wanted to have hordes of infantry trying to hold back mountain-sized behemoths and leviathans swallowing my ships in one gulp.  This game has that feel.  The world is alien.  The gameplay is different enough that it will take a little bit of time to optimize your play compared to the more traditional Civ:BE.  If I had to choose between the two, right now I'd pick this one.  Immersion > polish...at least while aliens (and Aliens) have a significant presence.
There are some cons though; spies are cheap and can be pretty powerful (you can easilly scout an enemy's ENTIRE empire with one easy to do scout mission to one city anywhere in the world?).  There is no traditional manual:  yes, there's a book full of backstory, but there are no. rules. anywhere.  There isn't even a decent wiki and compared to other 4x games out there hard info is difficult to find, so optimizing your play will be difficult
Overall, if you need the 4x on a distant planet game, I would tip my hat to this one.

-The dialogue: I simply do not care about these characters. The writing seems very amateurish. I like characters that I can relate to as a person, but every npc has a very dry personality and just sends you on boring fetch quests. Literally every line of npc dialogue can be summed up as "Oh here there sonny I lost my X, can you help me find them?".
Overall this is a really boring game for adults, and probably kids too. If only it had better writing and proper pacing, then it could have been so much more.

Okay, here's the short version of this review.

Now for the long version of this review.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is one of the most well-crafted video games I have ever played, and it's easily in my top 5 favourite games of all time. Picked this up based the Extra Credits endorsement, and I'll say out the gate that I don't regret the (sale price) purchase. The game does a lot of things right that Civilization: Beyond Earth -didn't- do, and if you're a fan of the classic Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri (I am!), then this will bring back fond memories.
THE GOOD:
Pandora plays like a rework of SMAC for the modern platform. The factions are very reminiscent of the original SMAC factions and the unit customizaton is well-done (if a bit lacking in variety). The interface is slick and easy to use - I had few cases where I couldn't find information I was looking for. Graphically, it's on par with competitors like Civ: BE or Endless Legend - while I don't necessarily play 4X for the graphics, these are well-done and I particularly like the look of many alien units (a Leviathan underwater looks impressive, and rightly so!).
Possibly my favorite feature is the resource pooling: instead of per-city farming/production, raw resources (food and minerals) go into a civ-wide pool, and each city has growth and production rates that use resources from the pool. This is a MUCH more modern take on 4X gaming - it's always frustrated me in similar games that I couldn't have a region producing a lot of food export that to other cities, and Beyond Earth's attempt to manage it with Trade Routes really didn't cut the mustard for a number of reasons. This hit the nail spot-on.
THE BAD:
Like Beyond Earth, Pandora suffers from serious balance issues. Some terrain features provide an overwhelming advantage through the entire game: a flat +50% to production or research for a city is unbeatable if you have it and someone else doesn't. The tech tree is reasonably easy to figure out, but its nonlinear (and randomized, game-to-game) nature make it easy to cherry-pick the techs you want and advance quickly. It would have been nice to see some variety in the tree: by the time I got to the second 'era', I was just learning bigger copies of buildings I already had, and my interest petered out. I also found that by the mid-game, the native populations had vanished and were no longer a threat (even after the major event adding new ones); this is a sharp contrast to SMAC where, if you polluted, the aliens kept coming and kept getting worse.
THE WTF:
The AI is completely irrational. I've had cases where it goes from denouncing me to praising me to offering gifts to declaring war, all in the space of a couple dozen turns. While the faction-customized dialogue options are nice, the 'locked-in' nature of each option means that I have basically no way of telling what I did to♥♥♥♥♥♥it off, either.
Overall, I like what I've played so far, (20 hours in) and plan to continue. The game is good, if not particularly challenging (due to the mentioned balance problems); I can see many places that it could have been better.

My guess is you're probably playing this because you got it for free along with Half-Life 2. I know that's why I played it. I suppose that's the joy of deleted scenes. It can really show who's smart and dumb in the entertainment buisness when it comes to what's exactly deleted. You've got the dumb ones like Lord of the Rings that throws out Saruman's last stand and the Amazing Spider-Man 2 which deleted all the important story scenes. And then there are the smart ones like Star Wars and Half Life 2, which you can go back and appreciate their deleted scenes for exaclty what they are. Would this have been fun in Half-Life 2? Sure. But it wouldn't add too much to the plot, so it's understandable.

I'll say upfront: Necropolis is best enjoyed as a coop. Myself, I've never played single-player and I wouldn't want to, for two reasons. First, I feel it would get damn near impossible to get through it alone around level 4, if not sooner (depending on what the Brazen Eye has randomly conjured up for you). But more importantly, Harebrained Schemes did an excellent job with this one: the level design, game-play, adversaries, lore, and atmosphere all instill in you a lonesome, bewildered and (sometimes) creepified feeling that you would expect if really stuck in a place like Necropolis, trying to escape. Playing with a friend makes it feel that less "threatening", and you really do want to share with another what you experience and come across whilst playing this great game.
Coop provides hilarious moments (check out some of my screenshots), and quite a challenge in its own right. You can damage each other ... you
damage each other,
put one another out of commission if you don't get a system of playing together down pat. If all go down, that's it, game over. But with Necropolis, restarting only complements it because it's so very random: every time I have played, there was something never before encountered! Also, there are codexes and cosmetic colours that offer special abilities and customisation, all obtainable only via multiple play-throughs.
With such a complex, randomly generated world, it is amazing that there is only one load time, the beginning (less than 10 seconds), and then no load screens,
. (This fact is made even more incredible when you get inside and see the world for yourself.) Joining for a coop is problem-free and fast. Every once in a while I have experienced some problem with sync, but that was due to ISP issues. The movement in and out of battles is fluid, well-designed and very "free-ranged" feeling; I wouldn't dream of playing Necropolis without a controller.
Even after 48 hours of play-time, I still get a chill, waiting for that door to open, to see what the Necropolis has in store for me. When you get inside this world, you will be in awe of it's design.  And when you and your buddy have wandered around for more than an hour--both marveling at how vast the level turned out to be and all the loots you plundered--before finally coming across that
door not yet opened, you'll both be made momentarily speechless to find the Brazen Eye at the end of that long corridor, expectant in unreadable glee at your startled figures.

This is probably the best roguelike (or roguelite) I've ever played. :-)
Why? Let's see...
-the theming: it mixes classic dungeon crawling with rhythm (or at least: sets you on a beat), and it maintains that position to the smallest details. From singing shopkeepers to music-themed bosses, it's neither too corny nor not flavourful enough.
-as far as variety in procedurally generated levels are concerned, things are pretty decent. There's a good amount of enemy variety and items, and all the systems seem to work together well (will you trade hearts for a better weapon? Will you fight extra monsters for gold to buy better gear? Will you risk stuff for diamonds to easy future runs?).
-the whole nine yards: in the lobby, you can practice fighting enemies, there are other characters to chose from, lots of unlocks, and so on. I even had problems finding the actual story mode. ;-)
-difficulty: as many roguelikes go, this follows the standard "extremely hard to complete" pattern, requiring many playthroughs from your end (reason why the variety is important). However, since enemies move to the beat in predictable patterns, all errors are technically your own fault. Still, even when playing as the bard (I'll get to that), it's pretty hard to actually make a good run.
-music: as you should expect, the music is great. And I may be underestimating it when I say that.
I've gotta say that Crypt of the Necrodancer feels like it has done its homework on the genre. It's like every plus point I find in spelunky, don't starve or nuclear throne is also somehow included here (though the beat-following is something of its own). The result is a very well polished and fun to play game.
As said, the bard deserves special mentioning. Where other characters have slight variations on the main character, the bard doesn't follow the beat. While this makes the game less hard (it's still in no way easy), it does change the entire gameplay. It also removes the only gripe I have with the game: that the constant moving in a beat can get pretty annoying if you just want to backtrack to another part of the dungeon. The bard changes the game so much it's an entirely different game (rather akin to Nova-111, btw). A better one, some might argue, though it misses a bit of the magic that makes the game special.
But whatever character you pick, this game has this addiction that when you die you immediately go "again! again!". So beware: your social life might suffer because of this game. ;-)

Necropolis is a really interesting real-time action dungeon crawler with plenty of quirky humor. The game is set within the titular Necropolis, wherein adventurers assist the Brazen Head with random chores, grocery shopping, and eventually decorating the hallways with their skeletons.
To aid them in the task of diving into the depths of the Necropolis, adventurers loot many treasures from all over the dungeon to assist in their longevity, be it scavenging weapons off of the corpses of the undead denizens, scrapping poorly crafted automatons, opening treasure chests, mixing together all manner of ingredients for alchemy, or taking advantage of the monthly sales at the local Ulzister Mart*.
Now, let's talk about the game stuff.
The combat in Necropolis is very reminiscient of the popular Action RPG franchise "Dark Souls" with a small sprinkling of the Legend of Zelda in some respects. The game doesn't rely on leveling up and making a proper stat build to viably reach the end of your journey, but instead has the player slowly upgrade their gear from start to finish, gradually becoming more resilient against the dangers deep within dungeon. It's not necessarily hard in most cases, but it is very unforgiving in regards to making mistakes.
Unfortunately, the actual act of fighting enemies often feels unrefined, with many weapon and enemy movesets often feeling less than impactful in their animations. A lot of the motions, especially with larger weapons, often feel to lack weight, instead opting to make things 'seem' more heavy by using slower movements rather than having more windup and recovery time. When there are multiple large enemies on screen throwing out many attacks, it may often leave one wondering exactly why something specifically did so much harm as they clipp the end of an animation where a weapon was moving with the velocity of a motorized shopping cart.
The Necropolis doesn't have many things one would consider a "boss", unfortunately. Most such things come down to being randomly-placed mobs that are essentially just bigger versions of other mobs (with said other mobs mingling with them) with very linear movesets and few hazards if you're attacking it using a ranged weapon. I personally would have preferred a more tailor-made encounter every two or three floors with something that required a lot of focus and arena navigation.
However, the game manages to keep things interesting with the use of randomly generated dungeons and encounters. This leaves the player pitted against a wide variety of many different types of mob scenarios, making it so that the player needs to rely on more situational awareness as rooms rarely generate with the exact same setup as before. A wise adventurer is less likely to be tackled by a Gemeater as they will look ahead before they progress, where an unwise adventurer will often land themselve's in trouble by rushing face-first into a waiting ambush.
The two character classes feel a bit imbalanced between one another in a few ways. The Black Guard seems as though they are to be the speedy and agile fighter who avoids taking hits while the Brute is the slower, tankier one. However, the way I-frames are distributed on dodges seems rather ill-planned, allowing the Brute to have an easier time avoiding damage as they have a rolling dodge animation twice the length of the Black Guard's side step that allows them more leniency with getting through attacks unscathed than their shorter ally. It's not all fine and dandy for the Brute, though, as some vertical attack animations, particularly with Greatsword-style weapons, tend to veer off to the side, often causing the attack to outright miss thinner adversaries.
Finally, the game shares one of the greatest difficulty-killers that plague many RPGs and survival games: Alchemy.
Every enemy drops some sort of crafting material. It's very rare that one does not drop some sort of crafting ingredient, and by the time one gets a couple of hours into the dungeon, they'll be able to fill Olympic swimming pools with buffs and restoration. The game lacks a true Pause feature, but it's not terribly difficult to step away from enemies to craft any given potion that you'd need to overcome a situation. The one thing that makes it difficult to become truly immortal (aside from the rare recipe for a literal potion of immortality to revive once on death), is that you only have ten item slots, and nothing stacks, forcing the player to decide if they want to hold on to valuable spell scrolls or keep space open so they can overdose on Essense of Vitality (that's not an exaggeration by the way, you can literally get sick by drinking too many potions in a short time frame).
Though the game has perma-death, dying in Necropolis does not deny the player completely of any progression. Side-quests from the Brazen Head and dying will reward the player for their efforts with Tokens of Favor. One token per completed quest, and a number of tokens are further rewarded based on the player's performance during the post-death results screen. The tokens persist between playthroughs and can be used to purchase alternate color palletes (so you may enter the Necropolis with more style on future adventurers) at the Old Man shop keepers and codices (permanent in-game unlocks that offer bonuses in the forms of buffs and bonuses) at the library pedestals.
So, you were worried about that codex you bought so you could recover stamina faster on your last adventurer? Don't be; just pick it up again on the next adventurer at the start of your next run.
The game features co-op, but it's a bit of a mixed bag. On the note of difficulty, all of the loot has to be split between each player, making it more difficult to just become a one-warrior army through lucky chests. Players also have to be very mindful of eachother's positioning and who is doing what as the game features full friendly-fire. A player who recklessly throws around power attacks will often cause a lot of harm to their friends.
However, co-op loses a lot of challenge in that it allows players to freely revive eachother on death, taking away a lot of the risks that come with playing the game. The only cost to trying to revive a fallen player is that they lose a bit of time spent in animations instead of progressing through the dungeon and are temporarily open to taking damage (though they may dodge out of attacks at any time), with no cost to their Tokens of Favor or Gems.
Furthermore, the game doesn't really seem to change enemy spawn patterns based on the number of active players, often making some situations in which one may have had trouble in a late-game floor a bit too simple to overcome.
But, playing with friends helps break some of the monotony of simply killing hoards of soulless beings, and it often feels more entertaining running around with someone else than simply taking on the adventure alone.
My one big issue is that the game doesn't have an in-game chat system or an alternative form of communication (example, Gestures in Dark Souls). Being someone who is incapable of making use of voice chat, I often find it an inconvenience that I have to open my Steam Overlay to say something to my friends who are currently dungeoning with me. It'd be so much better if there were some quick and simple way to just have the character make noise to call for attention and then point to things, show amusement with a sort of laughing behavior, or pointing to a corner so that the one friend we all have can sit and think about their mistakes.
Well, I'm out of text space. I just love game despite its flaws, and I hope to see further refinement in future update.

So with the release of the Witcher 3 i decided it was time to play at least one of the Witcher games sitting unplayed in my library and i decided to jump into the Witcher 2. I ended up really enjoying this game and it's one of the better RPG's i've played i a while. The quests are brilliant some nice depth and detail to them instead of endless fetch quests like a lot of other RPG's.
The games morality system is a lot superior is well with a lot of decisions not always being morally clear and with consequences or benefits not being evident till later. A decision you make early in the game greatly effects the story later giving you good reason to replay the game.
It's not all good though. I didn't really enjoy the combat system which feels a bit clunky and takes getting used to though it does promote taking a more tactical approach to combat utilizing different spells and potions.
The Good:
- great story of political intrigue with a really likeable protaganist in Geralt who seems one-dimensional at first but is actually a complex character
- brilliant quests that have more depth and substance compared to the usual RPG quests
- excellent morality system where the right (or wrong) choice is not always clear and keeps you guessing
The Bad:
-terrible tutorial that doesn't really help a whole lot
-clunky awkward combat that can at times be too easy or too hard when you get swarmed by enemies. Though it does encourage you to approach combat more tactically using spells and potions but the fact you can only drink potions outside combat can leave you ♥♥♥♥ed with a surprise encounter
-the save system is awful. You cant choose save slots to save in or to overwrite, instead each time you save the game creates a new save file leaving your save folder completely overloaded
Overall this is a really enjoyable RPG despite the few flaws and is still worth playing even though it'll be now overshadowed by it's sequel.

As the name implies, this is a hardcore platformer heavily inspired by I Wanna Be The Guy-based fangames. If you've heard of I Wanna Be The Guy before, you may know it's a mostly unfair trial-and-error based platformer focusing on comedic traps. Despite the mechanics and controls in this game being inspired by it, it's a very different experience. Rather than traps, this game wants you to methodically approach rooms, looking at what's going on before jumping in, since you have a limited number of lives. If you can handle difficult games, I'd recommend it - singleplayer alone is a great time, multiplayer races are chaotic and a ton of fun, and the developer has promised to add more stuff after launch. Given his previous game got a ton of updates after launch adding more content and fixes, and this game has already gotten two important patches very quickly, I have no doubt this'll be true here as well.

Although I've only had about an hour and a half with the game so far, I'm really enjoying it!
There are 3 options available as for difficulty of the game which you select before you begin a run. I've only attempted the "normal" setting (which is the lowest)  3 times as of now, and failed at about the 4th world each time. Each run was different, giving the best feelings of both hand-crafted and random design. I never saw any levels twice, and the level structure felt natural, with a steadily climbing difficulty curve that felt fair(still hard as stone though!). You get coins during the regular gameplay to buy items and perks from shops, and when you finally lose all 100 lives, you receive more coins to buy some permanent upgrades to aid in future runs. I may not be far enough in the game yet to make this call, but I thought this might make subsequent playthroughs seem more trivial. Even so, it seems the devs have balanced for this, and none of the items seem like they will make you OP in any fashion at all. There's also an option to turn them off altogether, for the truly daring and skilled.
Other thoughts:
The way the devs described this game on the Steam page with terms like "procedural generation" and "randomly generated levels" was really off-putting to me on first inspection. "IWBTG" and clones of it are in part famous for their pixel perfect jumps and the high skill/patience necessary to get through the stages. This basically had me picturing a HAL 5000 filling every inch of the screen with insta-kill spikes on level 1.. And because of that, I thought that I wanna be The Cat might fail by leaving the course of the game up to algorithm.
I was totally off the mark.
I must have missed the bit where they say 2000+ levels were designed by hand. I think that THIS is what they should be putting in bold for everyone to see. The procedural generation comes in the weaving of these levels together into a larger world (or, that's what it seems like to me!)  and seems to do an excellent job of it. I was a late-comer to the IWBTG world, but I am undoubtedly a huge fan of what it represents. It was both a throwback to the more "unforgiving" games of yesteryear, and even a reaction to the handholding fare of its time. It provided a challenge unlike any other, and most of that challenge was truly rewarding - its code was the one huge flaw, and has made the game unplayable in modern times for a lot of people, becoming a challenge just to get it run. I wanna be the Cat, as a game, gives more people the chance to try their hand at a would-be "official release" at this sort of game, and so far it seems to be an honest effort with solid gameplay. It is also the first non-free clone of IWBTG to have come out, as far as I'm aware, which might seem off-putting to some.
But I think it's worth the money.

Pandora is a re-imaging of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. During my first hour of play I think I came across about a dozen "Wow, it's exactly like Alpha Centauri" moments. I found that whereas with SMAC, a lot of my enjoyment was connected to grand strategic role playing, Pandora was at its best when I played it more as a board game ignoring the cookie cutter nature of the AI opponents and just concentrating on the 4X dynamics. You can have lots of fun with it but I doubt it will stand the test of time ala SMAC. For 4X devotees especially of a SciFi persuasion, I'd say it's a good purchase at a $20 or less price point.

The first thing you have to accept when coming into this game is that it is not a souls game. This has led to some being confused when they start the game for the first time. Ths is a gfantasy roguelike dungeon & biome, third person, adventure, looting, hacking & slashing, action game. The combat system is intuitive and filled with possibilites. The assortment of weapons and gear are large enough to pique your interest and give you plenty of options for each run through of the necropolis. Enemies have different tactics and attributes making choosing gear important if you want to easily dispatch them at later levels. THe difficulty curve is just challenging enough to keep you worrying if you have what it takes to survive the next corner of the dungeo right after finding a new weapon. Environments are pretty big with a remarkable diversity for a roguelike built upon modules being taped to each other. That being said. A few environments get easy to read leading to you losing interest in it. Crafting is a worthwhile feature giving you the tools to survive and the reason to go out andkilll that extra manshark for his alchemical ingredients. The soundtrack is pretty decent. The humorous dialog from your dungeon guide and writing on the walls is a nice feature that make the game worth listening to. The enemy AI is a bit lacking. They can attack and defend well, they just havve issues navigating trickky terrain and bump into eachother while in corridors. The build up to the finalé was unexpected sadly and the lag can be a pain if playing a few continents apart from one another. Over all the game could be better but the car still runs despite missing a rearview mirror. The journey is incredible with or wihout friends which is amazing that you can solo thos game and the changing situations really are endless. This game pleases an eight year old as much as an adult. You'lll get lost in its gloomy fantasy world.

Duck Game on its outside looks like a simple party game to play with your friends and have some laughs with goofy mods and easy to learn gameplay.
In reality, it's only fun if you've got a top tier internet connection with not even the slightest spikes during your match, otherwise you're likely to find yourself killed from several feet away from your opponent, or you shoot them and they don't die, despite you even seeing their feathers fall.
Local multiplayer has shown no issue, but Online Multiplayer needs a lot of tweaking. Overall the online is subpar at best, especially if you play with workshop mods, which requires every single player to have the same mods installed. Which, of course, is expected, but there is a system that is meant to restart your game to enable or install any necessary mods to connect. Seems good, right?
It's not.
This system more often than not fails and continuously gives you the prompt to install the required mods and restart your game. It's more efficient to just make sure you have the same mods beforehand, or play with no mods at all. Which is very disappointing, seeing as how many of the default stages and weapons get rather boring after the first 10 hours or so.
Also the armor system is garbage. You'll either take 10 hits before it breaks or you'll die with it on ever so magically.
TL;DR: The local gamemodes are great, but seeing as how most people are more than likely to play this game via the online versus, I don't recommend the game until they improve the online multiplayer.

If you're a fan of 4X and Sci-Fi, then you will love this.
Build improvements on your worlds (you start with earth and mars if you play as the humans), use the resources generated from those improvements to build starbases and ships and explore the galaxy, meet aliens, negotiate with them or destroy them!
The map size choices are amazing.  Playing a full game with the largest map size will take weeks, or using the small size play through in a few hours if you want a quicker game.
The different races you can choose from really are different.  War based, science based, trade based, cultural based.  Play it however you want to play.  You can even make your own custom race.
Build scouts, contruction ships, colony ships, warships, fighters, carriers.  Use the ships already built into the game, customize them, or build your own fleet from scratch.  I had a great time optimizing ships for specific tasks (low engines and life support on smaller ships with maxes weapons and shields for planetary defense, or gigantic capital ships with all the bells and whistles for leading a fleet of escorts into battle)

Addendum to the Might & Magic (World of )X(een) Legacy.
It's not a bad game, but it's pretty average and a bit too much on the clunky side with a lot less freedom than previous games.
This game is somehow like a watered down spin-off from the Might & Magic 3-5 World of Xeen. It uses the same base mechanics for Map layout, Movement and Combat, which was fine twenty years ago, but feels pretty clunky today. There is also a few inclusions from Might & Magic 6 like the use of Hirelings and a few categories for Spells and Skills and the use of a Skill and Promotion system.
Character creation is more streamlined, but also more boxed in, because everything each Class can learn and to what extent is laid out bare and square with progress bars and totally locked in. You can't add more Points to a Spell or Skill than the Limit of your Rank. There are four Races, each with three distinct Classes that each represents the Might, Hybrid and Magic Class of that Race. There are no limits in regards to which Race and Class you make for your Party, but since the game has no alternative Light Source other than what Magic provides you are going to have a really hard time dealing with Dungeons and underground Areas without a Dwarf (with Fire Magic) or a Class with Light or Dark Magic. If you decide to take a Shot at the Might Achievement you would be really darksided without a Dwarf in the Party, just saying. There are also no requirements for Grandmastery of Light and Dark Magic as there is no kind of Alignment or Reputation system at all.
Combat is quite clunky. You can only attack Enemies that are on the same Line as the one you are standing on and only within a limited Range, which makes Enemy movements look really silly as they slide sideways into Combat and the only Tactic that you can really apply to Combat is to make sure to stand in a Corner, Tunnel or Doorway where the Enemies can't attack you from more than one Side and there is also a limit to how many Enemies can stand on the same Square, which means they will just wait and queue up for the Slaughter. You can only Escape as long as you don't have direct Enemy Contact, but once an Enemy stands next to you you can't move at all.
I can understand why there is no water-walking (no flight, swimming and climbing neither), because that part have been tied into the Story and added as a Roadblock, but I don't understand why there are no Town Portals or Loyds Beacons. Alternatively, you can move around from Obelisk to Obelisk once you have unlocked them and you can add Markers to the Map to remember where they are and what they are called which is visible on the World Map, but they are all quite remote. There is a Spirit Beacon referred to in the description of Primordial Magic as a Spirit Gate, but you can only have ONE one-way ticket for the whole Party despite having several Characters with the same Spell. I really hate all this pointless walking, which it becomes once you have explored it all, because there are never any interruptions or encounters on the Path. The Area Map which is the only Map that shows all the paths can't be zoomed in or out and since there are a lot of Deadends you'll be wasting a lot of time moving from Place to Place, especially when you need to buy a Rank or Spells. There is no free movement at all, but a lot of Maze like Tunnels across the Landscape, through Forests and rocky Terrain. Once you acquire the ability to walk on water you realize that there is remarkably little water that you can actually walk on.
The only really nice thing the Game offers is that you can add your own Markers to the Map, which is visible on the World Map and Area Map and helps a lot to find Trainers again and to keep track of Obelisk and remember where you've been and so on, but unfortunately the Markers you add to a disconnected Area or City is only visible within that Place.
There is also no kind of permanent Item Enchantment in the game. You can't make your own Items or Enchant them with Magical Properties. No point in lugging around anything else than Magic Items, that you intend to use.
Each character has an action bar with ten Slots, but only one. There is no switching between them or making more, which is really too limited.
There is quite a lot of Puzzles and Riddles in the game, which is a bit of a testamony to the old games, but the ones that require you to move around a lot and step on plates in different order or keep track of teleportation Paths are really quite boring and tedious and the clunky Interface is not helpful at all in this regard.
There are a few funny references to Army of Darkness and other Race specific comments to nature and actions, but unfortunately they are just barely chuckleworthy. Your Characters really bark a lot in Combat.
The Story, Sound and Dialogue is pretty decent, but the Graphics are really low-res and it doesn't really support any Resolution at all. The game looks exactly the same in 1280x800 as it does in 1920x1200. It really looks at least ten years older than it is, but due to a tremendous lacks of optimization in the Unity Engine, which is powering the Game, it's actually pretty taxing on your GPU for no reason at all. The game looks nice from a Distance with Shadows and different Light Effects, but it's really blurry up close.
I bought the game on Steam, but I also needed to install Ubisofts UPlay and create an Account in order to play the Game, but UPlay is really half-baked. It tracks my Achievements and seriously slow down loading on Area transistions, but it neither record nor unlock Actions and Rewards and thus I can't unlock any new 'free' Areas. I can't unlock any of the Game Content with Upoints.
The DLC The Falcon & The Unicorn is really short. It's like an End Chapter, which isn't available until you've finished the main Game, and it's actually quite hard. It begins with a Blast of the most cumbersome tediousness of Puzzle solving as the worst parts of the game with a massive moving around. Once you get the hang of it it's quite simple, but incredible boring, because there is really no challenge at all. Until you get it right, until you understand the mechanics it's a massive waste of time.

Might and Magic X is an ok game that falls short of pretty much all its successors (the word is correct, as technically, MMX is supposed to be something like MM 5.5, hence why you get MM6 to complement it), even the mediocre Might and Magic 9. As if to add insult to injury, UbiSoft gives us the extremely good MM6 as a part of the deal as if to tell you - here, this is what Might and Magic 6 represented - tons of spells, water walking, flight, exploration, the ability to look under every nook and cranny and actually be rewarded for it. Might and Magic 6-8 were the golden years of the franchise, and every game brought the lineage to new hights. Then came MM9 which pretty much destroyed all the exploration, but added new 3D engine and interesting locales with roughly as much freedom as its forefathers.
And now, as a slap in the face comes MMX Legacy with its MM6 bonus. Let's compare the two:
1. Movement.
1.1. MM6 has free movement, turning, water walking, flight, strategic positioning even while entering combat AND during combat.
1.2. MMX is rigid as hell. You are forced into a square grid which not only makes the whole movement experince choppy and unpleasant, but also forces you to turn around just as choppily just to see if you haven't missed anything. Why were can't I enter water squares without having a certain god's blessing? Did people simply forget what a Water Walk spell is?
2. Combat.
2.1. MM6 has the best of both systems - turn based combat and real time combat. Turn based combat works like MMX, while in real time you could fly, play to the enemies' disadvantages (like use Water Walk and escpe on water while range attacking the enemies). It was liberating as hell and actually encouraged strategic thinking.
2.2. MMX combat is rigid and there is little need for strategy. Battles are best won if you can put yourself in a corner or a corridor so that only a few enemies at a time have the opportunity to attack you, while you pick them off easily as the others simply wait dumbly for their turns to enter your killzone. And people said that flying and water walking in MM6-8 was exploiting the system...
3. Exploration.
3.1. MM6 encouraged exploration on any level and at any time and actually rewarded you for it. And to prove that, the devs actually put a flight scroll in your starting city, so that you can go and explore. Opening every inch of a map in MM6 is exciting and rewards you with secret islands off the coast that have money or chests lying around, craters in mountains with obelisks, chests, and other rewards. I even found extremely rare items like artifacts and relics in such chests! Even if you encounter difficullt enemies (like even dragons or titans), you have a chance to fly or teleport away to escape and come back later.
3.2. MMX offers little in terms of exploration, mainly because everything is a corridor - and even if you get adventurous and press on, you get punished by it, because you encounter very difficult enemies and have little or no chance against them, which results in death. Artifacts and Relics are found in specific location, and up until now with 2 running play-throughs with 2 different groups, I found the same artifacts in the very same spots in the very sam dungeons. YAY!
4. Equipment.
4.1. MM6 has tons of gear diversity. You would just bite your nails before opening a chest or looting a body, looking at that hotbar right above your characters. Ding... You find 24 gold and an item (Axe)! - hell yeah, my guy needs a new one, is it better? Ding... You found 1096 gold and an item (Relic)! OH YEAH!!! What does it do? Can I even identify it? Can any of guys use it? OH it's a ring, all of my guys can use rings, but I don't know what it does! Screw that, I am porting to town to find out! This nailbiting, mouthwatering experience is very much gone in MMX.
4.2. MMX has a very rigid gear system. 90% of the time I have been finding better stuff in shops than in chests or the bodies of slain enemies. If you want to make a specific character build, you have to rely on the shops in the various cities. And yeah, just go to that same dungeon to get your artifact at the end. YAY...
5. Characters and classes.
MMX does have more diversity in Race/Class creation than MM6 (12 vs 9), but one can't escape the feeling that many of those race/class combos play and feel the same. They also reuse the MM6 system of making specialized fighters & casters, and then add hybrids of both classes. So in essense, you have 4 warrior classes, 4 Hybrid classes and 4 Caster classes. One nukes more, another heals more. One gets an extra attack, the other is better protected. Hybrids can really accomplish a lot and supplement your party well. A touch and go system, really...
In MM6 you had limitations - you Cleric was a poor fighter, but could heal and learn Light/Dark Magic and become an even better healer, buffer, or nuker. Your Knight could wear the best armor and hit like a ten ton truck, and get more attacks per turn. Your Paladin (the Knight/Cleric combo) could hit and heal, but had no access to the best healing & buffing spells from the light tree.
Here, you get a Crusader with Lay on Hands for max heals at any given time at the cost of all your mana who can learn Grandmaster Light Magic (cool heals/buffs), Grandmaster Sword (good fighter), Grandmaster Heavy (well protected), Grandmaster Arcane (Lots of magic resistance). Why not have a few of those in your party, then? IMO, Crusaders very much break the game.
6. To conclude: please don't get me started on the UDONTPLAY 3rd party DRM...
EDIT: As I put it in the comment: That being said, I am a completionist and I will still finish the game. I, however, cannot shake the feeling that it is inferior to all others though. It is like returning to the dark times before your golden age just for the sake of nostalgia.
In short, I would recommend that you buy an MM6-8 bundle and immerse yourself in the 3D-ish world of those games. Explore, fly, walk on water, steal stuff and have fun. Don't be swayed by this Grimrock-style Might and Magic game just because of the Might and Magic in it like I was...

Pandora: First Contact is an exceptional addition to the 4X genre. The graphics and music are amazing, animations smooth, the UI is easy to use to the point of being intuitive. I'd describe some of its mechanics--economy, trade, resources, and diplomacy--as being "Civ V Light". Unit combat is somewhere between Civ IV and Endless Space: each unit has a default power level, but units also have types, and as in ES you can customize your units to be better vs. one type of unit than another. The research tree is somewhat randomized, but sufficiently complex that most games will be won somewhere in the 2nd of three "Eras", depending on your victory conditions.
Of particular interest: the aliens of Pandora. Imagine you've turned the barbarians way up in Civ--in terms of their population, not necessarily their aggression, another setting that you can tweak when starting up the game. Additionally, though the game includes "a" sea unit--because they can be modded as mentioned above--one of the very early technologies allows all ground units to pack themselves up in a virtually unarmed naval transport. With the exception of the turn one needs to dis/embark one's transport, the archipelago set-up is not guaranteed to protect you from the other factions, but may expose your own ground units to the oceanic aliens.... Finally, there are a few pre-set events that will occur during the game at fairly predictable times (e.g. when nearly all factions have entered the 2nd Era of research) that, while thematically interesting the first time around, will continually serve to keep you on your toes.
Pandora was my first experience with Slitherine (the developer), and has been wildly successful. If you didn't like the lack of unit customization in Civ IV, or you wanted that sci-fi Civ V experience that we *finally* got in Civ Beyond Earth, or you'd like a very good, "easy-to-learn, difficult-to-master" 4X game, Pandora is for you.

I'll be honest, I don't think the rythym element works at all. Actual rythym games have you tapping out a tune, getting the feel for the flow of a piece, but here you simply have to tap to a beat, no variation at all. So what you're left with is a very competent roguelike with great music, gimmicks and enemies where you have to arbitrarily go at a fixed pace - no pausing for a second to take stock of a new room, no zipping through an empty corridor at speed, no control over the flow of the game in any way. It feels stilted and frustrating, failing to understand what makes rythym games a joy to play while simultaneously ruining a great roguelike with a poorly thought out gimmick.

Honestly, I don't care much for writing these glowing pieces on highly-acclaimed games. It's the whole "preaching to the choir" aspect that bothers me. I ran into this before back when I reviewed Resident Evil 4. Everyone knows FF7 is a great game, so why even bother with the review? I should just save myself the time & effort, make a humorous reference, then sit my♥♥♥♥♥down and drink...oh right. So I have to say something significant. I have to put words on a page that somehow match the importance and majesty of this classic JRPG. So let's get started.
Like any other game series, Final Fantasy has had its humble beginnings, its ups, downs, controversies, and even today we're uncertain of where it'll go next. Like any good lemming we follow along, buy the latest games, all the while hoping that eventually Square-enix will take the franchise back in the direction we want it to go in. The thing is, there's always been one path, and game-development isn't about what "we" want. FF13 might be a wildly different game compared to FF1, but if you played through most of them, you could see how such a divisive entry could be released. It's the accumulation of elements, taking what works, changing what doesn't, and evolving into something different. But we're getting a little ahead of ourselves.
Final Fantasy 7 is probably not the best JRPG of all time. When it comes to opinions; I don't touch best/worst anything. FF7 is a great JRPG, and certainly a remarkable entry in the series. Part of its quality is in its spectacle. Yes, I'm actually talking about the flashy stuff. Even in its earliest entries, Final Fantasy was always about grandness. In FF3 for the Famicom there was the discovery that your world, was just a tiny floating island in a much larger world. FF7 works in a similar fashion, with that tiny island being Midgar. The battles in FF games have always pushed for more special effects. Everyone remembers their first time casting Ultima in FF6, just like the first time they summoned Knights of the Round.
This touches on another aspect of FF. No effort (no matter how slight) goes unrewarded. One of the aspects I've always enjoyed about FF, is that I can wander into a forest in the middle of nowhere, and possibly bump into a unique monster. Perhaps this monster has a cool special move, that looks really neat, and maybe I'll be able to make it my own (via blue magic or otherwise). Other entries (like FF9) mix things up, like having mini quiz-shows hiding in the forest. It relates to one of my favorite aspects of the original Baldur's Gate. By simply wandering the outskirts you're bound to encounter more than just monsters. There's a lot of neat little discoveries in the dozen or so optional areas BG1 had. FF7 is a much more linear game, yet it still understands the importance of deviation.
The character models...I actually can't complain about them. Yes, nowadays we can simply mod everything so that it looks uniformly superb but...well I'm starting to see the appeal of those blocky wonders. This isn't nostalgia talking either, this is something I just noticed in my most recent play-through. Squaresoft put a lot of work into giving NPCs life. Even today, NPCs in RPGs are only good at standing around, walking in random directions, or (in the case of later Bethesda RPGs) doing a bunch of "radiant dynamic AI" actions that somehow look more robotic than if they were just scripted. A lot of NPCs in FF7 do things, memorable things, things that humans would actually do. Early in the game, there's this woman waiting at a train-station. Now this woman isn't anyone important. In fact, you're supposed to pay attention to the flashback this woman is a part of. Regardless, her boyfriend/husband arrives via train. He's back from war, and he's so happy he does his best Gene Kelly impression, by swinging around a streetlight.
I can't state enough just how brilliant these little moments are. There's no dialogue between these unimportant NPCs, they don't factor into the plot, and yet they add so much. The two most recent FF games I played through were FF13 and FF13-2. The few times I ran into NPCs they're just...standing around. Sometimes they walk, and they say a line or two when I walk past, but that's usually about it. Actually, FF13-2 did have the kids that run around the beach, one of them trips a lot. It might not sound like much, but that little bit of life makes the experience a lot more believable.
Complexity. The first Final Fantasy was practically Wizardry with an overhead view. Even then, it had numerous ideas that offered replay value. The most obvious one is the class system. Once you decided on your party, that was it. Whether you went with the traditional (Fighter, Monk, White Mage, Black Mage) the different (Thief, Thief, Red Mage, Red Mage) or the ridiculous (Four White Mages), you were stuck with that party until you won the game. FF1 was an altogether difficult entry, with numerous random encounters that could wipe you out. One of my most memorable party-wipes was when my party of 4 was killed by a handful of ghouls. Every round they did 1-2 damage, and every round they paralyzed everyone. That was about 25 years ago...sheesh.
By the time FF4 came out, the random encounter was no longer a serious threat. I never saw the easier battles as a "dumbing down" of FF. These RPGs have numerous mechanics and design decisions to keep track of. What better way to drill this into the player's head than through actual combat? The battles are there so you can figure out how everything works. Look at this way: You're always getting a new party member, new spells, espers, materia, junctions, jobs, gambits, etc upon etc. So naturally, you'll want to try things out, and not get killed in the process. It's like a tutorial...without actually being a tutorial (though FF has plenty of those as well).
Most of the depth and challenge in FF comes from taking away all of the stuff you receive. This difficulty has to be player-imposed, but it works wonders for extending the value of these games. FF7 is no different, as there are low-level runs, no materia runs, and so on. Even something as simple as choosing not to use limit-breaks can massively change the game. After all, once a party member takes enough damage, their fight command is replaced with limit. Now what? Hopefully that character learned mug, or has some items that do damage. Heck, you might have to kill them yourself so their meter will drain. Suddenly those bosses you meteorained through become a lot more interesting.
The best part is, even if you play through FF7 and take everything that's given, it's still an enjoyable JRPG. This is due to pacing. Unless you're trying to max out everything, FF7 is a +/-30 hour game. That is PERFECT! I can not emphasize it enough. Those hours are going to be spent in various locales, doing a wide variety of things, and having a grand adventure. I can't tell you the number of RPGs that I've given up on, simply because nothing happens for 5-10 hours at a time. A game having 100s of hours of "content" just isn't a selling point for me anymore. FF7 moves quickly enough, and still tells you all you need to know in terms of story/characters. It isn't spectacularly written, but it's an effective story that is appropriately-paced.
All of this is why I think Final Fantasy 7 deserves respect. It encompasses everything that makes JRPGs work. No really, I believe this game is an example of flawless execution. I mean, a game like Xenogears might have a better plot & more interesting characters (to me), but between disc 2, the platforming, and  t h e  s l o w - m o v i n g  t e x t  t h a t  c a u s e s  m y  b r a i n  t o  g o  n u m b, I regard it as a "more than the sum of its parts" kind of JRPG.
Still, it's like I said waaaaay back, FF7 is probably not the best JRPG of all time. It does a pretty good job of making you think it is though.

This is a review for the Brutal edition. Played around 9 hours, alone, in a party of 2 and in a party of 3.
Pros:
- Great art direction, looks fantastic, monsters are cool, level biomes are awesome, characters are neat.
- Great music in the few areas where you can hear it.
- Fun random spell/scroll system makes fights unpredictible.
- Challenging fight mechanics and friendly fire in co-op keeps you on your toes.
- Really fun co-op play.
- Lots of collectibles
- Every playthrough is totally different to the last. The randomly generated levels did not dissapoint.
Cons:
- Not worth £22.99, even after the Brutal edition update, this game is only worth it in the sale.
- Poorly optimized, encountered lag and framerate drop issues, which was surprising for a low poly game, since the levels aren't even that big.
- Non scaling difficulty! Playing alone was near impossible, whereas playing in a party of 3 was too easy. Playing with 1 other friend in a party of 2 was the sweet spot.
- Still pretty buggy. Clipping issues, in one playthrough a friend got stuck underneath two moving platforms. Also a reoccuring issue; when a friend dies while fighting, if you revive them, they still finish their attack mid-swing right after they ressurect back. (Since friendly fire is on, this usually means they stab their rescuer.)
- Issue with the probability of equippable armour appearing in chests? We were a party of 3, (2 rogues, 1 brute) however throughout our 6 hour playthrough we were only finding rogue armour. By the end of the game we were swimming around in tier 4 rogue armours but our brute was still wearing his tier 1 gear. At first we assumed there just hadn't been any armour made for him, but after viewing the trailer again it seems there just wasn't any spawning for him in our games...
OVERALL, I'm glad I played it, and thankful the dev team took previous feedback into account. It's a fun little game albeit needing some bug fixes and polish still. If it's on sale and 40%+ off, it's definitely worth getting into with a friend. Otherwise, hold off until then.

I'm iffy to recommend this.
The game itself is fantastic. The story is well written, characters are enjoyable, etc etc.
However, this game has been pretty harsh on me by changing my controls from Keyboard and Mouse to Controller in the middle of the game (So I have no idea how to do a majority of the things required in the cases) and NOT SAVING MY GAME AT ALL. (It happened four ♥♥♥♥ing times in the first three cases. Still haven't gone past Case Three since I lost my save.)
Some of my complaints may just be me, and if so I'm just unlucky, but that's not all.
Some of the games played in the cases (Hangman's Gambit, Make your Argument, BTB/PTA, etc) have been changed and not exactly for the better. For example: Hangman's Gambit was, in the first game, a simple word game where they'd present a word with some letters missing and you'd figure it out by shooting the letters. Simple, quick, fun.
In this game, Hangman's Gambit is a simple word game where they give you a phrase with no hints besides the length of the words in it, you must match the letters by pressing Z(Remember, I have had troubles getting my controls due to a random switch mid-game caused by the game.) on one and shooting it at the same letters by pressing LeftClick. Okay, doesn't seem bad at first. By doing so, they stay on screen without movement, and increase in size. You can get rid of the combined letter by either shooting them with Z, which gets rid of them entirely, or LeftClick which will act as you trying to place the letter there. Alright, still good. The letters now move across a screen and you must make sure they either touch the same letter and avoid all other letters. Still makes sense, but what was wrong with the other one?
A couple new mini-games were introduced like Logic Dive and Rebuttal Battles, both of which are fine.
Hell, I'd dare say Logic Dive is the best thing in Danganronpa 2. It adds a much needed action segment to break up the logic heavy segments. Sometimes it's nice to not think too hard.
Rebuttal Battles are a nice change into arguments since it adds a little more depth. Having to fight the counter-arguments of the classmates in order to continue the trial is cool. It's not much different from the actually arguments in how you complete them (SHOOT BULLET [Called Truth Blades in Rebuttals] AT LOGICAL ERROR AND WIN) but it's a nice little add-on.
So again, It's an iffy recommendation since I've had nothing but problems with it but the game itself is fine.

Final verdict: Great game, but not a Might and Magic game at all.
PROS
Yes they had some M&M lore and a really nice NWC type dungeon in the DLC.
The music was good but not M&M great
The graphic were spectacular for a grid based RPG
The voice acting was great and your avatars side comments were often excellent although they needed more (in particular, the male orc voice actor was spectacular)
The city sounds were also great but there were far too few and  and you had the same ones in all the cites and it was totally ridiculous to have Georgian chants coming out of a Orc healing center (chapel)
And finally the game story was surprisingly coherent and had far deeper elements than a typical Might and Magic game.
And there were bunch of puzzles. Most were fair, but they did have a couple really bad ones. There are riddle chests and puzzle dungeons ( fortunatly no monsters to battle in there)
Hireable NPC was handled better in this verions
CONS
Character upgrades are pre defined
A battle simulator (just like Lords of Xulima)
I think the developers wanted a cap on levels (prior M&M didnt give a lick about this)
Some battle last well over 20 minutes
No retreating from battles (either win it or reload)
No honorary promotions (although you can do the missions)
No experience points for avatars disabled at battles end
Many times the battle music would not stop after battles end (long time unfixed bug-you have to save and reload)
Audio did not work on my rig until i plugged in some headphone
Spell book sucked. Good spells but too many of the mage schools had little or no offensive capabilities spells.

So, just got the game today. I know it's in Open Beta, so I'm going to ignore certain issues I see with it, and dive into the core Pros, Cons, and Mehs. Lets get to it!
Pros:
Amazingly tight gameplay. The controls are very responsive, and I never feel as if I get cheated. If I die, it was on me, not on faulty controls.
Beautiful graphics. The game itself looks gorgeous at max settings. I'd like to maybe some particles/some sort of physics added in the future, but it's stunning!
Good character variety. If I get bored dealing a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of damage with Cassy, I can switch to Leonardo to tank for a bit, or maybe to Pip to heal. Overall a good system.
Cool ultimate skills! Almost every class I've checked out has a very unique skill that you won't find anything quite like in similar shooters.
Mehs:
Matchmaking. Finding games is easy, but all too often the teams are very lopsided in skill. You'll see a team of new players pitted against a team of level 5-6 - Not saying that thats a huge gap at all, but it kinda throws off the balance.
Server issues. I know that this is an open beta, so this isn't necessarily a huge issue. But the servers seem to have issues constantly! Looking at the game's error log is pretty overwhelming, simply because of the amount of times they have to shut down the server. Again, we're dealing with an open beta, but this issue NEEDS to be fixed.
Cons: This is a very short list, not too many things wrong with the game!
Little-to-no reward for leveling your Paladins. I'd love to see an RPG system implemented. I.E. +50 HP whenever you level up a certain paladin to level 2, or something like that.
Some of the community can be a little toxic. They have their mic unmuted, and they scream and scream... This is easily fixed with a mute button, but maybe a little punishment for them would be nice?
All-in-all, this is a fantastic game. Whether you look at the actual gameplay, the Paladin system, or the art, it's nearly flawless. For an open beta, this game is in great shape, and I look forward to watching it grow. I'd 100% recommend this game to any fan of online shooters.

Pains me to do so but Steam's inadequate yes/no recommendation system strikes again.  I'm not entirely sure of the development of this game but I suspect Ubisoft just threw these guys permission to use the license and very little in the way of funding.  The game feels extremely low budget.  Worse than some indie games.  Even looking past superficials like the unpolished graphics and lack of voice acting (things one would assume to be better with a AAA publisher) the mechanics are overly shallow such that most people will probably burn out on the excessive content due to tedium.
Melee is very basic with only one talent tree and limited attacks.  Range is pointless given the number of ambushes you face (and there's a penalty for shooting things at point blank/melee range).  The magic schools don't feel sufficiently different and mostly consist of nukes plus a couple of superfluous buff spells.  Yes, there are towns and quests and merchants and the occassional puzzle but all of it is very rudimentary.  Itemization is terrible consisting of a few hand placed relics with the rest being randomized Diablo-style crap.
MMX Legacy should be more polished and deeper than Grimrock (and not merely a turn-based alternative).  It isn't.  Moreoever it is arguably worse in some aspects like level design, character progression, itemization, etc.  You're better off playing the old Bard's Tale series as the graphics are only slightly worse but the gameplay is much deeper.   But that was funded by Interplay, right?  Well... this was ostensibly funded by Ubisoft.  Apparently not.  A shame.  Had they given this the funding they put in other iteration of the M&M series this would have been a fantastic game.  In its current condition it is mediocre at best.

I like the game, but it's not for everyone. Here's a tip for anyone that has trouble getting the game to remember your saves:
Find the folder with the U-Play exe, right click and set to run as administrator. Go to the main game folder (mine is programfilesx86/Steam/SteamApps/Common/MMX) and right click the exe and also set to run as admin.
For some reason the game requires admin privilege to make any changes whatsoever to a folder...even recording a save.
As for the game itself, it's basically like crossing Might and Magic III with Might and Magic VI...and then stripping it of virtually all depth in exchange for accessibility. I like the game...because I like the M&M universe and other games in the series (including the excellent Heroes games). But, like the Heroes games, it's weak sauce compared to the earlier entries. Judging it by Might and Magic standards, I give it a 5 out of 10...if that. But by gaming standards...it's not bad IMO. Maybe 7 out of 10....maybe too generous. I like it, but it's not for everyone.
While I recommend the game, I have to recommend you first watch some let's plays and get a feel for what the game entails before purchasing. It's NOT anything like Legend of Grimrock (which is what led a lot of people astray into purchasing the game...LoG and it's sequel are objectively better and vastly different). Also keep in mind the game is no longer supported by Ubisoft and the forums are dead...so you're on your own for the most part.
In short, I enjoy the game...but it's certainly a small niche type of game. Chances are, it's not for you. Buyer beware.

So it's a little slow to warm up, but it's worth persisting with. Or perhaps you'll feel differently to me and enjoy the opening as much as the ending.
This isn't Journey; there are no real puzzles and it's not a game that's going to make you think. The gameplay is very simplistic; you'll find yourself alternating between swimming around aimlessly in wide open areas and following a linear path in others. It is, however, a game that will make you
. That was my experience, at least. It looks great, obviously, but the music is what really did it for me. It's incredible. I couldn't tell you what the story is about but that didn't stop me from enjoying it, and I think it's supposed to be open to interpretation.
The frame rate dropped frequently to 40-45 FPS regardless of which graphical settings I chose, which was disappointing. I have a GTX 960, admittedly not the most powerful card around, but I think it might be CPU-limited rather than GPU-limited, since there are often hundreds of objects (fish, mostly) on the screen at once, plus all sorts of particle and lighting effects. For a swimming/diving game, the controls aren't as intuitive as they could be, and some menu options can only be chosen with a keyboard, despite the "strong recommendation" to use a controller. I'd like to say those are minor faults, but the truth is that they're not; I just ended up not caring because I was so drawn in by the music and the visuals. And by getting to ride manatees. Recommended.
