If you liked Gal Civ II, you should like this game. The hex grid suits the game well. The new adjacency system for planetary improvements adds some depth without increasing micromanagement. The new shipyard system streamlines ship production while also adding some complexity. Ship design feels a lot deeper, with no one optimal design, as there was in GCII. Overall, it's one of those games you can get sucked into for 8 hours straight, as any good 4x should be.
All that said, many of the complaints about the game are (still) valid. To name a few problems that caught my attention: the game crashes your entire system when you attempt to edit certain ship designs--avoidable, but still; Alliance victories are incredibly easy to get, even on Godlike difficulty, by simply rushing a few diplomacy techs and spamming diplo-boosting improvements; and the AI still needs a lot of work, particularly in that it rarely actually attempts to capture planets during war. I don't consider these flaws to be deal-breakers, though, and the game does make steady improvement with each patch.

I have very mixed feelings about this game, but I think it’s better than a lot of the RPG Maker junk cluttering Steam, though it’s also not as good as a large number of freely available RPG Maker games out there. I didn’t mind finishing it, but I loathed some parts of the game (core hunting, specifically). There’s also a new game + mode, apparently, and I’m not too thrilled about the prospects there. If you want a TLDR, you just read it - if you want to know more, I’ll start by discussing what I felt was poorly done in the game, then finish on the positive notes.
(Also, item farming spoiler below.)
The first real issue that I want to bring up is that the plot makes itself scarce. The game sort of hinges on being a simulation of an open world where the main character has no idea what’s going on (in a style similar to .hack and its game series), but that makes for very little character or story development. I’m pretty sure most of the game’s story-related dialogue would fit on 3-5 pages, depending on your font choice. It really reminded me of playing .hack on the PS2 because you really don’t get much back-story… but .hack had the breadth of the manga and anime to draw from, where this game sort of leaves you in the dark because you know nothing about the world going in.
Another flaw, or host of flaws, is the lack of polish that the game has in certain areas. To be fair, there was actually a massive graphics overhaul done on this game and it did make it much easier on the eyes… but it made it the spots in the game that were missed in the respriting effort and the quirks caused by bad QC during respriting much more apparent. For example, you can often find NPCs that are a few pixels misaligned on their sprite sheets, which causes floating pixels around them while they walk. Additionally, a number of the sprites weren’t updated to the larger side afforded by the graphics update, so they look *really* out of place when they show up.
There are also a number of typos in item descriptions and even one in the battle status ailment prompts. It’s pretty off-putting.
To wrap up negatives, I’ll bring up what is probably a personal issue brought on by my playstyle in both .hack and Data Hacker: the data core collection. I didn’t really spend a lot of time hacking enemies in this game (or .hack) when I realized that you don’t get experience for battles afterward. In .hack, there’s always the possibility of grabbing an interesting piece of equipment, but you usually just get data cores. In Data Hacker, all you have to look forward to are data cores. When Jaque, a main character to the plot, tells you to sell him your cores the second time you meet, it even makes collecting them seem pointless unless you need money - I can see people that haven’t played .hack making that mistake. But I digress. Farming for cores is time-consuming and rather boring. I spent several hours trying to locate a good dungeon to grab the final “Tz” cores from with any regularity when it came time for their use. In that vein, to anyone who reads this:
Core Farming Dungeons
AlZo Dungeon, second floor near the two doors: Al, Zo, Ki Cores
ZoTz Dungeon: Ma, Ge, Tz Cores
But, now, on to the good: this game is playable. If you like RPG Maker games, Data Hacker doesn’t disappoint because it’s very clearly an RPG Maker game. There are some interesting tweaks to the engine and some clever uses. Even a minigame (which I did manage to lock up the game with - don’t walk up to the tournament NPC from his right side) that’s… pretty similar to that card game from FFVIII. The creator obviously put a lot of work into it and, as long as you don’t focus on things you might want to nit-pick, you should be able to see this game standing quite a bit higher than many of the RPG Maker titles out there.

To be frank, I can't for the life of me comprehend why this game has so many positive reviews. I mean, maybe I'm not that qualified to give my opinion on this, because I was already not really a big fan of the first game; but even though the first one had quite a few flaws, like the ridiculous story and a few irritating characters, overall it was still enjoyable to me. The sequel on the other hand takes all these flaws and turns them up to eleven:
- The story and murder cases this time around are utterly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and nonsensical.
- While the first game had a desperate and isolated atmosphere, truly fitting for the overall theme of despair, everything in this game just feels so goofy, exaggerated and overblown, that I couldn't take half of it seriously. Oh, and expect lots and lots of 4th wall breaks and self referential humor. Gotta love those, right?
- Somehow they managed to make the minigames even more annoying and unintuitive.
- The various characters, arguably the heart of these games, are so much worse than its predecessor, that it's not even funny. They are way too over the top, to the point that they just become grating to deal with. It goes way beyond being one dimensional or stereotypical; you just can't imagine these lunatics ever existing or functioning in real life. Everyone is crazy, everyone has a messed up past and strange values. One person is a glutton, she will think about nothing but food even in life and death situations. One character is sad someone turned out to be a murderer, the next moment she happily forgives him and recites the catchphrase of this game: "We gotta do our best, for his sake!" It all just feels so artificial.  It's a flaw a lot of japanese media has IMO: style over substance.
Even if you bother to spend time with them, some character may reveal a superficial character flaw after a while, wich will never be brought up again and doesn't really matter. Oh, but you get their underwear as a reward. Aren't you glad you wasted time on this?
- The characters motivations for doing stuff and especially their motives for commiting murder dont make any lick of sense half of the time, which doesn't really help with endearing them to the player. It's probably not a good sign, that, while I was often saddened by the death of characters in the first game, I couldn't care less when someone died in this game. On the contrary, most of the time I was glad when someone finally bites the dust.
It's fair to say I was pretty much on Monokuma's side the whole time.
-As for positive things: music is still enjoyable, graphics are alright and I encountered no bugs or glitches while playing.
Damn, that turned out longer than I wanted. So in conclusion, if you are like me and already had to massively strain your suspension of disbelief and tolerance for anime tropes during the first game, especially in regards to characters and story, avoid this one. Seriously, it feels like a different dev-team worked on this game. If you don't give a crap about this, get it on a sale, because that price is ridiculous for a VN.

=Full disclosure=
I'm an original backer of this way back during the first campaign and I've already put well over 20 hours into the backer version before it hit Steam, thus my low playtime count as I've only just activated this today.
That being said; this is one of the rare few RPG Maker titles that I genuinely wanted to drop money on. It's fun and engaging and harkens back to the PS2 legendary series Dot Hack. I've had a blast playing this in the past and I'm looking forward to a replay once Reboot Initiative is ready to go, the new art style and enhanced atmosphere and mapping look great, and I know Ross - the main developer - has been busting his♥♥♥♥♥on the trilogy so far :) I do have to question the two negative reviews below, however, as they seem highly unfair. Games have bugs and issues, that's just what happens in development, but when it comes to indie devs they actually LISTEN to your feedback; so if you have any troubles, such as rare showstoppers or even just an impassable tile in some random dungeon, please.. take to the forum and report it! Leaving negative feedback on the game, especially on LAUNCH DAY, is really harsh and does more harm than good.
As a backer of the Kickstarter, I've been privileged to watch the game grow through the development process and it's been really enjoyable. You can really feel that a lot of love and attention to detail went into this project and while there's a fair amount of RTP present, it has been put to great use. The scenario of "Online World" is great, with an engrossing plot and an enormous amount of areas to explore and do battle in. Character customisation is extensive and the ability of Jay, the main pro(an)tagonist, to hack his own avatar and generate his own customised class is unique and enjoyable. What sets this game apart from others is the inclusion of the Hack ability, which allows you overwrite the code of enemies, granting you bonuses against them - or debuffs against your party if the hack fails, and even new and unique items as rewards.
Being able to hack enemies and gain Cores for use as currency, or even combinations to access new areas, is extremely satisfying - especially against tough foes. You can even use the Hack ability to hack other play characters, which you can do to acquire new members for your party, or even just massive amounts of experience points/cash for bolstering your existing one.
Audio and Visual wise, it's mostly standard RPG Maker, but NRG have put great attention to detail and the use of both custom and standard visuals in order to create the Online World. I have to say though, not once did I feel like the visuals were a detriment to the game, RTP or not, and the atmosphere itself was brilliant. Far better than a lot of other cut'n'paste - expensive - commercial RM titles, that's for sure. The custom soundtrack is especially enjoyable though.
All in all, I really have had a blast playing this and I'm eagerly awaiting the followups now. Good luck New Reality Games!
The showstopping bug has since been fixed (same day as release! Like I said; indie devs listen!) so having negative reviews up just harms public opinion of what is a truly great RM title. It's indepth, has an enormous world - worlds, for those familiar with Dot Hack - to explore and with the overhaul coming it's only going to get better. Good luck to everyone playing and I'll see you in Online World \o/

Time has not been kind to Final Fantasy VII.  Without the shock-and-awe stature of its graphics to cow naysaying new players, the JRPG’s many flaws are easy to see.  Marketed originally for a teenage audience, adult gamers will likely tire of the juvenile plotlines and offensively stereotypical characters.  Of course, that presupposes an American player can follow the narrative at all, since the translation to English is comically bad with its missing words and poor syntax.  An unholy hybrid of turn-based and real-time battles is the only reward for those who choose to slog on.
If I had played this game back in 1997, I would probably put it on a pedestal as its many adoring fans still do.  However, new gamers are not equipped with these rose-colored glasses.  While a playthrough makes it easy to see how influential Final Fantasy VII is, it is much harder to find enjoyment in the process.

I don't really want to give this game a thumbs down, but I can't recommend it when I feel there's another very very similar game that does what this game tries to do, but better. Golf With Your Friends is cheaper, and quite frankly is the superior game when it comes down to it.
Normally, I wouldn't mind some flaws, but this game has two major cons that I don't think will be able to be fixed without MASSIVE reworks to the entire game, sadly.
First and worst of all, the level design is extremely unforgiving. I don't mind a challenge at all, but this is mini golf. Meant to be a casual game to play with friends. I think maybe in the first level on maybe hole 4 or 5, you'll see the start of an awful trend in these levels.
There are MANY many times when you work your way to a hole, usually taking a few strokes to get there, only to find that if you make a mistake on the last stroke, the level will send you back to the very START of the level. It's extremely frustrating, and quite frankly too unforgiving in a game for casual minigolf.
Some more signs of unforgiving level design. There are QUITE a few spots where there's just holes in the map for what seem like the sake of frustrating you and your friends. This isn't inherently bad, but it's used MUCH too often in this game I'm afraid.
And worse still, there are a couple holes that are quite literally just RNG/memorization. I REALLY do not appreciate that kind of design in just about any game. By RNG, I mean pick a hole to go in, and it shoots you out to your death or back to the start of the level. Now, many minigolf type things do this, but in this game, its either you pick the right one and go to the hole, or you just fall into a pit and lose a stroke or are taken back to the start.
I will be fair on that last one, however, that there's not many RNG/memorization holes. Maybe 2-3, but, still, it shows off a lack of understanding to level design.
The next major con is the physics. The physics are not terrible by any means, don't get me wrong, but they're just not good enough, I'm afraid. When putting, you're meant to sort of "flick" your mouse and how hard you "flick" it is how hard you will send the ball. Unfortunately with this style, it is VERY hard to be precise with your power, and with the horrendously unforgiving level design that DEMANDS precision, it makes for an even more frustrating experience.
The ball itself also REALLY does not like to stop rolling. This is a big problem as well since most rounds are timed. I actually found myself having to increase the standard time by one minute simply because of these wonky physics. It also makes for a lot more downtime between shots, which isn't fun either I'm afraid.
I'll give a brief view on the Pros, though. The graphics are great. It's a nice looking game. The level editor is a super idea. The online is also quite good, however the UI needs work. (Have to start and host a new game every time a map is finished.)
My recommendation is just get Golf With Your Friends. It's cheaper, has better physics (slightly!) and has much better and more forgiving level design suited for casual golfing with well--your friends.  The graphics are not as pretty, and the online can be a tad wonky, but I don't find that to be a major downfall personally. There is no level editor in that game, yet sadly, so if a level editor makes or breaks your decision, then I suppose go for Golf It! for now. I assume Golf With Your Friends has plans for a level editor in the future.
Sorry for the downer review, it's not a bad game by any means, but simply feels inferior. Maybe the devs will prove me wrong and fix the issues I have with it now, but in its current state, I wouldn't recommend picking up this game.

Might and Magic X: Legacy: There's something to be said for a game to exist solely based on its legacy (pun intended). Unfortunately, Might and Magic X does not feel like a good entry in the series nor a good role-playing game. Personally I’ve never played a might and magic game (I am a huge fan of the Heroes of Might and Magic series however) so I'm coming into the series as a relatively new player. I have played one other game similar to Might and Magic X; Grimrock, which I loved and play completely through. I bought this game with similar expectations and was sorely disappointed.
First I was expecting clever puzzles and riddles, there are none to be found in this game. Puzzles are mostly switch puzzles and riddles don't require any sort of abstract thinking, or really much brain power at all to figure it out. Okay, lame puzzles, is combat any good?
Nope, in Grimrock you had four characters, two in front for tanking and two in the back as range or support, in this game they stand side by side, allowing your squishy magic characters to be hit alongside your heavy characters, it makes switching character places pointless and overall it’s annoying. Range characters are also pointless, most of the games engagements take place within melee range and range characters will get a penalty when in melee range and their shots hit random enemies so if there is more than one better hope the shot hits the enemy you want; they don't have strong enough magic or melee combat skill to be worth devoting a character to range, just use melee and caster characters. All classes can use a ranged weapon in any case, a much more preferable option to having a useless character. Combat itself lack strategy and excitement, it’s much quicker to just mash the attack button through fodder enemies; bosses are the only enemies requiring more strategy, but it’s not much more and overall combat is a bore and a chore, sadly the game relies on it heavily. Side rant, the final boss fight is bogus.
Visuals and audio are both pretty good, the game takes you to a great variety of locations and there is plenty of color in this game, it’s pretty. Music is standard fantasy fair, but it’s well done. Voice work is...ok, not sure why elves and dwarfs sound similar, I shake my head and chuckle anytime I hear my Scottish elf girl speak, it doesn't really fit in with the setting. So the other bits aren't too great, how about the story?
Well...that also is a letdown, actually the opening cinematic to the game spoils everything, the who, what, where and why. I can't compare it to other Might and Magic games, but as far as storytelling goes it’s pretty weak and not engaging at all and it’s extremely linear. The game offers you a very lengthy experience, so that’s something.
Honestly, I was really excited for Might and Magic X and wanted to love it after playing the disappointment that was Heroes of Might and Magic 6. It sapped my strength and will to go on by how boring it was. There's a lot of content for the asking price, maybe if you get nostalgic for these games it will win you over, but for $24.99 USD I'd recommend something else, like Grimrock.
TL/DR; Might and Magic X: Legacy is a long but, boring role-playing experience. None of its qualities are strong enough to make the long trek worthwhile. I’d recommend using the $24.99USD on something else or buy Grimrock. Also Ubisoft making me use U-play ticks me off.
-Thumbs down from Royial

I don't do reviews often, but having played the game for a length of time, I can safely say that I have a relatively fair opinion on the game so far. For context, I've played a number of 4x games and grand strategies. I'm generally a fan of what Paradox Interactive tends to produce, but I will try to maintain an objective opinion at all times during the review.
Firstly, Stellaris is an combination of a 4x (Explore, Expand, Exploit, Exterminate) and grand strategy game. You'll see and feel the 4x influence during the initial course of the game. I feel like it is this early phase that Stellaris has captured well and does incredibly well. You'll create your own race (or choose from the pre-mades) with their own government type, ethos as a government, native world type, what sort of FTL you use, and more. These decisions can and generally will set the pace for the rest of the game. Once you've picked your race, you're plopped into your homeworld's system and soon you're sending science ships off to explore the neighboring systems of the galaxy and expand your people. Eventually, you'll encounter sentient forms of life like yourself and they'll have their own set of ethos. One thing that I think Stellaris does well is that every race you meet will have a unique name, ethos, government, etc. every time you play. The only thing that generally remains consistent is the pool of portraits that both you and the AI have to choose from. There is quite a bit of variety, but you can sometimes end up with pictures repeating. Even so, I feel like a sandbox where anything is possible adds to the replayability. I'm not always going to encounter mammalians with the same portrait, strengths, weaknesses, etc. each time I play the game. Therefore, my strategy needs to adapt based on who and what I encounter.
As previously mentioned, Stellaris handles the early game very well. It's a constant state of exploring, your science ships uncovering new quests and anomolies in the galaxy, and expansion once you start building your colony ships. Another good thing about Stellaris, though some may disagree, is that research is handled on a card based system. There are three types of research (physics, society, and engineering) and initially most empires will start with three possible choices in each category. Pick wisely, as you may not see certain techs again or not for awhile. This adds another depth of decision making and changes the game up so you're not constantly delving into the same strategy each game. Additionally, it sets the empires apart a bit. Research possibilities can be locked or unlocked based on your ethos as an empire and the same holds true for the AI. Some techs are even marked purple as rare techs and some are marked red as dangerous. They're dangerous techs as the outcome of utilizing said dangerous tech can lead to a crisis happening in the late game. More on that in a bit.
Now to the part where Stellaris lacks. The mid game. Once everyone has settled, planets have been established, and borders are fairly clear, Stellaris can start to grow dull. This is a part of the game where you often have to make your own objectives because there isn't a lot of content in this part of the game. You'll either war, uplift pre-FTL primitive species, invade said species (if your ethos allows it), deal with the rare internal strife issue, or continue exploring as best you can. I feel like there's a lot of potential in some of the gameplay systems so far, but they definitely need more fleshing out. As many who play Paradox games know, this will generally mean that Stellaris is going to receive a ton of DLC in the near future. This can and will probably turn some of you off from the game. However, I can safely say that Stellaris is a complete game as of release and has enough that will keep people interested, especially as you transition to the late game.
At the late game, those dangerous techs I mentioned could've been researched by other empires OR you may have a situation where extra-galactic invaders have come to infest everyone. These are generally galaxy-wide crises that can snowball out of control if left unchecked. One criticism I have about these crises is that the AI doesn't take them seriously and this behavior can allow the endgame crises to snowball quickly, especially if you're on the other side of the galaxy from them and can't do anything about it. However, these end game crises shake up a common issue found in 4x. You'll find yourself possibly in a situation where you're not the top dog (if you managed to become that during play) and this opens up the potential for a situation where "losing is !FUN!" or you might solidify your strength in the galaxy by overcoming this obstacle. I feel like this is an area where Paradox can definitely add more to the future, as I'd like to see greater variety in the endgame crises. Most things in the game end up being original or different every time you play and I'd hate to see it where a similar strategy becomes common against the endgame threats every time.
In any event, Stellaris is very much solid as a base game and definitely adds a new take on the 4x genre by adding some GSG elements to it. However, the GSG elements are dominately on display during the mid game and sorely need some additional fleshing out and substance to make the mid game less of a drag. The early game exploration and late game galactic threats, however, make the game a recommended buy from me. HOWEVER, if you are not the sort of person that doesn't like DLC or want to wait for Stellaris to be more fleshed out and detailed like EU4, CK2, and other Paradox titles have become, I would not suggest Stellaris for the people in the anti-DLC group and recommend those wanting a more definitive experience until Stellaris has been built upon with additional content for the latter group. Rest assured, with how well Stellaris has done so far, it should be clear that Paradox intends to support Stellaris for a long time. Given the resources that Paradox has at its disposal by comparison to other strategy/4x developers, I look forward to seeing what they do with the game in the future. If you enjoy the 4x/GSG genre, I still recommend the game despite its few faults.

What an amazing game!  Dust really is a delight to play.  It throws you into the world of an amnestic rabbit ninja in a kind of Metroidvania – lite that sees you exploring levels, finding treasure, overcoming simple platforming, and then revisiting old areas as new abilities and powers let you access new parts of the level.  There’s also towns where you can chat to locals and pick up side quests, plus a fairly simple crafting system.  Dust doesn’t do anything revolutionary, but prepare to fall in love with this game if you have the time to invest in it.  Oh, and play it on the harder difficulty levels.  Easy is a joke and normal is also a cakewalk.
What I loved about it:
Art:  this is some of the best 2d artwork I’ve ever seen.  The world and characters are vibrant, skilfully animated and bursting with life and colour.  Even the stock fantasy settings such as forests, graveyards and snowy mountains are presented with the flourish of a true artists.  Ever wanted to play through an animated movie?  Dust is your game
Sound:  I’ve always thought sound is one of the most overlooked parts of gaming, and the incredible sound direction of this game is massive in building a stunning experience.  From the soft crunches of Dust’s footsteps to the screams of dying monsters, even the slight echo that accompanies the underground levels, Dust is also a joy to listen to.  The orchestral music also gives the world of Dust personality and atmosphere.
Combat:  The combat in Dust is visceral and frantic, sort of a 2d Devil May Cry (you even have some of Dante’s signature moves) as you soar through the screen, slashing enemies to bits, unleashing screen-filling magic and raking up combos in the 100s.  I think I got at 600 combo more than once in the sorrowing meadows.  I also very much appreciated how the game lets the player acquire almost all the combos and attacks very early on the game, so your primed for the chaos from the get-go.  Serisouly, the combat is so good it is almost ridiculous.
More than the sum of its parts : the overall experience in Dusts was just fantastic to me.  Add it altogether and you just have a wonderful, solid fantasy world to loose yourself in.
What I didn’t like
Boss battles:  too easy, and very underwhelming. I expected to find screen filling behemoths, but almost all the bosses are the same size as the player, and all were push overs.
Difficulty:  Overall, it was a bit too easy, even on the harder modes.  More than the combo-fodder enemies, I really thought the game would have benefited from some harder platforming sections too
Length:  It only took about 12 hours to complete the first time, but I was hungry for at least another 8 or so hours.  SPOLIERS  I wanted to know so much more about the world and the characters.  Who really are the Moonbloods?  Why does Gaius want to kill them so bad?  Who is the king we here of but never get to meet?  Many, many unanswered questions….
Back in the days of yore, when playstations and saturns ushered in the 3d era of gaming, I always felt like we left 2D out in the cold while it still had so much to offer.  Dust fulfils that promise.  It is probably the best looking 2d game I’ve ever played, and a lot of fun to boot.  I really hope this game is successful and there will be a sequel or another title from the developer.

While I'm recommending this --- for $30, it's a damn fine game --- be advised, this is largely a clone of Sid Meier's classic Alpha Centauri.  Also, I've only just finished my first complete playthrough, so my exposure so far has been relatively limited.
That said, it's a VERY good clone.  The flow and strategic depth are definitely there, and the musical score is splendidly executed throughout.  I found myself thoroughly immersed in the old "one-more-turn" addiction that Sid perfected so long ago.
THAT said, it has a few glaring flaws, mainly in its backstory and the factions resulting from it.  The story is ham-fisted, rooted deeply in the politics of the ecological left, taking itself deadly serious without a hint of irony or humor.  The result is a series of events leading to colonization which make zero sense.  Despite lacking the resources to maintain a massive population, and despite warfare that should kill off millions if not billions (it goes full-WMD at one point), the narrative demands that human population levels actually increase so as to ensure an overcrowded planet.
The result is that every faction EXCEPT the ecologists are thoroughly stereotypical.  Playing as the militant, for example, I found that suggesting a trade pact involved selling "huggable doll-mines".  For children.  Parody?  Nope, it's played completely straight-faced.  And the game is LOADED with similar dialogue... except for the ecologists.  For example, when given a gift of credits due to our Generous diplomatic relationship, I was told "this is so you'll hopefully chop down fewer trees".  There are one or two mentions of ecoterrorism, but it's very much dialed back and representative of real-world incidents as opposed to something as over-the-top as "doll-mines".
Aside from this dissonant style of characterization, though, it's an excellent game, well-worth your shekels if you liked anything the Civilization series ever produced.  I just hope the Steam modding community develops custom factions soon.

Hmmmmmm, where do I even begin with this kind of game? The concept behind this game made this almost an instabuy. A roguelike where the turns are locked to the beats? Yes please. I haven't seen a concept like this before, and I haven't heard about another one if it existed.
Unlike traditional roguelikes, there is no leveling system. You don't get "stronger" by defeating enemies or bosses. No, instead, you
from them. Killed by a blue slime? Don't stand above it or below it. Out of 80+ hours of play, I have had zero unfair deaths. I could look at the replay and see exactly where and how I screwed up. You get better after every death.
The music in this game is
. Seriously. I have (mostly) had nothing but Necrodancer tunes stuck in my head ever since I started playing. My only complaint is that Jules' soundtrack isn't the best for playing the character it is assigned to. I've had little problems importing music as well, but it isn't 100% perfect. Instead of manually tpping out beats, I just use a program that generates the file for me.
Make no mistake, this game is hard. It took me quite some time to clear the first character, and I am still working on the next two main ones. All zones mode is the main one for this game, and most of your character achievements will come from that mode. Play single zones until you're used to the game, then go for all zones. Do you think that being locked to the beat is too hard? Play as the bard. No beats and all the time in the world to make your decisions. Since you'll be dying a lot, it may or may not become repetitive. I haven't gotten bored in the amount of hours I put into it. This game is hard but replayable. Some characters are harder/more annoying than others. Experiment and see who you like best.
Like roguelikes? Get this. Like rhythm games? Get this. Want to be challenged? Get this. Want to get angry that you went to an endboss and died? Get. This.

A while back I stood out on faith of backing this game. I'm an avid fighting game player. Although my favorite genre is rpgs, fighting games have always given me the spriit for a competitive edge. Pocket Rumble definitely satiates this desire but why? First and foremost, Pocket Rumble is a retro style fighting game in the veign of old pocket handheld fighters meant to bridge the skill gap between the casual and competitive player. It does this by using simplistic controls. Only two buttons are used with regular normals, air normals, and special moves. At first, the controls felt a little strange because specials are done by holding down the corner directions and holding the button down as well. However, after figuring out the controls, the special moves were pretty easy to adjust to. Each character has four specials and a meter bar. However, Every character's meter is used in a different way. I'll use the first two playable characters as an example. Tenchi has traditional "shoto" character commands (I.E. Ryu and Ken) he utilizes a fireball and  anti air maneuvers and once his meter is filled he can use a special "super" fireball. Naomi, on the other hand, is strictly rush down. She uses a lot of forward advancing special moves with options to mix up the opponent. Her meter is used to make better versions of her specials and she is able to charge it up in the veign of king of fighters or dbz games. Each character moving forward is meant to specialize in their own form of meter building and special implementation, so much so that the characters become shout outs to many other famous fighting game series. WIth this variety in the style of play ,even though only 2 characters are available as of this review, there is going to be a lot of depth to the systems. Even now Its hard for me to stop playing this game online for any amount of time because I'm enjoying it so much. It feels responsive and brings fighting games back to the basics of spacing, anti- airing, and mind games. It is difficult for new fighters to break into the genre and make an impact so I hope that anyone reading this review can give it a chance. Right now it is low on content but once the final product hits we will really have something special on our hands. I recommend looking under the hood of early access to take a peak though. You'll probably like what you see.

It's hard to describe this game without comparing it to other games so I'll do my best to list the reasons why I don't recommend Paladins without regard to its competitors:
- Rounds typically last around 10 minutes but feel much shorter; simple run-and-gun-die-rinse-repeat mechanics.  Not much depth or variety.
- With the rounds being as short as they are, you spend way too much time waiting in the pre-game lobby.
- There are two different wholly arbitrary collectible card game mechanics. Neither are interesting or fun.
- The character power balance is out of this world.  It's not that certain characters are 'OP', it's just like the whole game feels... like it doesn't work correctly.
- Most deaths feel cheap.  (See above.)
- Maps don't appear to switch sides.
- The maps look cool but are extremely simple.
- Most players consistantly don't play the objective.  Normally I wouldn't blame the game for this but I have to think there's something lacking in design when the majority of people wander the map aimlessly or camp corners instead of standing on open objectives.
- The siege scoring system is butt-backwards mental.  You get a point when your team caps the objective but then the other team gets a point when you fail to deliver the payload.  I get how this is supposed to make it feel like both teams are doing something but capping the objective is a neutral objective for both teams; stopping the payload gives the defenders the advantage.  This actually rewards a team for not trying to cap the objective.  Your team can cap the point 3 out of 4 rounds and still lose the game.
- Payload maps are equally wonky and no-respawn mode seems entirely out of place.
- The mount system feels like it was put in to fix a problem instead of adding to the experience.
- Mounts constantly get hung up on terrain, making the amount of time they should save mostly pointless.
- Again I have to mention the outright shortness of each round.  You spend so much time waiting for queue to pop (due to leavers/afk'ers/spotty servers) and standing around in the countdown lobby it feels like the fun-to-waiting time ratio is drastically lopsided.  Very little actual 'fun' per time spent in game.
- The game runs excellent on older machines but at the same time it feels very 'floaty'; loose, lacking weight.
At the end of the day it feels like Paladins is a very shallow experience.  It's neither something you're going to commit to playing at a high level because of its lack of depth nor is it something you want to 'party up' and play with friends because of the outright shortness of rounds.  It is the core definition of a "Free to Play" game- lacking lasting value.

Pocket Fighter is another failed attempt at luring beginners into fighting games.
The main flaw here is that you hold down a button to perform a special move.
Why is copying smash bros so hard?
The main issues are that you hold diagonal directions for special moves instead of up/down/left/right and you hold the special attack buttons instead of simply pressing them! So what you end up with is input failure out the wazoo in a game about removing the barriers to fighting games.
Not since Rising Thunder has a "fighting game" been so bad.
If you have never played fighting games then you will enjoy this game possibly but if your intermediate or above then this game will be a difficult ride and honestly Smash Bros is a better entry level game for beginners.
The studio may bring it around and I hope they do because we do need beginner friendly fighting games but at present its not catering to the market it was designed for and its not catering to professionals.

I bought Final Fantasy VII more on a whim than anything. I'd heard it was a good game and had even heard that it was the best. I had the money, bought it, played an hour or 2 and then stopped for a long time. I started it back up again a little while back and I am glad I did.
Gameplay: 8/10
If you don't know how Final Fantasy works then you need a heavy dose of internet. This game holds the standard turn-based combat, however there is one difference I've noticed. This game can be switched into a real-time non-stop combat sort of deal. I don't mean being able to do whatever but rather the game doesn't stop for you. It may seem small but I am very glad this was a feature. In this game, the combat doesn't stop to let you think. If the enemy is faster than you, they'll attack more and if you take too long to think, they'll keep wailing on you. There are several times when I would be defeated because my character was killed before they could attack and I was never too angry. It was annoying on occasion, especially when an enemy turned me to stone or used that stupid FROG SONG but for the most part I could live with it. You level up by winning battles and so on. You also have Materia in this game which is basically something you can equip into your weapons and armor to give skills and boosts. A Cure Materia lets that character use Cure and if you link that with an All Materia then they can cast Cure on the entire party! The Materia allows for a lot of customizability in this game. You don't have to force Aeris into being a cleric (although character stats may influence things). I equipped Cure on all of my main party (Cloud, Tifa, Barret) and it worked out splendidly. The game makes a point that when certain Materia is equipped, certain stats are raised and lowered, however I never actually found this to affect anything. This game may also occasionally throw a special minigame sort of thing at you like the Chocobo Races later on and they're cool and all but the game has a habit of saying things like "Use [Switch] to do this" or something like that and it refers to whatever key that command is bound to and it gets annoying because some are rarely used. Combat has Ultimate attacks as well which are very powerful attacks that vary depending on which one you've earned, although they tend to be a nuisance a lot of the time. A bar fills when you get hit and when it peaks you can use any Ultimate of the level you have equipped, but you can't do a regular attack until you use it. This caused me a lot of frustration when I'm saving my Ultimate for a boss but don't have the MP to keep using spells.
Story: 9/10
Story is a tad cliche with the 'save the world' sort of thing, but it does so very well. Your character (I will call him Cloud) is an ex-SOLDIER who is helping AVALANCHE take down the Shinra corporation because they're killing the planet. He helps destroy a factory and leaves saying he doesn't care about the world. After some convincing he tries to be cool guy and helps save the world. The game starts off with you in Midgard, then after events you start exploring to save the world. You meet some interesting characters with some pretty good backstories. Cloud wants revenge on Sephiroth, Tifa is helping Cloud, Barrett wants to protect his little girl and many more. They're told much better in game, trust me. You travel around and fight monsters and travel some more. The traveling is where I feel the game lacks. A bit later in the game I found myself lost. I couldn't figure out where to go and I'm not sure if I missed key dialogue or what but there were times I found the way forward on accident. SPOILER ALERT! Later in the game you go to find Sephiroth. Where is he? Well I traveled all the way north to a fossil village and somebody there answered my question. He went through there to find the Temple of the Ancients which is on the exact opposite side of the world. Wait what?
Graphics: 7/10
I shouldn't bag on it too much because it was originally PS1 but I don't think they're the best and some CGI cutscenes weren't very well done in my opinion.
Sense of Progression: 7/10
This may be a bit of my personal getting lost, but any progress seemed lackluster as sometimes bosses would appear out of nowhere. I'm leaving a place, use a door and then BOOM! Wall demon? I'm not sure if I missed some context but... I never truly felt like I progressed at most times as I fought so much trying to find the objective I didn't know the location of that I would one-shot most normal enemies and bosses stopped being difficult.
Enemies: 8/10
Varied and special. Some had resistances, some used spells. Then there's the frogs... I don't like the frogs.
Length: 10/10
36 hours and only completed the first disc. I'm in for a long ride.
Overall: 8/10

Don't be decieved, only having two buttons and low execution requirements doesn't take away any of the fun from this game.
When I first seen it, I thought "Wow, two buttons and a weird way to input special moves? This is probably going to be whack."
I was certianly wrong.
At the time of this review, there are currently two characters playable in this build.
Both have four different special attacks, two to each button.
They also each have their own unique mechanic.
Naomi builds meter pressing A+B, and uses it similar to a Force Break, or an EX attack, while Tenchi has a meter that builds up with each special move you use, and gives him access to a super.
I'm very interested in seeing what other characters will have to set them apart from the rest of the cast.
Speaking of the cast, while not all characters are playable, you can actually look at them from the character select.
All the designs so far look good! The stage that you can currently play on, the school room, also looks nice.
The Training Stage is pretty bland, it's very reminiscent of Street Fighter IV, and V's training stages which I personally am not a fan of.
The game itself is fast, and fun. All characters have 12 HP, and each attack takes away one HP.
There's honestly not too much to say about the gameplay if you've played fighting games before, it's just fun.
There's no FADC, Roman Cancels, or anything like that, so you'll have to be careful just throwing something out on wakeup, though with how each character seems like they'll have a different mechanic, maybe a future character might have something like that? Who knows.
The netplay is wonderful, I've only had two or three bad matches out of the ton I've played so far. It's funny to me seeing a game as small as Pocket Rumble having excellent netplay while other, bigger titles like Mortal Kombat X being basically unplayable online, so kudos to the devs for not making that mistake!
So, overall, it's worth the $10 price tag it is currently at. I don't normally buy into Early Access games, but I'm always down to support a new fighting game. If you also aren't a fan of Early Access, I 100% recommend throwing it on your wishlist, and keeping up with the game until it fully launches, than picking it up whenever it does, because I think this game may have a good future ahead of it!

I don't do reviews often, but having played the game for a length of time, I can safely say that I have a relatively fair opinion on the game so far. For context, I've played a number of 4x games and grand strategies. I'm generally a fan of what Paradox Interactive tends to produce, but I will try to maintain an objective opinion at all times during the review.
Firstly, Stellaris is an combination of a 4x (Explore, Expand, Exploit, Exterminate) and grand strategy game. You'll see and feel the 4x influence during the initial course of the game. I feel like it is this early phase that Stellaris has captured well and does incredibly well. You'll create your own race (or choose from the pre-mades) with their own government type, ethos as a government, native world type, what sort of FTL you use, and more. These decisions can and generally will set the pace for the rest of the game. Once you've picked your race, you're plopped into your homeworld's system and soon you're sending science ships off to explore the neighboring systems of the galaxy and expand your people. Eventually, you'll encounter sentient forms of life like yourself and they'll have their own set of ethos. One thing that I think Stellaris does well is that every race you meet will have a unique name, ethos, government, etc. every time you play. The only thing that generally remains consistent is the pool of portraits that both you and the AI have to choose from. There is quite a bit of variety, but you can sometimes end up with pictures repeating. Even so, I feel like a sandbox where anything is possible adds to the replayability. I'm not always going to encounter mammalians with the same portrait, strengths, weaknesses, etc. each time I play the game. Therefore, my strategy needs to adapt based on who and what I encounter.
As previously mentioned, Stellaris handles the early game very well. It's a constant state of exploring, your science ships uncovering new quests and anomolies in the galaxy, and expansion once you start building your colony ships. Another good thing about Stellaris, though some may disagree, is that research is handled on a card based system. There are three types of research (physics, society, and engineering) and initially most empires will start with three possible choices in each category. Pick wisely, as you may not see certain techs again or not for awhile. This adds another depth of decision making and changes the game up so you're not constantly delving into the same strategy each game. Additionally, it sets the empires apart a bit. Research possibilities can be locked or unlocked based on your ethos as an empire and the same holds true for the AI. Some techs are even marked purple as rare techs and some are marked red as dangerous. They're dangerous techs as the outcome of utilizing said dangerous tech can lead to a crisis happening in the late game. More on that in a bit.
Now to the part where Stellaris lacks. The mid game. Once everyone has settled, planets have been established, and borders are fairly clear, Stellaris can start to grow dull. This is a part of the game where you often have to make your own objectives because there isn't a lot of content in this part of the game. You'll either war, uplift pre-FTL primitive species, invade said species (if your ethos allows it), deal with the rare internal strife issue, or continue exploring as best you can. I feel like there's a lot of potential in some of the gameplay systems so far, but they definitely need more fleshing out. As many who play Paradox games know, this will generally mean that Stellaris is going to receive a ton of DLC in the near future. This can and will probably turn some of you off from the game. However, I can safely say that Stellaris is a complete game as of release and has enough that will keep people interested, especially as you transition to the late game.
At the late game, those dangerous techs I mentioned could've been researched by other empires OR you may have a situation where extra-galactic invaders have come to infest everyone. These are generally galaxy-wide crises that can snowball out of control if left unchecked. One criticism I have about these crises is that the AI doesn't take them seriously and this behavior can allow the endgame crises to snowball quickly, especially if you're on the other side of the galaxy from them and can't do anything about it. However, these end game crises shake up a common issue found in 4x. You'll find yourself possibly in a situation where you're not the top dog (if you managed to become that during play) and this opens up the potential for a situation where "losing is !FUN!" or you might solidify your strength in the galaxy by overcoming this obstacle. I feel like this is an area where Paradox can definitely add more to the future, as I'd like to see greater variety in the endgame crises. Most things in the game end up being original or different every time you play and I'd hate to see it where a similar strategy becomes common against the endgame threats every time.
In any event, Stellaris is very much solid as a base game and definitely adds a new take on the 4x genre by adding some GSG elements to it. However, the GSG elements are dominately on display during the mid game and sorely need some additional fleshing out and substance to make the mid game less of a drag. The early game exploration and late game galactic threats, however, make the game a recommended buy from me. HOWEVER, if you are not the sort of person that doesn't like DLC or want to wait for Stellaris to be more fleshed out and detailed like EU4, CK2, and other Paradox titles have become, I would not suggest Stellaris for the people in the anti-DLC group and recommend those wanting a more definitive experience until Stellaris has been built upon with additional content for the latter group. Rest assured, with how well Stellaris has done so far, it should be clear that Paradox intends to support Stellaris for a long time. Given the resources that Paradox has at its disposal by comparison to other strategy/4x developers, I look forward to seeing what they do with the game in the future. If you enjoy the 4x/GSG genre, I still recommend the game despite its few faults.

This is a short review because I don't honestly know exactly how I feel about Pandora First Contact. Its certainly not a bad game, and I can't point to any specific part of the game that I don't like. It just didn't really excite me either. It could just be that this isn't really my kind of game. I've played a few 4X turn based strategy games, and I do tend to enjoy them, but its not my favourite genre and I'm also not a highly skilled player.
If you've played Alpha Centauri, then you can stop reading now, because PFC is pretty much exactly the same game, but with different faction names. If you've played any of the Civilization series, PFC is pretty much Civ on an alien planet with future tech. You can decide whether to buy PFC based off your experiences with those games.
PFC has all the standard 4X mechanics. Choose between 6 playable factions, create cities and construct buildings to improve your empire's level of food, research, production, gold, happiness and pollution. Train and upgrade military units, and then either wipe everyone out for a military victory or stay defensive and go for a technology or economic victory.
The two biggest differences compared to other 4X's are firstly the tech tree has a randomised layout with each new game. This is either good because every campaign will be unique, or bad because you can't pre-plan your strategy, depending on your point of view. And secondly, food and production is stored at empire level, meaning you can have a city producing zero food, focused entirely on research/gold/production/whatever and your people won't starve because they get food from other cities.
I played two full campaigns which took 9-10 hours each. I didn't encounter any bugs in game, but I have noticed that some achievements are bugged (I should have unlocked 2 faction wins and the medium world size win).
Ultimately I think fans of the genre will probably enjoy Pandora, but if you've never played a 4X before I think there are better games you should start with.

I am writing this review after playing the game to the end. I am also reflecting on a couple of criticism I read about the game.
- "This game is similar to Alpha Centauri (AC)". Partially true, but in the same time there are many new aspects as well. What I found painful and less than AC: lack of animations, movies and no spy games. I found more fun in the special operations.
- "Upgrade is costly". Correct, if you upgrade a simple guy to the latest technical level. If you upgrade one within the same era, it is more reasonable. Similarly to the real world...if you change catapult to ballista you can make it...if you change catapult to cannon it is costly....catapult to ballistic missile? probably you cannot afford it.
- Bugs. Yes, I found a couple. Drop Pod operation have dropped all of my active units (instead of the selected one) in one location. Upgrade unit is not always change the name of the unit, especially around the end of the game. I found a third problem but I cannot remember. However I cannot find any significant issue.
- Gameplay. Combat system, upgrade options, storyboard, unit and city graphics are good. Diplomacy and trade including economy have to be improved. You have only two goods on the market....why we are not having more, including special things like drop pods and even more, research results or blueprints...?
- City management. Similar to AC or any other Civs type of game. I found it easy-to-use, however a nice inside view of the city would be better.
- Combat. Overall is not bad, but strange things can happen. How can you shot down a warplane with flamethrower...I would see :)
- Aliens. Graphics and animation are OK, but they are simple. If you wait, develop yourself, you can rob the nests and wipe out all of them.
- Great surprise about alien invasion. I can imagine more surprises like that in the later stage of the story.
All in all, I like this game. What to improve? Animation + movies and economy + trade.

It is possible to enjoy this game without playing the first, but there are some plot points that will probably make more sense or hold more significance if you play the first one.
If you enjoyed the first game you will probably enjoy this game as well. It has the same dark bizarre humor and over the top characters, and clever murders. Although honestly I found the humor could be a little obnoxious at times as opposed to bizarely amusing, which wasn't a problem I had with the first game.
The gameplay adds a couple new elements, but gameplay is still obviously not the main point of the game, the main draw is solving the murders, particularly putting together small clues to form the whole picture, and of course, plot twists! There are very clever and intriguing mysteries in this game, and a couple I didn't even begin to figure out until the middle of the class trial
There are two main criticisms I have with this game, 1. There were a couple times where I knew the answer or clue I needed to trigger the next section of a trial, but the wording sequence needed in game was very counter intuitive. There were definetly times where the trial mini games just felt like chores
2. This was a criticism I also had for the first game: You can build relationships with characters, but those relationships don't matter. They don't make any difference when it came to the trials or the overall plot. It would have added so much more depth to the game and the characters if characters could decide to help or hinder your clue gathering based on how close you were to them. I was very disapointed that the developers chose not to add any more depth to this part of the game
Overall I enjoyed Danganronpa 2, and if you enjoy mysteries and story driven games with very morbid off the wall humor, you likely will too

First off, the game manual amounts to a .pdf of the backstory and no more.  There is absolutely nothing in it describing gameplay in any way, just a reprinting of the in-game descriptions of the factions, some modding advice, and a warning about epilepsy and video games.
My first impressions were very negative.  They have upticked some, but I still can't give this game a thumbs up.  Once I restarted over and over I finally got down what the manual should have told me in the first place.
Starting position is killer.  If you get dropped in the arctic/desert and have no mining special near you, you will have a nearly impossible time.  In the tropics or grasslands right next to a mountain with noxium in it: you're already 50% to victory.  This and other factors make save scumming and restarting all too convenient in this game.
For good or ill, the game has a difficult guns or butter start to it, as the only way to free up population for production especially is to develop the land around the settlement, requiring an expensive former unit, but things turn hostile so quickly that having a couple well cared for troops can be vital.  I have to rate that as a good thing.
Unit xp and technology uptick so fast that the differences between the starting factions are pretty moot.  Small game=zerg.  Big game=zerg anyone on your continent/island, then go turtle a while as the feral native aliens will get nasty for a good while and the odd faction will invade for no particular reason.
To me, the most delightful part was the first time the expansion kicked in, and (spoiler alert) the wormhole aliens invaded.  The AI was at least somewhat responsive (I got truces declared with the factions that had survived that long), the aliens picked on everyone, not just the human player, and I fought back the baddies and the creeping crud they induce after a long, desperate, and satisfying effort.
The Steam achievements were realatively easy to achieve, and account for most of the reason I kept trying to play this game.  Unfortunately, again nothing tells you that most achievements are out of reach if you click on the advanced game setup (somehow they consider it cheating).
The graphics are generally pretty until you build a lot of mines, then everything looks like an ugly sand dune and it's hard to tell a mountain from a hill.  This IMHO should be changed for no other reason than to clarify unit movement options.
All in all I could recommend this game if I didn't have to spend so much time trying to figure out the basic world mechanics.  Upgrade the manual, please.

I'll summarise Call of Duty Black Ops by highlighting the important points. Yes Black Ops has a strong cinematic singleplayer, with better characterisation and plot than World At War. Yes, Black Ops has made an intricate improvement to the zombies  mode, adding depth and the amount it has to offer. And yes, Black Ops on PC DOES have dedicated servers which eliminates the need for matchmaking and host transition. Yet despite this, the game's no better than COD 4. It does nothing new for the COD series, murdering the quality of the weapons, killstreaks and general balancing of COD's multiplayer. The COD points system is too shallow for what it promises and once again Call of Duty has a deadly short single-player lifespan too. The nail in the coffin for many though would be the outrageous system spec required for the game to run properly. Even a mid-range PC would struggle to play Black Ops without stuttering a chunk load and this is unacceptable. Get Battlefield Bad Company 2 instead.

Hmmmmmm, where do I even begin with this kind of game? The concept behind this game made this almost an instabuy. A roguelike where the turns are locked to the beats? Yes please. I haven't seen a concept like this before, and I haven't heard about another one if it existed.
Unlike traditional roguelikes, there is no leveling system. You don't get "stronger" by defeating enemies or bosses. No, instead, you
from them. Killed by a blue slime? Don't stand above it or below it. Out of 80+ hours of play, I have had zero unfair deaths. I could look at the replay and see exactly where and how I screwed up. You get better after every death.
The music in this game is
. Seriously. I have (mostly) had nothing but Necrodancer tunes stuck in my head ever since I started playing. My only complaint is that Jules' soundtrack isn't the best for playing the character it is assigned to. I've had little problems importing music as well, but it isn't 100% perfect. Instead of manually tpping out beats, I just use a program that generates the file for me.
Make no mistake, this game is hard. It took me quite some time to clear the first character, and I am still working on the next two main ones. All zones mode is the main one for this game, and most of your character achievements will come from that mode. Play single zones until you're used to the game, then go for all zones. Do you think that being locked to the beat is too hard? Play as the bard. No beats and all the time in the world to make your decisions. Since you'll be dying a lot, it may or may not become repetitive. I haven't gotten bored in the amount of hours I put into it. This game is hard but replayable. Some characters are harder/more annoying than others. Experiment and see who you like best.
Like roguelikes? Get this. Like rhythm games? Get this. Want to be challenged? Get this. Want to get angry that you went to an endboss and died? Get. This.
9/10

For example. there are reefs you can repopulate. I'm usually very critical in my reviews. I think the best I ever rated a game was 6/10 so far. Today will be a new record.
Lets see:
Stellaris is basically everything you ever wanted from a Master Of Orion game. Giant galaxies with up to 1000 stars, populated by numerous civilizations. I think the maximum is like 60 or so, but I didn't try it. But that's only starting civilizations, new ones can form later on. You can found federations together with other civilizations, with entirely self-declared rules. Those federations will vote a president from all the member civs from time to time which then controls most of the foreign and military policies. But it's not a simple alliance spam like in many other games. You'll find tons of civilization with which you won't even get close to an alliance, just because your own civilization's policies don't match with theirs.
The constant construction of more infrastructure like mining stations, research stations a.s.o. is incredibly rewarding. Warfare is not just like conquer as much as you can, but instead you need to keep an eye on resources. Can you maintain that extra planet? Is a war worth it for that incredibly rich border system?
Combine Master Of Orion with the complexity of a Paradox game (don't worry, it's not as complex as EU4, but still very in-depth) and you'll end up with Stellaris. I can already see my dump another 1000 hours of game time into this one.
Current flaws, early after release include:
- Some bugs with storylines. Like you can't finish a research project here and there because that probe you need to collect isn't clickable. Nothing game breaking, but annoying.
- Some balancing problems. Normal difficulty is way too easy and I easily stomped everybody. My attempt on hard was exactly the opposite. Feels a bit like too much depends on the starting position at the moment, but I'm sure Paradox will tweak it quite soon.
Overall: 8.5/10

Dust was a game that caught me by surprise. I have spoken often of games that deserve more recognition created by small teams, and in this particular case the story was written entirely by one man who also did ALL of the artwork for every location, animation and character in the game as well as being the organized lead of the project. At first glance I feel most will be turned away by the anomorphic art design as I was, but though the quality of production wavers at points, Dust is a game of immense substance.
So the sins of a low budget studio come into play. We have line readings that range from absolute cringeworthy all the way to BEYOND perfect delivery when a scene calls for it. The script dabbles between comical and serious to the same effect. I had a couple unexpected laughs, and was actually fairly impressed with some story elements that came into play despite the titles child friendly surface. Some parts of the script seem to try too hard to deliver it's point but others are spot on. When it manages to stave off cliche it goes in an interesting original direction that made me sure I saw the adventure through, you can tell the story meant a lot to guy who wrote it. The art isn't going to blow your mind, but the game has some really nice setpieces and effects. Overall it's extremely impressive as the work of one man.
Between the mixed signals I am giving, all subpar line readings and sometimes annoying characters, ALL can be forgiven for the most important part of any game, the gameplay. The combat system is fluid, over the top, and fun. To say it's devil may cry on a 2d plane just doesn't do it justice. Once you unlock enough abilities it is a total blast to just string up combos. It's one of those games that is so beautiful in motion that it's hard to critisize. There's platforming and a few mild puzzle elements as well, to round out the experience. The music is great throughout, and all and all the minor shortcomings were worth the entire package. There's some signs that the project was rushed and not drawn out to full potential, but such are the dangers of working with corperate buisness to fund your project. The game did well enough that they've even spoken about the possibilty of a sequel, of which I would be fully fledged to play.
A slightly rough around the edges hidden gem, I fully recommend this to someone wanting a charming fantasy tale or fantasically flawless 2d demi god slashing combat.

;This game keeps the charm and good writing from the first, but makes use of it a lot more. To the point where Monokuma gives huge spoilers to the first game, and pokes fun at it being cheap that the reveal was saved until the final moment.
;Compared to the first, characters are way more fleshed out.  I actually found myself liking everyone in this game, and relating to a lot of aspects of each of them. (Especially Nekomaru's obsession with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.)
;There's a lot more humour in this one, which makes the sad moments much more sad (but that's also thanks to better writing too).
;The story overall is pretty much the first game but on an island, and with a new protagonist as well. The traitor reveal was heart-wrenching, especially learning the events of the Danganronpa 3 Anime shortly after. But, there is also another plot twist in the ending that made me facepalm, though a little less than the first game thanks to being prepared for something cheap like that but also it just not being as bad.
;The trials are better, having more gameplay styles and a lot more to look forward to when it does come trial time. Older elements have been improved and the new additions are pretty well implemented.
;Killings and investigations are vastly more interesting than the first, creating scenarios that are a lot more creative than the first (and as a result, a little more of a challenge to figure out.).
;Free Time is pretty much the same, and this is actually pretty fine.
;Island Mode is like School Mode, but with a lot easier of a premise to grasp. More believable because it actually follows the plot this time instead of breaking the fourth wall constantly. Pretty much the same crafting and seaching game and the same great character building through Hanging Out and Trip Tickets.
;Monomi's Adventure Supreme can go ♥♥♥♥ itself, the sidegame itself is pretty lackluster and I was so unhappy having to spend about 5 hours unlocking all the items for 100%ing it. They're all random drops and you have to rely on pure luck for that♥♥♥♥♥♥to go faster.
;Finding the secret events was difficult, and finding the secret monokumas were also pretty difficult (there was only one I had to google, the one in the hospital room).
I'd recommend playing the game through, maybe gathering all the hope fragments and possibly beating Island Mode if you like the game. 100%'ing the game becomes boring and borderline frustrating. However, the base game is very solid and I'd probably even play it through again in the future. There is also Danganronpa Another Episode, as well as the Danganronpa 3 and 2.5 Anime series which I almost instantly watched as soon as I knew it even existed in the first place. I didn't expect for this game and DR1 to kickstart my love for this franchise, because I wasn't actually aware of how much I'd be into it. So I would recommend this game if you played the first and liked that, and would recommend this if you want to give it a shot too. It's worth it, but possibly not if you dislike the first game. It might be a VN, but it's not a bad VN, and actually tries with it's gameplay.

What if you could mix in elements of survival and epic future technologies, with a randomized tech-tree to keep it fresh? Pandora tries very hard to be a good spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri, but it falls down hard in several key areas:
1)It horribly, desperately, without argument needs a thorough and accurate manual. "Ask on the forums" does NOT cut it. Experienced SMAC players will likely muddle through, but only with a lot of trial and error. Novices will be completely lost.
2)The minimum requirements are not high enough. I exceed them and have all the graphic settings turned down (because, seriously, who needs fancy-pants animated graphics for a turn-based 4X game?) and the game can't even keep up with the mouse. The mosue focus keeps lagging behind the cursor, so the wrong things get clicked on. Annoying and tedious, which are not adjectives I like to apply to my leisure activities.
3)The description does not mention that the game is more focused on the combat side of things than most entries in the genre. There is no culture, no religion, minimal diplomacy and between two types of aggressive aliens and the other factions, expect to be pounded constantly. This isn't a bad choice per se, as there are lots of people who like this play style, but it should be clearly stated in the marketing text.

If I had to describe this game with one word, it would be "Addicting".
The music, the graphics, the combat system, everything is addicting.
But let's go in order, shall we?
Danny Baranowsky did an amazing work with the soundtrack, and that's an understatement. Just to make you understand: In over 8 years of gaming on Steam I've never even thought of buying a game's soundtrack, no matter how awesome it is.
This time I did. And I'll probably buy it too, when the chance comes up.
The tracks are energizing and the beats are well recognizable, which lets you concentrate on the game itself instead of the "beat bar" and adds that boost of energy that makes this game what it is.
Simple and colorful pixel art waits you in this game.
The graphics change from zone to zone, while keeping consistency in the 4 levels of each zone, plus a special boss level that changes every time you play.
The graphics themselves are not messy at all, but if there are many enemies on screen it could get quite difficult to concentrate on the rhythm enough to not lose track of a trap. But that's part of the game.
Oooooooh the juicy part.
The gameplay is innovative, a great mix of dungeon crawling, rhythm game, strategy, action and adventure.
Each level is randomly generated and gives the player a new experience every time. Diamonds allow you to unlock new weapons and abilities and the whole gameplay system gives the impression of getting better and better even if you're stuck in a certain level or zone.
The gameplay is relentlessly difficult, a single wrong move could ruin a whole great run, and you have really little time (usually one beat) to decide the next move. Even though it's difficult, the game is not unfair, it's just hard enough to make you keep trying harder and harder, to the point that you get worse instead of getting better (I'm talking from personal experience).
The game has unlockable characters, each one with its own way of playing, which gives the game a whole lot of replayability; additionally there's the mod support which extends the game life a little more.
If I had to say something negative about the game, it would be the first loading screen, before accessing the lobby.
On my system, playing the game means waiting at least 1 or 2 minutes at the loading screen, but the catchy tune that accompanies the loading makes everything better.
Instead the other loads are instant, which makes replaying or changing mode a breeze.
If you like hard games, great enegizing music and randomly generated maps. Get this game now.

If you've ever watched a fighting game and wanted to learn what was going on.
If you've ever wanted to learn how fighting games work and what all the fuss is about.
If you already play fighting games and have tried desperately for years to make your friends understand why you love them so much.
This is the game you need to play.
Fighting games always have a wall between the not-so-interesting "How do I do this?" and the much more interesting "Why and when do I want to do this?" This game takes that wall and turns into a tiny ramp that you'll climb very quickly.
You'll be able to take part in that mental back and forth between you and your opponent, of figuring out what your opponent wants to do, how to beat it, how your opponent is going to beat what you want to do, what your opponent can't deal with and picking apart the weaknesses in each other's playstyle rather than wrestling with the game to figure out what you want to do. You'll be able to see and experience why any serious fighting game player can't help but let their passion and excitement leak out when they talk about their favourite games or moments.
For more technical stuff  I'm based in the UK and had a number of very playable matches against folks in the US, the netcode is very stable. If you like to sink your teeth into the fine details of the game hitbox display and a frame data meter give you all the information you'll want are already in the game with full frame data in movelists coming later.
Training mode has all the essentials you need (most importantly a record function!).
Most importantly the game is absolutely adorable, the character designs are amazing and the stages have extra effects that trigger whenever you hit the final round to really get your pulse racing. This is a game clearly made by people who love and understand fighting games and the people who play them.
The game despite being in early access is already a complete if small experience and I'm certainly convinced that it'll only get better as more characters, stages and game modes are added.

Might & Magic X returns to the good old days of Might & Magic series (think World of Xeen) while retaining a relatively modern touch to it (think M&M6+). Possibly for the first time ever in the series even the inventory is (mostly) likeable! Power-up barrels scattered around the world, statues that buff the party, puzzles that have you scratching your head, quest lines without big yellow markers telling you where to go, and last but not least, completely unfair fights if you stick your nose where it doesn't belong. Welcome to the Might & Magic! I've missed being in the M&M world!
First and foremost, don't be put off by the rather mediocre ratings -- if you are a fan of the series since the early days, you will love this one too. For the most part I can't but praise the game, but I do have a handful of complaints:
* some of the (teleporter) puzzles are a pain (too much of trial & error);
* armor wear (i.e. items breaking) is completely useless and should either be redesigned or removed completely;
* the Falcon and the Unicorn DLC could use some tuning (it's incredibly challenging/frustrating for melee-oriented parties for example).
Some people have been concerned with the PC requirements. I ran the game on highest settings (i7-3770K + Ati Radeon 290) and 90% of the time it runs completely fine. The other 10% of the time there are significant slowdowns, spikes, possibly related to traveling to another section or perhaps from daylight to nighttime switching. Be what it may, the engine could use a little polish in that respect. Also, loading times when entering dungeons or cities are fairly long, up to the point where I would rather run around the city on map than enter to travel through it.
So much for complaints, because in nearly every other aspect Might & Magic X is a very fun and engaging game. I clocked 50 hours on my playthrough, and for the first time in years I was disappointed a game ended so "soon". More of this, please!
On a scale from 1-10, I will happily award M&M X a solid 9/10. For all oldschool M&M (and Dungeon Master / Eye of the Beholder) fans.
