To be upfront, I have not yet finished this game, nor have I played through it in the past.  That said, I feel I've gained enough of a feel for the game to write a useful review.  I'll update this once I'm done...
Quick Review:
Dated, yet lovable graphics.  Good MIDI soundtrack.  Enchanting story with winsome characters.  Fun battles with varied opponents.  Customizable fighting style to fit many approaches...
A little slow paced for the impatient people, but decidedly worth the time...
I recommend.
Graphics:
Not very impressive for the times.  I personally have some knowledge of how games are made, so I can at least partly appreciate how fantastic this must've looked on release.  It was one of the pioneer games that showed the incredible potential of what games could be.  That potential (graphically) is being realized today, so hats off to Square Enix for boldly helping kick things off for us...
However, it's not really all that great by today's standards.  The character models are so low-poly, it's near laughable.  The backgrounds are very nice compositions, but so heavily pixellated that it's sometimes difficult to see what's what.
The camera angles are creative and dramatic, and the special effects are varied and entertaining, but again, not even close to the same level as today's games.
Overall, it was hard for me to get past the graphics at first.  But as the game progressed, they were varied enough and creative enough to satisfy my experience.  Anyway, they get overshadowed by the rest of the game's magnificence...
Story:
Absolutely beautiful.  I haven't even gotten halfway through this game, and i'm already so invested with the story that I'm analyzing it and pondering it during the times I'm not playing.  Sure, there's a smidgen of predictability to it.  Sure, there's times where the "cheezy" is so intense you can taste it.  But the dialog is so brilliantly written, the flashbacks so creatively executed, the story so perfectly told, that it resonates with the player and draws them in.  You are fed a steady diet of backstory, side-details, and glimpses of the future the whole time.  Nothing is crystal clear to you, leaving you wondering over the mysteries all around you.  The characters are fleshed out until you feel you know them and feel a connection to them.  I felt my protective instincts awaken every time the hero's friends are put in danger.
NOTE:  No voice actors, the dialog is in text form.  It may sound bad in theory, but honestly the emotions are carried across just as well or better than voice actors could do.
Light-hearted, heartbreaking, infuriating, thrilling, etc.  The emotions are a roller coaster.  I've enjoyed the ride so far...
Gameplay:
The pacing of this game is a bit iffy.  So far, I would say that is the biggest obstacle to any player's enjoyment of this game.  IF YOU ARE A NATURALLY IMPATIENT PERSON, THIS MAY NOT BE THE GAME FOR YOU!  If you have any patience at all, it's worth pushing through the slower moments of the game.  The game doesn't hold your hand at all, so if you can't figure out what to do next, it can be frustrating.  I find it all the more rewarding and believable, myself.  It feels like your on an adventure where you don't know what's around the bend.  It could be just another monster, a friendly town, or you could be thrown into the middle of an enemy's fortress, or sent undercover in the bad guy's army.  You could find a potion lying around, or stumble across a weapon that packs some serious punch.  The feeling that anything can happen really allows me to enjoy every moment, even when I'm stuck on what to do next.
The battle system is intruiging.  It's turn based, so the strategy is in knowing your enemies' strengths and weaknesses, as well as your own.  The variety of enemies is great and keeps the battles fresh.  There isn't a book (in game, anyway) that you can consult to prepare for battles.  You can analyze your enemy only the first time you encounter them, and this contributes to the "anything can happen" aspect of the game.
The Materia system allows the player to heavily customize their party.  You can adapt them to your own playstyle.  Experimentation is necessary and encouraged.  Almost the only way you can learn new concepts is to try them out.  If you aren't the type of person that enjoys that aspect of gaming, there are tons of guides you could use to cheat with.  Us adventurous sort enjoy the thrill of the unknown, though.  And this game has plenty of unknowns.  There's a smattering of small, unimportant characters that you have to make decisions with.  Sometimes, the decisions mean nothing.  Other times, they can be rewarding beyond what you were expecting.
The world map is fine, but perhaps a bit slow to traverse with so many random battles popping up.  It can get annoying, but it's not a dealbreaker at all.
Music:
Good tunes.  A lot of folks seem really enamored by the soundtrack.  I like it a lot, but it's not the best part of the game for me.  It is well-crafted and enjoyable, though.  Not to be overlooked...
Playability:
SUPER IMPORTANT!!!!!  THIS GAME REQUIRES AN INTERNET CONNECTION AND MAKES YOU GET A SQUARE ENIX ACCOUNT!  Was very annoying to discover, but hasn't affected my gameplay yet.  I'm totally okay with it, but some folks have been surprised by this and it really threw them for a loop.  SO BE WARNED.
Overall:
This game is a story, one that you can influence.  It has a linear structure to be sure, but it's told in a way that makes you feel like it's all unscripted and untamed.  The characters will win your heart, and the battles will win your mind.  And the villain is epic.  So epic.  Sephiroth is a beast.  I am a Kingdom Hearts fan and that's the main reason I dove into this franchise.  No regrets...
Buy it, fools.
EDIT:  Finished the game!  It kept it's epic feel all the way to the end.  There were a couple times when it was difficult to discover where to go next, but it just took a bit of time and exploring.  The end game became so much more difficult than the rest of the game, that I actually had to consult a guide to combat Master Tonberry (who isn't even a boss).  But though I thought it was disproportionately difficult towards the end, it wasn't at all impossible.  The only gripe I had about the ending was the lack of save points (spots in the game where saving progress is allowed).  The last hour and a half of the game I played without a chance to save.  It probably doesn't sound like a big deal to some, but it annoyed me a good bit.
Good conclusion to the story, though.  Plus a fun batch of cutscenes to finish with.  Still two thumbs up to this fantastic game!

At full price? I can't recommend, for a number of reasons, of which I will go into further into this review. TL;DR would be that it is a pretty shallow and though polished, it is rather undeveloped and the developers have purposesfully left a lot to want in preparation for DLC spam.
If you want to know what sort of spam, just look at CK2's DLC list. Fourty plus items, if I recall correctly. Although you can get them pretty cheap given enough time during sales, it is still a hefty amount for a hefty sum.
At a sale price or after some updates and possibly an expansion or two, Stellaris could very well be worth the money spent. However, at this point in time it is impossible to know exactly where it will go.
Paradox is good at making feature rich games like Crusader Kings 2 (CK2), Europa Universalis IV (EUIV), but getting there takes time. Some of their games have had rocky starts and have a decent amount of content, others like Stellaris have had thus far a smooth and stable start, but are very much lacking in content.
+ Stable multiplayer. Did an eight-hour long game with twenty others in a group I play with without a single hiccup at all. Smooth as silk, with working hotjoin! A big surprise, given how broken multiplayer is in say, Crusader Kings 2 at times.
+ Diverse selection of species. Unfortunantly they don't have quite as big as an impact as one might wish for, more onto that later. But cool designs and a reasonably large number to choose from, which is always sweet.
+ You can customise your starting ethics and racial traits. All species have access to the same traits sadly. Ethics/Ethos allow you to be peaceful, militaristic and so on. You can make your political makeup somewhat unique compared to other playthroughs. Only a couple are actually viable for competetive multiplayer, though.
+ Ship editing and customisation. It's there, it does the job. Not the most sophisticated system around, and somewhat lacking compared to other games in the genre.
+ Purges, enslavement and eugeni- uh. Racial modifications. Uplift other species and over time force them to submit to your ethics, modify them as you will.
+ Political 'map' in mid to late game reminds one of games such as EVE. Large empires can wage huge wars, federations form and politics can get interesting. On MP, at least. AI is rather lackluster and not very good at that sort of thing. Or staying alive, either.
+ Large scale. Number of stars isn't everything, and games like Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion prove as much, but it honestly helps create a sense of awe in space.
+ Ship combat system is incredibly simplistic, in a very bad way. Factors such as range not being used (LRMs will engage in melee like every other ship, for example, instead of staying at their max range) and the complete lack of control over ship orders and priority targets leaves battles completely at the mercy of RNG and your ship compositions. AI isn't very good at countering player navy makeups, if it even tries at all. You can't even tell your fleet to target specific high value targets in a fleet.
= Could be fixed by moving the system to something closer to what is in Endless Space, as the combat system does sort of emulate what is used in that game, but is less complex for it lacks difference phases (Long range, medium range, melee and tactics).
= Could be fixed by moving the system into something closer to Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. Different ship types serve a different purpse; LRMs will sit back out of harm's way, whilst corvettes and destroyers armed with lasers and short range kinetics will engage in melee sort of thing. Give commander the ability to pick which targets (individual ships in an engaged fleet) the fleet focuses on, or what certain ships should focus on.
= Something between the two could be good, maybe. Really, anything other than what it is now would be better.
= Because come on, Star Ruler 2, Endless Space and Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion all do space combat far better. SR2 is made by a tiny (two?) man team in their free time, and is leagues better between the customization system and combat!
+ Planet classes only affect two things; when you can colonise it -> The required pre-requisite technology and the resulting habitability (which affects in turn how fast pop grows), which is based on your starting planet class. Then graphics, what the planet 'looks like'.
= Some planets, like Tomb worlds, being special planet types are somewhat unique. But even then the differences are far from significant.
= Many planets, such as toxic, barren or lava worlds can't even be terraformed in the late game.
= Could be fixed by adjusting what sort of resource outputs are given by different classes. Some should give more minerals, others more energy, some more of x or y tech, others biased towards having more space to build but less resources and so on.
+ Species and Phenotype don't affect what traits can be picked, only diplomacy. All of them live for the same number of (base) years, which is 60-70 years. No actual advantages or disadvantages to picking one or another. This means, at the end of the day, what you pick only affects the graphics of a pop you see every time you click on a planet, fleet or whatever unless you're dealing with people who've picked xenophobic ethos.
= Could be tended to by giving certain races unique traits, more or less slots for trait adjustments, different bases ages (possibly with some randomisation) so tree people and turtle people live longer than a human.
+ No trade systems. I mean trade as in trade ships - you can exchange planets, map information, vision, alliances and resources in deals, but you can't exchange the frequently mentioned (by capitalist-style empires) trade agreements.
= Would love to be able to build trade stations and would like to watch trade ships move back and forth, even if they are simply sprites for performance reasons. Come on Paradox! Every damn game has this sort of thing in as a default feature, yet you've left it out.
+ Ship customization is quite limited. Paradox should take note of Star Ruler 2 and their ship customization system. Not asking for that system exactly, but it is a damn good idea and is very well executed.
+ Stale mid to late game. I think they've done a seriously good job at the early game, other than the above problems which only become apparently later in the game and/or through multiple playthroughs. I've got a lot to say as to what could be done, but it is very likely that they have intentionally made these parts stale so to give room for extra $$$ DLC.
= At least if the host owns the DLC, all clients get it. They've confirmed it'll still be the case for this game, so there is that, thank paradox.
+ Feels quite shallow. I'd say it is quite shallow, for I feel it has less in it than EUIV did on release and many others say it has far less than CK2 did, too.

Dust is a serious adventure RPG that can be turned way simple for easy fun / exploration, or way hard into true hardcore 2D bash-em combat with an impressive combo system that can do various types of attacks, from ground to slide to jump and much fancier aerial moves.
The plot is relatively simple. You are Dust. You woke up in a field, not knowing yourself, when a sword... yes, a flying and TALKING sword floated up to you and addressed you as Master. Then Fidget, a Nimbat, showed up and wil accompany you on whatever quest you are supposed to go on since she comes with the sword. As you head toward the village in the distance hoping for answers, you hear fighting... Some sort of monsters are attacking the town, and you leapt into action...
The graphics are quite good, sort of Disney-esque type animal humanoid that looks far cuter than it should for all its seriousness, about finding one's true self and all the war and attack and civilian casualties, and good vs. evil and all that.
Sound is also quite good. There's some debate whether the protagonist voice sounds a bit too young, but sounds okay to me. (And you have to play the game to see why.)
There are basically three attacks (later there's a fourth, the ground slide/kick) blade, dust storm, and Fidget burst. It is the combination that makes things deadly. Blade plus jump is an aerial attack. Blade plus jump plus dust storm yields an aerial super attack. Dust storm and Fidget burst creates attack swarm. As you level up each ability through EXP (via quests and kills) you'll gain additional attacks and combos. (On casual difficulty this is done automatically)
You will also encounter various types of equipment: armor, amulet, left ring, right ring, and "augment" (weapon enhancement). You will often encounter blueprints to build more advanced equipment... provided you find the blacksmith and have enough materials. Some stuff are available at merchant.
There are many sidequests in the story as you encounter more NPCs. Some will ask you to find X ingredients, while others want you to retrieve something or someone, or reach a particualr area and search for something. Doing them yields extra EXP to level you up.
Other activities that yields EXP are just talking to every NPC you come across (but you only get that once).
There are special "treasure chests" in the world for you to find, and most involve some sort of a puzzle. Usually it is to pull a "bombfruit" toward an alloy gate to blast it open, but the bombfruit can be at a challenging place so it can be difficult to pull it properly esp. when the bomb fruit may come with a timer (after X seconds, kaboom!) There are also special "friend chests" (12 of them in the world) for you to find as you unlock your "friends" captured in the cages. It's another type of collectible, but a fun one.
As you learn new skills, such as floor slide (to get through narrow low tunnels), double jump ( to reach extra high places), iron grip (to climb the vines) , you will discover new areas you haven't been able to reach before, and often that is how you find these extra treasure chests and cages. So exploration is a must. You will be told percentage of areas you missed and/or treasure you missed, so don't fret.
The game autosaves when you pass through a "save point" (temple) which also heals you. You can also trigger a manual save on a savepoint. The savepoint also serves as a teleport point that allows you to leave the map region, if you bought some teleport gems (not that expensive, and you did get a few for free).
The game never felt too frustrating, except the problem of opening up a certain area before you are ready. For example, there's a mission where you need to find a girl in the "Hidden Cove", except you can't explore that area unless you have Iron Grip skill, which is only available at the end of Sorrow Meadows. The game doesn't always make this clear. There are also some quests that are a bit too whimsical, or even on casual, way too difficult without advanced skills like double jump. However, if you are the type that goes for every bit of completion, you will no doubt feel frustrated now and then, even on casual.
There are also six "trials", sort of a "speed-run" through a certain level where you try to take as little damage as possible, while fighting your way past monsters and environmental hazards. And they award high level equipment, depending on how well you do, with rating of up to 4 stars (depending on score).
All in all, Dust is a very good game that, IMHO, looks way too cute for its own good that people will have problems taking ti seriously. If you can get past it, you will find a rewarding action-adventure with good puzzles and challenging bash-em on higher difficulty levels.

Danganronpa 2 improves much of DR1's problems while still inheriting some of its flaws. WIthout spoiling too much, the game is structurally similar to DR1 in its premise and execution, but with quite a few differences in the details.
The first difference is an improvement in characters. Characters are much less one-note in this game.They are heavily-defined by their talents, but those talents are a small part of the characters and their back stories. If I do have one critique, there seems to be an over-reliance on sexual assault as a comedic plot device, as I've not finished every character's arc, but two of the handful I've done already have some form of (serious) sexual assault against them played up as really unfitting comedy.
Much like DR1's localization, DR2's localization has some issues. It feels like it's worse in the beginning, but there are a lot of just really weird dialogue moments that have some pretty unnatural sounding speech. It's not a deal-breaker, but I hope they continue to improve upon moving the game from East to West, as there are many more moments in this game where I felt like the localization team made some good strides in translating a character to Western audiences, and I hope to see them improve with each iteration.
The problem with the game's writing, much like DR1, comes at the end. I've got to say that the ending plot sequences are just the worst kind of anime crap. They are cringey, and throw in so many "plot twists" that the mystery sections they make you solve are nonsensical and and just end up tainting the better parts of the story.
The gameplay itself is quite similar to DR1. You get free time to spend with characters and do some side activities to pick up presents. There's a mini-game now also that lets you use up un-wanted presents to get bonuses, which is a welcome feature. Eventually, someone will get murdered, you'll have to find every clue, and then start a class trial, using logic and mini-games to solve the mystery. The mini-games are a mixed bag. Some like, the truth bullet system from the first game are alright, but others are a miss.
I'm especially not fond of the Panic Talk Action, which simulates you trying to shout through an opponent's flimsy defenses by winning a rhythm game. Unfortunately, there seems to be no actual sense to the rhythm as it doesn't really mesh up with any sort of tempo in the song, and seems to be more of a visual thing, which is incredibly distracting and hard to pull off without a power-up the game eventually throws you later in the story that almost completely breaks this. It's like the developers knew it was poorly implemented. Beyond that, there's a clunky snowboarding-esque minigame called Logic Dive that's a mixture of boring and badly made, but I didn't find too many other mini-games too offensive.
The mysteries themselves are part of the main appeal for me as I enjoy games like Phoenix Wright, and the only complaint I have is that the last trial, like in DR1 is a sort of plot deconstruction one where it feels like you have a dozen clues that are the exact same thing and the challenge is trying to figure out what the hell the developer's logic for the answers are.
Beyond the main campaign, there are some bonus modes. One of them is kind of like this task simulator that's mostly there to give you a chance to max out character arcs of characters who may have died too early in the main game or you just didn't get around to finishing. The other is a manga detailing events of the first game, and the other is a pretty boring and bad arcade action-adventure thing that gold old really quickly.
Despite those complaints, I really do enjoy DR2. Its story up until the end is engaging, the mysteries are creative, the characters are largely much improved over DR1, and I didn't spend 30 hours plowing through this over a few days for no reason.
Very interesting game. Highly suggested for mystery lovers or Anime Lovers out there ;)

PROS:
> Fun adventure story with a good sense of humor
> Really likeable main characters, both of them had an ample amount of participation and screentime

CONS:
> I encountered a few bug crashes during scenes and kissed my progress goodbye since I often forgot to save (so tragic I saved in chapter 1 but I was already in chapter 4, I had to speedrun it all over again)

Before you read my review, I'll just give my summary...
It's a less-than mediocre strategy game for its time, and your best call is to wait for this game to plumit in price (to around $10) than paying anything more and investing any time in to it.
Nothing spectacualr to report here.  I have played the previous games in this franchise, as well as their expansions.  While great games for their time, this just seems like a polished version of its most recent predecessor, with little addition of innovation or complexity (much like Civ:BE).   More so, the last incarnation of this game goes back to like 2008!  I really don't feel this game offers anything new, except for a massive upgrade in graphics and a campaign.  They still haven't caught up to Master Of Orion in the fact that you can choose to tactically conduct space battles, and they have even eliminated the animation aspect of planetary assaults/defenses.
Let's start with the tutorial.  It's basically a medium map skirmish that refuses to offer insight in to the finer points of the game (it doesn't explain the mechanics behind all of the myriad ways to govern a planet or manage an empire towards one's goals).  So, you're basically left to figure that crap out for yourself.  In short, if you haven't played GC2 and figured out how that game works, you're pretty much boned because the mechanics appear identical.
The campaign leaves way too much to be desired.  While I give props to Stardock for finally creating a campaign for their space strategy games, it is horrid when judged by any other metric.  It's only 3 scenarios long (I was hoping that each block of the campaign would have multiple scenarios), to begin.  Next, the first and third scenarios can be easily beaten if you just rush ahead with your uber-special capital ship.  This leads to being stagnated (technologically and/or economically) and viciously beaten by your opponent(s) if you don't just blindly rush ahead.  This takes any part of strategic planning out of the game.  Indeed, in the first campaign scenario, if you don't rush hard and relentlessly you're going to get overwhelmed by an A.I. that can see every action on the map and has a military production capabillity so diabolical that it would give Satan himself a raging boner.
As for the second campaign scenario, no matter how hard you rush, you're going to come across fortified planets.  It's basically a bunch of ships defending a planet that has stats so huge that you have to create a dozen (literally) orbiting war fleets to destroy, and that will take lots of time.  Alternatively, you can keep using turns to research better weapons/armor, but that will take even more time depending on your playing style (I've always prefered a tech-industry combo).  In any case, it's just sloppy game design.  The developers artificially force you to spend hours of real-time building armadas and researching specific techs just to conquer the last two planets on the map.
Next on the list of how this game is stagnant of any innovation, the tech trees are exactly the same (completely linear).  So, when researching better ballistic armor, there's no benefit to pursuing that particular course other than getter better armor.  This forces you in a rock-papper-scissors gameplay.  While not bad in and of itself, the game forces you to go certain routes unless you want to be pummeled by a specific opponent with specialist tech designs.
I mean, really, is it so much to ask of modern strategy games that they look at synergy bonuses for tech?  For all the HD space this game takes up, almost none of it has gone in to expanding the scope of the strategy genre.
In closing, this game is just not worth it at the current time.  While it has the capability to be modded through the steam community (which is awesome!), it just reflects on the attitude of the designers: "Buy this shiny, pretty thing and let the gamers add content to it!"  Don't spend a dime on this!  You're better off spending money on alcohol and pizza.

You know the kind of point-and-click adventures that are genuinely entertaining and give you that giddy feeling of accomplishment when you successfully solve their challenging but logical puzzles? Well, this is not one of those.
"The Next BIG Thing" looks awesome. It has a very good user interface. Dialogues are well written, and often very funny. Voice acting for the two main characters is excellent and at least tolerable for the others. The game has a goofy plot and quirky characters, on a level that would make even Japanese raise an eyebrow in appreciation, but that was only refreshing. There is enough content to justify the price. However.
The puzzles are horrid. They do not even make an attempt to be logical; literally the only way to figure out many of them is the age-old chore-fest of trying to use everything with everything. A very minor spoiler as an example: you are supposed to use a juicer on a fire extinguisher to gain a bottle of red color (there is no in-game logic for that either, the protagonist simply comments "oh well, this is the kind of weird thing I do" afterwards). Well then. With that, what should be a fun and exciting joyride frequently bogs down to a menial search for the one combination you have not yet attempted. And to top it off, there was one "puzzle" that stands tall among the most annoying and non-sensical puzzles of all time. I'm looking at you, tango flowers.
Still, other aspects of this game ARE gorgeous. So a very cautious recommendation: if you have stomach for subpar puzzles, get this on a sale and give it a try. Otherwise collywobbles may ensue.

This is the 4th Pendulo game I have finished.
The story is fun and fresh, the graphics is cartoon-like (which I love) and the adventure has some hilarious moments.
There are some quite original parts, like when you get stuck in the thoughts of one of the characters and you need to find a way to get out by collecting memories, interacting with family members, growing notebooks (yes, no mistake here) and some absurd stuff.
It took me about 5 hours to complete the game, although I was in the most difficult mode. It is not really hard, most of the time the next action you need to do is quite rational (yes, even when you grow notebooks).
If you like point and click adventures, I really advise you this game, especially if it's in a promotion pack with the other Pendulo titles, which was the case when I bought it.

The love for the point-and-click feel-good adventure is strong in this one. Playing the game, I had the impression that the developers had a lot of fun giving shape to their fantasy world.
'The Next BIG Thing' is certainly an exercise in creativity. Though some of the characters and settings pay homage to cult classics (anyone else remember the 1986 sci-fi horror movie 'The Fly'?), others are a delightful breath of fresh air in the adventure game genre.
Despite being basically a detective story involving mutants and robots, the tone is rather light-hearted and comical. Besides being a colourful and well-animated bunch, the characters also possess the gift of the silver tongue. Cynical remarks, sarcastic rebuttals, and laconic dismissives follow one another at machine-gun rate, all punctuated with wry smiles or sardonic smirks. Still, you never get the idea that the developers were trying too hard to be "edgy".
The puzzles offer decent challenges for experienced players, and the less hard-core ones can opt for in-game hints to avoid those shameful Google searches for a walkthrough. The voice acting was very good (note: I played the game with French audio) and gave extra character to the wacky array of misfits that you encounter during this ride, which will last you around nine hours on the first playthrough.
All in all, a great game for lovers of the genre. I'll be watching you in the future, Pendulo Studios!

short review: shallow rpg and rng point and click adventure.
I didn´t expect much and was still disappointed.
You want to set pause/popup/message options? Well, buy another game.
There are basically no options at all (besides turning the music on and off) -
no reassigning of fastkeys etc. .
The ui is a mess. for example: there is a list of all the other empires. I would expect to get to the diplo screen by clicking on one - nope. You have to search the map and click your way through - thats 90% of the gameplay, It´s a new genre: click´n´search.
No ledger, no mapmodes. You want to know, if there are unhappy citizens in your empire? Just click on every planet. Whos allied to whom? click, click, click.
The ui is poorly designed, especially when you consider, that it is made by paradox (lot of experience in strategy games) and not by some 12 year old kickstarter newbies.
All about luck.
Your leaders traits influence the game big time. Your leader has weak traits? bad luck.
Your starting system has no resources? Too bad.
You dont get the tech you need? oh well (it took 35 years, before i was allowed to build bigger ships).
Your explorer fails all the time, even with 93% success rate? nothing we can do.
Diplomacy went back to the basics. You like me, you good. I want fire, ugh.
Really wonder, how they couldn´t be embarrased by that poor performance. Worse than the original civ.
The "discovery" missions are 99% useless, a complete waste of resources, if you dont know, which to pick.
You will spend the first few hours micromanaging your planets, explorers and constructors (click, click, click). No production chain, or a "build-that-as-soon-as-there-are-enough-resources". Assigning sectors doesn´t really help. I gave them (3 different sectors) the task to earn energy (credits, money), gave them resources to help them grow, and they built spaceports. After that they upgraded the spaceports. Good job.
You get punished for success. The more population your empire has, the slower you tech up, for example. Which makes perfect sense, because reasons. You´re getting punished for exploring. You just want to expand and discover and don´t want to focus on military in the beginning? Have some space pirates. You want to play without space pirates? Just go to the option menu and turn off the music.
In the endgame I was thinking: do i really want to spend resources and clicking on building another colony, when it wont help much, but seriously harm my tech? why would i want to fight that empire? The game doesn´t fell rewarding. It´s more like: "great you achieved x, you really earned a kick in the nuts." (some achievements are bugged, but getting achievements didn´t really help.)
There has to be some kind of AI somewhere, but it´s really hard to find. The game is way to easy, because the AI behaves like a toddler. Good thing they´re cheating resources and tech, otherwise the ai would destroy itself, before you´re even able to attack.
This game might be interesting for roleplayers, who want a very slow paced game, with a lot of pointless clicking. But it just isn´t a grand strategy game. It´s the incestuous son of ck and eu, hidden away in a dungeon, screaming: ESMERALDAAA, playing hide and seek with his own snot and loses.
So if you like clicking, but flappy bird is too fast paced, if you have been overwhelmed by the option menu of super mario world and really hate it, when any of your decisions have influence on the gameplay and you love gambling in online casinos, this is THE game for you.

TL:DR Do I recommend this Freaking Awesome game? Yes, yes, yes. It's like playing out your own space opera.
Journey to the West.
The High Monkians, a race of spirtualists and individuals who aren't afraid to knock some heads in where needed. With the invention of warp drive, the Jade Emporer sought to bring The Order of The Monkey King to the stars.
From their home world Jade, a moon orbiting the gas giant known as the Mountain of Ice, in the Celestial Temple system, they expanded outward. Surveying systems looking for a new world to colonize. It needed to be the right kind of joungle world, not continental, nor oceanic.
Space Whales graced the skies, amebas and crystaline entities bared the path of exploration. But they found it, a new world filled with dangerous animals and thick jungle. They named it Emerald and soon a thriving colony arose.
Onward the Monkians progressed, spredding throughout the nearby stars in search of enlightenment. A distant world, Peridot, was next on the list. Local fauna proved... intoxicating. Work ethics fell, polititions got "groovy" and the society became difficult to maintain. The Emporer considered purging the planet of the plants responsible, but that didn't seem very enlightened. So Peridot became the center of a new sector, governed by it's own leader and allowed to function at %10 under capacity as long as they handled their own problems and continued to support the Order.
New alien races were discovered one after another. Some friendly, some smelly. A particularly vile smelling creature formed an empire on borders of the Celestial worlds, sending frequent insults and resisting attempts to trade and improve relations.
A new race, a young race was discovered, in a system with half a dozen habitable worlds. They inhabited the only Jungle world. The Monkians were too enlightened to take it from them. Instead they studied them from afar. They gained an immense wealth of knowledge, and passed laws restricting the interaction with such races. They even saved the world from an impending asteroid collision, though the child race may never know.
Distant alies were made, as the Monkians ventured further out. Trading star charts became their biggest leverage in gaining allies, as the Monkians amassed a wealth of knoledge about the galaxy before they had even ventured through a tenth of it. An aliance was formed, and soon a federation.
The Order of The Monkey King thrived in this new galaxy. There were greater civilizations out there, threats unseen, wars looming. But together, with other enlightened races, they stand a chance to continue venturing where no monkey has gone before.
Will their civilization continue to thrive or unexpectedly fall? What secrets await them in western half of the galaxy? Next time on Journey to the West. What happened to the science ship that discovered a fallen civilization?? We've lost contact for months, who are these superior beings?

I first heard about Dust: An Elysian Tail when a youtuber I'm subscribed to started playing it.
And my first impression wasn't good. I was pretty sure that it would be a game that I wouldn't watch him play. But I liked Fidget. She made me laugh. And I wanted to give the game a fair chance. So I figured I'd give it three episodes before making my final judgement.
This was a year or so ago, but I'm pretty sure that by episode two, I was HOOKED on this game. I was very sad that I didn't have a system that could run it (so when I discovered it was on Steam and I could play it on my computer, I immediately put it in my wishlist for when I had money for it).
The story is engaging, the game itself is beautiful, both in look and sound, and the main characters really grow on you. At least that's what happened to me.
It's not perfect, though. The platforming isn't easy even if (presumably) you're good at platformers. I am NOT good at platformers, so I'm pretty sure the game was trying to kill me. And it did. Many, many times. But I can't fault the game for something that's my problem. It's not its fault I'm horrible at that type of game. And I'm not sure if it was just a difficulty spike or if I was just underleveled and playing poorly, but the Cirramon Caverns, specifically when you're fighting two Trolks at once, kicked my BUTT. And this is ignoring the nightmare that is navigating bomb fruit things along spikey areas, sometimes with time limits that DO NOT feel long enough. The controlls also didn't always perform how I wanted them to when I wanted them to, but I'm going to blame that on my computer and not the game.
What is, possibly, the game's fault, however, is a glitch that I ran into a couple of times. There's a skill that you get that lets you slide along the ground. Sections of the game are impossible to get through without this skill. In one such area, I BELIVE it was Abadis Forest when you have to run a gauntlet of slime monsters able to attack you from below, when I had finally gotten all the way through the underground area and dropped down, I hit a glitch. In this glitch, the entire screen became the color of Dust's clothing and the only way to play the game was to restart at my last save point. Going to the help section, I received some very helpful, and very prompt, advice on how to fix it. It turned out to be a cache problem. Okay. Cache problem solved, on with the game! Then I had to revisit the area since I had missed some treasures. I hit the same problem. It had the same fix, but it was annoying.
But a few annoyances don't detract from my overall enjoyment of the game. Dust, Fidget, and Ahrah are solidly written and well voiced characters that I grew to love over the course of watching a youtuber play this game. I know some people don't like them. Dust becomes a whiny, angsty teenager mid-way through the game, Fidget has an annoying voice, Ahrah is all around boring, are the general comments I've seen concerning the characters, or at least the voice actors.
But I disagree. Dust is a blank slate. He's trying to do the good he can, without knowing who he is, and people keep either accusing him of doing something he can't recall doing, or expecting him to selflessly give of himself at every turn. In his shoes, I'd have sat down, cried and cried and cried, and then flat-out refused to do anything. I think he's allowed to let the frustration get to him and come out in the game.
Yes, Fidget's voice CAN be seen as annoying, but I'm in the camp that finds that voice to be part of her charm. I also like that Fidget brings humanity to the game. Ahrah is the Gandalf type of character. He's wise, he'll help Dust as much as he can, but he's always pushing Dust to make the decisions that will allow him to accomplish his end goal. Dust is, as said above, a blank slate, and placed in a frustrating situation. He's trying to do the right thing, but that's not easy to do. Fidget lets him laugh, gives him a friend to tease who gives as good as she gets, and just brings a lightness to the game that neither Dust nor Ahrah could give it. But at the same time, when the story calls for it, she can become as serious as any of them. There's a scene in Mudpot that, without spoiling it as much as I can, they're unable to bring a task to a happy ending for everyone. Ahrah is serene about it, taking the stance of 'Sometimes our best isn't enough, and there's nothing we can do to change this.' Dust becomes angry, lashing out at Ahrah who's frustrating him with his serenity. But Fidget is truly heartbroken. They did everything they were supposed to, and it wasn't enough. My heart broke for Fidget when that happened. And then when it happened again later in the game, my heart broke even more. Kimlinh did a fantastic job in putting that emotion into her voice.
And Ahrah is incredibely important. Dust is the warrior. Fidget is the humanity. But Ahrah is the glue that brings and then holds them together. Without Ahrah, Fidget and Dust would have never met. And I don't think that they would have stayed together without Ahrah. Ahrah is a magical sword. Fidget is the sword's guardian. Ahrah going to Dust is the only reason the two of them met, and I think that if he'd left, no matter how attached Fidget was to Dust, she'd have done her duty and followed. But more than that, Ahrah is the Gandalf of the group. He's wise enough to realize that you can do your best, and it's not always going to be enough. And to the best of his ability, he tries to comfort Fidget and Dust when they need it. One of my favorite things about this game is the Fidget/Dust dynamic. But at the core of that dynamic, at its foundation, Ahrah is the one who's there.
But this is running long, and I've said more than I really need to. I love this game. It's not easy, it can be incredibly frustrating at times, but this is a game that I believe will stay with me for years to come. If this had a rating system, I'd give it a 10/10.

Where do I begin?
Personally, I think this game is a masterpiece. After watching Danganronpa The Animation and got into this crazy fandom, I thought it was aight. But after seeing the games for the first time, I was simply blown away. Unfortunately, I didn't get the joy of playing it blind since I watched a playthrough of DR2 before I played it (NicoB, btw). But the fact that I got so many good reactions out of just sitting and watching sold me on this game and instantly made it my favourite.
Enough backstory tho. Let's talk about the things that this game does well.
-Characters-
For a game where you know way more than half the characters are gonna die, the characters here are really well made. I will admit, some more so than others. Now I could spend hours talking about all the characters and why I love or hate them, but for the sake of your potential uninterest, I won't. We'll cover this quickly.
The character variety in this game is pretty damn neat. There are some easy to love, and some easy to hate, and some you're not quite sure. And although there is only one character here that I hate, that's not a bad thing at all. I don't hate him because I think he's a bad character. Far from it. I hate him because his character was designed to be hateable. This goes to show that they did a good job at making this character. But at the same time, I know a lot of people who love him, so there's a lot of different ways that you can interpret each character, which I think is really nice and it helps keep the fandom alive. Of course no one's gonna agree. My favourite might be someone else's hated Mary Sue. And of course you won't get to know each character fully in the main story because they'll die before you get to. Luckily, there's a bonus mode after you complete the main story that lets you do so. And, trust me, you'll most likely get very attached to at least one of them. Just hope that they don't end up dead.
-Plot-
Much like the first game, the plot in this game rarely, if not ever fails to go into the perfect amount of detail. And at the same time, it leaves a lot of mystery. It's a really good balance of the two. This doesn't just go for the overall plot, but for each individual trial too. Admittedly, some have more questions left to answer than others, but that doesn't mean any of them are bad.
As for the overall plot, everything just seems to fit together so well, and that includes some details from the first game. It truly succeeds as a sequel by developing the series more and more with each chapter, and bringing it all together for what would have to be my favourite finale in any video game. And yet there's still more. But let's not get off track by talking about the other games.
-Challenge-
Now, if we're talking about this like it's an action game, I can't say that it has a huge difficulty level...or even a relatively high one for that matter. Rather than being challenging on the hands controlling it, it's challenging on the mind. It took me a while to figure out some of the solutions to some of the cases, but the feeling of satisfaction when you finally get it is awesome. There are a few minigames that require some action gameplay, and they can get quite difficult. Sometimes not because it's meant to be. But I'm not gonna sit here and tell you that this game is flawless. Luckily, you can set difficulty between 3 levels with both action and logic.
-Follow Up-
As I've already said, this game really succeeds as a sequel. I feel like it does almost everything better than the first game. The plot is more interesting, the characters are better, the trials are longer and more engaging, etc. Although this is the case, it is really worth playing the first game first if you're worried about spoilers.
-Waifus-
Okay, let's be real for a second. This game...no, this series as a whole has some great ♥♥♥♥in' waifus. Like oh my god. Like I can name 5, maybe 6 from this game alone. Sure, it's a silly point to make and coud've easily gone in the Characters section, but my bebs deserve more.
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is my favourite game of all time as of right now. And I don't think I'll be finding anything better any time soon. This game will keep you occupied for hours whether you're just in it for the plot or if you're an achievement hunter.
And as I've said, it's not perfect. I definitely has flaws. But the good points outnumber the bad points by a landslide.
For £23, this game is definitely worth the purchase, and that's true for whatever currency you might be using too.

A roguelike (meaning random levels and lots of dying) with relatively simple rules (making it approachable) that gains complexity step by step, as you come across different types of enemies with distinct patterns, unlock new items to find and characters to play as.
The game can be quite challenging but usually quite fair too, meaning it depends mostly on your skill and not on luck (for a roguelike) as you can even adjust the pool of items you can come across in your runs.
The most prominent aspect of the game might be the move-to-the-beat mechanic. This is not only a great idea but also very well executed: unlike in traditional roguelikes, you'll have to decide very quickly making it more of an action game. importing your own music works reasonably well, though its a bit clunky. My main complaint here is that you rarely get to finish a song, every dungeon-level has its own theme which also means you come across the same song again and again as you re-enter the dungeon. Still, it's a really nice mechanic overall.
Stay away if:
-You are quickly frustrated by easily dying and starting over from several minutes ago
-You have a lot of trouble clapping/tapping/whatever to a beat
-You don't like split-second decision making
It's pretty good.

If you don't want to use your brain in a video game, then don't play this game.
As innovative as it is inspiring, Crypt does so much with the Rogue-like genre as a whole.
It forces you to think of your next move, predict with the highest accuracy what your enemies are going to do next, and is ultimately 100% fair. Given that every run can be completed without picking up any items or money at all, it is impossible to say with accuracy "RNG screwed me over in this run", ala Isaac or Risk of Rain.
Though, it definitely isn't easy.
For a while (I think around 4-6 months), there was a character (Coda) absolutely nobody has beat on all zones mode. The character entails you to move to the beat twice as fast, not take any damage whatsoever, not pick up any gold, and finally not mess up the beat once. Tons and tons of strategies and streams were done, but for the longest time no one was able to beat it.
And, if you looked at the negative reviews of this game, you'll probably see the words "too difficult" many times.
It's also a hit or miss- people who would rather play a traditional rogue-like ala Isaac are likely not going to enjoy this game as much.
But honestly, I see no objective flaws with this game. It's definitely a hit or miss, and it can easily be a miss, but from my point of view there are no observable flaws.
The visuals are severely underrated. The contrast between the game's bright, changing colors when you are on a multiplier and the bland lighting when you mess up your multiplier is amazing. It encourages moving to the beat and develops the disco-esque atmosphere of the game. Soon enough, you'll feel like you're dancing rather than moving.
The music, arguably the strongest aspect of the game which is a shared opinion among even the negative reviewers, heavily contributes to each level and zone. Heavy metal music plays during the "Death Metal" boss, and he talks as if he's the stereotypical heavy metal singer. Blues-inspired music plays during the boss "Deep Blues" (cleverly named after the Deep Blue chess computer AI that beat a chess world champion), and the boss consists of a a chess set with all moves according to the actual rules of chess, but against you. Aria having a metal remix of the original soundtrack fits her character, since she's so damn difficult and absolutely hardcore. I can keep going on, but you probably get the point already. If you didn't worship Danny Baranowsky already, you might now.
The game design is phenomenal, where all deaths could have been avoided but happened due to a player's mistake. RNG doesn't decide if you survive or not- your brain and your skills do.
If you are struggling with a specific boss, you can practice against the boss in the lobby and learn strategies and other techniques you can perform, given the lobby also allows you to carry any weapon too.
The negative reviews of this game are mostly consisted of people frustrated with the game, claiming it's "too hard" or possibly even "unfair", but those are hardly objective flaws at all. I've already went over why Crypt is incredibly fair, and difficulty is not an objective flaw, otherwise chess would be painfully awful. I've seen one person complaining about how running into mimics kills you since you supposedly "cant do anything else", but I disagree completely. How about.. moving backwards? Each enemy has its own set of moves, and learning how to attack and defend against that whilst moving to the beat is the main point of the game.
In all, Crypt is an extremely refreshing game in the video game industry, and is very novel unlike all the other typical war FPS's out there. Games like halo, once inspiring and refreshing, have gone to complete♥♥♥♥♥♥and have followed the typical mainstream FPS BS. Crypt reminds us that we haven't run out of ideas for games- we just haven't been thinking enough.

The Next BIG Thing is a traditional point and click adventure. I am a big fan of this genre and I usually like most part of games contributing to it, but this game clearly makes an exception.
Two of the most important characteristics of graphic adventures are extremely weak. Although the story is indeed original, it doesn't make to capture gamers' attention and is somehow boring, if we exclude the mental trip part between chapters 5 and 6. Furthermore the story (and the game) is REALLY short. Puzzles are just poor, being way too easy and often illogic. Characters are not bad, I would define them average, since they are well defined but not able to intensively involve the gamer.
Finally the two strenghts of this game are the graphic interface, which is really user friendly and very well designed, and the graphics, that I rather loved both for the style, the colors and the attention to details.
Is this game worth to be bought? I am afraid that the answer is no. I can recommend this only to gamers who are very into graphic adventures, and even in this case only on a large discount.

For me, the strongest points of The Next BIG Thing separating itself from other point and click games are the bright, colorful graphics, the humorous dialogue between characters, how they interact with objects and the very helpful hint system.
Highly recommended for casual/point and click gamers.

Wow, huge step up from Pendulo’s Runaway series. Spot on story, comedy, characters, and puzzles. If this was released 10 years earlier it might have been an unforgettable classic.
Pretty much everything about this game is a massive improvement over the Runaway series. It still suffers from the wonky input controls, but the writing is by far a huge step up. Story has fairly straight forward plot, reporters must thwart a politicians evil plans. But the clever setting takes you to a variety of different locales without seeming over contrived.  While we finally have coherent plot, Pendulo doesn’t try for any depth.  The story revolves around monsters being marginalized and discriminated against being the motivation for the villain. While that may have been excellent foundation for a thought provoking moral on not judging other by appearance, no morals of any kind manifest.
No matter though, this is a straight up comedy and, unlike the Runaway series, it does not rely on racism or painfully dated references to make a joke.  Characters interactions are the main driving force. Dan Murray is a well-liked but incorrigible jerk, while Liz Allaire is a well-respected but disconcerting loon. They are surrounded by a number odd but likable monsters and robots. With flawed characters comes flawed motivations as well, Dan Murray’s goal in the game is simply to get a pair of boxing tickets. No heroism or romanticism here. It just works well for the character.
The puzzle are far better balanced than Pendulo’s previous games, most are logical and do follow some sort of logic.  But it does still suffer from some bad trigger design.  For instance, occasionally if you want to set off a sequence of events you might need to talk to same person twice in a row. This happened when I needed an item a character was holding, when he denied my request the first time, I tried again and it worked. It is weird why they set it up like that, but learned my lesson from the previous games. There is also a PAINFUL audio timing puzzle, but aside from that the rest of the game has that same 90s era twisted logic puzzle design, both fun and humorous.
Put simply, Pendulo nailed the Point and Click Adventure this time around. There is really very little to hate on and a lot that was just done right.
The overall game is good, the story is funny, the music is good and the puzzles are fun. Oh and beware the tango puzzle.

Might and Magic X - Legacy
+ Successfully emulates the old-school Might and Magic series, with a party creation system which feels very familiar. There's also other classic additions, such as portraits of your characters in-game. Many of the distinct Might and Magic sounds from the games 7-9 have been re-used, which brings back memories.
+ Graphically, the game looks modern and interesting, which is great.
+ A fairly large game world to explore with relative freedom, quite a few quests to engage in as well, along with class promotions.
+ Story is intriguing and lengthy, took me about 55 hours to complete all main quests, with side quests included.
+ Lots of different monsters to fight - naga samurai, air, earth, fire and water elementals, brigands, harpies, griffins, cyclopses, goblins, minotaurs...and many more.
- Turn based combat which is different from Might and Magic 7-9, but actually works really well, giving you a chance to tactically assess what spells you'll cast and how you'll attack.
- Throughout the game a lot of audio is constantly repeated (such as locals talking), and for some people this might get irritating.
- Decent amount of puzzles with varying difficulties, although I found some of these to be tedious, boring and annoying, resorting to simply googling the solutions.
- Grid based movement, which is a step down from conventional games where you can freely turn and walk in any direction. While this isn't ideal it doesn't drastically impact on the fun of the game, it just means it's not as fluid as it could have been.
Overall Score: 8/10
Might and Magic X - Legacy is an excellent RPG which mirrors the old series from the 1990s. Even if you're a Might and Magic 7-9 fan, you should still grab this game because it's awesome fun.

6/10 - AS SUCCULENT AS A PIECE OF STALE WALL CHICKEN
This is the first game with "Overwhelmingly Positive" ratings that i have been overwhelmingly disappointed with.
I'm objective with my reviews, giving unbiased detail about the games content. followed by how that content made me feel as the player.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ Starting off with the visuals and sound design, what drew me to Dust was the artwork. It's gorgeous and has certainly had a lot of love put into it. The environments look lush and the animations are great. The character design is generally typical of any furry humanoid world and fits well. The sound design fits perfectly and well there is nothing memorable it's all very beautiful, especially in the snowy area. Everything abotu the setting is easily the games main strength but unfortunatly doesn't save it from the very average gameplay.
+ The story Is actually rather interesting, but it's paced terribly. Nothing of any interest or importance happens until about the last quarter of the game, there's just nothing to be invest you in Dusts mission because you don't really have one. You have Amnesia, so as you progress Dust will recall small details about who he thinks he once was, but these are few and far between and don't give the player any joy in uncovering them. Nearer the end however when the past is revealed to you (oh sorry, spoiler alert, as if it wasn't obvoius that would happen) the story get emotional as hell and the ending even nearly had me sheding a tear. The music during the final cutscene really brought it home. It all came together beautifully in the end but it didn't really save the 3/4 of the game that was severly lacking.
- The game is a hack and slash 2D "platformer". I use quotations because there is actually very little platforming, and when there is it's very simple and short lived. The level design is very simple, without much change throughout apart from when you get the ability to slide through gaps or climb up certain walls. There are hidden keys and locked treasure chests you can use said keys on, but the chests just contain health items which you could just buy at the store and the occassional blueprint for an item that you generally won't need even on the harder difficulties.
- The combat is very simple, though it tries not to be by teaching you different combo attacks (though few), but these are quickly ignored by spamming your AOE attacks over and over in every fight, which keeps the gameplay stuck in a repetitive loop with no true feeling of progression. The enemies and encounters themselves have no feeling of progression either. You move from one horde of enemies to the next over and over again, and every fight starts becoming stale and similar very quickly. Every screen may as well be the same because you feel like you're repeating the same thing over and over with little to no difference in challenge. As i said, there is little to no platforming in the game, which means there really isn't anything in between these fights to break the tedium. It got to the point where i was just flying over all the enemies because fighting them became so boring.
- + There is one thing that interrupts the fighting more than often, and that's dialogue. The action is paused far too much to hear the protagonist and his sidekick talk about something less than important. On more than one occassion they would put in a dialogue section to literally tell me there were more of the same enemy ahead....the same enemy i had been fighting for the past 15mins. They also had to stop and point out there was a large hole directly in front of me. It all felt so unnecessary, and was very disruptive to the game flow. It's like the game was trying to force the characters personalities on to you in the non-story segments because they weren't well established by the story itself and didn't develop in an entertaining way. Some of the dialogue is funny, and Dusts sidekick, Fidget, made me giggle a few times. She breaks the 4th wall very often and i enjoy it when a game doesn't take itself too seriously.
- Dusts progression isn't based so much around sequential levels. Levels are selected via a world map, so you can choose to go to the area that progresses the story or you could go and do a sidequest somewhere else. The quests are incredibly boring though, simply put they are fetch quests and very easy to complete (Get quest - find item - bring back to quest giver - pat yourself on the back). Qusts yield little to no reward for the player either.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
All in all Dust is just bland. Everything works but is so shallow that it doesn't feel like an absorbing game experience. To begin with it feels great to play, but you soon realise that after an hour you've really seen everything the game has to offer.
BEST BIT - The visuals
WORST BIT - The bland and repetitive gameplay

I am currently writing this while at university, sitting in a web programming and php class, listening to the Necropolis Soundtrack.
When you read reviews of Necropolis from the pre-Brutal-Edition era, you generally find that people were dissatisfied with lagging movement, a frustratingly harsh combat system, a boring abundance of resources and - above all - not getting enough variation of content for their money.
Brutal edition, in my opinion, was able to fix most of those ailments.
The movement is fluid and well animated, the combat system has been tweaked at the right places, resource gathering rates are well balanced and certain algorithms have been fixed that prevented a large portion of content from even being shown... AND they added on to that content.
(This can be read in the patch notes of Brutal Edition)
It is, now more than ever, in the eye of the beholder whether or not to give this diamond in the still-a-bit-rough an honest chance for its medium-high pricing or not. Sadly, most beholders, when being thrown between a price of ~30€ and moderate reviews, will choose to step back from a purchase. In my opinion, that would be a step in the wrong direction.
Necropolis suffers from a misfired launch which Harebrained Schemes are trying vigorously to fix.
As someone who neither really likes roguelike games nor has ever played Dark Souls (a game Necropolis is often being likened to because of its difficulty and unforgivingness), Necropolis is an immensely enjoyable game.
There is a fluid, unforgivingly direct combat system that requires skill and tactical positioning - from beginning through to the end because equipment doesn't make you overpowered and enemies remain a threat even in lategame.
(The character-permadeath emphasizes the difficulty and pushes the player to keep a tight grip on the controls.)
There is a LOT of different and varied loot to discover and try out. There is an on-the-fly crafting system that never lets you forget you're short on resources.
The visuals are iconic and recognizable without ever being irritating, and though there is SOME repitition in the architecture it is balanced by the size of the levels not getting out of hand.
The soundtrack and sound design deliver flair and an appropriate feeling of desolation and danger.
The story, though minimalistic and cryptic, serves as a refreshingly loose and open-to-interpretation backdrop. This way, the game doesn't stop for extended periods of time and the atmosphere doesn't get interrupted by long speeches or lots of text.
Multiplayer is fun and - due to forced friendly fire - all kinds of challenging over again.
Definite recommend.
Don't be afraid to jump into the water.
If you read negative reviews that appear to be overly harsh on the game, check if they've been posted before the Brutal Edition Update, in which case they are severely out of date.

Only thing I'd change is add a 4th speed to make the game even faster, but then again as with EU and CK, by the end game the amount of processing required per day slows the speed down anyway.

There's a game with similar combat mechanics, it's called Wesnoth and it's a free (as in freedom) game. Wesnoth is a quite fun turn-based strategy which is easy to learn but hard to master, just like Pandora. Though Wesnoth lacks economy, politics, resource management, terraforming, units customizing and research tree. If you like Wesnoth and want a more deep and complex game, Pandora is your best bet. I haven't played Alpha Centauri so I have nothing to compare Pandora with, and many people complain that Pandora is too simplistic compared to AC. I'm not a hardcore 4X player and I quickly lose interest if the game is too complex to learn. I need too much time to invest just to start getting fun.
Pandora has a great, thought-out UI, it's really one of its strongest points — you jump in and everything is just in place. You want information about your income and what you need to improve, and find it right there. You want an overview of your units or cities and there it is, allowing quick resource redistribution and task management. Every control is commented with a tooltip so you'll grasp it all in no time.
Visuals are pretty, every unit is animated and looks great even in close range. Graphic is quite fast, I can play it even on Intel GMA (not HD), G620 on Linux. Not smooth, but playable indeed. Any GeForce of course would be much better.
Tech tree is randomized to prevent build orders, I don't know yet if it really makes any significant difference but it delivers some fresh experience and diversification among factions. It means you won't always have your favorite technology at the same turn and you'd have to deal with that. Unusual and interesting decision. You should also design units and can upgrade existing units to a more modern version (or downgrade and get money).
Audio is good, voiceover is nice for a sci-fi game, some quotes are voiced, some not, but every technology has a detailed description and own quote (some real, some fictional). Always interesting to read, you don't just get +25% to weapon but also a bit of sci-fi story. OST could be larger, music is fine but there aren't many tracks.
I haven't tried multiplayer yet, but it should be satisfactory as well. All game files (even models!) are in XML, so you can modify everything to your likes and even create new content like factions, units, terrain etc. I hope devs add the Steam Workshop support soon and if this game will take off, it may really become a big thing loved by many. We'll see.
If you're a fan of complex games like Civ5 or AC, have too much time to learn deep politics, many special events, cultures and controls, probably it's not your thing. Pandora is more oriented to fast combat and economics than diplomacy (which is like in RTS). I'm not a fan of diplomacy so it's perfectly fine for me. I also prefer sci-fi games over historical/medieval/fantasy and Pandora gives me everything I like. And best of all is that it's released for Linux, the port is really smooth!

A decent and fairly solid TBS 4x game that borrows heavily from Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. Does some things well, somewhat lacking in the other and doesn't reach the same level of personality and depth as SMAC. Surprisingly fast paced for this type of game. Resource system is global, which works fine.
+ Unit workshop. Build your own units like in SMAC, and with better interface. The chassis being the same things in 3 tiers is slightly boring, though.
+ Randomized tech tree (per era). Of course it makes the techs connect to each other a bit nonsensically, but it prevents "the one true tech path" that plagues other games from forming.
+ Allows unit stacking in such way that it still discourages the big "stack of death". OK, this is mainly here because of my opinion of Civ5's 1 unit per tile.
+ Good interface.
- Victory conditions are a bit meh. There is enough of them, though a few more wouldn't hurt, but the existing ones are just of the "reach 75% of X" variety.
- Tech tree has some cool stuff, but also has too much of things like "factory, tier 2".
- Diplomacy is kind of lacking.
- Could use more content.
Devs seem to be still working in the game, so it may improve.
7/10

Too unbalanced
The AI player is dead set on destroying you to the point that they get destroyed by your defenses and while this in itself is not a problem, the resources you spend on the "eternal war" put you behind other factions which will, inevitably, leave you vulnerable to their logical attack.
The research is randomized, not as in, you get diferent research options per game, but rather, your most important research can show up in the begining or at the end of the tier which makes this a restart game if the tree looks awfull. Much like when you are placed in a desert in the start, "playable but dont expect to win".
Your oponent show up rather close to you or not at all, again making restarting the game quite high, and yes you have to go back to main menu, not like civ that gives the option to reload if begining conditions are not decent.
It is more a war game than anything else which is good except for the fact that the game boils down into 1. who has the better tech tree? who has the best starting area? and Who is not getting attacked? which ussually mean that the factions that have combat bonuses ussually dominate.
yea the imperium has acheived a domination victory before any race reached tier 2 in the tech tree (mechanized era).

I've been playing turn-based strategy games a long time, and they always end up playing the same way. I was just looking for a graphics update out of this game, but it actually changed the formula for me enough that I had to change my playstyle to adapt to the game. I highly recommend this game. It's a serious contender for my game-of-the-year pick.

ABZÛ is a breathtakingly beautiful underwater walking simulator with a focus on exploration, and an amazing atmosphere. You are a diver set out to explore and restore life to the reefs. The story is told visually, but the plot is vague. I still liked it, but it seems like some things are left open to interpretation.
There isn’t a whole lot to say about the gameplay since the core of it is swimming around, admiring your surroundings, and exploring before moving onwards. There are some tasks you need to perform to open up the passage to the next area, but it’s all very straightforward. Between some of the different calm and open areas, there are these jet streams that move you quickly along with the current.
You’ll want to take your time to explore all you can to find new pools of marine life, and other collectibles. You can also grab onto the larger fish, and turtles, take them for a ride,and steer them. It’s really neat that you have this friendly interaction as you explore. You can also meditate at special meditation statues that let you get up close views of the different fish as they swim around in the area. It’s actually a bit informative too because it tells you the names of the fish you’re looking at as well.
Playing ABZÛ using a controller is strongly recommended. However, you can play with keyboard and mouse without too much difficulty, but it will likely take some time to get used to the movement.
ABZÛ is an incredibly gorgeous, and soothing game. If you’ve had a long day, and you just want to sit back, relax, and unwind, I highly recommend giving ABZÛ a go. It’s an excellent underwater walking simulator with a remarkable atmosphere. It is an incredibly short game though, so I do suggest waiting for a sale price.
If you like my reviews, please feel free to join my Steam group, and follow my curations
You can also check out my review on my website

+ Visually the game is incredibly beautiful.  Very cibrant colors, lighting, and so many gorgeous fish to gaze at.
+ The gameplay is very relaxing. The entire game takes place underwater in the ocean as you swim from place to place discovering new animals and exploring new environments.
+ The underwater movement is fantastic with great controls. It really feels great being able to swim around at pretty high speeds, and jump out of the water like a dolphin. The motion is so fluid.
+ The soundtrack is excellent, and really sets up the mood and atmosphere throughout the game.
- There could have been better "puzzles". Throughout the game there are doors that only open when you turn a valve to release chains. This is repeated multiple times in the exact same way.
- The "story" is extremely vague and a bit confusing. There are these underwater floating ancient-looking pyramids that act like mines and zap you when you get too close. For some odd reason you chase a shark throughout the game to these pyramids, and then at the end you destroy them.....  Yeah..... I don't even know...

A roguelike (meaning random levels and lots of dying) with relatively simple rules (making it approachable) that gains complexity step by step, as you come across different types of enemies with distinct patterns, unlock new items to find and characters to play as.
The game can be quite challenging but usually quite fair too, meaning it depends mostly on your skill and not on luck (for a roguelike) as you can even adjust the pool of items you can come across in your runs.
The most prominent aspect of the game might be the move-to-the-beat mechanic. This is not only a great idea but also very well executed: unlike in traditional roguelikes, you'll have to decide very quickly making it more of an action game. importing your own music works reasonably well, though its a bit clunky. My main complaint here is that you rarely get to finish a song, every dungeon-level has its own theme which also means you come across the same song again and again as you re-enter the dungeon. Still, it's a really nice mechanic overall.
Stay away if:
-You are quickly frustrated by easily dying and starting over from several minutes ago
-You have a lot of trouble clapping/tapping/whatever to a beat
-You don't like split-second decision making

I highly recommend this game.  What first got my attention for this game was the artwork.  And it is beautiful.  But then I found it's a 2D 'platformer' game, which I'm not that big on. . Dust has pretty much everything I want from a fun and entertaining RPG, and more. The
might seem straightforward at the very beginning, but as you progress in the game you understand that it's not as easy to predict as you thought. The
