To all turn-based strategy, 4x lovers (such as myself), I
. It's the best thing out before the release of Sid Meier's: Beyond Earth.
Anyone who is wondering what this game is like, I'll give you a brief idea on what it is like by saying that it feels like Civilization V with a few major differences, such as:
1.
- you also discover new technologies after every era you pass through, to give a sense of wonder of the future
2.
- infinite number of units per tile; like Civilization IV's stacks of death. The game has actually balanced it so that attacking with stacks is less beneficial; bombardments hurt all units within a stack, flanking (putting units next to each other in separate tiles) gives an attack/defensive bonus.
3.
- yes, you have a unit workshop and can fit different weapons/bonuses/abilities on them. There are a lot of different chassis to research (e.g. infantry, fast-attack vehicle, tank, watercraft, and more).
4.
- at the beginning of the game, they are not hostile. However, the wildlife can get more and more aggressive if factions fight against them, or produce a lot of pollution. They may then become the equivalant of barbarians, or even worse (if aggressive enough, they can launch a full-scale invasion on humans, threatening everyone. It could prove to be a good tactic, for militaristic players, to annoy the local wildlife so that peaceful players are threatened with annihilation). There are multiple types of wildlife, ranging from practically harmless little xenomorph drones to gigantic aquatic monstrosities.
5.
- it works something like this; morale (happiness) is local, rather than national. Local morale has an affect on local growth, and local growth depends on whether or not you have enough food stockpiled (food pool is national). Growth is also affected by habitable space; if you don't have enough space, migration to other cities (ones which have more habitable space) will occur. Production requires minerals (also stockpiled nationally). If you run out of minerals, production will be hindered but not stopped completely. Science is gathered normally (1 scientist = +1 science). There are buildings, natural resources and tile improvements which produce percentage increases and/or a small increase in that stat. You can also move your citizen's roles (there are four roles; farmer (food resource collector), miner (mineral resource collector), worker (city producer) and scientist (science producer)) around manually, and they will automatically go to the highest yielding tile. There are other factors as well (such as wars, pollution etc), but that's just the gist of it.
6.
- around turn 200 (normal pace), an alien force (size depends on how difficult you set difficulty level/alien aggression level) invades the planet and the world has to rally together to fight them off. It's a nice twist and a breath of fresh air, especially if the local wildlife is almost extinct by that time or if you have been playing a peaceful game up until that time.
In addition, the game's presentation is very nice (introduction video, graphics, artwork, quote voice overs), soundtrack is great, UI is intuitive and smooth, optimisation is smooth as well; never lags or crashes (runs a lot better than Civilization V). The game is, amazingly, roughly 500MB, so it's a very fast download.
What can I say which is bad about the game? Well, currently, the game has more focus on combat than Civilization. The game still needs, in my opinion, to add more content which aligns the player to a more non-combat style of gameplay (e.g. something similar to culture with wonders). There are multiple victory conditions other than conquest, such as economic and research victories, but it'd be nice to have more. There is also no indication of how far ahead you are when compared with your opponents, until the last few turns before your, or your opponent's, imminent victory, warning the player.
The good news is that the developers have pledged to add more content to Pandora: First Contact, maybe in the form of expansions, if it proves to be successful. So far I think the game has been successful, hence the Steam release (the game was released months before Steam).
: Just as I said before, they have continued updating the game to make it better and they have recently announced the first expansion pack, "Pandora: Eclipse of Nashira", to the game which adds espionage, better diplomacy, better aquatic gameplay (sea tile improvements etc), new factions and more.
For people hoping this to be the next Alpha Centauri, I wouldn't get your hopes too high. The game is good, and it is very similar to AC in some respects, but it's not exactly the same (e.g. no mind worms). Judge it for what it is. I played a lot of AC back in the day, and I thoroughly enjoy this game for what it is.
If you're still not convinced, or somewhat unsure whether or not to pay for the full price of £22 or $36, just wait for the eventual sale. I'd definitely call you mad for not getting it then.

Overview: Stellaris is off to a promising start. It has all of the base 4x systems - expansion, exploration, war, ship design, tech, diplomacy - and while few of these are stand-out incredible, they do yeoman's work and provide a base-platform for future improvements that will likely create a true gem.
I have played about 15hrs offline to minimize steam's resource hogging ;-) I will only go online for ironman or multiplayer.
The Delightful:
writing/scripting - incredible. Never thought I'd say that about a 4x. Interesting, branching event chains are well crafted with exquisite writing. The game has high replayability just for these stories :-)
Artwork - gorgeous.
Music - wonderful, per usual for a PDX title
Tech system - innovative and interesting. Unlike tech trees, you get a handful of options whenever you complete a tech. There is no guarantee that you will see the same option multiple times (you probably will with the essentials, but others are far more rare.) You can certainly start researching something and then change your priority & begin researching something else. Your progress will be saved, but if that card doesn't come up again, your research is lost.
The bland:
Politics - war, neutrality, (alliance/federation) are your only options
Trade - no civilian trade is modeled, and the options at the state level are typical. Moreover, there is no personality to it (explained below)
Leaders - get limited bonuses for a few fleets, armies, planets, but I don't get invested in them like I would CK2 rulers.
Domestic Affairs - at least by midgame,
Personality/Density of story? In ck2, I can get invested in the individual stories of my various leaders/vassals/characters. In EU4, my knowledge of world history fills my imagination with 'what if' scenarios, as I imagine the historical interplay and differences from the real world. In Vicky 2, the factions and (overly) intricate production/trade system helps bring personality to the domestic affairs of each country. I'm not much of a wargamer, but HOI3 benefits from the real leadership and well-modeled country ai. ---- In Stellaris, I tell my own story, but the game doesn't give me as much as previous titles to work with. Factions are fairly bland. International diplomacy is fairly bland. The leaders are merely bonuses to be added to certain stacks. While the ideology of different empires causes them to react in different ways, it doesn't appear to vary based on ruler or even POP-ideology (e.g. if half of my people are jingos, I should be more likely to go to war, even if my country was founded on peaceful principles)
The missing:
Espionage
Civilian trade (what can I say, Distant Worlds was a gamechanger)
Map modes ;-)
Lore - okay, again there are the great event sequences and some interesting things happened in the galactic past (and I'm sure I haven't begun to scratch the surface of this). BUT, for the individual procedurally generated empires? Beyond the story that you tell yourself about your empire, there is nothing. By comparison, when you encounter a HRE run by Ulm in CK2, you can speculate about how it happened, and read the logs to find some evidence of how it got to where it is. When you get an announcement in EU4 that Switzerland has declared war on the United Confederate States, you know something strange is going on and the historic backdrop provides fascinating context. Dwarf Fortress & Ultima Ratio Regum this is not.
The promising: PDX's expansion strategy, I love it.
For the next several years, I'll receive massive content updates, bringing in new mechanics, tools, systems; bug patches and performance enhancements will abound. And all of this for free.
PDX releases regular expansions and DLC. The base game receives much of the enhancement as a free patch, though some of the specific mechanics are unavailable for those who don't purchase the expansion, unless they are playing in multiplayer with a host who has paid for the content (then everyone gets all the toys.)
EU4 and CK2 are more nuanced, bigger, and better games today than they were at launch, even if you don't purchase any of the DLC. And, a base game is multiplayer compatible with anyone else. For example, with EU4's art of war expansion, the paid content included all sorts of new war mechanics, from allied objectives to marches to client states and new war goals. But if war wasn't your thing, so you didn't purchase it, you still got new provinces, awesome reformation mechanics, a complete overhaul and expansion of diplomacy at the vatican, trade goods, performance enhancements, etc. Not bad, eh?
*I play single-player offline so that I can minimize steam's resource issues*

Bought this game right after Brutal Edition came out.
Sure, it's still somewhat laggy, but overall, I fell in love with this game.
It's art style is something next level. Low poly, but yet never feels cheap. People tend to complain about how it's not as good as Dark Souls, but yet, there's a bit of a problem to that point. Even though I do understand how people tend to compare the two, I feel like Necropolis has more of Legend Of Zelda influence more than anything.
The game is difficult, but it really depends on the dice, as levels are procedurally generated. Because of that, you can have 10 runs in a row that look and feel almost the same, but on the next two, you'll find yourself in a completely new area with dozen of high-HP mobs. Beating off around 20 skeletons in one room really got me sitting on the edge of the seat.
Anyhow, first and foremost, this is a dungeon crawler with a strong Zelda influence, thus, if you're looking for something like Dark Souls, feel free to skip it. Other than that — I recommend it.

The Next Big Thing, is a point and click adventure game developed by Pendulo Studios. Being released in February of 2011 on both PC and iOS devices.
Gameplay in TNBT is your standard point and click action. You can walk around the areas fairly freely, allowing you to interact with objects and talk to other characters in the game. Obviously with all point and clicks the game play is not why you are playing. The puzzles in the game are somewhat entertaining as well, some of them really make you think, but are not so obscure that you have no chance of working them out. I had to resort to a guide for a few of them, but that is more than can be said for other Point and click titles out there.  The game’s UI is one of the better I have seen in this genre, it is very easy to navigate and to select objects and use them in different ways.  Even though the game doesn’t have any sort of in game tutorial, there is no real need for one since it is all so self-explanatory.
The game has a really nice art style. Whilst the game does have “cut scenes”, this is done in the same style and effect as the actual real time stuff. You can only really tell a difference with the frame rates.  The character animations are all fantastic too; there isn’t one weird looking walk, or strange facial expression to be seen here, a very nice looking game in my opinion.
As with all good point and click games, you should expect a half decent story, well The Next Big Thing certainly delivers there. I went into the game expecting it to be a sort of political tale, I was wrong.  The plot is set Los Angeles in an alternative reality. The two main characters, Murray and Allaire are both detectives and you set on the assignment to cover a kidnapping and conspiracy.  There is some witty banter between the two characters, and this is what drew me into the game right from the get-go. The dialogue between all characters is all top of the range and I was overwhelmed with how good they all sounded. The story does have a few clichés, but overall it is captivating enough that it kept me engaged right until the end.
There isn’t a real difficulty level to this type of game. It is only hard if you cannot work out how to progress with puzzles. But like I said above, none of the puzzles are so strange and obscure that you cannot work them out by using a little bit of thinking juice. This is something which I admire in point and click games nowadays and even though some may be a little let down by this, The Next Big Thing is a casual experience.
The full story took me just about seven hours to get through – for a point and click game I think that is just about the right length, it allowed the game to reach an end which tied up most loose ends, and it leaves you wanting more of the same, without over staying it’s welcome. There isn’t any replay ability sadly since it is very linear.
I didn’t run into any major technical problems during my time playing. The game runs at all resolutions and given that the game is mostly pre-rendered graphics, it can run on any type of hardware (it’s an iOS game so….).  The only slight problem I had, was that the game doesn’t lock your cursor in the game’s window; if this was any other game than a point and click, this would have been a major issue, but since it is a slow paced adventure game I can forgive it there; but honestly in this day and age, these types of issues should be mopped up.
The Next Big Thing is an absolutely stellar game and one that fans of the genre should really be checking out. The game’s interesting story line and good looking art style, on top of some quality voice acting, you can’t really go wrong with checking this title out.  The price tag of £6, 99 is well and truly on point with the amount of content and quality of it on show as well, so definitely picks it up when you can.

If you're a fan of the original Might and Magic games (And yes, I do even mean 6, 7, 8 and 9) you'll find many of the elements you enjoyed from those games here: Exploration, riddles, puzzles, and resource management. There are a number of interesting and unique quests which venture out of the normal "go here, kill this, gather that" formula, the best of which actually make an active effort to draw you into the lore of Ashan.
If you're concerned about the grid-based movement, or the relatively small size of the game, don't be. The developers know better than to get in over their head on a risky and much-beloved franchise. It may be small in scope, but I find it to be structurally tight and sound -- in the narrative/game mechanic sense, at least. There are a number of bugs that plague the game, but nothing that's really kept me from enjoying it.
The combat is frustrating in that you can't really run or reposition your party, but the resource management aspect of it is as satisfying and interesting as it ever has been, and there are still plenty of tactical decisions to be made in the course of your adventure.
Better than the originals? Definitely not. But certainly worth a look.

I would not recommend playing this game if you expect a hardcore hack-n-slash that is perfectly produced. It was made mostly by one guy and to be honest he's done a pretty darn good job of it too!
So, I was introduced to this game by a couple of friends who recommended I play it, not for its combat, but for it beautiful artwork and story.
I probably wouldn't recommend casual or normal mode as it is a bit too easy and the only reasons I've died so far are because (here comes the negative points):
- This game is meant to work with a controller or game-pad. Playing on keyboard like I am is a bit tedious and there are no keybind options (well, not that I can see). It does work with WASD and Mouse, but it's not the perfect fit for this game. This does make platform jumping (a core mechanic of this type of game) a bit difficult at times, especially in some of the levels where the platforms have an air current or (sorry to say it) badly made hitboxes on the spikes.
- There are very little combos meaning that during combat 90% of the time you're spamming right-mouse click
- Some of the levels are more side-scrolling puzzle, which does add a bit of thinking time and a small degree of difficulty, but it gets a bit old, especially at the end-game section where the AI can move through walls, yet you have to go through 10 different sections to get to the same spot
Really, I don't want to sound negative because the main reason I'm played (and loved) this game is purely for the gorgeous artwork and great story :)
So, it took me about 8 hours to get my 70% completion (I've completed the story and most of the side-quests along the way), but some of that time was re-running missions for materials for better equipment, so I will admit that if you rush only the story, the game will be quite short.
However I must stress to not judge this game on mechanics or core gameplay - you love it because of the story and graphics, not for the hack-n-slash side of it.
Overall:
Gameplay: 7/10 -  it gets a bit repetetive near the end and some of the puzzle elements are unecessary
Story: 9/10 - I would of given it the full 10, but for me, the story took a bit of time to warm-up and really get me hooked
Feels: 10/10 - play it and find out why ;_;
Graphics: 10/10 - gorgeous

While this is infected with Uplay it is a rather good game, but not one for Casual Gamer X because it is very difficult. Expect to start over at least once or twice until you get a good feel for all the skills and abilities. The biggest struggle is dealing with inherently scarce resources. Monsters do not respawn. The only cash is from chests. It's not just no grind, it is impossible to grind. Exhausting an inordinate amount of supplies to clear something is tantamount to losing a fight. You must pick and choose everything you do carefully, and you will still need to save and reload often.
It has some flaws (Uplay, bad graphics, you cannot flee period without reloading) but they're overshadowed by the fact that they simply don't make games like this anymore. This is a game to learn and master. You need both a plan and execution. No, the game isn't fair. Despite being open world it is quite linear, and if you go somewhere you're not supposed to you get destroyed often times. You have very few clues to tell you what's easy or hard until you get creamed. But you can just reload and continue. No big deal.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes challenging RPGs.

At a glance, ABZU seemed like a game I would like; breathtakingly beautiful, soulful score and wonderous moments as that was how the game, JOURNEY, was for me. I could not help comparing the two and that was the downfall.
Both games make use to the surroundings, music, sound, and environment to tell its story; disregarding words and written quests. However, where JOURNEY succeeded, ABZU failed. Certainly, ABZU is gorgeous but after just playing for a little under an hour I was overwhelmed by the vague emptyness of the game. JOURNEY always held its mountain in sights, wordlessly urging the player to new heights; to reach the apex where undoubtedly the game's lore would be revealed bit by bit. When you start ABZU, you are thrown into an underwater world filled with all kinds of marine life as well as seaweeds and coral, so much so that it gets a little confusing, since it's a bit difficult to tell which mound of dirt you discovered to the ones you didn't, as you explore and swim about trying to activate/collect things, which didn't give me a sense of accomplishment.
As you explore deeper into the underwater world, you encounter different regions. However to unlock the next region you need to uncover one robot friend...and that's the extent of the "puzzle". In some regions I only found 1 while another I found 3. Regardless of how many I find, they magically vanish at the next region. What was the purpose of unearthing them, as well as other marine life and the shells? I remembered in Journey where I had to go collect pieces of the player's scarf; the longer the scarf the further I can glide as I had to succeed in different platform levels to unlock the next area. I helped freed cloth creatures who would in turn help me obtain otherwise unreachable trophies and provided me with energy for my scarf. There was a purpose in collecting rather for the sake of just collecting to view; i.e. meditating.
Although both games' storyline are purpseoly abstract, in JOURNEY as you progressed you were shown bits and pieces of the story through glyphs/murals in which they tried to replicate in ABZU. However, it just didn't have the same satisfying engagement. Both games have substantial symbolism however because of it's ambiguity, it feels cold and difficult to connect with. The saving grace in JOURNEY was the unexpected anonymous online co-op which helped me connect with the game and it's progression as my unknown partner waited for me through the harsh wind of the mountains and accompanied me in the darkness as we once again try to reach the top of the glowing mountain. It's a key feature that touched my heart and urged me to replay the beautiful but short game.
ABZU rivals JOURNEY's beauty but lacks ambition with it's fruitlesss collecting, stale level progression puzzle and the charming warmth. I could only recommend this game for those who are looking to enjoy a game full the splender of an underwater world but aren't looking for a lot of depth and replayability.

Sometimes more is less.
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair has the unfortunate job of having to say "How do I follow up that?" The original Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc, had final relevations that would, without spoiling, make further installments tricky. Danganronpa 2, therefore, sidesteps the larger narrative already set up to tell a smaller but still engaging story. This one isn't really a standalone - though you can probably go through it without playing Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc, I would urge anybody interested to play the original first. While for the most part this stands alone, the parts that don't are pretty vital.
So, D2: GD keeps with the blend of visual novel text and minigames established in the original. There still isn't any signficant branching other than what students you choose to bond with during a given playthrough, though there's seemingly a hidden scene or two I may have missed, looking at the gallery. Instead, it relies more on the murder mysteries and minigames to engage, and those felt relatively strong, though one case left me rather cold. In general, those who have played D:THH will feel at home again. The core gameplay of "meet friends, watch them die, solve the mystery" remains the same, but there are a more few new distractions.
In keeping with sequelitis, some of the minigames have been changed and a new one has been added, but sometimes not for the better. The core debate mechanics are still strong and remain the core. A new debate style where you "cut" words is a middling addition - it's difficulty seemed to wander wildly to the point I felt one sequence was nearly impossible on Hard, but thankfully only nearly so. Hangman's Bluff gets a unnecessarily obtuse addition of moving letters that can crash into each other, which I just felt was distraction. A new minigame, Logic Dive, has you hoverboarding down the tube of... your mind?... and selecting different conclusions by boarding down different paths. To me, it felt like an unnecessarily reflex-and-memorization version of Ace Attorney Investigations' logic mechanic. Ultimately, though, they still fulfill their purpose of adding tension to the trial segments and breaking up what otherwise would probably be a tiring wall of text. Mystery deduction remains engaging for the most part, with only one mystery that had me squinting at how the player was supposed to puzzle a thing or two out.
Also new to the series are leveling and a virtual pet mechanic, which is easily the worst new addition. You can warp between locations quickly, or you can walk slowly from area to area on the new island environment. Walking levels your character, but also there's a virtual pet you get you can grow by walking as well. However, your virtual pet will♥♥♥♥♥♥itself to death if left unattended, so you have to enter a menu, select the pet option, and occassionally press "X" to clean its♥♥♥♥♥♥up and allow it to grow. Leveling can be done other ways as well, mind. Your level controls how many skills (gained by making bonds with others, still) you can equip for trails, and the pet can be given gifts to raise its "hope" to get it to evolve into different forms. It's all a bunch of fiddly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to reward people willing to play a Desert Bus-quality minigame that hopefully won't make a return, because it's real, real bad. The pets don't do anything interesting but shower your in monocoins, which are used once again to buy gifts to make bonds with the other students and unlock stuff in the gallery.
If that wasn't all, there's a fairly average arcade "magical girl" side-game to play, as well as a alternate story mode and novella that are unlocked upon finishing the game - I've played the former but not the two latter games yet.
As an aside, just get guides for gift-giving or pet raising in that regard. It's not worth sussing out on your own. Similarly, the random gacha machine tries to trick you into spending more than on monocoin at a time, but it's only worth it if you're buried in them and you're down to that last 10% or 5% of items to unlock. It retains the bad mechanic of just throwing in tens or hundreds of coins one at a time to get the best result.
This may sound all really harsh, but I still enjoyed it. And it's hard to talk about why, because the biggest elements of D2:GD are the relationships, reveals, and a deeply Japanese sense of humor and wit. If you've played D:THH - which you once again should have before playing this - you should already have a pretty good idea of what you're in for. The new characters are generally interesting and entertaining with only a few misses, and I wouldn't mind another go-round to see more once I have the time. It's unfortunate to have some of the albatross-like mechanics added to what otherwise is a fairly strong narrative, though hemmed somewhat by the relevations of the original. There are some handwavey portions that disappointed me somewhat, but overall it left me wanting to poke some more through the bizarre pile of questionable quality that is what the Danganronpa *transmedia franchise* at this point. Is it good? Hmmm. Is it fun? I think it's pretty fun so far.
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair remains a relatively clever visual novel with just enough spice of minigame and adventure game crossbreeding to keep me entertained, A lot of whether people like this depends on your tolerance for visual novels, Japanese quirk, and some degree of monkeycheese, but it's not the sort of experience you'll get much of anywhere else save perhaps the Phoenix Wright games, and those games aren't on Steam.

TL;DR: Easily worth your time for the narrative if you enjoyed the original, but it's not without some annoyances to put up with, so if you're easily bugged by some garbo mechanics or time-wasting elements it may not be for you. If you haven't played the original, don't play this.

Been playing this for a while now, already stepped up to Hardcore mode and I still love every single minute of this game. The graphics look as if almost every single piece of it, character models and attack effects included, look as if they were all hand drawn and that takes much effort and the game shows it. The characters are loveable (minus Gianni) and some you can actually relate too, or relate to someone else you know. My favorite support characters in the game are right now Sereth, the merchant that follows you around (ZOMG SPOILERZ), Cora because she reminds me of my own grandmother who passed away some time ago, and Haley the blacksmith girl for her spunky attitude and cheerfulness (*coughcoughshipwithdustcoughcough*). Dust himself is a rather interesting character, it starts off with him trying to find out who he is, and when he does find out, he now knows why he was created and leads the Moonbloods to take back their freedom. Fidget has my vote for best sidekick, she is by far one of the funniest and most loveable characters I've ever seen in an indie game, plus once you give her stats a higher number, she becomes a tiny power house of death.
But this is far from being called a "perfect game", like most it does have it's flaws that I've noticed in my time playing it. My biggest gripe is the enemies movements. The fact that most enemies become invincible when they jump can really hurt you in combat unless you have Fidget throwing out her magic to catch them when they land.
The second is the EXP system, I can see it's like playing the Batman Arkham series where you rack up the damage and combo number and the more you score, the higher the EXP bonus. But again going back to the enemies, it just takes one jumping and then ♥♥♥♥♥ slapping you from behind and you lose all of that hard work which made me rage on more than one occasion (example being Corbin's sidequest to do a 1000 hit combo...f*cking zombies).
And the third being your healing methods. I'm sorry to say but having to fully rely on healing items that are damned expensive if you need to buy any is rather bad design. I get the creator wanted the player to not HAVE to rely on healing items so much so you can perfect your combat skills, but when enemies surround you and you're near death, you blow through all of either one or all of your healing items just to get back a decent amount of HP to keep fighting. It probably would've saved players much more time and hassle if say, Aurora Village had an Inn of some kind so you can restore your HP if you don't have the gold for healing items, or rather recover Dusts HP when you go to the map screen to select a destination, giving Teleport Stones a more useful purpose.
Critics aside, this is still a fun game to keep you entertained for hours as well as emrese you in it's story to keep you on your toes. Many sidequests to keep you from being bored, and characters you'll love to keep you laughing and loving as well.

"A beautiful story told in a gorgeous handpainted 2D platformer. To think that this was made by a single person... - Buy it - play it - love it!"
In the game where everyone is an anthropomorphic animal of some sort, you play as Dust - a man who's lost his memory of who he is and why he's there. At his side he have a talking magic sword, called the Blade of Ahrah that guides him in what he could do to regain his memory. By wielding the sword he also gains incredible skills in combat. He is also accompanied by a small flying creature called Fidget, who reminds me a bit of Happy out of the Fairy Tail anime. In his travels through the land he encounters friendly people who's in need of help, a mysterious merchant from a distant land and strange lizard-like creatures that at first seems like monsters, but there's more to them than it seems...
The landscape is beautifully made and all handpainted with lots of color. All the characters have their own little personalities and are often a bit comical (for example- the flying creature Fidget has a fear of heights). The story is well written, but can be difficult to keep up with in the beginning. The combat mechanics are top notch and there are tons of moves and combinations to learn and use against countless enemies. Every move is beatifully animated and really flow together with the rest.

This game is fun, engaging, and deep. Unfortunately, the 'deep' gameplay is poorly indexed and described and so while you have a very firm grasp of the numerical results of your choices (20% is less than 15%) its unclear how the mechanics of the game use these numbers. For a 4X game that obviously wants numbers ascribed to everything, it is very frustrating not to be able to understand or and learn how those numbers affect the game. This game desperately needs a well written 'Civilopedia'. The Wiki's are still young and incomplete and all the players seem to be in the same boat about figuring out how many of the game mechanics really work.
Some examples:
Planet tile bonuses are for "Approval" when all the tile improvements actually affect "Morale". (once you do figure this out, this is actually one of the better presented mechanics: Approval = Morale/Pop, but poor labeling obscures this)
What does "Military" on a planet do?
How does Influence actually spread?
This is a fun game that unfortunately becomes less fun the more seriously you take it. This is super unfortunate because it presents itself as a game that should be taken seriously with the appearance of being able to customize and min/max everything about your empire. Which you can do, but without a solid mathematical understanding of how your choices will affect your gameplay experience, its hard to be invested in the choices you make.

While I applaud the developer's efforts to salvage a very rocky release, and while I always support people who want to make Soulslikes, no amount of additional content will fix the fundamental flaws in this game.
Before I can recommend this one, two things need to be fixed:
-Lack of combat variety: This is one of the big stinkers. There are exactly 6 attacks in this game per loadout: Shield Bash, Light, Heavy, Charged Light, Charged Heavy, and Falling Attack, the latter three of which reduce your max stamina. There are no Rolling Attacks, Sprinting Attacks, Backstabs, Parries+Ripostes, or any sort of replacement or equivalent. This, combined with the (in my current experience) very samey weapons and enemies, makes for a bland experience, and usually fairly easy/tedious. There are a few enemies that do provide trouble, but it's mostly because it's difficult to deal with their incredibly swift attacks.
-Stamina Bar Issues: There's a big difference between this and the Souls games, in one small area that turns out to be very vital. In Dark Souls, when you're fighting an enemy and running out of stamina, even if the amount of Stamina you have left is too little for the action you're trying to perform, you can still 'squeeze' a little bit left out of your Stamina bar. It's reduced to zero, AND you go into 'Stamina debt' where you don't have any stamina for the time it would take to regenerate the Stamina you used/went below 0 with. However, in Necropolis, if you attempt to perform an action that you don't have enough Stamina for, it simply does not occur. While this may just be muscle memory telling me that I should have enough Stamina to roll or attack one more time, there's a reason why Stamina debt exists: it's because an empty bar very visually communicates that you cannot do anything else with it until it comes back. When you have a sliver of Stamina remaining in Necropolis and can no longer attack or dodge... what exactly are you supposed to do with that remaining sliver? It might as well be empty.
And these last few are more nitpicky, but... crafting? Really? Of all the creative healing systems people have come up with for Soulslikes, based off the ingenious Estus system, you have to go for the game design equivalent of phoning it in? Enemies also seem to do little damage to compensate for the player potentially not having the proper items required to create a healing ration or something, except for the miniboss style enemies. If you ask me, I'd say to scrap the current drop system entirely and rehaul the healing system, make item and weapon drops random instead of constant, and make the special enemy weapons actually different from one another via expanded movesets.
My last complaint (and segue into what I like) is about the setting. I cannot take Necropolis seriously. I understand that it's meant to be funny or at least unserious, but I haven't even found myself cracking a smile at the attempted jokes. They just... fall flat. When I heard of 'Lord Abraxis of Mirrors, forever on his Onyx Throne' or something like that, I was immediately more interested than I had been since I began playing. I think the main problem is that you're just thrown in, without any sort of grounding as to the tone of the game, or why you should care about anything not related to the gameplay. Compare this to Enter the Gungeon, which immediately gives you a theme and a goal: Big bullet hits a planet (immediately establishes guns/sci-fi fantasy setting), and a dungeon is built over it, holding a Gun That Can Kill The Past (incredibly intriguing concept, introduces you to a story goal/reason to reach the bottom). In Necropolis, it's like... you're an adventurer in an abandoned Necropolis owned by a guy named Abraxis? And there's this Brazen Head guy. Go into the Necropolis because reasons?
But damn, the Necropolis itself is fantastic. You guys have nailed the vistas and the design, and it's just entrancing exploring. Enemies have interesting designs, but there's not much difference between a lot of them.
There's so much still waiting to be fixed about this game.
So much that, if fixed, could make this THE definitive Soulslike. Of that, I have no doubt. Continue the trend of listening to your fans, and you could even surpass Dark Souls with this and further efforts.
But with the gameplay stuck somewhere between Lords of the Fallen and Malebolgia, I can't really recommend this game to anyone.

If you like Dark Souls, rogue-likes, or dungeon crawlers, you'll love Necropolis. Put simply, you are exploring dungeons to find new weapons, armor, potions, spells, crafting recipes, level up, and fight a massive boss at the end and escape.
Now, I'll talk about some things Necropolis does really well.
PROS:
-Beautiful art style
-Drop in drop out co-op
-Huge weapon variety
-Armor buff/debuff trade-offs
-Huge enemy variety with different AI
-Solid progression from feeling powerless to almost unstoppable by the end
-Decent biome variety
-Hidden rooms rewarding keen adventurers
-Interesting lore
-Two unqiue characters
I want to re-iterate: this is a great game and you should buy it. Next, I'll talk about a few areas in need of improvement. Keep in mind the developers have promised to address each of these issues, but they still plague the current game.
NEEDS IMPROVEMENT:
-Only two characters
-Only a handful of biomes
-Final level too easy
PROS: (explained)
-The art style is complementary color palletes and low-poly, which is done so well Necropolis is one of the most beautiful games I've played. Several views have left me amazed at how good simplicty can look. The art drew me in and I love what the devs have done here.
-Imagine playing Dark Souls with your friends. The gameplay is more dungeon crawler, but this is a huge plus for Necropolis. I am not a big Souls player because the game is so hard alone, but dropping in with up to three friends at any time is a ton of fun and no less rewarding.
-You can find everything from shortsword and buckler, to heavy axe and tower shield, to greatsword and crossbow, to staff and wand. In Necropolis you can play as nearly any role given the right weapons. Some weapons come with damage types from fire to lightning. Some weapons have trade-offs like shields that protect against stagger, but cost more stamina to use.
-Armor drops are rare and random. Every set of armor is absolutely stunning to look at. Some offer trade-offs such as increased stamina and attack speed at the cost of health. Finding a set of armor is exciting and often marks a turning point in a playthrough, averting certain death in a tough fight.
-You'll encounter new and deadlier enemies on every level ranging from the standard dungeon enemies to the bizarre and terrifying. Many enemies have challeging methods of attack from slow debufs to teleporting to exploding and a ton more to keep you on your toes. I felt a sense of dread when I encountered a new enemy and that feeling of pride I felt when I geared up and defeated it was unmatched.
-The starting enemies can be quickly dispatched, but the difficulty curve ramps up very quickly. Enemies drop gems and with enough of them, you can and must level up if you want any hope of staying alive. Completing tasks for the taunting being that controls the Necropolis grant tokens that can be used to open golden chests with rare loot to buy expensive magic tomes that you keep when you die and grant powerful bonuses, or to buy new dyes for your armor that you also keep. With every death, the game gets even harder so that enemies that used to show up in the third dungeon appear right out of the gate. Some playthroughs even allow multiple final bosses to appear. Overall the game feels rewarding to conquer and play again.
-The deeper you delve into the Necropolis, the more biomes you'll encounter and it is thrilling to see the art style and new enemies each one has to offer. This gives a sense of exploration that is quite satisfying.
-Pressing on normal walls might reveal a room full of loot. Nooks and crannies can hide great secrets. In general, players who don't rush things are rewarded.
-Interesting stories about a strange world with a bit of snarkiness are what you can expect from reading the lore that appears on walls or at the end of levels.
-The first character is the Blackguard: a quick, fragile ninja capable of peppering opponents in light damage and out-manuvering attacks. He can side-step and stab enemies in the back. As the Blackguard, it is best to avoid damage all-together by dodging or using ranged weapons. The second is the Brute: a slow, damage spongey tank who can also deal incredible damage. As the Brute, it is best to run into a crowd of enemies and deal AoE damage using slow, but strong charged attacks.
NEEDS IMPROVEMENT: (explained)
-The lack of more characters limits playstyles and replayability. The third under-development character is the Arcanist: a mage of some sort. My best guess is that he will be ideally played using spells, potions, and bombs from afar while perhaps confusing enemies and buffing allies.
-I won't spoil the biomes as they are very rewarding to discover for yourself, but I will say you will encounter every biome in your first complete playthrough. I'd like to see many more biomes to make every playthrough unique.
-The journey is more important than the destination, but if you do manage to make it all the way to the final boss, you'll probably find it easier than the preceding levels, which is a bit unfortunate.
, but I would like to see an Arcane edition in the coming weeks to increase the amount of replayability.

Danganronpa 2 is a game i've already completed on both the PSVita and PS4. I've yet to complete the pc version but i think i've played enough to be able to write a review about it. Despite being a sequel Danganronpa 2 can in fact be played without playing the first game, although doing so isn't recommended. For this game a new cast of characters find themselves in a new setting, but the concept is largely the same. To escape from their island paradise/prison you need to commit murder and get away with it. If they do not then they face excecution.
The gameplay is very similar to the first though some changes have been made to the exploration and trial minigames. While the trial changes are welcome as they make some of the more boring minigames less worthless, i'm not to fond of the exploration, as i much preffered what was present in the first game instead. However, there being a fast travel feature alleviates this somewhat. The story itself feels like it takes a while longer to get going compared to the first one and i really wish it would hurry up a little bit in the beginning, the prologue especially. Thankfully the pacing is a bit more to my liking towards the end, and i do like the story quite a lot. Though, again, i didn't like it as much as the first. the trials are still as fun as they ever were, and its still a great feeling putting together the pieces of the cases.
Speaking of things not as good as the first game, let's talk about the characters. As i said before we get an entirely new cast of characters for this game(well, for the most part, at least). I do enjoy a lot of these new characters, don't get me wrong, but in equal regard, some of them irritated the crap out of me through the course of the game. First off, I really like some the concepts this game puts forward.  But I just can't recommend it.  Without any sort of tangible progress the game just feels empty.  You spend tokens of favor on codexes, which are the only real progression you get to keep.  All of your crafting recipes are lost when you die, which makes the crafting feel cheap and not worth pursuing beyond spamming rations.  You can only equip one codex at a time, and buffs they grant are wildly variable.  Some are entirely useless.  That said, the art style is amazing, and I love randomly generated dungeon crawls, but there's just no sense of progress or character growth. You worked really hard and found some cool armor and weapons only to die to a cheap group of mobs? Too bad you lose everything, time to start over.  The idea of permadeath is great if the goal of surviving is worth it, but the gameplay and character building is just too weak to support it.
Do you like 4x strategy games? Do you like strategy games? Do you like games? If you answered any of this questions with ''Yes'' or ''No'', buy this game.

Alright so, I'm your typical meat head shooter guy who screams over the mic while with his friends in TeamSpeak. I'm not the usual type to play games like this. But to be honest, this game sets its self apart from others like it in many ways.
The overrall diplomacy system makes up the bulk of this, making the game feel much more personal as the AI insults you,  compliments you, and tries to push their agenda on you. Each empire feels like it has it's own personality. The best part of this is that if an empire that has liked you for a long time ends up disliking you, they don't immediatley turn to a bland, blind hatred. They still acknowledge your former relationship and let you know that they feel you have strayed from the light. The only thing that I felt was lacking was more advanced Vassal interaction.
The ship customization is great, it's not overly complex, but just complex enough to make every ship between empires unique. The research tree leaves something to be desired. Until you've played the game through a few times you might find yourself a bit confused about what techs you're exactly heading for, though that might just be me and my lack of attentiveness towards research. The single player is excellent, but the multiplayer is where things really shine.
I highly recommend this game, especially if you have a group of friends that play it.

A brief summary of the below: I actually enjoy this game, and I plan to keep playing it. However, it's hard to get into, has a number of flaws, uses outdated soundbytes, and generally feels very unfinished. It doesn't feel like a betrayal to the series or anything like that, but this game is built from a lot of unrealized potential. I would not suggest this game to others unless they like the world of Ashan or want another dungeon crawler in game library. It's a solid turn-based dungeon delving game, but I wouldn't call the story I've seen impressive or the gameplay innovative.
Might and Magic X is a strange beast to me. It's an enjoyable game once you get past the ghastly introduction and a fairly deadly tutorial; however, it has a rather unpolished quality about it in general. As others have mentioned, the game has more in common with the original Might and Magic games (1-5) than it does the latter end of the series (6-9), at least so far as gameplay goes. It's based on the world of Ashan, which you will know if you've played Heroes of Might and Magic 5 or 6, on a peninsula consisting of a few towns and cities in an era of rebellion and religious turmoil.
First, since combat is so integral to any dungeon delving series, let's take a gander at the good side of that. Combat in Legacy is turn-based and square-based. As said above, if you're familiar with how old Might and Magic games played, or if you like Legend of Grimrock, then this will feel like familiar territory to you. The game uses this to its advantage as much as you do at times: enemies will sometimes move to flank you, doubly so if they "spawn" in a position from which it is perfect for them to do so, and opponents in dungeons typically attack from places that put your party at a severe disadvantage. This makes fights challenging, and forces you to make plans around the terrain you're fighting in if you can. Tossing enemies away from you with a gust of wind or immobilizing them before they can reach you so you can reach limit the number of melee attackers on you, or ducking around a corner so the enemy mage will have to walk into smacking distance to chuck a spell at you... This game encourages tactical thinking, and that's what turn-based gameplay is all about.
Now, let's discuss the bad part of combat. First, there's the fact that a lot of enemies do seemingly appear out of thin air. Ubisoft seems to be a fan of having your opponents, even when visible, be unable to be struck until  You will encounter this problem in the very first dungeon you ever touch, in the tutorial: spiders will drop from the ceiling and initiate melee combat with you immediately, before you can react. This would not be a problem except for the fact that entering in any melee combat prevents you from moving away from your current square. Let me repeat that: melee combat stops you from going anywhere. That means if you have even a single opponent on your face, you can't pull your part back a single tile into a defensible corridor to fight your opponents a few at a time. No, you're stuck standing in the middle of a terrible position where nine enemies can surround you, listening to your idiot adventurers screaming "Sorry, I'm a little busy right now!" when you're trying to get them to move somewhere they won't die. Apparently, the heroes of Ashan were never taught the intricacies of the tactical withdrawl. It's rather aggravating, and even after you've learned to deal with this limitation, you won't learn to like it.
There are a lot of other little problems I have with the combat system, such as poison lasting forever until cured (and you'll encounter a LOT of poison at level 1). They don't ruin the game, but combined these flaws make combat feel... well, flawed. A small aside: ranged combat can be fun, but in my experience you'll rarely get the chance to enjoy it due to being locked in melee combat most of the time. Your ranged damage will be negligible once your party is fighting in close quarters.
As I mentioned previously, the game lacks polish. I could talk about the graphics (though I'm not really a graphics-oriented person), which are lackluster, but I'm more inclined to talk about the various, small details of the game that could use changing. For one, Ubisoft has lazily taken sound bytes from previous games in the series - very outdated soundbytes, mind you - and slapped them into Might and Magic X. Perhaps they were trying to elicit some feelings of nostalgia from those who played Might and Magic 6, 7 and 8, but all the sound bytes taken from those games just sound so very out of place and old.
There are very limited voice options for your playable characters (a 'heroic' or 'cynical' voice for each race/gender combo), and several of them reuse the exact same lines. That is, the humans and dwarves say almost the exact same thing, everyone sounds like they came from the British Isles, and the characters' lines get very repetitive very quickly. (I left the first town in Act 1 as quickly as I could just to get my dwarves to stop talking about how darned boring the place was.) Non-player characters with a voice actor in the open world don't even move their mouths when speaking to you; games as old as Wizardry 8 have at least gotten THAT down.
The tutorial doesn't really cover leveling up well (if at all; I can't remember if it mentions it), which is annoying because players new to the series won't know to look for the 'skills' tab and place points there, and the skills tab being a subsection of the spells tab is very obnoxious, and... Well, whoa. Like I said earlier, there's a lot of polishing up and balancing that needs to be done to the game. The user interface and the tutorial just aren't built properly.
Despite this, I found the game fun; very fun. I'm going to keep playing it as I have been. However, if Ubisoft doesn't make improvements by the time the next game in the series rolls about, I'll be very disappointed, because the game could be so much better than it is right now. I like the variety in classes in the game; I like the ideas Ubisoft had in making race actually matter a little bit (as far as conversations with NPCs go at least). If you are willing to overlook this game's flaws, it will be great fun, and there's a rather rewarding experience awaiting you once you get past the nasty shell that is the game's introduction. If not, well, don't buy the game.

I’m not one who tends to be a fan of furries (not to mention the absolutely terrible pun in the game title), but I found myself surprised by this one. Let’s have at it.
I – Story [7/10]
Dust: An Elysian Tail is an indie, RPG platformer from Humble Hearts. I’ll be honest here, I don’t care about spoiling the story of D:AET like I cared about not spoiling the story of The Banner Saga, so there will be spoilers in this section. If you care about that, don’t read any more of this section. If you don’t care, do what you want. I’m not your mother.
Dust (the protagonist of the game) begins his journey by waking up in a forest with no recollection of who he is and is being hounded by a the Blade of Ahrah (a talking sword) and probably the most annoying support character I’ve encountered in a long time. (Her name is Fidget, by the way.) Thus, you set out on a quest to find out who you are and what is in store for you.
Eventually you find out that you (Dust) were created by a people known as the Moonbloods and contain the souls of two people who died simultaneously. After being presented with this revelation (and some slight bouts of identity crisis) you traipse off to confront General Gaius (your former friend and employer).
While the conflict of the story itself has been done before, it had it’s own spin on it and made itself unique. That being said, it was still a bit lacking in my opinion.
II – UI [10/10]
The user interface was as well-designed and easy to use as anyone could ask for. I navigated menus with easy and could see me stats in combat without a struggle. That just about covers it on this one.
III – Gameplay [8/10]
As I’ve stated before, I’m a big fan of platformer games and the fact that D:AET  was a platformer was about all I went into the game knowing about it. Also, as I stated above, I’m not really a fan of furries or the furry fandom in general, but that didn’t really detract from the experience of playing through this one. I found myself surprised by how much I actually enjoyed playing D:AET. The combat was simple, but fun. Navigating the world of Falana was (for the most part) a blast. Apart from a few lackluster boss battles and some cliched dialogue, the game as a whole is good (for at least one playthrough) and provided some laughs here and there.
Certain things in the game though could have, and probably should have, been done differently. Unless I’m mistaken, everything in-game is hand-drawn. While I personally love this when it comes to games, a few things really stuck out. Towards the end of the game, some big, flying spaceship-like enemies are introduced. These were poorly done and (while obstructing large portions of the screen) just seemed clunky. In addition to this, the snowy mountain region of the game could have used some tweaks. At times (no, not during the avalanches) the snow effects were so dense, it became incredibly hard to see your character.
Also, on topic of not being able to see your character, the last areas of the game sometime contain so many enemies and allies on screen, it is literally impossible to see where the character is standing. This was easily the most frustrating aspect of the game.
IV – Content [9/10]
The other part of D:AET I found myself surprised at was how much content it brought with it. While there are only a few regions in the game, there are a generous amount of enemies to steamroll and double that amount in items. The game even has a decent crafting system. Not only this, but the shop system was phenomenal. Merchants share stock and get new stock at frequent intervals.
The absolute best part about the shops though was selling a crafting item to any of them, which they would then catalog and start stocking so you could by more from them later. Why is this not a thing in more RPGs now days? Seriously though?
Regrettably, the items you equip don’t show up on your character, so you have no choice except to look ridiculous the entire game.
V – Visual [6/10]
Everything in D:AET is hand-drawn and, while that usually does it for me, I was a little disillusioned with the character art. The scenery was amazingly well done, but most of the characters seemed a tad rushed almost. There was a smattering of different enemies, which was great, aside from the ridiculous spaceship-esque enemies toward the end of the game.
VI – Audio [7/10]
The music of D:AET was fantastic. Easily one of the better soundtracks in a game that I’ve heard in a while. (It was very Sanctum 2-like too.) Really though, the soundtrack was just superb.
The voice-acting, however, struggled at times. While most characters were too minor to actually matter much when it came to the voice-acting, Fidget (who accompanies you the entire game) was utterly annoying. On top of this Dust sounds like an over-dramatic teenage boy who dreams of being a badass.
VII – Overall [7.8/10]
Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tail is a pretty good game from a fledgling developer. Would I have paid full-price for it? Probably not. I got this on a Steam Sale and am content with what I paid for it.

If you think you may be interested in this game, then go ahead and give it a shot, but I do not give it a high recommendation.  I rate it 5/10.
ABZU primarily offers great music accompanied by pretty and bright visuals that are perhaps a bit too cartoonish.  I won't deny that the game is beautiful and there are a lot of fish for you to encounter, but that's about it.  Some sort of story is told by murals on walls, but the story is not very intuitive and I'm still not certain I understood what the game was trying to portray.
On your first playthrough, you will be able to discover hidden pools that release new aquatic life into the world and collect hidden shells.  I did enjoy seeing the new sights that the game had to offer, but mostly I just enjoyed exploring to find the hidden pools and shells.  If you happen to play through a second time, the game offers nothing new to interact with.  I missed some shells in my first play so I played the game a second time.  About halfway through I realized that I was incredibly bored.  The environments really aren't so spectacular that they merit a second experience.
You are forced to swim through the ocean at a leisurely pace, allowing you to slowly take in the environments and discover all the wildlife.  This speed limitation is fine at the beginning of the game but grows rather tiresome later on when you are required to swim across vast open areas.  You can unlock faster movement speed but it requires you to find all the hidden shells (which means you'll have already beaten the game and therefore not need the increased speed).
I heard and read a lot of commentary comparing this game to Journey, and given that the development team of ABZU also worked on Journey, that's an understandable comparison.  However, this game doesn't come close to comparing to Journey.  Journey was a masterful experience worth playing over and over again.  ABZU is only worth playing once (and maybe not even once for some players).
A quick note on game mechanics: camera management and movement controls are not as intuitive as I would expect for a 3D environment, often leading to frustration.  I often found that the diver would swim in a direction that appeared completely unrelated to the direction I input.  Thankfully, you can't really die and the slow movement means you're not trying to get anywhere in a hurry, but it was still annoying.
Ultimately, I think ABZU lacks the direction needed to make the game great.  It offers really strong audio and visual stimulus, but it falls short in almost all other regards.  This game is essentially an underwater walking simulator with nearly no story and nothing to do except encounter the environments themselves.

Shadow Warrior is a great game being on par with other games of the time such as Duke Nukem 3D and Blood as one of the greatest FPS games of all time.
1.Story
In Shadow Warrior you play as Lo Wang an employee of the Zilla Coroporation, Zilla Rules most of Japan and decides to take over the world as he thought Japan wasn't enough, Lo Wang Doesn't agree with this and quits the job at Zilla Coroporation and sets out to destory Zilla and his army of ninjas.
2.Gameplay
Shadow Warrior Plays alot like Duke Nukem 3D as it is running on the same engine,the game has two episodes "Enter The Wang" and "Code Of Honor," The first episode has 4 levels and the second has 18 levels. Lo Wang is one of the most halarious portagonists in all of video games here are a few of his quotes "Row Row Row your boat gently down the stream why is my Dingy hanging out" and "Who Wants Some Wang" the game has an original weapon selection when compared to games like Doom and Quake, Lo Wang has his fists,A katana,Shurukens,Riot Shotgun,UZI SMGs,Rocket Launcher,Grenade Launcher,Railgun,Sticky Bombs,Guardian Head and a Ripper Heart.As far as I know, this and blood are the first FPS games to have ALT fire modes to weapons examples are the Riot Shotgun can shoot out 3 shots at the same time and The Rocket Launcher can Shoot Heat Seeking Missles and Nukes.
3.Presentation
Shadow Warrior looks very and I put very outdated for it's time in terms of Graphics, This game was released in 1997 by this time Quake was out for one year and it had true 3D Graphics not to mention 1997 was the year Quake 2 was Released so by this time the Build Engine was becoming outdated that is one of my major complaints with the Presentation, It's outdated and that can sum up the Presentation of the game.
4.Final Verdict
Shadow Warrior despite its presentation is a great game and there are so many ways to get it now. This particular version was included in the 3D Realms Anthology Steam Edition, You can also get it free on steam or you can purchase it on
and get its two expansions with it, Twin Dragon and Wanton Destruction you can purchase the remake Shadow Warrior Classic Redux (Which I also Reviewed) or if you are just old school you can pick up the boxed version but man I love this game so what's the final verdict?

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is an absolutely gripping role playing game. I can say with confidence that this game and its sequel Witcher 3 are two of my favourite games ever. Witcher 3 I would even say is in my top ten maybe even top 5 favourite games of all time. But this is a review for Witcher 2 not Witcher 3. Witcher 2 is an amazing game and it deserves more attention, while successful to a degree it deserves major recognition for its excellence in almost all areas.
The Witcher 2 is based on the Witcher fantasy novel series by Andrzej Sapkowski. The series takes place in a fantasy world filled with rich lore, great characters and dangerous beasts. It is a very serious and adult world, rife with mature social issues and Game of Thrones style politics. Blood and betrayal are every bit as prevalent in the politics of the Witcher series as debates and lies. Racism and inequality is a very wide spread issue between humans and non-humans (elves and dwarves). It leads to a lot of tension and violence. It is a fascinating world where I found myself wanting to learn more about it everywhere I went.
The Witcher series stars Geralt, who himself is a Witcher. A Witcher is a professional monster slayer by trade and masterfully trained in combat and possesses basic magic capabilities. Witchers are often thought of as freaks or dangerous weirdos but due to the high danger posed by wild beast and Witchers expert combat prowess they often find their services needed where ever they go. Geralt himself is a bonafide badass. He is pretty stoic but spending some time with him you learn he has an awesome dry sarcastic sense of humor and a deep loyalty to his friend’s fellow Witchers. He can of course fight amazingly well which is important because he faces an enormous obstacle.
Witcher 2 starts off with the Assassination of a powerful king, at the hands of a Witcher. Geralt finds that he is quickly falsely accused of the King's murder and with the help of his close allies’ searches for the assassin to clear his name. I don't want to go into more detail than that for the games story. The game has an amazing story with difficult and impactful moral choices. Story and player choice are for sure 2 of the games strongest areas, Witcher 2 excels greatly here. The game also has a great cast of characters. Geralt is a great protagonist; Triss is a very cool sorceress and potential love interest for Geralt. Iorveth the leader of the rouge elves is exceptionally cool and very interesting to talk to. The cast goes on and on with great characters. Too many great characters to name here.
Gameplay is Witcher 2 is stellar and thankfully is a massive improvement compared to Witcher 1. Witcher 2 plays very similarly to Dark Souls in combat. You balance sword play, magic and items simultaneously. Geralt is a very agile fighter and you will make use of the combat role a lot. Combat is very fast paced but is also surprisingly tactical. Different enemies require different tactics to overcome. Such as using Geralt's silver sword to fight monsters or taking a more defensive or offensive strategy. You can also make oils using Geralts alchemy skills that you can apply to your swords to do more damage to certain types of enemies to tip the odds in your favour. Outside of combat you will spend your time talking to NPC's to craft items or gain quests or learn more about all matter of things. You can challenge many NPC's to play dice poker or take part in fight clubs. There are lots to do and exploring the world is very encouraged, you will find many interesting things to see and do in the world of the Witcher 2.
Witcher 2 does have fantastic sound design and an excellent score. Each swing and hit with a sword sounds fantastic and the games score is awesome. The score might not be on par with Elder Scrolls and the sound design isn't as good as Halo or Battlefield but it’s pretty stellar and certainly is fantastic and satisfying.
Witcher 2 does have a few weaknesses though, the game isn't perfect. I found the game to be on the shorter side compared to most RPG's though it’s not at all criminally short. Some of the voice acting on some characters is kind of subpar too. The game can be very difficult too on any difficulty higher than easy, now that isn't a negative in itself but some users may find it too hard on normal but too easy on easy. I myself found the optional but smart to take tutorial level was not good in teaching me how to play the game and I found I had to learn it myself as I played. I also found the game far more playable with a controller than with keyboard and mouse which may be a bummer to players out there.
Overall I would give the game an 8/10. It just misses a 9/10 but the poor tutorial level and some subpar voice acting on top of some minor issues prevent the game from being higher scored. However despite and 8/10 I highly recommend this game to RPG fans. It’s fantastic and absolutely worth your money and time.

You cannot talk about this game without at least mentioning Journey, and considering that a few key people were involved with both games, Abzu can easily be viewed as a spiritual successor to its sandy, console-bound cousin. There are many parallels, but Abzu is its own unique experience, one that I believe is well worth it.
The story of Abzu is more abstract than Journey's, and it's less of an emotional ride, but that does not mean this game is devoid of story and emotion. I feel that the story in Abzu plays second fiddle to the experience of the game itself. It is a BEAUTIFUL game, and full of life (compared to Journey's equally beautiful, in its own way, bleakness). The controls, once you get used to them, make just swimming around in this world a joy. (Tip: Don't try to control the camera. It's always going to turn to point in the direction you are swimming. Just focus on your movements, and the camera will follow naturally.)
This is a very simple game with exploration and discovery at its core, so besides locating a few switches to flip and some collectibles for achievement-hunters, there are no real challenges or dangers to encounter. It is a very short game that can be completed within a couple of hours. These are not negatives, though, because I feel like Abzu accomplishes what it sets out to be. My only wish is that it included co-op because sharing the experience (and helping or being helped) was such a wonderful part of Journey that I miss it.
If you loved Journey, I believe you will at least like, if not love, Abzu.
If you loved Abzu, you owe it to yourself to play Journey.
If you are just looking for a short, beautiful, mostly relaxing, almost meditative experience, Abzu deserves a look!

Do you like rhythm games?  How about roguelike dungeon crawlers?  Well...  Why not both?!?  Crypt of the NecroDancer somehow combines the two into a challenging and absolutely addictive game, and manages to pull off both very well.  In the classic tradition of roguelikes, this game is unforgiving at times, however it is a game that rewards persistence.  After you die (and you will die), you get to spend  the diamonds you acquire during your run on various items which can spawn in the randomized dungeons.  The soundtrack here is really something else, you will frequently find yourself with the music from this game stuck in your head.  And oddly enough I really can't think of any one place where this game lacks, normally I can gripe pretty hard even about games that I do like quite a lot, but this one just manages to combine all the right elements with a stroke of simplicity that just ties the whole thing together very well.
Best of all, it only really requires 4 buttons to play:  Left, right, up, and down.  Thus, it can be played on a dance pad!  So if you've got the hardware laying around from your old DDR or Stepmania days, you can put it to good use here and get yourself some fit.
Do yourself a favor and get this game.

First off, I really like some the concepts this game puts forward.  But I just can't recommend it.  Without any sort of tangible progress the game just feels empty.  You spend tokens of favor on codexes, which are the only real progression you get to keep.  All of your crafting recipes are lost when you die, which makes the crafting feel cheap and not worth pursuing beyond spamming rations.  You can only equip one codex at a time, and buffs they grant are wildly variable.  Some are entirely useless.  That said, the art style is amazing, and I love randomly generated dungeon crawls, but there's just no sense of progress or character growth. You worked really hard and found some cool armor and weapons only to die to a cheap group of mobs? Too bad you lose everything, time to start over.  The idea of permadeath is great if the goal of surviving is worth it, but the gameplay and character building is just too weak to support it.

I've played all incarnations of Gal Civ II and loved them!  Gal Civ III is more streamlined of a game but there is a cost. There is no espionage, mining is now done for resources on constructed space station vs using mining ships and the tech trees seem to have lost a few things but this is not really a bad thing. Ship design is still solid and the use of strategic resources opens the possibility to prototype models that will enhance your ship's attributes based on the techs you have. AI is decent enough and if you are not careful one of you allies may win via an alternate condition that you did not see coming (example Altarians winning via tech victory). Game set up has a lot of nice features to give you a lot of variety to set the game the way you want. Map sizes can get to epic proportions for long campaigns. There are not as many races as Gal Civ II but you can create your own here. As with Gal Civ II this game is a great value due to its high replay appeal and addictiveness. As far as I am concerned the Gal Civ series is the best 4x strayegy turn based game series out there. Buy them.

First Impressions Video:
This game is fun. It's not groundbreaking, but I enjoy it.
The gameplay is very reminiscent of Dark Souls. You have a health bar and stamina bad and you dodge and slash your way through enemies. There is a hunger system. You slowly lose your max stamina and can replenish it by eating something. Really, the hunger mechanic ends up being more of a nuisance than an actual issue in the game.
In terms of combat, it's not bad. Enemies either telegraph their attacks too much or too little. There were few, if any, enemies that I couldn't figure out in a few seconds of combat. There is a good range of enemies. You have everything from the lowly skeleton to a vicious snail wizard. Each have a unique move-set and, thereby, present different challenges.
So what are the issues? For one, the weapons break down into three categories: swords, spears (of which I've only seen one), and clubs. Every weapon in those sets acts basically the same, but with different damage and speed of swings. This make the weapons very samey. There are a few special abilities, but they're few and far between. That being said, I do enjoy slicing up enemies with a little cutter.
The game is unbalanced. If you get a ranged weapon then you win. That's it. I beat the game because I picked up a crossbow and sniped EVERYTHING. The rain of exploding arrows was glorious.
The level design is what you'd expect out of a rouge like. It's okay, but not something to write home about.
The controls are not tight at all. I've pressed buttons and had nothing happen. The weapon attack don't always chain, leaving you fairly open. It really feels like lag coming from an internet connection, so that could actually be the issue.
In the end, I found this game to be enjoyable enough to pick up every now and again and do a run. I'd definitely say that if you're interested, you should pick it up if it's on sale. For full price? I'd wait and see if they do a few more updates. With a bit more content (and variety of content at that) this game could be great.

I'm a huge fan of the Might and Magic franchise, Heroes included, and that's the only reason I played through this. Unless you are REALLY desperate for your M&M fix, I can't suggest this as a viable purchase. For the same money, you can get much better titles, new and old.
As for the actual problems with the game:
-Graphics are laughable. Expect low res environs throughout the game
-Optimization is bad. I can run Skyrim on ultimate with no issues on my rig, but the turn based M&M is apparently too much, as even on middle of the road settings, there is going to be heavy lag in certain areas with dense foliage. According to the forums, this is a fairly common problem.
-No customization. There are 4 races with 4 hero type each (caster, ranger, tank, melee) and once you pick one of those, you get to decide on male or female. Oh, and also a name. Joy... There's no way to change the appearance of your characters and you never even get to see a model of them beyond a picture during character creation.
-Poor class balance. Rangers used to be completely useless, but after the patch they were upgraded all the way to just "meh". The game LOVES to spring ambushes on you (about 30% of the fights, along with most bosses), by dumping a ton of enemies at melee range, making bows and crossbows useless for the fight (once you engage in melee, you can't retreat till you kill everything in melee range). There goes a quarter of the hero pool. Tanks are also useless, since almost all bosses (and all undead, which are VERY frequent) are immune to taunt - your primary tanking mechanic. This means that 50% of the classes in the game have no purpose, except for flavor, at the cost of your party's strenght. That's just bad design.
-Turn based gameplay on a 2-dimensional plane. You can call this a throwback to the old M&M series, but it just doesn't work. Even the worst of Might and Magic games had a smoother transition between turns, than Legacy. The last ones even managed to mix real-time movement with turn-based combat. Also, turn based movement is not fun when on long treks between towns and quest points. This game has a lot of that, if you're looking for all the hidden little nooks and crannies.
-No voice work for quests. While it's not a necessity for every game, it would have been nice if M&M X managed to show off with something, at least.
-Lackluster story. Everything in M&M X screams "minimal effort" and the story is no different. It's painfully generic and set in a very boring world where every character is just a cookie cutter fantasy stereotype. There's just nothing new, even in the story: elves are elves, dwarves are dwarves and orcs wear fezzes (god damn it, Ubisoft...) You can't even augment your party with new and interesting companions. Once you get out of the hero creation screen, that's it - it's set in stone. You DO have the option of getting two followers, but with no voice work and characterization, all they offer is a boost to one (mostly unimportant) aspect of gameplay.
Relative to what else is out on the market, even at this price, Might and Magic X - Legacy is just a bad game. It has nothing to offer, save for the faint nostalgia of the franchise.
