While the humor is noticeably present, I don't really find this game to be THAT funny. That's not a bad thing, if anything, I feel like the humor lightens the mood, and keeps you from taking the game seriously. The game doesn't really take itself seriously, and I like that. I enjoy the dialogue (minus the "ayo" "aya" stuff), as well as the characters and graphic style. It really adds to the lightheartedness of the game. Every character is unique and entertaining. I also find this game to be pretty engaging, it makes what seem to be simple tasks mean something. I was into it the entire time. I really like the animation, like when you click on something in your inventory. It looks really good. I really loved the ending of the game as well.
However, some of the "puzzles" are frustrating. Some of them trick you. Some of them make absolutely no sense, for example, at one point in the game, you need to use a fruit juicer on a fire extinguisher to get the red paint off the fire extinguisher. Yup. You read that correctly. You can't make this stuff up... Some of them are just flat out stupid, like the Tango/Flower puzzle. It's sometimes hard to figure out what to do next. There is a help option included in the easiest mode of the game. If a game feels it's necessary to include a hint or help system, it acknowledges that some of the puzzles may be unreasonable or difficult to figure out. That's what I think, anyway. I don't feel it's necessary. Just don't make the puzzles so cryptic. You could make a fun, challenging game without cyptic puzzles. There's an option to play the game without hotspots/hints... I had hotspots on, and still had a bit of trouble finding some areas of the game because some of them are hard to see. You definitely looked at a walkthrough if you played on that option.
Is it a great game? No, I wouldn't say so. But I had a really good time with it. It's a lighthearted, quirky, entertaining point and click adventure game with a solid story, great characters, and humorous dialogue.

This game does a good job of being just about entertaining enough, just about engaging enough, just about funny enough and having characters just interesting enough to keep you playing to the end of its 5-6 hour story.
This won't shatter anyone's world but it's a solid Saturday afternoon adventure that might make you feel briefly a little younger, never a bad thing.

How do you review an expression of grief? Grief must take place somewhere beyond judgment. As an expression of grief it is faultless, but as a game, I have a few reservations. That Dragon, Cancer, is very much a mixed bag. It's a collection of touching scenes in the life of a sick child and his parents.
Some scenes express emotion quite vividly, such as when the parents meet their doctors for an update and prognosis, when you navigate Joel as he is carried on balloons made of surgical gloves, when Joel will not stop crying in the crib, and when he is cradled on the chest of his father Ryan during treatment.
Others were perhaps too abstract or left me confused about how to proceed, such as pushing Joel on the slide, helping Joel ride the animals created from constellations, or prodding Ryan to swim when he is submerged. On a few occasions, I seemed to - almost - perform the action that was required of me, but then the scene would reset for me to try again. It's possible that either these scenes were meant to evoke futility on the part of the player or that the game simply moves on if a player "fails" a scene too many times.
Through what is depicted here, we see hope and hopelessness, faith and spiritual doubt, helplessness, and confusion, among other powerful emotions. If nothing else, the game is entirely genuine and authentic - I've never played anything else like it.

I could not stop weeping. I even had to skip one of the stages because I couldnt emotionally handle it. This is an experience: one that will tear your heart out and smash it on the ground. I cannot express just how sorry I am to the parents who lost their precious child. As a single mother, SIDS was once my biggest fear for my son, and now cancer is. I lost my father to liver cancer, and the Universe was just kind enough to allow me to hold his hand and tell him I loved him just one that time. This game makes you realize that life isnt just about you, because its the truth. Its not. It never has been. Life is not kind to any human-being, man or woman, child or adult, black or white. Sometimes it can show favour, but it never makes promises it cannot keep.
Cancer is one of the most difficult things a human can endure: and the fact that a tiny child had to suffer through such pain is like a stab through the heart. Going through the "Waking Up" stage made me cry so hard that my stomach now hurts. Reading all of the cards of people saying goodbye to loved ones and trying to spread positive messages when cancer just makes you think so negatively. It gave me nostalgia because I remember those few months of hospital visits for my dad, and the thought that someone else, especially two parents to a small child, had to go through the emotions I did was just heart-wrenching.
I was hoping when I sat down that this wasnt a true story, that is was a fictional piece and was fabricated in the mind of a genius to wanted to bring awareness to cancer. But when I got to the end and summoned the courage to read the Steam description, I think my heart has physically broken. Its the fact that a child had to suffer such a terrible condition for such an extended amount of time is what pains me most and that two parents have to a lose their little boy. I just wanted to curl up and sob.
It doesnt matter that I didnt particularly enjoy how the game went very religious, it was an experience, one that will follow me for a long time. I wont forget this game so soon, and likely never. I would recommend without a doubt. It is worth the money and worth the time. Please, go into this game with a relaxed, peaceful state of mind. And beware: you will cry.

There are many parallels, but Abzu is its own unique experience, one that I believe is well worth it.
The story of Abzu is more abstract than Journey's, and it's less of an emotional ride, but that does not mean this game is devoid of story and emotion. I feel that the story in Abzu plays second fiddle to the experience of the game itself. It is a BEAUTIFUL game, and full of life (compared to Journey's equally beautiful, in its own way, bleakness). The controls, once you get used to them, make just swimming around in this world a joy. (Tip: Don't try to control the camera. It's always going to turn to point in the direction you are swimming. Just focus on your movements, and the camera will follow naturally.)
This is a very simple game with exploration and discovery at its core, so besides locating a few switches to flip and some collectibles for achievement-hunters, there are no real challenges or dangers to encounter. It is a very short game that can be completed within a couple of hours. These are not negatives, though, because I feel like Abzu accomplishes what it sets out to be. My only wish is that it included co-op because sharing the experience (and helping or being helped) was such a wonderful part of Journey that I miss it.
If you loved Journey, I believe you will at least like, if not love, Abzu.
If you loved Abzu, you owe it to yourself to play Journey.
If you are just looking for a short, beautiful, mostly relaxing, almost meditative experience, Abzu deserves a look!

Orion Prelude is an cheap FPS game.
Before the review, I would like to preface something, Orion Prelude is not the best FPS game. In regards to FPS, a gamer could boot up the classic TF2 for casual gameplay or CS:GO for a competitive, skill-based game. Orion Prelude is an FPS to play with a group of friends.
The player will usually play as a human (excluding game modes which allow the player to be a dinosaur). Playing a classic game against the AI is fun, until you realize the difficulty curve does not scale. The developers did not make the dinosaurs harder with each incoming wave, they only programmed more dinosaurs to spawn. Therefore, in games with more than two people it's simplistic to defeat the mission.
Playing with friends makes the game more fun. Doing 1v1 gun games can occasionally take 2 hours, while a deathmatch is full of paranoia and adrenaline. Every weapon in the game is more or less creaetive to a certain degree, whether it be light swords, arc guns, or giant robot mounts. The game can provide you and your friends many laughs in regards to dinosaur physics.
Should you buy Orion Prelude?

First, let's start with my history. I own all of the Might and Magic RPGs, the first nine or so, I picked them up off of
to make sure my collection was up to date and works on modern equipment. Be sure to check there if you're interested in the older titles. Now, I've played the first two briefly, but couldn't get into them because they were too old school, and mostly text. I've played 3, but haven't beaten it. I've beaten and loved 4 and 5. I've maybe gotten about halfway through 6, loved 7, got about halfway through 8, but couldn't really get into 9 at all.
So when I picked up this game I wasn't expecting much, different publisher, different writer and all that jazz. Most of the other reviews said if you liked 3-5 you would like this one, and that is a pretty fair assessment. This game dropped the real time aspects that were added in 6-9, and went back to pure stepper and turned based combat, very much like 3-5. But matching at least 6-8 (I can't speak for 9) it included the expert/master/grandmaster system of skills, and more widely implemented it.
So where is the real change, the real ground breaking moment? The game is more modernized, it allows level ups to influence stats, so it went one further than 6-8 did with allocating skill points at level up. This is a good and a bad thing. Stats are far more concentrated than in the other games, where multiples of 2 were generally points where stats saw increases, but it also made finding the next potion which raised your stats more of a treat than a requirement.
If I were to make one remark about the game that I didn't like, it is that they disallowed fleeing from combat. Or at least I couldn't figure out how to make it work. Even if the monster didn't chase me, as the case with the crystal spider, once combat started, it didn't seem to end. While in combat mode you cannot enter or exit an area so this means that if you're fighting a monster too powerful, you really have to load up a save. This is compounded by the fact that sometimes the game even prevents you from using certain tiles to your advantage by blocking them from you. It is all too easy to run into a monster too powerful for you to fight for the first half of the game, which means that the first time through, you may die a lot, just because you don't know where the easy areas to level up are.
Overall I found the game extremely fun, because I got back into the nostalgic atmosphere of the game, and once I had a handle on how the game mechanics worked, it seemed like the game could easily be completed with any party. Or, it doesn't really matter which classes you pick, you should be able to make it to the end of the game, as long as you keep in mind a few things:
1. You need a character that has a high strength, perception and magic. Not all necessarily on the same character, but it helps with opening secret doors, one of which early on actually blocks your way forward (a might door).
2. For your first time through, you need a free mage so you can find the hidden doors. When you're more experienced with the game, you can get by with scrolls or hirelings. Well I said need, but when you need to spot a secret door to get to the next spot, you'll have a hireling that can help you provided by the game. Finding secret doors though does get you more loot quicker, which means more money.
3. There is an overabundance of money in the game, so if worst comes to worst you can simply buy enough potions to keep your party going.
4. The first two acts are the hardest, because after those are completed you may be strong enough to work on promotion quests, and have access to far more master level skills.
5. While I said you don't necessarily need a free mage, it is by far my favorite class for expert level dark magic, not only do you get whispering shadows (which allows you to see hidden doors) but you get purge. Purge is a dispel spell that always succeeds, and works on a surprising amount of buffs.

Summary: The first official expansion to HOMM5, Hammers of Fate shares much of the same qualities as its' main counterpart, with slight improvements over the gameplay mechanics. With the notable addition of being able to queue large amounts of troops and caravan them to a specific castle with just the click of a button, it has streamlined and eased the process in amassing an army. I've personally experienced fewer bugs than with the main campaign, although the difficulty spike in the game is at times frustrating. The music and sound effects are still the same from the original, graphics for the most part unchanged, however the storytelling and cutscenes are vastly improved and do a better job of portratying the story. The bottom line is that if you were a fan of the original campaign and were just begging for more will find this right up your alley, otherwise it's the same formula and much of the same gripes from before. 3.5/5
In Hammers of Fate, there are three campaigns of five missions available to take on. There is a human-based campaign with Freyda and Duncan, then the fortress campaign with Wulfstan the dwarf, and then the shadow-elf Ylaya. Of the three campaigns, the fortress campaign presents some new gameplay mechanics that adds some flavor to the battle sequences. Namely each unit can be "enahanced" with a rune by expending resources throughout a battle. This can create a dilemma where you resources need to be set aside before a battle to maximize the use of runes and decrease on your overall losses. As far as the fortress town goes, they're also very sturdy and are resistant to siege machines which allows for a more defensive approach for the faction.
The missions themselves have some new variety, namely The Rebels and The Ambush are very event-driven and offer a new approach to the typical HOMM mission. Characters interact much better in cutscenes as they now utilize new models that actually articulate actions and expressions in a meaningful way instead of just going through random cast animations like in the original campaign. The story is a continuation of the original plot from HOMM5, picking up a few years after Queen Isabel returns back to the Griffin Empire. I did find the story easier to follow than from HOMM5, and maybe it's because I already know some backstory of reoccurring characters from the original campaign.
The music and sound effects are unchanged, it really could have needed a few new tracks to add some variety to the soundtrack but the effect of this is pretty minimal.
The difficulty in Hammers of Fate is much higher than in the original campaign, as I'm assuming that the developers anticipated it being played by veterans of HOMM5. Just playing through the first level, you'll find that it's much less forgiving and splitting your troops in a way to efficiently take on multiple objectives is imperative. The last mission in the game, The Decoupling is also highly frustrating as certain spells are necessary to complete certain objectives. Notably, there is a town to the east that needs to be taken to increase your recruitment pool but the gate to the town is guarded by 10,000 Enforcers, which is suicidal to take on with a conventional force but doable if you have Level 4 spells like an Empowered Meteor Storm or Armageddon. If you did not have the foresight to skill your hero to be able to gain these skills, you will have a tough time and in all likelihood will have to restart the campaign. If you want a challenge, if you found HOMM5 to be a cakewalk, you'll probably be content with Hammers of Fate.
In conclusion, if you liked HOMM5, buy Hammers of Fate. If you didn't like HOMM5, then don't. It's the same experience, just a few upgrades, but certainly nothing compelling enough that will change your playing experience. 3.5/5

After passing 60 games I figured it's about time I write some reviews about them as well, so here we go.
A few days back I bought this game as it seemed quite interesting based on the trailer and pictures. Truth be told it still is. I love getting together a nice fleet, build a bunch of ARC 170 fighters from Star Wars (I found it on Steam Workshop) and I simply love massive fights with them!
However this is also pretty much all I like about this game...
When I started I had no idea about designing ships and I just built the ones made by default and found myself having a quite weak fleet being massacrated over and over again. Not until I finally started to design my own ships and focus more upon economical and military research (and a lot on reducing size of everything, creating more space in the ships and get the logistics up) did I get any progress at all. I mean I seriously spent about 20 hours stuck in the first mission trying to figure out how I would counter all these continuous attacks coming from all sides! Don't get me wrong though, I got addicted to this challenge, but I feel that the default ships made by the AI should have more balanced in defenses (and not only go for either shield or armor).
After I finally won the first mission after 28 hours (I've never spent more than maybe 2-3 hours on the same mission in a game before <_<) I started playing the 2nd mission. This one came down as a real bummer because first of all I couldn't use the ships and planets from my past mission, secondly my designs were all gone and thirdly a large part of the research I had done was reset! This made the game feel unnatural and I felt I had been sent to a paralell universe or was playing a new faction or something. In my opinion a game should always continue where one left off and not ignore the players work and achievements. It just makes all the work and effort seem wasted...
Now despite this I would say that it is somewhat fun, but I think I will stop playing the campaign since I can't stand all my work being reset every time I make some progress in the story...
I overall I would say this game gets a 5,5/10. I don't want to give it a 6 as I am quite divided about recommending it, but at the same time I feel it barely passes the requirements for being recommended, mainly due to the challenge that took me 28 hours to solve.

It feels like someone invented the time machine, transported id Software team from 1992 to present day, gave them modern technology, and then they made this game.
All elements are there, like back in the day. It counts your score, died enemies don't disappear, there's a lives system, but this time a meaningful one - it allows you to respawn without losing progress unlike useless thing inferior to quickload we had before. And I even became interested in this game after playing shareware Episode 1!
AI is challenging. Enemies are able to predict where you're moving and shoot there, giving sense of accomplishment when you manage to overcome a hard battle.
The game is powered by DarkPlaces engine which is based on id technology, and it shows. Level editor gives you a set of primitives you can cut, shape and bend plus set of texture atlases instead of several pre-made models like engines do today. Thanks to it, levels are as interesting and imaginative as in other idTech-powered masterpieces such as Quake3, Quake4, Doom3, Prey.
And a feel of playing something of id Software quality wouldn't be there without modding tools, which are well designed. There's a NetRadiant editor to make new locations, and SandStorm editor to make missions. SandStorm is a wonderful idea: it allows you to place enemies, objects, triggers etc. in a separate file and test your mission instantly without waiting for a lengthy lightmap compilation. This approach also opens the door towards having multiple missions taking place on the same map to fully utilize its potential.
Excellent usage of the engine and classic design which make it feel like playing an old-school id Software release are an amazing accomplishment for a small indie team. If you're looking for a game that can make you relive the feelings from the 90s, you've just found it.

after playing several other rpg-style games from the M&M, the dark eye, D&D, gothic and alike series i was looking forward to play another nice game. After a quite nice start ( just a bit annoying expert/master/grandmaster-skillsystem ) the waiting on loads more and more angered me (takes 20s-1min per load).
later on you will find out that it really sucks to come to an area which might be relevant for quests without picking those quests before. The easiest Paradox grand strategy to learn and get into.
It gets you hooked with its sleak user interface, its extensive species customisation, its decent tutorial which will prod you in the right direction without holding your hand, its gorgeous sound design and soundtrack, its deep Empire-management, its fun and interesting 'quests' and stories as you explore the galaxy.
The game itself is a unique blend between classic Paradox Grand Strategy (Europa Universalis IV, Crusader Kings II, Hearts of Iron III, Victoria II) and 4X style games (Sid Meier's Civilization series, etc.), and this is partly what makes it an easier Paradox game to grasp the basics of.
Players striving to achieve greatness and min-max their Empire's may still wish to defer to the Wiki to learn how some mechanics work, as the tutorial doesn't go into much depth on a lot of these. However, this isn't strictly speaking required and you can still have heaps of fun going in blind (just be sure to read tooltips, people). Whether you want to enslave the sub-species of the galaxy, or establish a mighty federation of intra-galactic friends - there's something here for almost everyone with respect to playstyle within a 4X/Grand Strategy game.
Boldly go forth where no [insert xenotype name here] has gone before.
P.S: The game may have some bugs (I haven't ran into anything game-breaking yet), but in my experience Paradox is pretty good at fixing major bugs... usually. Also players coming from EU4 and CK2 may feel like the game is a little barebones compared to those game. I would remind these players that EU4 and CK2 as they are now are vastly improved in contrast to how they were on release (i.e. a lot of the features you see now in EU4/CK2 were DLC additions). Rest assured Stellaris will receive a lot of love with respect to DLC and added features in the future, I'm sure of it. Nevertheless, there is certainly more than enough fun game here to warrant the asking price.

That dragon, cancer是个有些特别的独立游戏。与其说是游戏，不如说它更像一种体验。不长的篇幅讲述了癌症儿童Joel短暂而充满爱的一生。
Joel从小就患上了疾病。因为疾病，他迟迟没能学会说话。Joel的父母抱着他四处求医问药，最终得知了他被确诊为癌症的噩耗。他们挣扎过，努力过，希冀过。Joel像是睡前故事中的那个骑士，而癌症则是一条恶龙。无论Joel再怎么努力想要击败癌症，无论他获得了多少帮助，结局仿佛从开始的时候就已注定。Joel还是走了。幻境中，他说他想养只小狗。他如愿了。他说小狗和他一样，最爱吃松饼上的糖浆。
本作大量运用了意象与意识流叙述手法。辅以独特的美术风格，本作营造出一种亦真亦幻的氛围。漫步于这些场景，就好像一帧帧穿梭于Joel的人生片段中。所有的人物都没有表情建模。但是优秀的配音和剧本演出使该有的感动没有损失分毫，而恰到好处的留白更是使剧本更加耐人寻味。在表现Joel被病痛折磨时，观众始终看不到Joel的身影，但却能通过他撕心裂肺的哭喊和父亲的焦灼感受到他的痛苦和不安。这种共情使我不忍心再玩一遍这个游戏。

Dust is a surprisingly good 2d hack and slash. The graphics are a little cute and cartoony, and run smoothly. One of the treats is the special effects -- It's colorful and exciting the first time you unleash Fidgets magic attack, and it gets more impressive as you play the game.
The story is decent, it keeps you entertained and has a couple of twists that are slightly unexpected. A few points are obvious, and there are some decidedly uninspired character motives, but otherwise it's an interesting romp through a fantasy world where you know nothing about the history.
Gameplay is where Dust shines. It's a fast paced hack and slash with a hint of magic. Reflex based combat and timing  based jumping puzzles abound. There are also many secrets and collectables hidden in the game, some with mechanical bonuses and some just for fun! The responsive controls and reasonable hit boxes mean minimal frustration with the game, only with yourself. A number of enemies require special tactics to destroy, while others are just a matter of a well timed attack or a beatdown. The real problem is when you're cornered by several types of enemies and no one strategy is likely to be successful. Hopefully you're fast enough to survive.
You can speck to wreck with your sword or become a whirlwind of magical destruction, the choice is up to you! The game forces you to balance your character as you level, only allowing you to be two ranks better at any given skill than any other skill. At first this is frustrating, but as you get up in levels the next tier of a skill is phenomenally more potent then the last and those skills you've focused on really shine.
The equipment allows you to specialize much more, providing bonuses such as X8 magic damage or massive health regen if you stack it correctly. equipment is where your real power comes from. Speaking of equipment, the crafting is just so-so. It's nice that it provides recipes and allows you to purchase rare ingredients as long as you've found one, so you won't spend too much time grinding. But most mid level items will be dropped long before you can craft them, and eventually you just end up crafting the top tier items so you can get copies of them. It's a decent system that could have been more useful.
My only real complaint about this game is the voice acting. I'm sorry whoever did it, but the voices are simply annoying. The developer really should have taken the time to get an honest recording studio or a professional sound technician to work over the audio files. While the rest of the sound is pleasant, I just can't stand the voices. They make me cringe. The well designed characters only make the voices even worse. Each voice has a serious case of try hard, and makes the characters feel like little more than charicatures of what they are supposed to be.
Ultimately, if you like 2d hack and slash RPGs, it's quite fun for what it is. Dust is no grand epic, but it's a fun way to waste an afternoon. Just turn the sound down.

For those who've never heard of it, it's essentially the story of the developer's son's battle with, and eventual loss to, cancer. Well, as the kid in question was only five at the time it's actually about the adults in the family and their experience. And given all that, it's a bit of a shame to call it out for being largely a load of balls. Mechanically it's primitive and odd to control even though you're mostly just pointing a character in a direction to advance the story. There are a couple of occasions when it tries to be more of a 'game' (a bizarre kart racing section and a puzzle involving candles that just had me clicking♥♥♥♥♥♥randomly until I could proceed) and those parts are arguably even worse as they're not only boring but just seem completely at odds with the subject matter. There are a couple of sections that genuinely take advantage of an interactive medium (e.g. a part where you can move between occupying either of the parents or the attendant medical staff while things are being discussed and 'hear' their internal monologue as bad news is being delivered and processed) and they show a glimmer of a good idea, but aside from that it's really just finding the next thing to click on to move your character through some landscapes. Coming off the back of something like Edith Finch which tells various stories of loss and heartbreak in incredible and moving ways this can't really seem like anything other than boring twaddle. Which is ironic given the very real basis here vs Edith Finch's invented story. The thing is, 'gameplay' aside, I was genuinely quite affected by the family's story in the beginning due largely to the voice work (the developer and his wife playing themselves as far as I know) doing a good job if putting you in the middle of the situation. However, not only is the wife's voice is incredibly grating after a while but about a third of the way through every conversation and line of dialogue becomes about their faith. Obviously I can understand the entire situation throwing up such questions and thoughts for a Christian couple but literally every scene after a certain point is a lengthy pondering on God and, frankly, I couldn't give a ♥♥♥♥ so I was left cold by it all.

The Next Big Thing is a solid adventure game with incredible visuals, a well-crafted world, and an interesting, yet very short story. The puzzles are easy and fun to do, yet there is one that will cause rage-quits in large numbers. Though its shortness hardly justifies the price, it’s a real deal even on a 50% sale: you get a fun and entertaining adventure for your money that won’t disappoint you later.
The Next Big Thing is one of Pendulo’s many point-and-click adventure titles with the studio’s trademark cell-shaded 3D characters and carefully constructed, astonishing hand-drawn backgrounds.
The game is set in another world, where the classic Hollywood movie monsters from the 1940s and 50s are real people who live among the humans. The story follows the adventure of two journalists– a cynical sports-maniac and an enthusiastic and downright loony investigative reporter– fresh on the trail of a new scoop that will eventually leave to kidnapping, brainwashing and of course lots of puzzle solving.
The style and the story is more cartoonish than horror-like, and this shown in the characters and the puzzles themselves. The latter ones aren’t especially devilish, but there is one that gave many people nightmares and caused many rage-quits and unfinished games. It’s a purely time- and rhythm-based puzzle which is hard to figure out, even harder to properly execute.
Apart from that the difficulty level may only come from pixel-hunting if you chose not to use the item highlight feature, as some of the objects you need to interact with can easily be missed.
Although the story is quite good and well-paced, and even the dialogues are well-crafted, the fact that the game is actually a sequel to Pendulo’s 1997 title Hollywood Monsters, and sadly for some reason the developers thought that anyone who plays this game will know the prequel: we learn next to nothing about the world and how it works in the first half of the game, and only small bits are revealed later in optional side-conversations and item descriptions.
Also, the game is short, even for an indie adventure game: shorter than their previous three title on Steam (the Runaway trilogy), clocking in about 4-6 hours depending on how much you may get stuck (especially on the aforementioned tango puzzle). The story itself compensates for it, but still, for costing as much as other Pendulo games, the play time feels awfully short in this one.

When I first saw this new sci-fi 4x game, I was excited for it. However, after playing for 46 hours, I realized that I was quite finished with it.
By far, the biggest problem is that you cannot in any way play out the battles. The only battles offered are cinematic views of your ships floating around, auto-fighting the enemy. This disappointing feature is compounded by the fact that a huge draw for this game – almost unlimited ship customization – is rendered pointless by your inability to actually use the ships you’ve created.
Some other problems are that the affinities unlock far too slowly to have much impact, the tech trees are all almost exactly the same despite promises of radical differences, and there is no feeling of depth, theme or personality to the game.
A much, much better alternative is Endless Space, although this game too suffers from a lack of playable battles. In Endless Space, at least, you can issue fleet-wide orders and change them during the auto-fought battle, which might have a significant effect on the result of the combat.

Review to Rant:
As a JRPG fan, I will praise its story as being well done and interesting as well as containing one of the most interesting villains in gaming *cough* sephiroth *cough*. The characters are diverse, amusing, and go well together (I will also admit to being a bit of a fan of Tifa's). However, The internet made me completely ignore the existence of a certain character, whose death was so tragic that I couldn't care less about them even then. But that's just me. The combat is well done, but I found it too easy. I felt no challenge while playing except from the "weapons". Even during the final boss battle, It's very easy and comes off as intense, but isn't. It is just time consuming, with an attack animation that gives you enough time to make a sandwich and be back in time to see the explosion. As far as side quests go, several are not really worth doing other than for killing time (DON'T BUY THE MANSION!!! YOU WILL NOT PLAY THE GAME LONG ENOUGH TO MAKE IT WORTH THE INVESTMENT!!!), but that does not mean they are bad (EXCEPT THE MANSION!!!). They tend to be fun and get you neat stuff.
That said, there are other things to mention as well. If you have played a great many JRPGS, FF games, or you happen to be an anime otaku, like me, then a massive part of the experience disappears as you start picking apart the faults. This game adheres to elements that is seen in a very large quantity of anime series and/or JRPGS. Once again, if you are an anime otaku, then this story will not surprise you and the characters will likely not particularly amuse you. Also the massively overhyped response this got from fans tends to blind people, including myself, into thinking this will be one of the greatest experiences in gaming. But it's 2015. There are new standards to be held for gaming, and a game from nearly twenty years ago, despite aging well, is not the mind blowing bonanza that people who played it in 90's claim it to be.
Allow me to be clear, This is NOT the best Final Fantasy, but I will not lie to you and say it is bad or even mediocre. Don't misunderstand. This game is great (Granted, being an Otaku took away from my experience), but it is also holding back a company that could be doing more than trying to live up to a game from so long ago. I feel that every JRPG fan should play this at some point, as this was a turning point in the genre's history, but also play some of the other entries in the series.
I played this game to see what everyone wanted back rather than a new entry to the main series, and found myself disappointed with the fact that this was the bar people held the franchise to, especially since the fans are stacked on each others shoulders, holding the bar so impossibly far out of reach that it is no longer possible to make someting that they will be satisfied with and WILL always be disappointed in the next game. The worst part is they demand a remake, when the company has already set their terms for a remake to be done, and the fans have no faith in the company. Frankly, it's disgusting to see fans of a series be like this and I sincerely hope they never get a remake of this game. Their only hope of getting one is in actually putting some damn faith in FFXV and hoping it is well recieved. If they can't even put faith in it, then they don't deserve a remake ever being made.
As a side note, people should stop ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the square enix login. If you are so lazy that making a login is an ordeal, then I have no idea why you are gaming on pc.

Well, I'll start with the good points. And probably the best aspect of the game are the graphics, the flame effects in particular. You'd expect that, right? In a game that's all about setting various things on fire that's probably a must. And the game delivers on that, the flame effects are very well done and looking quite realistic. Looking into the fire as it consumes each and every object placed in the fireplace has that mesmerising quality that real fire has. Or at the very least it's quite close.
Unfortunately that's the only good point for me. After all, it's a game all about setting things on fire. It's fun the first few times, it's fun as you discover new items to burn, but beyond that I found little entertainment in it. There is only one fireplace that doesn't really change through the game, and all the items take time to arrive, completing the simulated mail-order feeling. Sure, there's special stamps that can be used to instantly get the item, but these dwindle fast past the initial boom and getting them later requires completing combos (burn specific sets of items at the same time to get 1-3 stamps) -- a sort of an in-game achievement.
Contrary to what it seems the game does have a story to it, not a very robust and deep one, but I guess it's enough to serve as background for the pyromaniac frenzy that is the main point of the game. The story advances as more items are burnt and new ones are unlocked and finally reaches an end, offering a short epilogue in the form of a mini point and click adventure.
I can't say I disliked the game, I did enjoy it for a short time, even made myself finish the story. It just doesn't have enough to make me come back. But I suppose it might be a decent choice for a slow chillout evening when anything more than mindless clicking is just too tiring.

Little Inferno is an odd quasi-puzzle game with a similar style and consumerism narrative as World of Goo, 2D Boy's previous acclaimed release. The player is simply tasked with ordering items from a catalog and then burning them in the Little Inferno fireplace. The challenge comes from unlocking more advanced item catalogs, which require a certain amount of burn combinations to access, but you're really here to just be a virtual pyromaniac. Item design is excellent -- I love the screams from the school bus -- and the game's gradually unfolding story (told via snailmail letters) keeps you enthralled to the end. Little Inferno lacks the replayability of World of Goo, but it's an excellent experience on its own.

First off, the bad stuff. This game has a few frustrating elements put there by the developers. Poison will kill you, and quite quickly, and you get no warning that you need to get earth magic's cure poison or buy antidotes before you get poisoned the first time, although hopefully you will have picked up enough antifotes to be okay. Secondly, while both the team and monsters are locked in space when they enter a melee fight (which is fine), there is one boss that doesn't, and who is going to push the team to their death if the I guess random number generator wills it. Lastly, a couple of things are very difficult to find, and there's no abundance of hints to where to go and the voice acting isn't that great.
Apart from that, Might and magic X is a truly brilliant game. You start off choosing a team of four characters whose skills will complement each other on their Quest through the Agyn peninsula. From there on, everything is grid and turn based. You will move square by square through an astonishing world with a lot, really a lot, of cool secrets you may have to go out of your way to find. The game is really well made for people who like to explore places, as the world is big, and the only thing keeping you from going places are monsters. You will need to save often, as you may be ambushed by too difficult monsters in the early game, but even really difficult monsters can often be overcome if you employ the right strategy. Mages are given powerful but costly control options, and there are lots of different strategies to employ to get past the bad guys. Being turn based, you can even change your equipment during your turn in combat, yielding very interesting options if you stack up on cool equipment. This results in a lot of digressions from the tasks at hand; the party will find a new nook or cave they want to explore while on their way to the next location. Except for interdependent quests, you can mosttimes do any quest you have in any order you'd like.
While difficult monsters can often be overcome with the right tactics (or a couple of levels, there are always other things you want to do in the mean time), easy monsters can often kill the party if you don't pay attention. The simplest monsters give 5 xp, the toughest give you around 50, so you will never feel that you are too strong for an area, you simply spend less turns during each combat.
One of the aspects that really got me in this game was all the puzzles. All the way through the land they have put mysterious crypts, where you need to solve a puzzle to get to the treasure, with no dangerous monsters to distract you. There are a lot of chests which requires you to answer a riddle correctly, and they are very fun to ponder about, especially if you're playing together with someone. I already said there are a lot of treasure in this game, and it is sometimes hidden due to the movement in the game. If there's a chest to your side, you won't notice it unless you face that direction, and as you can't face every wall all the time, you need to keep looking for small boxes or camuflaged chests you need to face.
For the level system, I think it's good. every level gives you 4 attribute points, to be spread over strength, perception, destiny, magic, etc. with very clear effects. This makes sure your character gets better at what he/she does at every level. The character also gets 3 skill points, which can be spent on increasing skills. All the skills a character chan choose between, he/she can master to different degrees, expert (at 7 skill points), master (at 15) and grand master (at 25). At these scores, advancement needs to be bought from a skill specific trainer, which will give an extra boost and let the character advance further. There are 12 classes to choose between, and each has a different set of skill mastery possibilities, but each class needs to get promoted through a special quest to access gm training (range -> warden can gm bow, barbarian -> warmonger can gm two handed), so the game really makes you work to become better. I already mentioned that mages have interesting battle control options; the fighters also do. There's a skill called warfare, which grants spell like abilities (two more at each new level of mastery) like reducing armor or taunting enemies to attack that particular character. This makes any kind of team viable, and gives the game a lot of replay value. When I say any kind of team is viable, I mean it, character creation is not something you need to ponder a lot on, there will be ways to destroy every enemy with what you want to play. Also, at gm level, you will be insanely good, and your party will feel like living gods. This feels great.

The easiest Paradox grand strategy to learn and get into.
It gets you hooked with its sleak user interface, its extensive species customisation, its decent tutorial which will prod you in the right direction without holding your hand, its gorgeous sound design and soundtrack, its deep Empire-management, its fun and interesting 'quests' and stories as you explore the galaxy.
The game itself is a unique blend between classic Paradox Grand Strategy (Europa Universalis IV, Crusader Kings II, Hearts of Iron III, Victoria II) and 4X style games (Sid Meier's Civilization series, etc.), and this is partly what makes it an easier Paradox game to grasp the basics of.
Players striving to achieve greatness and min-max their Empire's may still wish to defer to the Wiki to learn how some mechanics work, as the tutorial doesn't go into much depth on a lot of these. However, this isn't strictly speaking required and you can still have heaps of fun going in blind (just be sure to read tooltips, people). Whether you want to enslave the sub-species of the galaxy, or establish a mighty federation of intra-galactic friends - there's something here for almost everyone with respect to playstyle within a 4X/Grand Strategy game.
Boldly go forth where no [insert xenotype name here] has gone before.
P.S: The game may have some bugs (I haven't ran into anything game-breaking yet), but in my experience Paradox is pretty good at fixing major bugs... usually. Also players coming from EU4 and CK2 may feel like the game is a little barebones compared to those game. I would remind these players that EU4 and CK2 as they are now are vastly improved in contrast to how they were on release (i.e. a lot of the features you see now in EU4/CK2 were DLC additions). Rest assured Stellaris will receive a lot of love with respect to DLC and added features in the future, I'm sure of it. Nevertheless, there is certainly more than enough fun game here to warrant the asking price.

I played this game a while ago and I decided to nominate this game in the Steam Game Awards in the write in category for "Games as an Experience." I nominated That Dragon Cancer for that category for several reasons. The first being because I think this game deserves more recognition, for the family involved, for those who have had an experince similar to this one, and even for those people who unfortunately may have an experience like this in the future. This game is impossible to truly describe with words, that's why I tell people just to play it, to experience it. It's not very often that a game comes along and causes so many of us to consider it not as a game, but as an emotional or existential experience beyond what we ever perceived games could be. To move us in ways none of us of expected. This I believe is important for not only gamers, but for games as a whole. That leads me to my next reason I nominated this game, for gaming as art. Game developers, people with interesting or engaging stories, or anyone that wants to express themselves in one way or another can look to this game as an inspiration. This game proves that video games can be the next form of art, and I mean real art. Games can be a way for people to express themselves just like conventional forms of art. They can be used to express beauty, emotion, passion, or even the entirety of the human condition like this piece of art does. Truly one of the most profound pieces of art I have ever experienced.
I just wanted to close this review out by thanking the Green family for allowing so many of us into your lives and helping so many cope with the losses in our lives. Also, I finally wanted to say sorry. I know it doesn't mean much, but I truly mean it. I hope that this game helped you as much as it has helped me.

The story of this game is around Dust, an anthropomorph that wakes up in the middle of a forest with no memories. You travel the lands trying to figure who you are while also helping out the people you meet along the way. I think the game focuses the most on its art and its story and although I don't have a harsh opinion on its game mechanic, I feel like there could've been more than just reworked art to same monsters-types.
Combat & Control
The combat system is based on a series of combos that is very easy to learn and different types of monsters & abilities are introduced along the way. The combos are easy to learn and pretty repetitive, but I didn't mind. Abilities were introduced throughout the game and are essential in being able to go back to previous maps to get previously obtainable treasure while also necessary to move ahead. I used an XBOX controller so it was a pretty easy ride for me and I liked playing this game when I just wanted to sit back in my chair and bash some buttons. The jumping was a bit annoying at first because I think it didn't have a "push down longer to jump for longer" mechanic so every jump was the same distance, even if you would give just a slight love tap to the jump button. Overall, I didn't mind the repetition of the combos and the new abilities   kept the combat and exploring the world a bit more interesting.
As for the monsters, there were a lot of variety but there was definitely some "reskinning" going on as you enter different zone. For example, there was a type of monster that would explode if you got to close and in another "snowy" zone, it was just redrawn blue with snow on it. I thought it was cute, but it did leave something more to be desired in fighting new types of foes. Still, I'd like to emphasize that there was still a lot of variety and there's no harm in using the same monster-type at a higher skill area.
World Exploration
Although there might have been some reskinning, I think I was able to look past it because each zone usually brought a new way to explore the world or puzzles that you had to solve to get the "treasures" scattered across the land. Like I mentioned earlier, you get introduced to new abilities and these abilities help you reach new places. For example, in the beginning of the game, Fidget points out a wall of vines that you have not yet learned how to climb and suggests we come back later. There are definitely some treasures that you would not be able to reach without certain learned abilities and would have to come back later to get them. And if you don't want to get them, that's fine too. The treasures are not vital in the end-game and are only for bragging rights and exploring the world. You also have to use these abilities and navigate around the map to get to the next zone so each area isn't just a mindless journey of button mashing.
Art (Voice Acting, Graphics, Music)
I've heard some people get really annoyed with the voice acting, and I can see where they're coming from. Fidget, your Navi-like companion, has a pretty squeaky voice and can be a little obnoxious to some and I found myself a little annoyed at some of the characters myself... Nonetheless, I think there was a lot of effort put into narrating pretty much every single line that is ever spoken in this game and I took the time to listen and read along. The backgrounds were pretty fantastic as well and there was just so much love put into every zone! I really loved the music as well and most them are very memorable! The only con is that there is just so much going on with aesthetic sometimes and there were some glitches with areas that were in complete darkness.
Story
Hey I admit it - I cried a bit and not just once! I can't really talk too much about the story without spoiling so I'll say this: they do have some cliche stories. Some "ideas" and plots didn't really resonate well with me either (e.g. Dust reacted differently than I expected to certain events, some plots didn't make too much sense with me, there were some missing plotholes...) Regardless, I thought it was quaint. Someone more critical than me might think the story was pretty sloppy... but who knows!
Basically, this game isn't perfect but that didn't stop me from finishing it and obsessing over the hidden treasures... oh the hours I wasted! I suppose I'd recommend this game, but it may not be some people's cup of tea.

That Dragon, Cancer is a narrative experience based on the cancer story of Joel Green, the son of the Developer of the game. I'm not going to go deeper into the story than this, but this is the basic premise. The game revolves about you taking control of one of the parents, with all the experiences they've had and what they had to deal with. The game is very confronting and as someone who has lost someone close to me to cancer, the progression of the game feels very familiar to me. It's very real and not shy to hold back on some depressing and crushing moments, which just need to be experienced. I can't recommend this game enough. A lot of forms of media (games and films) try to replicate what cancer does to loved ones, and this is the closest thing to that feeling I've seen so far. It's short yeah, but worth the money. Don't watch it, don't play it, just experience it. And then prepare to cry, a lot. Absolutely beautiful.

So we follow Dust, an amnesiac (which has been done to death) to discover himself and who he really is.  Odd title name aside, I really enjoyed this game as a guilty pleasure.
Ultimately, the story I didn't see coming, but the story tropes and cliches are a present throughout the game.  As far as learning indepth of all the other characters, it's kinda lacking outside of Dust himself and a few key characters unfortunately, and even the world and Villain's motives seem a bit cut and dry.  However the characters themselves are actually characterized amazingly well with surpsingly excellent voice acting.  I laughed quite a bit at some of the dialogue as well which is clever at times.
I've gotta admit, something feels just...great about cutting through a horde of enemies.  Controlling Dust, and the movement feels fun and fluid, with the game even providing certain button imputs to perform combos and special skills.  With that said, the enemies themselves could have been made a bit better.  The typical enemy wads do get a bit more challenging as you progress, and there are some creative attempts littered throughout but I felt they could've pushed it a bit more, especially with the bosses.  Oh god the bosses are terrible, and in a sense that I killed the first one without it getting a single attack out.  The later ones are no better, and your capabilities outclass the things you fight so bad that even on Tough difficulty settings you shouldn't have too much of a problem.  In fact by the end you are so overpowered the only challenge that you might have left is that god forsaken 1000 hit combo achievement/quest.  The platforming and puzzle solving is about average, but the hazards are appropriate even in later stages I felt.
Controls are surprisingly tight, if a bit too twitchy at times.  The game is kind enough to allow keyboard, keyboard and mouse and gamepad features, and all work splendid in my opinion.  The keyboard controls can be a bit finicky when having to climb vines and traverse narrow platforms, but otherwise it is unlikely you will get crapped on because a button imput didn't respond accordingly.
Sadly, due to all the bone crunching in the game you will be doing, it is unlikely you will hear the music too well.  When I did hear it though I thought it was passable, wasn't too legendary but wasn't atrocious either.  I love the Cave melody though, and I think the end boss fight but I hardly remember since it was too busy dying for me to be able to listen too it.
So, the animation and environments are all very lush and colorful...but...
The character designs, god help me they looked like Neopet rejects and I cannot fathom why they made the main hero (who I thought was a girl at first based on the trailer) wear turquoise and pink with some pseudo-Japanese Imperial outfit thing.  Animated cutscenes are pretty rough as well and feel like they were done in Flash by one person.  Thankfully the animations for character movement and actions are for the most part good though some extra frames would've been nice in some key areas such as when you begin to run or stopping as there is no median, it's either stop or go.
Ultimately this game is a fun romp if you just wanna kill loads of things.  The Easter Eggs in the game are also pretty ridiculous and cool, such as finding Meat Boy in the beginning stage (there's even more surprises besides him).  Because of the lack of complexity, if you want a challenging game I do not recommend this, as even on the hardest difficulty settings it is still rather easy compared to other things on the market.  Also, I don't know if mispelled Tale or...

All in all a technically very solid adventure, which, due to flaws with regards to the content, unfortunately did not become the (next) big thing. Recommended for lovers of other games made by Péndulo Studios. Not recommended for all others. You might take a look at the numerous other adventures which have been relased since then. There is a demo version as well, so if you are interested, check that out first.
Péndulo Studios' “The Next BIG Thing” presents itself as a classic point-and-click adventure. Connoisseurs of the “Runaway”-games will feel right at home. As before, the graphics are well done and nicely drawn. Some animations feel a bit chopped and not very smooth. Hints and hotspots are optional and can be turned off.
The developers kept their sense of special humour. The frame narrative takes place in a world in which monsters, robots with personality, and humans are living side by side. The introductory sequence shows the two playable characters (Liz and Dan), who are reporters for a newspaper called “The Quill”. Their boss sends them to the monster-movie producer FitzRandolph, who is a monster himself.
After getting there, Dan is hardly thrilled by this assignment, as he prefers sports over movies. Liz on the other hand wants to prove herself as a professional reporter and takes the assignment very seriously. The first dialogues between the two are overly clear about the two not liking each other at all. Even their personality could not be farther apart. Here Dan, the eloquent man about town, who could care less about authority. There Liz, being particular about everything and suffering from various psychological traumata as well as personality disorders.
This marks the probably weakest point of the game, which continues until its end. Some of the characters are bizarre to the extend that an identification with them seems almost impossible. The thoughts and dialogues are rather causing raised eyebrows and disagreement than a smirk. Whereas Daedalic's “Edna Breaks Out” integrated and established the (at least alleged) psychiatric disorder well as an element of the game, it feels overdone and out of place here. Péndulo should have taken a more careful and cautious approach.
During the course of the game, the player takes turns controlling Liz and Dan. The sections are pre-set and completely closed; there is no team-approach. The two meet the same characters. Those react, depending on whom they are talking to, differently; though comments or thoughts about the other main character remain sparse. It feels as if there were two parallel storylines. At least the voice actors are professionals and did a good job on sounding convincingly. At least in the English version of the game, characters often start or end sentences with "ayo", which becomes annoying rather quickly.
The story itself can be summed up rather quickly:
At least the ending holds a heart-warming surprise.

WARNING: THIS REVIEW CONTAINS MAJOR SPOILERS
I've played adventure games since the days when they were all text-based and required players to type in commands like "GO NORTH" or "LOOK HOUSE".  In all, I have probably played dozens (if not hundreds) of both text and graphical adventures over the years.
The fun in an adventure game comes primarily from the writing in the underlying story and the challenging nature of the puzzles.  Graphical adventures like this one can increase the fun by adding interesting visuals, good voice acting, and music.  The Next BIG Thing hits some of these notes, and either mangles or misses the rest.
The story in this game could easily be interpreted as racist.  Monsters are allowed to have jobs, earn money, buy homes, run businesses, have human friends, etc., but aren't allowed to hold public office.  The antagonist is trying to change that (albeit in a dishonest manner), and get his people equal rights.  Your characters stop his plan, and seem to feel no remorse for what they're doing.  The story could have been made more palatable with a simple line out of one of the good guys' mouths like "You know, we could have prevented all this if we had just given the monsters equal rights.  He had the right idea, but went about it the wrong way."  (There is even a reference at one point, admittedly within a dream-like sequence, where characters admit to enjoying staged fights between animals and get excited about receiving tickets to a fight.  Does cruelty to animals offend you?  It does me.)
Many of the puzzles in the game make sense and are somewhere in the easy to challenging-but-fun level.  Some of them, however, are very convoluted and make absolutely no sense whatsoever.  If it hadn't been for online walkthroughs, I doubt I would have ever come up with the precise combination of objects to solve those puzzles.  I don't think I'd have ever gotten there even by randomly combining objects in the game.
One puzzle in particular was very irritating.  There was very little intellectual challenge to it... I'm referring to the Tango puzzle.  You're required to click four flowers, each representing a musical instrument.  When you click one, it starts playing that instrument's part of the tango.  You click the next at the right moment in the first instrument's melody.  If you miss this by more than a fraction of a second, the puzzle resets.  Despite consulting the walkthroughs, only through dumb luck was I able to get them all four clicked at the exact right times.  I hate puzzles like that, and get no enjoyment from them.  (I find the mazes they used to slap into old adventure games irritating for the same reason.)
Some scenes in the game take your "suspension of disbelief" and stomp all over it.  At one point you're told a safe is too heavy to be carried.  Then the solution becomes hauling it around on a folding cart designed to carry cakes, cookies, and pies.  It's not too heavy for that?  The delicate contents of that safe can be tossed out of a flying zeppelin with a parachute attached and reach the ground safely?  And I can take an elevator to the surface, start a motorcycle, drive it into position, and be waiting when the safe finally hits the ground?  Really?
The dialog in the game has an annoying trait as well.  Characters, for no known reason, start conversations with the word "Ayo" as in "Ayo, Hello, Fred.  How are you today?"  They end conversations with "Aya" as in, "Well, have a good weekend, Ann.  Aya."  This is sort of amusing for the first five minutes of the game.  Do the developers think people really talk this way?
As for the humor, I don't recall a single "laugh out loud" moment.  I think I smiled at a few things.  Maybe my standards are too high.
Ultimately, this isn't a bad game.  It's just... OK.  I'd give it about a 6 out of 10. I've played many adventure games that were more fun (the LucasArts and Scott Adams games come to mind), but I've played quite a few that weren't.  The visuals are excellent.  The voice acting has its moments.  In the end, it's not a game I expect to ever play again.

I've been really looking for a game that allows me to be immersed in a world far away from my own. I've wanted to go into this mystical trance, experiencing something totally foreign to myself.

There is no reason to contemplate why you're doing what you're doing; there is a story to the game as well, but it's not necessarily the primary reason to play it - you'll see what I mean.
This is a game about Zen. This is a game about exploring the depths of a lost ocean. This is a game about feeling a sense of wonder you haven't experienced since you were a child.
In essence, Abzu is much more than just a breath of fresh air into a generation of dull and unoriginal titles, it's something that proves video games don't need to rely on violence, jump scares or utilize rpg mechanics in order to be engaging (in fact, I'd argue that the industry needs expand it's horizon a bit more).

Review to Rant:
As a JRPG fan, I will praise its story as being well done and interesting as well as containing one of the most interesting villains in gaming *cough* sephiroth *cough*. The characters are diverse, amusing, and go well together (I will also admit to being a bit of a fan of Tifa's). However, The internet made me completely ignore the existence of a certain character, whose death was so tragic that I couldn't care less about them even then. But that's just me. The combat is well done, but I found it too easy. I felt no challenge while playing except from the "weapons". Even during the final boss battle, It's very easy and comes off as intense, but isn't. It is just time consuming, with an attack animation that gives you enough time to make a sandwich and be back in time to see the explosion. As far as side quests go, several are not really worth doing other than for killing time (DON'T BUY THE MANSION!!! YOU WILL NOT PLAY THE GAME LONG ENOUGH TO MAKE IT WORTH THE INVESTMENT!!!), but that does not mean they are bad (EXCEPT THE MANSION!!!). They tend to be fun and get you neat stuff.
That said, there are other things to mention as well. If you have played a great many JRPGS, FF games, or you happen to be an anime otaku, like me, then a massive part of the experience disappears as you start picking apart the faults. This game adheres to elements that is seen in a very large quantity of anime series and/or JRPGS. Once again, if you are an anime otaku, then this story will not surprise you and the characters will likely not particularly amuse you. Also the massively overhyped response this got from fans tends to blind people, including myself, into thinking this will be one of the greatest experiences in gaming. But it's 2015. There are new standards to be held for gaming, and a game from nearly twenty years ago, despite aging well, is not the mind blowing bonanza that people who played it in 90's claim it to be.
Allow me to be clear, This is NOT the best Final Fantasy, but I will not lie to you and say it is bad or even mediocre. Don't misunderstand. This game is great (Granted, being an Otaku took away from my experience), but it is also holding back a company that could be doing more than trying to live up to a game from so long ago. I feel that every JRPG fan should play this at some point, as this was a turning point in the genre's history, but also play some of the other entries in the series.

Every once in awhile i like to buy an indie game to sink more hours into than originally expected. I went into "Crypt of the Necrodancer" not expecting much, it looked like a fun game to stab some monsters to while tapping my foot to the beat.
Necrodancer is a rhythm based rogue-like/dungeon crawler sorta setup with permadeath. And it's as fun as it is difficult.
Once I heard the soundtrack, I then got absorbed into the rhythmic gameplay. Goddamn it's top notch. Now for those unfamiliar, the game is played to the beat of the current level's soundtrack and you HAVE to move and fight and even reload your gun, to the beat. Now while you're bouncing around the dungeons beating up monsters you gotta keep your cool and each fight is very important as it could be your last, sorting out your combat techniques is like an artform once perfected, Especially in the higher levels when the screen is basically like an undead nightclub full of 80 things happening at once.
And once you fight your way through each zone, to the final bosses and eventually kick their decomposed butt, the satisfaction mirrors your badassery - It's indescribable.
The game obviously has a light heartedness going for it too, as all the monsters you're fighting dance while you're sparring to the death. Skeleton horsemen do the "My horse is amazing" while banshees "Hula" their way around the room screaming at you. Not only that but some of the opponents to find are things you really wouldn't expect like even walls coming to life and persuing you as well as various other interesting mechanics like the "conduits" in the amplified DLC where you can project bolts of lighting at monsters.
To wrap this up, It's a goddamn fun game, and cheap. The soundtrack is definitely worth buying too. If you're gonna buy the game, GET THE SOUNDTRACK TOO

Duck Game has quickly become one of my favorite games to play with friends, and one of the few that I've actually learned to play reasonably well, if not for the satisfaction of quacking on your opponents' dead duck face, for the fact that every time you strat it up, it never disappoints. - Very active Steam Workshop community (with great and numerous mods)
- Dev is still working on the game, including adding new features

Cons:
- Has some bugs, mostly in online play, but usually nothing gamebreaking
- Unfortunately online lag is frequent (the game is VERY fast-paced, rounds can last less than 5 seconds)
- Can be hard to find online games sometimes; more people should be playing this

Calling Little Inferno a 'game' is difficult for me, as it's really more of a interactive toy than a proper game. That said, there is a win condition and a ending leading to the credits, but there is no lose condition, no way to reach a game over screen, which is drastically different in comparison to World of Goo, where failing a level means you outright fail and have to start at the beginning again. World of Goo was a actual game with a heart, emotion and a wonderful soundtrack, but Little Inferno fails to really bring the game aspect to the table, making it hard for me to recommend as a video game purchase for longevity, but easy for me to recommend as a cheap purchase if you want to experience an odd story of pyromania.
Little Inferno has you becoming the 'proud' (large emphasis on those quotes, there) owner of the Little Inferno fireplace kit from Tomorrow Corporation, a fireplace that will incinerate anything put inside of it. Anything. From wooden blocks to squeaky toys to expired medication to miniature moons, you purchase items from catalogues supplied to you from the corporation which are mailed directly to you to toss into your fireplace to send up in a puff of smoke, leaving only ashes and coins behind. These coins always reward you with more money than the original purchase, and through this cycle you will burn more, unlock more, and eventually find out the 'secret' behind why you never tear yourself away from staring at the fireplace.
Now, I could sit here and babble on to you about the psychological fascination with just tossing stuff into the fireplace, dragging your mouse around and watch it go ablaze, but really, there's only one major reason to complete Little Inferno; the WHY. World of Goo had you wondering why the goo balls made their treacherous pilgrimage around the world getting sucked up by giant vacuums, and Little Inferno will have you wondering why the world outside is slowly freezing over, why your neighbor has downright gone insane with her own Little Inferno, and why you're eternally stuck there just burning things for money. To give any clue to what the answers are would be to spoil the 'story', which even if the game is shallow in its gameplay department, its big twist near the end is, I say, worth price of admission, even if a lot of questions are never truly answered. Like World of Goo, not much has to be said when the music grabs you, holds you still, and just shows you without the need for dialogue. I'll admit, when you heed your neighbors advice near the end of the game and something big happens, I was brought to tears. Not much was said, and not much needed to be said as things played out and the music did all the talking.
The eerie art style and somber, subdued soundtrack (save for more dramatic moments later) are easy on the eyes much like World of Goo, and it's kinda fun to try and complete the combination challenges, where a list gives you the name of a combo and you must burn those items in unison to complete it and gain stamps, which you can use to instantly have an item delivered to you. These combo's are also required to unlock better catalogues and complete the game, making it somewhat of a grind once later combo's requiring three or four items get in your way. I completed Little Inferno in a little over three hours (all in one sitting), and that's including me getting through all the catalogues at a pretty good rate while goofing around to complete combo's. Even if I blew all my money with failed combinations, spiders creep down your chimney to give you small amounts of money, again showing there is no way to lose in this game, only win.
At $14.99 (at this writing, it's currently $9.99 on Steam), I cannot tell you to go out and purchase Little Inferno, even if its ending is worth seeing for yourself after spending a few hours burnin' and burnin' some more. Due to Steam's Christmas sale, I bought my version for under ten dollars, completed the game in the one sitting, and have yet to come back to it, not even to complete all the combinations. Little Inferno is a one trick pony, plain and simple, but its one trick was one that brought me to an emotional level, considering all you do is just set♥♥♥♥♥♥on fire and get rewarded for doing so. World of Goo would be a much better use of your money since it's an actual game with conditions for winning/losing plus it has good gameplay, but if you ever have some money to burn and Little Inferno is on sale, go for it. You'll probably never come back to it again, but it's little, sweet story will certainly touch you, while it lasts.

If you like roguelike turn-based dungeon crawlers that force you to think on your feet and have a rad soundtrack, boy do I have news for you!
Rhythm and roguelike aren't usually genres that mix, but it actually turns out really well. In practice it means that you have exactly a certain amount of time for each turn, so you need to pay attention and go. The rhythm aspects are really pretty lenient, so that's not really a frustration. And also you can play with your own music, if that's a thing you're into.
There's a bit of a learning curve in figuring out how to deal with monsters and bosses, but the game's very fair about it, letting you unlock practice against them and offering some guides. And if you're terrible at rhythm, there's the bard mode, which has no timer on each turn, which I found was a good way to get started when I was much less good at this game.
All of the soundtracks are amazing and definitely worth getting the dlc for.

At first I enjoyed the game, holding my nose at the silly dual drm situation. It is mostly a fun game. It's far better then Might and magic 9, and feels more like the older games. Might and Magic Legacy contains considerable array of fun game play.
I enjoy its quests, puzzles, artwork and music. the class structure and progression is pleasing as is most of the game play. Over time, the game clearly has great re-playability and solid involvement from the community at large. However its likely too unfinished, too unforgiving  and too poorly balanced to recommend to most folks.
Prior to the end game (and often during the end game) I had to use cheat tools to transport my characters out of various places to sell goods, level up, stock up on porions and goods, etc breaking up the game play. This is really strange since in the prior games, you could just back track or teleport out when you needed to exit a dungeon.  Had there not been cheat tools I would have found the game unplayable.
I found I had to extensively use community generated hint guides since many  of the game goals are so arbitrary and poorly expressed I got lost easily. This is at odds with the other Might and Magic games and many modern games where I usually do not need to cheat and rarely need hints. Generally the only need I had of community tools in prior versions were for better maps, locations for alchemy ingredients  and trainer locations.
However as the end game approached the game has grown more and more tedious. The developer chose to lock you in a dungeon without escape on several occasions the worst of which is the end game. if you don’t plan especially well the game will grow tired and tedious or simply unplayably  difficult. Add to that that some quests can not be completed until you finish the game, and the general uneven game play, I simply cant suggest you buy the game in 2014 until the price comes down. I bought the game at 25% off and feel a bit cheated.
If you like the turn based style, consider the game only if its on sale (or has come down in price) and after you have exhausted other games in the series and general genre. As time marches on, the community will generate patch fixes , the developers may rebalanced the end game, and mods and such that will greatly improve the game , as it did for mm6-8. However as  the game exists now in mid-2014, it feels poorly balanced, arbitrary and a bit tedious now. Its not a bad game but its hardly excellent either. Its just not worth the high price the developer is asking.
All that said you will enjoy the game if you like the genre and buy it on sale. You’ll also enjoy the game if you buy it now and wait 6 months or a year for

I've been addicted to this game since I started playing it. I am not a big fan of rogue-likes in general, but this game is among few rare exceptions.
You have 4 zones to beat, each one contains 3 floors and a boss fight. Every zone has its own theme and enemies. But wait, there's more. The enemies each move to the beat in their own unique pattern, and you have to recognize it and adapt quickly. For example, some enemies might be moving along a scripted path, others try to go for you specifically, some might stay still for 2 beats and then move on the 3rd one, others might move on every beat, and so on. It's all very well done.
During your dungeon crawling you'll also come across a lot of items of varying degrees of helpfulness. You have healing items, weapons, armour, rings, spells, and even some unusual items. Some can spawn from the start, others require unlocking via collectible diamonds. You can even remove the less useful items from the dungeons via the janitor, so that there's more chances instead for chests to contain the items you find more useful.
There is of course a fair bit of luck involved, as is pretty common with rogue-like games. At times you'll be lucky to find a nice weapon and other useful items early on, other times you'll just be spawning with enemies all around you. It is a very challenging game. You will die a lot. But you do learn to recognize the enemy movement patterns and eventually overcome them.
I also really like the whole light-hearted theme the game is going for. I think the devs pulled it off perfectly. The music is also amazing and will just drag you in to the beat.
In addition to the regular mode with the main character, you also get to unlock several other characters, which seem to have their own unique abilities (for example one of them can only confuse enemies but not kill, another is only able to use bombs, and so on). It all adds an extra challenge for those who want it. You can even go and practice fighting against specific enemies and bosses if you wish.
Great game in general. Highly recommended.
