Aside from having the most generic title in gaming, Steel Storm also has a generic description: sci-fi shoot-em-up with loads of guns.
This is a top-down shooter (though there is an option for close camera third person, but its obviously not meant to be played that way) that takes place in 3D levels.  Ammo is limitless, guns are plentiful and varied, and there is little story to speak of, aside from the short briefings at the beginning of each mission that tell you what to do, and sometimes, where to go, in the expansive levels.   The main gist of it is: infiltrate enemy bases and blow up everything.
The 3D effects are neat, but they can be jarring at times.  Sometimes enemies or even your own ship can get hidden behind a towering structure, but rotating the camera might reveal it.  In a game so dependent upon positioning and reflexes, managing this can get tiring.
The levels are varied and interesting.  You’ll explore frozen planets, underground mines, and sky fortresses.  Some of the levels can be quite easy to get lost in, and it is easy to miss an important switch or key and have to backtrack.  Taking the player out of the action for such a mundane reason is a big problem.  The map provided is not very helpful, as it is full of icons that mean nothing to you, and aren’t explained in the legend.
Yet I still had a good time with this game.  The cel-shaded graphics are cool to look at and the guns are satisfying to use.  The enemies can be overwhelming, but with smart tactics and judicious application of rockets and plasma beams, they all explode eventually.  The few boss fights in the main campaign are loads of fun.  Repairs and shields can be obtained from crates lying around the battlefield, but it can be a little annoying to have to break open three hundred or so per level to find the few that contain what you’re looking for.  A more consistent labeling or telegraphing what is inside would have been welcome.
This game is a great diversion for a few hours, an easy way to shoot bad guys and feel almost invincible, at least until they swarm you and remind you that you didn’t search enough crates for shields.
There is a DLC campaign called “Forgotten Prison” but I didn’t feel the need to play it.  Steel Storm: Burning Retribution is a fine game in its own right, though it isn’t without its flaws.

No, but in all honesty, this is one of my favourite games; On the surface it looks like all it does is let you watch things burn, and  since I got this in a Humble Bundle some time ago I didn't particularly mind that. I like watching things burn and I wasn't expecting anything more - But it's so much more than that.
For one thing there's the variety of items - I'm not sure about the first few items but the further in you go the more variety you see in both what items do and how they react to fire.
That said, some items are, for all intents and purposes, the same as others - I think this is because there's a 'combo' list, which gives you more coins for putting together similar items, I figure a lot of the items were put in just so they could fill out the combo list and get it to 99 (Or 100, if you count the storyline one).
The second aspect is the humour, there's a nice mix of outright jokes and cult-references - As for the latter, I'm usually not a fan of games that make such jokes because the developers often think it's necessary to inundate the game with them, and that not only gets in the way of the game forming any of its own possible references but it also wears out the references that it makes (You know, like when a meme is overused and it becomes... Much overrated. Such boring. Wow.) - But again, it's a nice mix, the humour stays fresh.
The last aspect is something I've already touched on, and that's the storyline. In a way there isn't much I can say about it in that you only see the storyline in a couple of different points of dialogue, a small cinematic, and then in a cutscene-like-thing at the end where you move around and talk to people, tying up loose ends and whatnot - But on the other hand there's so much I want to say, especially about that cinematic, which was so unexpected - I remember at the time I was visiting home (I live away for university) and I thought I'd just play for a couple of minutes but NOPE it tore my soul out and broke me down into a puddle of fiery tears (Well, not quite, I was more like "Oh, I didn't see that coming, one day I'll write a review about this game because it just hit me that it's amazing")
If I had to pick out a downside I'd say it was the lack of Workshop-y features, if this game allowed people to put in any item it would have some sense of replayability - As it is, it gives a good couple of hours, though granted some of that time is spent waiting in the early game where you have little to no tokens. The closest this gets to such a feature is the picture frame thing where you can upload any photo and burn it.

Review of Might and Magic X: Legacy
What must first be said is that this is not going to be your average run of the mill rpg, the designers of this game has made it a somewhat old-school type game, and what that means is that the game will not hold your hand and lead you through it. This can be surprising and frustrating as you sometimes wander around aimlessly, having possibly missed some small detail that means that you are now on the wrong path. Since the name of the game is indeed 'Legacy', maybe we should have come to expect this and be completely ok with it, but I think it still needs to be said that the lack of descriptions of where to go in this game can be a problem. This problem can be more or less immediately rectified however, as long as you are willing to alt tab from the game to google, which is something that I personally ended up doing multiple times, even though I would consider myself somewhat of a veteran gamer.
The main plot of the game is convoluted, as it should be (follows the traditions of the older games), and there is a relatively little emphasis on story, as it should be. Most of what you do in the game is exploring, and fighting. Many npc's however have the option to spill some minor 'gossip' to the player, which is most of the time just random bits of lore of the gameworld. Scattered throughout the world is also many books, which holds a lot of lore of the world, if this is your thing.
The characters your party is comprised of are created manually by the player (unless you insist on letting the computer do it for you), and they all have lots of attribute points and skills that needs to be allocated. There is a nice range of depth to the character building in this game, as the 12 classes available all have different levels of potential with different skills. The mage characters can usually level up certain magic skills to the highest level (grandmaster), but also has the potential of leveling up certain weapon skills, armor skills, and passive defense skills. This well functioning skill system works together with your attribute system to give the player quite a lot of customization options for his party. It essentially *succeeds* in making the player feel like they are the one who created this team, as opposed to having few options and feeling like you are playing a non-rpg. The games skill and attribute system is sufficient, and well expected as it follows the traditions of the older Might and Magic titles. But that doesn't mean that it is fresh, or innovative. It also isn't balanced very well. The armor skills are shown to be very lackluster once you understand the games mechanics for example.
The game is entirely grid based. This is a design choice that has huge implications for gameplay, but it is an intrinsic part of the experience, and there is nothing to be done about it now. The entire game is built around this, and as such the environments of the game has the probability of looking quite odd and unrealistic, if you compare it to Skyrim for example. The world is also quite small, it would only take about 3 minutes to run through the length of the entire overworld map (once you have killed all the enemies, and opened everything). This is not because the game is small or short, but because of how compressed everything is, but this is a good thing most of the time, as otherwise there would have been an enormous amount of walking for you - that's a promise. The way the dungeons are built in this game screams 'gameplay' over 'realism', and thankfully so. Maybe it doesn't make any sense that the governor of a peninsula is living in a castle that effectively looks like a labyrinth? But it makes for fun adventuring, so I am pleased.
The main focus of the game could be said to be fighting, and fighting is done in a turn based tactical manner. You get to make one action with each of your characters during your turn, such as casting spells or attacking with weapons, (but this hardly has to be said I hope). You will encounter many enemies that will give you a run for your money, and I hope you will welcome the challenge. There has been a couple of posts both on Steam and on Ubisofts forum of players complaining about not being able to progress because their party is too weak. There is the hypothetical possibility that you might gimp your characters to the point of not being able to continue. But one must understand that this is a necessity in a game if you want freedom for the player to design their own party in meaningful ways, and still pose a challenge.
Finally, the game is produced by Ubisoft and requires Uplay to play, which can be a detriment, as most people don't want Uplay to clog up their computer as the millionth "gamehub service" program. Having popups that try to direct you to Youtube every time you exit the game is hardly a plus either, but that's something that Ubisoft thinks is a cool thing.
Score is a whopping 85/100 for me personally. It's the perfect blend between rpg and strategy, and will probably leave you with a feeling of satisfaction if you are a min-maxing geek like myself. But you have to look past some of the things mentioned earlier in my text to get the most out of it.

Stellaris is another magnificient grand strategy title from Paradox Development Studio that is incredibly deep, immensely detailed and highly ambitious. The game is also championed by a vastly improved user interface when compared with other Paradox games and has a far more inviting learning curve without losing the challenge or depth that the other games by this highly regarded developer offer.
Paradox are widely known for their catalogue of strategy games over the years which are of a very high quality but are also remarkably complex to an extent; some newcomers and even veterans of the genre felt alienated, confused and simply overwhelmed. Stellaris however, has a fully fledged tutorial integrated into the main campaign which not only guides you through the general mechanics along with each feature in a constructive manner; it explains aspects clearly and this is further supported by a far more user friendly interface. The screen is less cluttered when compared with the likes of Europa Universalis IV and all the information is clear, condensed and well presented.
The game takes place in space which is an almost Call of Duty style departure from the typical Paradox titles of classic eras and a real world setting. The premise is also slightly different as you create your colony from scratch or by selecting some preset examples instead of guiding an already established country. Your goal in the galaxy is to explore, build, research, expand, conquer and even exterminate all other races you come across - basically exactly what you'd expect from a 4X title. You can play this game however you wish and at your own pace -  you may opt to be a fanatic militarist or simply want to discover as much of the universe as possible whilst befriending and benefitting from other races you meet along the way. It is a massively detailed and highly engrossing experience in which the developers have made the transition from reality to sci-fi in a very credible fashion.
Stellaris runs superbly too and is bolstered by truly fantastic atmosphere enhancing audio that compliments your game throughout. The visuals are very good too and the galaxy map whilst despite looking rather basic, is easy to grasp and understand which is another massive plus. Overall; Stellaris is another superb Paradox title that is riddled with depth and a long term challenge but is also presented and executed in a far more appealling and enjoyable way than some previous titles by the studio. This game will have a bright future and is sure to provide many hours of entertainment.

The soundtrack is incredible as well. It's always well-placed, giving a certain atmosphere to the scene.

As a fan of the original Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc on the PSVita, purchasing Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair felt like a compulsory act. Never has a game quenched my highschool-murder-mystery-visual-novel thirst (which I never knew I had in the first place) like this series has.
Under the pristine, clean look of the UI, character designs, and flashy cutscenes, Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair eventually takes on an incredibly dark, sinister atmosphere contrasting mature and sickening themes with a clean and bright anime aesthetic. With the kickass soundtrack providing ample background music (even if it sometimes gets repetitive), as well as fitting themes for when the narrative gets tense, the game never feels empty like some other virtual novels do. You're exploring an entire "world" on the island your character gets stranded on from the very beginning, with the exactly the same amnesiac mindset of how he got there.
Eventually, however, Danganronpa 2 loses its luster with what amounts to a somewhat predictable story structure. While this is a series staple, it would have been a great addition for the game to mix up the narrative sequencing of this aprx. 20 hour experience. Aside from this minor complaint, the ever present mysterious and near-hidden gloomy atmosphere of this game never subsides, coercing the player into a constant questioning mindset in what amounts to a gripping experience.
Since I didn't play most of the added content mini-games (including the knock-off tamagotchi on the pause menu or the Magical Girl Usami themed battle-hybrid-thing, which both I assumed were stupid time sinks), I can't really fairly critique them. But, obviously, they don't really impact the story and are just optional filler that doesn't interrupt gameplay.
The classroom trial minigames, however, are another story. Point-blank: they're extremely mediocre but an improvement from the first game. My advice? Play on easy. You're not losing out on the pivotal narrative experience the game offers.
Overall, the anime styling, inside jokes, or not playing the first game in the series are the only things that should keep anyone from playing this game.

Okay I will start with saying this review is going to basically be gushing about how amazing this title is and how much respect I have for the man responsible.  I'll try to be unbiased but my love for this game is going to be apparent. Short summary will be at the bottom if interested.
Dust is a stylish-action 2D platformer that I would recommend to everyone.  I first became intrigued by this title just by the art alone. The visuals are stunning from the first second you start the game up.  When I did a little more digging I came to find out that nearly everything in this title was done by a single person.  After experiencing the final product, this fact itself blows my mind.  For one person to create this world and such a fluid action game other than the voice acting and the soundtrack (both of which I should note are adequate. Not amazing but not bad at all) is just incredible.
Where the game truly shines is the gameplay.  It can be compared to Muramasa: The Demon Blade, which if you are a fan of platformers that title needs to jump up to the top of your list. If you don't have a means to play it though Dust is a very comparable replacement.
The story, despite a few of the obligatory RPG staples, is not bad either.  Amnesia, high-pitched annoying sidekick, pallete swaps, etc are all present.  Although I will say that Fidget, your constant companion is actually not annoying in the usual sense, she's written to be that way and has some ocasionally funny dialogue. On the other hand she is a useful companion as well.
The best part of this title is definitely the gameplay, which would make me still recommend this game even if the world wasn't as attractive or if the story was weaker than it already is. There is something satisfying about just flying through the screen racking up 1000 hit combos taking down the hoards of creatures attacking you.
Sure it can be simple but can also be somewhat manipulated to stay difficult. That might not sound like it makes much sense but the leveling system doesn't just automatically make you stronger and diminish the challenge, which is sometimes a complaint about these types of games.  You get skill points that you can assign yourself, that in combination with not purchasing the strongest gear will keep the challenge up if you choose to do so.
There are many paths to take, sometimes you cannot access an area right away, so you have to gain an ability to bactrack...you know the routine.  Still, it is a blast to play.  This is my 2nd time playing through this title.  I did just about everything I could do in my Xbox playthrough, and when I eventually get a PS4 I will buy it again just to support Dean Dodrill and the magic he created.
To sum it up: This is a game some would call "Metroidvania" and it's top notch. One of my top 5 platformers probably.  The visuals are eye-catching, monster designs are intricate and characters are all incredibly detailed and look better than some big budget animation studio productions. By no means is it flawless but the minor gripes I have are easily overshadowed by how much fun I can still have. Highly recommend this game. Even if it wouldn't have been on sale when I first created my Steam account I would have bought it at full price without hesitation.
Pros:
Gameplay - Fast, can be intense at times, rarely is there a shortage of action and it's always satisfying to slaughter groups of enemies with just a sword and a flying chipmunk.
Customization - Outside of assigning your skill points as you level, you can also gather lots of equipment.  Enemies will sometimes drop Blueprints along with materials you will need to craft the equipment via the blacksmith.
Exploration - There are lots of secrets, and some collectibles to discover
Cons:
Poor map design - This is my main complaint. Every new area you enter is just shown as a small square up in the corner and will show if there is a another exit and if there are still any treasures to collect by either showing a full circle or just a dot if all the treasures in that screen have been obtained.
Writing/Story - Not terrible but just not really a strong point. Kind of hit and miss. The whole 'trying to discover your past because you have amnesia' story?  Not the most original.  I will say it is a little darker than what the bright colors and silly characters might have you thinking at first.
Buy this game you won't regret it.

Spoiler-free thoughts about the game, TLDR in the end
This review expects that you have already completed the first Danganronpa.
The story is bigger and better, but after the opening scenes it progresses quite slowly until the midpoint of the game: Danganronpa1 had a steadier flow going thorough the game, but the last half of D2 beats the ending of D1 hands down. To avoid spoilers I'm not going to say anything more about that.
Compared to D1, the main cast is much more eccentric. While the first game had pretty colourful characters set in a relatively dark athmosphere, D2 goes all out with the character designs, which might be off-putting to some people, especially if you're not used to Japanese style of humor. I personally would've preferred if the cast wasn't as weird as it was presented, but this wasn't a huge deal because:
a) There's actually some character development this time around, so some characters will grow as persons.
b) More information about the characters can be gained during the free-time conversations, which will help you understand the cast better, therefore they become more tolerable.
c) There's a good chance that the character you despise the most will die at some point lol.
While the main cast is mostly more one-dimensional than it was in the first game, the villains this time are just awesome. Instead of having arbitrary motives linked to the despair theme like in the first game, the reasons of the killing game and character actions become very clear. The case and story twists are huge and twisted af, I loved it.
The game had some of the best murder cases I've yet to play in any game so far (5th case omg). Most of them focus in small areas, usually just in the room or the house the murder took place, so the investigation, trial and logic proceedings stay more cohesive. Because of this there're less of those far-fetched moments where the player finds possible plot holes or logical near-impossibilities.
The trial mechanics are improved, tho I still dislike the action based logic games.
When it comes to the logic puzzles, the pieces of the puzzle should be the key to the solution, not vice versa, where the player already knows the answer, but the artificial difficulty of the puzzle makes him waste time and effort just for submitting the answer.
The best example of this is the Hangman's Gambit, where you have to shoot down flying letters to form a sentence to answer a question. The intention of the game is that the letters would act like helpful hints, but usually the player can figure out the answer after inputting a couple of letters. After that you're just waiting for the correct letters to appear on the screen, and the game becomes a time wasting formality. There is an option to turn down the action puzzle difficulty, but as I'm aware it doesn't really shorten the time you have to spend in those games.
The trial mechanic where the game really shines, Make Your Argument, is improved even further. The time limits are stricter, time bonuses have been nerfed, and because of the more compact theme of the murders the logic flows more solidly. There are still some moments where you struggle submitting the answer just because you can't figure out which statement to shoot down, but those are rare now, I had to dig a hint from a walkhrough only once during the whole playthrough.
The graphical detail and style are again excellent: the visuals have aged really well considering this was originally a PSVita title. There are some minor but very glaring issues though; I don't understand why the 2D hub world was put together so sloppily, because you'd figure that kind of solution would be easy to execute properly. The character movement animation is terrible, the sprites are jagged and pixelated, and the texture layers between the foreground and the character overlap incorrectly. Also when the background sprites happen to overlap each other, there're occasional graphical errors that are mostly caused by bad object cropping. Texture popping is also a thing, which is probably a remnant from the Vita version, it could've been removed from this PC version.
When it comes to selecting the voice acting language, I recommend Japanese due to practical reasons. This allows you to read the dialogue more fluently when the characters are speaking virtually gibberish, and moving to the next text box in mid-sentence is also less abrupt.
TLDR
The writing and dialogue are again excellent outside some "Japanese" moments, which this game has more than in D1. Especially the ending and the murder cases greatly exceed the first game, this stuff is wonderfully f*cked up.
The character designs are more eccentric and one-dimensional, but there's more character development around this time.
The villains on the other hand are superior, the motives and character actions are rock-solid, which was very satisfying.
Trial minigames have been changed for the better, tho they are still just artificial time-wasters if you don't like their core mechanics.
Play with Japanese voices, and be not afraid to max out the logic difficulty.

HOTLINE MIAMI
I've always been down to play pixel graphics game, and apparently i had my eyes on this game and soon enough i owned it. Now let's get on with the review.
|INTRODUCTION|
Hotline miami is a 2D topdown shooter with an amazing plot. I mean you will literally play because you will have the curiosity to know "what happens next".
The story is on a retro timeline during 80s era.
And it's developed by Dennaton Games and published by Devolver Digital.
|FUN FACTOR|
Want to be frustrated and taste what defeat feels like. Want to know what dying again and again and again and again feels like. Welcome to Hotline Miami.
There are guns with limited ammos, there are throwables, there are melee weapons and then there is your fist. It is an action-packed fast-paced shooter/melee/door bashing/skull exploding/head decapitation/eyes popping(literally)/and blood simulator. There is a grading system on each level whose points are based on how "murderous" you made you kill. Did you just shoot the guy and moved on or did you grabbed him and bashed his head literally to pulp? Well the latter method scores more point. Then there is one frustration of "dying from off screen NPCs". Yes you will be often shot by someone who is not even on the screen, so what do we do? Well we play and predict where he might be and shoot or do whatever to "kill him first".
My Verdict here : Kill or be Killed.
My points : 10/10
|GRAPHICS|
The game is really well developed in graphics front. There is details present in the game even though it is a pixel based. The retro coloring and the flashing lights looks dope af.
My points : 10/10
|SOUND|
Oh boy, the soundtrack of this game is lit af. The intro music of is so soothing to hear and the retro 8bit sounds are awesome. No wonder why Counter Strike Global Offesnsive has a Music Kit based on the soundtrack of this game.
My points : 11/10
|REPLAYABILITY|
The game has multiple endings and i personally have only unlocked one. So i will play again and this time get another ending, yes it is replaybale and not only because of the multiple endings. But because of the Fun-factor (read above again) it gives. Who the heck doesn't want to end their day by fighting in a retro game with 8bit music and chopping of head?
My points : 10/10
|CONCLUSION|
Don't think.
Just.
Buy.
PS : It's worth it's full price.

A very well made "point-and-click" game. The characters are likeable and emotional, and the story is well done, though quite simple at times.

The graphics are well done, in a cell shaded manner, and very aptly portray the emotions of the characters, seeming more so like an animated movie than a game.
The characters present are all very unique from each other, though I wish we got to see more of the ones that are so commonly mentioned, such as the Octopus Haring, who is mentioed to be a pretty bad guy. The game could have also done to be a bit longer, with a little more puzzles, and the ending before the final scene could have been a little more fleshed out, but I still finished the game satisfied. The final scene of the game was very well done, and actually caught me off guard. I applaud them for that one.

I want to start this review by saying that, when this game came out in July of this year, I actually stayed well away due to all negative feedback and attention it got; despite this, however, I did keep a close eye on it to see how the developers over at Harebrained Schemes dealt with all the bad press and negative reviews, and to my honest surprise they really stepped up and decided to take the community’s suggestions and ideas on board to make this game a much better game all round – Maybe the likes of Hello Games could learn a thing or two here…
The changes they made were the inclusion of a new playable character (The Brute), a completely new outdoor environment (The Black Forest), new and improved enemies, armour, potions, scrolls, weapons, and other big improvements to the game’s AI – Given this, however, were the changes that they made to this game in alignment to what the community wanted? Personally, I would say yes. Yes they certainly did.
Necropolis acts as a rouge-like hack and slash dungeon crawler, that’s not for people easily frustrated or stressed because after a while, you will want to throw your controller across the room and admit defeat! I will not lie, I did this a more than a couple of times but always found my self coming back for more pain like the masochist I am.
Necropolis requires you to actually think about your next move and plan a strategy as you play through, unlike most hack and slash games out there, and will most certainly punish you if you run in all guns blazing – The game comes pre-packaged along with permadeath, meaning that one wrong move, and you’re straight right back at the beginning! The way that the developers have prevented the game becoming stagnant is by adding randomly generated dungeons, so no playthrough is the same. At first i found the controls to be clunky, however after a while I realised that timing is more vital; once I had mastered this, the combat felt more fluid and smooth, and made the game that much more enjoyable.
There were many things that I loved about Necropolis, but at the same time I found aspects of the game more frustrating than fair; the fact you can craft food, potions, and other goodies was a big plus, but this can cause a big issue if you think there are no ghouls around the area, and decide to make some lovely meat, only to suddenly have a pair of teeth at your ankles and jugular, when you get wiped out by a hoard of skeletons that decided to creep up on you and ruin your meal! Another feature I loved was the easy drop-in drop-out co-op built in to the game, which made the adventure much more fun and much easier at the same time – My only gripe with this were the loot system, chests, and friendly fire, as you would have to somehow figure out a system of who would get what as only one chest would spawn as you enter each new level, items would only be able to picked up by one player, and yes, players can hit other players, leading to some awkward team kills…
Overall, I found this game highly addictive and a huge improvement on what was released back in July; the artistic take on the game really drew me in, as it wasn’t too over the top, and didn’t need to be – The game play speaks for itself! I believe that Dark Souls fans who maybe want a bit more of a challenge after pumping Dark Souls III dry will love this game, as well as fans of rouge-likes and dungeon crawlers in general!
I will happily give this game an 8.5 / 10 due to the massive improvements made in this game, and the dedication Harebrained Schemes put in to fixing it and not throwing in the towel!!

The worst thing about this game is that it sometimes forgets how much it sucks.
Dead Bits is a block-based first person shooter, which might seem a novel concept.  When I fired it up after hearing all the negative, I was pleasantly surprised that it actually ran.  Comparisons to Bubsy 3D were not right.  This game actually works.  It just sucks.
The first awkwardness is the intro to the levels, where you seem frozen in midair for a few seconds before dropping into a cube.  To actually play you have to jump down to the level.  But if you don't jump down right, you will fall and die.  In fact, the challenge of the game is not so much avoiding enemies as avoiding the crappy level design.
There is a nice touch for this kind of game, but not for a hardcore FPS, in that monsters have HP over their heads.  This is the only thing that makes Level 4 bearable.  But this doesn't make killing monsters any more easy or fun.  In Half-Life I can perfectly melee attack headcrab zombies, I can do great things with a sword in L4D2, I used to have a reputation of my skills with a lightsaber in the Jedi Knight games.  But this game's baseball bat weapon is hit or miss.  I take damage and don't even know why.  Which might not be the monster's fault, as I died in a corridor in level 2 for no reason once.  Something is very off there.
Then when I play level 3, and there's a wave of zombies coming down the hall, and I have to whack them with a bat and I'm actually doing it, it's kind of satisfying.  Then the game turns gray and goes into slow-mo, and whatever timing I had is gone.  Just another poor design choice there. You see, when you kill a monster, there's a chance the game will turn gray and slow down to make it more dramatic, which unfortunately is not disimilar to what happens when you die.
The biggest problem for me, though, is that you cannot change key bindings.  Left-handed players are pretty much screwed.
I can't help but feel there's an attempt at a game in here, but it's just not there.  The level design is what kills this game, more than anything.  Fortunately, there aren't that many levels, and they aren't that long.  I only managed to get through four of them before I gave up.

Pretty good overall.
The tech development around combat is 100% rock paper scissors (or beam, projectile, missile) and each has a defense (shields, armor, point defense) so it is easy to understand what you are working on attack defense wise, and you can react to your oponents' developments.
The other parts of the tech tree(s) are more dependant on your chosen race, so you may get some techs that your opponents will not.  The tech trees are fairly deep and in most cases you will not cap out before the end result of your game will be apparent.  So plenty to explore here.
The idiology choices are... interesting.  You typically get global benifits but sometimes you get ships or new buildings that you can make.  The big issue here is that you typically only earn idiology points when you colonize new planets, which on small maps or games where you want there to be fewer colonies you will some times be left with too few points to make idiology meaningful.
I think the game designers went for the "computer oppenents will get extra stuff to make them tough" approach, instead of having them "outthink" you, or plan better or what have you.  So expect to be outgunned and not out-thought.
The released updates to the game have been meaningful and generally nice additions.  (New races, new annomoly types, and of course bug fixes.)  The only bug fix that I have yet to see is the fix for text on small but extra wide computer screens (laptop), the text will sometimes be clipped in a location that will prevent you from reading all of it.
Multiplayer is a bit of a miss in my opinion.  They wanted the game to be "simultanious" as much as possible, so you can't just read a book during your opponent's turn, and you will want to because you won't have much to look at most of the time.  They should either provide a replay (so you don't miss anything), or go back to the drawing board on the concept entirely.
Overall I like the game, it's good, but it could be better in several areas.

long time dark souls fan, since the first one came out on PC I've been difficulty capping each one as they come out. I would get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and stare at my steam library just stewwing until the next game came out. Fast forward to the release, seeing in almost every review a dissapointed fanboy, seeing Totalbiscuit call it "okay" - not happy Kumabear.
So I waited, then I saw the update, the sale, figured at 20$ it was worth a shot. Boy howdy I was right. This game is phenominal.
The mechanics aren't quite up to dark souls standard, but they are tight, they are responsive, I feel as though my deaths are my fault and I have a long standing hatred of Gemeaters. The character of this game should be evident from any screenshots you see but I'll talk about it for a little bit here. The aesthetic is amazing. I love it, probably more than I love the aesthetic of Darksouls if I'm completely honest. There's nothing extra, it's simplistic streamline.
Probably a good moment to mention how it runs. I game on an old Alienware x-51, Nvidia gtx660, 16g RAM, i7 intel processor, etc. You can tell I got a big bottleneck in my graphics card, but this game runs great, somewhere between 50-60fps on average. I've had 3 crashes in close to 15 hours of gaming - solid by any metric, but even with crashes, the game saves whenever you cross through a door, so I lost 0 progress.
all things considered I definitely reccomend this game to anyone looking for more action adventure.

I really enjoy roguelikes, but in most of them I run into the problem of spending too much time micromanaging and deciding on how I approach the next encounter, which impedes my progress and I usually stop playing halfway through a character out of boredom.
However in Crypt of the Necrodancer, monsters make actions to the beat of the music. This brings back the reactive, time-limited critical thinking I enjoy and makes it a much more suspenseful experience. It will require you to study enemy patterns and figure out what type of gear you are most effective with. It has a gem system to unlock new items as well as the ability to filter out items you don't like from the spawn system. It also has multiple characters each with unique abilities, and a few training areas to help you progress.
If you like roguelikes in the slightest I highly recommend it.

Galactic civilizations 3 has implemented some really great features and the game has shown to have alot of potential.  Because of this potential galactic civlizations had the potential to become one of the greatest 4x games out there and all they had to do was improve on the neglected and bad stuff of galciv 2 because galciv 2 is still a great game.
The game has some really great features  but is incredibly sloppy.
The galactic world map feels like a mess and The ship icons on the map show barely any information. these are things that should have been improved upon because in a 4x game with the scale galciv has information is extremely important.
One of the greatest changes i have seen from galciv 2 to 3 has been the ideology system. This system allowes for you to pick between 3 ideological  idea groups wich has its own unique perks and benefits. This system effects both colonization and diplomacy and helps diversify playthroughs.
However this games diplomacy system is very lackluster and very barebones. Normally u would think a benevolent ai would choose to be very friendly and act like a general good guy but no matter their ideological path or relation to you they always talk about annihilating you, wich ofcourse is stupid and unimersive.
Galactic civilizations offers arguably alot more hours of content and variation to playthroughs then games like civilization. But the execution of alot of the content in the game feels sloppily implemented and buggy and the overal performance of the game is quite average.
All in all the game can be very enjoyable but the performance combined with the sloppily implemented features can be a source of alot of iritation.
In its current state i cant consiously give this game a positve recommendation. This is because they are trying to sell a buggy sloppy game for the full price of a regular AAA title wich is unacceptable to me. if u really want to play this game wait for it to be on sale.

My opinion after 16 hours of playing GCIII - game mechanics are almost identical to GCII, and the whole thing feels like a graphic remake of its predecessor, but it also feels incomplete. Here are few problems:
Beginning with Interface menus that do not offer even a half of the options you had before to customize your experience during gameplay. Resource icons for example make a mess out of the map when zoomed out, making it really hard to observe the gameplay. I haven't found any options to address this.
Taxing system for your colonies is removed and only way to manage your economical income is through single wealth/manufacturing/research slider. I don't yet have a definitive opinion on this, but for now this new income system feels little vague.
The hype about incredible AI that utilizes each core of your expensive i7 to provide you the best and most complex GalCiv experience is just hype. Reality is that for 16 hours of gameplay I haven't noticed any singe improvement compared to GalCIv II. The opponents react exactly the same in same situations, making same diplomatic propositions, and making same strategic mistakes as before (small example: just leave barely habitable class 5 planet next to your starting homeworld and AI rush to take it, spending a colony ship and bunch of money for improvements, just to loose the planet after few turns due to overwhelming influence of your nearby homeworld).
Spying is completely missing leaving you to guess what your opponents are doing, researching or building on their home planets. I read somewhere that developers plan to program "deeper" spying system than before, so they left it completely out. Really? Releasing a full-priced game without a crucial feature that existed in its predecessor, with a promise that it will be included in eventual DLCs that you have to pay for additionally?
Why developer haven't taken more time to finish their ideas and then release the full version, or at least implement the old style feature and then improve it later?
Speaking to another civilization should lead to trading screen right away (99% of the time this is where player wants to go), rather than opening a pointless splash screen. It is eye candy, but it is very inconvenient as you have to click twice. Furthermore, "trade with you", and "declare war on you" are two choices just next to each other making it a miss-click accident waiting to happen.
There are more smaller and bigger issues to remark and I will edit this interview if I find more or if I change my opinion on it, but in its current state this release is not worth the money as it offers less than GalCiv II.

Spoiler-free thoughts about the game, TLDR in the end
This review expects that you have already completed the first Danganronpa.
The story is bigger and better, but after the opening scenes it progresses quite slowly until the midpoint of the game: Danganronpa1 had a steadier flow going thorough the game, but the last half of D2 beats the ending of D1 hands down. To avoid spoilers I'm not going to say anything more about that.
Compared to D1, the main cast is much more eccentric. While the first game had pretty colourful characters set in a relatively dark athmosphere, D2 goes all out with the character designs, which might be off-putting to some people, especially if you're not used to Japanese style of humor. I personally would've preferred if the cast wasn't as weird as it was presented, but this wasn't a huge deal because:
a) There's actually some character development this time around, so some characters will grow as persons.
b) More information about the characters can be gained during the free-time conversations, which will help you understand the cast better, therefore they become more tolerable.
c) There's a good chance that the character you despise the most will die at some point lol.
While the main cast is mostly more one-dimensional than it was in the first game, the villains this time are just awesome. Instead of having arbitrary motives linked to the despair theme like in the first game, the reasons of the killing game and character actions become very clear. The case and story twists are huge and twisted af, I loved it.
The game had some of the best murder cases I've yet to play in any game so far (5th case omg). Most of them focus in small areas, usually just in the room or the house the murder took place, so the investigation, trial and logic proceedings stay more cohesive. Because of this there're less of those far-fetched moments where the player finds possible plot holes or logical near-impossibilities.
The trial mechanics are improved, tho I still dislike the action based logic games.
When it comes to the logic puzzles, the pieces of the puzzle should be the key to the solution, not vice versa, where the player already knows the answer, but the artificial difficulty of the puzzle makes him waste time and effort just for submitting the answer.
The best example of this is the Hangman's Gambit, where you have to shoot down flying letters to form a sentence to answer a question. The intention of the game is that the letters would act like helpful hints, but usually the player can figure out the answer after inputting a couple of letters. After that you're just waiting for the correct letters to appear on the screen, and the game becomes a time wasting formality. There is an option to turn down the action puzzle difficulty, but as I'm aware it doesn't really shorten the time you have to spend in those games.
The trial mechanic where the game really shines, Make Your Argument, is improved even further. The time limits are stricter, time bonuses have been nerfed, and because of the more compact theme of the murders the logic flows more solidly. There are still some moments where you struggle submitting the answer just because you can't figure out which statement to shoot down, but those are rare now, I had to dig a hint from a walkhrough only once during the whole playthrough.
The graphical detail and style are again excellent: the visuals have aged really well considering this was originally a PSVita title. There are some minor but very glaring issues though; I don't understand why the 2D hub world was put together so sloppily, because you'd figure that kind of solution would be easy to execute properly. The character movement animation is terrible, the sprites are jagged and pixelated, and the texture layers between the foreground and the character overlap incorrectly. Also when the background sprites happen to overlap each other, there're occasional graphical errors that are mostly caused by bad object cropping. Texture popping is also a thing, which is probably a remnant from the Vita version, it could've been removed from this PC version.
When it comes to selecting the voice acting language, I recommend Japanese due to practical reasons. This allows you to read the dialogue more fluently when the characters are speaking virtually gibberish, and moving to the next text box in mid-sentence is also less abrupt.
TLDR
The writing and dialogue are again excellent outside some "Japanese" moments, which this game has more than in D1. Especially the ending and the murder cases greatly exceed the first game, this stuff is wonderfully f*cked up.
The character designs are more eccentric and one-dimensional, but there's more character development around this time.
The villains on the other hand are superior, the motives and character actions are rock-solid, which was very satisfying.
Trial minigames have been changed for the better, tho they are still just artificial time-wasters if you don't like their core mechanics.
Play with Japanese voices, and be not afraid to max out the logic difficulty.

THIS is how you convey a message, bring awareness, interact with your audience, and touch souls. Depression Quest, take copious notes.
Its an interactive game/novel that follows the life of a family struggling to deal with the harsh reality of cancer overtaking their young son. Don't expect breathtaking visuals. Everything is kept very simple and I'm glad this choice was made because the narrative is the stand out star. The visuals and music are there to assist not overshadow. The presentation of this piece is what makes this a success, in my opinion, because it manages to leave an impactful mark without being too self-serving and pretentious. Focusing your narrative on a subject so real and so tragic is very, very risky but I feel that the risk was worth it.
The only issue I came across is muddled, garbled audio from inner monologues. I'm not sure if its intentional to add impact to the emotionally infused written letters or if my computer is temporarily on strike but I'm noting it anyway, just in case.
This is the second game that has driven me to tears and I'm okay with that. I will play this game again, most definately, after some time has passed. The journey may have been mostly sad but I will happily take it again until That Dragon, Cancer, is finally slain.

Directions

The Witcher 2 is a vast improvement over its predecessor, and, as the franchise is known for, has many new and variable tropes for a Fantasy RPG game. The combat is by far the most enjoyable, compelling, intense, and straight forward experience I've had in a while, and for the first time, the magic, enchanting, and alchemy systems aren't overly convaluted.

The only complaint is that the game takes too fondly to the objectification of most, if not all, of it's female characters. I won't get into detail, but if you're ok with that, then I highly recommend playing The Witcher 2 for a new Action-Adventure-RPG experience.

The worst thing about this game is that it sometimes forgets how much it sucks.
Dead Bits is a block-based first person shooter, which might seem a novel concept.  When I fired it up after hearing all the negative, I was pleasantly surprised that it actually ran.  Comparisons to Bubsy 3D were not right.  This game actually works.  It just sucks.
The first awkwardness is the intro to the levels, where you seem frozen in midair for a few seconds before dropping into a cube.  To actually play you have to jump down to the level.  But if you don't jump down right, you will fall and die.  In fact, the challenge of the game is not so much avoiding enemies as avoiding the crappy level design.
There is a nice touch for this kind of game, but not for a hardcore FPS, in that monsters have HP over their heads.  This is the only thing that makes Level 4 bearable.  But this doesn't make killing monsters any more easy or fun.  In Half-Life I can perfectly melee attack headcrab zombies, I can do great things with a sword in L4D2, I used to have a reputation of my skills with a lightsaber in the Jedi Knight games.  But this game's baseball bat weapon is hit or miss.  I take damage and don't even know why.  Which might not be the monster's fault, as I died in a corridor in level 2 for no reason once.  Something is very off there.
Then when I play level 3, and there's a wave of zombies coming down the hall, and I have to whack them with a bat and I'm actually doing it, it's kind of satisfying.  Then the game turns gray and goes into slow-mo, and whatever timing I had is gone.  Just another poor design choice there. You see, when you kill a monster, there's a chance the game will turn gray and slow down to make it more dramatic, which unfortunately is not disimilar to what happens when you die.
The biggest problem for me, though, is that you cannot change key bindings.  Left-handed players are pretty much screwed.
I can't help but feel there's an attempt at a game in here, but it's just not there.  The level design is what kills this game, more than anything.  Fortunately, there aren't that many levels, and they aren't that long.  I only managed to get through four of them before I gave up.

I bought this game after seeing the documentary Thank You for Playing, which tells of story of Ryan Green and his family as they come to terms with the terminal cancer of their son Joel. This game is his labour of love and lasting testament to his son.
The game is made up of dozens of scenes, some set in the real world of hospital wards and waiting rooms, and others set in imaginary allegorical places.  It does a great job of conveying things from different perspectives; sometimes you play Ryan, sometimes his wife, or sometimes a silent observer watching events as they unfold. This is one of the game's strong points, and lets you see things from a very personal perspective.
What wasn't so strong was focus and consistency. There were mini-games, linear set-pieces on rails, and in other scenes it wasn't clear at all what to do and where to go to progress. It felt sometimes like you were wandering through an art gallery but couldn't find the exit - some clearer hints might have been appreciated.
A lot of the symbolism and allegory was very Christian. As a non-Christian I found it difficult sometimes to understand the message, and I reckon a lot of it went over my head. Anything as deeply personal as this was going to be hit and miss against a mass market. Nonetheless, the environments created were simple, beautiful and imaginative.
For me I really, really wanted to like this game... but in the end I couldn't connect with it as I had hoped, but that doesn't mean that you shouldn't give it a chance.

There are many game series I came late into, and the second installment is usually a good indicator of what the development team behind a series is like in regards to how they feel about their game.
The console oriented approach of CDPR may have raised some eyebrows back when it was new information, and with catastrapohes such as Dragon Age 2 it's understandable to be apprehensive of what is generally seen as a focus on console in order to create more mass appeal and thus sell more copies, regardless of the quality of the game. People first assumed this was the case with CDPR and The Witcher 2, that the devs of a deep (if mechanically lacking) RPG based on a niche series of stories by a Polish author based on Slavic mythology had sold out to push more copies and make more money.
Whilst that goal is pretty much universal across game developers and companies in general, you need only play the Witcher 2 for a few minutes to see for yourself that it is not what drove the developers to make the game they did.
It cannot be said that The Witcher 2 is not flawed, it has difficulty with basic things such as inventory management being time-consuming and non-combat movement being janky, and numerous geometry issues in certain areas across the game. Where the game is successful however, is in it's design of location, character, story and monsters that make it interesting, and the brutal conviction with which it conveys to you all of this that makes it a game that is all to easy to get completely enthralled in, with plenty to do and plenty more ways to do them.

My actual least favourite character at the beginning was Fuyuhiko because he was rude, grumpy, didn’t care about anyone and was ready to let everyone die. I've been really looking for a game that allows me to be immersed in a world far away from my own. I've wanted to go into this mystical trance, experiencing something totally foreign to myself.
Abzu is as though you're reading a book about an infinite water, a world without land. It's a story, a piece of poetry, a sacred place to lose yourself. There is no reason to contemplate why you're doing what you're doing; there is a story to the game as well, but it's not necessarily the primary reason to play it - you'll see what I mean.
This is a game about Zen. This is a game about exploring the depths of a lost ocean. This is a game about feeling a sense of wonder you haven't experienced since you were a child.
In essence, Abzu is much more than just a breath of fresh air into a generation of dull and unoriginal titles, it's something that proves video games don't need to rely on violence, jump scares or utilize rpg mechanics in order to be engaging (in fact, I'd argue that the industry needs expand it's horizon a bit more).
Please, though, don't hesitate on picking up this incredible experience.
The $20 price tag is steep though, so I'd wait until it's ~50% off.

I do not know which was more impressive: the visuals or the music. They play off of each other so well that I do not believe the game would be nearly as good as it is if either were changed even a little bit. The gameplay, if it could be called such, is simple, as it is entirely based around movement and an activation button. The puzzles are as simple as the controls, which is fine in a game so focused on the exploration and the wildlife. At first I thought the animals you were going to see would be fantastical, but it is actually all animals that either are currently alive or existed on our planet many millennia ago. The story isn’t explained at any point, which is fine. You have to search the ruins of a (I assume) dead civilization and form your own guess as to what happened. There are one or two twists here and there that shouldn’t be to shocking for people with eyes. Very short. Less than two hours for me to beat, and I spent some time in each of the rooms. I will probably go back at some point and thoroughly examine every single detail I can find.
TL;DR: A beautiful, charming, and innocent adventure into an ocean of uncertainty and life. Definitely more of an experience than a game in the traditional sense. But that certainly doesn’t lessen its value. I walked away from Abzu feeling like I should go get my diving license before summer begins.

9/10. I was skeptical of this game at first and questioned if it was what I needed in a hack n slasher/beat em up game. I also expected it to be more "furry" cuz of how it looks on the outside. Glad to say it isn't and it's actually really damn beyond my expectations in what I thought I was going to play. I'll just put some pros and cons below and let you decide. Overall it exceeded almost every expectation and did more.
+The combat system while simple is still addictive as hell to play. There were times I just didn't want to stop playing at all because of how far my combo's would rise and I'd just wanna keep going and going. The controls/feel of the game isn't too floaty or "concrete", you feel very fluid and have lots of momentum/feel for your movement. Your attacks and movement can get out of control at first until you realize that "less is more". In the sense that you don't have to spam attack buttons and expect a win, in fact you'll prolly end up losing if you do that. You end up learning this game isn't just mashing buttons or combos to kill, it actually requires you to think out your movements/attacks accordingly, fast.
+It's VERY fast paced and intuitive to learn. The times I got "tutorials" on how to do something were only when I actually did need to know how to do something. The rest followed through as natural and didn't get shoved into your face by force. The game taught as you played and continued to do so just as Megaman/Metroid games have done. Without a "how to play" mode or a "press this button to do this" being told to you every moment. Again, the only time it did the latter was when it was actually something somewhat complicated. I never felt rushed or like I was being stalled on something I didn't know how to already do, I felt like I was taken through a breeze and did what I want as I please. (not to mention, Fidget can make some of the dialogue 4th wall breaking and hilarious, so even if you want to play without knowing anything at all on how to play from the NPC's, the dialogue is still pretty comedic to hear and very well done in terms of voice acting).
+Graphically stunning for being 2d, it feels like you're playing something truly beautiful despite it not being the typical 3d game
+The music and sounds are amazing sounding. I know it's silly but every explosion/cut really helps you feel the action.
+Gonna emphasize the combat system again, it's pretty simple again.. but it's also just so good that I sometimes would wish there were more mobs to kill because of  how often I'd find myself going into so many chains and slashing away to my will without end.
+The plot has it's touching moments, it's seriousness, and it's comedic loose bits to help you feel a lil at ease. In every case you'd expect the story to go how you think it would, it literally kept me from expecting anything. Every time I thought "oh, this is gonna happen", became the literal "wow...." and blew my mind.
+Metroid/Megaman-esque. The linear gameplay this game gave me had me in love. It was so good at directing me anyway it needed me to go while also giving me the freedom of doing whatever I wanted when I wanted to. It kept me from going where I shouldn't and kept me in order for the plot and correct areas to be in for my levels while giving me space to decide what I wanna do. No one likes being pushed around 24/7... this game doesn't do that, and actually makes you feel like you want to keep finding out more and do more, reaching both the plot's potential and your own skill's potential.
-As fun as this game is. After you beat the game and perfect everything 100%.. the replay value is lacking. I mean you can play it again on multiple modes but if you're like me and played it on the difficult settings and etc and got all the achievements in 1 go.... it can get old. It's well worth spending over 20 hours worth of playing but once you beat it to what you wanted to.... you'll feel like there's nothing left to do. The treasure hunting and perfection play of finding each map area helps in the replay value being less since you can easily figure out on the map where you haven't gone or what you should go to. Keeps a lil of the adventuring aspect out after you figured out how this game works.
-The plot is pretty fantastic, there is some lil bits missing here and there I still have questions about. Nothing too major or big, just personal lil bits that I feel like should've had some attention brought to.
-The combat system is a double edged sword. It's very fun and simple, but te part about it being simple is that it can get repetitive. Your attacks consist of about 3-4 combos, 1 button to do your basic attacks, and the other for an attack known as dust storm. A lot of the game's focus is around Dust storm, it was fun at first but after you play for a bit, sometimes it can get old or just simplistic. I loved combo'ing and chaining together but when you figure out you have magic and dust storm combined to make pretty good attacks that can handle everything for you. It can feel boring/tedious at times. It's controlled, and it's not like you can spam it, but you may get bored not having a huge assortment of combos/attacks available to you despite it fulfilling the need to hack away at millions of monsters.
Neutral.... Everyone's a creature. Everything is "furry" but I know most people see the word furry and think of the worst things. It's not that at all but tbh, the game could've gone without using that idea as the theme. That's me personally, some things could've looked darker or had more to them but were instead drawn cute and animal-ques. It fits for being nice/soft for being an E+ game but at the same time I feel it could've been more without the concept. It's up to each individual on this aspect and can be interpreted based on perspective. I didn't mind it at all and never felt it was overpowered in the game.
Overall, I give it a 9/10. The game's plot moved me and touched my heart, the gameplay was addictive and enticing enough for me to want to explore every area 100%. It was so linear and had amazing conveyance, I never once questioned "WHAT DO I DO?", or at least I didn't for very long at all without figuring it out myself. My opinion after 16 hours of playing GCIII - game mechanics are almost identical to GCII, and the whole thing feels like a graphic remake of its predecessor, but it also feels incomplete. Here are few problems:
Beginning with Interface menus that do not offer even a half of the options you had before to customize your experience during gameplay. Resource icons for example make a mess out of the map when zoomed out, making it really hard to observe the gameplay. I haven't found any options to address this.
Taxing system for your colonies is removed and only way to manage your economical income is through single wealth/manufacturing/research slider. I don't yet have a definitive opinion on this, but for now this new income system feels little vague.
The hype about incredible AI that utilizes each core of your expensive i7 to provide you the best and most complex GalCiv experience is just hype. Reality is that for 16 hours of gameplay I haven't noticed any singe improvement compared to GalCIv II. The opponents react exactly the same in same situations, making same diplomatic propositions, and making same strategic mistakes as before (small example: just leave barely habitable class 5 planet next to your starting homeworld and AI rush to take it, spending a colony ship and bunch of money for improvements, just to loose the planet after few turns due to overwhelming influence of your nearby homeworld).
Spying is completely missing leaving you to guess what your opponents are doing, researching or building on their home planets. I read somewhere that developers plan to program "deeper" spying system than before, so they left it completely out. Really? Releasing a full-priced game without a crucial feature that existed in its predecessor, with a promise that it will be included in eventual DLCs that you have to pay for additionally?
Why developer haven't taken more time to finish their ideas and then release the full version, or at least implement the old style feature and then improve it later?
Speaking to another civilization should lead to trading screen right away (99% of the time this is where player wants to go), rather than opening a pointless splash screen. It is eye candy, but it is very inconvenient as you have to click twice. Furthermore, "trade with you", and "declare war on you" are two choices just next to each other making it a miss-click accident waiting to happen.
There are more smaller and bigger issues to remark and I will edit this interview if I find more or if I change my opinion on it, but in its current state this release is not worth the money as it offers less than GalCiv II.

What can you say about Final Fantasy VII that hasn't already been said?  It's one of the best Final Fantasy games to date, which is easily said due to all of it's spinoffs like the absolutely thrilling Dirge of Cerbeus, the wonderful prequil Chrisis Core, and the ever popular movie Advent Children (just to name a few).
That said, there are some good and bad with this Steam version of Final Fantasy VII, so lets get the list going;
CONS:
- Requires you to be online and sign in via Square Enix before playing.
- Cloud saving is slow (2-5 min pause) and you can't Save/Load until it's ready.
- No additional content added.
- Subtitles have been censored, which actually removes a bit of character emotion.
PROS:
- Final Fantasy VII
- Graphical Enhancements (allowing high resolutions).
- Video and Overlayed characters are better synced.
- Music has been updated (uses the higher-quality playstation audio tracks)
- Subtitles have been "repaired" to remove "engrish" language.
- Fully mapable keys & controller support.
- Ability to disable cloud saving.
So is the game something I would recommend?  Of course it is!  It's Final Fantasy 7 for cryin out loud!  But...  If you already own a copy of Final Fantasy VII on a console than there is no real reason to get this one.  There isn't any new content, just updating for modern PC technology.  That said, if you have the older PC version (and love it) then replacing it with this one might be a good idea.
As far as the price, I don't actually believe this game is worth $17.  I'm willing to bet most individuals who are looking to purchase this game are doing so because they already have Final Fantasy VII and are simply looking to update it...  I purchased it during a 50% off sale for $8.49, which I consider a decent price.
All in all I'm giving this a NOT recommended.  Shocked?  Well it's true that I love Final Fantasy VII but Square Enix screwed up with a few things.  First, this is a single-player only game so an internet account should NOT be a requirement.  Second, the regular price is a little high for a game that is almost 20 years old (no matter how good it is).  Third, the Cloud Save feature (which is the only real reason for being online) is so horribly slow you'd be better off going back to CD swapping.
So as much as I'd love to give this a thumbs up, because I really love this game, I simply can't.

Well well, what must I say about this game, voted as one of the greatest video games of all time, seen as one of the best games in the Final Fantasy franchise, and known for its colossal impact on gaming? Well. If your a gamer like me, who plays games by heart and not eyes (heart being story and eyes being blown away from games featuring explosions guns and violence), then this is a game for YOU. Before I go in depth of how amazing this game is, I must tell you how I got into the Final Fantasy franchise.
As a kid I shied away from the series because honestly the roman numerals in the games was just too confusing and at the time I was a strict Nintendo fanboy. Times have changed, I am no longer a strict Nintendo fanboy though I still am but now I accept other games. I gave Final Fantasy 1 a try and quickly got hooked. Then I moved on to 2 and at that point it was clear I am now a Final Fantasy fanboy. I then went to 3, and at the time (all of this happened recently btw), there was a Steam deal going on. The Square Enix publisher discount stuff. Final Fantasy 7 and 8 were in that, and I had some spare change and decided it would be a fantastic idea to purchase two Final Fantasy games with the highest amount of reputation within the franchise. I did not regret that decision, it was clearly worth buying. Now, back to our discussion on why the game is great.
This game, is addictive. No, not addictive in a bad way like Minecraft (You know, playing all day losing your mind). Addictive story-wise. The story in this game is ENGAGING ON SOO MANY LEVELS. IT DOES NOT AT ALL FEEL LIKE I AM PLAYING A GAME ITSELF, BUT WATCHING A MOVIE WITH A DEEP STORY AND AMAZING CUTSCENES AND FLASHBACKS. The gameplay itself is interesting and apealing to me. When I play the game, I don't care for the gameplay, I am anxious to see what happens next in the story. When a game gets you feeling like this, it is clear why Final Fantasy 7 is regarded or arguably one of the greatest games of all time. Its games like this one we just don't see anymore, it really does suck because I myself wish that these games with all these DLC's and micro-transactions would just STOP and use this game as an analogy to what a perfect game should be. This game is a classic, I had no problems with it other than how frustrating it was to get my freakin Square Enix account setup. If you can get past that one problem, you got yourself a perfect beautiful game right here. In conclusion, I say if you are one who enjoys a great story with fun gameplay, then this game is worth your 12 dollars. Or, at the moment if the deal is still going, its half off.

I was unable to play the game once I entered the lighthouse due to what appeared to be a bug in the game, resulting in a downvote. I submitted a helpdesk ticket to ubisoft (I'm on mac, but they apparently don't admit to have a mac version, so I submitted it to the windows help desk) and got a useless response. They basically had me install every OS X update and some flash installers, none of which really helped. I felt like I had just called comcast and the script the "helpful" individual on the other end had them read the same thing, even if it was totally innappropriate.
However, I changed my recommendation after following the directions in one of the steam forums. Apparently, this is a 32 bit game and, for mac users, you must find the actual program and mark it as such in order to get decent playability. Once you do, it is fine (though, not a stellar experience). I'm pretty sure Macs have been 64 bit for over 10 years now. But, maybe the code they are using is still 32 bit and they can't afford to have someone actually update it? Even the PC version isn't 10 years old...
The game plays more or less like the old M&M games that came before it, but with better graphics. Having grown up with games like this, I prefer the turn based combat. There are some real problems, such as situations where the enemy you are fighting doesn't actually appear on your screen. However, you can still blow them away with fireballs, even if you have no clue where they are. I've seen pirates walk through walls to fight you, and combat turns for the opponent can take several minutes as the animations dig through to find you.
All in all, this is a decent remake of those old school dungeon grinders that were king back in the 90s but modernized for semi modern hardware. If they put some work tuning the engine itself, it would probably be a great iPad or android game. Hopefully, it will get some attention and they'll fix some of the more annoying bugs (and maybe bring it into the 21rst centry of 64 bit hardware?). But, even now, it's a fun game that can be enjoyed for hours.
