I'm going to slog through this game anyway out of dedication to the series, but honestly... it's pretty bad. If you've ever played any of the original Might & Magic games and were excited to play the much-hyped revamp... well, that's too bad, because there isn't really anything they have in common with them aside from some loose superficiality.
Character creation:
There really isn't any. This may seem surprising at the outset -- after all, hasn't this kind of always been a hallmark of the entire series? Tweak your character and your party (because, hey, who wants the default party, right?) and test your theories to see if it's survivable. Sometimes you may not even find out until halfway through the game. Balance your party with early, mid, and late-game classes, and grind your way up to success, right?
Well.. no. There are four races, and each race has three classes (a 'might' class, a 'magic' class, and a hybrid class). Each one gets one or two special abilities once they're promoted (like MM6), and also like MM6, you have to receive 'training' to go from novice to expert to master to grandmaster in your skills. Like MM6, these trainers are also spread all throughout the world, and you have to learn where they are (or read a spoiler). Your class choice feels almost entirely flavourless, and pretty much only determines what skills you can raise to what caps (and at times, what skills you can even learn at all). Also, you only get four party members.
Control and feel:
The game is on a grid, like Xeen-style era of Might & Magic, and things only move when you do. Monsters don't patrol, however, and unless they 'see' you, they won't go anywhere. When they do see you, the 'danger' light turns hostile, and they will proceed to chase you... forever. You cannot outrun monsters or get them to some kind of 'tether' range, so if you step into the wrong area, your only option is to reload the game. There is no fleeing.
NPCs are also like the Xeen era of M&M, in the sense that they appear to only be found in towns (or in map objects on the main map), and do not move. They CAN be found standing around in the game world in towns, but do not actually move. The ones that you can't talk to (which is most of them) do, however, tend to say one of possibly four or five quipped lines, which will replay, endlessly, every time you are standing near them. This is also true of 'environment' sound effects like mumbling, people shuffling things, hammers on anvils, etc. It is generally one sound that loops forever until you step away.
UI:
The UI is pretty minimal, which is OK. There is an 'action bar', akin to the one on most MMOs, with 10 slots that you can set for each of your 4 party members. Frequently, however (particularly on a mage), you will have to go to your skill book and manually cast from there, as it's simply not feasable to have everything you need on the bar. Not a big deal; it's split up intelligently.
There is a minimap, which autorecords your progress on a gridded map. Unfortunately, however, you can not scroll this map even when you make it larger, so if you're looking for somewhere that's off the side of the enlarged map, too bad.
Gameplay:
There aren't terribly many spells per spell 'level' per school, but there are a lot of schools, which means there's still a hefty amount of spells. Unlike previous games in the series, there are not 'master' or 'grandmaster' schools of each element, there are simply libraries in each town that have all the spells and you pick from there.
Weapons and armour can break (this appears to be random chance -- I had a new item I just picked up break in a second combat, and a weapon I used the entire game until then -- 17 hours in -- never break), which degrades their stats until you go to town to repair it. There is no 'mobile repair' that I've encountered yet, though perhaps there is a spell for it that I'm unaware of.
Like previous Might and Magic games, you can have two 'hirelings' (sometimes one or both may be a mandatory 'quest' hireling), but these hirelings do not participate in combat as they did in the later versions -- they are back to simply providing an auxiliary benefit for a small percentage cut of your gold and a hiring fee.
There is no grinding, not because grinding is not necessary, but because monsters do not respawn. Ever. If you have killed a monster, it is permanently gone. This means that there is a *fixed* finite level of gold and loot in the game, and even things like the "well, it'll respawn in a few months" option in previous iterations of the series is gone.
There is no party formation -- each spot in the party lineup is equal, and it doesn't matter if you get flanked or attacked from behind. Everything does the same damage with the same random odds of it hitting someone as anything else.
Like some later M&M games, you get food (called 'supplies' in this one) to camp, and can only camp so many times before having to resupply. Camping cannot be interrupted.
Areas are 'gated' by progress -- did you put points into 'shield' to get it to expert level (the first tier past the starting one) so you can have that extra edge on the boss you're fighting in the beginning? Well, too bad, because that's in the second town, and you can't get there no matter what because some NPC is standing around saying the bridge is off limits, or the gates are shut, or what-have-you. Everything is limited in this fashion -- you may be given a region to explore in that's open (and consequently, may have monsters too hard for you -- which, again, you can't run from, you simply have to reload), but anything outside of that region is always gated. Don't know what trainers are available in the area and don't want to read spoilers? Sucks to be you, because if you opted to put things into your skills and got to a skill tier that's in the next 'zone', you don't get to use it.
You have one single inventory, and it's on a grid that does not get larger. Later you will find yourself needing to stop your dungeon delve to go back to town to sell everything, which is mildly obnoxious. I don't yet know if the Lloyd's Beacon spells have made it into this game, however, because...
Faithfulness to source material:
None. This isn't Might & Magic, this is Heroes of Might and Magic: the RPG, which is a *distinctly different game*. The original Might & Magic games were a kind of silly but fun hybrid of extreme sci-fi with high fantasy. There were spaceships and computers and people and races from other planets, and later your samurai would be dodging ray guns from robots. There is and will be none of that here (one early NPC, in fact, says he was exiled because he thought that stars might be other planets), because this is all set in Ashan, the world from the Heroes of Might and Magic games. This is actually *incredibly irritating*, much moreso than I thought it would be or than it sounds on the surface, but I think it has something to do with the fact that this was touted as a long-awaited return of a game for the fans, and then (presumably Ubisoft) proceeded to crap all over everything that would've actually done that.
Conclusion:
The game basically feels like Grimrock, except there aren't any secrets you can spy (you just cast the detect secrets spell, and if you don't have it up, the secrets don't show up, period) and the plot is less interesting. Yes, the plot is *less interesting* than "yo we put you doods in a hole gl hf." I've dutifully been reading everything that I've come across, including all the lore books, and I really just don't care at all about it. It's extremely low-tier regional politics (that will, I'm sure, eventually involve demons or angels or both), and I'm 20 hours in (the amount of time sunk being telling, given that everything is gated and linear).
I'm really not happy with it. The entire game plays like a demo game that's a lead-in for user content. Sad.

There are many game series I came late into, and the second installment is usually a good indicator of what the development team behind a series is like in regards to how they feel about their game.
The console oriented approach of CDPR may have raised some eyebrows back when it was new information, and with catastrapohes such as Dragon Age 2 it's understandable to be apprehensive of what is generally seen as a focus on console in order to create more mass appeal and thus sell more copies, regardless of the quality of the game. People first assumed this was the case with CDPR and The Witcher 2, that the devs of a deep (if mechanically lacking) RPG based on a niche series of stories by a Polish author based on Slavic mythology had sold out to push more copies and make more money.
Whilst that goal is pretty much universal across game developers and companies in general, you need only play the Witcher 2 for a few minutes to see for yourself that it is not what drove the developers to make the game they did.
It cannot be said that The Witcher 2 is not flawed, it has difficulty with basic things such as inventory management being time-consuming and non-combat movement being janky, and numerous geometry issues in certain areas across the game. Where the game is successful however, is in it's design of location, character, story and monsters that make it interesting, and the brutal conviction with which it conveys to you all of this that makes it a game that is all to easy to get completely enthralled in, with plenty to do and plenty more ways to do them.

In short, this a 3D top-down shooter with maps - typically urban environments with grid-like streets - and objectives for each level/map. As far as arcade action goes, it is pretty entertaining. You have your infinte-fire machine gun, and then gain the ability to add other secondary weapons as you progress - such as rockets or a beam. Mission objectives vary from map-to-map/mission-to-mission - generally destroying certain targets (such as boss enemies or crates), clearing the stage of enemies, or simply reaching the exit. The latter generally requires deactiving force fields by roaming the streets looking for red lights to run over. There are items to find on the map to increase your score, and of course you're free to kill as many enemies as you like, even if that isn't the objective. You'll probably find yourself doing so anyway, given their aggressiveness.
The controls are pretty tight, and aiming feels very natural. I do wish the player's ship was a bit more agile, making it easier to dodge bullets. All in all, it seems like a good distraction, but more structured than other twin-stick shooters like Beat Hazard. I don't know how long it would take to wear out its welcome, but given the amount of weapon upgrades, and the ability to easily play in short 15-30 minute bursts, I'd give it at least 4-5 hours.

Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is a sequel to its first game and developed by the same company. Every single aspect from a first game returns to this with an even more mini games introduced and overall even more engaging story and debating. Danganronpa 2 is not a copy paste of the first game, it's an upgraded version of the game itself. Danganronpa sets a good example of how sequel game should be made.
Just like everything else from first game, the extraordinary students once against are forced to murder each other so that they can get out of mastermind's prison, now takes place in the whole island called jabberwock island. Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair puts you in the shoes of Hajime Hinata, a students with unknown talent because he doesn't remember it (Sound familiar?). The game played exactly like the previous game, you will need to find a clue, ask your friend and figure out each incident to find the bottom of this, as well as the mystery of the island itself. Class Trial will be held once the dead body is discovered and students have completed their investigation, all other survivors students are forced to debated at each other until they figure out who did kill their friend. You will need to reconsider your clue, find contradiction in between each debating and shoot them all down with your truth bullet, if what they say and your clue matches, then the mystery is broken down and thus another step close to the truth. The rules are the same as previous game, if murderers success in not letting anyone find out about them, they will be freed as all other students will be executed, but if all students find out who're  murderers then they alone will be executed and all survivor students can live for another as killing game continues.
As ones would expected, the story in this game once again contain so many twists. The murder scenes are executed flawlessly with the even more reasonable motivations behind them. The warm, humorous and heartbreaking will be waiting for you. Stellaris is another magnificient grand strategy title from Paradox Development Studio that is incredibly deep, immensely detailed and highly ambitious. The game is also championed by a vastly improved user interface when compared with other Paradox games and has a far more inviting learning curve without losing the challenge or depth that the other games by this highly regarded developer offer.
Paradox are widely known for their catalogue of strategy games over the years which are of a very high quality but are also remarkably complex to an extent; some newcomers and even veterans of the genre felt alienated, confused and simply overwhelmed. Stellaris however, has a fully fledged tutorial integrated into the main campaign which not only guides you through the general mechanics along with each feature in a constructive manner; it explains aspects clearly and this is further supported by a far more user friendly interface. The screen is less cluttered when compared with the likes of Europa Universalis IV and all the information is clear, condensed and well presented.
The game takes place in space which is an almost Call of Duty style departure from the typical Paradox titles of classic eras and a real world setting. The premise is also slightly different as you create your colony from scratch or by selecting some preset examples instead of guiding an already established country. Your goal in the galaxy is to explore, build, research, expand, conquer and even exterminate all other races you come across - basically exactly what you'd expect from a 4X title. You can play this game however you wish and at your own pace -  you may opt to be a fanatic militarist or simply want to discover as much of the universe as possible whilst befriending and benefitting from other races you meet along the way. It is a massively detailed and highly engrossing experience in which the developers have made the transition from reality to sci-fi in a very credible fashion.
Stellaris runs superbly too and is bolstered by truly fantastic atmosphere enhancing audio that compliments your game throughout. The visuals are very good too and the galaxy map whilst despite looking rather basic, is easy to grasp and understand which is another massive plus. Overall; Stellaris is another superb Paradox title that is riddled with depth and a long term challenge but is also presented and executed in a far more appealling and enjoyable way than some previous titles by the studio. This game will have a bright future and is sure to provide many hours of entertainment.

First thing: know what you're getting into.  This is a personal-narrative driven game (I hesitate to call it a game because it's more of an interactive story which lasts approximately two hours).  Gameplay is NOT the point of the experience.
The audio is incredibly well done.  I played with headphones (as is recommended), and was completely drawn in by the music and the voices of each person, especially knowing that Ryan and Amy's voices were their own--it was not "voice-acting."
It's the genuine touches that make it so emotional.  You look at the pictures within the game, you read the letters, and it moves you because it's REAL.  I think it's important to differentiate between entertainment, which likely includes most of the content in our steam libraries, and representations of Real Life, which is how I would categorize That Dragon, Cancer.

You may end up loving it.

An amazingly relaxing and moving game.  Abzu is similar to Journey in many ways in that you are a traveler in a strange, beautiful world, a story told without words but which moves you through music and visuals.  Abzu doesn't quite eclipse Joureny for a few reasons, but it's an amazing game, with calming, tense, and angelic music in places.  The environmental story telling is top notch and can convey emotions and feelings without any words.  There's even a few surprising twists in the game's story, which is surprising because it's...you know, a game without words, told entirely through visuals.
Abzu doesn't beat out Journey for two reasons.  The first is, this game is underwater, which, while providing some breathtaking visuals, sealife, and a feeling of exploration...can be a bit fiddly to control.  The choice for movement will leave your trigger fingers sore and sometimes a bit confused as to how to move your guy.  Underwater is harder than a simple desert, like in Journey, so this is understandable.  Something that bothered me here was an inclusion of collectibles.  Some people like them, but for me, they distracted from the beauty of my surroundings.  There's not many and you can ignore them, but I'm a bit OCD, so...it bothered me a bit.
All that said, those are very minor nitpicks.  Abzu is a breathtaking game that will make you feel, with moments of joy and sadness to eclipse many modern releases.  The scenes of a world being reborn rival Okami in their beauty when they happen.  The visual style may not be complex, but it can do so much more through stylization than any AAA title could do with realism.
Abzu is an absolutely amazing adventure and while a bit pricey at 20 dollars, is absolutely worth the plunge.  Dive into uncharted waters and find an amazing world waiting for you.

I enjoy the game.  I've played through every race at least once. Some races are much easier to play than others, in my opinion.  My review shows the hours I've spent in the game, so it should be clear that I like the game, so I'm just going to list what I don't like.
Cons:
- Difficulty levels are wonky as hell. The same difficulty will be super easy one game and unbearably difficult the next.
- No ability to disable animations for combat.
- No ability to "ignore" or "auto-fight" planet battles. This is important on big games when you get a little behind and the AI camps your planets attacking 20 different planetary defenses each turn.  Each time, you have to click "quick battle" and then still wait for the animations to play.  While "neato" the first few times, it makes the game unnecessarily long.
- No way to filter ships other than "Core" (built in formats) and "User" (your custom designs).  This is especially hampering in late game stages when you have every possible ship format for Cargo, Tiny, Small, Medium, Large and Huge, particularly so when you change races often so the default ship names become meaningless.
- Queued ships don't automatically upgrade to the latest vesion, this feature was present in both 1 & 2.
The worst:
Sometimes the game will get into a runaway loop.  The worse I've experienced so far ramped RAM usage over 16gb, disk I/O to 99% and all 4 cores at 99%.  Before I could get the process ended via task manager, the system was comletely unstable and even wiped out display on both monitors.  Before you say I've an underpowered machine, here's the specs:
4770K OC @ 3.9Ghz
32Gb RAM (1866)
GeForce 980ti 6gb
Samsung Solid State drive
Modular 1200W power supply
3 extra 120MM case cooling fans
I'm hoping Stardock will improve on some of these issues over time, needless to say, I will continue playing regardless.

I genuinely forgot about Steel Storm until the trading card update. The 90 minutes I played some years ago wasn't impressive. And coming back to it today, the game is shockingly familiar. The single-player campaign is the same, no improvements or changes stuck out.
Unfortunately, that campaign is pretty boring. I played a few more missions this time, but according to the only Steam guide on the game, I've seen almost every enemy except the final boss in just a few missions. The levels are bland, focused heavily on backtracking and trap sections. The AI is nothing impressive, even for 2011 standards, with most enemies being simple to fight. The only challenge of the game is the approach of traps and spawns. Even though these traps quickly become predictable, you can still be quickly overwhelmed as enemies spawn in all directions. Basic enemies can be threatening, and I've lost 100% of my health to a salvo of rockets I couldn't avoid. Due to this, the best approach is to exploit corners and weapons so enemies can't get a clear shot. Going toe-to-toe with hitscan enemies is a fight you can't win, so the strongest approach is to kill them blindly.
Pretty simply, the game is very underwhelming. It feels mediocre for a shooter, especially at the price point. Maybe multiplayer is better, but the community is not very active. Steel Storm doesn't really do anything special or noteworthy, and really isn't a game worth remembering.

The deeper you go in this game, the better it gets. The first few floors are very grindy and repetitive. This game has been in development for many years and boy, does it show (in a good way!). It SHINES with polish and the excellence and bug-free experience ANY game can have with sufficient, dedicated development time constructively spent by active developers on working out the kinks, improving and optimizing the graphics, ramping up the coolness factor of the bullet streams, increasing the enemies' intelligence and their pathfinding and tactics, increasing the detail of the textures and improving the lighting and gameplay and...
...well, Steel Storm: Burning Retribution (SSBR) has been through the equivalent of many "early access" development cycles without having used early access time.
I believe I first downloaded it on Sourceforge long ago when it was available for Linux and Windows. I think.
Back to the point: SSBR is a polished, satisfying game. You might find yourself spending more time playing SSBR than you anticipate!
And that's just the single-player part. I haven't even delved into the multiplayer portion of the game with its collection of multiplayer variants
. SSBR is like a third-person Unreal Tournament or Quake with modern graphics and mechs and hovertanks instead of humanoids. And limited, rather than infinite, respawns. And double kills, triple kills, quadruple kills, etc. And a LOT of weapons.
SSBR is, by default, played while viewing your HoverTank from a top-down, third-person perspective. There's an automap in the corner and a larger toggleable map, but don't give up on it if that's not your cup of tea: the main camera can be positioned anywhere you want near your character (unless the camera options have been altered; I remember on an old build using a primary camera a little above and behind my vehicle with other buttons bound to cameras looking in forward/back/left/right/etc. directions from the POV of my vehicle. I remember lots of clipping errors in that build from many years ago, which was probably using a different engine.) When I played it today
, I noticed no clipping errors at all. Two camera options are available to choose as defaults, but individual features (e.g. speed of camera movement, camera response delay following your having turned or moved your vehicle, angle of camera relative to ground, angle relative to the vehicle, angle relative to a fixed base, etc.)) within those options can be changed, etc.
I don't know if the multiple access-anytime camera angles are possible in the current build, but it would not surprise me. If you like games with lots of options to play with, SSBR can probably help to satisfy you.
If you like playing HoverTank DM/CTF/etc. or the much larger than I remember single-player tutorial and campaign(s), this game is different enough and contains enough similar and different features that it's an enjoyable experience.
By default, SSBR's controls are mapped to keyboard, joystick, X360pad, and mouse. The mappings can be changed at will from the main menu or the in-game pause menu.
The detailed and varying barrels and crates and bins and boxes and scenery are gloriously destructible. Unless it's a legitimate barrier (for which you will be grateful after you learn they can provide good cover from behind which to snipe turrets and other baddies), it can be destroyed... and what will the destruction leave in its wake? Repair parts to give you more health? An additional vehicle respawn ("life")? A new weapon? or a huge number of parts exploding all over the place, adding only to your score? The number of 'gibs' an exploding item releases can be set to preference.

This is my review for The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings (4/10)
(Negative Review)
1/5 - Annoying
2/5-Frustrating
3/5-Bad
4/5-Very Bad
5/5-Extremely Bad
I'm going to focus only on the negative things about this game, which made me uninstall and stop playing this game, after 11 hours.
1) Quests : (3/5)
Some quests (Side quests mostly) don't have a waypoint so you will spend minutes figuring out where to go, and each place is big enough which makes it frustrating and eventually you will not have enough powers to continue and end the quest.
2) Enemy AI : (4/5) -
The enemy AI is annoying in some points because you will see your health get lower for no reason, or too soon, and then you are dead within the first seconds.
Not even mentioning fighting bosses (like the Kayran, which made no sense at all).
Also, you will find yourself fighting an enemy multiply times because you will have to reload the checkpoint because you keep dieing.
3) Game Features : (4.5/5)
Alchemy, Potions, Enhancements, Skills , Crafting Items - All of this and I had no idea what to do with those.
Alchemy - Useless, Complicated, hard to understand.
Potions - How can I even use them?
Enhancements - Complicated,
Skills - Why in hell, I can't pick/choose a skill when I'm a level 7 already?
Crafting Items - Some items I didn't even know where to get.
4) Level of Boredom/Frustration : (4/5)
I did enjoy playing this game in some moments, mostly because I enjoyed fighting different types of enemies, using different tactics including swords/bombs/signs etc..
But, leave all of this and what do you do in this game? Just traveling from place to place figuring out what to do next.
You will either get lost, or get bored in some quests which lead to nowhere.
If you don't have patience, don't play this game.
5) Health System : (5/5)
Last thing which made me quit the game. Why? Because you can't regenerate the health during combat (Potions don't work, and there is no other way)
So, in one time you will fight multiply enemies and doing one mistake, so you die.
Or in other time, you will fight some big♥♥♥♥♥enemy which hit you so hard that you forgot or couldn't dodge, and lower your health down to -50% in one hit.
So this was my review, a generous and not so harsh even tho I did get annoyed or angry in some points.

Updated after 40+ hours of gameplay.
In short: Stellaris is an engaging and hugely promising 4X game. It's a blast to play, and does a masterful job at combining 4X and Paradox-style grand strategy. Patches and DLCs will only make it better.
=== The good ===
Graphics and artwork are great, and the music is simply wonderful. They both set the mood so well, along with all the "plot events" related to anomalies your research ships discover and various random events like the ones you find in EU, HOI, and CK.
Exploration gameplay consists mainly of assigning scientists to research projects and science ships and using them to explore the galaxy and unlock new techs. The random nature of both anomalies, story events, and technologies sets an atmosphere of exploration and disocvery, and you really feel like you're a species setting off to brave the cosmos. There is great variation and creativity in the techs and story events, too. I also love how there are three means of travelling between systems and that you have to pick one and stick with it for the whole game.
The way you decide on policies, ethics and government types for your species reminds me of other Paradox games, and helps make the various speces feel diverse and immersing while also having a significant impact on what you can and cannot do in-game, increasing replayability value.
You also manage your "pops" and buildings on planets, and use a Stars!-esque ship designer to design your ships. Battles are largelly automated, so winning them depends on good ship designs and finding a good fleet composition.
It should also be noted that the game is incredibly stable, both in single-and multi-player. There's apparently a bug where your friends may not see the gamer you're hosting, but we fixed it by simply launching a hosted game for then to use Steam to send an invite directly to the person who was to join.
=== The bad ===
Earlier I complained about user interface and balance -- these have been improved by patches. The game still doesn't have the depth of the rest of the PDX games, but is still incredibly fun.
One problem is the lack of victory conditions beyond the ones requiring conquest, however, which is a particularly big problem when playing as a pacifist species.
The main problem with the game in my eyes is the lack of depth we've come to love in PDX's games. Diplomacy has been improved greatly by patches, but warfare still easily becomes a battle between stacks of doom.
Also, the various species lack personality. They basically all play the same pretty much regardless of how you design them. Far from the differences between the nations in Crusader Kings II, for example.
All told, however, I find this to be a *great* 4X game, and I can't wait to see what Paradox has up its sleeve for patches and DLCs!

Steel Storm is a retro styled shoot'em up with good controls and reasonable AI that actively tries to avoid your fire.  It's fast and fun with a need for good reflexes.
The addition of a level and full map design tool is also a boon though there are only a few extra campigns out there.  Which do vary in quailty but also offer a good challenge for when you've finished the official campaign.
If you prefer a different challenge then you can also change the view to more like quake and games of that ilk.  This change of view angle makes the 360 field of attack much harder to cover.  Often the tactic you have used to survive in the more top down view will not save you here.
The visual effects and sound effects suit the game perfectly as does the music for the most part.  As with anything however music is down to personal taste and you can always turn it off and play your own if your hardware can handle it.
I've played this on both aging AMD units and state of the art Intel gaming rigs and it played perfectly on all.  For those who have discovered issues there are work arounds which I've also used successfully on some rigs.  Find these on the forums.
Now I'm not going to indicate that the game is perfect.  It does for sure have its flaws.  While it does have plenty of different weapons to sate most play styles the number of types of enemy is limited.
1x Fast and light tank that can zap you and disable all but your starting loadout.  The handicap is temporary of course.
1x Light tank that fires a single plama shot in each volley.
1x Medium tank that fires 4 shots in a volley, as the class implies has more hit points than the light variant.
2x Heavy tanks - one with a plasma turret and minigun turrets and the other with three rapid fire heavy plasma turrets.
4x Types of fixed turrets, plasma, laser, missile, repair.
2x big bads, a carrier and a super heavy tank.
The AI also has a few other problems that occur when there are player friendly or other players in a game.  Often the AI has problems locking on to a target and will constantly change target while never firing a shot.  On occation in multiplayer mobs will spawn and not attack making them easy pickings.   Thankfully a recent patch looks to have reduced these annoyances to virtually zero.
As for DLC, the extra weapons are a nice touch but too few.  The second DLC is a better addition with a whole new campaign with some new game twists which I'll not spoil if you've not tried it.
Overall I found the game to be enjoyable if not a touch repetitive.  If you don't like shoot em' ups this game is not going to change your mind about them.  If you do then give this little overlooked gem a blast.

Another aspect of this game that shines is the music and overall sound of the game. Given that the games visuals are more simplistic in nature, the audio really needed to shine and it does easily.
Overall this game is a solid two hour experience that is great for those looking for a genuine and emotional story. if you are looking for gameplay, this is not the game for you since it is an emotional narrative driven game. I really tip my hat to this family for using such a tragic time in their lives as inspiration for a game. I hope it helped them through the grieving process, knowing that these stories helped people like me deal with similar situations.

An amazingly relaxing and moving game.  Abzu is similar to Journey in many ways in that you are a traveler in a strange, beautiful world, a story told without words but which moves you through music and visuals.  Abzu doesn't quite eclipse Joureny for a few reasons, but it's an amazing game, with calming, tense, and angelic music in places.  The environmental story telling is top notch and can convey emotions and feelings without any words.  There's even a few surprising twists in the game's story, which is surprising because it's...you know, a game without words, told entirely through visuals.
Abzu doesn't beat out Journey for two reasons.  The first is, this game is underwater, which, while providing some breathtaking visuals, sealife, and a feeling of exploration...can be a bit fiddly to control.  The choice for movement will leave your trigger fingers sore and sometimes a bit confused as to how to move your guy.  Underwater is harder than a simple desert, like in Journey, so this is understandable.  Something that bothered me here was an inclusion of collectibles.  Some people like them, but for me, they distracted from the beauty of my surroundings.  There's not many and you can ignore them, but I'm a bit OCD, so...it bothered me a bit.
All that said, those are very minor nitpicks.  Abzu is a breathtaking game that will make you feel, with moments of joy and sadness to eclipse many modern releases.  The scenes of a world being reborn rival Okami in their beauty when they happen.  The visual style may not be complex, but it can do so much more through stylization than any AAA title could do with realism.
Abzu is an absolutely amazing adventure and while a bit pricey at 20 dollars, is absolutely worth the plunge.  Dive into uncharted waters and find an amazing world waiting for you.

I really want to recommend this game, but there are some serious problems. The look, sound, and antmosphere of the game are incredible, and the basic gameplay loop of clearing out rooms is addictive and challenging. However, the AI is incredibly spotty. Sometimes I can walk right in front of a guy and he wont notice me, other times I can kill someone and the guy next to him will chase me, only to get caught in a doorway or forget about me after a few seconds, meaning strategies like baiting guards into rooms are fairly ineffective. Hit detection is also unpredictable, especially using the spacebar to finish off someone who's already down.
The biggest problem, however, is the constant crashes. I never had a session over the 45-60 minute mark that didn't end in a crash. Imagine this: you've cleared two rooms so far and are on the third and final room of the stage. You're starting to get frustrated and your playing is getting a little sloppy, but you're still confident that, given time, you can figure it out. However, you look at the clock and realize you've been playing for a while, and now you have the pressure of finishing this room and completing the level quickly, or otherwise you risk losing all your progress because it's not IF the game crashes, it's WHEN. It adds another layer of tension that the developers didn't intend, and not the good, "I have to kill this guard quickly before the other guard gets back" kind of tension, and more the "If this game crashes again I'm done" type of tension. It's disappointing especially since there is genuine challenge and fun to be had here, but it's balanced out by occasionally unfair gameplay and the looming threat of losing your progress if you don't move fast enough.

Recommended, with reservations. Read below:
ABZÛ is a linear exploration "experience game" from some of the devs who worked on the PS3 masterpiece, Journey.
With this pedigree, I was quite excited to check out what the creative team behind one of my favorite games of all time had to show us next. However, I was pretty disappointed.
ABZÛ follows roughly the same structure as its predecessor, the problem is that it drinks too much from the same well, retreading ideas we've seen before.
ABZÛ tries to hit most of the same moments and setpieces as Journey, in some cases down to the same camera angles and similar musical direction. The problem is that in ABZÛ these setpieces feel unearned. The game is trying to convey this sense of elation and joy without really providing the connective tissue to relate emotionally with the player. The end effect is comparable to that weird remix of a favorite song of yours that, while not ruining it, doesn't quite feel completely right.
It's no surprise that ABZÛ's best moments are the ones that haven't been cribbed directly from Journey, where the game can speak with its own voice. Sadly, they don't occur often enough to elevate it to the same level as its predecessor. While both games feature a unique mythos that the player progressively learns about, the worldbuilding in ABZÛ feels much more unintuitive to grasp compared to the effortlessly integrated lore in Journey.
While retreading similar imagery (historical glyphs, islamic inspired architecture such as gates and corridors, a magical world with its own rules) ABZÛ's version doesn't compare favorably in any aspect to Journey, which makes it feel less elegant in many respects. There's even a collectible aspect that feels like a tacked-on afterthough as opposed to a similar  system in Journey, which was perfectly integrated with both mechanics and narrative and worldbuilding into a holistic component of that game.
I can't really give ABZÛ a "not recommended", because it's not a bad game. The game is gorgeous and features really technically impressive elements like massive schools of fish and wavy seaweed. Swimming around and controlling your character is a joy, the lighting and mood are fantastic and the acuatic flora and fauna are great. It even has manatees! Manatees, you guys!
On its own it holds up as an impressive, if fairly soulless, audiovisual interactive experience. Unfortunately, I can't avoid being disappointed in a game that misses an oportunity to explore new territory and instead just retreads previous ideas, all of which have been executed better in Journey.
If you haven't played Journey. Get hold of a PS3 or PS4 and give it a playthrough before ABZÛ. Otherwise, ABZÛ is still alright, but as harsh as this sounds, you'll be basically getting a low-rent Journey.

When I first became a PC gamer and got Steam, I already knew GMod is a must. It's one of the most amazing sandbox games pretty much ever. The community is huge, despite it being a bit of an old game. The whole purpose of the game is to get mods from the Steam Workshop, and there's always new mods being added. If there's a fandom you like, such as Star Wars or pretty much any other movie or game, chances are there are mods for it on GMod. I love the Star Wars vehicles and the Carter modpack (Stargate mod). If not, you can create your own content and contribute to the community yourself. In sandbox, you can build structures and machines, create your own scenario for a shooter deathmatch (with friends, with NPCs, or both), and explore maps created by fellow players. There's also lots of gamemodes other then just sandbox, and it's easy to invite friends to play since it's integrated with Steam. The only things I don't like about it is it can take a long time to load, especially if you're joining a friend with a lot of mods. Also the  physics can be a little bit crazy. For only ten dollars, this is a must for every PC gamer, in my opinion.

The rhythmic approach to traditional dungeon-crawling (ironically, the very mechanic that left me convinced for the better part of a year that I would not enjoy CoND) distinguishes it from nearly all others. I would draw your attention to interesting titles such as FTL and 868-HACK.  For me, at least, having to move rhythmically (with the exception of at least one character) lends CoND a real time feel.  I know it sounds crazy, but it's quite literally a "turn-based, real time dungeon crawler" with an amazing soundtrack and great controls.  The rhythm sort of compels you to act even while considering enemy movement patterns.  Don't get me wrong: I'm terrible at CoND. It can be addictive, though.  I often have terrible runs followed by better runs that end terribly, which is frustrating.  But the effects and music give it a special charm.  Plus, I can endure such crushing defeats in very short bursts.  I've only played a handful of games each day for that very reason.  Though the pace can feel a bit frenetic at times, enemy patterns are predictable. That's where the turn-based elements come into play.  My many deaths are usually due to a lack of dexterity, but that happens because you don't feel like you have quite have enough time to consider moves.  This is a fallacy, of course, because you can always retreat a bit here and there.  I often feel that the only barriers to success are my own gaming history and preconceived notions.

Bad Things: The game is open world yet it still feels very linear. This is due to the fact that you are stuck in the area in which the story takes place in. If you play all of the side quests along with the main story then you will have explored 100% of the area before you leave. Some bosses give you little warning so that you can not drink potions before battle. Also there isn't a fast travel system so walking back and fourth from quests can be tedious.
All in all I would definately recommend this game. I only wish that I had a next gen or rather current gen console to play the next game on.

Necropolis... There are an abundance of tough-butt games coming out, especially with the success of our beloved Dark Souls series and alongside the plenty of games comes plenty of failures; Necropolis is not that. While many games boast a truthfully brutal environment and tough-as-nails experience, very few truly deliver it and Necropolis succeeds in many ways.
First, the atmosphere: it's beautiful. There's a sense of emptiness and death while parodying many clichèd stories from films and books. You can see the plethora of inspirations and what is trying to be made fun of. You can feel the fog or the snow on the ground because it is so well put together. Nothing seems 'out of place'.
Secondly, the multiplayer. While my gripe lies in the fact that it's dependant on each player actually succeeding and working together via communication (if there is an in-game chat, I've yet to find it) it seems really stressful to have it limited to four players, when I could personally see it supporting six. But, four is better than one - so that isn't so much an issue. It's a fun and easy to do multiplayer set up and with four players you literally could demolish just about any level of the dungeon.
An added point to the multiplayer - people are very, very stingy and will refuse to help you out in purchasing the gates/doors to move along, or will rush to be the first to open a token chest (since only one spawns.. Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥. If you can, set up a system.
The third thing that has a heavy placement, is the looting. Looting in this game (can) be fun, but most of the things require searching or purchasing it from some vendor. Do not rely on the linearity of specific paths to find the things that are hidden away. Explore a lot. Jump on those floating rocks, backtrack a bit and look for the jutting off steps - odds are they lead to something more interesting.
It seems that the freedom and openess of each individual level allows for many different approaches to not only looting, but combat, how to pass by an enemy you may consider tough, or how to provide aid to your companions from a ways away.
This wasn't so much a review, was it..? Either way there's a certain air to the game that makes it great.

In it's current state, Stellaris is far too rough to be great. It isn't bad, it just isn't really meeting expectation for me.
First, the midgame drags just incredibly. Once you stop having things to explore, or at least a point to exploring them, the universe loses a lot of it's charm. To add to this, quite a few of the event chains i've run into have been bugged and are uncompletable or uncontinuable past a point - I have completed the objectives, but they just sit unfinishable in the event log. Past the first 150 years or so, the game slows massively (just processing time-wise) on the default-sized galaxy, adding to the feeling of drag.
The AI isn't aggressive at all, or at least hasn't been in my game, so I have only been in wars I have started. All fleets seem to be largely the same speed, and the retreat option is extremely powerful, so actually chasing down a fleet that uses the same travel method as yours is almost impossible. My transports have also been unupgradable, so while my fleet's warp ranges have increased, I can't actually bring troops to land on the planets I bombard - all I can do is chase down every military ship and station until the enemy surrenders, which is painstaking and a bit boring.
The UI is very clunky in places - the 'e' (galaxy map/system view toggle key) only works properly if you have the system highlighted 'perfectly', so I often end up snapping the camera to somewhere that feels utterly random. There is no way to center the map on a fleet in the galaxy map, only in the zoomed/system view, after which you have to rely on the toggle key to hopefully leave you still looking at your fleet. The research screens do not indicate when you have more than 4 research options very clearly, so it is very easy to miss until you get into the habit of trying to scroll 'just in case'. There is no event log, so it is very easy to miss things if you accidentally clicked through something or want to remember what just happened. It does not seem possible to change the notifications at the top of the screen like it is in other Paradox games, so there is no way to add pauses on important events, nor is there any way to hide the dozens of 'hostile fleet detected' popups during a war whenever you detect a science ship or single corvette, apart from just clicking them all away.
I trust Paradox to make this extremely good in the coming months, but I regret trusting them enough to preorder this. It needs a serious dose of patches before it should be honestly recommended.

this is one of the first games that truly makes me confused on whether i like it or not. nearly every aspect of this game has a bittersweet feel to it. the co-op, vagueness of item descriptions, combat flow, and the lottery of loot are all equally rewarding and punishing, good and bad, fun and exhausting. honestly every aspect of this game has qualities i love and hate. more to the point, im not sure how i would score this game, a 3/10 or a 9/10.
In many ways the combat, co-op, and crushing failures remind me of dark souls co-op play. however, this is more akin to the 3d platformers of the ps2 era rather than any more modern game. and the lack of documentation in a game so dependant on specialization of skills reminds me of the age before internet walkthroughs. The combat is a learning process in the timing and range of different enemies and a completely random but methodical progression in gear. honestly if this game were to get just a bit more quality of life additions it might be my favorite co-op game ever. friendly fire is a very interesting take on this type of co-op dungeon crawler. normally friendly fire drives barriers in friendly, cooperative play, and encourages greifing. however, in my experience the ability to accidentally injure your teammates while also being forced to stay on your toes fighting the monsters fosters a sense of respect instead of a grudge. It encourages communication and protectiveness as you try and somehow use your numbers to an advantage in a crowd of friend and foe.
However, there are many crushingly depressing aspects of this game. the randomly generated levels are amazing, but incredibly easy to become boring and disorienting after getting lost. The possibility for a huge crowd in a tight space on the other side of every door is a huge cause of unneeded stress. Another unnecessarily obnoxious feature is the lack of individual money drops. this means that for every person playing, each has less much needed money to purchase upgrades. this, along with the lack of reliably strong and effective equipment, can make many playthroughs tiring and boring.
This game has strong bones, and my hope is that with frequent and meaningful content updates, such as the brute update, the game will continue to grow and adapt to become a household synonym for teamwork and cooperation.

Bonus points for having an honest F2P model, in which the ONLY advatage of spending cash is cosmetic items and unlocking champions faster (but there is  a generous free rotation - so you can realistically play it forever and not pay a dime assuming the developers keep up this honest model).

Cons:

Having played The Witcher 1 for many many hours on the GoG version, I was eager to continue Geralt's story on this sequel. Alas, stuff, life and other games got in the way and it took me a few years before truly playing this game. Now that I have finally played and finished one path (sided with Roche, never liked 'em elves in Witcher world), I can say that this is a very good game.
You get to know some more into the Witcher's world however, this iteration puts you in a political turmoil as mysterious assassins are killing Kings in the North. Chaos ensures and despite having "friends" or "enemies-to-be-friends", you get to see what the hell is going on from what path you choose, the path that you forge yourself from what decisions you have made (same thing occurred on TW1 as well).
Eventually, you get to see the "big picture" and from that moment, you gotta decide who's worth killing and especially, who's worth NOT killing. It should all come down to the big latest sequel, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.
So, without wasting more time, here's the pros and cons:
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings Enhanced Edition is a fine great game! I may be seen as nitpicky of it but I still hold TW1 as the best of the series yet. TW2 feels dumbed down at places and even gameplay mechanics. TW1 had more areas to explore and venture forth. Characters are better on TW1 as well. TW2 is a very good game, but not a masterpiece in my book.
For newcomers of the franchise, I'd always advise to start with The Witcher 1 at first. You get some more information about lore, characters, setting, etc. TW1 is a superior game in my opinion and it deserved to be played! As for TW2, it is a good sequel however, maybe I expected too much out of it. For what it's worth, TW2 introduces the gameworld and main elements for newcomers, in case you just want to jump right into the setting. Like any sequel you do skip in a game, especially a RPG, you will be missing out but that is your prerogative!
But since this is 2015 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt recently released, you may as well simply jump right into that game instead! I've "heard" TW3 introduce new players rather well into the gameworld but again, you will miss out on the previous events and may not care what you pick on the possible choices and scenarios that occurred on past games.
Do yourself a favor and if you do skip TW1 and TW2, do your homework and get informed on Witcher WIKI. Loads of good information there!

In short, if you like pretty, hack-n-slash, Metroidvania games you owe it to yourself to pick up this Indie title.

Updated after 40+ hours of gameplay.
In short: Stellaris is an engaging and hugely promising 4X game. It's a blast to play, and does a masterful job at combining 4X and Paradox-style grand strategy. Patches and DLCs will only make it better.
=== The good ===
Graphics and artwork are great, and the music is simply wonderful. They both set the mood so well, along with all the "plot events" related to anomalies your research ships discover and various random events like the ones you find in EU, HOI, and CK.
Exploration gameplay consists mainly of assigning scientists to research projects and science ships and using them to explore the galaxy and unlock new techs. The random nature of both anomalies, story events, and technologies sets an atmosphere of exploration and disocvery, and you really feel like you're a species setting off to brave the cosmos. There is great variation and creativity in the techs and story events, too. I also love how there are three means of travelling between systems and that you have to pick one and stick with it for the whole game.
The way you decide on policies, ethics and government types for your species reminds me of other Paradox games, and helps make the various speces feel diverse and immersing while also having a significant impact on what you can and cannot do in-game, increasing replayability value.
You also manage your "pops" and buildings on planets, and use a Stars!-esque ship designer to design your ships. Battles are largelly automated, so winning them depends on good ship designs and finding a good fleet composition.
It should also be noted that the game is incredibly stable, both in single-and multi-player. There's apparently a bug where your friends may not see the gamer you're hosting, but we fixed it by simply launching a hosted game for then to use Steam to send an invite directly to the person who was to join.
=== The bad ===
Earlier I complained about user interface and balance -- these have been improved by patches. The game still doesn't have the depth of the rest of the PDX games, but is still incredibly fun.
One problem is the lack of victory conditions beyond the ones requiring conquest, however, which is a particularly big problem when playing as a pacifist species.
The main problem with the game in my eyes is the lack of depth we've come to love in PDX's games. Diplomacy has been improved greatly by patches, but warfare still easily becomes a battle between stacks of doom.
Also, the various species lack personality. They basically all play the same pretty much regardless of how you design them. Far from the differences between the nations in Crusader Kings II, for example.
All told, however, I find this to be a *great* 4X game, and I can't wait to see what Paradox has up its sleeve for patches and DLCs!

On the surface, Abzu is as casual as a Pot and Parma at the local pub, but beneath its unassuming appearance is a game replete with beauty and positivity. Unlike many other games in my library, I don’t feel I have to actively draw a sense of achievement, success, or fulfilment from Abzu – it simply unfolds in colourful flourishes as soon as you enter the game.
The best way to describe Abzu is as a spiritual exercise. The controls and functionality of your avatar are simple, as are the hurdles you must overcome to progress through the game world. You don’t have to think about anything but the world, pulsing with life all around you. The game encourages you to slow down and relax by using a meditation mechanic, which allows you to follow the different creatures of the ocean and witness how they interact with each other and the environment. If I had to place Abzu in a genre, I guess you could call it a walking sim, but that would be like saying limes and oranges are the same because they are both citrus.
Matt Nava has created a world brimming with life and colour, and there’s a real sense of being allowed to witness something that’s fragile and secret. There is a masterful juxtaposition of the desolation of the surface with vivid colour and movement underwater. The way that claustrophobic tunnels and ruins suddenly open upon verdant pools, or azure panoramas of the open ocean, superbly portrays the sense of scale and grandeur you would expect from oceanic environments. Possibly the most effective technique used to immerse the player is the addition of each new species you discover to the world around you. Be that humble Nautilus to float amongst, or Orcas to ride around on, the player gains a real sense of bringing the world around them to life.
There’s no wonder Abzu was named among Steam’s 2016 Best Sellers, and I can’t wait to see what Giant Squid do next. There are a few things that could have been done a little differently, mainly to do with the robot companions, but that’s purely as I don’t think the game actually needs them. I have to say though, that I did get somewhat attached to the little blighters though, which became abundantly apparent when the first was taken from me (intentional spoiler diversion), so they certainly added something to the game.
If you like to have a nice variation of games on the go, or if you’re looking for something to freshen the palate after that last big title, Abzu could fit the bill for you. It definitely gets the thumbs up from me!

Dust: An Elysium Tail is an indie action & adventure platformer with basic RPG elements. The game was developed by Dean Dodrill. The website launched back in 2002 and was supposed to be an animated film, but in May 20, 2009 in his development diary Dean said he was going in a different direction and expanding the universe in the form of a video game titled Dust: An Elysian Tail, instead of Elysian Tail the animated film. Originally released for the Xbox 360 then ported for PC with Steam on May 24, 2013 the feedback for the game has been extremely positive.
In Dust: An Elysium Tail you play as Dust, a sword wielding animal of sorts, with your flying companion Fidget, who constantly pesters you throughout your journey. You wake up in a small forest not knowing who you are or why you’re there, a magical talking sword known as Ahrah leads you on your journey to figure out your identity while also stopping the evil forces terrorizing the world.
During your adventures you will fight a large variety of different monsters and traverse through all sorts of different terrain, whether it be icy mountains or around a dangerous volcano. You will craft weapons and armor using materials you found while slaying your foes which will increase your offensive and defensive capabilities. You will find all sorts of treasure chests that you can loot from and friends that you can find throughout each of the levels.
I have spent over 16 hours playing this game from start to finish while searching for all the hidden secrets within the game and completing all the side quests.  So depending on what kind of gamer you are, whether you like to stay and search for secrets and unlock achievements or just go from point a to point b, you are looking anywhere between 10-15 hours of gameplay on the normal difficulty, and possibly even more on the tough and hardcore difficulty settings. The replay ability is there for playing the game on the higher difficulty settings to take advantage of the games combat mechanics while also unlocking an achievement for finishing the game on a higher difficulty.
What makes this game different from the others of its genre is the real emphasis on storytelling, you develop such an emotional connection to these characters, you feel for them and their struggles, you genuinely want to help them. Another thing that Dust: An Elysium Tail has done is implemented a color blind mode for people who are color blind, which I think is absolutely necessary for games that revolve around colors, if your game does that, do your consumers who are color blind a favor, and implement similar settings.
Personally, I enjoyed Dust: An Elysium Tail. I thought the game had a very engaging story with unique character development. I loved the simplistic yet smooth and appealing hand drawn feel to the art style. My only concern with the game was the difficulty, or rather, the lack thereof. The bosses were pretty weak on the normal setting, so I would highly suggest when you are starting your journey, you set your difficulty to a higher setting. Another issue I found is the amount of bugs and crashes I experienced while playing the game, it got worse closer to the end, it might be something on my end though. The character leveling and the crafting system to increase the power of your character and equipment, I thought it felt pretty rewarding. The voice acting I thought was pretty well done, especially for Dust. I did however find Fidget to be a bit annoying, but that is what they were going for. I thought the music for Dust: An Elysium Tail was good, the composer for the soundtrack was HyperDuckMusic and here is a link to their Youtube Channel.
If you are a fan of the Metroidvania-esque  type of genre, I think you would enjoy Dust: An Elysium Tail.

I picked up this game after hearing nothing but good things. Every review I read was a glowing recommendation. 3.4 hours is not exactly a lot of time to have played this game, but considering how short the chapters can be, it is definitely enough to learn what it has to offer. And here is what I found.
Yes, this game does have a unique visual aesthetic and pleasingly trippy soundtrack... But that's only on the surface. What I have not seen in any one of the many reviews I have looked over, is the answer to the question "Is it fair?"
In my personal experience... No.
There are underlying rules in video games. A basic structure of logic. Simple things. You perform X action, you get X result. But what happens when you perform X action, and get a different result than promised? Or none at all? Is that fair?
I accept certain mishaps as player error. There were many times I made small mistakes, and I acknowledged them as my own fault. But I cannot accept blame for my efforts being actively thwarted by the game itself going against its own logic.
Examples:
1. I fired 2 shotgun rounds into a standing enemy, only for him to remain unharmed.
2. Standing behind an enemy in a bathroom with a clear shot, I fired at him with a shotgun, then watched in disbelief as the entire spread of shot was stopped completely by a single pixel of the environment.
3. Using an assault rifle, I opened fire on 2 enemies, killing 1. The second managed to walk through at least 5 bullets without damage, before killing me.
4. It is entirely random if guards hear gunfire or not. You are told they will hear it and come running. Not always the case. You can fire multiple rounds from multiple places and still not draw their attention, whilst a guard in a far room will hear it and come running. This changes often, and the same guard will react differently on your next attempt.
5. The worst one of all, and the final nail in the coffin. 3 guards made their way towards me, I aimed my shotgun and fired a shot that would have killed at least 1 or 2 guards. I watched as my shot did absolutely nothing. There were no obstacles in-front of me, yet the shot was completely blocked. That's right. The shot was stopped by the empty space in-front of me.
Do any of the examples listed above seem fair to you? Multiple times across various chapters, I failed by no fault of my own. That is not logical. That is not challenging. That is not fair. I do not see how such a significant aspect of this game can be overlooked by countless players. On the surface, Hotline Miami has unique visuals, pretty good combat, and a nice soundtrack. But does that excuse it for cheating the player? Personally, I don't think so.

On first blush, it looks like a modernized Crimsonland clone, and although there is something different here as well, that analogy doesn't far miss the mark. Like CL, this is a game that circles some well-trod terrain, but does it so smoothly that it feels worthwhile and satisfying. As I alluded to earlier, the arena feels much tighter than Crimsonland's, but that's a good thing. Close-quarters makes it possible to become overwhelmed much more quickly and with fewer monsters biting at your personal pieces.
Nation Red is not a game where you level your character, crafting a killing machine to stand against the ages or even to stick around for future gaming sessions for that matter. In NR, you build for the moment, leveling up in the hope to live long enough just to level up again. You know that eventually you are going to fall, but in the meantime take as many of those undead mooks with you as you can. It's bragging rights in the halls of Valhalla. That's the ShMUp-blood flowing through this genre's veins. Go until you can't go any more, and have fun in the fire.
The game retails for $10 and does go on sale occasionally. That said, 10 bucks is an honest price for this game and there is
of gameplay and enjoyment to be found here for the price of half a Jackson. If you like top-down, twin-stick shooters with satisfying, crunchy effects, pick up Nation Red. Those zombies ain't gonna shoot themselves.*

I can't recommend the game at this time. It's fun, but the physics bugs that let you get stuck in level geometry and force you to restart your run from the very beginning are a showstopper. Would change my review if there was a way to get unstuck, something like a "teleport back to starting room" 0-cost spell that takes 10 seconds to cast seems fair.
Alright, a few more hours in and I haven't experienced the issue again. I'm changing this to a POSITIVE review, but the above caveat stays, so keep in mind that you don't walk by mistake in any tight corners. The levels actually manage to keep surprising me and the difficulty curve is well balanced. In a way the design reminds me a bit of the megastructure from BLAME! but you're traversing it down instead of up. And it's magic-flavoured rather than scifi-flavoured.
Combat takes obvious cues from Dark Souls or whatever it is Dark Souls took inspiration from, but feels a lot more responsive. I'd say it does Dark Souls combat better than Dark Souls does it, except that game obviously had other design considerations. Enemies, weapon and armour variety are kind of repetitive, but that's offset by the sense of exploration you get, I'd say.
I wish there was some way to know what things do stats-wise, i.e. is weapon X better than weapon Y. At this time I haven't found a wiki with stats listed, so your best bet is to experiment with the weapons. Nothing tells you whether enemies are weak to a given elemental damage or if there's any elemental damage system in the game at all. This sword is electric, but does it do more damage to metal enemies? Less? Who knows. Does the ice sword apply some DOT? No idea.
On the other hand, if you keep your wits about you, the above doesn't matter much, just the game might be a bit more tedious. Play it for a few hours and you'll know what it is like. If you like your first hour and just want a few hundred hours of more of the same, you'll like it.

Having played The Witcher 1 for many many hours on the GoG version, I was eager to continue Geralt's story on this sequel. Alas, stuff, life and other games got in the way and it took me a few years before truly playing this game. Now that I have finally played and finished one path (sided with Roche, never liked 'em elves in Witcher world), I can say that this is a very good game.
You get to know some more into the Witcher's world however, this iteration puts you in a political turmoil as mysterious assassins are killing Kings in the North. Chaos ensures and despite having "friends" or "enemies-to-be-friends", you get to see what the hell is going on from what path you choose, the path that you forge yourself from what decisions you have made (same thing occurred on TW1 as well).
Eventually, you get to see the "big picture" and from that moment, you gotta decide who's worth killing and especially, who's worth NOT killing. It should all come down to the big latest sequel, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.
So, without wasting more time, here's the pros and cons:
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings Enhanced Edition is a fine great game! I may be seen as nitpicky of it but I still hold TW1 as the best of the series yet. TW2 feels dumbed down at places and even gameplay mechanics. TW1 had more areas to explore and venture forth. Characters are better on TW1 as well. TW2 is a very good game, but not a masterpiece in my book.
For newcomers of the franchise, I'd always advise to start with The Witcher 1 at first. You get some more information about lore, characters, setting, etc. TW1 is a superior game in my opinion and it deserved to be played! As for TW2, it is a good sequel however, maybe I expected too much out of it. For what it's worth, TW2 introduces the gameworld and main elements for newcomers, in case you just want to jump right into the setting. Like any sequel you do skip in a game, especially a RPG, you will be missing out but that is your prerogative!
But since this is 2015 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt recently released, you may as well simply jump right into that game instead! I've "heard" TW3 introduce new players rather well into the gameworld but again, you will miss out on the previous events and may not care what you pick on the possible choices and scenarios that occurred on past games.
Do yourself a favor and if you do skip TW1 and TW2, do your homework and get informed on Witcher WIKI. Loads of good information there!

For those of you who've already played Trigger Happy Havoc, you should have a general idea of what Goodbye Despair is about: Students at the upper-tier Hope's Peak Academy are forced into a Killing Game, where victory is only possible if you kill one of your classmates and not get caught. The difference here? You're on an archipelago called Jabberwock Island, there's a rabbit version of Monokuma that's more obsessed with Hope than Despair, and things got a little bit MORE complicated in terms of gameplay... And all of this is wonderful.
Like the previous game, gameplay is split between three main segments: Daily Life, Deadly Life, and the Class Trial. Daily Life and Deadly Life are more-or-less the same as in Trigger Happy Havoc, however the new mechanic of Hope Fragments as a form of currency to buy skills for the Class Trials AND the addition of the Level System allows for some more diversity than just talking to someone and hope you get either a good skill or a boost to your PP limit.
Class Trials have kept their normal finding the contradictions, hangman's gambit, Bullet-Time-Battle (now called Panic-Talk-Action) and the Closing Argument Recap, but a few newer events appear, alongside revamped versions of previous events: Including the Rebuttal Battle (engage in one-on-one arguments with your classmates to cut through their beliefs with your blades of truth) and the Logic Dive (an obstacle course-like trial in which you evade various obstacles to solve the trickier questions). The new additions, as well as the old spins on the classics, are a welcome bunch to the hectic and dramatic Class Trials.
Lastly, but CERTAINLY not least, the characters are phenomenal. While the Trigger Happy Havoc cast were enjoyable, many of them fell into character archetype pitfalls that made them feel predictable. The Goodbye Despair cast, although also being archetypes themselves, feel even more real than compared to the previous cast, each one bringing something new to the table that you probably wouldn't expect, including a few surprising choices like the Ultimate Yakuza and even a returning face nobody really expected (and surprisingly thought they wanted). Of course, Monokuma is in full-swing, and as much as he is a despicable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a bear, he's still too much fun, especially when using his little sister Monomi as a foil.
My review wouldn't do this game justice, all I can say is that Goodbye Despair is definitely a must-buy for anyone who enjoys mystery, comedy, and above all, enjoyed Trigger Happy Havoc. So, I give this game a 9/10 "Must Play" recommendation, and hope you all give it a play.

I Am the Hero is a solid beat-em-up game with well-done pixel art and fitting sound effects and music. Unfortunately for me, after having completed the main game and enjoying ~parts~ of it, such as the funky character design and the combo heavy combat system, I also couldn't help but feel like the game "tried too hard" to convey its coolness. Being able to charge up a heavy-hitting Falco Punch / Shoryuken esque uppercut is cool and all, but it's nothing that hasn't been seen elsewhere before. The enemies bouncing around the screen after particularly heavy attacks is cool, and some of the boss fights have fun patterns / attacks to them to dodge, but I felt like every encounter in the game -and the game at large- was pretty forgettable in hindsight.
The locations of the levels have some variety, from fighting on desolate streets at night to lab areas, but large swaths of the levels also feel like they lack any distinction and have just been copy and pasted to draw out their length. This aside, the game's main story mode clocks in at a bit under 2 hours to complete, which is in line with the length of other beat em up titles, but at the 9.99 price tag you're not getting a lot of content.
You are able to select to learn a new skill or the option to swap to a new character at the end of levels, which I often chose to opt for the new characters. These are fun to use as they each have their own set of useful attacks, such as a body-building, effeminate character in a leotard or a G type character with reversed hat, shades, chains, and breakdancing / crip-walking attacks. The G character cracked me up the most of what was present in the game, but from a brooding, silent, raincoat-wearing enemy to a 'mad scientist' boss, many of the game's portrayals of characters felt very overdone and cliche to me. They fit their purpose, but they do very little to break the mold or provide anything new or fresh, despite however much insistence the game keeps heaping on that it's so cool and stylish.
I didn't hate my time spent playing the game and its pixel art from the characters to the backgrounds is all well done, with fitting sound effects and music. I enjoyed myself initially with this game but felt like I was just finishing it after the first couple of levels to do so rather than really being all that interested in what the next levels or enemies would be. It's not a bad game, it just didn't add up to anything very memorable or enjoyable for me.

In one word, "meh." All the basic ingredients of a great 4x are in here, but they're soured and hamstrung by a host of poor design decisions. The game starts out feeling expansive and interesting, but then very quickly becomes repetitive.
Take exploration, my favorite of the 4X's (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate).
You begin the game with a 'survey ship', the GC3 equivalent of the starship Enterprise. It has some decent weapons, but leans more towards sensors and speed. With this ship. you can explore your neighborhood and (more importantly) pop the various sorts of floating relics (starship junkyards, random floating capsules, etc.). Sounds good, right?
Unfortunately, these relics are one-shot deals which rarely give any sort of meaningful reward. Further, with just one survey ship each, the whole galaxy's allotment of relics is quickly used up. At the same time, in the early game, it is hugely important to find an colonize habitable worlds as fast as possible, which means that one survey ship isn't enough. Rather, you'll want to pop out 3-5 tiny scout ships (one quarter the size of your 'Enterprise') to help you find those worlds. In combination, this means that your survey ship - which began life as a source of pride and a flagship for your civilization - quickly begins to feel dull, like a one-hit wonder.
Lastly, all strategic resources are visible from the very start. So really, there's not much mystery to the galaxy. Your first impression tells you all you need to know. From that first impression, you can either decide to exploit that system, or to ignore it, and if you ignore it (because it lacked resources or habitable worlds), there's no reason to ever go back.
While each X connects to the game mechanics in different ways, they all suffer from the same basic design flaw - a lack of mystery and a lack of interesting choices such that the whole thing gets repetitious rather quickly. I've played two half-games of about 8 hours each, but haven't had the heart to finish either. Maybe I'll come back in another year. Stardock say that they've got a development timetable going out to 2019, and good things may happen, but given the lack of imagination that they've shown so far, I won't hold my breath.

Whoa! What a little gem of a game. I was not expectng the level of polish as far as mechanics that Paladins offers. This game runs very smoothly and feels ready for release. The gameplay is very fun, combining (some may say "copying") Overwatch's somplistic-yet-profound combat with some MOBA elements (like leveling during each match to unlock power-ups, in-match item shop). That said, this is definitely more Ovewatch than Dota2, as the MOBA elements are just icing. The gameplay is very fast and unlike Overwatch, you don't change "champions" after the match starts. This games, in my opinion, fulfills the promise that Battleborn failed to deliver: an alternative to Overwatch with fast, fluid, technically sound combat and additional depth.
Bonus points for having an honest F2P model, in which the ONLY advatage of spending cash is cosmetic items and unlocking champions faster (but there is  a generous free rotation - so you can realistically play it forever and not pay a dime assuming the developers keep up this honest model).
Pros:
-Very mechanically sound
-Simple to grasp, yet deep combat
-Fast matchmaking
-Similar to Overwatch with MOBA elements
Cons:
-Maybe "too" similar to Overwatch
-Matchmaking sometimes misses on parity

I'd get my one criticism out of the way now though... I played on a fairly powerful gaming laptop and can run most games on high settings with ease.
