Too many modern games hold your hand and take the excitement of exploration away from you, because you know you're never in any real danger. In Might and Magic X it's nothing like that... take a wrong turn and you may get rinsed into oblivion by some elite water elementals you had no right to be near... but that's all part of the games charm. Some people won't get it, and you may hate that sudden, seeimingly unavoidable deaths can occur from nowhere, or you may not enjoy an epic 20 minute struggle to overcome 3 goblins and a big dog that leaves you mentally exhausted (and your characters bereft of potions)... but if you're one of the people who does get it, then get this game... it's ace :)

After putting 80+ hours into this game with two ongoing playthroughs I definitely recommend Might and Magic X: Legacy.  At first I was slow to succumb to its charms.  I felt the controls and immersion were a little clumsy, the voices and sound effects cheesy at best, and the visuals less than stellar.  When I got to the heart of the game, however, all of those things faded to the background and I found a lot to enjoy in the party building, monster smashing, and exploration.  I encourage newcomers to begin with an open mind and to be prepared to invest some solid time with a trial party to get acquainted with the mechanics and to learn what works well and what doesn't. Then once you have a vision and some goals it makes the challenges in front of you - and your progress - much more rewarding and motivating.
I'm enjoying mysecond playthrough even more, this time using my knowledge of trainer and gear availability, what works best in combat and what doesn't, and an understanding of the pacing of the game to make a challenging party that beats the odds.  What's more, the game is deliberately set up to prevent you from trying all of the skills and classes in one go.  At first this frustrated me; now I appreciate the built-in replay.  A tip on that note: Don't try to do it all, do just a few things really well, and then try a different mix in another playthrough.

Now, let's talk about something more important. Is the plot really that good ? Well.. of course it is, but how good is it ? Like I said, Danganronpa 2 really is better than the previous game, in every aspect. I have to warn you, though. Don't play this game if you expect a ""realistic"" story. You'd better play games where you play the role of a spiky-haired lawyer in blue suit, which fits better your expectations. Just like the first game.. I have my doubts as to whether or not the writers took some illegal drugs before writing the plot. Anyway, if it doesn't bother you, then I can assure you that you will enjoy this story, it can't be otherwise. There are so many good mysteries, murders..
As for the music, they're not exceptional but still enjoyable. If you've played the first game - and you should because this game is full of spoilers - then you'll probably be happy to rediscover the "Closing Argument", a bit better than it already was. In fact, pretty much all sequences from the Class Trials have been improved since the last game, but the Closing Argument is by far my favorite.
In conclusion, this is a must-read. Don't lose any more time and just take the plunge.
And now, New Danganronpa V3 is waiting for me... :-)

Perhaps the worst problem with stellaris is its glacial pace, in Endless space there are multiple game speed options in addition to the total map size option, In Stellaris the only option affecting the pace of the game is the size of the map. This means that a stellaris game can easily run for 10 hours and still leave you with barely any progress into technology. Overall I think that time for mroe development will greatly improve stellaris' viability as a game and look forward to seeing how paradox chooses to improve on the foundation theyve built with this release but I can't help but feeel I migth have been better waiting for a year or so before purchasing stellaris.

* Well-Crafted Crazy Combo Streetfighter Beat-em Up *
I bought this game during the Steam Sale after a friend of mine demo'd it.  I was always kind of interested in it and would highly recommend purchasing at full price unless your funds are extremely limited.
The game is cute, well animated, with a lot of thought put into the combo system.  In short, this is the game River City Underground wants to be (as it sure as heck does't seem to want to be River City Ransom).  Button mashing won't avail you here; you need to time your moves and execute your combos precisely if you want to really string them together, but even a raw noob like myself can still eek together a 100-hit combo.
This is a game where with practice and finese you can really make some impressive looking fighting sequences.  The enemies become playable and it shows in their design as they all have enough moves on their own to be viable, and they are a great assistance since they're your only equivalent to a second life -- having separate power meters and life guages.  They can be tagged in easily, and while nowhere near as versatile or as overall powerful as The Hero they are still quite usable and in some instances are extremely helpful.
Lots of very fine pixel animation, a pounding soundtrack, a good sense of humour and excellent pacing.  This arcade game-play at its finest, discarding the bad and keeping the good.
The only criticisms I have at this moment is that you can't out-right skip the cutscenes -- not that they're BAD but after a point you just want to keep the beat-down flowing.

This is a very short experience but that didn't stop Portal of being an awesome game.
This game more than a game I think is an experience, something between a movie and a videogame, perhaps we could call it an interactive movie.
Commands are simple, there's a bit of exploring, a bit of puzzles and a whole lot of artmosphere (yes, I just created a word).
The game uses an art style that evoques games like Journey, combined with an exquisite art direction and we have one of the prettiest looking games I have ever seen.
There's an story and there are things to do but the game never feels exhausting at anything. Abzu is a game in which you can die but is not frustrating, it wants you to continue all the time. This is the perfect game to relax after being under stress, it will calm you down in no time.
The atmosphere feels aweome, the music complements the game perfectly and while the plot is simple it has it's share of mystery and twists.
I wish there was more to do in this game because the world of Abzu is certainly one that you want to come back again and again but the replayability is poor.
Just like the original Portal, this game is the perfect proof that games are art and don't need to be stupidly complex in order to be enjoyable or connect emotionally with the player.
Play this with headphones for the maximum inmersion.

The game revolves mostly around co-op, and playing with a friend who has this game can be rather enjoyable, so I recommend getting the 4-pack. It's not perfect, but the game is, what, a dollar. However, to pass it up as an AAA game or any game over $10, I'd rate it a 6/10.

I've always been interested in Necropolis since the PAX demonstration From the start I loved the art style and the concept.  My experience on launch week was a good 5-8 hours due to a friend owning the pre-order edition, during that time I enjoyed the game but was turned off by the obscure descriptions, repetitive evironment zones, enemy variety, and etc. As a result I didn't buy the game as it didn't seem worth it's pricetag for the mixed bag of enjoyment and frustration it offered. Cons:
Seems to be a bit poorly optimized for Mac.

Controls cannot be rebound, some may find it awkward at first.
New game plus mode would be great to boost replay value.

Really enjoying this one so far. If you've played Dark Souls, you'll find the gamepad control scheme comforting.
Overall, the experience is a bit short (I still haven't beaten it, but I'm having tons of fun trying and  want to beat it all the way through a few times to unlock all the items) but it's very memorable. Currently, there are 9 "levels" in the game, each level is essentially a large, randomly generated floor of a dungeon, with safe-rooms connecting each floor. I went in expecting more floors than this, but considering I've put a good 15 hours into honest attempts and still haven't reached floor 9, I think it's in a comfortable place right now.
The combat feels fluid, a lot like Dark Souls. The dodging, blocking, time-sensitive swinging, and lock-on function will feel familiar to any players of that series. The enemies are varied enough to where I still am seeing new ones on the lower few levels. I am also still finding new armor and weapons, as well as discovering new magic scrolls and potions.
In total, the tokens (in-game currency) needed to unlock all the items in the game totals somewhere around 100 or so. You can also spend 1 token at the start of each floor to open a fancy chest. In my 15 hours, I've collected around 20 or so tokens, to give you an idea of how long it would take to completely unlock everything.
The design of the areas can start to feel a little bland once you've been through a certain biome a dozen times, so the game can certainly benefit from more tilesets. I would not be surprised if more biomes are added in the future, however, as the variety was just increased with the last major update.
I don't feel that I've wasted my money. $30 seems a little high, but I'm hopeful the game will be expanded, considering the developer's obvious intent to create more content.

Over all, for the price and type of game, I'd recommend it. You just don't see a lot of games of this style being made anymore, so it's almost a matter of "beggars can't be choosers," unfortunately. That said, the game does come with a caveat emptor or two - when I played it, well after release and the first patch or two, I didn't really experience any huge problems. That said, some people do experience some game-breaking bugs, so your mileage may well vary!
Tha said, it's a spot-on solid homage to the older style of party-based first-person turn-based grid-based adventury games! There's secrets, spells, NPCs and quests, puzzles aplenty, riddles to answer, quests to do, etc. etc. At this point the game seems to be pretty playable and most bugs are work-aroundable at worst, though again it may just be that I got lucky, it's hard to say!
Each race has its own set of classes with their own unique promotion/promotion skill, skillsets, and so forth. The game starts out pretty smoothly and progresses nicely in terms of difficulty and character strength - I did feel my melee characters ended up a bit too strong by the end, but my magey fellow caught up right at the end-game, finally. It's really a pretty solid RPG of the style, and the only thing around since Grimrock (which isn't quite the same, anyways, though solid in its own right.)

Vietnam is a lush and heavily vegetated area of the world. A lot of the actual war didn't actually take place in the jungle, but it was certainly a different arena than US forces had ever been in before. Likewise, Battlefield Vietnam is one of the first games we've seen that really tries to take advantage of this kind of dense cover in a multiplayer arena. Horribly long load times, easily 15-30 seconds for an area.  There are cases where if you want to run back to town, you will need to run through 4+ areas.  With movement and load times this can take easily five minutes.  Too make it even more annoying the loading of an area STOPS if the screen loses focus, so no alt-tabbing during a load time.
This is simply too immersion breaking.   There is a good chance you will hit a point where you have to run back to town realize this could easily involve five minutes to get there and then ANOTHER five minutes to get back.  If you’re the type of person who will drop this game and forget it with the above scenario don’t buy it.
Pros
Probably the best combat system for a turn based RPG I’ve seen in a long time.
Melee for example you have the three styles, duel-wield, shield and two-hander each one has situations where one is better.  A monster has the ability vindictive, for every miss on him he gets one more hit, which might damages your whole party.  Duel wielding dagger wielders with 4 attacks might get you killed if they miss too often one round, while a two handers one swing mass damage won’t cause a wipe.   Conversely a monster might be able to block the first swing against him 75% of the time, making the duel wielder at worst lose one attack and the two-hander do none.
The spells are just as varied and important as well with their effects frequently being more important than their damage.   Pushing a monster square away, putting a monster to sleep, reducing the number of attacks a monster gets, buffing the party, removing block attempts or armour from monsters, AoE spells, and many more effects.
Although some fights do break down into a simple damage race, knowing what type of melee and spell to use and the correct order actually matters in this game.

I enjoyed Strike Suit Zero: Director's Cut. It's a fun, often thrilling, 3D space shooter with a transforming giant robot, different abilities and weapons, and it is challenging enough without being overly frustrating. The missions in the game are generally the same, go here, shoot this, but the narration and specific mission structure keep the game fresh. I blasted through the initial campaign pretty methodically, acing every possible mission, then came back for a few of the harder missions. I imagine just going through the game normally wouldn't be terribly difficult.
The story is standard Sci-Fi, but I enjoyed the dialog and voice overs. The OST is pretty good, with a few tracks that really stood out to me, and it compliments the main game well. And the game generally looks good, too.
There is a huge con to the Director's Cut: there are no shadows. None. Nothing casts a shadow, and that makes the Director's Cut look arguably worse than Strike Suit Zero (the vanilla version of the game), and the development team is no longer involved with the game. If that's something that doesn't really bother you, go with the Director's Cut. It's the expanded, better version of the game for sure. If you can't live without shadows, then you're best to stick with the vanilla version.
My preference is that I would recommend Strike Suit Zero: Director's Cut.

Much of what I said in my review of the first Witcher game will still apply here.  That being said, you are doing yourself a disservice if you don't start with the first game.  But, that's my opinion and it is subjective.
Once again we find ourselves in the boots of the Witcher, Geralt of Rivia.  They are much shinier and detailed than before. Also, I think my pants are tighter.
The story is still amazing, the characters are life like and reek of complexity.  I found myself, on more than one occasion, staring at my screen trying to make a decision that I knew was going to effect everything going forward.  The Npc's in the towns and so forth could use more material. I get it, you're upset you got syphilis from a ♥♥♥♥♥, but I don't need to hear it everytime I run past you.
While the areas you are adventuring in are not massive, after running back and forth 5 or 6 times it feels rather large.
The world looks great, from lush forests to open fields, towering mountains, bloody battlegrounds and dirty ♥♥♥♥♥houses.
All the different characters style and facial construction from the first game have been updated and I feel it better shows their personalities. Oh, and hairstyles, you have a few choices.  I tried them all, but Geralt's standard Witcher cut fits best.
I found the music to be buggy at times and kind of hang on the same three notes over and over.  A quick f5 then f9 solved the issue. I can overlook this issue because the soundtrack fits the game world so well.
I don't feel as though the sex and violence overshadows the development of the story at all.  In fact, I think it fits well and was executed just fine.  It's a violent time and people like to get laid, it happens.
Combat has been somewhat redone to be more fluid and enjoyable, still very clicky, but in more of a mash kind of way.  I don't dislike it at all.  Dodging and rolling around just feels better than the first game. And although I didn't use a single bomb or trap after the tutorial, having them equipped in quickslots(called pockets, heh) allows you to use them quickly. It seems like a nice touch.
The changes to how potions and meditation work feels well thought out as well.  Not being able to use pots during a fight puts it on the players to be prepared for the road ahead.  But, you can meditate pretty much anywhere you want(unlike the first game where you needed a campfire).
Now it's time for me to continue my chase of the Wild Hunt.

Stellaris is a fantastic game developed by Paradox, and scratches an itch I have always had for a game. The concept is fantastic, and the execution is better than I expected. It has a solid base game, however many features that I would see as needed are still not in yet, and will most likely be in DLCs and expansions.
Pros:
There is quite a lot of depth to this game, lots of things to do. Science is divided into 3 types of science, with each of these 3 having their own tech pool. Techs that are available to research are random.
Lots of things you can do with your own race, creating your own can is honestly my favorite thing to do, and seeing them in the singleplayer games makes my heart soar.
Lots of buildings, government types and ethos are important, and open up new technologies while also closing down some, or makingi t extremely unlikely to find a tech.
Music is really good.
Graphics are good, but I only have a GT530 so I can't say how good they are compared to high end games with excellent graphics.
Cons:
AI can be really derpy. Frequently empires will not see you as a threat or identify they need to stop you to have a chance at winning the game.
Early game is a lot of fun for me, but mid game it starts dying off, late game it just isn't overly fun anymore.
A few government types are better than others without question.
Overall I would say this is a really solid game in the strategy category, and especially if you like sci-fi games.

ABZU is fun enough and pretty enough for kids to play over and over, but meaningful and involved enough to have replay value for adults.

Play it for the fun and pretty fishes, for the ability to swim with whales or giant squid, or for the beautiful underwater environments. I have 111 hours on record as of this review, so I have played it a bit.
Now, I'm sure whomever is reading this is looking at those who do not recommend the game, and take their criticism into effect when committing to purchasing a game. I do that as well. When I say I would not recommend this game, it is not because it is not a good, or even great, game. I absolutely love it. However, this is not a game for everyone. This is not a game most of my gamer friends could get behind, even those who love strategy games. It is far too...exotic, that it almost feels like it strives for a niche market instead of a mainstream game. Thus, I would not 'recommend' it. But, if you are reading this, then you have interest in 4x, grand strategy, or at least some form of strategy games. And in that regard, consider it, at the least. It is one of the most intricate and complicated strategy games I have ever played, from Warcraft to Total War. But I do not recommend it for the following reasons.
1) This game is hard to learn. Or at least quickly. My first few playthroughs on the campaign, I was always beaten, and on a custom game, I was crushed. The learning curve is brutal. It was very oppressing to have enemies invading you with these advanced ships, or with many times your own fleet, because you don't understand the minute specifics of the game. Once you grasp it, it becomes SIGNIFICANTLY easier. But for those whom do not have the patience to learn it, or are just not willing to reduce themselves to learning strategies online, this game will likely disappoint.
2) The A.I. is far too predictable. Now, perhaps it is simply me, but after a few playthroughs, each race had a fairly predictable course of technology and action. Some focused on creating a tremendous amount of influence to make others not hate them, some tried to be great merchants and sell and buy everything, some tried to bully their way into everything. It eventually comes to a point where the game is far more interesting to craft races to combat.
3) Military might is overpowered. Now, I understand why, at least a bit. However, those races that choose the malevolent path, and focus on building the power and size of their fleets, will utterly crush the opposition. Playing on the largest map setting, by the time I had started exploring the galaxy, I found that those who were invading conquerers were plentiful compared to the other paths, as they did not have the means to survive their enemies. This could be overcome by enemies that split their focus a bit, and researched technologies in other trees, but for the most part, opponent A.I. is very singleminded, and thus, only the strong-minded survive.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Abzu is alot less comfortable for me to play than Journey - this is mostly to due with my Logitech controller whose triggers are significantly less comfortable to use long term. But this is also due to the fact that to move in the game, you must hold the right trigger at all times to move, versus using the control stick. Plus, in order to move fast, you need to smash A to boost - leaving the entire game of pressing R + A from beginning to end.. Also because of full three-dimensional swimming space, I had to fight the camera a few times in this game - this didn't affect the entire game, and maybe deinverting the camera would have helped me, but it was an annoyance nonetheless. That said, the controls are responsive and it is satisfying to breach the surface of the water or flip around and swim.
Abzu has fantasic artistic visual design, with good color choice, smooth animations, and beautiful visual effects. Many objects and "characters" are a bit flatly shaded versus having detailed textures - This gives the game a Zelda: Wind Waker quality that doesn't take advantage of modern texturing details which argurably makes it look not as good as it should, but will still look good ages into the future. My problem is the model quality of some objects, which sort of detracted a majestic moment while looking straight into the eye of a whale. I have no complaints for the Austin Wintory soundtrack.
I feel there is less gamplay and interactivity than Journey here, making this akin to a Walking simulator. Not as bad as Dear Esther, but the only thing you do in 90%+ of  Abzu is swimming or blipping your sonar with X to interact with occasional objects. This will vary from gamer to gamer on whether this is a problem, but for me, this was an uninteresting experience versus Journey which was a reduced down, but still relatively engaging platformer.
I won't spoil the story, but also I can't. I kinda know what I did, but I don't know why I did what I did and what effect it really had other than to make things look pretty. Who am I? What am I? Where am I? Who and what am I interacting with? Why do the fish reflect our own world, having same taxinomic names of fish in real life, but the player character and "levels" have a fantastical, unrealistic appearance? WHAT IS GOING ON? While I only spent two hours here, I'm not convinced I was satisfied with my entire exprience.
Still, if you loved or like Journey, you will more than likely enjoy Abzu. Going forward, if I heard of any Journey/Abzu-esque games, I will resort to watching somebody else playing it - it's better to look at in game than on video, but I didn't love playing it (also, I had inconsistant frame drops from 60fps to 30). Like Journey, the game is short - so short that I finished it before my Steam Cards could drop. I'm glad I got it on sale versus full price.

It feels like Demon Souls mechanically, but not at the same time, mostly because once you die you need to re-earn everything you lost. The main problem with this is because of the RNG involved you don't always get a weapon/armor/consumables that are not utter crap that you're using for multiple floors. Of course there's good runs and bad runs, but bad runs seem to be prevalent in this game, to the point of not being able to complete more than one objective if any. If you run into a certain enemy who can kill you in one hit on the first floor as well, you're better off resetting than trying to fight it.
There's no bosses either for the first five floors, I haven't made it any farther than that to say if there are any at all. Because of this, there's also no dedicated rewards so you usually end up fighting with tier-0 gear until you are lucky enough to find something that's actually usable.
It's a good concept, and I enjoy it to a point. But in all honesty, it really feels like a niche game until additional mechanics are added to it and some rebalancing of the content.

Surprise, surprise, a new Might & Magic in 2014. And it's turn based. And has grid based movement. And is in first person. I had to do a double take, too, after that announcement. Although we had some Japanese games carry on the torch of such RPGs (Etrian Odyssey, Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls etc.) in recent years, they were fairly combat focused and simple.
This here is the real deal. It has (light) puzzles, lore in the form of books, an expansive overworld and multiple cities with shops, NPCs and quests. Character generation and development has a lot of options and you have to make hard choices because there are a lot more skills to develop than there are skill points.
The game has two difficulty modes and I played on the easier setting. I think I made the right choice as I felt the challenge was always so that I had to pay attention to enemy weaknesses and positioning but was never totally outmatched besides a few badly balanced battles. Oftentimes, in these "new old school" games, you have to go straight to a higher difficulty to get a decent challenge but this just felt right. The game loves to ambush your party from all sides with no escape possible so I think this could get frustrating in a higher difficulty quickly.
The main satisfaction in these kind of games comes from getting loot, killing monsters, developing your characters and exploring new areas. I think the game absolutely delivers in these aspects, I almost never was bored in my 40 hours which it took me to beat the game with most sidequests done.
The graphics are nice and adequate for the budget they probably had but the performance could be better. Loading times are fairly long, too, for 2013 mid-range game computer hardware with an SSD.
I would welcome a Might & Magic XI after this successful revival of an old franchise.

Well, isn't this little gem a treat.
Space Combat games are making a bit of a resurgence these days (thank god) and it was titles like this that started it.
The Director's Cut is basically the spruced-up version of the original Strike Suit Zero, so this is basically identical to the console release.
Imagine if Wing Commander had been made into an anime, and you're pretty much there. The base campaign sets you on a war for Earth's survival against the Colonies, and casts you as a pilot doing undergoing disciplinary action for turning up on an orbital platform with no idea how he got there. You're taken out for your flight certification with the intention of sending you off to war asap, until you get updated orders to escort a freighter to the middle of nowhere... game on.
As a story, it's pretty good - there's a decent range of missions that cover the typical Defence/Raid/Bombing Run/Epic Fleet actions that this genre typically runs, with the campaign starting off mysterious and handing you the titular Strike Suit, with it escalating through various missions to the point where it's basically the Battle of Endor from Star Wars.
The Strike Suit is your main fighter - it's described as being able to shift between fighter and mech, but as you're no doubt aware, you're in space, where there's no ground - it's less a 'mech' than it is a spaceborne gunship. Typical tactics have you dogfighting and swooping to build up Flux (aka Magic Suit Juice) then shifting into strafe mode and blasting everything to pieces with your crazy cannons and hilariously anime-esque multiple missile system. It's great, but much more Star Wars meets Anime then anything vaguely realistic. When in 'Fighter' mode, you have a good selection of unlockable guns and missiles to use for loadouts, and it's pretty decent - plasma guns, machine guns, missiles of every stripe - completing the game also nets you a mad Railgun (that looks more like a Beam cannon from the cruisers in the game, but mounted on your fighter), so you have plenty of choice.
You do get other fighters - standard fighter, interceptor and bomber - and the odd mission where these work better than the Strike Suit, but in general they're relegated to mission re-runs. They don't really give you anything the Strike Suit can't but it's nice you've got the option.
Graphics and Audio are spectacular. The art style for pretty much everything is an awesome anime style reminiscent of appleseed or robotech/macross. The music was done by the same guy who did the Homeworld games, explosions, lasers and gunfire criss-cross the screen, and the backdrop of nebulae, planets and asteroids looks stunning. It's hard to believe this was released back in 2014.
Specific to the Director's Cut, they've rewritten a lot of the dialogue - the whole campaign flows much better and tells a very interesting story compared to the original (in which I struggled to understand wtf was going on). They've upped the textures and polygons on everything so it all looks that bit more crisp (although the strike suit has lost it's cool Silver finish and now sports a slightly-out-of-place blue and yellow scheme, but it's a minor nitpick).
This edition comes with all the DLC, and it's broadly good - three new specialised Strike Suits and a new campaign. The Strike Suits are ok -  they all look good, with the Raptor broadly corresponding to an Interceptor variant and the Marauder as a bomber - there strike mode comes with weapons suitable for their role. The Revenant was a later release and is a stealth variant with bad handling and heavy armour on top of a cloaking device... no, I've no idea how they came up with that one, but it's pretty cool. The only issue with these is that they're generally overpowered as hell, so will imbalance the campaign - the Raptor's shotgun-style cannon does insane damage and can rip up cruisers like nobody's business, so remember to up the difficulty. The extra campaign are simulated missions which add a little more backstory from the early days of the war, complete with a GlaDOS-esque AI controller that makes the later missions rather amusing (albeit crazy difficult).
If I had to find a negative.... look at my playtime. It's 12 hours at time of writing and I have 100% achievements - that's two runs of both campaigns in there. Suffice to say, it's very short.
However, if you like space sims... I'd argue this is one of the best choices on Steam.

Foreword:
My grandpa died in June last year (2016) after a six month  battle with pancreatic cancer. This January my nannie (my grandpa's wife) died within a week of being diagnosed with late stage pancreatic cancer. We literally had a week notice. To be honest, it still doesn't seem real. It still makes my chest ache with sadness to think of them both. It hurts, alot. Regardless, I cannot begin to comprehend the pain the parents felt when they learnt that their son had cancer. The pain, the sadness, the numbness and all the other roiling emotions must have been unbearable. And yet they chose to share their story with us. And it's beautiful.
Gameplay:
This is essentially a walking simulator with cutscenes, audioclips, reading and some minor interactions to keep you "entertained".
Graphics:
Whilst the graphics won't blow you (or your GFX card) away they do serve their function perfectly. In fact, I'd call the graphical styling 'charming'.
Audio:
Background music is simple but fits the mood perfectly. Audio clips are clear as are the SFX.
Replayability:
There isn't any.
Verdict:
If you've been touched by that dragon, Cancer, directly or not, you should give this 'game' a go. It will run you through all of the emotions we humans enjoy so much and you gain an insight into the experiences of two loving parents watching their child fading before their eyes. The only negative aspect of this 'game', for me, was the mountains of Bible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Fine, you believe in God, but please stop stuffing it into every bloody note and audio clip. I get that their faith is part of their lives but the sheer amount of it began to make me feel ill.
Score:
8/10 - Highly recommended

Not a bad game but I cannot recommend it. Buy it if you want to support the devs. Finished it in under 2 hours and will be getting a refund. Wasnt worth the price tag for so little content
Pros
+++Retro graphics
+++Soundtrack
++Story
++Level design/Progression
+Decent variety of enemies
+Old school feel
Cons
---Combat: Fun at the start but gets boring fast, revolves around juggling/stun locking enemies. Lacks depth. The only real block you have costs energy, no grappling/throwing enemies, ZERO usably weapons its your fists all game. Some older beat em up games have better combat than this. Falls short when compared to modern games of the same genre like Shank that offers so much more. By the time you learn all the cool moves the game is pretty much over and you are done with it. Late game bosses often require cheesy tactics like stun locking them in a corner otherwise they are a pain to beat and take forever
--Environnement: Lack of breakable items. No weapons/items to pick up and use/throw. Only 2(3) kinds of powerup items +HP and +Energy and some green goo that makes you feel weird but does nothing.
--Game lenght: Finished in less than 2 hours
--Lack of online coop: Storymode coop would have added replayability.
-Weird end of level rewards: You get to choose between 1 new combat move for your main char or unlock 1 new character (which is not a new hero but instead 1 type of enemy/boss youve beaten). The new char comes with much more restricted combat moves that makes combat even more bland and repetitive, so they are only worth unlocking for the sake of trying a new char.
Also you dont get to choose which skill you unlock, so theres 0 character customization
TL;DR : Good attempt for a beat em up game, but falls short when compared to other modern fighting games like Shank.

I highly recommend this if you are in for visual and audible art in our favourite medium.

I was loving this game, I was so in love with it right away that I wanted to do a review immediately. The graphics are cute, the jokes are funny, the gameplay is pretty solid and flashy for a beat 'em up. That's when I hit 4-2. 4-2 is a super long elevator ride with a bottomlest pit that restarts you all the way at the top and enemies that love to kick you long distances. Then it suddenly all broke down;
1/ The enemies tend to stunlock you, I noticed this earlier but dismissed it because I could fight back. The way you usually get out of it is the Phantom Dodge, a recovery dash, out of the ground. I say usually because the move has a pretty big range and will almost always dash you off the WAY TOO SHORT elevator platform which means you're left victim to being hit and kicked off the platform anyway, yeah you can be hit on the ground, no invincibility frames.
2/ That's not too bad though, if you get lucky you can spam your Forward+Light move and doing so will simply push the enemies off the platform, however, if you're not fast enough, a rather large mob can gather and most enemies have the ability to kick you around so you'll fall right quick too. They also all have quite a bit of health which works normally to pull of nice combos but you don't want to do that because:
3/ A lot of your offensive techniques move you around the screen a whole lot and if you cut a combo short you'll be stuck, inresponsive for about a half second, enough to.. you guessed it, get kicked off the elevator and start all over. So either you ♥♥♥♥ yourself or you get ♥♥♥♥ed as it turns out. This is especially bad with later mobs, the first few waves are fine, simple enemies you can kick off pretty easily. It's when the large boxers with super armour and multiple assassins and hooded guys who can just kick you off the platform if they so choose that there's a problem.
I can't recommend this game, the music is amazing, the art and gameplay are really good, but that elevator ride is egregious enough that it easily ruined the whole experience for me and at this point I haven't finished it, nor do I plan to. I get that it's meant to be arcadey and all but that's just bad game design, either put checkpoints on it or make it reduce your health but not kill you. Otherwise it's unbeatable unless you're absolutely perfect AND get good AI RNG.

This one doesn't even deserve a review but I insist on making one anyways. It's just another inane addition to the already vast conglomerate of zombie games with the omnipresent propensity for violence. I managed to demean myself by undergoing 2 hours of shooter/platforming gameplay with the slipperiest of controls since Sonic Heroes. This mindless piece of work was fun for the first 10 minutes, but many functionallity problems blight the experience overall.
I can't vent too much since I obtained this on the 97% sale, but I want my time back.

Video Review Here:
I am the hero presents itself as a tongue in cheek 8 bit beat em up where you take on the role of “hero” who travels through time and worlds looking to beat up bad guys. From the start, the story immediately dismisses itself as there is no true motivation. Perhaps this was for the best however as the game’s current translations leave a lot to be desired. Many of the story sequences fall flat as the translated text made me tilt my head trying to understand exactly what they were going for. I am the hero begins to show its stuff however, in its sharp and deliberate design.
Each environment and enemy are inspired and full of life. From the outset, a sign showcasing the controller layout blips into existence in an organic and interesting way. It immediately caught my eye and gave instructions without taking away from the game itself. Later, there are some minor tutorials but giving that up before the game began was a nice and novel touch. The core gameplay, as mentioned before, is a beat em up where your character has access to the typical arsenal including punches, kicks, and grabs as well as a whole lot more. The developers seem to be fans of street fighter however as they also added in certain button prompts that can activate EX moves as well as air juggles.
The EX attacks can be done by doing a quarter circle forward and an action when you have enough meter. The whole system takes a little getting used to but once I got enough experience in, I became able to juggle and manage hordes of enemies at once. Hero also has access to a juggernaut type ability that makes him unable to be stopped during combos and was essential for certain encounters.
The bosses in the game are the true adversaries as they embody the full ambiance of the level and often have ex attacks of their own.  It was satisfying to be able to also juggle these bad boys after a little effort and effectively get rewarded for our increasing skill with the game. While the game does suffer from some minor text translations, the combat and visual style more than make up for it. What stood out most to me was how sharp and amazing the sound design was. Specifically on one level, you can hear the footsteps on the water as well as thunder in the distance. Not to mention every punch sounds meaty and adds a nice weighty feel to the combos.
Overall, great game and I hope they can fix the tiny translations within it to really make it an even better game. Recommended to anyone who wants to give it a shot. There is a slight difficulty curve around 4-2 but as a masochist gamer, I enjoyed the change of pace.

Geralt of Rivia has returned, and with warm welcome. The Witcher series is becoming one of my favorites within my list of fictional sagas, and this game certainly delivers on all fronts.
Assassins of Kings pulls no punches. It starts off with an incredibly beautiful CGI introduction that rivals even the best studios. Once you start the game, you're thrown right into war, and the rollercoaster ride hasn't even reached the first hill at this point. Geralt's adventures are plentiful - every quest, whether tied into the main questline or just a trivial matter, fits within the world and doesn't feel disjointed or forced.
The graphics are certainly a huge step up from the original, and still hold up well as of this review (May 2015). I have a AMD 7970 3gb card, and still can't even run this game on 'true' max settings - mind you, the only thing holding me back is the 'Ubersampling' option, which looks unreal, but cuts framerate to a halt on most systems. It's reserved for the 'best of the best' and not many can run it, even today. Aside from that setting, the Witcher II is still beautiful in every respect. The coastline city of Flotsam feels salty and dirty. The nearby marshes displays a sticky, dense fog that utters caution within the unknown. Details such as these are scattered throughout, and you'll never find yourself tired of the eye candy.
For those who played the original, the combat is a huge breath of fresh air in comparison. Gone is the timed left clicking jumbled mess, replaced by real time combat. You can light attack, heavy attack, or block/riposte. That's it. Despite this well-needed change, however, the fighting can get rather intense, especially on harder difficulties (I played on Dark). Dodge (basically roll) is your best friend. You will find yourself rolling out of harm's way so often, it's not even funny. Roll or die, that's about what it comes down to. 95% roll, 5% swordfighting. Apparently Sonic the Hedgehog is Geralt's spirit animal.
All the original Signs are back - Aard, Yrden, Quen, Igni, and Axii. In this game, Quen is your best friend. It will save your life countless times - my advice is to invest in upgrading it early. That said, there is a simple yet effective skill tree for Geralt's Signs and other abilities, split into four parts - Training, Swordsmanship, Signs, and Alchemy. Allocate points to the playstyle you like - you'll typically never level them all, so choose wisely.
Briefly touching on loot here - swords and armor are much more plentiful than the first game, which is nice. However those who import Witcher 1 saves will find that their imported content won't last long until a trade in, which is disappointing, especially with one particular weapon you acquire from the first game that its storyline seemed to hold in high regard.
The story is certainly good, and not too over the top (well, aside from a detail or two). Geralt's choices have much weight in this game, and you'll find more impactful choices than in the first iteration. Also included are various ways to get information in the dialogue options - persuasion (Axii), intimidation, and so forth. I'm not sure if its based on your current skills or a random number roll, but its a fun take on the 'click to ask X question' bit.
My only real gripe with this game, other than the occasional dodgy combat roll, is the Steam achievements. The game practically forces you to play twice to get absolutely every achievement. 100%'ers, beware. The insane mode alone is risky - one death and your save games become null and void.
Overall, this is an tremendously enjoyable sequel. Not as long as the first, but it has depth and production quality. Definitely worth a playthrough or two! (Note: This game has 'something after the credits'. Stick with it!)

And the most important part - keep the awesomness of soundtrack by Danny B and blend it into gameplay itself (oh wait, the latest isaac installment has no Danny B soundtrack, too bad)
I'm not underestimating the efforts of programmers and artist behind this game. They've made a great job, but for me this game was and always will be "the next game with OST by Danny B"
And the result is absolutely awesome. Gameplay is tense, challenging and rewarding. It pulls you in entirely and gives a lot of emotions - hard boss fight left me with tears in my eyes couple of times. Not because of a weepy story (hey there Undertale) but because of sheer excitement and willingness to win.
Just like the Undertale I've mentioned above this game gives you an idea of how the soundtrack may enhance and multiply the enjoyment of simple in its greatness gameplay mechanic (Crypt of the NecroDancer, VVVVVV) or style and story (Undertale). As to the isaac game, it was great in it's time but now McMillen has to leave it and make smth new. I'm glad that Danny B eventually participated in such fresh project that once again proven his composing skills instead of making soundtrack for another game about weeping at piles of poop.
And final thought - play it with gamepad. Assign controls as the developers recommend and you will never want to play with arroy keys again!

Okay. Now that that is out of the way..
This game is truly a worthy sequel to Trigger Happy Havoc. The new little mechanics (quick-travel, running, the ability to MOVE THE DAMN CAMERA WHEN YOU HIT "TAB" INSTEAD OF BEING LOCKED IN PLACE FOR A SOLID 4 TO 5 SECONDS EVERY TIME) make gameplay much more enjoyable. The courtroom minigames are engaging (though at times near the end of the game, the Revised Hangman's Gambit killed my no-damage streaks... I probably just need to Git Gud) and the new ones are pretty cool!
As for the characters; wow! What a colorful and cute cast! I was afraid I'd forget half the characters by the time I was done since I'm really quite awful with names, but much to my pleasure, I was able to remember everyone's first and last names, their talents, their personalities, and all that good stuff! (By the way; Chiaki is the only GF that matters. I'll fight anyone that says otherwise.)
Aaaaand Monokuma is a lovable pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥as always! The quips and throwbacks to the previous game all really make dealing with his presence again worth it.
Then there's the storyline. I've made my way through a handful of visual novels with crazy twists in them, and this one's twists... Well. I won't say much for fear of spoiling the end, through there is a lot of foreshadowing (and thinking back, it all should have been obvious from the beginning) and the shock factor is constantly raised so every time you think you've hit the climax and you try to breathe for a second it turns out that something more dramatic was lurking right around the corner! I don't cry easily, but my vision got all blurry during the ending credits because my silly self was teary-eyed!
Ah, I almost forgot! The other minigames! Island Mode and the Usami side game! Because of these minigames I am still not done playing this game to its completion. I will probably be investing another handful of hours while I try to hunt for achievements (and while I read the included novel; Danganronpa IF!). Not that that's bad!! I am very pleased that this game includes good post-game content. The more hours I can invest in this game; the better.
In conclusion! If you enjoyed the first game, I can guarantee (with 97.3%* certainty) that you will enjoy its sequel!
(The remaining 2.7% is for the people that may be unsatisfied with the ending since
. I think it suits the story well, though, seeing as how the creators of this wonderful series love to pull stunts like these often.)

Dialogue is filled with plodding exposition and internal monologues, which to some extent was a part of the first game, but here much of it feels lazy and unoriginal with people droning on about doing their best and not giving up. One of the major twists from the first game is just casually mentioned to everyone and people accept the idea of the killing game pretty quickly, with one character threatening everyone else not long after a motive is set.
even the item system seems to have somehow gotten a downgrade. many of the presents from the first game are still here, but everything has turned 8bit. I have to assume it is supposed to go along with some kind of tamagotchi type subgame they have, that works by running from place to place, but it is still an odd change.

Danganronpa is something of a mixed bag of different mini-games and modes, so I find it a little too weird to write about it as a whole. I'll split this into chunks:
Story: The main story is a mildly interesting framing device explaining why so many different people (from a jerk of a little girl dancer to a trenchcoat-wearing man who speaks of how evil he is and is utterly devoted to his Four Dark Devas of Destruction-his pet hamsters) have been brought together to try to kill each other to escape. The story reuses some general themes and devices from the first game, and although there's something of a justification in some later-game twists, I would have rather they came up with something more original. The story really shines when it comes to each murder mystery, however; I have never seen mysteries written this well in a game. Even when the answer is obvious, it's usually a trap or things aren't quite what they seem. Attentive players can pick up on some of these thanks to choice foreshadowing and less obvious clues, but plenty caught my trope-overdosed brain by surprise.
Gameplay: Gameplay consists two parts: visual novel/investigation segments, with standard "talk to NPCs, find clues, etc" that anyone who's played a game in this genre should be familiar with. I have little to say about this save that it's straightforward and doesn't waste your time with much backtracking or pixel hunting for clues. And then there are the trials, the other half of the gameplay, which consist of a mixed bag of mini-games and logic puzzles to determine who killed the latest victim, and these range from excellent (Nonstop Debate) to inexcusible (Panic Talk Action) to perfect in every way (Closing Argument). On the whole, they make for an enjoyable experience, and I have to say no game like this has given me quite the sense of accomplishment that Danganronpa 2 gives when you piece every little bit of the case together and lay every mystery bare to shove it right in the villain's face, all to haunting yet upbeat music.
Sound: Voice acting is on point here, even in the dub. Special mention should go to the VAs for Gundham, Nagito, and (SPOILER) for really owning the characters and going the extra mile to drive home the lines. I usually skip ahead in games like this because I read much faster than the characters speak, but I found myself often letting the lines play out with the game's Auto mode. The music is also fantastic, suiting the mood from calm exploration to tense interrogation.
Extras: There's a surprising amount of unlockable content the game hands to you. There's the expected art and sound gallery, along with cutscene theater. However, the game has a few side stories that are completely optional, some of which don't relate to the game at all and expand on the greater universe of the franchise. Unfortunately, these to me felt unimpressive and lackluster compared to how tight and rewarding the base game feels. Although, being able to get everyone's visual novel sections was appreciated.
On the whole, this game is well worth your money for the core experience. If you like solving mysteries and can roll with the game changing up gameplay with some action in your sleuthing, this game will be absolutely perfect for you. Highly recommended for any fan of murder mysteries.

I love spaceships. Always have, always will. In particular, I love fictional spaceships blowing the snot out of each other with lasers, missiles, and giant machineguns. Among that category, I especially love small-scale dogfights between small fightercraft. The careful maneuvering. The tense lining up of the perfect shot. The inadvisable victory flourish of flying through your vaporized enemy's debris cloud.
Problem is, I suck at it.
The venerable Freespace 2 is widely reputed to be the master of this genre, but buying and playing it left me cold. It seemed to expect that I would have the reflexes, dexterity, and coordination to be an actual fighter pilot, with the ability to juggle power systems, track objectives, use a target-lock system that was like finding a needle in a haystack, command allied wingman, find and execute a target that seemingly has no bearing on the overall battle, all while worrying about pesky enemy fighters that seem infinitely faster and more maneuverable than I am. When all I wanted to do was fly around shooting stuff, this was simply not fun. I have been searching for a game to scratch my Luke Skywalker itch for years, and with Strike Suit Zero, I have finally found it.
This game is the master of making me feel like an ace pilot, without dumbing it down enough to stop being challenging. You only need to juggle shield, boost, and flux, a recharging resource that allows you to transform into the titular Strike Suit. Dodgy physics aside, the ability to halt dead in space and move laterally adds a very interesting new dimension to the old fighter combat formula. Few things are more satisfying than transforming mid-dogfight, watching your would-be pursuer overshooting you while you send a swarm of light-trailing missiles up his tailpipe. I also found it a useful tactic, when I inevitably misjudge my strafing run, to transform right as I am about to collide with an enemy capital ship, halting my forward motion, before turning ninety degrees, changing back to fighter mode, and zooming along the length of the hull like I'm skimming the Death Star trench. This game is the master of making even your screw-ups look awesome.
By and large, it looks fantastic. Beautiful ship designs and backgrounds, and each ship leaves a trail of light from its engines that makes every dogfight look beautiful. There are little touches, like the way the Strike Fighter's wings will expand and contract with speed and direction and, best of all, a visible cockpit overlay while in first-person mode. It isn't perfect. It is quite short, the story would be lacking even if most of it wasn't told in exposition-dumps over the radio that you'll be too busy dogfighting to pay attention to. And the final level is crap. However, if you're looking for a modern spacefighter game more in the spirit of Rogue Squadron 64 than Microsoft Flight Sim, definitely give this little gem a look.

This game is both solid as can be and at the same time unpolished. The gameplay is great but in these days of so-called "AAA" titles people turn their nose up at the aesthetics. I think this is why metacritic gave it a low score. But in any case the game deserves some respect due to a few things that in a very noble move, it did not advertise as a feature.
One of these things is the fact that it uses netradiant and the darkplaces engine (themselves a fork of GtkRadiant and the Quake engine). Both of these are free software and licensed as such. The source code and what modifications were made to the editor and engine respectively are included on zip files with the distribution.
To my knowledge this is one of the few games on Steam that have free code and moreover ship that free code along with the install. It is very humble about this fact, and I am guessing I am one of the few people aware of this as it requires looking in the install directory.
In other words, this video game is a massive open source/free software and classic-game-nostalgia love-fest.

I am the Hero is a 2D beat ’em up fighting game with a nice pixel-art style, music and fighting system.
You play as a mysterious “Hero”, a very relaxed and cool looking guy who can stomp any enemy into the ground. The game looks very fancy and beautiful. It reminds me much those old 8-bit games, but it’s more polished and has to offer more, it’s something like a modernized old-school game. In addition to the nice visuals and music, there is plenty of humor in the game (great dialogues and enemy design. For example, there is a rapper, who is battling you, literally throwing words and phrases at you!).
The gameplay is quite challenging but easy to get into. As the game supports gamepads, I used my Logitech controller. There is quite a big skill list in this game. The controls are quite similar to those in fighting games like Street Fighter or Mortal Combat. You can use different combinations of buttons for different moves, combo them into an infinite chain of kicking around your enemy and use your energy for super moves or a buff, making you immune to stuns and stuff like that.
After each level you have can choose between unlocking a new move for your main character or unlocking a second character (you can switch to him whenever you want in the game). But I found most of the second characters quite useless as they have a very limited move-set and aren’t really strong.
The enemies are quite easy in the beginning but throughout the game you meet new bad guys and bosses with new types of attack and you have to face more and more of them at once. Luckily, they sometimes drop burgers and coke (fills up your health and energy).
The game also offers a local and online multiplayer mode but I couldn’t test that aspect of the game.
The translation also needs some polishing in some moments but it’s OK in the whole.
Positive:
+ nice pixel art
+ great soundtrack
+ quite a big move list
+ unlocking more moves and characters
+ amazingly long combo chains
+ humor
+ trading cards and achievements
Negative:
- second characters are weak
- some mistakes in the translation
- sometimes difficult to make the moves you want
All in all this is a great game and I had fun with it. The game could need a multiplayer story mode and maybe a versus mode (choosing between the second characters and fight each other).

So they were just♥♥♥♥♥♥at the game, not the games fault at all. I also have seen people complain about input delay? I have no idea what they are talking about tbqh, I didn't notice any whatsoever (maybe the fight stick+gaming monitor has something to do with it being good for me)
A bit short, imo (3 hours on my first playthrough, the time of writing this review, and I got stuck at one part for maybe 30 minutes that was pretty tough) but I guess most beat 'em ups are short, it isn't really a genre I like. This was an exception though, I fell in love with this game.
That said, I still feel far from done playing. There is plenty more to do. I still have characters to unlock, along with quite a few moves, and I am excited to try the next difficulty level, even though I died many times at the standard level. Worth the $10
-Tons of fun to pull off the air combos, you can make them very, very long, and it is satifying when you do it right
-I love the art/style. Good animations, character design, enviornments, the whole shebang
-I love how fast paced it is, you can really zoom around the screen once you get the hang of it
-Terrific music, I hope the soundtrack is release I wanna buy it
-Had some humor, which was often made even funnier by the translation, but some of the jokes themselves were good too
-The choice between unlocking EX moves or a character at the end of a level is an awesome idea (the characters won't be as good as your main character, for the most part, but you can switch to them whenever, and once you die they come in basically acting as an extra life, giving you a chance to finish off whatever killed you and the level. You can only have the hero and 1 other character at a time though, having a bunch of lives would be too easy)
-The meter system is good, you can use it do dodge after being hit so you don't get combo'd (takes a very small amount of meter to do this), preform EX moves, or my favorite: the endure status. When you activate it, your meter starts to drain, and you attack faster plus you don't flinch when hit, you can just continue your combo.
-At the end of the game, final boss, after my main character died, my backup got switched in, but the sound effects stopped working. There was only music. I then died, and when I started again there was no music OR sound, except for 1 sound effected when I beat the boss. Final scene played, confirmed unlocks, then I went back to the main menu, neither of those had sound either. Pretty anticlimatic, thanks to that. I should have restarted the game when it first happened instead of continuing. However, that was the only glitch I experienced while playing.
-I found it difficult to input the EX moves. Using a fight stick might have had something to do with it, it wasn't smooth like street fighter at all. I tend to stick to just using my meter to activate Endure, for the most part, as I found that to be very good
-Menu UI and the information within them could be better, no big deal though. Just play the game.

The Witcher 2, the game that was forgotten after Skyrim was released. But now you're here whether to buy this game because you hear Witcher 3 is amazing. One thing that this game is most praised about is its story. But honestly, it's not that impressive. The plot was not boring, but after you finish the game and sit to think about it, it's pretty basic.
There are also some characters that are mentioned who were never introduced. An example is Ciri, who does not appear until the third game. Sometimes there are characters that are mentioned and I'm completely oblivious to. Also, once you take a few days of break, you're likely to easily forget who is who.
Second complaint is that the game feels too clunky. The combat system is a lot better than the first Witcher, where you just click to hit. But it's annoying when you cannot pick up items, jump down cliffs, or open doors until Geralt is relaxed. You can tell that this game was made in mind for consoles first while playing.
Definitely, the most annoying problem is that you cannot overwrite saves. I don't know why they decided to do it this way. You're able to do this in the first Witcher. The problem is that when you make too many saves, the game crashes. I've tried to follow different solutions but the game is still crashing for me.
You also have to finish the game twice. [MINOR SPOILER] There's a point where you have to decide between Roche and Iorveth. Picking one side completely changes the story. It's interesting to see the different perspectives of both sides, but if you only play one side, you're only playing 50% of the game. And it's a little annoying when playing the second time because you already know what the ultimate ending is.
Overall: 7/10
There are some annoying problems here and there, but the game isn't a complete mess. Darts and bombs are useless (imo). Only 5 sex scenes in all that look the same. And frequent crashes towards the end of the game due to not able to overwrite the wall saves. The story isn't the greatest, but I'd praise this game for its combat system. It really is a huge improvement compared to the first Witcher. You hit when you want to, and the signs are actually useful. A decent game if you're into fantasy RPGs.

Looking at the store page
looks cliché, yes, another zombie survival bloody shooter with nothing particulary new
in game design. It's a few years old & easy to overlook, but I am glad I tried it. It is reasonably priced & surprisingly looks & plays gruesomely well!
Imagine a claustrophobic top-down arena, twin-stick shooter with a bit of a Left 4 Dead flavor to it. No story, just a smörgåsbord of Power-ups & Perks, to accompany the never-ending horde of thousands of mindless zombies to slaughter "cooperatively" with your friends .. this is
!
It's simply addictive in its psychopathic repetition. This is accomplished by offering simple responsive controls, with unique classes that can be greatly modified with the perks, weapons & power-ups each  session. Then combine this with inherent co-op multiplayer mechanics in reviving dead players, covering each other & the like, and you have a lot of variables to change the outcome of the game. It might be the same map you have played 100 times already, but every session has randomness & feels unique to a degree.
Difficulty is very scalable, but with an experienced group it can feel like it becomes a
sometimes
. Controls you will understand after a min or two of gameplay, but as you last longer you need to start working on your crowd control & aiming, plus using the right power-ups or weapons for the situation. If you want go all
into it, you will also need to learn to work closely as a team! All this can take a bit of practice, but does keep you wanting to come back for more to see if you can survive longer!
There are also an extensive list of achievements to challenge you - some really cool ones too, kudos to the devs for their creativity! Thankfully as well, the devs saw fit to let you
your favorite weapon so it doesn't get replaced by a new pickup you run over
- nothing worse than having your assault rifle replaced by a crowbar in the thick of taking down a boss! Something all new players should know about :).
There are really no in-game annoyances at all, its all well balanced & easy to distiguish visually amongst all the blood & guts. Meaty Metal/Rock riffs keep the adrenaline pumping throughout! Soundtrack & effects complement the style of game perfectly.
Solo mode offers a few more tailored challenges too in a series of missions. You can also play all the Multiplayer modes in Solo. Solo, I would argue, is harder than co-op but both have their merits. The pure Survival mode I found to be the toughest out of them all.
Even though the game is over 5 years old, I was still able to find some online games without too much trouble. Even if you don't see any games hosted, you can start a public match yourself, & others can drop in and out whenever. This makes online mode a breeze to use & keeps you from waiting in dreaded lobbies.
reminds me of earlier times .. classic gaming days. Days when FPS weren't trying to be an action movies, when RTS
was popular & when 'simulation' in the game title actually meant the real deal. And most importantly, when shoot 'em ups were .. all about the survival & scores. Refreshing, addictive, simple & fun!

I can't say I can really call this a good game so much as I call it a fun toy. The fire physics are fun to play with, and this game is guaranteed to make the pyromaniac inside you cackle with glee as you burn stuff. Some items are fun just to play with instead of just burn right away (Manly Razer comes to mind). A lot of the things react in unique ways when burned, others... do nothing at all. But if you ever wanted to burn an opera lady or a pirate or... well, this is the place to do it. In that regard, Little Inferno is fun. Some people will say that's enough. It's made more appealing by the story that goes along with it, told through the letters you receive from three different people. While I kinda like the story itself, some of the themes lose their impact due to their overly repetitive nature. I invite you to take a shot every time someone mentions something not lasting forever or never being able to go back.
Another thing I don't really understand is why after buying something, you have to wait for it to ship to you. Some items take a few seconds, others take a couple minutes (I believe the longest you'll wait for an item is five minutes). So if you run out of stuff to burn and are waiting for your next batch to arrive, the gameplay grinds to a halt, leaving you sitting there like a putz while you wait for your stuff. If you happen to get some Tomorrow Bucks, you can use those to skip the shipping time, but the game is very stingy about handing them out. The best way to get more is by finding combos, which is also required to unlock the other catalogs. Oh, and did I mention after buying something, not only does it take a while for it to ship to you, but it takes even longer to restock?
So to some degree, it feels like I'm playing a free to play game where if I don't have or don't want to spend money (or Tomorrow Bucks in this case), I have to wait to keep playing. I'm not convinced that's a good choice of gameplay mechanic. At least it isn't riddled with microtransactions like free to play games.
I wouldn't say Little Inferno is bad, but my biggest gripe is the waiting system; it's just an unnecessary feature that gets in the way of what's otherwise a fun little experience. You'll have an enjoyable time when you're not waiting for more things to burn. I think the story is the strongest point of the game, even though themes are repeated to the point of losing most of their impact.
You're more than likely to play this game, finish the story, maybe mess around with burning stuff for a little while, and then get bored and uninstall it. Worth checking out, but I suggest you wait for a sale; this fun toy of a game isn't worth full price.

SO primarily, I do not really write reviews on anything. I generally take all opinions with a grain of salt and keep my own to myself since the opinions of others matter very little to me, but in this case I will make an acception.
First off, I am not saying this game s free of problems and is perfect and so on and so forth, it has bugs, it needs some TLC and so on, but it is a good game. So first off, no this is not a "Lo-fi dark souls" not in the slightest. Just because it has a stamina bar, a health bar and you stop moving to use items does not make it Dark Souls. Those that tend to believe this likely have not really played Dark Souls all that much. WIth my being a Dark Souls veteran since Demon Souls actually I can say this feels nothing like Dark Souls.
Now that that's out of the way, on to the complaints about it being linear or some such. The simplest way I can put this is... NO... My word if someone believes it is linear apparently never ever explores. I got lost for an HOUR on floor two because I saw another door and was all "Oh hey, another door, lets go look." And found out there was a TON on the other side of it and it looped all the way around the whole floor. By floor 3 there were so many different paths to choose from I had no idea what to do and most of the grand total of 6 hours I have had time to put into this game was on floor 3. SO no, it is not linear at all, i suspect those that believe this were Un-lucky enough to pick the right path the first time and didn't care to explore.
And lost but not least the difficulty.... This game is not hard to me.. Again, Dark souls veteran.... Hardly anything feels difficult anymore... Anyway moving on, the reason it is not BRUTALLY hard as people make it out to be, its literally as hard as you make, much like Dark Souls. If you run into a group of enemies like a moron, you will get wrecked or barely survive. If you dont watch your surroundings and run around like an idiot, you will get wrecked or barely survive. If you swing your weapon with reckless abandon you will get wrecked or barely survive.. Maybe that is where that Dark Souls comparison comes in but it isn't a Dark Souls only concept, it's the concept of OH! this game doesnt let you charge in like a moron and go super Saiyan on everything and bottle feed you regening health like a baby like modern games!! WHOA!... so yeah.
Anyway, all in all this is a good game, is it GREAT? No not really, not yet anyway, but it is good, and it is worth the cost in my opinion. So I would recomend this game to anyone sitting on the fence with the fore warning of this is not a game dumbed down in difficulty to modern standards, so be ready to change how you play games if you are used to that kinda deal. That is all, as you were, have a nice day.

If you didnt play danganronpa 1 and are only reading this to get a look at both games reviews, i will just say this game is as good if not better than danganronpa 1. For those who already played danganronpa 1, let's start by saying what is worse because that list is much shorter.
-->We start with the ambiance of danganronpa 2, which is different than the first game. The game feels much more open because of the size and the way you move between places and islands, that doesn't mean it's worse, but you feel much less claustrophobic which in my opinion is worse because of the nature of the game.
-->The second aspect of the game which is, again, subjectively worse than the first one is the balance of the characters personalities. the characters are just as good or even better than the first game, but the balancing is off in terms of seriousness, that means the cast become much more silly or serious ( not gonna spoil) and doesnt achiev the same cool balance of the first game.
With that out of the way, we can go to the pros. The game is absolutely fantastic, you can feel improvments in almost every aspect of the game execpt maybe the tutorials for the minigames of the class trials. The story manages to also impact the story of the first game in a very positive way, shedding light in a lot of elements that the first story left pushed aside. The game immediatly throws you 2 very mysterious characters, that forces you to think about the characters in the first game, and with that you are left with not even knowing if the events of the second game are after or before the events of the first game at the start. This time, in a tropical island, you are going to feel much more connected with the characters because of the better balancing between the plot and the social events, you will feel even more part of the group, and, therefore, feel much more despair as things go ugly. The class trials are better in a lot of ways, the main aspect is the difficulty. The game feels like it knows you played a full game already and its much less kind with the difficulty, making the trials much more challenging in a good way. The minigames are, imo, better but still it's subjective, aside from that, the trial shows quality of life improvments, only the tutorials are bad.
TLDR: the game is better in almost all aspects but the ambiance is less claustrophobic and the cast has problems with the personalities balancing throughout the story. Overall, the game is a must have for who played danganronpa 1 for sure, and the majority will probably like the second game even more.
