welcome to the most recent addition to the Might & Magic series, Might & Magic X Legacy. Developed by Limbic Entertainment and published by Ubisoft, Might & Magic X legacy was released on January 23, 2014.
The game is a throw back to the RPG's of old, adopting very traditional PC RPG mechanics. You start the game with the option of customizable character creation or the choice of choosing a default party of characters. Character creation is limited in terms of real personalization, you have the option of basically choosing a heroic voice or a cynical voice and that is about the depth of their personalties. My advice is to choose heroic every time as the cynical characters tend to repeat the same god damn four lines of speech every five minutes and it becomes tiresome. Other parts of character creations are good, there’s four races to choose from which span your clique elves, orcs, dwarfs and men. Each race has three unique classes to choose from, one might class, one magic class and a hybrid class.
Legacy injects a lovely sense of nostalgia and really does bring you back to the series of ten plus years ago. However once that nostalgia ends what are you left with? Well a combination of good mechanics, dated mechanics and strange design choices.
Lets start with movement outside of combat, I have no idea why the developers and ubisoft went for grid based movement outside of combat. Wanting a grid based combat system is one thing, out of combat grid based movement is quite another. While going for the retro feel is one thing, using dated movement that becomes boorish and frustrating is quite another. I really do feel that grid based world movement is a relic of a bygone era that does not need to resurface. The developers of the old might and magic games did not have grid based moment because they wanted too, it was a technological limitation of the time period, that limitation no longer exists so the lack of free world movement feels very contrived.
The over world design itself doesn't really make sense you have a little lighthouse that nearly spans a 5 by 5 area and then a supposed huge castle that takes up the same amount of space. Places and objects in the world are not in proportion and it actually becomes immersion breaking to the point of silliness. Someone should also speak to the builders of the island as they need to be introduced to the concept of roads, how any of the citizens travel in that place is beyond me.
The games graphics are confused too, you'll go from a really nice looking area, to areas riddled with poor textures, draw distance problems and outright texture load issues. I feel that Ubisoft really didn't give the game the budget it deserved and while the games graphics are in no way bad they are comparable to that of older games like elder scrolls oblivion even on its highest settings.
Combat is where the game shines, the combat system is very traditional Might & Magic combat which is by no means a bad thing. I am certainly a fan of turn based combat and always have been, it is a solid mechanic that remains fun to this day. Fights are challenging and fun making you really consider each action you take to ensure your teams survival. The problem with the combat lies in smaller design choices I don't understand. Without any warning the game seems to regularly bump up the difficulty for no logical reason, for example you can clear the first two levels of a dungeon with no fuss then suddenly on the third the enemies are a lot tougher sometimes to the point of killing your entire party in one fell swoop. You can regularly run into much higher level opponents in the world that will just kill your characters in one move, which is fine in one sense but not in other. I like the fact there are enemies you cannot defeat yet, however having one of these enemies in a cave right outside of the first starting town is annoying. You cannot choose to escape from battle, so once you accidentally stumble into an area to high level for you and engage in combat, you might as well load your last save right there. Barring the few minor annoyances combat does remain fun, engaging and challenging.
Levelling up again while simple suffers from strange design choices. When you level you receive attribute points to improve your base stats and skill points to improve your proficient with skills. Now any logical person would think to place tab these two menus right next too each other but no. instead you have to press the absurdly small level up button to place attribute points then close that menu to press the other small button to open the skills menu. The is a good amount of depth once in game to tailor the characters to the way you want them, there’s plenty of stats and skills to customize as is always the case in Might & Magic. The game doesn't do well in explaining skill related mechanics to players unfamiliar with the series, in fact the game has no tutorial at all and while I am a fan on games not holding your hand. It would be easy to miss that to improve skills you need to find a trainer, which by the way a spread out in an unhelpful way.
The reason I love RPG's so much is due to their rich, well told characters and story. Might & Magic X Legacy's story is about as deep as a puddle in the middle of the desert, on the sun. There is no reason what so ever to care about the characters in the game, they are all as generic as any clique uninteresting fantasy characters. The back story of your characters goes as far as, your mercenaries looking for adventure, quaint. The games main story itself, is little more than a pointless excuse to visit the various dungeons with even the governor of the island basically stating that you hold no ties to the empire and thus have no reason what so ever to help them basically by saying (office space style) 'uhhh, if you could go ahead and restore all the elemental altars... that would be great.' it makes even less sense considering the empire has an army, paladins, griffon riders and a myriad of resources available to combat the threat, the reason they don't? Who knows.
In all the game provides a good nostalgic feel but past that I feel disappointed. Those looking for a old school RPG will find it here. I feel that instead of trying to push the franchise forward Ubisoft have created a dated RPG experience and cashed in on the franchises name. I have to ask why this game needed to be made, yes make more Might & Magic games but don't replicate the mechanics over and over. Push forward, make better experiences, I'm not saying take out what makes Might & Magic, Might & Magic but at least bring the franchise into the modern era. Also Uplay is awful, stop putting that♥♥♥♥♥♥in your damn games Ubisoft.

So in the late 90ies, when the N64 was picking up speed, Factor 5 released
for the platform. It was an arcade style Star Wars flying game where you pilot a variety of Star Wars vehicles while trying to defeat the Empire. It was intuitive, fast paced, fun, and varied with a tonne of easter eggs and cool reasons to come back to it. Sadly, Factor 5 was shut down after the release of
. Leaving behind a gaping hole in the arcade Space Combat departement. Enter
, a high energy, fast paced, blindingly awesome space fighter.
Takes you into the far future. Mankind has taken to the stars and has gotten in a right kerfuffle. Renegade colonists and a mysterious militant faction called the Black Fleet have taken aim at planet Earth. In particular the former have come in possession of a planet busting weapon and seek to destroy the Earth. You're an ace pilot going by the name of Adams. After being reprimanded for disobaying orders you're stuck on mundane duties. During a routine escort, you and your wingman are drawn into a galaxy wide conflict with the existance of time and space in the balance.
The game dumps the Sci-fi and space opera blabble on you thickly right off the bat. Part Star Wars, part Mass Effect and part War of 1812, the story takes you through a bunch of scenarios where you attempt to disrupt the Black fleet or the Colonials. Every scenario throws you a different curveball. Defending, attacking, raiding, bombing, dogfighting; it's all part of the changing palatte of challenges the game throws at you. Every mission comes with a choice of fighters to use and customisable armnaments. Beating the stage unlocks more ships to use and so the games keeps you coming back for those shiny platinum medals.
The game's namesake; the Strike Suit, is the poster boy for cool. It is fighter craft that can transform into mobile weapons plaform. The ship turns from a jet fighter into an attack helicopter on the fly. In fighter mode you're fast and nimble. In Strike Suite mode you can strafe and fire a plethora of weapons with deady accuracy. Strike Suit mode however consumes a special energy that can only be replenished by waiting, or by dealing damage in fighter mode. It creates a high energy tango that rewards an agressive and fast playstyle that requires a traditional degree of skill in flying games, as well as new control scheme.
The controls are perhaps my one gripe. I had to remap the entire layout before I was comfortable. It is a small matter, but once you got it all in order, the game is a blast from start to finish. Everything is unlocked by being good at the game; not good against others (there is no multiplayer to detract from the core game). I would really like to see more from this developer, as well as more of these games.

There's three difficulty settings, each one unlocked after completing the one before it. Beating the game on each difficulty actually reveals different endings. Just good luck with beating critical mode. It's not really fun or fair. Also, the unlockable characters are a little underwhelming. Only a handful of them are actually somewhat useful in combat.
In summary, I can say that this game is a solid beat-em-up experience. I'm kind of itching for more bosses and levels in the future. The one thing that bothers me about the game though, is its story.
- SPOILERS -
Beating the game on critical mode was not only a painful experience, but a bittersweet victory as well. I got the achievements and unlocked some new characters, but the ending you get for beating critical mode felt like a giant middle finger. I don't know what to believe, was the adventure real? Was it all a kid's imagination? Does the adventure actually mean nothing and was the main character dead from the start? I love the game's style and such, and I still find it very fun to play, it's just that these questions and that ending really do bother me. Just a personal thing I wanted to mention.

That Dragon Cancer is an extremely personal and, at times, deeply moving videogame. I really do applaud the bravery of the Green family, who have chosen to share such an intimate and tragic part of their lives. They, and the rest of the Numinous Games team, have created a game with such overwhelming emotional moments that forces even the biggest of cynics to feel something at their very core. This, quite frankly, is an incredible achievement for any piece of art.
Unfortunately, there are times were this connection is ripped from the player due to frustrating control issues and design choices that just feel ‘off’. The prime examples of this are the kart racing and church scenes, which simply break the intense immersion that is otherwise prevalent and make the experience feel unpolished. Thankfully the frank sincerity with which the Green’s tell their story is so touching that these minority of disconnecting points do not become a burden.
Players’ reactions to That Dragon Cancer may vary depending on their opinions and outlook on life. For instance, I struggled to feel as empathetic as I could have done at points due to the discussion of the family’s religious beliefs. This isn’t a slight against the game, it is simply a part of their story and just one of several elements of it that are ripe for post-play conversation. Couple this push for discourse with the emotional impact provided, and you get an experience that players will be thinking about long after the credits roll.

A solid but flawed beat-em-up that came out of nowhere. Great pixel art, fun combat, and a good overall presentation make it worth the asking price. However, the game will be polarizing for many. If you enjoy beat-em-ups that are more grounded and less combo-heavy, this isn't the game for you. If you like fast-paced action games with a combo system that allows the player to make their own identity in combat, you'll love this game despite its flaws. There are a large amount of unlockables and online co-op for the Workshop (think Bloody Palace), along with three difficulties for the single player campaign. For $10 you'll get about 3-4 hours out of the first mode of the campaign, and many more if you choose to unlock everything and go for records on the Workshop mode.
Sadly, the game isn't without its flaws. The movement controls are mapped to the left analog stick by default, but this can be easily fixed via the Steam beta client. Even with the movement changed to the d-pad, the game seems to have difficulty reading certain inputs, which can lead to disaster if you're trying to get a super move out in a pinch. Bosses are a mixed bag with invincible supers (although the player has these as well) and seemingly random rules for when they stagger and when they have super armor. This makes the ground combat borderline useless on them without taking a risk, and charge attacks or supers are the only semi-guaranteed way to start a combo. They will also tech out of juggles at random instead of at set times, which can be frustrating if you stagger them with a super and don't get to capitalize on it for full damage. The defensive options are lacking; you have a tech roll that spends your super meter, a dash with a significant cooldown, a hyper armor mode that also increases the character's speed, and a pursuit move in the air that doubles as an airdash. None of these defensive options seem to help much against the bosses or large crowds of enemies; if you dash through one enemy and whiff your dash attack, the long recovery will put you in trouble. Punishing a boss after dodging their super feels off since there's no guarantee you can get any significant damage off it. When the bosses don't stagger for long periods of time or basic enemies combo you, it often feels like the game is missing a few mechanics. The offensive options are solid, but the defensive options feel half-baked. In general, the boss battles feel slow-paced and a bit too random given how controlled everything else is. The critical mechanic is supposed to serve as your main crowd control tool, but due to the vague timing to execute it, it feels more like a random bonus. If the enemies had an indication/tell for the timing, it would be a much more viable tool for the second half's large crowds and difficult to stagger bosses. While this is nothing that couldn't get fixed in a patch, the game starts to feel a bit unfair and random towards the end of the second half.
The difficulty curve is high and it definitely rewards execution, but the aforementioned issues can sometimes make it feel like taking damage isn't entirely your fault. For the asking price there's a lot of content to go through, but seeing as the game is quite difficult on the first difficulty, factoring the other two modes into the overall replay value may not go well for anyone but the most experienced beat-em-up fans. The developers are open to feedback, so hopefully these issues will be ironed out in due time. These games don't come out often, so definitely support it if you can. The passion in this game is obvious in every aspect, from the art style to the animation and gameplay, but the flaws may turn some people away.
I finished the campaign in about three hours with some deaths and running through a few levels extra times for Youtube footage. The campaign is long for the genre, but the solid combat keeps it fresh. It can easily be finished in one sitting, but playing through it in chunks might be better due to what the game asks of the player. I will update this review if the boss mechanics and control issues are fixed.

Not as good as Journey.
Like, nowhere near.
There's just not enough of a "gaming" element for me. Journey had great core mechanics revolving around platforming and puzzle solving. Abzu has swimming. Just swimming. There's no challenge and 0% skill involved, other than using the sometimes awkward combination of camera and player controls. This gets particularly bad in corners or other tight spaces.
Journey's narrative unfolded through sound, ambience and visuals, with a real sense that the player is driving towards somthing. The problem with Abzu is that it's not just inferior in terms of gameplay mechanics and challenge, it's also a far less engaging narrative. After an hour of swimming around going vaguely forwards, I was still completely lacking any sense of purpose, and was struggling with any reason to keep playing at all.
If you want to go exploring in a pretty underwater world, then Abzu will probably do you fine. But it lacks the depth and engagement of Journey, and you'll probably get bored quickly. I did.

A little too wacky for my tastes.  The game also has this horribly long buffering time where you'll end up executing moves just because you tilted up on the stick.  It functions similarly to Smash Bros, where directions inputs change up some attacks...which is good in theory.
Trying to execute a simple combo like Punch, Punch, Up+Kick, VERY often has you actually performing a Punch, Up+Punch because of this.  It's pretty hard to get in specific directional moves and makes for a unsatisfying experience.
Also, you can't remap directions from the Analog to the D-Pad by default.  While I normally wouldn't care AS much, the "EX-Moves" (Supers) are formatted in something like "Down, Forward, Punch". If you try a Hadouken/QCF input, the move doesnt come out...it uses the old school "mortal kombat" input, where you have to tap Down, then Forwards to get it to work.
While I enjoy the juggling aspect, the issue of this format (and other games similar to it) is that it puts too much emphasis on it; air juggling enemies infinitely more or less takes the challenge out of it and the only way some enemies and bosses can counter this is by having random moments where they become invincible and dash out of the combo.
The super-moves are nice, but since they're trouble to execute, and since air juggling is much better 9 times out of 10, you're better off just juggling...or waiting until you unlock the Air EX move so you can juggle and chain it into a super.
No grapples, either, but that's a personal gripe.  If you want a game where you -can- juggle, but dont -have- to, and want a game that feels more solid over-all, albeit slightly buggy, check out Devil's Dare.
Most of these issues can be cleared up in a few patches, but I'd stay away for now.

I was kind of looking forward to playing this game, and I can't help but feel a little disappointed from the result.
Well, okay, I wasn't expecting something that fantastic. But I was expecting something that made me- you know- FEEL something!
ABZU is the first creation from Giant Squid, created by the art director of the games Flower and Journey, Matt Nava. Now, before I talk about what ABZU is about or the gameplay or all that whatnot, I think it's fair that I shoot off my opinions about Flower and Journey first.
You know how much I love to do that.
Flower is pretty average. The visuals are stunning and it controls marvelously, but the story behind it is pretty bland. It focuses too much on the nature vs. man conflict and doesn't do anything that creative or new with it. I get it, Flower. I'll start using eco-friendly lightbulbs. Get off my f***ing case!
Journey is pretty damn good. Again, it's conflict is too similar to Flower and I didn't get much out of it. I didn't feel that the threat was that imposing, but I loved the visuals and controls once again. I also think the puzzles, silent storytelling, and link-up play with strangers made it feel a lot more genuine. Did it deserve game of the year 2012? Not really. But it's still worth a look at.
ABZU follows a lot of similar themes to these games, which is to be expected after coming from a guy who worked so hard on these previous games. I may not love them as much as other people, but I do think there was a lot of effort put into them nonetheless. However, ABZU feels a bit lazily made in some regards.
How? Well, that's the tricky part.
I think, yet again, that the visuals are stunning. The underwater world of ABZU is breathtaking at times. The sea floor is designed in a cell-shaded cartoony theme but each environment you explore varies enough in structure and color palette to give a sense of discovery and each looks unique and beautiful enough to warrant appreciation. The fish that habitate the world make it feel alive and bustling with energy and each fish is designed uniquely with different swim patterns and tendencies. To be brief, this game really makes you feel like an scuba-diving explorer.
Along with that, Austin Wintory makes his return to composing another excellently-done video game soundtrack. He did a fantastic job in Journey, and I personally think he outdid his work with ABZU. Some of the songs that play are so seamless that they help draw you further into the action or calm that happens within the game. One of my favorite tracks is "Delphinus Delphis", that really captures the essence of swimming through a fast jetstream filled with millions of fish swimming about all around you. It captures the wonder, the danger, and excitement within ABZU wonderfully, and I think Wintory is definitely getting the recognition he deserves. I certainly hope he keeps going on to compose more video games, or even some movies in the future.
Well, it does sound like I like ABZU a lot, doesn't it? But you know me. I can never truly love anything, especially a game revolving around the sea. It reminds me of when I was a young boy, living alone on a small island in the Pacific when I would sleep alone, shivering beneath the palm tree as the waves would bash the eastern side of the island, as if to frighten me. I've been scared of the ocean ever since.
If you believed that story, congratulations. You're gullible.
No, what does bother me about ABZU is the laziness of the story-telling.  For one, it relies on you befriending this shark that's introduced in the game but I didn't have much reason to do so. He acts very showy and aggresive, but after saving him he doesn't really do anything. And when they try to pull on your heartstrings, it just felt very rushed and forced.
Along with that, I groaned when I saw events unfurl in ABZU the exact same way they did in Flower and Journey. Yet again, there is an all-powerful, dying, destructive force that is imposing itself on the environment and nearly overpowers you, until you find the magical power of "the first thing we pulled out of our a**es" and you finally crush the big, evil... thing and save the world! I was hoping it would do something a little different, but the writing fell back on the same conventions built on Flower and Journey which are, in my opinion, weak. I never felt that intimidated by the big-machine-thing because it didn't pose a real threat. I'd already restored the sea-coral-magic-things and the mines set up all over don't even kill you, they just stop you for a couple seconds. That's not scary. That's annoying and tedious.
The gameplay is also significantly weaker in ABZU than it was in Journey and more on par with Flower. Oftentimes, you're left to explore a large room with two switches put somewhere randomly around the room that will both open the door. It's not challenging or engaging. It's boring, and far too often does ABZU rely on the big-room-two-switches-one-door idea that it feels very lazily designed. In Journey, you often had to use teamwork or your own know-how to solve the puzzles set before you. They weren't that challenging, but they were something! With ABZU, it feels more like you're doing the same thing over and over. You swim down a jet stream, follow some whales, go through a giant robot door, find two switches, open a door, wash, rinse, and repeat.
I still think ABZU is worth playing, if you like this sort of game. I'm just disappointed that even with a fresh new design team, ABZU can't help but feel like just another game made by thatgamecompany, but this time it's underwater. It's certainly beautiful and excellently-scored, but the execution of the story is so bland and forgettable that I couldn't be bothered to remember it within the next week. But that scuba diving and underwater exploration was so engaging that I might go back and play ABZU simply for that pleasure alone. I'm giving ABZU a 7/10.
Also, don't worry about the warnings for having a controller in this game. It controls just fine with a keyboard and mouse. Take my word for it.

The Witcher 2, the game that was forgotten after Skyrim was released. But now you're here whether to buy this game because you hear Witcher 3 is amazing. One thing that this game is most praised about is its story. But honestly, it's not that impressive. The plot was not boring, but after you finish the game and sit to think about it, it's pretty basic.
There are also some characters that are mentioned who were never introduced. An example is Ciri, who does not appear until the third game. Sometimes there are characters that are mentioned and I'm completely oblivious to. Also, once you take a few days of break, you're likely to easily forget who is who.
Second complaint is that the game feels too clunky. The combat system is a lot better than the first Witcher, where you just click to hit. But it's annoying when you cannot pick up items, jump down cliffs, or open doors until Geralt is relaxed. You can tell that this game was made in mind for consoles first while playing.
Definitely, the most annoying problem is that you cannot overwrite saves. I don't know why they decided to do it this way. You're able to do this in the first Witcher. The problem is that when you make too many saves, the game crashes. I've tried to follow different solutions but the game is still crashing for me.
You also have to finish the game twice. [MINOR SPOILER] There's a point where you have to decide between Roche and Iorveth. Picking one side completely changes the story. It's interesting to see the different perspectives of both sides, but if you only play one side, you're only playing 50% of the game. And it's a little annoying when playing the second time because you already know what the ultimate ending is.
Overall: 7/10
There are some annoying problems here and there, but the game isn't a complete mess. Darts and bombs are useless (imo). Only 5 sex scenes in all that look the same. And frequent crashes towards the end of the game due to not able to overwrite the wall saves. The story isn't the greatest, but I'd praise this game for its combat system. It really is a huge improvement compared to the first Witcher. You hit when you want to, and the signs are actually useful. A decent game if you're into fantasy RPGs.

Necropolis was a beautiful mess when it first came out. It was fun, yes, but it wasn't polished. The game was playable, and fun, but it wasn't great. Then the devs put out 1.0.1 and completely finished the game. And 1.0.2 made it amazing. And how 1.1 is out, and Necropolis is wonderful. It's unique, with the Dark Souls: ROGUELIKE EDITION theme going, with sarcastic and humourous dialogue, and just overall interesting styles. The art style is very nice, and fits well, being geometric and simple, but serving the game's theme perfectly. The combat system is well developed, and as they've added special effects to weapons, it's gotten better. The enemies are unique, interesting, and fun to deal with, especially when you realize that you walked around a corner into 3 Gemeaters and a huge Grine colony, plus a bunch of skeletons. The game's revive system is now balanced, so MP isn't just a free ride to the end, and the game does scale in difficulty, because I got 3 shot on the third floor, and I was STACKED.
While I dislike the inability to customize your keyboard and the reccomendation to play with a controller, the keyboard layout isn't terrible, for the most part, and it isn't unplayable without a controller.

Changing my review back to positive since I have not experienced any bugs since my last review a couple weeks ago.
You can see by my time played that I've put more into this game a lot of the others who have reviewed.
I have beaten the game with the Brute and have made it pretty far with the Blackguard
Pros
- Very appealing art style
- Game is more random that it appears at first, even with my time played I am still coming across new arrangements and biomes, hidden routes, etc
- I play solo,  and personally find the game to be very challenging in it's current state. It feels like it's balanced for a multiplayer game. Have only managed to beat it once, and am still trying with the Blackguard
- Combat system is simple, very similar to Dark Souls, but has more depth than it seems at first. The types of weapons and armor you have, their attributes (weight, speed, element type, special abilities) can really change your strategy up
- Armor sets, once you start finding them, are all wildly different (and is the biggest difference between the Brute and the Blackguard) and probably do more than any other item to change up your gameplay. I still haven't tried them all
- Doing an entire run take a reasonable amount of time if you don't try to speed run it (5-6 hours if you play at a normal pace and explore everything). I usually do 1-2 levels at a time
Cons
- Sometimes buggy. They seem to have fixed the serious issues, but I still get occasional annoying glitches, things like chests not being interactable, etc
- The 2 characters are good for variety, but aren't balanced properly. The Brute is much better. Either make each character more or less or mark The Brute as 'Easy Mode' because he kinda is
- Despite what I said before, the level of variety could still be improved. A game that's all about replayability should feel as fresh as possible every run through
- The new mob, the bandit, isn't balanced properly. He is fast, has long range weapons and bombs, spawns repeatedly behind you (discouraging exploration :/) can steal items AND can steal practically all of your gems, which you need to progress. Later in the game they aren't so bad because you have stronger weapons, but they can pop up very early in your playthrough, and in groups, and it's way too much. Make it weaker (so they can be fought in earlier levels). And if you kill it you should at least get most of your gems back. The constant spawning is also super frustrating. In my mind it really turns what is normally a great thing about this game, exploring the beautiful environments, and makes it into a frustrating slog. To be clear, I think the bandit was a good addition to the game (variety!) but needs some fine-tuning
- Cost is a little much, even with the update (although I certainly felt it was worth the money)
- Really feels like it was designed for multiplayer and seems like it would be a great multiplayer game, but there is no group finding. So yeah, unless you know 3 other people who want to pay 30 bucks for a really hard rogue-like, no multiplayer
To sum up:
A challenging, visually unique rogue-like that needs a bit of polish; but still worth getting if this is a genre that interests you. If you have friends who would purchase and play this game with you, then definitely get it. If the devs keep releasing updates, could be one of the best out there

Previously my review of the version of this game which came out back in July was less than positive. And, despite what people wanted to fanboy about (the level of negative reviews backed up a lot of my claims), perfectly fair. However with the new Brutal Edition update, and an apparent uplift in the positivity of the reviews, i felt almost obliged to take a step back in to this game with a fresh perspective.
And wow, it has changed. Not necessarily to the level of it being an amazing game, (it still has its issues), but it feels far more like its actually worth the cost of the game.
Ill start with the good stuff, just to make sure you all realise that while im still not the biggest fan of the game, i dont feel outright disappointed. Now i just feel like its not for me, and i can agree with anyone elses praises of it for the most part.
++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
+Graphics Style: I said this before, and ill say it again. It looks good, and its not because the devs are lazy (you idiots who claimed that back in July). No it doesnt require two GTX1080 SLI to reach 30fps stable, but for all the ACTUAL gamers out there (as opposed to tourists like the graphics elitists are) know that it takes more than sparkles to make a game good.
+Combat: Previously i believe i may have given this a con, due to it being rather generic and uninteresting for how easy the fights were. But with the addition of larger and varied troops and enemy combinations, the simplicity turns completely around and actually shines. Also they nerfed the block, which is good.
+Enemy variety: While in the time i played i only encountered one new enemy than i did back in the July version of the game, the actual combination of enemies within the maps are far more varied. You no longer deal with just 3-4 basic soldiers over and over until you encounter 1-2 bigger dudes. Youll frequently stumble into 1-3 little dudes, 3-4 larger ones, a spider or two and even maybe a street shark.
+The Maps: Thanks to the addition of a lot of mapset pieces, and (i dont doubt) effort on the devs part, the maps you move through are no longer incredibly linear. Previously you would have a side passage here or there, but ultimately leading to the same room to progress. There wasnt much alternate areas or approaches. This has changed a lot. Hell, it doesnt even feel as horizontal as it did before.
________________________________________________________________________________
-The Usual Soulsborne-esque sins: Now, im not going to right out and say that this game is TRYING to be dark souls/bloodborne, (in the way kids these days would say "ripped off") but it certainly is influenced by that type of gameplay. Unfortunately, like many similar to it, it fails to grasp the whole concept of WHY dark souls did what it did so well. It was never the raw difficulty, but a large number of elements combined together to bring out a strategic and intimidating world and experience for all. Enemys had certain attacks, or combat styles or approaches which would force you to think about how to adjust your playstyle to them, or use the world to your advantage.
Necropolis STILL doesnt do this. In this, and many others like it, the 'challenge' can be summed up in three different ways.
"Cluster♥♥♥♥ the player"
"Its totally logical for the player to be hindered by things the enemies arent." (and Vice Versa, though)
"Lots of fast, nearly undodgeable damage."
Take these away, and the fights would be trivial. Except for those Street Sharks, those seem to be pretty well designed, if a little powerful to encounter early on.
-Still a large lack of replayability: Not to say its anything near what it was previously (the addition of a lot of map pieces means you dont feel like youre trekking through the same map over and over), but its still nothing close to what games like Binding of Isaac (for a Rogue-like example) or Neon Chrome (For a Rogue-lite example) might bring you. You genuinely need to enjoy ALL the aspects of the game to get replayability, theres no real material motivation.
That being said, its likely that as the game is built more and more upon, it will gain a lot of it. Assuming it doesnt go all Hero Seige and wreck the gameplay without fixing many of the issues.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
In addition there are some small opinion based issues i have with the game, but they dont belong in a proper review. Theyre also really insignificant for the most part, so it would be unfair to list them.
In summary, while its a game that still doesnt really provide an entirely new or innovative experience, it has definitely become a game worth its cost (especially if you take into account the likelihood of more content in the future). The co-op is probably a huge + too. I cant comment on it though because im the only one of my friends willing to play Necropolis.

Still being updated occassionally at the moment, but these are tweaks rather than serious changes to gameplay, which is already excellent.
The AI can be very challenging at times, which is a nice change from many strategy games (you can also play Multiplayer). Theoretically, the game can support hundreds of factions on a single (huge) map!
There is genuine immersion, and the game asks serious questions of you at times: deciding whether to prioritise research or ship construction can be a serious concern, and you'll find yourself falling behind with the other even as you gain an advantage with one. Even if you had comfortably decided that research is key, you still have to decide whether economic or military would better serve you - and all the while the AI will be hatching schemes of its own.
Furthermore regarding military research, this game is unique (to me at least) in how it can propagate arms races between factions. There are three basic weapon types: lasers, kinetic and missile (and their defences). If you focus on missiles for example, you may be able to ruin anyone lacking missile defences but would suffer miserably if your opponent has anti-missile defences aplenty. You could even build up a balanced military, but this would take time, rescources and leave you with few obvious strengths.
Diplomacy is failrly intelligent, and gives a wide veriaty of options regarding tech and rescource trades, alliances, pacts, threats etc. lastly, the modding community is incredible - there are modded races and ships for almost everything, from the Tardis to Star Trek to Battlestar Galactica to Warhammer 40K!
I utterly love this game, and if you enjoy 4X style games (or turn-based strategy generally) you can't afford to give this a miss.

Spotty textures, limited descriptions, annoying glitches... and yet something about Might and Magic X: Legacy is so very, very Awesome.
Thanks to Legend of Grimrock (a game I also recommend and IMHO better than this), there has been a resurgance of grid-based dungeon crawlers. Legacy follows suit and provides hours of singleplayer entertainment that many RPG fans will likely enjoy. While anyone trying out grid-based rpgs first time should try the cheaper and more polished Grimrock first, Legacy will scratch that RPG itch whenever it comes up. If its too much for you now, save it to your wishlist for a future sale.
Legacy's combat and character management is where the game really shines. Many of the toughest boss fights are challenging, unique and provide a great sense of accomplishment after bringing them down. You might find yourself reloading a save once or twice as you figure out a bosses mechanics. Even the common enemies can't be taken down with just basic attacks and rightfully punishes players who underestimate their foe. Large variety in classes and skills makes every character level up feel meaningful and potent as you mold your party into your own. You'll find yourself using nearly every skill you acquire, from minor spells like Light Orb or Fire Ward to the warfare skills of your melee classes to powerful grandmaster spells like Thunderstorm. The default party offers a great balance to different playstyles, but there are so many different class/racial combinations its worth building your own unique party, especially if you plan to only make one playthrough.
Different scenery and enemies throughout the game offers much needed variety, which the Legend of Grimrock lacks. Dungeons are engaging, fun and filled with secrets; which are found with a perception check rather than the players own cunning and discovery. That said, the developers have wisely taken many of the games puzzles and placed them in "mysterious crypts" dotted around the map, rather than amongst the major quests which could serve to only slow the pacing. Even than, the crypts offer excellent items worth trying to get, but by no means necessary to complete the game. Storyline is your typical fanasty affair with an unseen villian who needs stopping, but interesting enough to provide some entertainment.
Fantastic RPG specific qualities aside, you will find some pretty horrid textures within the game. Even after changing the options from the main menu (a MUST), the game was filled with some objects and characters that are something you'd expect from 2003. Most of these seem to come from the unit models brought in from Might and Magic Heroes VI, which were likely not optimized or polished for upclose inspection. On the other hand, some charecters are quite detailed. It seems that Ubisoft has tried to spend as little as possible on this title and the wide margin in texture quality shows as a result. I myself have run into a graphic glitch where most of the world area's cities and castles disappeared from view, resulting in me wasting a good 15 minutes trying to find a particular castle, until I figured out what had happened. Thankfully a simple game restart solved the problem. Judging by the forums there are other graphics glitches and some quest breaking bugs, though I haven't run into them myself.
Many of the quests also lack enough description which might leave you trying to figure out what exactly your looking for. World map is also painfully simple, providing markers for only the most important cities and main dungeons, yet neglecting to identify individual sections of the map which are often given as your only clue about where to go for a certain quest. You'll also need a pen or pencil once or twice as your party seems to have none of their own for a couple critical details.
Might and Magic: Legacy X is a fun addition to grid-based RPGs and I felt was worth the $25, which I luckly didn't have to spend due to the recent Ubisoft sale, though others might consider it too much at its current price. However, it is definitely worth keeping on your wishlist for an appropriate sale or price drop. Those who haven't picked up cheaper RPGs (especially Grimrock) should get those first before putting money in this new title.

This is a good game, but not a great game. If you don't expect more than an arcadey good time, you'll be fine. On sale, this game is a very good deal, with friends, it's a great deal.

The single player stuff is fun. The multiplayer is really what sets this game apart. You're still doing the same or similar stuff, but with a few other people, everything is amplified. It's more frantic, and that really makes this a better game.
The menus and some game decisions are a bit odd, not very friendly, but not so bad as to ruin the game. But things like showing a button to go back, labelled ESC, that you can only operate with your mouse... what?

'Strike Suit Zero: Directors Cut' is a space combat game that lets you fly a handful of different spacecrafts, each with special abilities, on a mission to save earth from final distinction.
It is impossible to write a review about this game without mentioning 'Strike Suit Zero', the game that came before 'Strike Suit Zero: Directors Cut'.
The expression 'Directors Cut' automatically makes us believe that 'Strike Suit Zero' and 'Strike Suit Zero: Directors Cut' have to be more or less equal games, with only a few tiny variations, as we know from so many movies. This however, is not the case. IMO 'Strike Suit Zero' and 'Strike Suit Zero: Director Cut' are very different games. And while I do recommend the directors cut I do not recommend the original game 'Strike Suit Zero'.
So what's the difference?
Well, the main difference is that you have a chance to complete the game in the directors cut. You might also be able to finish the original game, but according to Steam statistics only 5.3% of all players managed to see the end of the main campaign in 'Strike Suit Zero'. So the major difference is the difficulty. 'Strike Suit Zero' gets incredibly hard at some points, even on easy, while the difficulty in the directors cut if very fair.
Besides the difficulty developers changed the graphics and made the directors cut more colorful. IMO this makes the original game look more realistic. But both games look very nice.
They also changed the sequences of the story dramatically. I would not say it's necessarily better, events just unfold very differently but eventually lead to the same end.
Controls are also different in both games, although only slightly.
One outstanding aspect of the game is the music. IMO the music of 'Strike Suit Zero' is on of the best game soundtracks ever. And while the original game comes with soundtrack and art-book, the directors cut does not. I even had the impression that not all parts of the soundtrack appear in the directors cut, although I might be wrong about that. I've started playing the music on my stereo via a MP3 stick. It's great. Go to the shop page of the original game to hear what I mean.
Strike Suit Zero: Directors Cut
Pros:
- nice graphics
- great music
- additional simulation levels beside the main campaign that are very enjoyable
- good controls, although I needed a while to get used to them
- some space crafts can convert into strike suits, a space robot that can kill scores of enemies in single attacks
- good, interesting story
- very good voice acting
- balanced and fair difficulty
Cons:
- disappointing final level of the campaign
- short campaign (13 missions)

I was surprised by how good this game is. Gamers old enough to remember the older Might and Magic games of the 1990s will recall that they were some of the best open-world RPGs of their time. MM3 through MM7 were absolute classics that I still play once every couple of years. MM8 showed signs of decay and MM9 was a flat-out disaster. So when I heard there was a new one coming after several years, I was skeptical...but this game captures most of what was really fun about the old ones.
I do wish that there was more customization in terms of character design in terms of appearance, the party members are only ever represented on screen by a little portrait, so letting players have more power over how they look wouldn't have been especially hard. The options for different classes (i.e. sorcerer, knight, etc) also seemed surprisingly limited. The older games actually gave you more options in this regard.
Gamers who didn't grow up with Might and Magic could find this tedious and primitive - the tile-based movement and turn-based combat are relics of a past era. But those of us with fond memories of the old games are in for a nice round of nostalgia.

I totally forgot to comment on the voice acting in my review for the original SSZ! Now that I think about it, it was essentially that at its best: forgettable. The only times it ever really made any impression on me at all were when the line deliveries were weird. For example, every time I played the mission Thule Station I took notice when Captain McCallum told Control, "Flight Team Leader Reynolds is the best we HAVE..." in a slightly incredulous tone that would only have made sense if he'd said it in response to Control requesting for Adams first. Instead he says it apropos of nothing.
To remedy that slight fault, the Director's Cut adds a lot more voice acting in the form of expositionary dialogue AND re-recording some of those awkward lines from the original so that they sound more natural. The story and background have been fleshed out into something that's actually worthy to say something about: it was good. Not the most original but there's actually something there now that piques my interest. I want to know more about Akira 5. I want to know more about Dr. Abram. The fact that I'm interested in the story at all means they succeeded in something. This game isn't just a series of disjointed combat missions anymore. The character of Control has a lot more lines and her characterization also changes subtly. All of this improves the game as a whole.
All the ships and space platforms have been retextured to have more colour. Personally, I actually preferred the staid colour-scheme of the original. Chalk it up to my childhood impressions of spaceships being formed by Star Wars and Star Trek. White, grey, and bands of glowing blue are the proper colours of spaceships in my mind.

It is hard to explain what this game is about. The "base" is a top down shooter. You have guns and melee weapons. All items can be thrown. Some, like knives, are lethal. Others, will just knock the enemy down for a few seconds. Most important thing is that, everybody dies pretty quickly, including you.
On top of that base game is a puzzle game. At least, it seems to me that way, considering how every level is built. The goal is to kill everyone in a level in one go. There are some rules in the game. Like if the enemy is standing behind a door and you just run into the room, you will knock the enemy down. The enemies do not react to dead bodies, but they do react to you, and anybody who sees you will run after you. But if a gunshot is heard, everybody will be alerted in that level. As said before, everything pretty much kills you in one hit, but you always have one advantage over your enemy because of your vision and the masks. Masks are basically collectables, that grant you abilities. There are a total of 26 in the game.
A note on why i think it has features of a puzzle game. I feel this way because the game always has some people that are much easier to kill. Some enemies patrol the level, and you can take them down from behind, so long as they are not looking. Others, pretty much intentionally, walk by the doors for example. It just feels like the game was designed this way, so that you would kill these people first.
The trick is to kill as many people in the level without alerting anyone before actually going guns blazing. You start off with nothing at the start of the level, though having some masks equiped can change that. You work your way up, find better items throughout the level.
As you progress through the game, the levels will start becoming harder, there will be more enemies and they will have better weapons. Personally, i am not much into puzzle games, but this one i liked, probably because it is more action oriented.

There are quite a few things to like about Crypt of the NecroDancer, and there's no question that it is the result of having an interesting crazy idea and running with it - and I love seeing game writers taking risks and doing crazy interesting stuff.
But.  This just doesn't work for me.  I'm probably not really the target audience - I have never gotten into the rhythm/dance games at all, and am now probably a bit old and just not generally able to slip into the "zone" when playing.
Playing the game 'properly', with the beat (not as Bard) is frequently just too chaotic and confusing - particularly when starting out with this constant time pressure (not just the urgency of keeping to the beat, but also knowing there's only a limited amount of time until the song ends and you get forcibly moved on).  I frequently couldn't work out what items were - reading the text was problematic at times, and if I'd picked something up that I didn't already know I found it quite difficult to work out what I had picked up and what to do with it.
Playing as Bard (not the default for a Newbie, and I understand why because it doesn't really represent the 'core experience' of the game) sort of solved a lot of this - the time pressure is removed so you can spend as long as you need to look at items and play around with them and learn the enemy behaviour.  But playing as Bard is just dull for the most part.  Removing that core mechanic does drain the game of any particular interest.  I thought it would make sense to play as Bard enough to learn what I needed to learn and then go back in with the beat to enjoy the game, but frankly it just didn't hold enough appeal to do this.
The music is great.  The graphics are ok.  The roguelike stuff is ok, although the upgrade system is a bit thin, a bit poorly implemented and a bit ... I don't know, just patchy.  Not enough richness to make it feel worth crawling through the dungeon again and again like a good dungeon crawler does.
And there are bugs.  Playing on Windows it just dumped me out of the game every other hour or so.  Not such a big deal, but not great.  And a few possibly deliberate gameplay choices that seem like bugs - the mimics that reveal themselves when you stand next to them, but are still counted as "fail" moves to attack until you take a step and get them to move off their square.  It's sitting right there pulsating, I know I need to kill it, but you just fail me for swinging at it?  Minor, but annoying nonetheless.
I think there are people who will enjoy this, but it frustrated me too often for too little reward and too little motivation to keep playing.

Queen's Quest 3: The End of Dawn isn't related to the previous part of the series and could be labeled as a seemingly decent hidden object game: it tries to do everything right, but overall it feels like another run-of-the-mill product and thus it's easily forgettable. The plot is predictable despite the double twist, the fantasy world it takes place in is characterless, the puzzles are plentiful, but either too easy or time-consuming.
According to the story we play as Eliana, a young female alchemist who was dropped off at the doors of an alchemy academy as a newborn and had been raised by the Headmaster of the institute. An ancient dragon, once defeated by the combined forces of humans, dwarves and elves is about to awaken and threatens the world again. As the chosen one, we have to stop the dragon.
The role of alchemy is subsidiary in this game, as opposed to Queen's Quest 2: Stories of Forgotten Past, where we consantly had to shapeshift into forms of different creatures by drinking various brews. Sometimes we have to concoct potions and take the forms of others to get past guards, but most of the time, we are going to have to use our amulet and shoot energy rays at our enemies to defeat them.
There are literally tons of hidden object scenes, as we are going to need plenty of items which require multiple parts (marked as 1/2 and 2/2) and so we'll have to look for them through these. Needless to say, these will take away most of our time and it feels like an unnecessary method of prolonging the duration of gameplay. The background story is also told through simplifed hidden object scenes, where we have to find 3 runes on the picture in order to progress. There's an alternative method solving the HO scenes, a pairmatching minigame, where we have to match  related images, which is certainly an interesting feature.
The minigames are similarly numerous, but unfortunately they are either too easy (most of them are) or just frustrating, stretching gameplay time. All these (the overuse of even twice used hidden object scenes and frustrating minigames) are especially true for the bonus chapter, in which we have to help one of the characters from the main game and it's a totally uninteresting add-on. Less, but more creative puzzles and minigames would have been better.
There are some strange examples for item use, like breaking a padlock with 2 wrenches (?) or not having to use a fireplace poker to remove something from amidst embers. On the other hand there are some imaginative portions of the game regarding items which I liked, for example where we crashland with the balloon and an emblem disappears from our inventory, which we have to find and reassemble again.
The game features a helper (much like the circus monkey from Dark Arcana: The Carnival): Dahlia, the fairy, which is a welcome addition, but her role narrows down to reach some items that are either too high or far (even then sometimes we have use a stick to reach these, despite the fairy being there with us). Another character however, the rogue/merchant is amusing and it's a good thing we meet him several times throughout the story.
There are 3 kinds of collectibles for achievement enthusiasts, but one of them (crest) is very hard to spot since its appearance changes in each chapter.
Graphically the game is nice, but nearly not as beautiful as recent HOGs, or just to stay at the series, the previous installment. The animations are usually the weakest point of this genre, but Artifex Mundi originals still manage to produce decent ones. Here however they are below average and could have used a bit more frames.
The music for the most part is good and relaxing to listen to and the same can be told about the ambient effects.
The written text and the narrated speech don't always correspond to each other, but contentwise they are pretty much the same.
My feelings towards Queen's Quest 3: The End of Dawn are quite mixed. The over-enthusiasm and its negative effects on quality clearly show, but still, I can't say that the game is bad. It's just an average hidden object game with some nicely done elements. It can be easily skipped, if you are not a hardcore fan of the genre, but if you are, you can give it a try.
PROS
+ plenty of minigames and hidden object scenes
+ has almost all the elements a HOG needs, pairmatching game, fairy helper
+ good music
CONS
- way too many hidden object scenes
- most minigames are either too easy or time-consuming
- items consisting of way to many parts
- plot is pretty generic
RATING
5/10

This game tries hard, but with the awful animation, bland story, disinterested voice actors, and tedious hidden object scenes, it simply doesn’t work as a decent hidden object game.
It is rare to see a new hidden object game series nowadays where every game has a completely different basic premise, but looks like Queen’s Quest is like that. The third instalment, The End of Dawn not only lacks any kind of royalty, but even the second game’s fairy tale detective premise was dropped to replace it with a generic formula: we play as a young alchemy student, who finds out that she plays a central role in a prophecy about an evil dragon.
This plot feels thin from the start, and this is just the first warning sign of the many issues. The story is bland. The voice actors were so bored out of their minds that they did not even try. The animations, especially the facial ones, are terrifyingly horrendous. The hidden object scenes are full of similar-looking tiny objects, making them tiresome and tedious.
The list could go on, but I think the point is clear: Queen’s Quest 3 is simply not a good hidden object game. The level art is nice and it lasts long, but that is all it can say about itself.

I was kind of looking forward to playing this game, and I can't help but feel a little disappointed from the result.
Well, okay, I wasn't expecting something that fantastic. But I was expecting something that made me- you know- FEEL something!
ABZU is the first creation from Giant Squid, created by the art director of the games Flower and Journey, Matt Nava. Now, before I talk about what ABZU is about or the gameplay or all that whatnot, I think it's fair that I shoot off my opinions about Flower and Journey first.
You know how much I love to do that.
Flower is pretty average. The visuals are stunning and it controls marvelously, but the story behind it is pretty bland. It focuses too much on the nature vs. man conflict and doesn't do anything that creative or new with it. I get it, Flower. I'll start using eco-friendly lightbulbs. Get off my f***ing case!
Journey is pretty damn good. Again, it's conflict is too similar to Flower and I didn't get much out of it. I didn't feel that the threat was that imposing, but I loved the visuals and controls once again. I also think the puzzles, silent storytelling, and link-up play with strangers made it feel a lot more genuine. Did it deserve game of the year 2012? Not really. But it's still worth a look at.
ABZU follows a lot of similar themes to these games, which is to be expected after coming from a guy who worked so hard on these previous games. I may not love them as much as other people, but I do think there was a lot of effort put into them nonetheless. However, ABZU feels a bit lazily made in some regards.
How? Well, that's the tricky part.
I think, yet again, that the visuals are stunning. The underwater world of ABZU is breathtaking at times. The sea floor is designed in a cell-shaded cartoony theme but each environment you explore varies enough in structure and color palette to give a sense of discovery and each looks unique and beautiful enough to warrant appreciation. The fish that habitate the world make it feel alive and bustling with energy and each fish is designed uniquely with different swim patterns and tendencies. To be brief, this game really makes you feel like an scuba-diving explorer.
Along with that, Austin Wintory makes his return to composing another excellently-done video game soundtrack. He did a fantastic job in Journey, and I personally think he outdid his work with ABZU. Some of the songs that play are so seamless that they help draw you further into the action or calm that happens within the game. One of my favorite tracks is "Delphinus Delphis", that really captures the essence of swimming through a fast jetstream filled with millions of fish swimming about all around you. It captures the wonder, the danger, and excitement within ABZU wonderfully, and I think Wintory is definitely getting the recognition he deserves. I certainly hope he keeps going on to compose more video games, or even some movies in the future.
Well, it does sound like I like ABZU a lot, doesn't it? But you know me. I can never truly love anything, especially a game revolving around the sea. It reminds me of when I was a young boy, living alone on a small island in the Pacific when I would sleep alone, shivering beneath the palm tree as the waves would bash the eastern side of the island, as if to frighten me. I've been scared of the ocean ever since.
If you believed that story, congratulations. You're gullible.
No, what does bother me about ABZU is the laziness of the story-telling.  For one, it relies on you befriending this shark that's introduced in the game but I didn't have much reason to do so. He acts very showy and aggresive, but after saving him he doesn't really do anything. And when they try to pull on your heartstrings, it just felt very rushed and forced.
Along with that, I groaned when I saw events unfurl in ABZU the exact same way they did in Flower and Journey. Yet again, there is an all-powerful, dying, destructive force that is imposing itself on the environment and nearly overpowers you, until you find the magical power of "the first thing we pulled out of our a**es" and you finally crush the big, evil... thing and save the world! I was hoping it would do something a little different, but the writing fell back on the same conventions built on Flower and Journey which are, in my opinion, weak. I never felt that intimidated by the big-machine-thing because it didn't pose a real threat. I'd already restored the sea-coral-magic-things and the mines set up all over don't even kill you, they just stop you for a couple seconds. That's not scary. That's annoying and tedious.
The gameplay is also significantly weaker in ABZU than it was in Journey and more on par with Flower. Oftentimes, you're left to explore a large room with two switches put somewhere randomly around the room that will both open the door. It's not challenging or engaging. It's boring, and far too often does ABZU rely on the big-room-two-switches-one-door idea that it feels very lazily designed. In Journey, you often had to use teamwork or your own know-how to solve the puzzles set before you. They weren't that challenging, but they were something! With ABZU, it feels more like you're doing the same thing over and over. You swim down a jet stream, follow some whales, go through a giant robot door, find two switches, open a door, wash, rinse, and repeat.
I still think ABZU is worth playing, if you like this sort of game. I'm just disappointed that even with a fresh new design team, ABZU can't help but feel like just another game made by thatgamecompany, but this time it's underwater. It's certainly beautiful and excellently-scored, but the execution of the story is so bland and forgettable that I couldn't be bothered to remember it within the next week. But that scuba diving and underwater exploration was so engaging that I might go back and play ABZU simply for that pleasure alone. I'm giving ABZU a 7/10.
Also, don't worry about the warnings for having a controller in this game. It controls just fine with a keyboard and mouse. Take my word for it.

Strike Suit Zero - Directors Cut - Like the original Strike Suit Zero and Strike Suit Infinity this title is massively under-rated; if you ever wondered what life as a fighter pilot in the homeworld universe (pretty much the same art style) was like then look no further! You assume control of the Strike Suit, an experimental fighter that can transform itself into an even more immense strike craft. The campaign has been slightly reworked to make the story flow better, the visuals also slightly tweaked to make the game more immersive and the music is composed by Paul Ruskay; the chap who brought us the delightful yet sinister sounds of the homeworld franchise. The gameplay takes place in the third person perspective and pits your ship against the full panoply of space based enemies, from fighters and bombers to destroyers, cruisers and capital ships. The gameplay is also surprisingly challenging and you will often find yourself overwhelmed if your concentration levels drop off even for a momment. Highly recommended if you enjoyed any of the following; Xwing, Tie Fighter, Wing Commander Series, Homeworld 1, Homeworld Cataclysm and Homeworld 2.

In Little Inferno, you sit in front of a fireplace and burn everything. It is absolutely brilliant. Before the brilliance, however, a few words of warning to the wary buyer. There's a fair amount of waiting in the game, and the puzzles you complete to progress are by no means difficult. If this does not trouble you at all, then stop reading this review right now and buy the game.
For those who remain, I present some positives. Little Inferno isn't the most technologically advanced software ever, but it looks very pretty. The bright fire effects and "JUST BURN EVERYTHING" gameplay will satisfy your inner child and pyromaniac alike. The things you're burning are quite entertaining in themselves. The game gives each a humorous name and description, and each reacts to being set on fire in a different way. An alarm clock rings until its untimely demise, a model bank churns out money, and firecrackers do exactly what you think they'd do.
So, LIttle Inferno is a solid fireplace simulator. But is that it? Is it worth $10? Go watch the trailer, and think about it. There is most definitely something more. As you start up the game, Kyle Gabler's incredible soundtrack dares you to say otherwise. And that is exactly everything I can say about that without ruining it.
tl;dr
Little Inferno is great. There's fires, and a bunch of other really great stuff that you need to play to find out for yourself, so go buy it. Also, the soundtrack is amazing.

The Witcher 2 as a game is the meaning of the word progress. Everything from the graphics to the systems behind the game are an amazing feat, one you would expect from a big named developer backed up by a huge budget. The looks of the game are not only unparalleled due to its PC only nature, but also because it presents a world that feels hand crafted. The attention to detail borders on the extreme: the clothes, the houses and buildings, the faces of the characters their weapons and in general every corner, nook and cranny of the world has a distinctive touch. The scenery is simply breathtaking, and if you are like me you will want to make a screenshot out of every frame. It also shows that you don't need an overabundance of browns and blood reds in your palette to show a gritty dark fantasy world. This game shows its maturity not through a pretense of adult topics or over the top action animations, but through a careful use of its elements and by showing the player some respect: yes, you are an adult, and you can handle these topics, because indeed the Witcher's is a dark world filled with conspiracies, racism and characters in between every single shade of gray. It is a living, breathing, unforgiving world.
The story is as complex as in the first game, filled with twists and choices that may change the fate of many, and forking paths that make a replay of the game not only encouraged, but required in order to see the extent to which they occur and diverge. Normal and hard difficulties are recommended and will test your skills if you don't face every battle with all seriousness, preparing beforehand by brewing and drinking potions and using all of your abilities during the fight, i.e. your swords your magic signs depending on what enemy you face and traps and bombs for your crowd control.
The actual combat is in no way dumbed down. It will still punish you if you go unprepared and you can't mash your way out of battles. It is in much better shape than in the first game, and friendly to both the use of a gamepad or mouse and keyboard. The user interface is slick and great looking.
The ending of the game comes abruptly, and you might feel that it doesn't solve every issue the game presents (the main storyline issues ARE solved, though). It is no excuse from what many will consider a downbeat ending, but in all honesty it doesn't detract a single beat from what this game does right, which is almost everything else. Even if you don't like the ending you will feel that the journey was worth it.
In the end I feel like I'm required to praise this game so high despite its shortcomings not because it is a perfect game, but because it is an honest one. When more and more AAA releases are done with specific quarters or demographics numbers behind, or executives who never play games are calling the shots, The Witcher 2 really feels developed to please it audience, to show them they too are tired of these.
There is a certain level of quality you expect from bigger developers which have more of a history and a name, because they deliver experiences that go way beyond what you might get from the indie guys. It is OK, they have the money and the numbers behind. This is a trend that has been changing in the last years and that no longer holds true in most cases though.
In this case in particular neither of these apply. In my mind CDProject RED are already the big name, from whom I will expect unrelenting quality. Because after what they achieved they can't be considered the little guy any longer. With the Witcher 2 they delivered a game that is truly above and beyond any RPG from the last years, that feels like a product of love, careful planning and an overall shout to fans and the gaming community that says "we know what you want, and we can deliver. Where others have failed you we will prevail." And God if they don't.
A serious contender for the best game of 2011, and frankly there is little in the horizon that looks like it might compete with it. Five years from now when other games made by bigger companies are all forgotten in the $5 bargain bins of the world, many will be reinstalling this game to reminisce and fondly say: "yes, I played a game was this good in 2011, and it was glorious."
Congratulations CDProject RED, you just released your first masterpiece.

This game has been in my library for awhile now and with the Witcher 3 just having come out, I decided to retry the Witcher 2. I thought early on that the game was a little hiccup-y and slow. The early Flotsam quests are kind of boring, but I stuck with it and actually enjoyed myself quite a bit once I stopped trying to 100% the game on my first runthrough. Some of the missions were very well thought out and the decisions I made through the game actually felt pretty meaningful and held my interest. Many of the characters were intriguing and generally cool to listen to. Some of them had some neat stories and held secrets from you, making the NPCs actually rather worth to talk to and hear everything. If you're good at reading between the lines, then you'll learn that a lot of the NPCs have plenty of things to hide. Geralt isn't an altruistic main character (unless you really want him to be) and I rather liked that. He's in it for himself at times and if he can get some gold for helping people, then so be it. I really liked that there were no "good" or "evil" answers. Each answer had a realistic response to a scenario and could swing a few ways depending on how you want people to view Geralt. The different characters and questlines over the game kept me generally interested till the end. Some of the few gripes I had with this game were that: sometimes the game will just crash for no good reason (I started save-scumming after this happened a couple times), some of the VA sounded a little deadpan next to excellent VAs for Geralt, Letho, and Iorveth, and lastly, I just really did not like early parts of chapter 1. The last point is just my opinion, but damn did early Flotsam turned me off to this game originally. I felt like I really had to force myself through some of those missions. In the end I'm glad I did however, since the rest of the game afterwards is VERY good. If you're looking for a great 30+ hour RPG with great dialogue and a pretty fun combat system, then pick this game up for sure.

A serviceable Space Shooter that doesn't raise itself above other games in the genre, let alone compare to the classics.
Total Playtime: 9 hours on hard (all achievements unlocked)
Going in the first thing I've noticed is how strange the control is compared to conventional aerial shooter. AD are used for tilting while x-axis mouse movement are for turning, which felt quite strange but it's not impossible to get used to. While the controls are responsive, the actually game mechanic leaves much to be desired. There's little to no momentum and the acceleration is way too fast for my taste. Adding into the mix the fact that your auto-fire's range is ridiculously long and we have a game with little to no finesse when it comes to aerial combat. The game also went for a approach of quantity over quality when it comes to enemy and enemy AI are near non-existent. If you expect to have epic dog fight while pulling off complicated menuever then sadly this game will disappoint you.
Moving onto the graphic, the game looks almost nice but the lack of attention to detail holds the game back in the end. While the particles and background are great, the models and textures show the game for the low budget small team project it is. For veteran of the Space Shooter genre, it looks nice enough to satisfy but not to impress.
Sound is definitely the best part about this game. There're a fair number of memerable tracks and while it never really goes into full blood boiling epic mode like the Ace Combat games, the score has enough high and lows to convey the right type of atmosphere and emotion for each situation. The distinct Eastern vibe also really make the soundtrack standout. Plasma blast and explosion all have enough kick to keep the tension up and the improved voice over is much appreciated.
Story is a bit cliche but the plot is generally straight forward with clear-cut goals that the players won't feel lost or confused by it and doesn't get in the way of the gameplay. While there're moments where things don't make a lot of sense such as sneaking up on a space station through a Nebula when you can just warp right next to it it never really get to the point where it'd make the audience cringe. I really wish they'd have given Control a bit more personality and have her relationship with the player build a bit more, but considering the length of the game, it's probably too much to ask.
With three levels of difficulty and online leaderboard there's significant room for replay. The fact that the developer put so many different models of space crafts and Strike Suits with distinctly different playstyle in also work in the game's favor. Playing a level with a Generation 1 Strike Suit and a Raptor felt very different and while the combat itself is rather uninspired, it's still very statisfying to blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up with big guns and bigger explosions.
In conclusion, SSZ Director's Cut is the definitive version to get and while it has some good moments, it never really pull itself out of mediocrity. However, with so few Space Shooter around, it's definitely worth a look at if you're fan of the genre and can be entertaining if played in moderation. However, I'd recommend waiting for a discount due to the low production value and how quickly the game become repetition due to the shallowness of the gameplay.

Overall: Recommended for fans of the genre but don't get your expectation too high, best to buy at a discount.
