Need to blow off your steam? Why not shoot some zombie scum to pieces? Yeah, I know - sounds pretty psychopathic, but keep in mind: It's fiction. And in this game's fiction you simply shred zombies to pieces. Simple as that.
First of all: It's your quasi "casual zombie massacre game". Quasi casual because it offers the possibility to descend into Zombie County for 10-20 minutes and get back to work, family, whatsoever after. If you're looking for a longer shot you may try the challanges, so it works both for those who are taking a short time out as well as those who want to get some challenging progress.
Second: It is a zombie massacre. Nothing more, nothing less. If you're looking for a thought-out plot (or a plot at all), you'll be disappointed *massively*. If you're looking for a fun, fast-paced and action-packed top-down shooter with zombies (a whole da*n lot of zombies), you're in for a gory treat.
The look is great. It's your typical scrapped, end of days atmosphere combined with your typical zombie settings, including the "usual suspects" as a cemetary and the obligatory gas station.
The areas of the levels/maps are pretty limited, which of course intensifies the action.
Keeping in mind that this game already has some years under its belt, the graphics are still ok (and what's important for me: working on my netbook), but not top-notch. However the atmosphere gets delivered perfectly.
- metal riffs, shots, explosions, gore & splatter - "Nation Red" delivers an absolutley convincing and genre complimentary sound design.
The concept of "Nation Red" is simple, yet addictively entertaining: You'll be confronted with hordes of zombies and you'll gain experience points while shooting, chopping or stabbing through your undead enemies. Power-ups like "Bullet Time" or mines drop sporadically, alternate weapons and grenades offer some tactical variations.
The game itself is being played via gamepad or with mouse and keyboard. Shooting, evading, switching weapons, grenades - you really don't need more than these. And, granted, you don't get more options than these. So summing up: Simple concept, simple and extremly easy to master controls.
If you're looking for a diverting, entertaining zombie shooter with a "casual" touch ("casual" not meant in the negative way), lots and lots of gory fun, fast-paced action with easy to grasp controls and a grand combination of metal music and booming sound fx, "Nation Red" is your game.

Played this back on the ps1, one of my favorite Final Fantasy games.  Has a few bugs and some glitches, i cant remember where in the game, but they are easily bypassed.  Other than the few bugs, fantastic port, great game, brings back all the great memories from the original game on ps1.  This game also has a a massive amount of save blocks (unlock final fantasy 4) so you can save your game at all the cool parts in the game.
If you dont know the game, the story is detailed, the characters are awesome, and the game has tons of extras throughout the game.  The materia and limit break system takes a bit to get used to if you have never played this but its not difficult.  The game also has a feature to turn on max levels if you dont want to grind and work the trenches.  The game is not HD remastered, it is pretty much exactly the same port as the PS1 version, we are still waiting on that from squaresoft.  Considering this was made in 1997, its very impressive.
It is worth nothing that skill wise many of the characters are the same.  It is not like ff4 with a specific dragoon or ninja, or ff6 with a specific thief, or a specific martial artists.  The characters are differrent in look, have different weapons and limits, but they all have access to the same materia.  It would have been cool to have unique skills for each character to really set them apart not just from the story and visual, but in battle as well.

Danganronpa is one of few times where a despair-fueled experience comes highly recommended. THE FIRST GAME IS VIRTUALLY MANDATORY in terms of narrative, so pick that up first.
PROS:
+Great characters, with plenty of potential waifus - just don't get too attached. One character who started as a total A-hole turns out to be one of the biggest bros as time goes on.
+Plot makes twists and turns at varying levels of 'bonkers', and at a constant high of despair.
+Incredible blend of Persona and Phoenix Wright, as written by George RR Martin (not really, but the way characters die...)
+Investigations and trials are compelling, with surprising turns that change how you look at a character you THOUGHT you knew.
CONS:
-As is usually the case in games like Phoenix Wright, there's a specific chain of logic you have to follow in trials; it can be frustrating to understand where the plot's going but not know how to progress. Which piece of evidence do I present? Who do I accuse?
-Get ready for LOTS of reading - but considering half of this game is a visual novel, that's par for the course.
-So many dead waifus... :(

Since I played the first game, I've been eagerly awaiting for the localization of Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair.
I knew that fans who already played the japanese version were stating that this sequel was even better than the first episode - and after playing it myself I can easily understand why.
As usual with Spike Chunsoft games, Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is essentially a visual novel.
Expect lots of reading, but despite a not exactly "top class" translation the dialogues and writing is captivating and definitely interesting.
The pacing of the story is great, gradually ramping up until a finale that left me with my jaw open. The last part of the game is really something that must be experienced. The first game is known for its plot-twists, but the sequel blows that game out of the water. You will not expect what's going to happen, and this is good.
Having played the first game, Trigger Happy Havoc, is requirement if you want to fully understand and appreciate the whole storyline. The developers are expecting the players to be up to speed concerning the plot of the series, so do yourself a favor and get both games if you can.

I have always loved a good mystery, especially when it's a dark as possible. That's why I loved the first Danganronpa game as it fufilled that and even more, but Danganronpa 2 takes what the first game built on a takes to a whole new level of despair and hope. I honestly never really expected for a PS Vita game to make to the Steam store, let alone for it to one the best ports out there as you can hardly tell that it was originally on another game system, unlike some ports. COUGH! COUGH! Tale of Symphonia. COUGH! COUGH! This game is great for those who love game like Ace Attorney, but want a little more than a visual novel with no gameplay mechanics that couldn't be done by a 3 legged turtle. It's also nice that it has a difficultly setting so you do not have to worry about being too stupid or not being able to use logic like you want to, and before you say I'm calling anyone except myself an idiot, I am directing this comment at myself. I can be very stupid at times and an essential idiot handicap is almost always appericiated with me because I do not know when my moments of sheer "why isn't my brain thinking the bestest" will happen. Now while it is not necessary to play the first game and be able to understand this game's story, I would highly recommend playing the first game before this one as it will make the storyline the last few chapters a LOT more clearer. Playing the first game is also a good way to understand if you really will like this game as the game mechanics are a bit easier to learn and you'll get an idea of what you're getting into by the end of the first trial. It's really incredible though because *insert spoiler here*! Overall, if you're looking for a good visual style novel to get into on your day off or you'd like something that'll make you question the state of the world and why aren't you doing anything about in the wee hours of the night, then Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair (and goodbye any peaceful dreams after beating it) is your horror story to play through!

Exactly what i was looking for in a new installment to the Might and Magic franchise but not without its faults.  It's a very good tip of the hat to the old school play style of rpgs that this game is based off of and I'm really glad that the mastering system was kept over from MM6.  Much improved graphics and a great story and surprisingly well paced.  Bosses fights were surprisingly well designed and had much more to them than I initially expected.
On the downside however, this game is much more linear than previous titles and it is NOT OPTIMIZED PROPERLY.  Doesn't matter how much a beast your machine is.  This game won't run right on your PC in its current state.  Still playable of course, have no doubt about it but you will need to reduce the graphic settings and deal with a lot of stutter in some locations.  Mountain tops and waterfalls did it the most for me.  This game also, in the spirit of the franchise, doesn't exactly hold your hand so you will probably make mistakes in character class and master choices through your first play through.  Also.... bows are worthless in this game, but after replaying MM6 i'm reminded of how OP they were there so i suppose this is a lesson learned.

No its not diablo, torchlight, etc. Spelunky didn't need a million items or some epic story to be a masterpiece. Necropolis IS a great rogue-like that presents the genera in a darksouls esq format while preserving may of the elements of classic rogue-likes and if you treat this game like what it was supposed to be, I genuinely believe you will be more than pleased. The game is cheaper than a night out at the bars and I certainly don't regret buying this like i did that last round of shots I don't remember...
In summary, if you dont know what a rouge-like is go find out before you buy this. If your a fan of nethack/adom/spleunky/etc. I think you will like this game, I certainly do. In addition just about everything i would have complained about has been rectified in the last few patches.

I dont know how to start this review because i normalt dont write reviews for games, but this story deserves a lot of attention! (Alot more than it already have)
okay, let's start:
It took me a while to collect the courage to finally sit down and play this game!
I cried so much that i needed pause my game a few times and dry my eye!
Never in my life have I played a game which has impacted me on such a level..
Its really difficult to put into words how life changing and eye opening this story is.
It is a travel through love, despair and hope from two loving parents to their dead son Joel.
Cancer and other terminal illnesses are something that almost all of us in the world have been touched by in some ways.
Whether it is ourselves, a person close to us or just someone who have influenced us or been there for us in some ways.
Diseases like this can effects us in many negative and tragic ways. But it also shows us that love and hope never dies!
This was an emotional rollercoaster for me, because i felt each and every emotion a person can feel.
It reminds you of how precious life is and how scared we are of death and the unknown!
It is NOT just about cancer,but it is more than that, it is about life and all the struggles some of us face in life. (life is not always fair, but we need to stay strong)
It also shows that even when someone is gone, the wonderful memories and their love is always with us in our mind and heart.
That Dragon Cancer is an experimental game that is focused on telling the story about a little boy named Joel, who has been diagnosed with cancer and his parents, who have to deal with all their concerns and hopes for the future of their beautiful son.
The way that this game captures emotions, and the way it depicts Joel in particular, is astonishing.
Making Joel laugh and talk makes it feel so real.
Watching Joel play just adds more and more authenticity to the story of a little boy who dont know the horrible reality of his life and his future.
There is nothing i can say bad about this game/story!
The use of audio from the home movies made every bit of the unscripted dialouge feel so authentic and genuine, it made me break down and cry!!
And dont let me start with the storyline and the voice acting it is so breathtaking and so unique!
IT makes you feel that you are by their side fighting cancer!
If you dont have this game please go and buy it
(It is worth the money)
I cannot reccomend this highly enough!
This is a game that every person should experience!!
This is to Ryan and Amy Green and as well as everyone else who is affected by this.
I am so sorry for your loss and thank you for sharing your sad and beautiful story about Joel...

It's not a prefect game (so very few are), and this one could definitely use a little more work. That said, I would still call it a diamond in the rough. The game starts out fine, and the controls are pretty standard. Forward thrust, back thrust, barrel roll if you don't accellerate while rolling. But it's fun and nice to see a dogfighter again. Added points for the dated transforming ship, once a trope but now a relic.
The programmers do need to work on a few key details, however. The background radio drama doesn't start up until after you've cleared a wave of baddies, and it forces you to simply keep flying around doing nothing while it carries its tune. Then there's the final level, which goes from an open air game to tunnel crawler rather abruptly with no prior buildup. This is made worse by the fact that you have learn to manuever in tight spaces, but also do it while your ship is constantly speeding up. The radio does take this time to do the story right, so it wasn't a total bust, except when you inevitably died and had to start the whole damn tunnel over. Finally, the last and most glaring problem, especially on that last level, the controls are designed specifically for an XBox controller, definitely not for keyboard and mouse. I had to go out and buy a logitech game controller to actually finish the game, which might not have happened if the tunnel crawling had been introduced and practiced before that last level.
Also, i want more of the music. It was absolutely beautiful, and props to the company for getting the immensely talented Kokia to do the vocals. That being said, the stylized Middle-Eastern music is just scattered too thin. I would love to be able to complain that the music was too saturated, but most of the soundtracks are 2 minutes or less with no good way to repeat them smoothly. There is only so long that one can listen to laser fire and engine thrusts before wanting to shoot something, and not in the way the game was doing it.
After all of that, I would love to have see this fully fleshed out. Some tight corner missions to introduce and teach the concept before going into the ever speeding up final mission would be awesome; longer versions of the musical tracks would be wonderful; and please, PLEASE, air your radio drama DURING the firefight so I (and everyone else) don't have to get bored and see how close to a cruiser I can fly without damaging my shields or hull.
All in all, I love the game. I just think that those specific pieces of laundry need to be aired.

I have played many hours on this with friends and we've had some epic hours gaming on it. I must admit the game has been buggy from time to time, problems with friends joining and some of the AI can occasionally be glitchy whilst playing like for eg. once I got killed by a raptor roughly 4 seconds after I'd already headshot it clean dead with the Longshot sniper rifle with the damage increase augment purchased. I suspect these glitches are simply down to internet lag between players. I plan to play this game over LAN (1 Gb/s) soon with friends at which point I will update this review.
I would like to note that I don't normally suffer issues gaming with my friends online, We play often on a variety of games and 99% of the time its perfectly smooth. My connection speed is 100 Mb of which I'm receiving speeds of 106.9 Mb/s (12.6 MB/s) Download and 6.09 Mb/s (0.7 MB/s) Upload (results from
tested via closest server). In my rig I'm running an i5 quad core CPU @ 3.3 GHz per core (Corsair H55 Cooler + 2 x Fans), 16 GB (2 x 8 GB) Corsair DDR 3 @ 2400 Hz, MSI NVidia GTX 760 2 GB (NZXT GPU Bracket + Corsair H55 Cooler + 2 x Fans), Asus Z97-P Motherboard, 2 x Kingston 60 GB (RAID 0) for Windows 7 Ultimate and 2 x Kingston 120 GB (RAID 0) for games powered by EVGA 500 Watt 80 PLUS 12v+40A PSU.
My friends whom I play online with the majority of the time are on similar spec rigs with similar speed internet connections and we all live within a 10 mile radius. I suspect where some of the issue is coming from is there are 2 of us using the same internet provider and package, we get the same speeds. My friend who is on the same provider and speeds as myself actually has 2 people playing from the same house which will obviously greatly affect internet throughput. My other friends have much higher upload speeds, up to 20 Mb/s or 2.5 MB/s for those who'd like it converted :) We all suffer these glitches from the AI, some of us more than others so clearly its a common problem which leads me to internet connection issues must be the root. I have also forgotten to point out I also get these glitches when playing with newcomers when I host an open game although I haven't noticed them during solo play however I must admit I tend to mainly play this game multiplayer 90% of the time.
Additionally we tend to get these problems the most when playing Conquest mode which is a 30 round game mode which can last a good hour or more (depending on how many players have joined). I intend to play a Conquest mode game with my usual 4 companions on this game in a LAN situation. The same computers and players as usual, same game mode, rules etc but connected via a 1 Gb/s network switch and see if the problem subsides. If this is the case then it is clear that the most effective way to play this game with friends on this game in Conquest mode would be to get together to play via LAN instead of struggling with glitches via online play.
I have been very specific with this review to help those who may still be pondering over buying this game. It really is a good game, hours of entertainment, loads to do on it and its 95% smooth gaming but there are those little issues from time to time sadly. This is without a doubt a really fun game to play solo but even more fun with friends, as long as you are happy to live with a little lag if you gaming online.
All in all, long review aside, great game, well worth what I paid for it (got it in a sale happily) but its worth the full price in my opinion. :) Hope my review has helped!

This isn't the first Final Fantasy game I ever played, but it's definitely the best.
Pros:
Engaging and well-crafted story and setting with detailed and likable characters.
The complexity of materia (which allows players to wield magic and summon creatures in battle) allows for endless customization and tweaking to suit a specific play style.
The battle system, while technically turn-based, demands good timing making the battles feel more urgent and alive.
It's a lengthy game with plenty to do without relying too much on grinding to pad out gameplay.
Plenty of secrets and hidden things to uncover throughout the game.
Absolutely gorgeous music.
Cons:
Have to make an account to play (thankfully, it is a fairly simple affair and took about two minutes).
Although the 2D graphics have aged fairly well, the 3D models have not often making it difficult to judge where you can and cannot move.
The FMV looks very poor.
Default keybindings are bizarre (Insert for Switch?!) and impractical.
Many of the required mini-games are bland and generally boring to play.
Verdict:
10/10 This game highlights the best of the Final Fantasy series. It's an absolute blast to play, with an incredible narrative, detailed characters, and some of the best gameplay I've ever experienced in a RPG period. If you've given the series a try before and didn't get in to it (as I had) I urge you to reconsider and pick up this game. It's a masterpiece that is well worth playing.

Short Review:
Improved since Orion Horde, but largely remains to be seen. There's still plenty of room for improvement.
Full Review:
- Gameplay
The game concept is simple. For campaign, you have to survive a group of invading dinosaurs that will only invade you after you start your first generator and after which, you have to drive/walk/fly a long distance to activate your inappropriately-marked second base. The "Capturing Base" message only appeared after I was some distance away from move the marker and the base itself.
For survival, it's self-explanatory. For PvP, it's self-explanatory. For sudden death, it's self-explanatory (if you've played other games that have this). Every other mode other than campaign revolves around these 3 modes, only difference lies in whether it's a team or one man army or which weapons you get to use.
- Changes in Gameplay
The last time I played this game was close to a year ago. I played only Singleplayer and gameplay was at best average. You go around capturing bases, shooting dinosaurs, and perhaps exploiting the map to your advantage. Everything else was left to yourself. There are 3 markers indicating where to get weapons, skills and vehicles. That was about it. Even after the transition from Orion Horde to Prelude, I found it rather boring. Along with a non-existent support team, I decided to abandon the game.
Many months later, I saw their latest video advertisement showcasing "how much their game has improved". Reluctantly, I decided to give it a try. (To my surprise,) they had actually improved on Singleplayer mode. You no longer fight alone and have four (relatively dumb) teammates which will help you when you go down, without desperately trying to get a last wind. Campaign-wise, I haven't managed to get pass the first few bases because the AI wouldn't follow and I ended up getting plummeted by two triceratops. That wasn't fun (to die and lose), but nonetheless interesting.
- Graphics/Visual Appeal
Despite the "massive overhaul" from Orion Horde to Prelude, there was not much change in the menu layout and character design. Pretty much every customisation requires you to buy for real money (or earned by unlocking numerous achievements), and the graphics are rather dated (pixelated with its bad geometrical shapes). The only thing that impressed me was the main menu background and that's about it.
In the game itself the developers have noticeably added the weather effect. Your screen will occasionally blur due to the snow and there is a consistent (but annoying) white border around your screen because of snow blowing on your face (at least that's what I interpreted it as). The added weather effects are appreciated and helps you to "focus" on the game. However, other than that first glance, every other models such as the vehicles, weapons, et cetera are pretty much mediocre. The text do not scale well with the resolution and exceeds the screen (so the skill name and description is cut off for me) and the border between the background and the text is not consistent. Skill icons are also exactly the same as when the game costed USD15.00 before the overhaul to Prelude, which would have been fine if the icon were not extremely visually unappealing. Think of the icons as having secondary school or fresh college students (not graduates) drawing them. It's not simple enough to be "simple" or complex enough to be "complex". It's just... Well, the trailers don't show you the skill icons, do they?
- Bugs (?)
There are some noticeable features that I can't really describe it as bug or glitch or whatsoever, because I have no idea if they were meant to be a feature or a bug. For example, you are able to buy the same skill as many times as you want, so long you have the credits from killing dinosaurs. I have no idea whether buying the same skill again have any upgrades (because the skill description remains exactly the same and there is no indication of current level) or it's just bugged and wasting my credits (because even the skill icon colour, everything else remains the same). Sometimes I am also spawned way, way, too far away from the base when I just started the campaign and have to activate the generator to start the game. Again, I have no idea whether being spawned 400 metres away from your main and first base is a feature or a bug.
- Verdict
By now, you'd probably wonder why the hell am I recommending this game after such negative experience and I have only 3 hours on record. I'd say the game is actually worth that $1.00 if you have friends to play with. It's fun for a while, and you could probably find some easter eggs here and there and explore the terrain. The terrain is rather big, but there's no sandbox option for me to explore so I can't rate the maps very accurately and I'll leave it out from the gameplay part. After all, with dumb AI, you can't do much (albeit more than without AI). However, if you got no friends who will play this with you (or can't seem to find one) and/or the game reverts to its original Orion Horde price of USD15.00, I'd say skip it. It's seriously not fun playing alone. I would have given this a mixed review if possible, or else a bad review. But for its price, it's hard to argue.

Pros: If you're an old-timer longing for the good old days of min-maxing stats/skills for a party (and you don't play JRPGs for various reasons), this will be the game for you. Your gameplay rewards will mostly come from seeing your carefully-planned party composition hit its stride around the mid-levels, when your bladesinger has enough stats to chunk mobs for big satisfying criticals. This game will mostly appeal to RPG fans born in the very early 80s or older, since it's a throwback to the Xeen/Terra style of gameplay. It includes all the quirks of those previous games such as tile movement, turn-based combat, random stat-increasing barrels and high-level party-oneshotting dragons in the midst of a lowly bandits and wolves. Full shameless nostalgia.
Cons: It's still buggy. Your party can get stuck around teleporters, music and ambient sounds can loop forever, and some events don't trigger. Also many parts are under-developed. Armor system is underbaked (you can finish the game with your warrior wearing cloth), a couple spells are placeholders (eg liquid membrane), some classes are more fleshed out than others, tanking is near-useless, there is an overdependence on specific spells (eg Celestial Armor, Burning Determination and Whispering Secrets) which make or break your game.

The Witcher 2 as a game is the meaning of the word progress. Everything from the graphics to the systems behind the game are an amazing feat, one you would expect from a big named developer backed up by a huge budget. The looks of the game are not only unparalleled due to its PC only nature, but also because it presents a world that feels hand crafted. The attention to detail borders on the extreme: the clothes, the houses and buildings, the faces of the characters their weapons and in general every corner, nook and cranny of the world has a distinctive touch. The scenery is simply breathtaking, and if you are like me you will want to make a screenshot out of every frame. It also shows that you don't need an overabundance of browns and blood reds in your palette to show a gritty dark fantasy world. This game shows its maturity not through a pretense of adult topics or over the top action animations, but through a careful use of its elements and by showing the player some respect: yes, you are an adult, and you can handle these topics, because indeed the Witcher's is a dark world filled with conspiracies, racism and characters in between every single shade of gray. It is a living, breathing, unforgiving world.
The story is as complex as in the first game, filled with twists and choices that may change the fate of many, and forking paths that make a replay of the game not only encouraged, but required in order to see the extent to which they occur and diverge. Normal and hard difficulties are recommended and will test your skills if you don't face every battle with all seriousness, preparing beforehand by brewing and drinking potions and using all of your abilities during the fight, i.e. your swords your magic signs depending on what enemy you face and traps and bombs for your crowd control.
The actual combat is in no way dumbed down. It will still punish you if you go unprepared and you can't mash your way out of battles. It is in much better shape than in the first game, and friendly to both the use of a gamepad or mouse and keyboard. The user interface is slick and great looking.
The ending of the game comes abruptly, and you might feel that it doesn't solve every issue the game presents (the main storyline issues ARE solved, though). It is no excuse from what many will consider a downbeat ending, but in all honesty it doesn't detract a single beat from what this game does right, which is almost everything else. Even if you don't like the ending you will feel that the journey was worth it.
In the end I feel like I'm required to praise this game so high despite its shortcomings not because it is a perfect game, but because it is an honest one. When more and more AAA releases are done with specific quarters or demographics numbers behind, or executives who never play games are calling the shots, The Witcher 2 really feels developed to please it audience, to show them they too are tired of these.
There is a certain level of quality you expect from bigger developers which have more of a history and a name, because they deliver experiences that go way beyond what you might get from the indie guys. It is OK, they have the money and the numbers behind. This is a trend that has been changing in the last years and that no longer holds true in most cases though.
In this case in particular neither of these apply. In my mind CDProject RED are already the big name, from whom I will expect unrelenting quality. Because after what they achieved they can't be considered the little guy any longer. With the Witcher 2 they delivered a game that is truly above and beyond any RPG from the last years, that feels like a product of love, careful planning and an overall shout to fans and the gaming community that says "we know what you want, and we can deliver. Where others have failed you we will prevail." And God if they don't.
A serious contender for the best game of 2011, and frankly there is little in the horizon that looks like it might compete with it. Five years from now when other games made by bigger companies are all forgotten in the $5 bargain bins of the world, many will be reinstalling this game to reminisce and fondly say: "yes, I played a game was this good in 2011, and it was glorious."
Congratulations CDProject RED, you just released your first masterpiece.

Gameplay 1/10:
No failure states, no success states, the gameplay is just the vessel upon which the player's boredom rides to reach the auteurs' conclusion.
Plot 3/10:
Told through letters, and some exposition in the end, it's essentially irrelevant to the experience. One could argue that there are two stories being told: the story of the main character, told via traditional means, and the story of the player, told by the timers on the boxes as they're being stared at by pairs of eyes round the world, eager to discover the next nothing. Finally, there's no closure given, instead the player returns to the start screen, able to pick up from where they left.
Character 5/10:
Ms. Plumps is a classic example of a hamartanousa heroine, who, after being punished, distances herself from the tragic hero, who keeps committing the same crime till the ultimate hubris that will set him free, as it did her. However, none of the characters seems to have any more depth than their cardboard representations: Plumps is the ditz the PC should strive to follow, PC is a blank slate, Weather Man is stuck in his balloon, and Nancy is just someone with a plan that came to fruition regardless of any actions or omission by any other character.
Thought 2/10:
Only there as background noise, seeing as all the characters are single-minded pyromaniacs.
Diction 5/10:
It's what could have saved this game alone, if it was given a little more love. The message is simple, yet powerful. Any gamer has probably felt it (more so any critic/reviewer), however a simple mention of a deep thought is not the same as exploration of the same. In the end it felt like a cheap cop-out.
Melody 6/10:
The music has the decency to not overburden us with its presence.
Spectacle 7/10:
It manages to be pretty throughout; be it through sleek flammable objects, or haunting character design later on.
Final verdict:
Recommended only if you are willing to suffer mild boredom so that you can appreciate its half-baked message.

Dust is a great game.  The whole cutsy animated look isn't really something I'm used to so there's moments where I'm thinking "Wow that's really overly cutsy borderline furry"  lol  like the Figet character whos your sidekick in combat throughout the game, but the game has a very deep and rich story with a tremendous amount of voice over content.  There's a lot of talks with characters in the game and the way Dust doesn't remember anything makes for a very rich and engaging story where you are constantly discovering in pieces what hes about and what your purpose in the games story is.  It's the kind of deep story that most games lack now days.
The learn as you start playing way they teach the mechanics of the game is also very well done.  All of the little tutorial tips as I learned new moves actually displayed the name of the button that I had remapped certain actions to instead of a preset default key mapping.  I was glad to see that the game knew I'd changed primary and secondary fire and correctly displayed it when guiding me through, most games fall short with this but not Dust.  This game really has a very polished and good feel to it.
The combat is great hack and slash fun and the secondary fire with the ability to add in extra damage from Figets ability gives it some fun choices that work better for certain enemies.  Overall this is a definite must buy for anyone who likes a good hack and slash game.  Cutsy animation that some may hesitate at but if you want a taste of that hack and slash fun and the deep story I mentioned just watch the video trailer on the Steam Store page here and it's clear that this game is standing above most other games in its class.

How on earth can a creative little toy such as Little Inferno be so linear? While "playing" this game you feel like you are just burning things to unlock the rest of the things so that you can throw away this monstrosity, because Little Inferno is awful. It could have actually done rather well if the unlocking system was sorted out, but since there are so many restrictions on what you can burn and when you can burn them, it’s a losing battle trying to have fun with the toy.
You start the game with a catalogue and only the first few objects are available for purchase. You get coins from burnt objects and every object coughs up more money than it was bought for. After you burn these items to a crisp, you go back to the catalogue and buy the next few items. Another problem the game has is that the objects that you buy from the catalogue don’t appear on your shelf immediately. Instead you have to wait for the objects to ship to your house, like freakin’ Amazon. If you really can’t wait, you can use a stamp (which is basically a rarer version of a coin) to knock 30 seconds off the delivery time. That’s right you can get a faster delivery. Like freakin’ Amazon. What makes matters worse is that there are seven catalogues and each one has items with longer and longer wait times for delivery until the last item which takes an outrageous five minutes to arrive.
The only actual gameplay involved is making combos, which is where you are given a clue, then have to work out which two objects to burn together to complete the challenge. The only problem is, the clues are unbelievably obvious, for example “Bike-Pirate” is the clue for the combo involving the bicycle and the pirate. What fun.
The developers even added a storyline in the form of very burnable letters from people you never actually meet. Almost every single one has the phrase “This can’t last forever” in some shape or form, and this could be like a side-plot except I don’t care in the slightest.
I was put in mind of FarmVille and all those other Facebook games that spanned out their gameplay by having users spending most of the time waiting. I can only assume that these games were the developers’ only points of reference when designing. I know I’m probably being a little harsh since it’s only an indie game made by a tiny team of people, but if we can produce something as illuminating as Bastion, there is no need for Little Inferno hiding in a mass of smoke, getting in people’s eyes and making them water.

After watching Ryan Green’s emotional award reception for the “Games for Impact” category at the 2016 Game Awards, I immediately picked this up. And as hard as it is for me to speak negatively about a game that carries such emotional weight, I just can’t recommend this game.
is the swan song of Ryan Green’s son, Joel. The story is deeply personal, and in my opinion, therein lies the problem with this game. I don’t know Ryan or his family, but for them, I can only image the solace that this digital immortalization of Joel will bring them, ensuring that he will never be forgotten. The narrative is told through memories Ryan shared with Joel, but it’s constantly interrupted by an incoherent telling of Ryan’s own religious struggles. I completely understand the comfort that is found in religion during difficult times, but as a non-religious person, this was just way too preachy for me to relate. By the half-way point, the game was no longer about Joel, and was almost entirely about Ryan’s personal struggle to maintain faith in a god he felt was causing such pain to his son.
I want to feel the same emotions that I’m sure Ryan felt while creating this game, but I just don’t. If religious ramblings can evoke emotion from you, then please, play this game, as I’m sure there’s a beautiful story in here somewhere. Otherwise, spend your money elsewhere.

I went in to this game skeptical on weather I would like it or refund it after 5 minutes of play. Fortunately the game hooked me and I played everyday for about a week until I beat it. I still have to go back and collect all the masks as well as do any of the side content I did not complete. Overall Hotline Miami was a fun, enjoyable and awesome experience for the money. The soundtrack is also a masterpiece and is definitely one of the reasons why I loved this game. The story is amazing if you decide to pay attention to it, and the artstyle is one one of the best I have seen in a video game. The gamplay however is the main selling point of the game that differentiates it from any other title out there. If you take a single attack, whether it be a punch, pipe, bat, or bullet your going to die instantly. Because of this when you first start a level you will most likely die quite a few times (25-60 on average) depending on the difficulty. You also kill enemies with one attack as well. The A.I. isnt the brightest since you can easily camp in a corner with a shotgun, let them charge at you and then blow them to smitherines, but I think the A.I. was designed that way on purpose, since the gamplay is already difficult enough so having somewhat dumb A.I. makes it a lot of fun to take advantage of. There are also leaderboards, so if you're in to that sort of thing than you will most likely spend a lot of hours on it. There are also two bonus missions after the main story and epilouge and they will give you an extra 30-70 min of gameplay on top of the base game which took me about 5 hours to complete. (I suck at the game so people who are more skilled may take 3 hours to complete). Also after beating the game you can collect any other extra masks, as well as unlock any other weapons that you did not obtain, which could take up to another hour or so. In the end if you fully take advantage of all the features the game has to offer your looking at around 7-10 hours of gameplay, and that's not including any other replays of levels to get a higher grade on them.
In conclusion:
If your in for a hell of a challenge and some trial and error levels, as well as constantly dying and respawning then pick this game up cause it is definitely up your ally, and it is the perfect fix of adrenaline, intense fast pace moment to moment gameplay and stress and anxiety. However if you want something casual and chill and just kinda want to relax and turn your brain off then I would recommend another title, since this one is anything but relaxing.

No real difference between GC3 and GC2 might as well purchase the cheaper GC2. A much larger focus should have been put into how the planets are managed; the current simplicity aspect is annoying to true civ fans. Wormholes are one of the least enjoyable aspects of the game in that it's only purpose is to force player vessels to meet and greet other civs while removing surveyor ships from play. Another aspect of utter annoyance is the blocking factor of asteroids, worlds, starbases etc. The game is supposed to mimic space exploration and yet the game system is dominated by a 2D travel aspect. Guess what? if asteroids are in your direction of travel in space all you have to do is go up or down it's rather easy to escape an asteroid field in space especially since they conform to gravitational bands around the object they are orbiting and yet the spaceship, per typical sci-fiction capabilities, does not. This game should have been so much more especially with today’s computer power. It should have been a more modular game in that the player should have been allowed the type of play he/she would like to enjoy (such as more control over world management with smaller tiles and the ability to manipulate the planet builds more. Stacking of ships onto solid objects since space is 3D and the allowing the player to choose whether he/she wants to enter the object or not. An emphases on mining/utilizing all asteroids even dead worlds for mineral required resources (Oh, by the way current research is showing for as many worlds found around stars there should be 20% in deep space between the stars)). I will say that I enjoy the game about as much as the original GC2 but since there is little difference between the two I have am starting to get bored with GC3 already. There are a few better items, special resources, better A.I., improved diplomacy but for all its benefits, in my mind, they do not make up for the fact that there is little difference between GC2 and GC3 so for this reason alone I would inform anyone to wait three to four years when the game will be $10 before purchasing because it does not offer much more than GC2.

Transforming space plane has interesting dual mechanics. Default plane mode has ok maneuverability, and Gundam-form has limited time where it can't boost as fast as a plane, but is highly agile (strafe in all directions) and different weapons.
Story is given by good voice acting & optional subtitles. Short cut scenes only show entry/exit/explosions of fleets, but doesn't really show any story. While story has somewhat interesting details, it's delivered during frantic dogfights, so you can ignore most dialogue, but objectives/priorities are important (top-left UI list). You will lose if trying to shoot everything, since there are time limits, priority targets, targets to protect from incoming torpedos etc.
Main game took me 12hrs (might update this once I get to the included DLC). Most missions seamed similar and somewhat monotonous, save for occasional beautiful interstellar backdrops. Enemies are only fighter planes or various large cruisers, and passive targets like supply/fuel ships. There's some plane variety, but like most space/air combat games, enemies are 5 pixel dots with missiles/lasers swarming everywhere, so unfortunately there's less variety in choosing how to approach certain plane enemies. Fighting various cruisers was more entertaining, as their weapons variety/count is more apparent and deadly.
Weapons: choices increase as story progresses. Vague paragraphs describe various weapons, so it's necessary to test out each one, but this is aggravating when you cannot switch loadouts once a mission starts (with multiple checkpoints, even on death you cannot change a bad loadout combo). 3 difficulty levels is nice, but also behaves same as loadout, so if you're stuck at 4th of 4 checkpoints for a mission, you can't start the 4th with an easier mode, or fix your bad loadout (must exit game & redo the first 3 checkpoints with new settings).
Planes: There's a few plane choices, but by the time I finished the main game, only 2 ships were unlocked: ordinary plane, and transformable strike suite. The other 4+ planes are still locked, probably will unlock after achieving certain optional objectives. This might help replayability, but the 2 planes choice certainly caused some monotony.
Controls: Amazing support, especially for indie game. Game auto detected the joystick brand, and setup reasonable buttons. It auto set a joystick+keyboard combo, weird, but after some missions default setup seemed fine. I heard mouse & gamepad also works. With joystick, sometimes plane has some roll wobble, but it's more stable than other flight games (ace horizon and warthunder have some awful yaw+roll wobbles).
Problems: Shadowless issue didn't really bother me, as the textures, nice bg, dark ships you can hardly tell apart from dark bg, nice weapons/explosions are all visually rich (runs fine on laptop).
4 plane speeds: there's static, slow forward, forward, boost. I was confused by the redundancy for many missions. Additionally, a bug where either boost is always on (shift-key, uses limited fuel), or never on. I had to restart game, or pull/put the usb joystick, or external keyboard. Tip: start with only static (s) to turn faster, and boost (shift, use fuel). Use forward (w) only build up fuel.
Suggestions: More plane varieties available at start and clearer weapons differences. It would really help to have scene variety of interiors/above planet combat or meteors littered areas (only one short mission was interior).

It's quite funny that two years ago, I looked at this game and went "Ewwww! It looks like garbage and somehow it has good reviews? How..?." I kept on seeing this game everywhere in top 10 lists and I figured that at least trying it couldn't hurt, right? I got this game for, like $2.00 and it's honestly worth every cent. Although this game is simplistic, it is a hell of a lot of fun. If you've read any of my other reviews (Please do! They're very good. ;)  ) you'll know that I love a good story. Stories, in my humble opinion are one of the easiest and most effective ways of making a game charming. If Undertale had no story we would be left with a bunch of loveable characters and a semi-unique fighting system. Story just adds that "Umph" That every game needs.
Hotline Miami tells the story of a person who gets strange phone calls telling him to do normal things like fix the plumbing or cleaning the carpet at a hotel. Almost like their boss is calling them to work. The phone call gives an adress and when the player arives, all they see is men wearing white coats
the player then puts on a rubber mask and thengets the urge to murder everyone in the building without knowing why. At first the player is disgusted and throws up after one of these mass genocides. But soon the player can't stop. The player likes to kill and slowly starts to go insane. Killing is the only thing it knows. The player is sometimes visted by 3 people in rubber masks. They talk as though he is a lesser lifeform and mock him. The player is then asked 3 questions. One of which really stood out to me. "Do you like hurting people?"
Gameplay is simple and fun. It only takes one bullet to kill you but everything else also dies to one bullet. Some levels require a lot of planning and practice in order to not die. This game is challenging but not hard for the sake of being hard. Movment is fluid down and your reactions must be quick. You can play sneaky and pick people off one by one OR charge in sword drawn and hope the enemy isn't fast enough to pull the trigger. This game is very violent and at times a little too violent. For anyone complaining that it's similar to Overwatch, I suggest you play it when you become somewhat tired of Overwatch. The gamefeel of Paladins is completely separate from Overwatch in three major ways. The first is that teams are made up of five players, rather than six. This means that an individual player's skill can heavily influence the match, for good or for bad. Secondly, every character feels somewhat tankier and can regenerate health when out of combat for some time, which changes the overall feel of engagements. Some may think that this takes the focus off of reactions and skills, but it creates a much more emotionally charged environment. It also makes 5v5 team deathmatch all the more exciting. Thirdly, the pacing is somewhat more gameplay-oriented. Maybe it's just because I'm far better at this game than I an at Overwatch (or all the players are bad) and die less, but I feel that the game wants players to meet each other around the objective. The maps are somewhat less nuanced and are shaped for engagement. The game also allows players to rush into the action after death on a horse.

I imagine this is a game I will continue playing for months, if not years, especially as new content is released. Stellaris is a STRATEGY game, and makes no bones about it, as there is barely even a nod towards tactical elements.
The one thing I love about Stellaris above most other games in this genre .... there are actual STAR SYSTEMS, not just planets floating in space or arbitrary placeholders. Ships which warp or jump into a system have to traverse the system or wait for their jump drives to cool down before they can jump again. As an immersive factor, this WORKS for me.
The nature of the game is TOTALLY suited to modding and customisation. I can imagine people designing the entire star wars galaxy or star trek galaxy or empire of man or warhammer 40k universe or starcraft universe in this. I literally cannot wait to see what modders will do in terms of race design, 3d models, static galaxy designs, story driven gameplay, event chains, etc.
Stellaris has given a massive POKE IN THE EYE to those who think 4x games cannot encompass multiple stardrive types and should be simplified to managing hyperlane bottlenecks.
You will love it if
- you like sandbox games
- you want control of customisation
- you want to set your own goals, and drive your own agenda
- you love science fiction stories, as the anomalies and events in the game are like a story unfolding, absolutely amazing.
You will hate it if
- you are a twitch gamer wanting a rail-shooter in space
- you want the game to drive the agenda for you
- you just wanna kill things and couldn't be bothered to read.
Being a sandbox, i imagine it will suit the multiplayer environment much better than the single player environment, but it is still an awesome single player experience.
There are a few things missing, but they detract very little from the game experience.
- there are only randomly generated games, no campaign modes
- there are no freighters, passenger ships, trade routes, etc.
- the game is pseudo 3d, and effectively plays out on a flat galaxy map
- no tactical combat mode, but its well done, with combat seamlessly playing outin real time on the strategic map.
- current diplomacy is not that complex, no espionage, sabotage, etc. But the sheer number of species and diversity adds its own complexity.
- being a sandbox, there is currently no campaign, but I am sure the modding community will solve this.
- while there are leaders (governals, admirals, scientists, etc) with traits, experience and skills, they are randomly generated, not a result of a complex relationship engine as in CK2. Not a big deal to me, but I imagine some would have hoped for this. I can imagne a system like rome total war with governing families leading factions might have worked.
Many of the tricks the designers missed in the realease version, I imagine can be added in future content, or through modding.

It's been quite a while since I played the original SSZ, swearing to never go back to this pile of... disappointment.
Then SSZ DC came out, and I decided to take it for a spin. Why the heck not.
Has the game changed much since the days of the original? Yes. Graphics have been ramped up, textures reworked, the story makes a little more sense now, mission design was improved a bit...
How about gameplay, then? Well, difficulty has been scaled down, going from "batshit insane" to "barely managable" (on EASY). Controls have improved a bit, all those bricks they call fighters and interceptors now turn a bit better yet do not loose precision aiming. Capital ships now have their weak points displayed on the HUD so you at least have some help with destroying those monstrosities (and you will be doing a whole lot of that).
And this is where it ends.
You still need MAD PILOT SKLZ to have a paper cat's chance in hell to get to the good ending. Check out the achievements ranking to confirm this.
The Strike Suit itself still feels flimsy and underpowered - so still no piloting a big indestructable mecha with a can of whoopass In Space. (at least you get it sooner, if that's any consolation)
And the music? If you expect a pounding rendition of something like, say, MUSIC FROM THE LAUNCH TRAILER, turn around and walk away. Because this is where the composer that wrote that piece went - and you'll never get a pleasant beat in the whole game.
Was I expecting much? Well, yeah, it was supposed to be a game about War Mecha In Space, and those are generally expected to be made of awesome.
Did I get much? Not at all. Even in full cheat mode the game is a chore, flooding you with dialogue when you are way too busy to pay attention, and staying perfectly silent when there's a lull in a battle.
Can I recommend this to anyone I know? NO.

Based on it's simple ultra low poly chibi characters and it's low resolution, pre-rendered backdrops, younger gamers would have a hard time believing that Final Fantasy VII was a cutting edge title in 1997. In addition to being a technical marvel in it's day, along side Resident Evil, Metal Gear Solid, Super Mario 64 and Ocarina of Time, it was an important ambassador for the potential of 3d graphics in gaming. Squaresoft had been working for some time to make their characters more emotive in order to sell their grand fantasy stories. With it's pre rendered cut scenes and fresh diesel punk and cyber punk informed sci-fi setting it allowed JRPGs to explode in popularity in the west.

Boasting one of the most thrilling openings in RPG history, players take control of Cloud Strife as he joins the terrorist group AVALANCH in order to destroy a Mako reactor. Cloud's former employer, an evil corporation named Shinra, is using these reactors to harvest a new form of energy that is destroying the planet and each of AVALANCH's members has a personal reason to fight against Shinra except for Cloud. Annoyingly enough, Cloud starts off as an angsty, aloof♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥but slowly opens up, dealing with his own bag of issues over the course of the game. The rest of the cast is colorful and generally likeable. During the fight against Shinra a new threat emerges, shaking the plot up and introducing players to one of the most iconic villains in history. It's a narrative that is compelling though it seems a bit more silly now than it did upon release. Square has desperately tried to recapture the magic of Final Fantasy VII and often it feels like they have only managed to parody their own classic game. Final Fantasy VII established several character archetypes that are regularly found in many modern Final Fantasy titles and they have never been as likable as they were in VII.

What hasn't been cheapened by the failures of subsequent Final Fantasy titles is the combat mechanics. While the turn based structure may feel slow by modern standards, the materia system remains a phenomenally flexible system that effects everything from what weapons you want to use to your character's stats. Materia are magic crystals that are a byproduct of the mako reactors in the game world and allow characters to use magic. Each materia falls into one of several catagories: spell, command, support and summon materia. Each weapon and piece of armor has a number of slots to place materia in and some slots are linked allowing support skills to compliment offensive materia. For instance a poison materia linked to an added effect materia on a weapon allows characters to poison enemies or deal elemental damage. Final attack materia combined with life materia will instantly revive characters when they fall in combat giving yo a second chance during tough encounters. Characters don't really have classes, statistically some are better suited for certain roles than others but the right equipment allows any character to function in a desired role.

Personally, what has burned Final Fantasy VII into the deepest part of my memory for the past 17 years has been the soundtrack. From it's delicate melodies to it's whimsical themes, the soundtrack to this RPG classic is every bit as ambitious and epic as the rest of it's design. Since characters relay their dialog in text, the soundtrack serves as their voice. Hearing a character's theme several years after playing the game is like hearing the voice of an old friend. There is more humor, love, suspense and wonder in this game's sound scape than many entire franchises.

Final Fantasy VII is a classic and it's certainy worth revisiting for even experiencing for the first time. Thanks to a recent re-release on steam as well as versions available on the PlayStation network that's pretty easy to do. Unfortunately the port for steam isn't exactly exemplary. The controller support requires a mod to function properly, there are a handful of bugs and it requires registering with Square Enix. On the upside, there is cloud save support and achievements. In any case, I'd buy a lackluster port of a bonna fide classic if it convinces Square Enix to take a break from releasing embarrassing new entries into their flagship franchise in order to give gamers new and old a properly remade version of what is, arguably, the most popular game in their company's history.

Can't get enough of that sweet 'Half Life' action? Yeah, I understand. With everyone patiently awaiting the arrival of the highly sought after 'Half Life 3', some of us are forced to take more drastic measures in getting our 'Half Life' fix. We're forced to replay the original 'Half Life' games, yep all three of them, even 'Opposing Force'. We're forced to replay 'Half Life 2', yep every episode, and eventually, when there's nothing 'Half Life' related left to play, we must play through this early tech demo of a removed section of 'Half Life 2' redesigned to showcase Valve's HDR lighting.
But in all seriousness, 'Lost Coast' is a twenty minute demo where you basically walk around admiring the world's surroundings. And when I say admiring, I mean admiring. Seriously, I must have taken in the scenery for over an hour while walking through this demo. And I especially loved the area with the staircase where you get to see Valve's fancy new lighting software and how it mimics what the eye sees in real life. It really is quite impressive, and still is, seeing as how I played through this demo in 2015; 10 years after it's initial release.
You also get the chance to fight some bad guys, solve a very simplistic puzzle that honestly took me way too long to solve, and shoot down a black helicopter (yep, those black helicopters) with a rocket launcher. The real reason however to play through this demo is to get a chance to hear from the developers themselves with the added in commentary. Aside from that it's pretty much everything you'd expect to see while playing 'Half Life 2'.
Let the numbers speak for themselves. ;)

So. I have hundreds of hours in dark souls and bloodborne. I love those games. In my honest opinion, Necropolis is not in line with these games.
Necropolis is a rogue like game with combat that requires more thought and strategy than a classic 'run and gun'.  It punishes poor timing and lazy execution. The combat may seem 'clunky' to some, but I think it works just fine. Using a steam controller, the movements and combat feel fluid.

In summation; I would pay $30 for this game. It's similar, yet different enough to keep me interested. Highly recommend it.

I effing love turn-based RPGs. I also love any game where I can create my own party and try to make their unique skills work together into a harmonious vision. Also I love exploration. Also dungeon-crawling, especially the type that rewards searching walls and floors for traps and other dangerous things.
Might and Magic X - Legacy contains all those things.
Don't buy it.
It's like everything I like about the genre has been taken, then subverted to make it ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
There is a turn-based system, but the turn-based movement ceases to work when in combat. There is no maneuvering once enemies are in melee range. You can never take a tactical withdrawl or move to bottleneck your foes. There is no party formation, so your characters stand in a line up front. This is not Grimrock, where the people at the back of your party are mostly vulnerable to attacks from foes that have specifically flanked you. This is Might and Magic, where your unarmored mages hurl themselves in front of every stray arrow or blade they can find, as though their torso posessed by the ghost of a weapon collector.
You can, however, make your own party. I meticulously used all four available races (Orc, Human, Dwarf and Elf) to make what I thought was a balanced party that would have unique skills that complemented each other. A true adventuring party, if you will. It turns out what I wanted basically didn't matter, because the level of party customization in the game is basically like paint over a piece of cardboard. There are 'classes', but they just determine how far your skills can advance, which has no bearing on the early game. They have 'advanced classes' that are unlocked at some point, but just one per class, so really it's just the inevitable progression of your class' skills. No class starts with a special ability that makes it unique. Only advanced classes get those. So your Mercenary (a might-based fighter) that's dabbling in Air Magic is -just as good at it- as the fully-specialized Freemage. Wait, you say that the Freemage is more heavily invested in the Magic attribute and is better with magic? Yeah, 8% better at the start. Hot stuff. That might increase by a whole 8% per level, too! All the while you're completely neglecting your mage's ability to stay alive by investing in Vitality or Perception, so really it's closer to 2% per level.
Basically your meticulously planned party is going to be ineffective, because the game doesn't really want you to experiment with the parts of the skill system that you like. Want to invest in Warfare (a fighter's equivalent to casting spells) and have a battlefield commander? ♥♥♥♥ you. Now your fighter can't hit anything to save his life, and you need to land your Challenge attacks to draw the attention of enemies, who will then proceed to mangle your fighter that didn't invest heavily in their armor skills.
Basically there are no good decisions, and that seems to be how the game likes it.
Monster fighting is tiresome. The earliest quests have you dealing with spiders that poison you with their basic attacks. Poison never goes away without a (fairly expensive) antidote or specific spell that nobody can start with. So any of your characters that get poisoned by this frequent attack will inevitably go 'unconscious' without immediate medical attention. Being unconscious doesn't clear the poison. The poison is eternal. My Dwarf Defender didn't recover from poison after resting for twenty-four hours. Or ever. Not without help. So 'camping' to tend to your wounds just refills your health bars and then you watch them rapidly deteriorate from the poison that never disappeared. It takes about six 'steps' in game for people to keel over dead after getting up from their nap.
What.
Monsters don't get any better. Naga in the second dungeon (the first after the 'tutorial' with the spiders) dual-wield and attack twice per turn, gaining more damage if they hit with the first swing. They regularly one-hit your spellcasters and cannot be provoked into attacking anyone wearing armor without spamming 'challenge' attempts, which costs mana and rarely lands. Naga priestesses spam ice spells just as strong as the party's, but don't suffer from mana conservation. Everything crits. You guzzle mana and health potions every three rounds. I don't want to say 'unrealistic' when talking about my fantasy dungeon crawlers, but my god...
I don't even...
I hate to compare this game to Grimrock (which was brilliant), because it doesn't feel fair. Grimrock was a labor of love for people that love this genre. Legacy was a kick in the nuts trying to cash in on nostalgia with a low price tag and promises it doesn't deliver on. Exploring dungeons doesn't have player attentiveness rewarded by secret passages and vast loot. Instead, your characters bark out their discovery of things, waiting for you to mash your face against every nearby wall until something glows and you open a new passage with the spacebar.
Riveting.
Traps are mandatory. Often they just sit on a required pathway, and almost always just spawn more monsters. Usually in flanking positions. Even if you detect a trap your only choice is to mash your face into it, or, in rare circumstances, walk around the otherwise empty room.
Loot is a mess of +2 to damage and +5 to some nebulous resistence stats. It's also completely random and there's no such thing as farming, so if the wrong loot drops for your party...♥♥♥♥ you. I guess you can reload, save-scumming for better loot, but is that something we really want to encourage?
I've been told the game opens up, both in terms of exploration and tactics, but after my first party (which I was a fool to put on the harder of the two difficulties, which made it nearly unplayable) couldn't pass the second dungeon, I don't think I'm going to make it there. My second party has the exact same problem in the exact same dungeon, you see. On the 'much easier' difficulty.
Developers and veterans will probably giggle because someone can't handle their hardcore game. Their perogative. I'm still not going to reccomend this steaming mess to anyone.
Slow, unsatisfying, tiresome. Avoid it.

Though I could see why at this game's initial release people were hesitant about it and claimed every level looked the same, I would have to say that with all of the updates up to this point this game has become a complete and worthwhile game.
I am mostly writing this review as a response to a lot of the reviews I've seen that, even after all of the latest updates, still claim each level looks alike and that there is no complexity to the battles you'll have in this game, because honestly I think we must playing different games. I'll give it to you that in the fist few levels there isn't much in the way of difficult 1v1 battles, however anyone who tells you they are absent from the game clearly hasn't reached the mid-to-late levels because there are in fact quite a few enemies that fulfill this role, and in the last few floors the game often gives you one or two, plus ads, to fight at one time. These guys practically feel like mini-bosses and really do force me to think about how to take them on.
As to the levels all looking the same, in my first few runs I thought the same thing, but now I feel the complete opposite way. I'm not sure if it's a mechanic of the game to simply make the levels look cooler on subsequent play throughs, or if a recent update changed how the game determines which modules to load on each floor, but I never have a run where each floor is just the standard series of rooms and hallways, there are always outdoor sections, and each floor really starts to take on its own theme. In fact, I often STOP seeing those normal hallways around floor three.
When it comes to the weapon selection, It may look like there are only two different kinds of weapon (light and heavy), but experimenting with all the different choices I have available proved to show a big difference between shortswords, longstowrds, axes, hammers, greatswords, staves, etc. I can feel the difference in how each kind of weapon stakes up against the different enemies this game throws at me.
This game is great, as you can see I've put a lot of time into it. Are there things that could be better? Sure, but there are so few I can't even think of examples. Do I think the games few weaknesses take away all the fun? Absolutely not. People have complained that after beating the game once, there isn't much intensive to play again, other than trying to 100% the game. I'll give it to you that a run done before completing the game and one done after don't have much of a difference (aside from the fact that you probably can afford to purchase some of the better upgrades if you've beaten the game), but I feel like the game doesn't need to give me something to convince me to play it again. This game is fun, getting to play the game is enough of an insensitive for me to want to play again. Honestly the first time I beat the game I was sad because I thought "If I win I might not want to play this wonderful game more" but that was about a month ago and I've clocked another 20 hours in just the last 2 weeks.
And this is all my opinion of the game before Brutal adition. I already thought it was a great game and then the devs made it bigger and better. I haven't had a chance to play it too much but from what I've played I liked.
TL;DR This game can't be judged in just a few minutes, honestly I think it can't really be judged in just a few hours. This game takes a little bit of time to figure out, anyone who tells you its missing: level variance, weapon variance, or battle variance hasn't ACTUALLY played the game yet. They most likely haven't gotten through the first 3 levels, and to quote the Brazen Head (the games quasi-narrator) "Most people still consider this to be the tutorial part of the Necropolis"

I wouldn't call this a game so much as I would call it a memoir that you can personally experience with the help of a computer.  But for the sake of the review, I'll call it a game.
I honestly don't know how to review this game.  It runs fairly like any game should, though I often felt a bit lost at various times since the game was vague about what I needed to do or where I needed to go.  The graphics are decent despite everyone being a faceless being and the voice acting is right on point.  But those things aren't really what the game's main draw is.
The game does an excellent job of allowing you to experience the family's grief when their son is diagnosed with cancer and their struggles with it.  It's not "hollywoodized" and melodramatic, instead being very much how people do react in situations like these in real life.  Sometimes you don't always cry when someone you love is discovered to be terminally ill, but instead convince yourself that you can fight the disease and win in the end.  Or, perhaps you don't feel anything at all and the grief hits you many days later when you can actually process what you've been told.  It's different for everyone.
I'll admit that I didn't cry at any point throughout this game, despite what everyone else says.  I knew how much pain the characters were in and how upset they were, as the game developers did an excellent job with showing their grief, but I never felt overwhelming pain myself.  I don't know if it's because I'm emotionally dead at times or because I'm a nurse and it's my job to keep professional distance from heartbreaking situations like this with my patients, but that's just how I felt.
But despite my apparent semi-apathy, I'd still reccomend this game.  It's a short experience, clocking in at about 2 hours depending on how much time you take to explore the environment.  It's a wonderful experience and it does provide a good sense of closure to all those who might have perished because of unfortunate reasons.
And maybe in that time, you can feel what I couldn't and cry the tears that wouldn't come for me.

Duck is the common name for a large number of species in the waterfowl family Anatidae, which also includes swans and geese. Ducks are divided among several subfamilies in the family Anatidae; they do not represent a monophyletic group (the group of all descendants of a single common ancestral species) but a form taxon, since swans and geese are not considered ducks. Ducks are mostly aquatic birds, mostly smaller than the swans and geese, and may be found in both fresh water and sea water. The word duck comes from Old English *dūce "diver", a derivative of the verb *dūcan "to duck, bend down low as if to get under something, or dive", because of the way many species in the dabbling duck group feed by upending; compare with Dutch duiken and German tauchen "to dive".
This word replaced Old English ened/ænid "duck", possibly to avoid confusion with other Old English words, like ende "end" with similar forms. Other Germanic languages still have similar words for "duck", for example, Dutch eend "duck" and German Ente "duck". The word ened/ænid was inherited from Proto-Indo-European; compare: Latin anas "duck", Lithuanian ántis "duck", Ancient Greek nēssa/nētta (νῆσσα, νῆττα) "duck", and Sanskrit ātí "water bird", among others.
A duckling is a young duck in downy plumage or baby duck.
A male duck is called a drake and the female is called a duck, or in ornithology a hen.
The overall body plan of ducks is elongated and broad, and the ducks are also relatively long-necked, albeit not as long-necked as the geese and swans. The body shape of diving ducks varies somewhat from this in being more rounded. The bill is usually broad and contains serrated lamellae, which are particularly well defined in the filter-feeding species. In the case of some fishing species the bill is long and strongly serrated. The scaled legs are strong and well developed, and generally set far back on the body, more so in the highly aquatic species. The wings are very strong and are generally short and pointed, and the flight of ducks requires fast continuous strokes, requiring in turn strong wing muscles. Three species of steamer duck are almost flightless, however. Many species of duck are temporarily flightless while moulting; they seek out protected habitat with good food supplies during this period. This moult typically precedes migration.
The drakes of northern species often have extravagant plumage, but that is moulted in summer to give a more female-like appearance, the "eclipse" plumage. Southern resident species typically show less sexual dimorphism, although there are exceptions like the paradise shelduck of New Zealand which is both strikingly sexually dimorphic and where the female's plumage is brighter than that of the male. The game is awesome. It's smooth, elegant, sounds great, looks great, and is stable.
This is no trivial game that you can master, finish and discard in a couple dozen hours.
I imagine this is a game I will continue playing for months, if not years, especially as new content is released. Stellaris is a STRATEGY game, and makes no bones about it, as there is barely even a nod towards tactical elements.
The one thing I love about Stellaris above most other games in this genre .... there are actual STAR SYSTEMS, not just planets floating in space or arbitrary placeholders. Ships which warp or jump into a system have to traverse the system or wait for their jump drives to cool down before they can jump again. As an immersive factor, this WORKS for me.
The nature of the game is TOTALLY suited to modding and customisation. I can imagine people designing the entire star wars galaxy or star trek galaxy or empire of man or warhammer 40k universe or starcraft universe in this. I literally cannot wait to see what modders will do in terms of race design, 3d models, static galaxy designs, story driven gameplay, event chains, etc.
Stellaris has given a massive POKE IN THE EYE to those who think 4x games cannot encompass multiple stardrive types and should be simplified to managing hyperlane bottlenecks.
You will love it if
- you like sandbox games
- you want control of customisation
- you want to set your own goals, and drive your own agenda
- you love science fiction stories, as the anomalies and events in the game are like a story unfolding, absolutely amazing.
You will hate it if
- you are a twitch gamer wanting a rail-shooter in space
- you want the game to drive the agenda for you
- you just wanna kill things and couldn't be bothered to read.
Being a sandbox, i imagine it will suit the multiplayer environment much better than the single player environment, but it is still an awesome single player experience.
There are a few things missing, but they detract very little from the game experience.
- there are only randomly generated games, no campaign modes
- there are no freighters, passenger ships, trade routes, etc.
- the game is pseudo 3d, and effectively plays out on a flat galaxy map
- no tactical combat mode, but its well done, with combat seamlessly playing outin real time on the strategic map.
- current diplomacy is not that complex, no espionage, sabotage, etc. But the sheer number of species and diversity adds its own complexity.
- being a sandbox, there is currently no campaign, but I am sure the modding community will solve this.
- while there are leaders (governals, admirals, scientists, etc) with traits, experience and skills, they are randomly generated, not a result of a complex relationship engine as in CK2. Not a big deal to me, but I imagine some would have hoped for this. I can imagne a system like rome total war with governing families leading factions might have worked.
Many of the tricks the designers missed in the realease version, I imagine can be added in future content, or through modding.
