NOTE: This review below is based on the original Strike Suit Zero, as I'm still playing through it. The Director's Cut improves pacing and voice acting, adds much of the original game's DLC, as well as provides a visual upgrade. However, it is much more demanding on systems and ditches the (rarely used) Steam Workshop support. You're probably better off getting the Director's Cut as a new player (unless your system cannot run it), but veterans of the original probably don't need to double-dip.
Strike Suit Zero is a intense and frantic game with a lot of significant flaws. Controls can feel complex and cumbersome, often akin to patting your head and rubbing your belly as you constantly shift between various weapons systems to chew through energy shields or armor more efficiently, time your EMP to throw off enemy missiles, manage weapon and thruster energy so as not to be left vulnerable while also keeping tabs on numerous objectives, enemy types, and friendlies that need more protection than Slippy ever did. Flipping into 'Strike' mode (AKA Mech mode) is only a temporary respite, cutting your maneuverability and boasting a whole different set of controls that must be mastered to maximize it's enormous firepower. It's overwhelming at times all of the stuff that needs to be kept track of, and the cluttered, boring missions don't help. However, when the game is firing on all cylinders and you get into a stride, there's absolutely nothing like SSZ in the genre that makes you feel like an ace pilot. The climax of one mission, for example, sees you screaming into combat as an outgunned allied battleship is melted, corkscrewing through a swarm of enemy fighters blasting at everything to build up flux in time. From there, you flip smoothly into Strike mode, strafing along the broadside of a massive enemy cruiser mashing turrets and hoping to god your shields can hold on for just a few milliseconds longer before shifting back to fighter mode and wheeling out for another run, eyes constantly watching the armor melting off your allied ship. Moments like these will be among the most memorable moments you can have with this game. Unfortunately, they'll also be peppered with hatred for the accursed bomber missions, long missions of "kill this group of enemies, move, repeat ad nauseam", and the boring story.

Ah, zombies. We're all sick of them in games, aren't we?
Nation Red is a game with a simple premise. You're one of four classes each with their own perks and you have to fight off the zombie horde! That's basically what this game boils down to, it's almost exclusively a horde mode. Even the "Mission" mode is just fighting off a series of hordes except the match changes after you hit a certain amount of kills.
What makes Nation Red unique and rather fun is that it's very comparable to twin stick shooters/shmups. The zombies keep coming at you and your goal is to stay alive. Like most shmups, as you kill zombies there are weapon drops, perk drops, and you successively upgrade your character to help you defeat the horde of zombies.  There are a couple of maps and modes and the game is excellent fun solo, but when you have four people on your fireteam, that's where the game shines.
This game is excellent for killing some time and the style (twin stick shooter) is a style I particularly enjoy. If you enjoy shmups, if you enjoy zombies, and if you enjoy testing yourself to reach a high score, Nation Red is an interesting twist on tried and true gameplay experiences. It's fast paced and has a couple of modes and maps to make you want to come back.
As a caveat, I cannot really suggest it at its full $9.99 pricepoint, but if it hits a sale/bundle and the style of game is up your alley, you may find Nation Red is just your ticket. I'd also suggest playing with a controller, because, well, its a twin stick shooter and you're far more lethal with a controller in this kind of game than you are with a mouse and keyboard.

+ Nice combination of old school turn-based RPG and modern comfort features (annotatable automap, easy comparison between different items via mouse-over, rest anywhere instead of only in safe zones etc).
+ Turn-based battles require a lot of micro-management of your character's spells and skills. For me, it was a great part of the fun of MMX - for other players this might be a turn-off.
+ Thoughtful management of your character's attributes and new skill points is a must - but it's also very rewarding when you reach a new weapon proficiency or finally master a new, powerful spell.
+ Decent variety of enemies, though there are only about two to three different types per dungeon / overworld area. Each type of enemy has different resistances and skills - you have to adapt your attacks / buffs / debuffs accordingly.
+/- Loads and loads of loot, but too often enemies drop only useless stuff (weak weapons and armour for the most part). On the other hand, a decent number of powerful "relics" (weapons, armour) can be found in the most remote and dangerous areas of the game. These relics make a real difference in battle, especially as you can level them up (4 levels each) by simply having them equipped in battle. Levelled up to max, these relics are the most powerful items in the game.
+/- You will often run into enemies who are simply too strong for your characters, requiring you to level up and get some better gear before you return. A classic feature, yes, but this can be annoying if you haven't yes found an area / dungeon where your characters can level up without the constant threat of getting killed by strong mobs.
- Story is okay, delivered mostly by NPC "talking heads" (text only, speech in very rare cases) and books containing background information about the world and its history. Almost no dialogue choices for your characters. All in all, the story of main quest and side quests is serviceable, but not very engaging.
- Quality of character models and textures ranges from "serviceable" to "eyesore".
- No crafting. Would have been nice because too many of the weapons in shops or dropped by enemies are useless.
- As of mid February 2014, annoying bugs still remain (parts of the environment turn invisible, quest rewards not given etc). Your mileage may vary; I did not encounter any quest-breaking bugs.
All in all, I wholeheartedly recommend this games to all fans of classic, turn-based RPGs. It's not perfect and still needs some patching - but there are simply tons of fun to be had while fighting and exploring.

In the Witcher 2 you play as Geralt of Rivia, a witcher. Witchers are humans who go through intensive mental and physical training and are genetically enhanced in order to become itinerant monster slayers for hire.
The game plays out as a RPG, with a deep combat system, which actually requires you to prepare for fights by oiling your swords with special ointments and drink potions to be able to come out on top. The morality system is very ambiguous, with you being able to take decisions that will alter following events in a meaningful way, but with no clear "right" or "wrong". The graphics are extremely good, but to be able to take full advantage, you will need a high end pc.
The strongest part in the game is the story, which takes place in a rich medieval world comparable to the one in The Lord of The Rings, and Game of Thrones. The plot is filled with war, intrigue, twists, backstabbing and colorful characters. The Witcher games are actually based on a fantasy series by Polish writer Andrzej Sapkowski, but take place after the conclusion in the books.
If you are interested in RPG's set in immersive worlds and with solid mechanics, the Witcher 2 is a must buy!

As someone who only played one other game in the series, Might and Magic 8, Legacy feels to me as both a nostalgia trip and a game which tries a bit too much to be similar to previous games in the series to be its own game, but too little to be a remake.
The most obvious differences between 8 and Legacy are that the former is semi-turn-based with free movement and the ability to swap out any party member except the leader, while the latter is completely turn-based with grid-based movement and your party is fixed from the start which, as far as I know, is what the series was like up to around the 6th game.
The biggest disappointments in Legacy are that the game is significantly more linear than 8, and the world is significantly smaller. A large part of the enjoyment of Might and Magic, to me, was exploring new locations, seeing how quickly enemies can annihilate me, then finding ways to sneak or fly past the enemies and try to acquire the loot they are protecting. However now most enemies you encounter will be roughly as powerful as you are because new towns are unlocked only as you progress through the main quest, as opposed to them all being available from the start, the starter island notwithstanding. And if you do encounter enemies that are more powerful than you, which is either in mini-dungeons that simply have 1 very powerful monster, or, more rarely, on the world map, you may as well simply reload your most recent save, because once combat begins it is impossible to escape, save for perhaps some spell I have not yet discovered.
There are also a couple of mechanics which are nearly pointless given how the game is structured, namely the fact that trainers for skills are scattered around the world and buying a ride to another city. In 8 trainers for skills could be in any of the several towns or out in the wilderness, particularly if they're the highest rank trainer, and if you looked and asked around you could generally get to the trainer no matter where he was, because even if he was in the highest-level town, you could simply get a ride there and find the trainer, despite the fact that a single step outside would spell your doom. But since you cannot move on to the next town without completing a number of quests, for balance reasons the trainers are much more cluttered. Nearly every rank 1 trainer is in the starting town, most of the rank 2 trainers are in the second town, and after exploring for about an hour I've found 3 rank 3 trainers pretty close to each other in the wilderness. As a result all that's left of a mechanic that encouraged exploration is the requirement to walk all around town until you find the right house, as well as limiting your skill progression if you haven't gotten far enough through the storyline. In a similar vein, buying a ride to another town is essentially pointless as it only takes a minute or two of walking to cover the distance on foot.
I also have a few more minor complaints. There is no tavern card game, which was a great time-waster as well as an interesting way to get some artifacts, and there are barely any traps in any of the dungeons, whereas in 8 nearly half of all chests were booby-trapped and taking one wrong step could lead to ambushes, fireballs or even falling into a pit of snakes.
Despite these complaints, I've enjoyed my time with the game so far. While not as much as in the game I played all those years ago, exploring is fun as is slaughtering weaker monsters and barely defeating monsters that are more powerful than you. The grid-based movement, while more restricting, also means that you can't defeat monsters that are significantly more powerful than you simply by kiting them or by flying above them while they gather underneath, vainly trying to reach you. Similarly, while the fact that your party cannot be changed after you start means you can't be as versatile with your group of adventurers, it also means you can't simply cast an invisibility spell at level 10, sneak through a cave full of high-level dragons and recruit a level 50 dragon into your party. It's a different experience to Might and Magic 8, but a fun one nonetheless.

A Brutal Edition Review Update
Brutal Edition, which should probably be called "Hey guys you like Dark Souls?" edition, adds a new player class and a new tileset, while making some fundamental changes to mechanics.
The new class, the Brute, has more refined and useful animations for many weapons than the Blackguard, while also having a Dark Souls style roll dodge. The entire feel of the Brute solidifies the idea of "low-fi Dark Souls" that Necropolis puts forward, without really solving any of the inherent problems the rest of the game has. The Brute is probably an objectively better class than the Blackguard, almost going so far as to obsolete the first class.
The new area, The Black Forest, brings to mind more Dark Souls comparisons. Snowy, ensconced in dark, fallen trees and thin corridors between tall cliffs, it feels like an extension of the swamp tileset, rather than something truly its own. It's an inoffensive addition at worst, and a nice change of pace from endless stone corridors and dull swamps.
Finally, Brutal Edition adds new enemies, but none of them make a meaningful addition to the combat systems or any encounter you'll find, as most enemy groups are still single unit types.
Unfortunately, many of Necropolis' fundamental issues remain, now exacerbated by balance changes to mechanics. You still face swarms of enemies (check my one single Necropolis screenshot to see a only-slightly-larger than typical mob of enemies for level 2) with AI that only has two modes; run at you or find more guys to run at you with. The endless mobs of enemies that can do enormous amounts of damage are still fatiguing and not particularly varied to fight. For some reason, drinking unidentified potions and using unidentified scrolls still doesn't identify similar items, ignoring every other roguelike with randomized items.
Shields are no longer unstoppable god machines of blocking, but the bleed through of damage with the new balance is somewhat poorly tuned. The only things you ever really need to block are the super enemies and some of the nastier variants, and now blocking them can be a risky proposition at best. Many of the enemies worth blocking retain zero windup attacks that can combo you or take huge chunks from your health. The overall combat of Necropolis remains unsatisfying and fatiguing, a trudge uphill both ways in the snow while being beset from all sides by brigands.
Finally, monsters drop considerably less crafting materials, and you no longer start the game with Iron Rations as a crafting option. While in a vacuum this is a good change, as reaching floor four or five in previous Necropolis patches ensured an endless supply of Iron Rations, none of the other changes (or lack thereof) to the game support this. You still face huge swarms of enemies, but now without the ability to mitigate the slow, almost unavoidable drain of your health. Roguelike? Certainly. Fun? Not so much.
And that's kind of the final tune Necropolis sings. It's doing its best to be a compelling roguelike, but even with these updates it just doesn't quite reach fun. It's a slog to play, it makes some baffling decisions that exacerbate the issues it has even before thos decisions, and it just isn't worth $30 of content, gameplay or updates.

This is essentially "Human Suffering the Video Game". Now that may sound like I'm insulting the game, but nothing can be further from the truth. 'That Dragon, Cancer' is a kind of quality that words cannot adequately express; a deep, meaningful look into a real family's struggle with cancer and the complexity of everything they went through. You don't so much play as anyone or anything, but rather you fallow the family through the experience. You're introduced to their son Joel, and from there the game takes you through the story switching from vantage point to vantage point. There's a haunting, almost dream-like, pressence that lingers througout the experience and really gets across the full emotional weight of this very sad story. I caution any particularily sensitive players to play this game with discretion as certain portions of the game are very graphic, for instance the inclusion of real audio of a dying child screaming in pain from dehydration, actual CAT scans of the child, and some extremely emotional testimonies of the whole process. Truthfully this experience shouldn't be handled like just another piece of entertainment. The game goes far beyond just being a game. In this documentation lies the power to make you question, to make you appreciate the people around you, and to change the way you look at certain things. I personally am more appreciative of my health and the health of those around me for having played this game; that's the sort of powerful experience That  Dragon, Cancer really is. It's a very short game that can be completed in just over an hour, but what it does in that time is remarkable, beautiful, terrible, and deeply meaningful all at the same time. In short, That dragon, Cancer is a beautiful documentation about suffering, loss, faith, endurance, and perseverance made by two loving parents in memory of their son. It's a brutal look at the depths of human suffering, as well as a testimony of love and faith all executed in a masterful way and made all the more intense by the fact that every bit of it is authentic. I absolutly recommend that you support this game and the family it's based off of with a purchase.

For anyone complaining that it's similar to Overwatch, I suggest you play it when you become somewhat tired of Overwatch. The gamefeel of Paladins is completely separate from Overwatch in three major ways. The first is that teams are made up of five players, rather than six. This means that an individual player's skill can heavily influence the match, for good or for bad. Secondly, every character feels somewhat tankier and can regenerate health when out of combat for some time, which changes the overall feel of engagements. Some may think that this takes the focus off of reactions and skills, but it creates a much more emotionally charged environment. It also makes 5v5 team deathmatch all the more exciting. Thirdly, the pacing is somewhat more gameplay-oriented. Maybe it's just because I'm far better at this game than I an at Overwatch (or all the players are bad) and die less, but I feel that the game wants players to meet each other around the objective. The maps are somewhat less nuanced and are shaped for engagement. The game also allows players to rush into the action after death on a horse.

Ah, zombies. We're all sick of them in games, aren't we?
Nation Red is a game with a simple premise. You're one of four classes each with their own perks and you have to fight off the zombie horde! That's basically what this game boils down to, it's almost exclusively a horde mode. Even the "Mission" mode is just fighting off a series of hordes except the match changes after you hit a certain amount of kills.
What makes Nation Red unique and rather fun is that it's very comparable to twin stick shooters/shmups. The zombies keep coming at you and your goal is to stay alive. Like most shmups, as you kill zombies there are weapon drops, perk drops, and you successively upgrade your character to help you defeat the horde of zombies.  There are a couple of maps and modes and the game is excellent fun solo, but when you have four people on your fireteam, that's where the game shines.
This game is excellent for killing some time and the style (twin stick shooter) is a style I particularly enjoy. If you enjoy shmups, if you enjoy zombies, and if you enjoy testing yourself to reach a high score, Nation Red is an interesting twist on tried and true gameplay experiences. It's fast paced and has a couple of modes and maps to make you want to come back.
As a caveat, I cannot really suggest it at its full $9.99 pricepoint, but if it hits a sale/bundle and the style of game is up your alley, you may find Nation Red is just your ticket. I'd also suggest playing with a controller, because, well, its a twin stick shooter and you're far more lethal with a controller in this kind of game than you are with a mouse and keyboard.

Dean Dodrill single handedly managed to take elements of pretty much all the best 2D platformers that have appeared in video games over the last 30 years & combine them into a singular work of genius. The graphics have the Disney-esque fluidity of Aladdin on the SNES & mechanically the 'Dust Storm' at second glance could be Rocket Knight's rocket charge attack. The obvious Metroidvania map exploration and ability tree is present & finally taking a cue from games such as DMC & Bayonetta is a combo meter system which keeps the combat from being 'mashy'.
Not since Shadow Of The Beast on the Amiga have you seen such lush, hand-drawn & vivid backgrounds. The character design, voice acting & level layout is far what you'd expect of an indie developer, let alone one person. It's such a feat in itself that it's hard to not overlook any shortcomings the game may have.
Finally, the best (semi-secret) part of the game is the ode to all his indie developer friends (circa 2010-11) where he has made similar levels or rooms represeting the game they were working on at the time. The Fez & Braid room are particularly inspired!
I'm certain to buy whatever Dean & & his studio Humble Hearts decide to work on next.

Abzu is… wow. It’s just wow.
It’s visually the most striking thing I think I have ever seen running on my computer. The use of colour is stunning. Animation is mesmerizing and the amount of individual fishes and plants is mind blowing. To see this world live around the player and to interact with it left me at times speechless and at times just giggling with myself. Music is also excellent and with the visual style creates an unique mood. Controller is recommended and with it the game is really fluid to play.
Abzu is one of those games in which the player doesn’t actually do much and it offers no challenge. Navigating is simple thanks to visual cues such as light shining somewhere or the camera pointing to next thing. The game basically moves from one “room” to another and sometimes a door needs to be unlocked. This is always as simple as finding two buttons to interact with. A lot of the game is also spent in underwater currents which are basically on rails with very little to interact with. Personally I didn’t mind these because of the look and atmosphere but could be an issue to those who want more game in their game.
I completed the game in a single sitting which took a little under 2 hours. I wasn’t even trying to rush through it, but progress is so easy and at times automatic that the end just happened. In those 2 hours is included some time spent just playing with the fishes and swimming around. There are some collectables but I think those do not fit the game and I really don’t see the point in searching for them.
Because the game relies so much on visual elements, a solid 60 fps is the absolute minimum. For me, with a 760gtx this turned out to be hard to achieve. In screenshots the game may look cartoony, but with so many moving elements, it really takes some horsepower to run the game properly. This is why I recommend that you have a decent pc before buying, as low frame rate takes a lot away from the experience.
As an experience Abzu is absolutely fantastic. In its short running time it manages to tell a touching story and stun with it’s presentation. With a sale price of around 6€ Abzu is with every cent and then some. Thoroughly recommended.

Galactic Civilization III is a great update from GC I or II. Best thing is to go 64bit, so there is plenty room for an upgrade.
...and upgrade is badly needed, btw.
Game is playable, but sometimes still feels like a beta which was released way too early, while all buyers are getting used as semi-proffessional-testers. There is so much to do, that you have enough fun to explore all aspects of this game. They had some rather good ideas...unfortunately they didn't follow the road to the end.
As in shipyards. You could sink hours into building your own custom designed ships....but you can't lead them in a battle. All you could do is to have higher numbers then your enemy and wish good luck. They brought in a cinema like view on the 'battle'...but you could do NOTHING to change the outcome.
As for multiplayer. They totally forgot about founding different versions by simply translating the game without compensation. Us players had to bring voice toward the devs about their hard to stand mistake. About half a year the game wasn't playable in multiplayer. Lately us players found the missing key inside english localization files. But...at the end game is still not working in multiplayer...not for technical issue, but for bad design. All players are in LOCAL lobby to find mutliplayer games. If your local area has no GC3 players, you paid for a multiplayer game which you can't use. There is another bad design....they sold the game on GOG, but GOG players' versions are not compatible with STEAM players' version. They even didn't bring up a simple IP-connection...for their own reasons. Looks like GC3's multiplayer was just announced to have it but never implemented for internet users. Just a word: if I would like to play multiplayer with my neighbour I would have bought a tabletop. Multiplayer is used to be played worldwide not local.
As for creating your own custom faction. Factions aren't anything other then branches from only one alien race. All do compete on the same ressources, all do compete on the same sort of planets. All 'aliens' do start on little sunshine world same as all other. Devs changed the way those custom factions were stored several times...but you could never find out which one use old (=obsolete and gamebraking) design when you subscribe one from workshop.
As for Steam cloud. GC3 offers steam cloud for savegames, custom factions and your very own ship designs. Unfortunately it's simply impossible to delete them. Even Steam is not able to delete them completely. But if you have saves from earlier game versions...it is able to break your game. Instead of offering a simple switch to turn Steam cloud on/off for GC3 they just tell you to switch off Steam cloud for your entire account to avoid issues with GC3.
As for diplomacy. It's there...rudimentary, but it's like living in the '60 where all things are good or bad but game shows no offer for playing it other then by force. Still you can't prevent aliens from spreading colonies or outposts...even within your own zone of control. Player is still forced to run and hestitate to get some of the planets and goods before the aliens grab it.
My first guess is, the devs cutted out deeply needed parts to sell it later for good money as DLC. Worst of all decissions in my eyes. First one has to bring a totally satisfying game, then one could upgrade his good product with more flavor. Stardock may learn it from Paradox...
I'm really dissappointed about the game in current state and also frustrated about it for a very long time, where no one was able to adress multiplayer issues for longer then half a year. It has great potential to be better then the actual design...but I fear the devs are a) unwilling or b) unable to do better.
Have to adress my good impression about Stardock's helpdesk, those guys really try to fix issues...but unfortunately they can't adress bad design from devs. Yeah, one could say it's all merchandizing...but if I stop to buy things from Stardock, they defenetly regret. Seems there is no other way to get the message through.
Besides there are allready competitors underway which avoid those issues.
Have a look at 'Stellaris', 'Endless Space 2' or even new 'Master of Orion'....all announced 2016.

This game is fantastic.  I dont normally play 4x type games, but the exploration mechanic and the randomised skill tree make this enjoyable because it is not simply a race down a tech tree, like it has been with every other 4x game I have played.
Also the whole politics/populations/science interplay is a really nice thing.  For example I am playing a religious and militarist fascist dictatorship.  One of my science teams finds some beautiful alien tombs on a far away planet.  I allow the knowledge of them to be spread within my empire because its a nice thing for my population to look at.  Some of my population become xenophilically inclined, realising aliens might have value.  A little while later I enact a policy of fullscale strategic orbital bombardment, in order to allow me to quickly massacre the colonies of another empire that I am at war with, due to not being expressly allowed to simply butcher them and needing to damage them collaterally.  The populations which began to value dirty xenos life didnt take too kindly to this.
The only problems I have encountered are wierd restrictions.  Like mentioned above I can only directly cleanse alien species if I am officially xenophobic.  Why?  I mean I can understand not doing it as effectively in terms of time and societal reaction if I am not fully committed to solving the xenos problem.  But just not being allowed to do it at all is odd.

Edit: Added some thoughts regarding the content updates since release.
Update 2: As of April 29, 2017 Stellaris has had it's first major expansion. Which along with the free update that came along with it have further improved the game and also fixed one of the big issues I had with the game, the Ethics Divergence system. I look forward to even more updates and expansions for this game.
Update 1: Since release, Stellaris has now had three content updates in the form of patches and one story pack DLC. The three updates for the game have added new content/features, refined and update older features, and overall have improved the game significantly since release. The DLC, Leviathans, added some new things to do in the typically boring and slow mid-game of most 4X games.
Original: Stellaris is a great mix of 4X and Grand Strategy. It plays alot like a mix of Civ, with exploration and meeting empires in the early game, and then shifts over towards a more grand strategy like feel as you start establishing both friendships and rivalries with neighboring empires and your borders began to collide. If you've been wanting to try other Grand Strategy games such as Europa Universalis, Hearts of Iron, or other Paradox games, but have felt intimidated by the depth then Stellaris is a good place to start to get the feel of the genre.
I fully recommend this game and consider it a definite buy if you are interested in this genre!

Sound - Great track and good background audio.  Lots of attention to detail.  I have a bug where sound gets weird and I have to restart the game.
Gameplay - Very replayable.  Big world, lots of secrets, cool classes, tons of lore.

If you like Legend of Grimrock or old school games like M&M's, Wizardry, Anvil of Dawn, Dungeon Master you'll love this game.  They got the nastalgic feel with the modern style. The first thing I fell in love with when I started the game was the music. The soundtrack is amazing and captures the atmosphere in each individual level very well and there were even moments when I just laid down my controller and listened to it during my playthrough.
That's not to say the music is the only thing this game has going for it. For reference, I'm not that good at classic sidescrolling games like Castlevania or Metroid, but once in a while I'll take the time and learn a game like that. Dust was one of them. I played on Normal, and it felt really well balanced as it constantly challenged me more and more. The boss fights were somewhat easy, but besides them I can't complain.
The art is absolutely beautiful. Backgrounds look amazing on the highest settings, the characters' movements are fluid, and the visual effects for certain moves are really nice to look at. I really loved exploring all the different areas with their unique atmospheres and themes that clearly distinguished them from one another. You never lose sight of where your characters is though, so you won't find yourself dying because of the background distracting you.
Look, all I'm trying to say is, go play this game. I finished it on Normal after collecting everything there is to collect in 18 hours, so if you're less of a completionist freak you'll make it through even faster than that. It's worth playing, and while the story does have some pretty cliché moments the game makes up for it in the way it presents them. Cutscenes are beautiful hand-drawn sequences and while the voice acting is not the best I've ever heard, it certainly isn't bad either. Also it's fully voiced, so that's a thing.
Play this game. Do it.

I can recommend this as a slow-paced, somber, impressionistic storytelling experience with only minimal "gaming" elements. If you're into that sort of thing.
I commend the game for providing neither "too little" nor "too much" interactivity. I felt like I was getting into the parents' headspace, and I appreciated the ability to dwell or not dwell on certain things. (E.g. you can read as many or as few notecards about people with cancer as you'd like.) I did cry a little. The mini-platformer was cute in a way.
A few reviewers have complained about the religious aspect. While I think this story perhaps could have been a little more powerful for me *personally* if it had been about people struggling with cancer without the belief in God, it is in fact about a family that *does* believe in God, and so it's basically imperative that the game touches on that and shows how the family deals with cancer in a religious context. What's more, you hardly have to be religious to empathize with the suffering and struggle that's going on.
On the downside, I unfortunately got very frustrated in the church scene, where I couldn't figure out how to advance the narrative to the next scene, even after googling for how the scene was supposed to work. Maybe I was just being dumb somehow. In any case, I had to resort to manually skipping to the next scene.
For the price, it's too bad the game doesn't also include the corresponding documentary, "Thank You For Playing".

You will always have an opportunity or a chance to train and grind before a mandatory fight, so if you're struggling with a boss, it's not impossible. Just get out there and start levelling first. Although, you'll be suprised. I accidentally managed to save up limit breaks for the second boss and two hitted him so...
Story is great, a bit of a mess to get your head around first time through. This is one of those games that when you replay, you suddenly find yourself noticing lots of little references and allusions to various events. It all makes a lot more sense then. Although again, last time I played it solidly, I was like 10. I wouldn't have understood♥♥♥♥♥♥ May just be me. Anyone who remembers the PS1 discs will understand when I say that disc one is the best and why you may want to take a break when the point in the game is reached where disc one ends. One last nitpick is that the script is altered slightly to make it more accurate (I think), but all swearing is censored. Now I can't remember if it was in the original (I believe it was, otherwise this wouldn't annoy me so much). So now it's just a bunch of random characters like !"@'~# instead of♥♥♥♥♥♥ that is a bit irritating, but that's just me.
All in all, fantastic game, great quality port (suprisingly so tbh), could do with a graphical oevrhaul. Definitely worth the buy, especially if the glorious steam sales come on.

MDK is a 1997 third-person shooter video game developed by Shiny Entertainment for Microsoft Windows. It was ported to Mac OS by Shokwave, and to the PlayStation by Neversoft. It was published on all systems by PIE in North America, with Shiny Entertainment publishing it themselves in Europe. The Windows version was released in April 1997, the Mac version in June and the PlayStation version in November. The game was released on
in September 2008, and on Steam in September 2009.
The game tells the story of Kurt Hectic, a janitor who reluctantly must attempt to save Earth from an alien invasion of gigantic strip mining city-sized vehicles named "Minecrawlers". These Minecrawlers are removing all of earth's natural resources, and crushing any people and cities that get in their way. Aided by his boss, the possibly insane inventor and scientist Dr. Fluke Hawkins, and a robotic two-legged/four-armed dog named Bones, Kurt must infiltrate each Minecrawler, and fight his way to the pilot, whom he must then kill before returning to Hawkins' in-orbit space station, the Jim Dandy.
Conceived and co-designed by Nick Bruty, MDK was Shiny's first PC game, and was notable for using software rendering, requiring a Pentium or equivalent microprocessor, rather than necessitating any GPU enhancements, despite its large 3D levels and complex polygon-based enemies. As the developers were attempting things never before seen in a PC game, they had to write their own programming language from scratch. Additionally, when in sniper mode, the player has the ability to zoom up to 100x, but the developers chose not to employ any of the standard solutions to pop-up, such as clipping or fogging. They also worked to ensure the game ran at a minimum of 30fps at all times on all machines. The game's original system requirements were a 60MHz Pentium, 16MB of RAM, 17MB of hard drive storage, an SVGA compatible video card, and a Sound Blaster or equivalent sound card; modest specs even by the standards of the time.
MDK received generally positive reviews, with critics praising the gameplay, the level design, the sardonic sense of humor, the game's technical accomplishments and, in particular, the use of sniper mode. The most oft repeated criticisms were that the game was too short and the story was weak. The game was a commercial success, and Interplay approached Bruty to work on a sequel immediately. However, he was already developing Giants: Citizen Kabuto, and so BioWare was hired to develop the game. MDK2 was published for Windows and the Dreamcast in 2000, and for the PlayStation 2 (as MDK 2: Armageddon) in 2001. In 2007, Interplay announced a third game was planned, but it was never made

Having played MDK2 extensively and also having loved it extensively, I was naturally curious to see what the original game looks like since I didn't get a chance to do so back in the day. In short, it does not disappoint, but it does seem a bit underwhelming (especially compared to the sequel). Let's take it from the top.
Graphics wise, well... it's old and it shows, for some reason the texturework and visuals remind me of Star Wars Dark Forces II: Jedi Knight, but for it's age, it has decent 3D modeling and animations. Performance wise, it has trouble without a patch, but luckily there's a very good community patch available (link:
that solves most of the issues in the game, including widescreen. Sound design is pretty good - the music and effects are minimal, but effective.
Gameplay wise, we have a 3rd person shooter with just one weapon (your arm-mounted chaingun, which can be upgraded temporarily to a superchaingun by means of a pickup), some very fun items (World's Smallest Nuclear Bomb <3) and a fairly basic but enjoyable enemy roster. The premise is such: the Earth is being destroyed by aliens using giant minecralwers that literally plough over entire cities in one fell swoop. Your job is to parachute into them and work your up way to Gunta Glutt, the alien leader and take him out before he takes out planet Earth. Every level begins with a parachuting mini-intro and then follows into a series of VERY intense arena firefights and ending with a boss battle.
These firefights are pure 90s shooter joy; if you're not sidestrafing, prioritizing targets and using your items (grenade, decoy, Thumper - a giant damage inflicting hammer- and tornado) smartly, you'll end up a stain on the alien minecrawler floor. Like I said, the best word here is intense; this game is never boring. There are also some short platforming sections and they are done well (something that would be greatly expanded upon in MDK2). The sniper and its various ammo types (homing bullet, mortar, grenade, homing grenade) are satisfying as hell to use and popping headshots is just plain fun. The boss fights (each minecrawler has its own boss) are also fun, but not terribly hard. In my book, the gameplay gets top marks, and it gets even better in MDK2.
I just have to mention the tone and humour as a separate thing of beauty. This title doesn't take itself seriously at all, and while there is very little content compared to MDK2, there are still awesome and hilarous moments. For example, you have campy "chomp" sounds when you pick up health (apple for +10HP or a roast chicken for +50HP), enemies make very exaggerated and silly pain sounds, the boss designs are also very cartoony and hilariously deformed, and, my favourite moment (spoiler),
.
What about the bad, then? Not a lot to hate on, to be honest.
Firstly, the controls take a while to get used to and are a bit of a pain to re-map, but once you do get used to it (I suggest trying MDK2 first and mapping a control scheme similar to that), it's not that bad. You can't really look up, but auto-aim is very well programmed and forgiving enough for it not to be a problem.
The item system and switching ammo types in the sniper are a bit less intuitive than in MDK2; it gets the job done, but it's a bit clumsy.
The main fault of this game, however, is that it's EXTREMELY short. There are only 5 levels and a rather short boss level; you can literally finish the entire thing in about 2-3 hours without rushing it. Since there are no secrets or collectibles, there is also very little replay value other than maybe completing it on hard; the short length also means the story is practically non-existent. It is also fairly expensive at 15€ for such a short and old title, so it's definitely not worth full price. If you see it on sale and have an afternoon to kill, definitely go for it, it's an awesome little title sets the tone well for one of the most amazing 3rd person shooters of the early 2000s, MDK2, which would greatly expand on everything and make me wonder why MDK3 never came out.

Some of my population become xenophilically inclined, realising aliens might have value.  A little while later I enact a policy of fullscale strategic orbital bombardment, in order to allow me to quickly massacre the colonies of another empire that I am at war with, due to not being expressly allowed to simply butcher them and needing to damage them collaterally. The only problems I have encountered are wierd restrictions.  Like mentioned above I can only directly cleanse alien species if I am officially xenophobic.  Why? I can't seem to shake the feeling that I will get crusified on a professional level for praising a game that was originally dispised as much as Hitler himself, but I have to give the game it's due; it's pretty fun for a while.
Not that I didn't try looking for problems with the game mind you, the game has those in spades. That said however, it still manages to be entertaining for a few hours despite those drawbacks.
Firstly, the entire game looks like a unreal tournament 2004 mod. Most of the textures are early xbox 360 levels of detail, the model work is both clunky and ugly to look at and things seem to clip though solid objects often (especially dinosuars). The game also still has optimization issues to this day, consistently dropping frames on a 660 TI on high and even causing some stutter issues on a friends 980. However, dropping the game down to medium settings seems to help with the frame issues, but you shouldn't have to as the textures on high are 360 quality anyhow. The game does have neat water and sunshaft effects though.
The game options menu is very good. You have standard sound sliders, resolution and appect ratio options, texure and lighting quality and even a FOV slider with numbers for those that get motion sick. Both the game controller and keyboiard keys are entirely rebindable, which should be industry standard by now(shocker, it's not). The only real problem I have with the game menus is no colorblind option and that the only AA it has is FXAA, which really doesn't detract from the game since it looks like 2006 barfed up on the textures/models anyhow.
Sound quality is well...passable at best. The guns have no real meat to them when firing and the dinosuars sound run the guantlet from not remotely terrifying to amusingly bad. The placeholder eagle screech over the Pterosaurs for example is downright laughable. Also some creatures lack sound altogether, that giant croc may as well be solid snake for as much sound as he makes. (Also, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ biologist in me needs to point out that crocs are NOT dinosaurs, nor are Pterosaurs. Really wish folks would get that right already.)
The sound track itself is hit or miss as well. Doesn't hurt the game, but it's one of those personal preference things. Your milage may vary if you decide to mute the music.
Lastly, the gameplay. So you have a game thats fairly ugly, sounds meh, poorly optimized, but has good options and acceptable controls. Surely this game must be terrible to play and that is where you would be wrong. Despite all the games harsh drawbacks it still amnages to be an amusing game. The amount of game modes is kinda on the meh side and the larger dinos are a easy target, but everything else from the death matching to team wave play is a blast. At the worst it's a few hours of fun before you uninstall it and never touch it again.
Did I also mention it's cheaper than a whopper Jr? this game goes on sale for a low as 50 cents sometimes and even now on steam it's all of a buck. If you ask me a dollar is worth 5 horus of entertainment the game provides, easily. There is however a micro transaction system in game, but it all seems really cosmetic (IE you can't buy power) so it's not really bothersome.
So should you buy Orion Prelude? Well, that depends. Is a single american dollar worth 3-6 hours of entertainment for you or do you REALLY want to eat soemthing from BK(I suggest you don't because eww gross)? If the answer is yes, then at worst you get some trading cards and entertainment. If no, then I guess you REALLY must like processed half- soy beef right? (BTW I'm presenting you witha false dichotomy here, it's satirical in nature and in no way represents your eating habits, at least I hope you don't eat too much fast food. Especially shitking, ick).
I tentatively endorse and suggest you pick up Orion Prelude. It may be a ugly, semi buggy mess of a game, but it's a fun mess of a game that costs you less than a  bag of chips. I mean honestly, the game can only get better from here right?

A surprisingly good sequel to a classic game series, quite unexpected from Ubisoft to be honest. Just don't expect a cutscene-heavy, "cinematic" RPG, MMX is pure gameplay with a very basic story, but a nice balance between open-world exploration and turn-based combat, tons of dungeons, creatures and powerful items to find.
This is one of those games that gets the character progression just right - you feel really helpless in the beginning, struggling to kill a bunch of wolves without someone dying, and the game stays difficult until the end (on warrior difficulty), but in the end, once your characters have earned their promotions and have got grandmaster ranks, they finally begin to feel powerful, annihilating hordes of monsters with a few spells, which feels really satisfying.
One thing that I didn't like about the combat mechanics was that once you enter melee range there is no way to move around, and no way whatsoever to escape from a bad encounter. Because there is a lot of exploration involved, and because even the starting area contains some creatures that are unbeatable until much later, this results in frequent save/load abuse. Scripted "trapped" chests or doors that cause enemies to spawn behind your back are also quite lame for the same reason, thankfully there are not too many of those.
Only in Chapter 2 but this game is spectacular. Highly recommend picking this up.

After completing Little Inferno, it's a game that I would highly recommend for a tablet / mobile device, but struggle to recommend for PC. The biggest issue I had with the game was the time I spent doing other stuff. The basic mechanics of the main game are buying items from catalogs and burning them in the fireplace. The developers implemented a timed "shipping" mechanic, where once you buy an item, you must wait a certain period of time. In a way, I understand a bit what they were doing, but the last couple catalogs feature items with shipping times well into the 3-4 minute mark, and the final item takes a mind-numbing five minutes to ship. This is inexcusible for a PC game, waiting five minutes for no other reason than waiting. This absolutely drives pacing into the ground as you search for combos.
Speaking of combos, the combos fall into one of three catagories. There are some well thought out combos that, after about five minutes, you will figure out and maybe even smile at the logic. The vast majority of the combos are very easy to solve and you end up wating more for the item to show up than solving the puzzle. There are some combos that, unless you follow the same logic trail the developers did, you will need to look up. This happened about 3 or 4 times to me, with a couple combos I simply got lucky on guessing / happened to get while burning stuff for money.
This is a quite fun time waster, or if you are doing something else like playing a turn-based game online, but they ask 10 dollars, and there's no way I can recommend this as a full-fledged game. For a game this short and this expensive, there should be far less waiting around. Unless the game looks very interesting to you, wait for it to appear in a bundle or on sale and pick it up. I can recommend for 2-5 dollars, depending on interest level, but ten is just too much for a game this short and with this many delays.

So NECROPOLIS: A Diabolical Dungeon Delve... What do I say about you?
First off, I think this is a game where friends are a MUST unless you enjoy a very, very difficult challenge. The combbat is solid enough, yet simplistic in many cases. The allusions to Dark Souls aren't unwarrented yet, anyone who is a hardcore Dark Souls fan will immediately see where the comparisons fall flat.
Controls are just about what you'd expect from a Dark Souls title and yet, its lacking in a few ways. Dodging doesn't quite feel as good in my opinion and there's no counter attack that I could find/or was aware of so parrying isn't an option. The lack of information given to you can also be a little frustrating if you're expecting a Souls experience yet its hardly fair to ding this title for it as so many rogue-lites follow this same pattern of obfuscation and discovery. If that's your jam, you won't be disappointed with Necropolis.
However, the lack of I-frames when you get hit can be a little annoying because that means should you get surrounded, or if you're dealing with a large mob and happen to get knocked back a little thanks to an unlucky hit, the rest of the group is free to pile on as much damage as quickly as possible. A small annoyance but then, for those looking for a challenge? There it is.
The procedural generation seems pretty good. I had to do quite a few runs through before I could beat the game and each time, while each layer of Necropolis did a decent job of adhering to the aesthetic for that specific area, it felt new and different each time. I felt compelled to explore or sometimes to make the painful decision to get the hell out of dodge while I was still alive.
The loot could be improved upon, as I'd like more silly and crazy weapons that make you feel like an absolute badass when you finally get them, but then, what's currently available is diverse enough that I felt free to find a weapon that suited me and I had a good chuckle at some of the weapons I picked up. Don't know if I got unlucky with RNG but I tended to get the same armor time and time again which was a little boring but I still had a lot of fun.
Looking at the hours I put into this game, I'd say the price point was fair. I have some amazing stories that me and my friends still laugh over and we had a genuine good time. What more can you ask?
Overall, I had a BLAST playing this with my friends. The combination of friendly fire and the insanity of the rooms, dealing with the spawns. It was a GREAT multiplayer experience. I will say the distinct lack of boss fights until the very end was a little disappointing but I'd still jump back into this game again in a heartbeat. If you can pester your friends into picking this up with you? You're going to have a great time.
Highly recommended

This game is two things:
- A fun casual game where you save up money to burn things by, well, burning things. Gameplay is simple, but the results are a lot of fun as each object you burn has a different reaction. You can also find specific combos (hinted at cryptically) that give you extra coins and speed-up tokens, lending the game a puzzle-element.
- An unsettling setting and theme, accompanied by an absolutely amazing score and an ending that had me thinking for several days. This is not something I expected when starting this game, and it took me by surprise, and a delightful one indeed.
I would recommend this game to anybody except perhaps for people that are looking for a challenging experience. Little Inferno offers a wide range of emotions, some not seen nearly enough in videogames, and you owe it to yourself to give it a try.
(...maybe not at full price, but that's a decision I'll leave to you)

Alright I don't write reviews often, but this game deserves it. NECROPOLIS has seen a number of bad reviews that quite frankly, are wrong.
I'll start by appealing to one of the game's tags - indie. The game is made by a small group of people, so we should all probably stop comparing it to other games of its genre IE: Darksouls, and start looking at the game itself.
It's not perfect. I'll say that much, but the developers are constantly working on adding content, and trying to appeal to the game's players.
The combat system in the game works like this - should you rush into a room swinging your sword everywhere, you're going to get swarmed, stun-locked, and most likely die. End of story. The game is punishing in this respect, you aren't invincible after taking damage. That means you have to think a little. Survey the room first, find some smaller enemies and take them out, then focus on taking out the larger enemies. There will be a lot of waiting. Waiting for a large enemy to use an attack that leaves them vulernable, or waiting for an opportunity to attack a smaller enemy without being swarmed. You have to find the right time to attack, because much like enemies, you also will be left vulnerable.
Difficulty in the game may vary. If you're willing to take your time and kill enemies one by one, the game is considerably easy. If you get lucky with RNG and obtain decent gear fast, the game can be easy. But unless you're lucky or very cautious, the game can get difficult fast. First off, enemies will swarm you if you panic and aggro too many. Also, you can (and probably will) fall victim to some of the enviroments, whether it be falling of the map or jumping into lava. The enemies also benefit off of the enviroments typically more so than you do. Getting trapped in a room with a spinning laser ball of death is never fun. Some people say the game is too easy, some people say it's just right, it really depends on the player.
I said we should look at this game by itself without comparing it to huge titles such as Dark Souls, well I'm a hypocrite, because that's exactly what I'm about to do. Dark Souls has some multiplayer to it, invading people and summoning people to help in certain areas, but that isn't enough to make me consider it a multiplayer game. you can play through 100% of NECROPOLIS with your friends. Friendly-fire is defaulted to be on (I actually don't know if you can turn it off) so it means that you have to work together rather than rushing groups of enemies with 4 people. This adds strategy. Also, the multiplayer works off of a drop in/out system. A player can enter the game at any point and time, and just as easily leave, which is an amazingly convenient system. Not many games with this style have co op, which is where I tend to have the most fun when gaming.
In my opinion, other than some performance issues the game has been having as of late, the only thing that this game needs is more content. That being said, I can still happily play the game with the amount of content it has, but more variety is always welcomed. And guess what? That is the main focus of the game's development. $30 is a little pricey, but if you have the money to spare, or just wait for the game to go on sale, I think that NECROPOLIS is a great buy. The game itself is good. Not fantastic, not game of the year, it's good. But it has so much potential to become a fantastic game that everyone should play.
My guess is that many of the bad reviews are coming from people who just played huge titles and expect the same from a little indie game like NECROPOLIS. Having played Dark Souls, if you are in it for just the combat, I'd pass on this game. But I'm more of a fan of the roguelike genre, which has been flourishing with new games lately, and this is definitely one of the better ones out there.

Replaying this game on the ps4 made me realise that i should write a review for this game, not because it needs it but because i want to pay my respect to the person that made it, because this game was largely made by a single guy over the course of 4 years.
-The gameplay-
This game is a sidescrolling Beat's em all with some light metroidvania and rpg elements which mean you will learn new moves throughout the game, those moves will allow you not only to fight enemies but also to reach places that you could not reach before.
The controls are responsive and fast, this makes for very fast paced combats with combos reaching sometimes the thousand of hits. It does, however, feel a little bit repetitive like most games of the same genre, the game would have benefited from a little bit more combos.
Sadly the game is also too easy on Normal difficulty, i died only once on the second boss, i would recommend you play on hard from the get-go if you are an affecionado of the genre.
That being said the gameplay is solid, fun and works well for the 13-14ish hours it takes to finish it(20-21 if you complete everything.)
-The presentation-
Dust AET is visually stunning, featuring some of the most beautiful 2D i've ever seen in any games, the animations are also really impressives, fluid and detailed.
The design may not be for everyone with it's anthropomorphic cast of characters but i found them quite charming and it did not bother me in the slightest.
The story is nothing groundbreaking but has the merit of being interesting and fun to follow with some strong moments here and there thanks to the duo of Fidget and Dust.
The music is really good and has a few memorable themes which is quite rare nowaday in video games.
I will also point out that the voice acting is very well done but only available in english.
-Overall-
If you don't mind the repetiveness inherent to the genre then you will find here an amazing game that is well worth the 17$ full price.

In 1997, Shiny Entertainment — the makers of acclaimed hit, Earthworm Jim — set out to create a darker, more violent videogame. Their hard work resulted in the creation of the unofficially titled: Murder, Death Kill.
Officially: MDK.
Much like Earthworm Jim, this game is weird at its core. You play Kurt Hectic, the janitor to famed mad scientist, Dr. Fluke Hawkins. One day, while minding his own business, aliens invade Earth. They drop these enormous strip-mining vehicles on various cities throughout the planet. Hawkins sends Kurt down with his own creation, a strange power suit with a sniper cannon on the helmit, and a ribbon parachute. Throughout the game's six, multi-stage levels, Kurt will shoot and jump his way to completion with the aid of Dr. Hawkins and his other creation, a four-armed, cigar-smoking dog named Bones, and his flying bomber. The game is both violent and humorous, making it an instant cult classic in its time.
Playing this game on Steam is challenging, mostly because it is broken from out the gate. In order to get the game to work properly one must download an unofficial patch (MDK Steam Fan Patch by Alyxx). This patch fixes issues with Direct 3D (such as not loading any objects aside from Kurt, in levels), as well as regains access to the off-the-walls weird music video at the end of the game. The original game was set up for all keyboard controls, but the Steam version allows one to map keys to a more modern-shooter arrangment that makes the game play much better. That said, there are still some moves like weapon and ammo switching, that remain clunky. I would also recommend using the caps lock to toggle the turbo mode to always on. This will ensure that Kurt is always speeding around the enormous levels, and will get rid of any feelings of tedium. Plus, it makes the firefights more engaging.
This game comes recommended with the caveat that you also install the fan patch. This is an old title, so don't expect many graphical bells and whistles. That said, if you were a fan of Earthworm Jim, there are a few nods to that game in the original MDK. Further, if you enjoy violent, and absurd stories, this game will be right up your alley.

VIDEO VERSION:
STORY
Winner of the “Games for Impact” prize at the Game Awards 2016, “That Dragon, Cancer” is a game about developer Ryan Green’s son Joel and his 4-year battle against cancer. From the first minutes, we learn from narration that Joel Green is not like a regular kid at his age, since he can't speak properly at the age of 2. At age 1, Joel was diagnosed with an atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor and developed seven other tumors through the four following years. During the gameplay, we see his improvement through chemotherapy, but things turn dark when doctors bring the news that Joel’s treatment is not curative and other tumors might develop. All in all, we follow the part of the parents who spend sleepless nights and live in a roller coaster of emotions towards a child that will hardly survive. The game’s title is taken from a story told by Ryan and Amy to Joel’s siblings about him being a brave knight that has to fight a powerful dragon named Cancer. In it’s gameplay, you play a mini platformer as Joel the knight and need to avoid the dragon’s constant attacks.
GAMEPLAY
As the story suggests, this is a walk through the lives of Ryan and Amy Green and their struggles while facing their son’s sickness. From time to time the playability will vary from first person, to third person, and even to a short platformer. Gameplay is mostly walking and moving to places, and the interactions are focused on selecting story frames, paintings, cards and certain actions the characters do. It follows a single storyline, so you won't have choices, except for the order of elements you want to see or even if you want to see them. At some points, you can change your “perspective” and jump from character to character and listen to their thoughts and feelings. Though it doesn't give you much choice-making opportunities, this game’s intention is to tell a story that has happened and unfortunately happens to tons of people every day. So if you are expecting an exciting gameplay full of choices that change the story, you should probably reconsider playing this game or opening your mind to this kind of experience.
DESIGN, PRESENTATION AND MUSIC
This game has had some negative reviews, specifically about its design, playability and specific parts of the story, so let’s calm down and chat, shall we? For the design, it is as simple as it can be: the characters and scenery are modeled in a simple 3D texture and characters are faceless, the color palette is simple but changes according to the scene and the characters’ feelings and thoughts. On the first scenes, we can notice black spiky balls and dark trees surrounding the scenery, even contrasting to the rest of it. Those are the representations of cancer, sometimes far from our perspective but always present. On some scenes we see imaginative recreations from the moments the Greens have been through, such as the heavy rain inside the room when the doctors talk to them about the treatment options for the tumor that don't guarantee other tumors won't grow and a wagon ride in the hospital imagined as a car race. As psychology suggests, we all experience things differently, and metaphors can help others to try and understand how we feel and think, so I’ve found the fantasies created relatable to the actual experiences. The soundtrack is very good, specially on touching scenes. But what broke me were the narrations from Ryan and the recordings from when Joel was alive. This is not just a fictional story with good interpretations, it is the real documentary of real people’s lives, so even though I myself don't have kids and don't even plan to, I cried as hard as if it were my actual son that I was hearing screaming and crying in pain.
CONCLUSION
Before we move on to the conclusion, there are a few thing I’d like to address. This game has a very present religious theme, so very often you’ll hear Amy saying just how much she believes in God’s power and His plans for Joel and for their family. Though Christianity is the world’s largest religion, obviously not everyone can relate to their thoughts and world views. I for example had nearly zero reasons to relate to this game at all: I am not a parent, I am not a Christian and the people I know that have had cancer at some point had it diagnosed quick enough to give it proper treatment. But there is something that should probably be louder to people who gave this game a try than just the game’s design, it’s gameplay or even the religious themes. This game is about Empathy. “That Dragon, Cancer” is not about the possibilities of playing, it’s about putting yourself in someone else’s shoes. It’s not about having beautiful graphics, it's about showing that this could happen to anyone. It's not about a God or faith, it's about human hopes and doubts. It’s not about you or me, it's about someone other than us. And, above all, it is not about Ryan or Amy: it's about Joel. This is his story. Unlike games, life sometimes doesn't give you choices. Cancer is not a choice. The treatments available for it are and we must deal with the consequences of the choices we make, at times dealing with stuff we didn't even get a saying in. This story is the unfolding of the choices these parents made trying to save someone's life. A child’s life. The amount of courage necessary to make a game out of such a personal and painful experience is indescribable. For that matter, I must leave my recommendation of this game for anyone looking for something to help them feel empathetic. It is a short game, you can finish it in a couple of hours, but for the personal growth it can bring, I do think it is a priceless experience.

Many games try very hard to quirky or outlandish, be it's Portals pin point precision writing or Borderlands trite characters equating shouting to zaniness. None though seem to quite so effortlessly succeed as Shiny Entertainment.
MDK basically has no writing or characters. It has briefings, announcing "giant mine-crawlers" comically attacking tiny inconsequential British villages (most likely the developers home locations), but aside from that, anything approaching characterization or plot is non existent.
Instead, it uses that vagueness to enhance it's otherworldly feel. This, combined with a juxtaposition of dark cyberpunk imagery and Tommy Tallarico brooding tones working against self-aware buffoonery, gels together to make a wholly unique game unlike any other third person shooter before or after.
The visuals are especially worth bringing up. This game is now 20+ years old. Around it's release (1997) when 3D graphics were still emerging, it's remarkable how good this game looks. Against contemporary peers Tomb Raider, Mario and Zelda, there is really no competition, MDK looked light-years ahead, you only need look at the screenshot to see this.
The game-play also holds up remarkably well. If you're modern gamer wanting button combo's, leveling up or wall-cover based combat though, this is not your game. It's charm lays in it's simplicity.
It's operates very much like a third person Doom. Aiming is automatic, all enemies fire dodge-able projectiles with levels scattered with resources, and similar to Duke3D, usable items.
It has a few sporadic platforming sections, and the rare "figure it out ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" but nothing taxing, acting as a nice diversion from the wide arenas the encompass much of the game. Arenas tend to be full of dozens of enemies at once or varying types, but all are perfectly defeatable simply by avoiding projectile attacks, death never feel cheap.
This is one of the first games in memory with a sniper. It's used rather well. Instead of specifically used for redundant head-shots it has multiple mods of fire with specifically designed sections to take advantage of it, while also remaining optional and useful for arena battles themselves.
Usable items like grenades, a decoy dummy come in very useful in the harder difficulties, typically serving against enemies with large HP pools. Optional Bonus pickup's and the scarce secret area comes in handy, such as the eccentric "groovy" (with a nod to Earthworm Jim) that drops cows from the air.
If I had criticisms it would be the default control layout which is obtuse, and doesn't meld well with it's "tunnel" stage. By and large though, once this is worked around MDK is an incredibly slick third person shooter, never outstaying it's welcome like so many titles today - pointlessly padded. On the downside, it's simplicity lacks the replay of other modern action titles.
MDK is a game designed by English speaking people, with a French music video for an ending, a game where beating the end-boss involves turning a 4 armed dog into a seal, where you are running around as a Dark Knight like character chasing a physically running health pickup screaming like a chimpanzee.
MDK is odd, simple, short and now old as hell, but it works.

The Hotline Miami soundtrack is something I don’t think we’ve seen in the video game genre until now. The soundtrack functions as a mechanic of the game, playing inside Jacket’s head as he crushes in the skulls of his “enemies” like all of our 80’s action heroes dishing out justice as he see fit. This is where Hotline Miami really shines, the soundtrack, one of the only that I listen to outside of a game.
When I first played Hotline Miami it was on its release in late 2012. I was working in a kitchen with a 40 minute drive to work, only to end up making minimum wage. A couple years out of High School and barely able to afford the gas I needed to get to work, I spent the little allowance I had on this game. I was never much into the electronic music scene, and in the early 2010’s there was a small push against in within the music industry in the form of “indie music” in the likes of Mumford and Sons and Sufjan Stevens, and with that push it was also a time of change mentally, expansion of the mind and acts of humanism. I think Hotline was a push back on that progression; the soundtrack poured gasoline on the pseudo-hippie culture of intimacy and friendship and in lighting that fire told us it's okay to be alone. In 2012 I was living a fairly lonely life and it was a psychological challenge for me to change from having all these people in my life to having none, it was perhaps the feeling of alienation of Hotline Miami that called to me at a time when I barely knew anyone, even myself.
I don’t make it a habit to review every game I play, but for the love of the soundtrack itself I felt like I needed to write this. At the risk of sounding like a pretentious jerk, the devs managed to create an absolute masterpiece; a collage of violence and ambience. Hotline Miami redefined what a video game could be to me. All you need do now is ask yourself a simple question.

Artistically, Dust is truly an amazing button-smasher. Oh, no, whooops, RPG-Platformer, what am I saying...
Silly me.
So, yeah, while it feels really (REALLY!) unfortunate to give this game a negative review, I'm going to have to do that, because Dust eventually ends up being, as I just said, a button smasher. Merely and mostly a button-smasher.
And the sad thing about it, is that this is pretty much the only thing about the game that is actually bad, in my opinion. And so, all of Dust's good aspects are going to waste on the final result....
At the very beginning of the game, Dust reminded me of Rayman, and in a good way. Meaning that, it reminded me the glory days of platforming games, or at least that glorious series which had somehow managed to keep some of the first installment's magic in it towards the years.
Dust begins with that magic as well.
It gives you a feeling of an aspiring Disney film.
It has lush and colorful graphics, which seems hand drawn, and seems even more terrific in my opinion with the post-effects turned off, in the so-to-speak 'lower' quality.
It also has a magical soundtrack, combines many sort of genres, catchy and dramatic moments, and it fits the game perfectly.
The different areas of the game are very immersing and seems like there was much though put in their design.
So, really, the developers had prepared a great ground for the actual game. Really incredible atmosphere and environment.
Too bad the game starts to fall short as we reach the actual content.
The plot is nothing special, it isn't too bad but not much good either. It is mostly predictable, it starts alright but then you see it really isn't anything interesting, with the exception of just a few moving moments.
Still, it isn't enough to push you forward AND make you enjoy yourself.
Towards the end, unfortunately, I didn't even care much what the characters were saying, but just kind of wanter to get this over with...
Of course, a game with terrific gameplay doesn't HAVE to have a good story.
But sadly enough Dust won't deliver on this aspect as well.
Dust is mainly a platformer, and therefore its gameplay isn't that complex and you can imagine how it plays out.. Of course, there are some terrific platformers, some mediocre, and some bad ones... Depends on the execution, right?
Well, here the execution didn't go so well to my taste.
The gameplay is basically a simple platforming gameplay, and you'd slowly gain some abilities, and yet it becomes incredibly repetitive and boring, and also somewhat annoying. It isn't even too graceful, as as the game progresses you'd find yourself among more and more HORDES of enemies, and not single enemies. It actually becomes the core of the game pretty quickly. And what will you do then? As I said at the very beginning, you start Smashing Button! Three buttons, smash them with all might. At the very beginning of the game you'll learn the different 'moves' you can do with those buttons but soon enough you wouldn't care, as it doesn't make that much difference. Why, you might ask? Because you wouldn't even see much of these moves. As you amash the attack, jump, and moving buttons, pretty much all at ones, at many times you can't really tell for sure what's going on on your screen. You're just watching Dust jumping from point to point as there are lights and bombings and explosions and hurt enemies faltering anywhere, as even you're sidekick says once in the game: "Seriously, have you seen the screen? He goes VOOSHWOOSHSHWOOSHVOOSH". And that's an understatement.
Last but not least, let's not forget that's a RPG-Platformer. Of course. The devs tried to add some RPG elements, but personally I found them very weak and not integrated to the game so well.
Yes, there are side-quests, there are exp points, leveling up, so-to-speak abilities to improve, some 'crafting', some stats, some clothes which would raise those stats....
All these features just felt very out of place to me, they weren't that interesting or crucial to the game, and didn't add much challange to Dust, which I completed on Normal with all sidequests and most achievements done, and pretty much with ease.
I can't say this is a BAD game. It does have magic in it, and many good aspects. But only halfway through the game I just felt it was more of an annoyance to me than fun. And that definitely shouldn't be that way, so, no, I wouldn't really recommend on this one.
Unless smashing-buttons aimlessly and watching your screen goes VOOSHWOOSHVOOSH is you're thing, of course.

Indie Game Mini-Review: That Dragon, Cancer.
I've heard of this title months ago but it was brought to my attention again after it won the Games for Impact Award at the 2016 Game Awards so of course I had to get it... and oh man was I wrecked.
You play the parents of little Joel who is diagnosed with terminal cancer. Through their eyes, you experience all the different coping mechanisms they go through as Joel slowly fades away. To say this game is depressing is an understatement. It tricks you into thinking you can fix an issue like this if you just solve the puzzle or find the right solution only to be hit with the harsh realities of life and death. I imagine this is how parents of sick children feel. There is no "win" condition to "beat" this game and that's not the point. The goal is to make you feel every ounce of helplessness and despair as a loved one suffers and die. You WILL cry during this game. The moment came for me when the game FORCED me to listen to Joel cry in pain and I had to hear the father plead with Joel not to bang his head on the cradle bars because there was nothing else he (and by extension, me) could do. 😢
Can I recommend it? Objectively speaking, it's not a good game. It's more interactive novel than game (and even the "interactive" sections aren't true choices), the controls and interface needs work and it moves too slow. However, this didn't win best game... it won best game for impact which was set up for titles that deal with important social issues and on that metric That Dragon, Cancer shines. No other game will make you experience grief and mourning nor make you aware of the effects of cancer to a family. On that immersive trait alone, I can highly recommend it... just be sure to have tissue nearby. :(
