I'm assuming most of the reviews here are from early access, here's one from someone who did not play early access and has also not played any previous games in the series.
This game is very good.  It's expansive, challenging but not unfair, and there's a good amount of character and party customization.  It's the most RPG-y RPG I've played in a long time.
You'll travel the open world, come across riddles, puzzles, enemies and dungeons - some of which will be too high level for you.   There is no level scaling and the world is crafted in a way that you're going to want to backtrack often to try and kill that boss you found who one shot you 10 hours earlier.  And that's awesome.  You're going to be battling your way through dungeons, barely surviving by the skin of your teeth and have to make runs back to town (actual runs, no instant click travel here) to restock on supplies so that you can continue.  And that's awesome.
It's not going to be for everyone but this is a really solid, lengthy and replayable RPG with lots of substance that's built on its RPG systems and its gameplay rather than a story or dialogue choices or any of the usual modern stuff.
The only con is performance.  Performance is poor in some places, and loading times especially are poor.  This is exacerbated by the fact that the game freezes in the background, meaning you have to sit through the 30 second-1 minute load screens.  This can get very annoying because you will often be making trips back and forth to town and there's a loading screen each time.  The game also doesn't exactly look amazing and the dialogue and story are generic and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  But from what I understand this is a game made by a small team mostly as a proof of concept to get this series back up and running, and it did what it set out to achieve and then some.

Might and Magic Legacy goes back to the days of RPG youth putting you into a first person perspective, grid and turn based combat with puzzles, riddles, exploration, sidequests, lore and combat all aplenty.
The game lasts in the ballpark of 40-50 hours and I enjoyed it the whole way through. You create your party from 4 races with 3 class options for each race, any combination is probably viable on the normal difficulty (Adventurer) however if you play on the warrior difficulty you will want to look into optimizing your party a bit. I completed the game on the warrior difficulty but started over about 10 hours in and remade the party.
Combat can be difficult the whole way through the game depending on how much side quest stuff you do, I did virtually everything the game had to offer and the final fight was still a bit of a challenge. If fighting against the random number generator is not your thing this game may not be to your liking - I could have a party member go from full health and shielded to dead in 1 combat round from bad dice rolls.
There are some bugs still in the game as of the time of writing this (Graphical slowdown issues at points, Had the last boss bug out during the fight on me to name a few) but they are minor and didn't detract from my opinon of the game much.
All in all this is a fantastic RPG and anyone itching to explore a new world, loves turn based combat and wants to actually have to use your brain on occasion I highly recommend the game to.

Damn, this game gave me a headache. Should I recommend it or not? Is it, in the end, a good or a bad game?
Well it is both. You're welcome. ;)
In fact, MMX is a great old-school RPG, and some might hate it. If you don't like turn-based games, forget about it right away. It will appeal mostly to people who started playing computer games in the 80's and 90's. This said, this category of gamers will regret going back to another feature that was typical of the era: infinite loading times. This is, by far, the most annoying thing in this great game. You'll have to suffer long loadings every two minutes, because it makes you travel a lot, and reload saved games a lot. It is, apparently, very badly programed and suffers from huge stuttering issues on any machine. It runs "smoother" on 64-bit systems but doesn't really take advantage of huge amounts of memory as it could. Maybe it emulates floppy disks, I don't know. Let's call it a feature. Oh, and the world looks more like a maze than like an open world, making it difficult to find your way, even if you've discovered every square inch of land (or sea). If you were used to rushing from west to east in a matter of seconds in the old MM series (by tapping arrow keys madly, like Stakanov), you'll be disappointed by how long it takes to travel. It expands the world size artificially, but it works eventually.
Now that's all for the bad stuff.
Good things about this game? Mainly all the rest. First thing first, it is DIFFICULT. You'll spend hours trying to find the few roads/places where you're safe enough to gain some experience while avoiding dying every minute. Then you'll come back to places that were previously unaccessible to your party and kick some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Or not, and die again. And again. More often than in the old games, except maybe MM6 which was very open and very difficult too.
You'll soon discover that you have to make careful choices in your skills, for every character in the party. At first, you'll also be poor as hell, which means that you'll have a hard time training your party while in the meantime healing it, buying new stuff and potions, identifying loot, etc. And then, half way from the end, you'll have not to care about money anymore since you'll have a good 100 k that will never be spent.
But don't be fooled: money is one of your problems at first, but not the only one. Money will not buy you extraordinary items that can save your♥♥♥♥♥♥ It will help, but it is not the solution to all your problems. Exploration is much more rewarding than shopping, and as soon as two of your party members will be equiped with fine stuff, things will get easier. A few relics later and you'll be able to deal enough damage to cyclops. Yeeha!
Then, there's magic. Remember the title, Might & Magic? Right, you'll need both. All the time. You'll need healing all the time, and above all, good warding spells. With good loot and a good spellcasting timing, you can take on almost any mob - if you're lucky. Yes, luck counts a lot. On the good side, it allows you to do critical damage. On the bad side, so it does for monsters. So you might litteraly obliterate a monster to 10% of its health, then it will do a beautiful critical strike and kill two party members in one blow. And they will not benefit from the experience gained from the fight...
Now, should you reload or deal with it and visit a temple ASAP? It's all up to you. You can try again until only your party makes huge amounts of damage, or play fair. You can think hard about a specific puzzle's logic and finally understand how it works, or you can try any combination until the damn chest opens. You can take notes (real notes, on paper) or look for answers on the internet. Play fair and suffer a lot or play safe and... suffer a lot, but a bit less.
This game rewards people who like exploring, and who are willing to come back to the same place they died a dozen times before just to see if now, it might be ok. And yes! It opens a new area. Now I can die again! Oh God, now I remember how loud I yelled at my computer in 1994, and why. And I also remember why I kept on playing. Damn, it's good.
BUT PLEASE DO SOMETHING ABOUT THE LOADING TIMES.

This really isn't much of a game, but more of a tech demo for the technical geeks. This little gem includes most elements found in its complete game, Half-Life 2. Originally planned as a section of the Highway 17 chapter of Half-Life 2, this unused concept was scrapped, possibly due to time constraints or maybe based upon the fact that this game is a prototype all on its own.
This demo details various visual and graphic capabilities that are found in that said complete game. All the while, this ''game'' just shows how immensely strong the Source engine is, considering it was pretty new for its time back in 2004, and how it would become the most essential game engine to date, what with various Valve and 3rd party games being built on top of this incredible engine. The most clear concept that is shown off is the high dynamic range lightning that is now most commonly used in nearly all of Valve's games.
There isn't much of a story or a narrative in this demo, you're none other than Gordon Freeman, who is stranded on a lost coastal cliff, (The clue is in the title.) that you must climb up to destroy a Combine artillery launcher in a monastery, which is rebelling and attacking a nearby town. Though this is just one massive chunk of a technological demonstration, it has several story elements that didn't make the cut in the final game. As a result, this level received a good response from the community, as if the fans haven't been missing anything at all.
While I would say, this game is very interesting if you love to dig down and unearth various unused game content and maybe discover a little of the history that had been closed.

I'm going to start with the obvious: this game is not the Neverhood, and if you go into it wearing your rose-coloured glasses and expecting it to be exactly the same you will be disappointed.
Now that's over with, I can say that I very much enjoyed Armikrog.
Controls/gameplay:
It's a standard point-and-click, pretty self explanatory. The mechanic of switching between Tommynaut and Beak-Beak is really neat, as was being able to feed Beak-Beak the seeds to make him fly. It would have been interesting to see some other types of seeds, perhaps one that makes him swim, and I feel the mechanic was a little bit under utilised. For me the game is still buggy. Tommynaut would get stuck on things or randomly stop moving, and sound effects and voice lines would sometimes not play. These bugs aren't exactly game breaking, but they are a bit annoying.
Puzzles:
The puzzles were pretty standard and not too difficult or too easy. There were some early puzzles (push puzzles) where I found it was way too easy to render the puzzle unsolvable and have to reload a save. However, this was an isolated incident. I would have liked to see a bit more variety in the puzzles though.
Story:
The story was interesting enough, though I feel it was a bit rushed. It would have been beneficial to have the story be more fleshed out. I didn't really have any feelings towards Mother, Father, or P. I know I've said you shouldn't expect this game to be like Neverhood, but who could forget the discs you collected to watch Willie Trombone explain the story in charming 2D claymation. I really think the story is where this game most suffers. We don't get to see the personalities of any characters aside from Tommynaut and Beak-Beak. The events surrounding Numnaut and Vognaut should have been given more attention. As a villain Vognaut feels very cheap, his motivation is paper thin at best.
Visuals:
The visuals are where Armikrog really shines. I went into this game hoping for stunning visuals, as I absolutely love rough claymation, and I was not disappointed. The incorperation of other materials, such as fur and paper, only add to the charm.
Overall:
To me it feel as though the game was rushed. Maybe it's because they didn't have the support of another studio (remember, Neverhood was released under DreamWorks), maybe they were just feeling the pressure of having to please the kickstarter crowd. I honestly don't know. But, I do think the game would have benefitted from a few more months development time.
Despite its flaws I still list Armikrog as one of my recommended games, with a few conditions. If you haven't played Neverhood, play Armikrog first. If you have played Neverhood and are using that as a base for your expectations, don't play Armikrog.

When I was a little girl, The Neverhood was, and still is, one of my all time favorite games, to the point where I even found a way to play it still on Windows 10 this past year. With that in mind, I was ecstatic when hearing about the news of a "spiritual successor" to the game. However, the game came out, and when I finally got around to being able to buy it, I was disheartened to say the least at seeing the reviews. I mean, 90% negative? Surely something had to be wrong. I thought to myself, "Clearly something is just not right here, clearly these people missed something or were looking too hard". However, I can say now without a doubt, sadly, that they were right.
It's downright depressing how upset I am. I waited 20 years for something to do justice to the memory of The Neverhood, and was instead handed this game. Now, to be fair, and give credit where credit is due, it's one of the most gorgeous looking games I've ever played. It is so seriously well produced that it's insane, and makes me upset it isn't just a short film, because my god, the visuals are amazing and you can tell some seriously talented artists worked on creating this world, but that's the thing, it's not a "world" as much as it is just a bunch of small, random buildings with some of the single most unintuative, infuriating "puzzles" to ever grace a puzzle adventure game. I am not even being facetious about this, believe me. Like I said, seeing the reviews, I thought "No, this can't be right" but no, they were totally right. Everything about this is, aside from the visuals, is so sub par it broke my heart.
The music isn't anywhere as memorable, the "plot" is nearly nonexistent, and told to you in really cool looking story scenes in a dialogue you can't understand so you're sort of just grasping at straws to make a coherent story out of it, the characters are pretty plain and uninspired with no real personality behind them and the gameplay, oh god, it's just sad. The game works (at least when I finally played it across this last summer after it's been properly patched and updated, and also thankfully dropped down to a 10 dollar price ticket) totally fine, but it's so poorly conceived puzzle wise that it just makes you mad more than anything else that somebody thought these were acceptable puzzles.
I usually don't harp on things like this, but man, I was so excited for this, I'd waited so long for a Neverhood successor, and then to get this game, it just....it really did break my heart in two. I can't even begin to explain how depressed I am about how this game let me down in so many ways. I wanted to like it. I even thought some of the stuff in the game was cool and interesting at points, but on the whole, I just cannot recommend this title because it frankly is just boring and felt put together for the sake of putting something together to cash in on the memory of what was a great PC adventure title back in the day. All that being said, I would like to say that I'd be very curious to see if the people behind it were to make something else, even in the same style, how that might fare with this as a learning curve, because I think they have potential, it just wasn't with this title.
Armikrog is labeled an puzzle game, sure, but the only thing I found puzzling was how this managed to get published in the state that it's in.

A lot of fantastic games came out in 2016, but ABZU is definitely one of the best. Having loved Journey, I went in with high expectations... only to have those expectations absolutely smashed in the face of a simple, but beautiful game. Where Journey was a quiet journey of self-reflection, ABZU is busy and joyful, absolutely teeming with life, to the point where the quieter parts are almost haunting. (Most people have a very similar relationship with the ocean - equal parts fascination and dread - and the game captures this feeling perfectly in its atmosphere. Diving deep is scary, but always worth it.)
Like Journey, ABZU tells its story mostly through murals, leaving the player to piece together what happened to lead the story to this point. Despite this, there's a real sense of connection and emotion. There were several moments when I actually cried out in pure glee, and moments when I felt like my stomach was made of lead. And after finishing, I immediately replayed it, looking for things I'd missed the first time.
I couldn't possibly recommend this game more.

The graphics are very nice, there is some humor and a decent but short story, and burning things in the fireplace is actually quite fun for a while. But, the fun wears off fairly quickly. I take it that is the point since the game is supposedly a commentary on the free to play model which involves a lot of clicking and waiting. There are waits as the items that you bought are delivered, sometimes up to a minute or two. If it was just burning things in the fireplace the allure might have held on a little bit longer, but the waits do become irritating.
Overall, interesting game to get if you can get it on sale. Don't expect to be able to replay it or get more than a 5-10 hours worth of entertainment out of it though.

Summary:
You're an adventurer delving into Necropolis, searching for a mystical amulet while surviving the various denizens and traps the dungeon has to offer. Look for potions, food, weapons, and armor anything to survive in this extremely hostile enviroment and remember: Watch your back! If you die you're dead for good!
Classes and Customization:
So far there is only ONE class and it can be customizeable though the loot you find along your jouney though the dungeon and depending if RNGesus will on your side. You can even change the color of your adventurer too though color palets you can buy from merchants.
Gameplay:
The gameplay of Necropolis is much like Dark Souls, roll and backstep to doge your enemies attacks while timing your attacks to defeat your enemie(s). Each weapon has it's own combo attacks and movesets ranging from Shortswords, Longswords, Greatswords, Maces, Crossbows, and so fourth each weapon catagory has weapon tiers ranging from tier 1 to tier 4 as the highest possible rareity and can be found though merchants, chests, or enemies that you've defeated. Enemies that you've defeated will drop valuable resources(and currency) for you to make food, potions, and bombs provided that you've bought the blueprint from one of the merchants.
Enviroments:
Currently in Necropolis there are 5 biomes:  Dungeon, Swamp, Sewer, Anamatron Forge, and Skyland(?). Each enviroment is procedurely generated meaning that each playthough is different so in one playthough there may be a nice "Bigboy" chest the next there could be a anamatron ape wanting to play football with your corpse.
The Deneziens of Necropolis:
There is quite a large amount of enemy variety in Necropolis and each have their own deadly attacks and surprises. Many of them can call for reinforcements and some and punt you off a cliff if you're unfortunate enough to be standing near a ledge. Some can teleport behind you and surprise you while your in the thick of it and others will wait till you're close enought for them to anbush you while you least expect it.
Overall rating:
With a little over 10.5 hours in this is one of the funnest Rogue-Like games I've played. I've never really liked these types of games personally but for Necropolis I'll make an exception. On top of that, the developers are listening to our feedback and in the coming months there will be A.I improvements, a new class, and new enemies to fight. Now I don't think there is enough content here for a $30 asking price more like around $20-25 until they add more content that is.
Now as for my recommendation for Necropolis it's hard to say honestly. There isn't much content but the gameplay itself is a awesome experince especially with friends so I'll have to say "No" for right now. In the coming months more content will be added and more after the coming content update. By then the Winter Sale will be around the corner and you can get this 25-50% off that in my opinion will be the best time to pick it up.
My overall score for NECROPOLIS - 4.0/5

Recomending a game is all about the value-proposition. Do you get a sufficient amount of enjoyment for what you pay? I payed 50 cents for currently 30 hours of game. That's a 60 hour per value ratio. 60 hours per dollar is equivalent to 3600 hours in your standard $60 AAA game. Very few people spend 360 hours on a game, much less 3600. I am completely satisfied with my purchase. Even if I don't play another hour of this game, the value of my 50 cents is apparent.

This game has some potential, but the irritating design choices overwhelm that potential in my mind.
First off, "open world" this game is not.  You have exactly one direction you can go through the first town, you can't even leave town without finishing a railroad quest, unless I missed something.  And even after leaving your world is made up of "you can go to X different dungeons, but X-1 of them will kill you instantly" so you really just have the illusion of choice.  Maybe it opens up past the first region, but if you have to get that far in to a game for it to be open world, it isn't.
This railroading leads to the biggest issue I have compared to the old games, party composition.  I'm sure some dedicated players will be able to prove me wrong but I honestly don't feel like most party combinations will be viable in this game because of the mission you have to do before leaving town.  In the old games you could run a full ranged party and soften things up enough before they get to you if you were willing to accept that sometimes you don't soften them up enough and you get stomped.  This game doesn't seem to make that an option since there is no way to skip the first dungeon and it railroads you in to melees without the chance for an opening volley.  And that's not even considering the spells you have to run if you want to be able to explore everything.  Don't have a good coverage of the spell schools?  Prepare to miss a lot or use a guide.
Even with these issues aside the mechanics just don't feel like they're there.  Outside of your weapons skills skill increases just don't seem to do much. For instance, armor skills reduce your penalty to wear armor, so if you've already negated the penalty it's just a waste of a point to put them there until you find the trainer or better armor. Unlike the old games you can't increase skills past a certain point without finding a trainer, so you end up maxing out your barbarian's mace and two-hander skills and then just throwing points into other things at random, or saving them until you can find the trainers, making your progression slam in to a wall.  Battles are just slug fests with both sides having what feels like high chances to block or dodge, which makes poison especially irritating since there's no, apparent, way to resist it and you can go three turns without anybody hitting someone if you're unlucky.  Any sort of incapacitation keeps that character from gaining XP, yes, even stun, so you find yourself stalling a battle so your tank will wake up and gain XP from the kill, only for the mage to get stunned and you to have to wait again.
Overall there are just too many little issues that build up to make this game not fun, and there are too many games out there to waste time on one that's frustrating and not fun.  I feel bad for Limbic but hopefully this game got enough attention that Ubisoft will get someone that knows what they're doing, and has at least played a Might and Magic game before, for another attempt, because this could have been good.

A Welcome Return To Old School RPG Gaming
For the tl;dr crowd:
Pros:
* Really truly does recapture the feeling of old school Might & Magic games, particularly the World of Xeen games (which was what this was patterned after)
* Tough but fair
* Strategic combat
Cons:
* Optimization issues
* Requires UPlay (It's Ubisoft, no way around UPlay, unfortunately)
Now for the long winded review:
When I first heard about this game I was first of all shocked, as it had been so long since a core Might & Magic game had been released (I bet there is a contingent of people that prior to the release of this game though Heroes of Might & Magic was the core series, rather than the spinoff it is) that I just assumed the series was dead and buried.  I was both excited and a bit scared.  Excited because holy smokes a new core Might & Magic game!  Scared because it was being made by a developer I didn't really know and that had, to the best of my knowledge, no prior experience making an old school RPG like this.  Would they be able to recapture the Might & Magic feeling?  Would they get the mechanics right?  Would they try to modernize it too much?
After reading up on the team and following their blog for a bit, it became apparent that these people were a fan of the games and genuinely passionate about making an old school RPG.  They also revealed that they were patterning this game after World of Xeen (M&M 4 & 5), going with turn-based and grid-based, rather than free movement and real-time, like M&M 6-9.  While I enjoyed M&M 6-8 quite a bit, 9 not so much, I was also a huge fan of the World of Xeen games and was happy with this decision, so I decided to pull the trigger and get this.
I can now happily say that I chose wisely.  This game has exceeded my expectations.  While the game isn't exactly pushing graphical boundaries and there are some jarringly low res models and textures mixed in, the game is plenty pretty enough for my tastes and it has a certain charm to it.  I suspect Ubisoft didn't exactly give Limbic a massive budget to work with, so I wasn't expecting The Witcher 2 levels of eye candy.  Much more importantly, this is an honest to goodness old school Might & Magic game.  The setting and story follow the Heroes of Might & Magic games timeline rather than M&M 9, but mechanically they really did a great job of recreating the World of Xeen gameplay.
There are 12 classes among 4 races to choose from (3 per race) filling the roles of fighters, casters, and various hybrids in between.  The game doesn't hold your hand and you learn on the job, which may be a turn off for some gamers, but is very welcome in my book.  Certain class combinations will work better than other, and it's certainly possible to build a party that's going to get stomped in the game, but there is room for a variety of different viable combination.  Balanced parties (a mix of warrior and mage types) will naturally work the best, as they usually do in RPGs, but it's possible to go mage-heavy (though you will burn through a lot of mana potions) or warrior-heavy and still succeed.
The game is quite challenging, but not cheap.  There are 2 difficulty settings:  Adventurer and Warrior, corresponding to Normal and Hard respectively, though, compared to the average game of these days, they're more like Hard and Very Hard.  This game will kick your behind and you will die.  There is no sleepwalking through fights except for the most basic of weak enemies.  If you try to sleepwalk on simply brute force your way (even with a warrior-heavy party) through battles you will get destroyed.  You have to use your head to survive.  The game constantly puts you into confrontations where you are surviving by your wits and the skin of your teeth, and that's on Adventurer difficulty.  Warrior difficulty is straight up punishing, and I love it!
There is a good bit of strategy in using your various spells and abilities to protect yourself, buff your allies, debuff enemies, debilitate them, and deal damage.  Plus the grid-based movement adds another layer of tactics, making for a chess-like game of maneuvering where you try to lure ranged enemies into melee without getting pelted by arrows and spells while advancing on them, or getting as many "free" volleys of arrows on melee enemies before they close to melee, all while being mindful of the terrain to position yourself in a spot to prevent being flanked or surrounded.  It's a well thought out system that forces you to use all the skills at your disposal.  It can seem overwhelming when you're caught off guard and a group of enemies creeps up behind you while other enemies close in from the front and you're caught in a vice in a seemingly hopeless battle, frantically trying to keep your party members alive while trying to take out key enemies before they can demolish you.  But when you survive a battle like that, it's that much more satisfying, so much better than mindlessly steamrolling through trash mobs like in so many RPGs.
In conclusion, Might & Magic is a throwback to the RPGs of the 80s and the 90s, with much of the good and the bad that comes with that.  It's a wonderful nostalgia ride and Limbic did a terrific job of delivering an authentic old school RPG experience.  It's thoroughly challenging and quite satisfying.  If you're looking for an old-school turn-based RPG romp, look no further.

I'm going to state up front that this game is carried by its aesthetic and presentation. It brought me the good type of nostalgia... not a cash-in or an appeal to a sense of reclaiming something specific from my childhood. These forms of nostalgic entertainment are typically simple, and amount to glorified references to an older piece of media that brings you to a certain age. Armikrog bears very little, if any resemblence to anything from my memories. It feels like a lost episode of a pilot that aired one saturday morning, at 5 AM, feeling just a little off; but with all the pieces seeming to fit into place. It's more a nostalgia for a feeling, a time, or a place that the art style and characters capture wonderfully, but is equally as hard to place. That being said, I would have preferred if this was the satam cartoon format that it was presented in.
The gameplay is decent, only had 1 or 2 bugs while piloting Tommynaut(bad name)'s totally rad shapeshifting dog sidekick, and it's standard or below-average point n' click fare. It fell into a trap which keeps me a little distant from the genre, however, and that's difficulty vs accessibility. With this type of game falling into relative obscurity, it still is one of the easier genres to produce, and therefore it has more creative individuals drawn to it, as it can be designed and released for fans of the niche. And this is a good thing. What almost every one I've personally played does though is fail to properly accomodate modern audiences while simultaneously utilizing GOOD difficulty.
An example of the above is in the last big puzzle of Armikrog, and countless other point n' click last puzzles. The subtlety at recognizing which are the correct keys really comes down to trial and error, which is difficulty by way of obscurity. Scrounging the details, while partially signalled, still becomes more tedious than it is even difficult. Having only really played contemporary adventure games, I can't be the judge of older materials, the oldest I've played dates back to the late 90s as the genre was starting to fade. Broken Age is another notable offender, with similar backgrounds albeit with a larger budget.
Several puzzles are simply too easy, or are entirely guesswork to properly solve, even if unintentionally. They make any sort of context clue useless by being unneeded or unhelpful. Some were rewarding, but a large amount felt filler-ish. One appreciated component is that the game was structured in a progression that was mostly modern-influenced, I believe. It required only a little backtracking and inventory management, which I believe eased the process between different point n' clicks out there.
But it's a game that made me think, more than others. Not because of its content but because of the surrounding details, the feeling, and the fantastic aesthetic. For this reason, I reccommend it, and to be quite fair to the game, claymation is such a rare thing any more, I would have purchased this even if it was unplayable to help support a dying form of animation. If you're expecting revolutionary point n' click gameplay, look elsewhere(and tell me where to look myself), but if you want to relive a moment from your younger days that may not even have existed, I highly reccommend this game.

The 4x genre has been long overdue for a renaissance, and it couldn't be more fitting that Paradox put it into motion. Long known as the father studio of Grand Strategy, the numerous systems and mechanics at work in those games often made one think of how they would work outside of historical fiction. Now, we finally know, and the result is an experience that is incredible in both form and function.
It must have taken a lot of courage for Paradox to try their hand at a 4x game as it's not the genre they know best. It's clear that they had to leave their comfort zone to make this game, but they did so with a level of elegance and grace that speaks volumes to their skill and dedication to making damn good games.  Stellaris is just that, a damn good game.
The artwork of Stellaris pays tribute to longstanding Sci-fi behemoths such as Eve and Endless Space. It is clean, yet abstract just like space itself. Playing gives one a sense of whimsical fantasy laced with the Austere beauty of precision you'd expect from an exacting and scientific game. The result is artwork that is both beautiful enough to be admired, yet  clean enough to prevent sensory overload. Stellaris is simply beautiful to behold.
As for music, there's hardly a moment where the pacing doesn't fit perfectly with what happens in game. One would think this is entirely the kind of music you'd play if you were on a ship, in interstellar space. It's a cross between modern sophistication and classical sensibility. Clearly, the art and music team worked very closely, and the results show.
Gameplay is the heart of any game, and it's something Paradox has long been masterful at delivering. Here, they took bold steps to try their hand at systems they don't have much experience with while blending them with those that they do. In the end, the combination of these systems proves to be more of a match made in heaven than anybody could have predicted. There are some flaws, rough edges, and missing pieces, but as a 1.0 game, the foundation is hands down the best Paradox, and the genre have yet put out. Given Paradox's track record, within one year this game will have more features than the next two 4x games combined. Already, it proves to be a perfect blend of two similar, yet distinct genres.
For those unfamiliar, you will play in real time managing a fledgling empire. You can colonize planets and configure them for specific types of production. You can build fleets of ships and wage wars, or you can diplomatically isolate enemies while strengthening alliances. Hire leaders to manage your affairs from afar, and explore the frontiers of the galaxy to uncover secrets, technology and unfathomable dangers. For the first time in a 4x game, exploration is both fun and integral. The blending of strategy and RPG like elements means you will feel completely immersed in the lore of the galaxy.
I simply can't speak highly enough about this game. As is, it is perfectly playable and utterly refreshing. As a longtime Paradox fan, I am more excited about the future of this game than I was about its release. There is no doubt in my mind that this will be the definitive space game if it isn't already. Please buy to show your support for Paradox. They aim to do one thing: Make damn good games.

Little Inferno is one strange beast of a game. Upon startup, the game immediately presents nothing but a fireplace, and tasks players with simply burning the few letters they have with them. Immediately afterward, a catalog is sent, and the rest of the game is spent purchasing items and setting them aflame, watching the strange animations each item has. My first reaction, upon realizing what the game had in store for me, was "They made a whole game out of this?"
The humorous thing about this game, though, is that it WANTS you to feel that way. In fact, it encourages it by making you wait long, painful periods of time - upwards of a couple minutes - for your new kindling to arrive. And yet, for whatever reason, I found myself enjoying the experience. It was strangely appealing, setting things ablaze, and I wanted to see what would come of my neighbor, who continuously sent me letters. So I kept playing for 3 hours straight.
In the end, the game throws a massive twist on you. I don't want to spoil too much, but let's just say that I was completely thrown for a loop and felt like quite a fool for having spent such a long time playing the game. This isn't a criticism to Little Inferno; rather, this is the highest praise the game could achieve, because it is exactly what the developers sought to accomplish.
A couple of days after playing Little Inferno, I can't help but reflect on it fondly and reminisce. A remarkable work of satire, I truly believe this game will be remembered for all time as one of the most humorously self-aware experiences this medium has ever created. Well done, Tomorrow Corp.

Picked this game up on a sale for 50 cents. Haven't tried the PvP modes, but right now I've sunk about 30 hours into the PvE wave mode. Sure the bots are absolutely terrible, the graphics aren't at Crytek levels, and it gets fairly repetitive, but I've enjoyed all 30 hours. The survival mode is fairly simple: defend a generator for three waves, move to capture an outpost somewhere on the map, repeat twice, then finish with a final tenth wave. The waves of small enemies, ground and airborne, are accompanied by a few very large, very strong dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurs and Stegosaurs. The game can be very challenging or very easy depending on the settings. A personal favorite of mine is to turn the dino health down and spawn rate up to dramatically increase the size of the wave.
Recomending a game is all about the value-proposition. Do you get a sufficient amount of enjoyment for what you pay? I payed 50 cents for currently 30 hours of game. That's a 60 hour per value ratio. 60 hours per dollar is equivalent to 3600 hours in your standard $60 AAA game. Very few people spend 360 hours on a game, much less 3600. I am completely satisfied with my purchase. Even if I don't play another hour of this game, the value of my 50 cents is apparent.

There is something really really special about Steam. You know what it is? It's social part.
When I was just a student and couldn't afford to buy games and I was pirating them, it was kinda hard to track and to remember about every game you wanted to play. But still, it wasn't a good solution, because all these games weren't at one single place and it still was kinda uncomfortable and one way or another, but I started to forget about games I wanted to play at some point.
Now I have everything that I need here, on Steam. And the most important part - communicating with other players. Some of them can be really helpful and remind me of games I wanted to play and never had a chance, or simply forgot, because of my unorganized past. Right now, I have another problem, even having my own library, it's so huge already, that I need a lot of time to categorize every game. So, that's how talking to other players really help.
That was a little interlude about how I was reminded about Hotline Miami. I was speaking to a guy, who have hundreds of hours on this game and also creating levels for its sequel. We never spoke about the game itself, but I really felt like a dumb, calling myself a gamer and never finishing Hotline Miami - amazing, brilliant, unique game, that blew millions of gamers minds in 2012.
Hotline Miami is a masterpiece. I am not afraid to call it this way, because I know it for sure. What do you call a masterpiece? A well-made product, which combines amazing interesting gameplay, unique and inexpressible atmosphere, astonishing WOW-effect driving soundtrack, colourful characters with its own story and charisma, intriguing plot with twists and cliffhangers, mind-blowing graphics, special visual style and possibility to replay. So,HM has everything listed above, maybe except mind blowing graphics, but to be honest, this is not that type of game, where you want to care about this.
Sets in alternative 1989 Miami, this game provides you an interesting thrilling story, about a mysterious guy, who keeps on getting messages with new contracts on his answering machine. First levels you will be getting in a mood of the game, trying to understand the whole mechanics and how everything works in there. The moment you will already fall in love with game, you will begin to understand, that the whole game and story is not only about a random person, killing others for money as a mercenary, it’s something bigger. But, no spoilers ahead, you gotta see and feel everything by yourself.
For a new players, game can seem ridiculously difficult, but it’s only for the first few levels and the moment you’ll understand how it works you will be enjoying it for a long long time. This game can be challenging at some levels and you can be mad af on yourself, especially when you are trying to finish the level with an impossible scenario and outnumbered enemies for 30 minutes and then you are distracted by the phone call and the last guy on the floor kills you. BANG! You are dead and have to start all over again! So annoying. The whole game is about quick actions and good reactions, one shot/hit - you are dead, so you always have to be first. And one quick tip - you will start to hate doors after this game so much! The whole door mechanics in the game is just insane and can make you lose your mind. But, when you’ll realize how it works, you’ll start to use it in a tactical way, that can lead you to the win easily.
So, to make a long story short and to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:
+ Love action games
+ Love fast paced games
+ Want to experience something new and unique. Even now, in 2017, game looks fresh, amazing and really special with its own style and flow.
+ Really love challenging games, I wouldn’t say that this game is either hard or difficult, but some levels can be really frustrating and make you wanna kill yourself
+ Music lover, seriously, music is, probably, one of the most important ingredients in this game, I bet no one can imagine this astonishing game without it
+ Enjoy games with a cool visual style and unique gameplay
+ Like indie games and believe, than sometimes, you don’t need million of dollars to make another AAA project for making a masterpiece
+ Love rich interesting stories
You should avoid this game if you:
- Don’t have any patience. This game literally is all about patience. You can stuck on some levels for hour or even more and you will need your patient skill to hold yourself and finish it
- Can’t stand repetitivity in games. First of all, the whole game based on one mechanics, which is, basically, running over different levels, one-hitting enemies faster than they will and escape. Plus, sometimes music can feel a bit annoying, especially if you die a lot, just so you know :)
Enjoy!

+ Environments and visuals are absolutely stunning; everything, form lighting effects, to foliage, to textures found throughout the world, are incredibly well-rendered and captivating
+ Solid, well-implemented control scheme that makes good use of large swathes of keyboard real-estate; I have grievances regarding a few of the keybindings, but these are easily remedied via the menu
+ Inventive combat system; it takes a bit of a push to get the hang of, but one will quickly find themselves enjoying a comfortable proficiency (with practice)
+ Admirable level of PC optimization
+ Impact of choices made are readily apparent, have incredibly far-reaching consequences, and lend astonishing gravity to each selection
+ Top-shelf voice-acting and written dialogue
+ Side-quests often have substance enough to rival the main plot
+ Ending spells out in wonderful detail the consequences of your actions, often within the specific areas in which you've visited
+ Very story-heavy game, and is therefore rife with lore-friendly collectibles and references that greatly enrich one's sense of immersion
+ Everything, from textures to NPCs, is meticulously crafted, and the game does not rely on cookie-cutter pasting techniques
+ Choices made throughout the game don't rely on a standard good/evil system, and therefore allows more flexibility in terms of character progression
+ Signs, potions, oils, enhancements, and traps all combine to lend tremendous depth and freedom to combat
+ Excellent game length and, due to multiple endings and story paths (which differ wildly depending on choices made during the first chapter) give the game an alarming amount of replay value
+ Successfully mature, somber tone pulls the player in, and manages to do so without coming off as overbearing; definitely not a 'tryhard' game
- Somewhat poor targeting mechanics
- Occasional bugs that require a restart; may not be prevalent for everyone, but I certainly noticed them
- Following NPCs can be tricky business, in that they often get stuck, block hallways and doors, and display poor pathing in general
- Comparing equipment available via trading with that which is currently equipped is not possible, making it necessary to exit from the trading screen to check stats, etc.
- Waypoints and objectives occasionally will not update properly

The Witcher 2 Assassins of Kings is by far one of the best RPG's ever made.
I will attempt to explain the why in my review. I will cover all levels of the
game, graphics, story, combat etc.
I will start off with the story that is being told. As someone who loves a
deep immersive story and world this game is a delight. The characters are
all well voiced and feel like they have a lot invested in the world as well
as them not appearing to be cardboard cut outs just conveying the next
plot entry to the player. You have to make choices in the Witcher 2. Which
for those of you who played the first will find a bit urking if you enjoyed
taking the Witcher path (neutrality). However the stakes are greatly raised
in the sequel. The fate of the entire northern realm is being decided and
your choices as Geralt will have long term ramifications on the world.
This is the only game I have ever had to sit back, get up out of my
chair and weigh the pros and cons of my decision. I have never felt
more invested in a series than the Witcher series. It is such a believable
world, so well crafted with so much attention to detail and love it is
unmissable. The story is exciting, if it does feel over a bit too soon. In
my 2nd playthrough I played on normal, did just about everything you
could do with some additional grinding out levels etc and that took me
about 45 hours. Where as my Witcher 1 play through took me 60+.
That being said the enhanced edition of the game that I played for the
first time since the games original launch has added a lot of content
and interesting things that make the game a bit more fleshed out to
give players a bit more of a satisfying conclusion leading up to the
third game.
The graphics to be honest are still the best we have seen on the PC.
I believe that if they released a brand new game (story, combat etc)
with the existing engine everyone would still be blown away. The fact
that CD Projekt said "Nah its not good enough" and created a new
engine for the Witcher 3 is insane especially by todays standard of
lazy♥♥♥♥♥developers copy and pastaing as many god damn games as
they can to meet their annual release schedule (♥♥♥♥ you Call of Duty
and Battlefield) is a breath of fresh air in a stagnant market. I bought
a 980 superclocked for the Witcher 3, and I can't even run Witcher 2
with ubersampling (I don't even think it does anything other than
cater to the egos of nerds with quad titan blacks) but other than that
I can ultra this game at 80-100 FPS constantly at 1080p. The game
is absolutely beautiful, the textures the character models. Everything
is picture esque. It is the exact thing we pc gamers love to see. Detail.
Now onto Combat. As a fan of the original games fighting style ala
Jedi Knight esque "stances" combat which I know a lot of people hate
because it can come down to just button clicking at the right time. I
initially hated the Witcher 2 combat, it was sluggish and felt rather
consolized. After 4 years passed I picked the game up again now that
the enhanced edition has improved combat it feels much more
responsive and fun. Even if it still feels to be a bit of a "Roll fest". I
do feel that combat still needs improvements to make it more
interesting, a hybrid of one and twos combat systems could work
out incredibly well and make the game feel unique in its own right.
That being said the combat has been improved and I have heard
there are mods that made the combat even better.
I have a lot of love for this game and for this series. I think that
CD Projekt red has proved themselves among the best developers
of games to this day. Their mentality is that of the days of old.
When people who loved games, made games. It wasn't a day
to day job. It was done with passion and commitment. You can
tell CD loves their IP, and their franchise. Their commitment
to their fans has been something truly admirable. They give
free content out that most companies would charge a boat load
for. Most of you would say "Well that's nothing special they should
do that anyway" I agree with you in theory but that is not the
point. The point is they do not HAVE TO, but they DO. They
care about the people who play their games. That is why I
love them and am eagerly awaiting The Witcher 3 Wild Hunt.
This game is a must if you love RPG's. It is an absolute must.

A lot of fantastic games came out in 2016, but ABZU is definitely one of the best. Having loved Journey, I went in with high expectations... only to have those expectations absolutely smashed in the face of a simple, but beautiful game. Where Journey was a quiet journey of self-reflection, ABZU is busy and joyful, absolutely teeming with life, to the point where the quieter parts are almost haunting. (Most people have a very similar relationship with the ocean - equal parts fascination and dread - and the game captures this feeling perfectly in its atmosphere. Diving deep is scary, but always worth it.)
Like Journey, ABZU tells its story mostly through murals, leaving the player to piece together what happened to lead the story to this point. Despite this, there's a real sense of connection and emotion. There were several moments when I actually cried out in pure glee, and moments when I felt like my stomach was made of lead. And after finishing, I immediately replayed it, looking for things I'd missed the first time.
I couldn't possibly recommend this game more.

That Dragon, Cancer is an adventure game developed by Numinous Games. This game has gotten a lot of mixed reception with gamers, however the game has gained critical acclaim with reviewers and critics across the board and I can understand both sides of the picture
That Dragon, Cancer is a linear short story adventure. A videogame developer's love letter to his son. The game is a poetic and playful interactive retelling of Joel’s 4-year fight against cancer
The length of the game is extremely short (I finished it in over an hour and in one whole sitting) and the asking price is a bit too steep and some of the mechanics are a bit clunky, however, That Dragon, Cancer's story and character development especially with the Green family are nailed perfectly in the game
The story is well written and travels through the struggle that the Green family had to go through to help Joel's four year fight against cancer and the pain and thick and thin that poor baby Joel had to go through to fight against cancer
I can understand the mixed responses from gamers about That Dragon, Cancer and I can also understand why critics and reviewers gave this game a near perfect score and to me personally I really enjoyed playing through That Dragon, Cancer. True, the length of the game is ridiculously short, however, it was interesting watching the sturggles that the family and Joel himself had to go through fighting against cancer
That Dragon, Cancer will and has mixed reception but if you are reading this review, then you are dying to know my recommendation. That Dragon, Cancer is a game everyone should try and play and finish in one whole sitting, however, for the retail price it is offering, I would not recommend it at its full price and rather wait for a price drop or a sale
That Dragon, Cancer is not the game for everyone, especially with the subject matter it is dealing with, however, a majority of gamers should at least give it a try...

Yes, the first couple runs you will likely only see a few enemy types and at most two biomes, but that's the first couple runs.
The odd thing about Necropolis is that you need to die to see things. As you do more runs things begin to open up with sewers and factories and hanging gardens and swamps and who knows what else, each with new weapons to loot and enemies to kill.
I've played about thirteen runs so far and have seen levels lower in the Necropolis transform from single biome spans of gray corridors into mixes of three or four tile sets each, like a factory with pits of blue lava surrounding a garden of floating platforms connected by rickety bridges.
What I can say for this game is that it is a lot more than the first few runs, and instead of your character progressing, the Necropolis itself becomes more interesting and varied as you play.
If you want to burn all kinds of stuff this is your game!

Okay, to write a review of Final Fantasy 7 is not a simple task, believe me it's not. Now you've probably heard this before from dozens of people, whether it be your friends, gaming magazines, internet or basically any other form of communication; written or spoken, Final Fantasy 7 is one of the best games of all time, and though now it may seem like an overrated, outdated RPG nearly 17 years later, it deserves the title.
I only beat this game once, and have dived back into it thanks to this updated re-release on Steam. Visually, it's eye-candy to me. Though current-day gamers might turn thier heads, this game looks awesome and if it weren't for the PlayStation's graphical limits, i would say that this is the way the developers originally invisioned the game back in 1997, fluent animations, sharper character models, and just overall better looking port.
The Story is something else, The story of Final Fantasy 7 is not a forgettable one. You begin as part of an eco-terrorist group who is hell-bent on destroying the world's biggest power company for killing the planet, hours into the game later you find yourself on a mission to save a world that is doomed to complete annihilation at the hands of a super-soldier who is "taking back the planet". (i hate to give away to much spoilers.)
As for the gameplay it is your typical, run-of-the-mill, turn-based JRPG. for a series who practically invented the genre, this game doesn't stray to far away from it's predecessors in terms of the battle system and means of progression, hell if you're having trouble understanding how to play, there are countless websites dedicated to this game as well as an in-game tutorial, have fun.
If you are a fan or RPG's, JRPG's, or curious about the genre, PLAY THIS. you are doing yourselfs a huge injustice by reading this and playing some damn Final Fantasy 7, you will not be dissapointed.

I actually played Final Fantasy 7 for the first time several years after it was released. A friend of mine gave me both the FF7 and FF8 discs at the same time. I initially decided to play FF8 as it was the newer and more graphically realistic of the two games. FF7's blocky and cartoony graphics initially turned me off and I didn't get around to playing through it until after I finished FF8. I liked FF8 well enough at the time, but it wasn't until I went back and played through FF7 that I realized how superior of a game Final Fantasy 7 is. It taught me an important lesson that I still think about when playing games now: graphics are just not as important as good gameplay and an interesting story
Final Fantasy 7 was the first game in the series released on the PS1 and was also the first game in the series to not appear on a Nintendo console. More importantly, it is also the game that is credited with popularizing the Japanese role playing game genre for western audiences. It is also the first game in the Final Fantasy series to fully embrace a futuristic sci-fi setting as opposed to the Tolkien-esque fantasy settings found in the previous games. Earlier games in the series had some futuristic and science fiction elements, but Final Fantasy 7 really embraced this aesthetic and fully built its characters and setting around it
Final Fantasy 7 follows the story of Cloud Strife, an amnesiac mercenary who joins a band of freedom fighters who call themselves Avalanche and are trying to stop the money-loving Shinra corporation from installing environment polluting "mako reactors" across the planet. The first part of the game deals with the Avalanche vs. Shinra conflict, but then the game and story really opens up as you begin to uncover the details of Cloud's past, his lost memories and how a mysterious man known as Sephiroth ties in to the story. You'll also of course explore the backstory to all of your party members, who are all well written and interesting characters. It's a truly gripping and mysterious story that had me hooked from the beginning and kept me interested to the end. It's a difficult game to put down because if whatever's happening in the story doesn't hold your attention, the addicting and well designed battle system probably will.
Just like any other entry in the Final Fantasy series, the battle system in FF7 is completely unique, but I believe this is my favorite battle system found in any of the Final Fantasy games. This battle system allows for a high degree of character customization through the new "materia" system. In the game, materia are basically little magic jewels that characters can equip on their weapons and armor to grant additional stat bonuses or new abilities. For instance, if you want a party member to learn a fire spell, you simply place the "fire" materia into one of the materia slots on that character's weapon or armor. What makes this system interesting is that some materia can be paired together. For example, if you wanted to be able to cast fire on all enemies at once, you can pair a "fire" materia with an "all" materia, assuming you have both. Players have to make some fun strategic decisions when building out their party as some weapons may be statistically better, but have fewer materia slots. Further adding to the strategic complexity of this system is that materia can gain experience and level up, granting you further statistical bonuses or more powerful spells. Another smart piece of game design is that some weapons and armors can increase the growth rate of the materia, but at the cost of fewer total materia slots. It's an excellent battle system that forces the player to think carefully about their party's build.
Adding to the perfect harmony of excellent gameplay and well-told story is the masterfully composed soundtrack. I know I've said it before, but Nobou Uematsu is a genius. The PS1 sound chip makes the tracks sound very MIDI-ish, but pay attention to the composition of the pieces. It's genius. Even more mind blowing is the crazy musical variety found in each track. There's the sleazy "Oppressed People", the dark and beautiful "Anxious Heart", the playful carnival-like "Gold Saucer", the nightmarish "Those Chosen by the Planet" and of course, the rockin' boss battle anthem "Those who Fight Further". But really, the whole soundtrack is totally amazing from top to bottom. Give it a listen if you're into video game music
Final Fantasy 7 is a masterpiece of a game. It's a perfect blend of engaging story, smart game design and a top-notch soundtrack. I've tried many times to recreate the experience of playing FF7 for the first time be trying various other Japanese role playing games, but none can quite recapture the brilliance of FF7. It's a must-play for fans of RPGs with great storytelling, don't let the blocky graphics scare you off. Speaking of which, I'd love to see that FF7 HD remake sometime in my lifetime

My first impression was that it has significantly more simplistic visuals than I'd expected, not very engaging gameplay and unremarkable game mechanics.
Honestly, I just wanted a bigger Grimrock, which IMO was a masterpiece, in all of its humility. Not having played original M&M games I'd hoped there would be lots of lore to pick from and create a huge, immersive and rich environment. Sadly, the lore and opportunity may have been there, but the implementation went someplace else.
Scale-wise it certainly is no Skyrim - a dozen of locations or so. To call it an "open world" is almost laughable with all the progression-based obstacles you coincidentally encounter at every turn - ranging from guards blocking a bridge and impassable terrain to hopeless fights. Talking about rich environment - there's not much role playing, aside from listening to gossips from NPCs with sporadic voice-overs, sifting through loot to find something that suits your party and wondering about the way you were supposed to distribute your skill points to not get brutalized all over the map after act one.
In short: the dungeons are there, the quests are there, the loot is there, but it still feels like a farm sim - and not the best one.

To be honest I have never been a hardcore 4X gamer and my only real experience to 4X was way back in the day with Birth of the Federation (good times) and then more recently Civilization V. So as more of a casual coming into Galactic Civilization 3 I didn't know what to expect due to the numerous comments on the learning curve and crashes/bugs.
I will have to say that the game isn't too hard to pick up honestly. I've played far more difficult games as far as entry level is concerned (Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis 4). The tutorial campaign could use a little more polish to teach you some of the more unexplained nuances, which sadly there is a lot of. For example, it doesn't explain very well ship roles. It also doesn't explain the more intricate part of starbases and just how important they actually are.
But really I was off and racing experimenting with a few practice games and I also picked up a few tips outside of the game online. However that doesn't mean I have become by all means excellent. I feel like I am picking up new techniques and research build orders everytime I play. In addition to that the difficulty does seem really challenging even on normal. I am very calculated and careful in my play yet the AI always seem to end up leaps and bounds ahead and this is usually due to the fact that faction power is calculated largely off of ships you have on the map at any one stage.
The game runs very smoothly for the most part. I have a decent gaming rig with and SSD, 16Gb Ram and a GTX960 and the graphics are nice and smooth, however I feel it does need a little optimization. For example when scrolling the map especially on large and above maps with the anti-aliasing tunred up and draw grid map enabled there are little pauses here and there. So bare in mind it is good but not perfect. Lowering the AA down to 4 or 2 especially for large maps and above is pretty useful to iron out the tiny half second lag you get on large and above maps. However having said all that it's a treat looking over the bright star and nebula filled galaxies in the game. Turns in later games and on larger maps are pretty quick too so far (now about 18 hours into it). Granted I haven't started a super huge map loaded with races just yet but I aim to do that in the near future.
The honey moon period is starting to wear off the game but so far it's still okay, honestly this game can keep me glued to the computer for hours. I don't even realise sometimes how much time has passed. If a game can do that to you, then it's clearly a good game right? The game has a great ship creator (love the 3D printing support by the way - regardless of me not having a 3D printer).
The depth of the game really comes from the way you pick your research and how you manage your resources and planets and diplomacy and a little more annoyingly starbase management too. It is a fun game and I could honestly if it weren't for kids and work sit there for hours and let the days and months dwindle away until I have completed a huge map and emerge from my cave soiled and hairy.
Anyways give the game a go, the developers are great and are working closely with the Community to better develop the game. I have however become skeptical of the price of the DLC vs actual content. This does feel al little over the top to pay $5 for "events". The game is no doubt fun but I see many online starting to call out Stardock on their DLC content. Give it a go you may just become addicted like I have!

***This review contains spoilers, mostly from The Neverhood***
I don't know how many attempts at writing this review I've had before. And to be honest, I still don't entirely know how I feel about this game - but I'll do my best to express all that comes to my mind.
Let me start by saying that The Neverhood is my ultimate favourite game. As in, for me it's an absolute perfection, a masterpiece among games, my favourite game ever since I first played it as a ~6-year-old.
The Neverhood has everything.
Its story, although short, is deep and reminds me of biblical genesis. We see the creation of the clay world, we see its first inhabitants, living happily in peace, we see one important rule, a forbidden fruit, and a corrupted unit that breaks that one rule. We see the peaceful world being broken, and finally - we see a saviour, a Messiah, the chosen one, who can save the world and make it a happy place again. But there's also a plot twist. We can choose an alternative ending to the story and rule the world ourselves instead of the original creator.
Along with the main thread there are also some short stories that add to the plot - we get to see some bits from Willie and poor Robot Bil's struggle to get the teddy bear (and more). The story is good. Involving, entertaining and keeping us interested thanks to the way how we learn random parts of it.
The Neverhood has the most amazing graphics. Let's be real, games released in 1996 were nowhere near the photorealism we see in the newest titles - I think everyone remembers what Lara Croft looked like in the first Tomb Raider game. A game made in claymation must have been visually appealing at that time. More - a game made in claymation is timeless. Sure, we have better recording devices and some easy ways to polish the recording now, but the difference isn't that notable.
Soundtrack... an absolutely flawless background of the game. Critically acclaimed, no need to go into details.
Sense of humour. Ah... crème de la crème. Who didn't laugh seeing Klaymen's escape from the monster after playing with its music box? Who didn't laugh at the amazing facial expressions? Who didn't laugh seeing clay turtle smashed by a mushroom house and then its clay guts dripping on the ground? And if you played the game, did you jump into the giant drain hole? If not - you have mistakes to fix! Those might be details... but even the tiniest details build a perfection.
And finally, the puzzles. Tons of puzzles, often difficult ones. It's not a game where you're guided from the start to the end, it's a game in which you have to explore the furthest corners of the world to find hints for whatever you're stuck at. Every puzzle-adventure game I play I compare to the Neverhood. And trust me, proper puzzles are a rare.
Needless to say I spent most of my gaming life wishing for the continuation of The Neverhood. When the news about Armikrog heading to Kickstarter came I was both over the moon and concerned. Will that long-awaited game live up to its expectation? Let's see.
Story-wise, it's not The Neverhood. Probably not much can be added to the original story, so the choice to make it an independent game didn't come as a surprise to me (although I'd much rather see a story set in the exact same universum, just from a different point of view and maybe set in a different time). That didn't happen. Instead, we get a story about Tommynaut and his dog Beak-Beak. We need to navigate through a fortress and - again - learn the story of the creation of the world and a special unit (the child - P). However, the story is short, not as interesting as the one in The Neverhood and to me it feels a bit like the designers tried a little bit too hard... you know what I mean? It's not a completely atrocious story, no. It's an okay, solid mediocore story. Nowhere near as good as the plot of the Neverhood though.
In terms of graphics Armikrog is good. Really good. Reviewed as an independent game (which it is, in fact) - it looks amazing with its polished claymation. As The Neverhood's successor it feels a bit... too shiny? The Neverhood had its visual imperfections, but since I love the entire game with all its tiny flaws, they were the most perfect imperfections I could imagine. Armikrog looks great, but as it often is with perfected appearances, it's easy to make that perfection seem bland. Nonetheless, the game is visually appealing, points for that.
Soundtrack fits the game and was made by the same composer who made music for The Neverhood - nothing to complain about. Well, maybe the fact that the overall feel of the game is more shallow, in all aspects, so the soundtrack couldn't really be any better.
Humour and puzzles... those are my main complaints about the game. It has some funny bits and it has quite a few puzzles. But compared to The Neverhood? Please. Not even remotely close. Although I have to admit that games nowadays are generally a lot easier than those released ~20 years ago. So it's not only Armikrog's issue, it's a problem I see in many many games and I believe the developers wanted to fit in the market.
Bugs! I played the game shortly after its release, having promised to myself that I wouldn't use any walkthrough guides. Well... I got stuck at the very beginning when an item I was supposed to get disappeared. Spent some time walking around to make sure it was a bug and then quit playing. I then returned to the game a few months later - fortunately, this time noticing no major bugs.
You might be wondering why this review is positive. I'm assuming that most of the people who haven't yet played or heard about Armikrog aren't The Neverhood fans. They'll judge this game without comparing it to the old classic. And despite all I wrote - it's an okay game. Not a masterpiece, but a solid slightly-above-average title, especially now, with gamebreaking bugs fixed. If, however, you've come here knowing and treasuring the legacy of The Neverhood... I would probably advise you to try to forget about Armikrog and keep cultivating the perfect image of the old masterpiece in your heart and memory.

Uaggh.  I really want to recommend this game, as it's super-rare we get games like this.  I only found out about The Neverhood until later, though I was familiar with TenNapel's work on Earthworm Jim.  When I heard about Armikrog I was like, "oh awesome!"  I really enjoyed those quirky, FMV-rich point and click adventure games from the 90s.
But Armikrog?  I like the story, I like the setting, the world and presentation.  Tommynaut, voiced by Michael J Nelson?  Rob Paulsen as Beak-Beak?  Napoleon Dynamite plays the villian?  Mixed with the quirky, weird music stylings of the original Neverhood composer?  This sounds great.
But I saw some negative reviews, particularly those from long-time fans saying the game was short, shallow and very buggy.  I decided to wait until it was on sale, and here I am.
The verdict?  I wish those reviewers hadn't been right, but I fear they are.  And what's worse is that I am playing the patched verison;  I can only image what it was like on day one.  The game just isn't very well coded.
Visual glitches, physics weirding out, or even the fact that cutscenes will trigger where it's clear they expected me to be standing at point A but I'm over at point B, so things don't sync up...
It's also very short.  As in, I beat the game in just a few hours.  (And I could have shaved off 30 minutes if I hadn't decided to back-track to re-experience parts of the game which will only make sense once you unlock something later in the game.)

Yo, real talk, homes. Imma sum this bad boy up with some pros and cons, yo. Check it. Prep yo aniz for some deep shiz, fam.
Pro: Long, rich lore fo' days. Seriously. There's a lot here in general.
Con: If you're new to the series, there's so much lore and so many long fantasy names here that it makes this game confusing AF if you take more than a couple days break. Still kinda confusing if you don't play it consistently.
C: Also the story, to me, seemed really generic at first, but. . .
P: The story gets a lot better in chapter 2, when there's a little more going on underneath the surface of kingslayers and amnesia.
P: Several decent sized, open locations for you to explore.
C: Garry of the Riviera can only move so fast.  If you get lost (which you will) and need to go from one part of the map to the other (which you will), then you'll be soaking a lot of time into just running around (which I believe maybe the number 1 time killer in this, yes, even more than talking.) I think the game would be over a lot faster if Geraldo Rivera's top speed was more than that of a lax jog.
P: Good base for deep combat, but it's not without its flaws.
C: Combat isn't actually all that great, it's good and showed promise, but not great. Even with the FCR mod, Geralt is a bit unresponsive at times, leading to inevitable frustration. Another frustrating bit is the sometimes long melee animations that open Geralt up to the enemies sometimes quicker attacks that cannot be dodged, blocked, or parried once the attack animations are started (looking at you, sword twirl animations), this has got me killed quite a few times when I pressed X for swift pokes or slashes and instead got short dance routines. It's actually making me really mad thinking about it.
P: The choices you make ACTUALLY, TRULY, like, FOR REAL affect the story quite a bit, unlike other games that claim to.
C (imo): The game a lot of the time doesn't tell you where to where to go, or if they do, how to get there, which can lead to running around (all over the local map in some cases) and wasting time either getting lost, or just jogging from point A to B in general. I don't know how many times I had to google how to get somewhere when I failed to memorize the map in it's entirety since the overworld maps can be pretty bad, especially when you need to revisit a hidden path. Some enemies also share the problem of withheld information, they have weaknesses, but they aren't conveyed by example or even described in the in-game books that document the creatures. They don't need to hold my hand, but when the game gives you so much detail, you should be able to find more than just lore in the in-game books and conversations.
C: Oh and even in the Enhanced Edition, the UI's kinda bad, but you'll get used to it.
Closing Statements - It's a long, solid ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) game that I recommend for the story, but the actual gameplay left me questioning CDPR's actual gamplay design decisions almost all the time. "Why did he twirl for a slash at 3 ft away when he could've done a quick thrust or slash? Where on earth do I find these creatures/people? How do I get across the forest or these trenches with an overworld map that looks like a maze with only dead-ends?" Though it looks like they may have fixed some of these problems in The Wild Hunt, (which, at the time of this review is only 12 hrs away,) my only hope now is that they fix or improve upon the rest of those things.
P.S. For me, it's easy to criticize and harder to praise. Not just this game but all things, I list so many flaws in ill-fated hopes that some recognizes these faults so that the same mistakes can be prevented in the future, should they be avoidable, as not all mistakes are.
Update P.P.S. The Witcher 3 pretty much fixes all of my gameplay related complaints. I'd thumbs up the s♥♥♥ out of it if I had it on Steam.
