Crypt of the NecroDancer is a roguelite game based on the "bump to kill" mechanic. Games based on it (e.g.
) are usually turn-based, focusing on the strategy and effective enemy killing. But necro
is different, everything is done in microturns - All actions (both yours and enemies's) have to be correlating with the soundtrack's rhythm. Each beat is a single action for every character.
That makes the game pretty hard, especially in later levels - but it's definitely a pro for the game since I'm talking about roguelite game. This genre only deserves hard but fair difficulty. You have to deal with the press that requires you to feel the rhythm and remember specific dances of your enemies; you need to train proper dodges for each enemy and keep yourself concentrated (and if you don't, you'll can consider yourself dead in less than a minute).
As I already mentioned, all attacking is done just by moving to enemy's place in the grid (to "bump" them). If you do that at the beat the enemy's ready to fight, you lose your health instead and you have to quickly reconsider your (necro)dancing. There are many pickups through all levels, you can find both melee or ranged weapons, spells, armor pieces, or other passive and consumable items. There're also two resources: Gold, used to buy items for your current run, and diamonds, which are used to unlock more items for your runs (in the game's menu).
You might be scared about the controls for dancing, but they actually couldn't be more simple. All you need is arrow keys (or a dance pad), since you can only move in basic four directions on a grid. All spell casts and item uses are done by combinations of those keys, e.g. arrow up + arrow right to cast a fire spell.
All levels have procedurally generated groups of enemies and rooms, that's nothing unique for roguelites, but I am really happy for secrets in Crypt of the NecroDancer. In most roguelite games I've played, secrets were mostly placed somewhere in level's corners but this game does something completely different - secrets are always somewhere near the level's center, that means you don't have to explore borders in each level to get an advantage. On the other hand, secrets can have many deadly enemies and traps, you have to be wary. Also, you can dig through all walls in every level (besides the border blocks), making your own way through the level!
Talking about graphics, there's nothing to criticize. I love the precise pixelart design with sweet animation the game has! Since it's all about dancing, seeing every NPC to dance with the rhythm is truly satisfying. Soundtrack is amazingly well made, each level has its own song that has even more variations: There is a shopkeeper in every level, and when you'll be near him, you'll hear him sing to the current song. Also, there's a level that perfectly uses genre variations for a song - in hot parts full of lava you'll hear heavy metal, and in icy parts you'll hear electronic version of the same song. In the later levels (zone 4) the soundtrack isn't that good (for being more on the hard electronic genre, so it may be just my personal issue) and it's hard to move with the rhythm of the song properly. Considering everything about the game, I think it's rather another feature to bring the difficulty even higher near the end of the game.
Crypt of the NecroDancer comes with an unique idea for a roguelike game; to change casual turn-based strategy into rhythm driven game. This change may seem small, but it makes the game distinct, harder and much more entertaining! The game also have a lot of replayability for all achievements (which are hard to unlock), so don't expect getting just few hours of gameplay from it if you want to get everything. Add great pixelart graphics and perfect soundtrack (mandatory for a rhythm game) and there's nothing to stop me from recommending it to you. It's great! Now let me go "necrodance" a bit more, I haven't got enough yet.

I actually played Final Fantasy 7 for the first time several years after it was released. A friend of mine gave me both the FF7 and FF8 discs at the same time. I initially decided to play FF8 as it was the newer and more graphically realistic of the two games. FF7's blocky and cartoony graphics initially turned me off and I didn't get around to playing through it until after I finished FF8. I liked FF8 well enough at the time, but it wasn't until I went back and played through FF7 that I realized how superior of a game Final Fantasy 7 is. It taught me an important lesson that I still think about when playing games now: graphics are just not as important as good gameplay and an interesting story
Final Fantasy 7 was the first game in the series released on the PS1 and was also the first game in the series to not appear on a Nintendo console. More importantly, it is also the game that is credited with popularizing the Japanese role playing game genre for western audiences. It is also the first game in the Final Fantasy series to fully embrace a futuristic sci-fi setting as opposed to the Tolkien-esque fantasy settings found in the previous games. Earlier games in the series had some futuristic and science fiction elements, but Final Fantasy 7 really embraced this aesthetic and fully built its characters and setting around it
Final Fantasy 7 follows the story of Cloud Strife, an amnesiac mercenary who joins a band of freedom fighters who call themselves Avalanche and are trying to stop the money-loving Shinra corporation from installing environment polluting "mako reactors" across the planet. The first part of the game deals with the Avalanche vs. Shinra conflict, but then the game and story really opens up as you begin to uncover the details of Cloud's past, his lost memories and how a mysterious man known as Sephiroth ties in to the story. You'll also of course explore the backstory to all of your party members, who are all well written and interesting characters. It's a truly gripping and mysterious story that had me hooked from the beginning and kept me interested to the end. It's a difficult game to put down because if whatever's happening in the story doesn't hold your attention, the addicting and well designed battle system probably will.
Just like any other entry in the Final Fantasy series, the battle system in FF7 is completely unique, but I believe this is my favorite battle system found in any of the Final Fantasy games. This battle system allows for a high degree of character customization through the new "materia" system. In the game, materia are basically little magic jewels that characters can equip on their weapons and armor to grant additional stat bonuses or new abilities. For instance, if you want a party member to learn a fire spell, you simply place the "fire" materia into one of the materia slots on that character's weapon or armor. What makes this system interesting is that some materia can be paired together. For example, if you wanted to be able to cast fire on all enemies at once, you can pair a "fire" materia with an "all" materia, assuming you have both. Players have to make some fun strategic decisions when building out their party as some weapons may be statistically better, but have fewer materia slots. Further adding to the strategic complexity of this system is that materia can gain experience and level up, granting you further statistical bonuses or more powerful spells. Another smart piece of game design is that some weapons and armors can increase the growth rate of the materia, but at the cost of fewer total materia slots. It's an excellent battle system that forces the player to think carefully about their party's build.
Adding to the perfect harmony of excellent gameplay and well-told story is the masterfully composed soundtrack. I know I've said it before, but Nobou Uematsu is a genius. The PS1 sound chip makes the tracks sound very MIDI-ish, but pay attention to the composition of the pieces. It's genius. Even more mind blowing is the crazy musical variety found in each track. There's the sleazy "Oppressed People", the dark and beautiful "Anxious Heart", the playful carnival-like "Gold Saucer", the nightmarish "Those Chosen by the Planet" and of course, the rockin' boss battle anthem "Those who Fight Further". If I had to sum this game up in two words, those two words would be frustratingly addictive.
You will die. A lot.
Don't make the assumption that this is a run-and-gun game. This is a thinking mans psychedelic 80's murder simulator. You will die learning a map layout. You will die figuring out when enemies will respond to gunfire. You will die due to glitchy doors. There is a lot of you dying in this game. But guess what there's also a lot of?
Heart-pumping Adrenaline-gorged violence. No other game evokes the same sense of crazed desperateness as you pummel some poor Russian mobsters face into the dance floor, only to get up a split second later, grab his shotgun, and blow away the other Russian Mobsters who've been unfortunate to be in the same building as you.
While the action is split second and fast-paced, the game rewards tactical planning and thinking more than twitch reactions. You will not succeed trying to run through a building swinging a baseball bat like a madman. You're going to have to bait enemies, burst into a room when no one's looking, and die several times perfecting ways to murder people.
My only complaint is how vague the boss fights are. While I've only encountered two thus far, both of them have been pretty vague on how you actually win them. How the hell was a I supposed to figure out that I could only damage biker once he's throw his weapon when that isn't how the gameplay mechanics works at any other point previously?. The boss battles are inconsistent with the rest of the game.
It can get frustrating, but it is intensely satisfying when you've cleared four separate floors after countless deaths trying. 8/10, would recommend.

This game is about experiencing a very short life through poetry, imagery, visual art, recordings, everything that can be poured into your soul and your heart will be if you play this game. I recommend this game to poets, gamers, artists, and anyone who holds hope close to their heart.

I bought this game a while ago.. but, for months, I couldn't dare to play.. because I knew what it would bring to me. I knew I would feel sad and might cry.. and it did when I finally clicked the play button today.
I was always thinking games can be better than movies in engaging the emotions. Players have to think and move to get through the games. In some games, your moves are everything. You constantly move and do something. This is not that kind of game. You don't need to move much. You can get through it pretty quickly if you want to. But you don't play this game to see the ending. We all know the ending; the ending that nobody wanted. You play this to "feel"; and the developers, the parents of Joel's, take you through their emotional turmoil. It's a rather tightly set story. There's one storyline and it seems like there's mostly one way to make progress. You cannot skip a part or scene. You have to go through it like the parents had to go through it. It is painful. However indirect, watching a little baby son dying in your arms is painful; and that makes this game great. After playhing this game, you remember at least three names: Ryan, Amy and Joel Green.
The part where I felt the power of this medium called "Game" is when I was walking down the hallway in the hospital full of cards. I literally opened all the cards. Every single one of them. And I cried. They were the messages to their moms, dads, grandmas, grandpas, uncles and friends who had fought or are fitghting the dragon. While opening them one by one, I was so glad that I was playing this game and that I could open all of them. If it were a movie, they might open one or two of them to tell you what they are and the long shot of the hallway full of the cards would be it. I won't have a choice of acknowledging the messages someone sent to their loved ones.
All in all, it is not an easy game - playing itself is easy, there's nothing much you need to do. But digesting it is what I mean. But I didn't even get distracted once playing this game for 2 hours. Mesmerizing.

I was concerned this wouldn't be a recommendation after participating in the Early Release, which was incredibly disappointing. However, I was pleasantly surprised when the final release came out that a large number of the issues I had with the game had been addressed. Overall, M&MX does a good job of capturing the old school vibe of earlier entries in the system, while taking advantage of some of their later design improvements first seen in their Heroes series of games.
That said, the game misses the mark in several ways. First, the graphic performance is very disappointing. It looks like a game optimized for 5+ years ago. The creation and skill system does a poor job of helping new players understand pros and cons of the abilities and how they impact gameplay. The amount of running through previously cleared areas is frustrating. The limited voice acting is grating and repetitive.
Despite those disappointments, this does scratch the itch for a classic, party-based, first person roleplaying experience. The exploration, discovery, hidden bits, and character classes do feel like previous entries in the system. For a truly authentic experience, and to help off-set the disappointing graphics, I strongly recommend selecting the "classic pixelated" display found in the gameplay settings menu.
Other pros - once you're familiar with the game, the classes are diverse and offer a lot of variety in how you want to build your party. Combat is tactical enough to be satisfying without slowing the game down too much. Boss fights are brutal but winnable with careful play. The cool epic items that level up with your character are awesome. It's casual enough to be approachable by a wide audience. It's a fairly good value for its pricepoint. It has a strong nostalgia element.
I think people familiar with other games in the series will be most likely to enjoy this version, but it shouldn't stop new players from giving it a shot!

This game has something that I like to call "Sonic 06 Syndrome". You can see what the developers were going for, and in those brief but fun moments of gameplay, you see what it could have been. The difference is that this wasn't a game rushed out to meet a specific date. Nobody was waiting for this, there weren't millions upon millions watching a trailer. If the developers took their time it would be good.
Each level begins with you falling into a box with a few weapons. These weapons will be used to kill the zombies(?) you are going to encounter. Well, except level 4. There's no weapon like the game has been showing you at the start of each level. Also, you only see a small island leading to a tunnel so there's no reason. Tunnels have been used since level 2 as a way of continuing the stage. So no weapon, that's cool. But NOOOOO; there's a bat to the right. YOU HAVE TO LOOK TO THE RIGHT TO SEE AN ARROW POINTING AT A WEAPON. This is unneccesary. What they should've done to show that weapons can be elsewhere in the level is by putting them elsewhere in the level. How about the sewer system you were just in? That could make the player realize that weapons aren't only at the start.
Next, the levels. The design in this game is...odd. It's jumbled islands that look like they belong in Super Mario Galaxy. Zombies are laid out that you'll have to beat. What if you die? Back to the level select screen. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would I want to go aaaaaaaaaaaall the way back to the level select? I'm advancing in a level, let that be my own damn choice.
Killing zombies is fun, but killing zombies in any game is normally fun. Considering the odd layout of the levels, dumb design, easy to beat enemies, and weird game design, I say avoid it. There are plenty of good zombie games that do much more right (Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2 are as good as zombie games will get) and keep you wanting to play. But hey, if you like games that feel as though they belong on the Xbox Market's indie game section then whatever! It's only 99 cents, so just sell some Steam Trading Cards and get it if you really want it. I'm sure there's also going to be constant giveaways (which is how I got this), so eh. But avoid it unless it's free or you're crazy.

I haven't experienced any bugs yet, but I don't doubt they are around. I suggest taking your time with this game and doing the same.

Crypt of the NecroDancer is a roguelite game based on the "bump to kill" mechanic. Games based on it (e.g.
) are usually turn-based, focusing on the strategy and effective enemy killing. But necro
is different, everything is done in microturns - All actions (both yours and enemies's) have to be correlating with the soundtrack's rhythm. Each beat is a single action for every character.
That makes the game pretty hard, especially in later levels - but it's definitely a pro for the game since I'm talking about roguelite game. This genre only deserves hard but fair difficulty. You have to deal with the press that requires you to feel the rhythm and remember specific dances of your enemies; you need to train proper dodges for each enemy and keep yourself concentrated (and if you don't, you'll can consider yourself dead in less than a minute).
As I already mentioned, all attacking is done just by moving to enemy's place in the grid (to "bump" them). If you do that at the beat the enemy's ready to fight, you lose your health instead and you have to quickly reconsider your (necro)dancing. There are many pickups through all levels, you can find both melee or ranged weapons, spells, armor pieces, or other passive and consumable items. There're also two resources: Gold, used to buy items for your current run, and diamonds, which are used to unlock more items for your runs (in the game's menu).
You might be scared about the controls for dancing, but they actually couldn't be more simple. All you need is arrow keys (or a dance pad), since you can only move in basic four directions on a grid. All spell casts and item uses are done by combinations of those keys, e.g. arrow up + arrow right to cast a fire spell.
All levels have procedurally generated groups of enemies and rooms, that's nothing unique for roguelites, but I am really happy for secrets in Crypt of the NecroDancer. In most roguelite games I've played, secrets were mostly placed somewhere in level's corners but this game does something completely different - secrets are always somewhere near the level's center, that means you don't have to explore borders in each level to get an advantage. On the other hand, secrets can have many deadly enemies and traps, you have to be wary. Also, you can dig through all walls in every level (besides the border blocks), making your own way through the level!
Talking about graphics, there's nothing to criticize. I love the precise pixelart design with sweet animation the game has! Since it's all about dancing, seeing every NPC to dance with the rhythm is truly satisfying. Soundtrack is amazingly well made, each level has its own song that has even more variations: There is a shopkeeper in every level, and when you'll be near him, you'll hear him sing to the current song. Also, there's a level that perfectly uses genre variations for a song - in hot parts full of lava you'll hear heavy metal, and in icy parts you'll hear electronic version of the same song. In the later levels (zone 4) the soundtrack isn't that good (for being more on the hard electronic genre, so it may be just my personal issue) and it's hard to move with the rhythm of the song properly. Considering everything about the game, I think it's rather another feature to bring the difficulty even higher near the end of the game.
Crypt of the NecroDancer comes with an unique idea for a roguelike game; to change casual turn-based strategy into rhythm driven game. This change may seem small, but it makes the game distinct, harder and much more entertaining! The game also have a lot of replayability for all achievements (which are hard to unlock), so don't expect getting just few hours of gameplay from it if you want to get everything. Add great pixelart graphics and perfect soundtrack (mandatory for a rhythm game) and there's nothing to stop me from recommending it to you. It's great! Now let me go "necrodance" a bit more, I haven't got enough yet.

TL;DR: The Christian morals and story about struggling with faith was very refreshing to see, and its art style is very nice looking, however its wonky controls, campy tone, ridiculously slow pace and heavy reliance on artistic scenes did not immerse or interest me in the way I had anticipated.
Let me start this review off by saying that I loved the Christian morals and ideas shown in this game, and I enjoyed the story about battling with faith and tragedy. However, regretfully, I don't think I can wholeheartedly recommend this game.
First off, the art direction is very pretty and contemporary, and I liked looking at each set piece in the story. It's a shame then that the wonky controls withheld me from fully imbibing them. The mouse sensetivity never seemed consistant, or if there was mouse acceleration on, there was no setting to turn it off, unfortunately. Also, I would've definitely enjoyed an option to choose to use WSAD to walk instead of point-and-click. I thought it was annoying to use most times and probably lessened my immersion in the game.
Also, I think this game might have been too short, or maybe I was expecting too much from it. The game felt quite short and anti-climactic, however the pace is painfully slow. Usually scenes will last as long as you let them, which can make certain scenes go on for what feels like forever. It felt to me like they would rather show a slow, symbolic, campy scene rather than the intenseness of how real life must've felt. I dunno. Maybe I was over-estimating this game.
All in all, there were a few scenes I thought had a very clever mechanic or idea, but I never really felt immersed in this game like I wanted to be. I loved its morals, but sadly I didn't love the game.

(Experienced in VR) No spoilers.
A unique and emotional experience that was extremely immersive in VR even though it was like a semi-cinema mode.  I loved this game as a whole and the vast majority of the different parts within it.  For me, and I would dare say any parent, it was intensly cathartic.  There was one part that was so perfectly designed to provide the perspective of a parent going through this experience I could barely make it through the game.   When I was done with that part, I don't want to spoil it, my mind was blown!   I barely made it through, it was so emotionally traumatic, so painful, so uncomfortable.   I think if I wasn't so thoroughly enveloped in the experience at the time, and had actually remembered I was using a VR headset, I would have pulled off the vive during the specific part metioned previously!  I was shaking, crying, practically balled up on the floor in agony.   Right after that sequence pulled the tear soaked Vive off my face and I thought: "WHOA, what was that!  How...wha....WOW!!!"
My poor little three year old son was excessively snuggled, hugged, and kissed a lot more than he was used to after I experienced this game!
Obviously, I highly recommend this game!   I am not sure if I have even reviewed any game before in my life!   Seriously though, it is unique, powerful, and I cherish it's influence.  I think any person, and especially any parent would feel similarly.  I plan to share with some of my friends and family.
To the parents this story involves:  Thank you, I am sure this was difficult to make.  It is beautiful, I honestly would describe it as a masterpiece!   Ironically through experiencing something where your hope was lost and tragically, dare I say violently and cruelly murdered even, this story inspires hope in people who may have to endure a similar experience.  You showed others that you can survive it.   You may not come through it the same, or without painful or crippling injury, you showed everyone it is at least possible to get through it.
I know it may not be possible but making a full VR/native VR experience of this with a few adjustments to take advantage of the increased immersion VR provides would be AMAZING!!!   Even a much shorter version that uses the core of this game would be great to see!   I loved the concept and how well this was implimented.  I just can't get over how much the VR factor seemed to matter and influence the experience for me!   It was revolutionary!

I took the two hour journey into this game, knowing full well that I was going to be going on an emotional rollar coaster.  Needless to say, I was correct.  Not only did I feel the sorrow and sadness that the Green family felt, but I also shared in the joy of Joel's laughter and beautiful ending.
As the player, you switch from third person to first person as different people.  For me, this gave me the opportunity to understand how the different characters were handeling Joel's situation.  The graphics are stunning but different from other games as they show no facial details on the characters, making you imagine what the characters are going through.  I did not know going into the game, but the voice actors were the actual family, and the adorable laughing is Joel's himself; looking at this, I would not want the voice acting any other way as it adds more sentiment to the story.
Many people are cautious about playing games with sadder topics like about cancer or death, but I think that everyone should give this game a try as it will affect anyone who plays it.  Overall, finding the correct words to describe this game as a whole is difficult as it makes you question uncertain topics on death or if there is an afterlife as well as questioning what would you do if you were in this situation.  These philosophical questions only make the game better, and it is by far one of the best games I played.  I would highly recommend playing this game with a box of tissues at your side because you will need them.

Years back, I played a game called Odin's Sphere on Playstation 2. It was unique and I'm engaged by it, but I haven't got the chance to finish it as I already gave away my Playstation 2 . On the other hand, Dust: An Elysian Tail kinda makes that compensation.
a.Gameplay
The gameplay itself is not really complicated, but I feel it is a difficult to master kinda game. Timing is essentia for a counter-attack. Long story short, it has satisfying combat and rewarding quests.
b.Story
There was a war between a powerful race, who run a campaign to dominate the world, by crushing other weaker races to their ground. But then, there was someone, who mysteriously reborn to this world with an amnesia. War and a reincarnate? Is it a sign for something great is gonna happen?
c.Graphics
Dust has a cartoonish graphic, but that doesn't it's a bad thing. In fact, the graphic is beautiful and it's HD. For those who don't like cartoon graphic, you might wanna reconsider before buying.
d.Replayability
Most of the time I enjoy the fighting, crafting better equipment, and do the side quests. There is no new game plus feature, but we can always start over with different stats build.
Verdict:

Ah yes the sequel to Danganronpa one of my favorite video games of all time. After playing the original game I naturally had a set of expectations going into the sequel. This game exceeded my expectations for a great sequel and as a result I think the sequel is better crafted than the original game.
First off, I think the sequel has a better written story that is just as engaging if not more engaging than the story in the first game. Not only is the overall story better, the cases are so much more complex and better written than the cases in the first game and as a result they feel more satisfying to solve. I also think the sequel has an overall better cast of characters because most of them have character development outside of filling out of their report cards and I became more attached to these characters as a result.
Secondly, I think the second game has a better set of minigames than the first. There are returning minigames that have been improved such as the Nonstop Debate, M.T.B Battles which now go under the name P.T.A, The Closing Argument, and Hangman's Gambit which feel more satisfying to complete than the versions in the first game. The two new minigames go under the names Rebuttal Showdown and Logic Dive. In Rebuttal Showdown a character will usually object towards one of your statements and come up with an argument of their own. You must cut through their words and come up with a counter argument which will prove that they are incorrect. In Logic Dive you must surf through a matrix obstacle course and answer a series of questions and piece them together to form an answer which will help move the case forward. Both of these minigames are very fun and satisfying to complete.
Thirdly, I love how much more expansive the island of Danganronpa 2 is compared to the high school enviroment of Danganronpa 1. I also think that Danganronpa 2 is more visually appealing because of the more varied enviroments of the individual islands. I also like the small features that they added like the ability to raise different kinds of virtual pets, hidden monokumas in each chapter, and Island Mode a mode which is a what if game mode where no murders happen and you can get different endings for each character. As a result this gives Danganronpa 2 a lot of replay value.
Lastly, Danganronpa 2 still has an amazing soundtrack which plays in all the right moments and overall has a better sound than Danganronpa 1.
Overall, Danganronpa 2 is an amazing sequel which I think surpasses the original in every way. 10/10 one of my favorite video game sequels.

I strongly recommend this title to players who remember the golden age of cRPGs. This may not be everyone's cup of tea but if you like a good old-fashioned dungeon crawl, no other modern titles can touch this.
Graphics: The graphics are good but the performance is a bit spotty. Still, if you ever wanted to try an old school dungeon crawler but were put off by the graphics, this will help you get into them.
Sound: The sound is wonderful. The music, the voices, the effects, etc all work well.
Story: These are not the kinds of games you play for story purposes. Still, if you bother to read all the text, there is a decent story there. There are even texts you can find to figure out the back story of the world or characters.
Gameplay: This is where the game scores the highest marks. There are 4 races with 3 classes per race. You assemble a team of 4 from those choices. This makes the game immensely replayable. I have just finished the second act and am already planning my Hard mode playthrough.
Also, the game has many nice touches. It has mechanics to limit rest abuse. Potion overuse is limited by hefty potion costs. Over-levelling is slightly limited by the lack of respawns.
Overally, I love this game. It was a great surprise.

I'm a big fan of The Neverhood and backed this game on Kickstarter, but somehow never came around to finish it until a few weeks ago.
In three words: I am disappointed. I'll try and explain why.
One of the first teasers we got from Doug & C:o was a song that sounded very much like the music from The Neverhood. The music in the game, however, sounds nothing like it. We also took part in livestream Q&A's where he showed us his models of the Armikrog fortress. The concept and the models were epic. The game, however, is very constrained and take place inside four towers. You barely even see the world outside, only glimpses of it. It would have been much more fun if half of the game took place inside Armikrog and the other half outside. The developers did very little with the story. The concept is epic, but the execution is very straight forward.
And so it goes. This game has enormous potential, but, somehow, it falls flat. The music is fine, but not remarkable. The characters are fun, but in the end not very interesting. The puzzles are boring, repetitive and too easy. The clay world looks great, but you don't see a lot of it.
Compared to The Neverhood, it's nothing special. Compared to other games today, it's still nothing special.
I don't really recommend the game, but even with its faults, it's still playable, at least once. But it's not mind-blowing and apart from the claymation graphics and the voice cast, there's nothing note-worthy about it. As a fan of The Neverhood, I'm still glad I played it and I'm glad that it exists, even if the feeling of "meh!" hangs over the game.
Oh, and it's definitely not worth 25 euros. I mean, come on...

Hello,
here is my review of Might & Magic X - Legacy:
first off there is no free modding kit like advertised in the shop. To use the mod kit you have to download UnityPro, after 30 days unityPro costs 1500$ once or 75$ per month to use. 32 bit users are getting screwed because they have no sound effects and are reduced to middle grafic settings. So false advertising at work in the shop.
It uses Ubisoft launcher as second layer of drm, isnt it fun? Problems with your internet connection? Bad luck you will not be able to play it.
The technical aspect of the game is horrible. On 32 bit system the game is incomplete, you get only middle textures, no party sounds, no monster sounds and other features are missing. The overall performance is bad. On 64 bit you get hight textures, animations and all but it does not look too good at all. That would be tolerable, roleplaying games are mostly about gameplay and not super grafic quality. But the performance is supbar compared to the grafic quality delivered. It runs really choppy and many systems. Even on the latest 780 gforce power rigs it does not run smooth so that is that. Performancewise it is a catastrophe.
Gameplay: 12 classes Defender, Bladedancer, Ranger, Mecenary , Freemage, Shaman, Druid, Runepriest, Barbarian, Scout, Crusader. Unfortunately ranged classes like the ranger and scout are useless farther into the game. You have very little opportunity to fight monsters at range, in melee they do next to no damage, because the main ranged stat perception does not improve the damageoutput of melee much.
The Ranger gets a point blank shot, this does not really help to improve his damage output. Magic classes are strong until the monsters get rediculous high resistance against their magic school. Most monster are resistent against a magic school or general resistent against all magic, so tough luck if your chosen magic school like fire or wind does nothing against that special pack of monsters or the boss. Magic user tend to burn your mana potion resources like mana addicts.
Defender, Bladedance and Crusader perform very good, the blade dancer with daggers buffed up by crusader spells is the best damage dealer in the game by a wide margin. He is so op that it brakes the whole class system. You will struggle without a bladedancer or barbarian as damage dealer in your party.
The whole class system is borked and unbalanced
The combat relies very much on luck and potion chucking, It does not feel very might and magic like in the later stages of the game. With a suboptimal(no bladedancer or two)  party you get one tough as nails fight after the other, in m&m series the game would throw many easy monsters at you to test your resource managementskills and use of aid spells, but not one hard battle after the other. The pacing is frustrating and not fun even on the easier adventurer mode. The encounterdesign is not good, it is one overly hard battle after the other, even for trash monsters. There is no respawn, the monster count is too low to succed by grinding. M&m x is the only rpg i know where i can't win through overleveling, so for me it is no rpg at all. Leveling your character through grinding, getting better equipment, farming gold, leveling skills is what makes a good rpg for me.
the skill system is more might and magic like. It is very rudimental and easy. You have 4 skillpoints per level to invest in your skills, after 7 15 20 skillpoints you can upgrade to a new skilltier, expert, master, grandmaster, you will get boni for each upgrade. Some skills are more powerfull then others. So magic skills get 5% 10% 15% spell penetration and more resistance against that magic school while the infamous dagger skill gets expert 1 extra attack and plus hitrate, and on grand master 2 extra attacks and plus hitrate. Combined with dual whield skill you can get a staggering amount of 6 attacks per round, your bladedancer becomes a weapon of mass destruction. Compared to this all other skills and magic school are just a joke in terms of damageoutput. You will need some skills/spells to progress like protection against status ailments, healing spells but for raw damage dagger and dual whield is greater then none.
Per levelup you get 4 attribute points you can allocate where you wish. For a seasoned rpg player it should be easy to get a deasant build. Melee 2 strength 1 perc, 1 vit, magic 1 magic, 1 vit 2 spirit in the beginning and 2 magic 1 vit 1 spirit later when you have enough manapoints (never).
I think the game release was rushed, the gameplay is boring and frustrating, the encounters are onesided against the player to the extreme, you cannot grind in a rpg!, the performance is bad even for the grafics and on excellent gaming rigs, the skills, classes, monster encounters are not balanced at all. I do not recommend this game.

Allrighty, first things first, for those that are curious : this game is not worth the money, it was a massive disappointment for me after spending years waiting for a new might and magic and overall it just feels like a downgraded version of legend of grimrock - the only upgrade being the price of the game - i will go into details below.
Also note that you have to use Uplay to start MMX
---General Stuff---
Settings used : 1600x900 windowed, everything set to high
- Game crashes a lot, for me it averaged around 1 crash per hour, sometimes crashing more frequently, sometimes less, depending on where you are in the game. (crashes more frequently at night)
- Huge FPS drops, even bigger at nighttime or when using teleporters. MMX goes down to like 1-5 FPS and apparently tries to reload all the trees and other objects in front of you, there are tons of people with that problem in the Ubisoft forums, so it is related to the game, not computer specs (my computer can handle all new games anyways)
- Annoying loading times, when loading savegames or quickloading. Can take up to 30 seconds when transitioning in and out of dungeons. (this is most fun when you are trying to navigate the optional dungeon with instant kill traps, leading to a quickload if you make a wrong move)
These three points alone ruined the game for me, because it feels like trying to play skyrim on a pentium 3.
But let's also take a look at some of the games "Key Features" from the store page.
- This is pretty misleading. Most areas are sealed off at the start and have to be opened with quest items from main quests. for example you can only access around 20% of the world before completing Act 1, around half of the areas can't be accessed before you have the swimming and teleporting abilities.
Also, most of the areas accessible are "sealed off" by monsters, so if your level is too low, you can not get past them (example : cursed ruin spectres, blackguard mages before karthal), which leads to the area also being inaccessible until you made some level progress via main quest. This makes the game feel rather linear, you can only explore freely if you are nearly done with Act 3 (aka 75% of the game) but at that point you have been to most areas anyways thanks to the main quest.
- The game has a variety of quests, sure. But are they "fun and original"? Not really. About 80% of the quests are your basic stuff, "get item xy", "bring item xy to person xy", "escort person xy to location xy", "visit dungeon xy". The rest of the quests is pretty fun though, especially the more puzzle related, for example getting asked questions about various locations in the game by a guard (you have to input the answers on your own, no multiple choice) was a neat quest.
- While this is true, they forgot to add the fact that around half of those dungeons only consist of a single room with a single monster guarding a single chest. Most of the other dungeons are pretty generic, however there are also some exceptions, like the Enigma Tower or the Tomb of Terrors that are really well made and fun.
- The ingame Beastiary shows that there are around 140 enemies in total in the game (i only found 130 by visiting every location in the game, so the rest is probably for the upcoming dlc) which sounds like a good amount of enemies. However, the developers counted every single variation of those enemies as a new creature. Lets take an example to make it more clear. Throughout the game you will fight a variety of Humans, of which there are also some swordsman. In the beginning you fight against Militia(1) and Elite Militia(2), afterwards against Militia Captain(3), Elite Militia Captain(4), and even later against Black Guard(5), Elite Black Guard(6), Black Guard Captain(7) and Elite Black Guard Captain(8). They all look the same and have the same abilities, only difference are the health, attack and defense stats, but the game counts them as 8 different creatures, so you can imagine how many "different" enemies you will have to face. Bosses are no exception, most of them just look like random normal enemies with a red name (Luke for example looks exactly like a Militia)
- Here they just forgot the most important information : to use the ModKit you have to buy Unity3D which comes at the small price of 1500$
---Gameplay---
The Difficulty Level of the game is extremely broken.
The beginning of the game is challenging and somewhat luck based, with crits being able to oneshot mages and rangers, with you not being able to cure crowd controls reliably and with enemies dodging and blocking like there is no tomorrow.
Ofcourse this also depends a lot on your party composition, but it gets easier after some level ups. In fact, if you have a healer - especially the druid - and just max out his heal (earth magic) everything becomes a piece of cake.
With both of the druids healing spells healing you for absurd amounts every turn, for 4 turns, you can take on as many enemies as you want, even the final boss can't do♥♥♥♥♥♥ This is just one of the balance flaws that the game offers.
Don't have a fire mage? Well ♥♥♥♥ you, this boss will paralyse you and only fire magic can cure it in the early stages of the game. Don't have a dark magician? Well ♥♥♥♥ you again, you are not gonna find secrets because only dark magic can detect those. (you can buy scrolls for that, but they only last 50 turns and are rather expensive early on) Have an archer? Well ♥♥♥♥ you as much as you want, but the bow is absolutely useless in this game, since enemies will just spawn in melee range every time. Good thing you can also skill daggers on an archer. Oh, daggers are the most broken weapon in the game, being able to dual wield them and getting 3 attacks per turn per dagger will 2 or 3 shot every boss later in the game when you have elemental daggers.
tl;dr = Difficulty level and class balancing is terrible
Also Side Note : You can sometimes even accept quests a second time after doing them, yup nice bug. example : get a doctor from village a to village b, afterwards get him some reagents to fix someone up. quest done. go to his house in village a, woops suddenly he is here again, giving you the same escort mission again.
---Story---
The Story could not be more casual (spoiler ahead)
There is basically no character development, they all feel like puppets saying the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over again,so you will probably stop caring about the story after the first act.

Right off the bat I have no idea why this is compared to Dark Souls; having played and beaten Demon's Souls, Bloodborne, and Dark Souls 1, 2, and 3 (feel free to look at my profile for proof), the only similarities between this game and Dark Souls is the controls. That's it. Dark Souls has many unique areas filled with carefully crafted encounters designed to test temptation and patience, and that isn't here because this game is randomly generated. Not that that's a bad thing, just that everyone saying this is like Dark Souls is wrong. It's just a buzzword like "rogue-like" or "metroidvania"
It's so sad, I want to recommend this game to everyone, but it's pretty short. Easily worth $15 or $20, but 30 is a lot for a game with little polish and little content. It's way more fun with friends, but $120 is a steep price to pay to get four friends together.
Good things now: Tight controls and interesting gameplay. Gameplay is the windup/cooldown combat of many hack and slash games, but enemies hit hard so you have to kite or dodge frequently. The levels are randomly generated so exploration is required, especially if you play solo. Enemies drop the weapons they're holding, so if you want that massive sword you have to kill the thing holding it. Enemies usually appear in hordes so gameplay revolves around crowd management, ideally with charged attacks that cause AOEs; your max stamina drops when you use these attacks, but they can be restored via rations, craftable via enemy item drops.
This game is fun and addictive if you go in with the correct expectations rather than expecting Dark Souls, which this is nothing like. Combat is a bit janky 1v1, but most combat is against hordes of enemies, so you notice it a lot less. Final boss seriously sucks though, on top of there only being 9 levels; many changes are coming to fix glitches and add more content and stuff so that's great.
HIGHLY recommended on sale.

TL;DR: 9/10. They did almost everything right. Mostly boils down to how experienced you're willing to get, because it's tricky to get used to.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is about shanking monsters to a kickass beat. The game stars a girl named Cadence whose entire character, backstory and development can be summarised by "a girl named Cadence". It is very much centered around the gameplay and music working together, which works super well in a pretty flexible way compared to other rhythm-based games. The introduction is short and doesn't add much to the game other than justifying the mechanics, so you'll pretty much have the same experience regardless.
The game takes 'turn-based' in a slightly different way. Each beat of the song is represented at the bottom of the screen and symbolises a turn each. If you miss a beat or do something you're not supposed to such as walk into a wall of stone, every enemy still gets a turn while you're standing there hoping nobody noticed that your pants just fell down. Each time you miss a beat, your current combo is broken, meaning you don't have any time to stop and read useful information as even standing still will bring it to a screeching halt.
Combo, you say?
Why yes indeed, a combo.
Maintaining the combo gives a boost to the amount of gold you pick up. Items that you pick up such as weapons or rings may give additional boosts to people who haven't accidentally thrown their flimsy shovel into a solid wall or stood around stroking themselves for too long unless they're a Monk, who for whatever reason is allowed to stroke himself for as long as he likes, which pretty much defeats the entire premise of the game.
Comparing two items is a pain, as stopping to read the item's description will cause you to lose your combo, meaning you have to do a god damn raindance around the item just to read the stats and figure out if it's going to increase your chance of winning by 0.3%.
The ENTIRE game can be controlled using only 4 buttons/keys, which is about as convenient as an enemy who you can't actually hit with default gear because it won't line up next to you. I'm looking at you, golden slime. Sure, it's an interesting mechanic, but its main flaw is replacing memorising which key to press with memorising which combination of the same keys to press. It does show appropriate key combinations beside relevant items, but stopping to read it in the middle of a room more undead than a haunted mass grave is usually not worth the time. Guessing which combination is hardly worth the risk; you may be trying to heal in the middle of battle and end up throwing your sword across the room.
Using your own (or someone else's) music instead of the original game's works pretty decently in terms of functionality, although the soundtrack is good enough that you wouldn't want to replace any of it in the first place.
Local multiplayer is an interesting feature, although playing it with a first-timer was akin to participating in a three-legged race with a monkey who has bricks for feet. Unless you're both relatively similarly experienced, one of you is going to drag the other behind. Well I wouldn't say drag behind as much as them stumbling about while you're already buying everything from the shop with a stack of gold, which for this game was about as fun as letting a monkey with bricks for feet kick you in the shins after you finished the race without him, because now neither of you are having much fun at all.
And that was after they went through incredibly short tutorial. Sure, it taught the basics, but you only really got to do everything in the tutorial once before it was over and it was clear that it didn't adequately equip a person with the experience they needed to survive unsupervised inside a padded room.
If someone wants to play for the first time on your copy of the game, let them play singeplayer first.

Like some other reviewers, I'm stumped by the hate this game has received from some folks. The haters don't seem to understand how the game industry works or have any understanding of context. For instance, for some reason there are a lot of comparisons to Dead Souls. I'm not sure why that is, if it came from the devs or a critic or what, but it's a silly comparison. Dead Souls is a AAA title produced by a huge team, with a huge budget, by a huge megastudio. HBS is a small indie studio. Granted, they are not as small or as indie as some game developers. But the Necropolis team only had 5 engineers on it.
I'm a game engineer myself, and appreciate this game on that level as well. As a player, I'm happy to pay a premium for quality indie games that break the boundaries of genres down and inject some fresh content into the market. Indie games tend to run a little more expensive relative to the content because they can't leverage the same scale that the big studios can. They have less money for sales and marketing and have fewer customers, so they have to charge a bit more to make a buck.
That said, the game isn't perfect to be fair. Some people report having beaten the game in 2-5 hours in multiplayer. I played this game in single player mode and it took me several playthroughs to survive to the last level and beat the game. So it would seem that either these players are just much better than me, coming from games like Dead Souls; or, what is also likely is that the gameplay difficulty doesn't scale for multiplayer. That certainly is a flaw. For single player, I felt the amount of content was worth the price. I wouldn't pay a mega-studio that much money for the same content, but I felt fine paying that to a smaller studio to support their efforts. Sure, given the way the levels are generated they could easily have allowed you to play to level 100, or even, in all honesty, infinitely. But do you really want to? This game isn't designed to be a 100+ hour experience. For instance, I've put I think over 500 hours into Fallout 4. This isn't Fallout 4. It's a refreshing palate cleanser between games like Fallout 4.
A better comparison than Dead Souls might be a game like The Long Dark, in my opinion. Despite their many differences, the games do share several similarities. Both games use low poly models and simple textures and shaders to maximum effect in order to offset the small team size and focus on gameplay with the resources they have available instead of burning their budget on AAA art. And honestly, it works very well, in my opinion. As with The Long Dark, I became immersed in the environment very quickly to the point that I forgot about the low-poly art completely very quickly. And in any event, I'm a fan of different art styles anyway; even AAA games use this technique sometimes, the Borderlands franchise comes to mind, for instance. That franchise of course is made by a much larger team, and so the art is much more detailed - but not on the level of more photo-realistic games. I think the amount of content, variation of enemies, quality of the art, et cetera, is well scaled to the size of the team.
I found the soundtrack refreshing and interesting, and overall enjoyed the minimalist aesthetic. If you're not into that sort of thing, maybe this game isn't for you. But that doesn't make it an objectively bad game; it's just a matter of taste.
As an engineer, I found the procedural level generation fantastic. There is no level design in this game; the levels are generated on each playthrough. The last level may be an exception, but I don't know since I've only played that level once. Single player seems much more difficult than multiplayer, so I died several times and got to really put the level generation through its paces. Actually, I'm not truly 100% sure it is procedural; it could be pseudo-random and/or modular, or a combination of all 3. Procedural generation is difficult to pull off with architectural spaces as it doesn't tend to produce a lot of right angles or grids of columns, for instance. Then again, this game has a lot of organicly shaped spaces as well. In any event, it's very well done. Little details of this system surprised me several times. There were also a few other pleasant surprises I discovered that I won't spoil for you, which I wasn't expecting.
I played this game with an XBox 360 controller, which made the most sense to me. I prefer controllers over keyboard and mouse, especially for this kind of game, so I can't speak to the keyboard and mouse controls. I know a lot of folks really like keyboard and mouse because they allow faster movement. Personally, I don't like that freedom of movement even in something like an FPS because it ruins the immersion for me to be able to turn instantaneously on a dime, which you can't do in real life. I will say the controls are a bit limited; I found myself wanting some combo attacks or something. There is also a lot of potential for parkour-like/Prince of Persia-style moves that I feel would have added a lot to the game. However, again, given the resources the team had available, I understand why these sorts of features are not present.
I also wish the codexes that are unlocked were better balanced; I found myself only ever equipping the crafting codex, because the potions it lets you craft are invaluable in single player mode. It might have been fixed by adding, say, a second codex slot, or giving crafting away for free rather than requiring a codex for it. I'm willing to overlook this, however, in light of my overall enjoyment of the game.
To be honest, I also wanted to support the team and have a lot of goodwill for the studio because I have purchased, played and enjoyed all of the Shadowrun titles they have produced, which for me also added additional context to the purchase.
Lastly, I didn't encounter a single bug playing this game. I'm sure it has a few, but I didn't encounter them. That deserves credit in my book.
In short, in my opinion, buy this game if:
- You are willing to pay a premium to smaller studios to reward them for making innovative content
- Specifically, you like HBS and want to support their continued efforts for games like Battletech and the Shadowrun franchise
- You enjoy short palate cleansers between longer gaming experiences
- You like intentionally minimalistic, low-poly or otherwise less-than-AAA quality game art in indie games like The Long Dark, Fez, Primordia, Gardenarium, Dust, et cetera, et cetera
- You have nostalgia for roguelikes but don't want your character to be wiped when you quit the game
Don't buy this game if:
- You are expecting a AAA, 100+ hour, Dead Souls-like experience
- $30 is too rich for 10 hours of single-player content, regardless of the studio or other context like economies of scale
- You don't give a toss about HBS or Battletech, Shadowrun, et cetera
- You demand only the best, AAA-level, bleeding-edge production quality for art assets in any game you might purchase
- You don't own a controller, or don't want to use one, and you don't think you would like the control layout of this game, which cannot be changed

What a gorgeous game. I got it when it was on sale, because I thought it's not really a kind of game I'd enjoy, a platformer/simple beat 'em up game with cutesy cartoonish graphics. Then I started playing, and I still wasn't convinced. The beat 'em up part seemed rather limited, a talking item, a sidekick I though I wouldn't like... but I couldn't stop playing. The graphics are great, the story is interesting enough, the moral/ethical part is believable (hey, it's a videogame), and the levels just feel so polished, everything just works. I was really surprised when I read that this game was basically made by one man, but it makes sense. Everything fits together nicely, the story, the graphics, the gameplay, the music and the voice acting.
Yes, you might not enjoy the visual style, or some of the characters, or the action part. Grinding isn't really necessary, you don't have to solve 100% of the game, I certainly didn't have the patience to find every treasure or friend, or to craft all items. I played for 20+ hours on the default settings and enjoyed almost every minute of it. The game could be even better if it had more than one linear main plot, and the player could influence it with their actions and play the good or the bad guy. The background story seems to be perfect for that. Still, an extraordinary game.

Gameplay
The Binding of Isaac is a 2D action-adventure-arcade video game where the player controls Isaac. It's not your usual platform game, it's kinda a "rogue-like" game where the player traverses through the dungeons located underneath his mother's basement and try to finish each levels without death. Gameplay style and elements mixed up the dungeons of The Legend of Zelda series with randomly procedurally generated floors. Like traditional roguelikes, death is permanent and the player is forced to restart with nothing if they die!
Visual
The art style of The Binding of Isaac is cartoonic, monsters look good and disturbing. The scenery of the levels is darky and give the feels that you are the only one there. Overall it has a lot gorish element. If you don't like blood then this game will not catch your taste!
Music
The Binding of Isaac has a very ambient,atmospheric soundtrack. Boss fights theme is a rock on! Unique effects sounds! Cooooooooooooooool ^.^
Final thoughts
I recommend to everyone this masterpiece. Isaac's is a killer,mass muderer but that's ok! :P

So this was a case of needing something to occupy myself with while my wife worked on her second and third playthroughs of Dragon Age: Inquisition, so I went through my Steam library looking for something I hadn't tried yet. After seeing that Dust was an RPG metroidvania I decided to give it a try.
After playing this I'm realizing I have a fondness for metroidvanias; while Guacamelee is the golden standard against which I will judge them all (that and Symphony of the Night, of course) it turns out Dust was pretty decent. The art style was pretty, though why all of the characters were anthropomorphized animals (aka furries) is beyond me. It didn't really help or hurt the game, but it did take me out of it a little. Why do some of them wear clothes, but your sidekick doesn't?
Speaking of your sidekick, Fidget, ohmygoodness is her voice annoying. The game is well acted, but getting past Fidget's voice is a challenge. That said the dialog is surprisingly funny. Fidget does work as decent comic relief, "Why does it have knives for hands?! KNIVES FOR HANDS!" The overall plot is meh (evil general with ambiguous motives is trying to kill off the natives - I mean Moonbloods) though I liked the section where you are helping people in Mudpot. I found those characters way more interesting.
Gameplay is solid. Standard unlock-powers-to-access-new-areas stuff (though, again, nowhere near as awesome as Guacamelee). There's also RPG stuff such as leveling up and managing gear. You can find recipes and make your own gear out of stuff you pick up from bad guys. There's a nice mechanic where if you sell an ingredient to the shopkeeper then the shop will periodically restock that ingredient, so later when you find a recipe that needs it you don't have to go grind a mob.
The game's difficulty was all over the board. Sometimes I would feel like I was burning through all of my healing items and revival crystals (generally when I pushed forward in the main questline without doing side missions/looking for all the hidden treasure chests) yet by the end I had zero trouble with the final boss. Seriously, he was a chump. Also not interesting. If you're going to have me empty a boss' health meter 4 times at least have him change forms or vary his attack pattern. Not that it mattered because, as I said, he was a chump. I didn't need to bother studying the attack pattern.
This game was a pleasant distraction for roughly 10 hours (didn't collect EVERY item, but did get most) and was well worth my time (especially considering I don't even remember buying it). That said, if you're looking for a metroidvania and you HAVEN'T played Guacamelee then, obviously, play that instead. If you're a fan of the genre then this is probably worth your time.

I was really looking forward to Armikrog.
When it was first released, I played for a few hours and hit a huge game-breaking bug (along with many many other less game-breaking bugs). At that time, there was no autosave, and I didn't know I had to manually save, because, for whatever reason, saving is hidden in the Options menu. Once I realized I had to start completely over, I decided to wait to play until it had a few patches under its belt.
Well... it's been awhile and it seems like the devs have decided not to patch it anymore. It's at least playable now, and beatable, but there are still many bugs.
Besides that, is Armikrog worth playing? Sadly, no.
There are other more in-depth reviews, but the jist of it is this:
-The puzzles aren't really that interesting (Tzurk seems to enjoy removing the levers from his machines aparently).
-The puzzles also really don't fit within the context of the environment in many cases. They're just kinda there.
-The story is incredibly thin, both narratively and environmentally.
-The repeating baby puzzle was about as enjoyable as sitting next to a crying baby on an airplane.
-The game breaks its own internal logic a lot. For example, there's a door that requires Beak Beak to sit on a button to stay open... except later in the game when it doesn't?
-The ending left me with a "that was it?" sorta feeling.
Again, I was really looking forward to Armikrog, and I wanted to like it. There were moments I enjoyed, but they were too few and far between. Ultimately, I was disappointed. (Sorry Doug and Ed!)

I'll weigh this game with yes/no answers in my opinion.  I love point-and-click adventures and was biased to like this game due to The Neverhood.
-Is this game as memorable as The Neverhood?
No, but now that that's out of the way, let's stick to questions about adventure game quality.
-Is this game created with compelling artwork?
Yes, it is impressive and fun to look at.
-Is the game world full of interesting beings/machines/locations?
No, sorry.  The game world isn't huge, you don't interact with many beings, the machines are not very fun to use, and many screens have no more than one or two interactive spots.
-Are the puzzles satisfying?
No.  They repeat in frustrating ways and most give no sense of satifaction at all.
-Is the difficulty challenging but beatable without a walkthrough?
Yes.  I found the difficulty to be about right, but I did roll my eyes when confronted with the same puzzle again and again.
-Does the game run smoothly, and is it easy to move around and use items?
No.  Expect to click in the wrong place and accidentally walk out of the room or change characters multiple times (to the dog who is used in almost exactly the same two ways repeatedly throughout the game), not to mention the weird save menu and the inability to see your inventory.
-Is it bug-free?
No.  It is pretty glitchy, especially the sound for me.  At least I never hit a game killer or lost a save.
-Is the length appropriate?
Yes.  Many people would say no, but I don't generally have this complaint about games.  Most adventure games pad out their length with tediously long conversations, and for better or worse, this game doesn't have conversations.  If I hadn't gotten stuck a couple of times, I'd place a no-hint run-through at around 5 hours or so depending on your luck and observation skills.  I did, however, notice one or two places that seemed to me to hint at unfinished areas that were never added.  I could be wrong.
-Is the story satisfying?
No.  You spend most of the game watching the story only as cryptic scenes deliberately delivered in gibberish.  Then you find the backstory written on a wall that is, although reminiscent of The Neverhood, far too long for most people to read.  There are also places that get blatantly interrupted by credits and shout-outs thrown in as Kickstarter tier rewards, especially in the story wall, making me less than satisfied for having read all that otherwise pretty creative stuff.  And it still has typos.
-Am I glad I played it?
Yes.  I can't really explain why, but this answer trumps the tally from the list above, and the game gets a thumbs-up.  I think you can see that it is a highly conditional thumbs-up.  I've played some crap adventures over the years, and I don't regret playing this one.

When I first heard about this project, I was excited that one of my favorite games, "The Neverhood", was getting a spiritual successor. After seing the other negative reviews, I was hoping that the issues wouldn't impact my experience too much. I was wrong.
What can I say that hasn't already been said? Many of the puzzles are either too easy or too annoying. A lot of the cutscenes explaining the story are in gibberish until the end of the game, meaning most of the time I had no clue what was going on. The environment feels very enclosed since most of the game takes place inside of buildings. Lastly, the game is quite short only lasting about 3-4 hours. This wouldn't be too much of a problem if the game was a bit cheaper.
As for the positives, the soundtrack is nice to listen to. Terry S. Taylor has once again proved his musical expertise. The claymation used in the game is also great to look at. The only problem is that there's not enough cutscenes showcasing it.
Overall, I would only recommend this to fans of "The Neverhood" or anyone interested in claymation. Even then, I would only recommend this during a sale. I would honestly recommend "The Neverhood" more than this. Although rare, it is a far more enjoyable experience.

This game captures a certain era and type of first-person party-based dungeon crawler that Legends of Grimrock couldn't hope to cover, and it does a good job. The Witcher 2: Assassin of Kings is the sequel to the first installment by CD Projekt Red. Making drastic if not numerous changes on the original. With a much more expansive open-world, compared to the first a very large decrease in invisible walls, much more gestures when talking to the NPC's wherever Geralt travels, fast paced combat, no more of the ridiculous click to win like in the first. The styles of fast, group, and strong have all been discarded in favor of just fast and strong attacks with either sword. Dodging is more tactical and in fact encouraged due to Geralt not being someone who can roll over an enemy A.S.A.P. Potions make a return, as well as signs, oh and armor and weapons are even more extensive and wide ranging than the select amount you gain from the first game.
All in all, the second game represents more in some ways the transformation CD Projekt Red has done, and this is displayed by Geralt's ageing self. The game in so many ways becomes unhindered by its limitations of old(usage of the old Bioware engine for the first.) Quests are even more diverse and can take a while to figure out which one you would like to do(what I mean here is there are a load of quests you can start and optional that can converge, so u can do a part of a quest here while also doing another part of another quest here and perhaps another). It's a complicated jumble of chemicals mixed into one potion with a wide variety of effects!(Get the pun?)
Nevertheless the game also gives two major paths to follow that can be completed in one play through for one path and another play through for the other. And yet if you choose to play a third play through you will(I can guarantee you will make some changes from your 1st and 2nd play through to see what the game has to offer). Much of my game play was spent either using quick save and quick load to see how a scene will play out the way i'm most comfortable with my decisions I made as well as listening to the crowd of NPC's muttering about their life in dreary detail that contain both morbid, fascinating, gritty detail of events past and present. All, in turn create a vibrant atmosphere that game shares with the player to behold in the eyes and body of Geralt of Rivia.
*Below is a short but detailed account of the game play mechanics.
Magic, for a Witcher is comprised of 5 basic spells(In Witcher terms they're called signs), you are able to utilize when you first start the Witcher 2.
The Fire power or Igni is a spray of well fire to a directed enemy of which can burn an enemy or distract them by having to fan out the flames on their bodies.
The Force power(I'm not joking) or the Aard sign gives you literally force powers to either push, stun, or break handy(breakable walls).
The Shield power(my personal favorite: because it allows me to charge madly on my enemies) or Quen is an electrical shield conjured around your body in a 360 degree radius which is displayed as flying blue sparks (Not a bloody eye-sore of a yellow shield around your character). Which WILL SAVE YOU(notice the caps?) when attacked by monsters, humans, or traps, it doesn't give you 100% protection from snarky people that love to toy with you nor does it give you invincibility to allow yourself to go crazy on the enemies regardless of health. No The Quen merely gives you a 1 free chance to avoid being damaged. Though you can recast it with Vigor(Basically, how many times you can use any sign[pro-tip: upgrade yourself for more vigor=more spells]).
The Trap spell or Yrden is a semi-invisible trap(Don't worry enemies don't see it) laid on the ground to essentially immobilize a single enemy for "x" amount of times. This sign can be upgraded to have two traps and even slow enemies(provided you can upgrade it).
And last but not the least the Mind Spell or the Axii Sign. Basically what this sign does is brainwash an enemy to fight for you. To be honest i rarely used this spell(apart from using it in conversations for more details huehuehue....) because of it's inconsistency to really work as intended. For example: when cast on an enemy the mind controlled enemy can't seem to detect i'm an ally and thus attacks wildly to either their comrades or me. Which is quite troublesome to deal with a crazier enemy.
While the Signs are essential in turning the flow of battle in your favor, one must also remember to use the right swords and also the right potions to aid you in combat. While the signs are helpful in many ways, it does not mean that you can rely solely on magic to save you. For at the end of the day you have low health, no vigor to use signs, and forgoing a potion in favor of dashing through will you realize "Perhaps I should've thought this more thoroughly."
- a random child says.
Geralt doesn't lose them if ever(except if he's captured and well detained without weapons then I guess you could say he temporarily lost them). However! The two swords in Geralt's disposal are vital in his hands because:
1: Steel sword deals with the bigoted humans foolish enough to cross a Witcher's path. So please advise children not to learn this at home lest they too carry two swords for fun. And accidently maim a neighbor/acquaintance in a game.
2: Silver sword deals with the wild creatures that seek to disrupt every nook and cranny wherever Geralt goes. In Swamps, jungles, caves, dark caves, and more. It is essential for Geralt to carry a silver sword for only silver can hurt a monster(except humans you need only steel for that). Honestly, Geralt needs not a silver sword, but fate loves to kick his pants and send every raging monster after him whenever he ventures beyond a town's borders. To be frank, it's as if Geralt is a Monster slayer than a Witcher!(Though Witcher does count as a monster hunter I think...)
In any case, that is why he carries two swords! Just so yall can remember that when you wonder "Huh, so that's why he has two swords."

Powerful stuff awaits. What I mean by powerful stuff is how Geralt can be powerful(I bet your eyes are glued here now haha), And I'll tell you his wee li'l secret. Potions, crafting, decisions, and a slice of tactical pies.
For starters potions like the first game are essential to the game play, for not only can they aid you in dark, very dark caves, but enhance Geralt's abilities of vigor regeneration, health regeneration or buffing his damage for either swords with oils or runes, It is important to note you cannot overdose in so many buff potions because you can only drink 3(you can drink more if upgraded), but some potions carry a negative effect in favor of boosting an ability to keep that in mind. To remedy this I recommend a healthy dose of reading books in crafting diagrams to make traps, bombs, daggers, to also aid you. Making you one hell of a versatile fighter. It is also important to note of crafting, because it WILL be helpful in upgrading your White main character you control over. Making you last longer in combat while giving special buffs huehuehue.
And last but not the least most important thing of all are the choices you make! Yes yes yes, your probably eye-rolling me right now given the game says it's an RPG, but i cannot stress this enough because your decisions will have MAJOR COSEQUENCES. So think carefully and for goodness sake make use of the quick save and quick load to witness what the game has to offer. Because playing one play through on 1 path isn't enough and only marginally covers 50% of what the game has to offer. So again choose wisely.

That Dragon, Cancer is an interesting attempt to share the experience of seeing your child suffer from cancer. It's more like an interactive movie than a traditional video game, which makes sense for this story. I liked the way the game incorporated a mix of video game formats (like a racing game and platformer), though the majority is point and click.
I expected this game would make me feel as if I personally had a child with cancer, although perhaps that was a ridiculously high bar to set. In the end, I felt like I better understood the experience of one family's battle with childhood cancer. I sympathized but couldn't really empathize. This was particularly true because the parents in the game are strong Christians, and I am not very religious. This game is one family's story, not any family's story - which I say mainly to help set others' expectations.
I enjoyed the game overall and felt a range of emotions reinforced by the music and art. I'm glad I picked it up on sale and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys story-rich games or indie innovations.

Let me qualify my review: I'm a first-time father with (as of this writing) a 7 month old daughter. It is through that lens that I played this.
It's impossible to overstate how heavy and depressing this game is. I suppose if you're knowingly playing a game about a child with cancer, this is not a surprise, but I found it to be unflinchingly devastating even knowing that and setting my expectations appropriately. The scene where the father is trying to calm his very sick boy and failing is far too real for my liking. I sincerely hope I never experience anything like this.
It's also worth mentioning that this is a "walking simulator" - there's no real gameplay here, you merely exist to move the story along. It's true that there are some mini-games - a racing one and a metroidvania bit, but they require no skill and offer no reward other than doing them.
I know that most people deal with and process grief in their own way, and in that light, I don't begrudge anyone's path through such a horrible event.
That said, the game takes on a very, very strong religious tone about halfway through, and I found it offputting. In way, this was a relief, because it allowed me to take my focus off the true grief of the game's events and turn it into eye-rolling at the game designers. I found it ham-fisted and at odds with everything else going on. Take out the parables about Jesus, Lazarus, the Jesus in the boat with disciples thing, and the game would take on a much more univeral tone.
But as I say, I don't begrudge anyone their own personal path through such an event. If it brought them peace, more power to them.
With that in mind, I'd recomment this with the caveat that the strong Christian preaching may take you wholly out of the experience at key times. Also, be absolutely sure that you're ready to experience a magnitude of grief unlike most anything else.
I'd give this a 3/5. Unforgettable, but with a few deep flaws.
