Behind a deceptively simple premise hides one of the more engaging, in-depth, and downright addictive top-down/endless shooters I’ve ever played.
Start game, click mouse, shoot zombies, last until you die. On paper this is what the game appears like but a well-rounded and extensive list of gameplay altering perks to choose from allows each player to cater their character to a very specific combat style. With every wave of enemies that passes you gain a little more of a specialty for dealing out damage, but of course the difficulty ramps up as well. A fast frenetic pace means that boredom never sets in as you’re either going to succeed until you find yourself neck-deep in enemies, or you’re going to fail in which case you can instantly try again; getting right back into the meat of the action while trying a completely different build of perks.
Perhaps not the prettiest game but good enough for what it wants to do and very well optimized.  I’ve played it on several PC’s including an old clunker that didn’t even meet the minimum specs and it still ran fine. Needless to say on a modern gaming rig there’s no problems at all, even during the most hectic moments.
A long list of achievements (for those that care) and a decent match-making service provide longevity beyond what the base game offers (which is already quite extensive). Add in its low entry price and a committed fan-base and you have a recipe for one of the best hidden gems I’ve managed to find in recent memory.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a truly special game.
Done in the style of hand-drawn animation, while playing it I couldn't help feeling like I was back in my living room watching the Saturday morning caroons of my youth.  I did experience some display issues (flickering on the screen) but if you're like me, a child of the 80's,  and you experience it, I recommend pretending that you're just watching a well-worn VHS tape.  For me, that just added to the experience and even made it all the more endearing.
The story is compelling and you'll likely get sucked in and want to play this exclusively until you get through it.  There are some fun Easter Eggs that you can unlock as you go along as well.  Additionally, the progression is nicely paced between leveling up and the gear that becomes available throughout - I never felt like Neo until the very end despite rarely feeling like I was in danger of dying.
I chose not to 100% this game becuase I wanted to save myself some aggravation.  The collectables can be quite challenging to get (or even to find) but there is a wealth of information out there online should you choose to go that route.
Between the nostalgic feel and comfortable gameplay, I would recommend this game to anyone.

I'm a huge fan of Might and Magic IV and V, which Legacy is heavily inspired by. Indeed, in many ways this is almost MMIV/V with 3D graphics, and more text.
That said, while MMX is definitely fun, it lacks the sense of humour and scale of its predecessors. MMIV/V had you exploring an entire planet, while Legacy keeps you on a single archapeligo. Despite the fact that there's still lots to explore, this does make everything feel oddly cramped. While the cities in X are about as far apart as those in IV and V, they feel much closer (and there's fewer of 'em). It's a minor issue, really, but it kinda sums up the game: The same as what came before, but somehow cramped.
As for the style: The old Might and Magic games didn't take themselves at all seriously. Well over 3/4 of the people you talk to were jokes. X is much more serious. It certainly has jokes, but there are fewer of them, replaced with lots of text. Usually I love lots of text in games, but here there are so many characters and factions to keep track of (and it definitely helps to have played Heroes VI by the same devs and set in the same world) that it becomes hard to really care about them, which is a shame, because the actual plot has loads of potential.
All-in-all, it's a buy if you like games such as Legend of Grimrock (though that's real time to MMX's turn based), Etrian Odyssey, or the old Might and Magic titles, then it's well worth a buy. If the idea of slowly working your way through a dungeon where one bad decision or unlucky chance can doom you, then this ain't for you.

This game is simultaneously a more complicated version of Galactic Civilizations 3 and a dumbed-down version of Europa Universalis 4/Crusader Kings 2.
It introduces a lot of new concepts to the typical Paradox strategy game formula, all of which are borrowed from 4x titles, such as population, ship customization (though not as in-depth as other 4x space titles), happiness levels, et cetera. These are all new to the series, if one considers Paradox grand strategy to be a series, but they're not new to strategy gamers. That's not to say this is a bad thing; it's certainly a welcome "starting point" for a first-time Paradox strategy player. It's not too complicated to be a good entry point, but it's certainly not detailed enough to be able to jump straight into one of the other titles, such as EU4 or CK2, without still needing to do quite a bit of learning - though the player will certainly have a decent head start!
As for Stellaris itself, it's pretty great. Creating a race is fun, and while surveying systems can get a little tedious at the beginning, you really grow attached to your neighboring systems in doing so, and you really feel possessive over them as soon as you find your first neighbor. Keep an eye on those mineral levels, too! I've found, personally, minerals to be way more important than energy credits. Don't forget to keep upgrading your fleets with your new technologies, either!
In typical Paradox fashion, I'm sure that a slew of expansions are sure to release every few months for the next two or three years and I'm excited to see what they do with the game as it is now, already full of things to do.

This is not a game for all gamers.
Action-oriented RPG gamers will find something more valuable -and probably more challenging- on the Dark Soul's path.
Story-driven RPG gamers will get upset with the underdevelopment of certain fabulous and then dismissed characters.
Adventure-fueled RPG gamers will probably spend hours gathering tons of loot after hours to battle against the menu's map.
So why should I recommend you Assassins of Kings?
Because the world feels REAL both in their beauty and in their ugliness, a living, breathing world.
Because it is SO well written and putting Jaskier as the narrator is one of the greatest literary high-fantasy ideas ever conceived.
Because the amount of effort put by hundreds of people in and out of CDProjekt shows in every pixel of it, technicalities and menues interactions aside.
It is easier to say that Assassins of Kings is more of a cinematic experience than a game (think of Mass Effect as a prime example), specially compared with The Witcher 1 which is more on the novel's line when it comes to storytelling (and equal to none when it comes to gameplay).
Mind you: as a gamer, some technical things will heavily disappoint you.
If you are able to see yourself as an actor rather than a gamer, you'll probably understand lots of things about this unique world and their characters.
I'm not trying to scare you off this game, on the contrary...
Every single minute of it must be your personal choice.
THERE is when the magic happens.
Have fun.

If you're looking for that one last cheap game during the Steam Winter Sales, and you like exploration games, you should give this game a try.
Note that the game is only about 2+ hours long and there's nothing to do outside of exploration. That said, the game seems to be based on Unreal engine 4 tech but with more of a cell-shaded type of look. The lighting and underwaterworld as a whole is very convincing and can sometimes be surprisingly assaulting on the senses (in a good way). Without spoiling anything, the scenes with 1000's upon 1000's of fish swimming around, each seemingly individually lit, must impress anyone who sees them for the very first time (unless you hate fish). The music is appropriate and varies during the six or so chapters, as are the sounds. Controls are simple enough with options for inverted (standard) controls. Note that I played with a controller. Performance of the game was great, even with the highest settings (running on an RX480 8GB) and VRAM usage did seem to over around only 2GB or so (great news for those with older graphic cards).
I usually am not very much into indie titles but was interested in this game after reading some reviews online and here on Steam. this is a serene experience that is all about exploration (although very linear), and suggestive story-telling through images and sound. And it does a great job at that.
In my opinion, the regular price of €20 is a bit steep but the current Winter Sales price of €5,99 feels just right to me.

Necropolis feels very much like someone took everything DSP whinged about the Souls series for, verbatim, and made that into a design document to make this game from. Slap onto that some 2004 spriterip webcomic level humour and some mind-blowingly /strange/ design choices, and you get something that would feel like a stretch at £10, let alone -£23-.
I say strange because, think about this. What kind of person would think "You know what a Souls-like Rogue-lite needs? Respawning enemies." And what unfortunate arguably humanoid entity would approve the pause screen not actually pausing the game, while said enemies continue to respawn in close enough proximity to you to trigger their attacks? In a perma-death game.
Enemies will shamelessly spawn within camera view within a metre of your character, and the lack of variety quickly makes every one a slog. You'll be well acquainted with A) Screaming zombies who fight like humans, B) Robots that fight like humans and C), Spiders after a single hour of play. Occasionally a larger version of one of these three will appear. More often many of those larger versions will appear and wedge you into their hit-chains, where a stamina bar that over time permanently depletes will slowly doom you to losing all progress. This is then followed by the ever-present 'narrator' saying something passive aggressive and unfunny.
Speaking of, it's clear they weren't trying to go for anything interesting, and we should accept that that's fine. Sometimes we have to aspire to Fallout 3, and there's nothing wrong with that. But playing for more than an hour will show all the achingly stale memegenerator .com-tier humour the programmers communal lunch-break had to offer, and it will repeat quickly enough. Unfortunately, everything carries a sentence talking about how someone with a silly name was a doody-head, most especially when that space could be filled with important information about stats or the items actual purpose.
In Necropolis, you have a stamina bar that functions much like the one from the Souls games series. It temporarily depletes on attacking, dodging, running and blocking attacks with your shield. Unlike Souls however, your maximum stamina also depletes on top of that passively until you very slowly eat one of the many items from it's throw-it-in crafting system. Does this ever become a worthwhile issue? I am tempted to say no as you gather vast amounts of resources quickly, but with how many enemies the game can sometimes respawn midcombat, it's uncertain. Performing heavy attacks takes larger chunks out of this maximum cap, and using charge attacks will slice huge amounts off, actively punishing you for doing anything but kiting with tiny slashes here and there.
On the topic of combat, you have a wide variety of weapons to choose from with differing stats and random enchants, which the game tells you nothing about. If one is upset by the complexity of styles in the Souls series, then they will find these are very thoughtfully contained to 3 styles; a Heavy style that knocks down every enemy type, a Medium style that you will pass over for the Heavy, and a Fast style that lets you do less total damage than the Heavy at a higher speed with no knockdowns. If you were worried that the Heavy might ask you to sacrifice something for its power, fear not, since every weapon is held one-handed alongside a shield. You might sometimes find a ranged weapon that depletes your actual stamina meter, but you'll be switching back to a shield in no time. It doesn't matter which, they appear to be all the same.
Even the level design suffers, being made of generated chunks fixed together at points. This coupled with the surface-level sleekness in its graphical style leads to a tediously large, frustrating to navigate series of mazes that will have you backtracking only to suffer one of the (somewhat common) performance hitches, suddenly swinging free of it and becoming lost.
All petty jokes and memery aside, this just kind of feels like a game that took many many ideas from Souls, but doesn't consider why it does those things in the first place. Somewhere in the muck is the potential for a fantastic 4-player dungeon delver, but it's smothered by irritating decisions, frustrating design and trudging, repetitive gameplay.
For £23, don't even consider it, especially since it appears the devs are looking to make paid expansions.

This game is so good, it ruined my life. I actually pre-ordered this on Stardock before it was on Steam and *totally* forgot about it, which worked out for me I guess since there's like a zillion user-made ships now.
The ship design system is better than it was in GC2, and there's LOTS of nice ships on the workshop (personally I love using the Covenant ship hulls from the Halo series for my fleet), but the vanilla ship designs look better as well.
The mining system is a general improvement over GC2, taking cues from games like Endless Space that have strategic resources instead of just building a facility on every asteroid to get extra production value on planets. Another point on the mining, the black holes and nebulae/gas clouds/radiation storms are a nice touch to break up the map design.
The minor races also seem to be improved over GC2, they feel a lot more fleshed-out now rather than just generic civs you beat up and take the lunch money of. I haven't yet tried Revenge of the Snathi, but it certainly looks like some good silly fun.
The only complaints I can really think of at present are the planets and losing excess research points; I feel like there might have been more variety to palents in GC2, but that could just be nostalgia goggles. Also, as others have said the game will often place your colony capital in stupid or entirely useless locations (like a tile with no adjacent tiles). If you generate more RP in a turn than you need to finish whatever you're researching, the rest just go into oblivion, rather than being saved up. This is a common problem for me since I usually play research-oriented civs, maybe it's less noticible if you play a military/production focused civ like the Drengin.
Edit: I totally forgot, Espionage didn't return from GC2, which was a little bit disappointing but not a huge deal to me.
But overall, this game is pretty great and gets an 8/8 from me, mate. That said, you should probably wait until it's on sale, unless you're *really* itching for a 4x game with a good ship designer and fancy graphics.

This game shows how you can still do some impressive stuff in two dimensions. The animations are wonderful, and there's so much fun to be had while slashing down enemies and finding loot around. The story itself is well developed and has several sidequests which make sense, and while there aren't dozens of them, they provide several hours of gameplay along with the main storyline.
Graphic (and sound/music) wise this game is really well done, mostly in a way that makes it fun to watch and play through rather than for sheer beauty, but overall all of the characters and the places are well designed and stand out perfectly. If anything, sometimes the gameplay is repetitive, but that has mostly to do with the platform design rather than with the plot or the level design (imho), as the 2D nature of the game has some limits, but in the end the game makes really a lot to overcome each of its dimensional limits.
For that matter, the amount and quality of both combos and movements of Dust make it fun to even just watch the character jumping in the air!
In fact, while fighting you can also count on Fidget abilities, and some rings/pendants/etc greatly improve Fidget's combat skills, up to a point that lets you draw the fight style that suits you the most.
RPG wise, this game allows you to craft several items but most of the crafting makes use of loot you can only find while killing enemies. That in turn makes for a solid system (as much as some backtracking) as it pushes you to play each area throughout, instead of buying most of what you need from a merchant.
Overall, a really good game and especially a really good 2D platformer (with rpg elements), a good plot and a fighting system that makes for a lot of fun.

This game probably started F2P now it seems more P2W. It gives you that same mobile feel where there are multiple currencies and the only ones that matter are the gems.
I read a few things about how this was better  than overwatch and though on a fundamental side they are both FPS games with heros. I don't feel like they are enough a like to compare.
The game is not polished at all though it is still in BETA which wouldn't bother me if there wasn't so many options for micro transactions. I have played other F2P games like LOL and spent money on them and also other games where it is a grind to get things, but in LOL the things like RUNES can be used across a range of Characters. In Paladins you purchase cards for each individual hero.
So, if you buy a hero you start over.
The fact that the card system and the Epic stats(?) that you pick at the beginning are one currency and the characters are another then you have the gems you buy with real money as a third.
It wouldn't be as bad if the cards were not so important in the game. They completely change how your character is played and its strength and after awhile they feel under powered with out the correct ones.
On gameplay side i feel like it could be a unique game. The matches are way to short for my liking and the hit boxes are HUGE  or maybe its the lag in the kill cams, but you can obviously see huge gaps in crosshair placement and when people are getting hit markers. The game has it share of bugs and glitches and the player base just isn't there so you end up with either slow ques are people with huge range of skill levels.
Pros
+Cool concept with what could be a fun game
+Free as long as you don't mind grinding while getting destroyed
+Looks like they are making a large hero list
Cons
- buggy with some more annoying than game breaking things.
- Card system is a bit much having to grind huge amounts of currency to buy a very small amount of cards for one character. Then if you get a new character you have to repeat the process on it.
- P2W feel
- low player numbers so you get thrown in with a range of player skill levels.
It is free try it if you want. Just wasn't for me.

I am a great fan of Neverhood and as most of people who backed the game on Kickstarter, we expected at least to see the spiritual successor. No such luck. No luck at all.
The game is too short, if you're good at adventures and concetrate a bit, you can finish it quickly. Okay, perhaps creators offered something other in exchange for short playtime.
Good story? Nope, it's short and not interesting.
Okay, is the music good? It's decent, but like everything else in this game, it feels slacked off. Which is suprising, seeing how the same guy composed the soundtrack for this game as for the Neverhood.
How about cutscenes? Are there any funny movies? Nope, they' are short and often don't contribute much. And there is too small number of them.
Okay, final try : the puzzles, are they any good?
No. They repeat themselves too often, and this game is actually the sum of three of four types of puzzles. Most of the puzzles are actually asking from you to write a thing down here, and enter it there. They aren't demanding. What's even worse, one of the last puzzles in the game is actually totally random, asking from you to click on something you wouldn't even do, because you tried it before with Tommynaut and with his dog and it gave no result. So, near the end of the game, thing that doesn't work suddenly works. That's some design.
I can't say that this game is bad. It's not bad, but it's lacking. It feels rushed and like every corner was cut so it would get done. It's not worth it's price. Perhaps if it was 5-10 bucks it wouldn't be too much.
I wasn't really sure whether to recommend this game or not. But damn, it's disappointing.

is my favorite game ever, so I was excited by the news of this project a few years ago.  When
was finally released in its patently unfinished initial state, I decided that I would wait at least a year before playing it, in the hopes that my experience would not be spoiled like so many others'.  When it went on sale last weekend, I took the opportunity to snap it up and play it at last.
I was immediately struck by the obvious necessity of features not in the original release, especially the hotspot indicators for the cursor and in "Beaky-Vision".
had no need for anything like that, but
is both more complicated and more finicky, and I occasionally found myself having to waggle the cursor around what I knew needed clicking until I found where I needed to click.  (The "octovators" were frequent offenders in this regard).  Without these helpful indicators, I would have been stymied uselessly; for example, I doubt that it would ever have occurred to me to click the octovators while in Beaky-Vision without the giant, obvious spirals swirling around them.
As it is, I still managed to trip myself up on things like this three times.  Between a missed hotspot, neglect of an irritatingly arbitrary mechanic (for

reason, only Beak-Beak is allowed to press buttons placed low on the walls, and one of them was at the end of an upward-sloping floor that threw off my sense of its height), and a baffling phantom hotspot, I wasted hours trekking back and and forth between rooms, trying different combinations of levers I'd already pulled and buttons I'd already pushed, combing empty areas for items I might have missed.  One hallway infuriatingly had an open skylight and a black suction hose that, while both tantalizing, turned out to be completely superfluous.  Finally, when I got to the phantom hotspot, I actually started over completely, convinced that I'd triggered a game-breaking glitch.
Unfortunately, once I'd surmounted these obstacles, they turned out to be the only real difficulty I had playing the game.  I had no problem blowing through the rest of it, and I even played through it again in the same sitting for good measure.  With the exception of the
(the sole part of the game that required any real analysis), the puzzles all have immediately obvious solutions, and mechanics are repeated to exhaustion.  See a
the second, third, or fourth time, and you immediately know that you'll be spending a few perfunctory minutes with Beak-Beak and
before you can move on.  Detached cranks and levers are littered all over Armikrog, to the point that it's a surprise to find one already in its place.  (It was in one of these cases that the phantom hotspot occurred: I had picked up a lever, and there was a socket that I could click on, but Tommynaut wouldn't put the lever in.  It turned out to be for a different socket; why I was able to click on that one at all is still a mystery.)  It's even easier on replay, as the answers to the symbol-based puzzles (barring one near the beginning) aren't even randomized - a feature that
managed twenty years ago!
Additionally, the structure of the game is very linear compared to
's entertaining tangles, with each tower discrete, self-contained, and visited in sequence.  Between this, the aforementioned ease and repetition, and the regrettable absence of
's distinctive first-person traveling,
oddly feels smaller than its predecessor, despite almost certainly being larger in absolute terms of space.
All of this having been said, while the gameplay overall fails to approach
's standard (or that of most good adventure games, to be completely frank), there are some intriguing elements that save it from outright mediocrity.  Beak-Beak, while not integrated as well as he could have been, still provides an entertaining dynamic in his capable assistance of Tommynaut.  He can sit on buttons, crawl through tunnels, and even fly in certain areas, and where he can venture on his own away from Tommynaut, his Beaky-Vision presents the world through a swirling, hazy lens that, while purely cosmetic, is still pretty cool to see.  The game also does a few entertaining things with space, like
or
.  And while it was trivial to figure out, one puzzle built around colored light remained entertaining to solve through all three of my playthroughs.
Ultimately, though, the gameplay (at its best or worst) is trumped on some level by Armikrog itself.  While less compelling as a whole than the Neverhood, I have to admit that it's a more visually impressive setting on a screen-by-screen basis.  As lovely as the Neverhood is, Armikrog simply has more to look at, with hardly a wall, floor, or ceiling not adorned with some striking detail or texture, and it's crafted with finer skill.  Next to
's flashy flair,
lumpy surfaces and solid colors look downright crude.
's music is also impressive, if not as memorably kooky as that in
or even
.  While it has its crazy moments, it's mostly subdued and occasionally downbeat, especially later in the game.  Surprisingly, it's the softer, sadder tracks that work best; songs like "Nocturne in Blue" or "Mother Is Near" are genuinely emotional in a way that you'd be hard-pressed to find on the earlier soundtracks, and they give the game's dramatic inclinations a touch of much-needed gravitas.
"Much-needed" because they unfortunately don't do a whole lot to generate it themselves.  The backstory, whose bulk is told through a dishearteningly typo-riddled counterpart to
's Hall of Records and whose remainder is related by
is most interesting when it is furthest from Armikrog itself; initially promising elements like
gradually become displaced by
and eventually
as the plot approaches the present, and no matter how much metaphysical weirdness it's strained through, there's nothing going on after the written account ends that hasn't been done countless times before.
used basic ideas to tell a simple story;
uses comparatively sophisticated ideas to tell an ultimately
story, and that's not a good change.  The game initially makes a point of being mysterious about its details, but they're compelling only for as long as they're hidden away.
Still, I don't want to be too hard on
, especially given all the trouble that it and its creators have been through.  It doesn't cut it as a follow-up to
or even really as an adventure game in its own right, but the power and charm of its spectacle are undeniable, and it's worth playing through to at least experience its fantastic visuals and music.  It might sound shallow, but they really are that special.  In the end, I have to recommend it on that basis, with the extremely strong caveat that it should be nobody's introduction to
- play that timeless classic, then enjoy this game as the pleasant expansion that it is.

I am NOT going to spoil the story for DR2GD for two reasons:
I can, however, summarize the basic gist of the story so that you know what you are in for. If you've played the first Danganronpa game, then you know what is basically going to happen:
The story is kinda sad, honestly. The main game is split into two styles: Daily Life and Deadly Life.
Daily Life is when you can walk around the island and talk to the other students! You can use these opportunities to give them gifts that you can buy with coins that you collect from
! By giving characters gifts, you can become closer to them, and learn more information about them. A lot of these characters are very interesting, so I think you'll find at least one person that you'de like to get to know better! However, becoming friends with characters DOES NOT CHANGE THE OUTCOME OF THE MURDERS! You may end up becoming friends with someone who gets killed or is the killer! Your heart may be broken by this, and it sucks! You'll sometimes be trying to get to know everything about someone to get an achievment or just to know them as another character, BUT THEY'LL DIE BEFORE YOU EVEN GET THE CHANCE!
Spoiler about this game mechanic:
The second part of the gameplay is the Deadly Life. Deadly Life is the investigation part that happens after a body has been discovered. You will look for clues and then participate in a class trial to find the true killer! Finding evidence involves
walking around, but is mostly just pointing and clicking things in rooms that pertain to the case. The class trail is a bunch of minigames that revolve around everyone trying to answer questions about the case, defend themselves, or piece together the events of the case. Most of this is also pointing and clicking, but there are sometimes word-puzzles, multiple choice questions, a platformer-decision-making minigame, and rhythm games.
This game involves a lot of clicking. You will sometimes use the keyboard to get to the main menu and walk around, but most of the game is clicking.
Another big part of the game is reading! Please be able to read when playing this game! ALSO BE READY TO SIT THROUGH A LOT OF DIALOGUE! If you are the kind of person who hates cutscenes and would rather play the game, ignore the urge to skip through text. THE DIALOGUE IS IMPORTANT! Stellaris is a 4x/Grand Strategy game from Paradox.  Fans of other Paradox titles such as Crusader Kings II or Europa Unversalis IV will enjoy this game.  While not perfect I find this game to be rock solid so far. I haven't run into many bugs and none of them have been game killers.  Ethos and traits give a large variation to the races you can create, which supports a large number of personal playstyles.  Everything from ruthless space slavers bent on galatic conquest to alien space hippys can be created.
There isn't really anything in the game I dislike, it's more that I hope Paradox improves on in follow up DLC's. The areas I find a little lacking is Diplomacy/Trade. Both are lumped into one window and are simple. Its not bad just simple. The other aspect which I think needs improvement is the limit on managable planets. Your can manage 5 planets before penalties kick in. Now you can run a few overr that limit and its not a big deal but I can already see that when I'm deeper into the game splitting my planets into various sectors could become a pita. The game is highly moddable so there is already a mod getting rid of the limit and allowing sectors as you wish.
All in all this is a rock solid game and given Paradox's habit of improving their games with DLC's gives me a positive outlook on Stellaris going forward. I would recommend this game to any strategy fan.

This is not a game for all gamers.
Action-oriented RPG gamers will find something more valuable -and probably more challenging- on the Dark Soul's path.
Story-driven RPG gamers will get upset with the underdevelopment of certain fabulous and then dismissed characters.
Adventure-fueled RPG gamers will probably spend hours gathering tons of loot after hours to battle against the menu's map.
So why should I recommend you Assassins of Kings?
Because the world feels REAL both in their beauty and in their ugliness, a living, breathing world.
Because it is SO well written and putting Jaskier as the narrator is one of the greatest literary high-fantasy ideas ever conceived.
Because the amount of effort put by hundreds of people in and out of CDProjekt shows in every pixel of it, technicalities and menues interactions aside.
It is easier to say that Assassins of Kings is more of a cinematic experience than a game (think of Mass Effect as a prime example), specially compared with The Witcher 1 which is more on the novel's line when it comes to storytelling (and equal to none when it comes to gameplay).
Mind you: as a gamer, some technical things will heavily disappoint you.
If you are able to see yourself as an actor rather than a gamer, you'll probably understand lots of things about this unique world and their characters.
I'm not trying to scare you off this game, on the contrary...
Every single minute of it must be your personal choice.
THERE is when the magic happens.
Have fun.

If you're looking for that one last cheap game during the Steam Winter Sales, and you like exploration games, you should give this game a try.
Note that the game is only about 2+ hours long and there's nothing to do outside of exploration. That said, the game seems to be based on Unreal engine 4 tech but with more of a cell-shaded type of look. The lighting and underwaterworld as a whole is very convincing and can sometimes be surprisingly assaulting on the senses (in a good way). Without spoiling anything, the scenes with 1000's upon 1000's of fish swimming around, each seemingly individually lit, must impress anyone who sees them for the very first time (unless you hate fish). The music is appropriate and varies during the six or so chapters, as are the sounds. Controls are simple enough with options for inverted (standard) controls. Note that I played with a controller. Performance of the game was great, even with the highest settings (running on an RX480 8GB) and VRAM usage did seem to over around only 2GB or so (great news for those with older graphic cards).
I usually am not very much into indie titles but was interested in this game after reading some reviews online and here on Steam. this is a serene experience that is all about exploration (although very linear), and suggestive story-telling through images and sound. And it does a great job at that.
In my opinion, the regular price of €20 is a bit steep but the current Winter Sales price of €5,99 feels just right to me.

Necropolis is a A Dark Souls-like game with procedurally generated dungeons in an atmospheric world.
The first thing I want to say is if you enjoy Dark souls, Lords of the Fallen or any other similar game, you know what you're getting into with this game. It plays very similarly in a lot of aspects. Although simpler, and not in a bad way.
When it comes to melee combat, you can choose between a weak but fast attack, or a strong but slow one. On top of that, you can charge both to unleash a deadly combo of very powerful hits.
However, none of that is free. You have a stamina bar that recharges very quickly, but slow enough to not allow you to spam attacks. As you sprint, jump and attack your character will become exhausted. This reduces the size of your stamina bar, and in turn reducing the amount of stamina you can recharge. You can increase your stamina bar back to normal by eating food. Depending on the food, you will increase more or less stamina. You may also take a risk and eat rotten food, which will not grant you much stamina, and has a chance of making your character vomit, leaving you vulnerable to attack, but it's a good option for desperate situations.
You also have the ability to dodge attacks, as well as block them with you shield, or shield bash enemies to knock them over. You may also replace your shield with projectile weapons.
As mentioned earlier, this game is simpler than most, and I personally enjoy it. You don't have to spend time upgrading yourself, or checking the stats of weapons and gear. Everything is split into tiers. If you find a sword that is tier 2, it's better than your tier 1 weapon. Simple as that. Now you can simply decide based on looks, or small custom attributes like fire effects on the weapon.
So the game is relatively rogue-like in the sense that every time you die, the entire world is reset and randomized. This doesn't mean you find completely random layouts. It's more like the developers created a set number of rooms, and the game randomly puts them together, and then fills them with random enemies & weapons. It's good enough for a few playthroughs, but then can get stale after a while.
Even though you technically lose everything when you die, you can get credits for completing quests that the game gives you, which you may then use to purchase permanent items that will carry over playthroughs. Things like dyes for your clothes, or a codex. A codex is a passive upgrade that you can equip onto you character to do minor things like cheapen prices on stores, or jump higher. Barely game changing, but it's nice to feel like you haven't lost EVERYTHING when you die.
If you play the game in Co-op, it's much more fun in my opinion. If you lose all of your health, you will be downed. Your partner has a bit of time to fight off some enemies and then come revive you for no cost at all for both of you. This can happen as many times as you want. However, if your partner does not revive you in time, you will lose all of the gear you carried, as well as your money, and re spawned nearby. I personally think this is a pretty good system, as it's a decently balanced penalty. Although you can easily find some good gear again, it punishes you in case you found a super rare weapon or armor, and it will take you quite a bit of time to regain all that money you lost, which was quite valuable. It can also create for more co-operation between teammates because they can craft and drop items for you since you lost all of your stuff.
Speaking of crafting, it's quite a simple system. When you kill enemies, you gather money and crafting materials. Simply clicking on a recipe in you inventory will craft that item, as long as you have the needed materials. That's it. You can craft any item as many times as you want. As long as you have the recipe and the materials. There are tonnes of unique potions and bombs you can create to tide the battle over to your side.
Something I love about the game is that when you pick up a magic scroll or potion in the world, it won't be identified to you. You have no idea what it's attributes are until you drink/use it, or use a "scroll of identification". This means that you could drink a potion and gain super strength, or be paralyzed right where you stand. It adds an interesting aspect where you aren't sure if you want to risk drinking an unknown potion during battle because it could help save or ruin you.
The game isn't as difficult as it makes itself sounds. You will die a few times, and it isn't easy, but I beat it with one friend of mine in around 5 tries. It was a super fun playthrough, and I can't wait to play it again with even more friends, but I won't be getting back to it immediately due to the fact that it does need a little bit more variety in between multiple playthroughs. I'm hoping the devs will add even more monsters, rooms and loot in the future. It's by no means empty, as it has quite a good variety, and a lot of surprises that will really come out of nowhere. I jumped quite a few times when I wasn't expecting something.
I need to mention the stylized aesthetic. I personally love it. It's got a dark atmosphere and the world and characters look very cool. Despite that, the game actually manages to sprinkle in a bit of humor too. The lore you find on walls, or descriptions of items can have a few jokes, which can be funny, but sometimes slightly frustrating. The point is to make you try figure out what some items do without being too straight forward, and I like that, but I felt like some descriptions were a little bit too vague. Just a little.
Also I love the soundtrack of the game. It really sets me in the environment and mood. Really great job!
Overall, I am really surprised to see the "mixed" steam store reviews at the time of writing this. Sure, the game has a few problems but overall I really had a blast playing it.
I personally got a review copy for this game, and want to mention that it in no way affects my opinion. I'm always honest, and have given countless negative reviews to games.
I want to point out though, that if I hadn't gotten that copy, I probably wouldn't have played this game so soon, as I think the full asking price is a bit high. 30 Euros or your regional equivalent is a little bit too high in my opinion. I'm sure the amount of work put into this game justifies it, and it really is a great and polished game for the most part, but I just didn't get enough time out of it to justify that price.
Another issue is I don't think I would have had anywhere near as much fun if I played through solo. It's a fun game, but can get repetitive at times. It's definitely not often, but sometimes you will find yourself grinding just a bit. I didn't get bored for a second playing with my friend, and it's not just because of his company. It's an entertaining game, but I'm sure I would have felt a bit worn out on my own.
Finally, my biggest complaint. When playing in Co-op, you can't both access shops at the same time. It's just a big waste of time. Me and my friend need to take turns waiting for each other to browse the shop selection and make our purchases. I would love if they updated the game to allow all players to talk to the store owner at the same time.
Overall, I really had a blast playing through the game and look forward to my next playthrough. If you enjoy Dark souls or any other game that plays similarly, then you will enjoy this as long as you know going into it that it is simplified in a few aspects.

Every once in a while, you come across a story that genuinely moves you.  Makes you feel something deep inside of you.  It's the difference between laughing out loud at something versus typing LOL as a rote response to what you read on your feed.  This story went beyond any that I had ever experienced.
It didn't make me cry.  Crying can be done with your dignity intact.  Crying can be a quiet means of expressing grief. This is not something everyone will enjoy.  I would specifically recommend you shy away from itnfor a while if you recently lost someone close to you due to cancer.  That Dragon, Cancer will dig up those feelings, will force you to deal with them even if you thought you had long since come to peace with them.
This game tells a story, one too familiar to too many people.  If you play this, you must do so prepared to grieve.  This is a game worth playing, a story worth experiencing.  It is worth your time.  Just be prepared for how it will affect you after you finish it.

This is one of those titles that transcends the label "videogames".  It is an experience.
In terms of storytelling That Dragon, Cancer is one of the most significant games ever released.  Rather than tell a story through heavy exposition or narrative TDC simply shows disjointed moments of one family's experience with tragedy.  It is vulnerable and raw in a way rarely seen.  I don't think I've seen a description of pain so naked since reading C.S. Lewis' "A Grief Observed".
I can't say that this really feels like a game.  There is little interaction in terms of gameplay.  It is mainly in the genre of point & click adventures but rather than convey a feeling of exploration and choice TDC conveys a feeling of powerlessness.  This fits the experience that TDC is attempting to communicate perfectly.  It is beautiful and emotionally exhausting.
This is one of the best "games" I have ever "played".  These terms dont' do justice to this amazing and deeply personal accomplishment.

I can't really say that That Dragon, Cancer is much of a "game" in any sense. If you're looking for a game, this isn't going to satisfy. This is really an "experience" of the emotional and spiritual varieties, so if you're looking to not shed tears, this will disappoint you on that front.
Saying all that, do I find this experience to be worthwhile? Yes. Very much so. That Dragon, Cancer contains a story that can only really have been done as interactive software. Never in my years growing up playing on various systems would have I believed that someone would someday use video games to tell a story like this. Its runtime is no longer than that of your average movie, and in that time it shows the whole spectrum of the Greens' experiences with Joel, from the highest joy to the deepest despair. I can only imagine the pain and bravery from the Greens that was required to recollect these experiences to share with us. I also appreciate the way they portrayed their faith, as it was honest, held nothing back, and wasn't there to preach. Rather, it was there for the player to experience and do with what they will. If what the preceding words describe interest you, please, do not hesitate to give this a run. I think you'll agree that this is worthwhile.
And Joel, if you can see this, I can't wait to meet you someday.

This game is pretty fun for a while, until the novelty fades. But as some others have pointed out, it's not just really difficult, it's just flat out unfair at times. After countless deaths, and getting nowhere with certain characters (which you need to finish the game with to unlock others) such as the Monk that DIES when he touches gold, the game just becomes a frustration and it's obvious the insane difficulty is being used to pad the game which has quite a lack of content. There are only four levels (with four stages each) and if you are able to complete the game you can do so in about 30 minutes or less. Now, I could understand the Monk being harmed for touching gold, but dying just for touching it seems a bit ridiculous to me. Then there's Eli, who can kick bombs (of which he has an infinite supply). Sound badass? He's not. That's his only weapon and when you come across the enemies that push you around the map it's almost impossible to kill them without hurting yourself first. To make matters worse, instead of having several completely different sounding songs to play on each level, there are only a few (you need to turn them on by yourself) that are more like remixes. You have the option to add your own music to the game, but no random option for that. This has apparently been in the works for 2 years. Unless you have a lot of patience to lose over and over, playing for hours and accomplishing nothing, I wouldn't recommend this game. Once again, it was fun for a while, but I think I will quit before I break another keyboard.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a 2D metroidvania game. You are Dust, an amnesiac furry thing without memory. Your only companions are an adorable flying cat named Fidget and your intelligent weapon, a blade named Ahrah. Your goal? Stop the evil general Cassius from committing genocide on the Moonblood people, using your blade and Fidget's magic to beat back monsters and his army and keep the people safe.
Story
The story of the game is largely an excuse plot; your goal is to defeat General Gaius. There are only about two dozen characters in the game, and most of them are minor NPCs you only interact with occaisionally; only a small handful of them do you interact with more than once, typically for some quest (either main story quest or sidequest) that, once done, you are done with the NPC.
Ultimately the plot is a bit of a mess. It is obvious from the beginning that you are, in fact, a member of General Gaius's army despite your amnesia, but your companions - Fidget the Nimbat and Ahrah the Elysian Blade - encourage you to do good. The problem is that not only is there very little mystery in the plot, towards the end of the game there is a rather poor plot twist. It seems that you are not only Cassius, the general's right hand man, but also Jin, a man who was trying to protect the moonbloods. You have both souls in your body, but are in truth neither one, but some sort of gestalt entity who is under control of neither of them.
The problem with this is, beyond being rather dumb, it is completely unnecessary. He could have just as easily rejected his past and chosen to be good, but instead there's some silliness about multiple souls which was never really hinted at before the last couple areas of the game and really adds nothing to the story. You wander around solving problems, but several of them feel rather forced - while the fight against the first boss and the last boss make sense, you fight the "rage" or "inner demons" of two other bosses, and it really is a bit silly.
In the end, the major saving grace of the story is Fidget, who is a wonderfully adorable companion. Dust himself is okay, but Fidget steals the show with her adorable shenanigans throughout the game, and she is really what sells the game.
Gameplay
As a metroidvania, you would expect over the course of the game that you would unlock additional weapons, techniques, and maneuvering abilities. This is partially true - you do unlock a couple new attacks for Fidget, but they are fairly interchangable and there is only one point in the entire game where they matter. Otherwise, while different, there isn't that much point to them - I mostly stuck with one and it served me fine, but you could use the others and fight decently as well.
You do, however, use the same sword for the entire game, and you really never gain any sort of significant change as far as that goes. Your attacks are identical throughout the game, only the enemies vary, with the only new attack move you gain being primarily a maneuvering ability which sometimes can be used to attack - but generally speaking you have better options.
As far as maneuvering abilities go, they're dead standard - a wall climb (only on special walls, of course), a double jump, a slide that lets you navigate narrow passages, and a super jump that is very situtional and almost never useful.
The gameplay in general is fairly mediocre - the platforming is decent, but the actual fighting - and you do quite a bit of it - is not. Virtually none of the enemies present any actual challenge - in the entire game, only a handful of enemy types are actually dangerous, but you will fight through hordes of enemies over the course of the game. Most of these enemies, while they have unique appearances, are not all that different to fight tactically, and unfortunately a few techniques - particularly spinning through the air while unleashing projectiles, then beating on the enemies while they are in hitstun from the projectiles to recharge your magic meter - works against every single enemy in the game, and quite effectively. Indeed, you can defeat all the bosses in this exact same way, and fairly effortlessly at that. There is one enemy type that you must counter their attack to kill, but they telegraph their attack so blatantly that it is never an issue, and they are seldom encountered, let alone alongside other enemies, making them rather trivial once you figure out the timing.
The overall difficulty of the gameplay is quite low as well - playing the game on Hardcore is the only way to go, because it is the hardest mode and it is still too easy. While if the enemies hit you they can do very significant damage, it rather quickly becomes evident that you can easily trap them in hitstun forever and avoid their attacks, thus completely negating the threat that they should present.
Graphics
The game's graphics are 2D hand-drawn sprites and they look alright. In conversations, there is a more fully animated version of the character speaking, and they all have multiple poses, though they get repeated somewhat, which becomes especially noticeable in longer conversations. The character designs are appealing, but in conversations, the character sprites are bizzarely low-resolution - there is no clear reason for this, but they have a grainy appearance, and the cutscenes also look a bit off as well for similar reasons.
Fidget, however, is completely adorable, and Dust looks quite decent, meaning that the two most commonly appearing characters look just fine. Most of the minor NPCs are decent but unamazing. The entire game has a very furry aesthetic to it, likely to appeal to said fandom, but it is not offensively so - the graphics are quite generically appealing.
Final Summary
Dust is an alright game but nothing special. The gameplay is bland and it is mainly the game's aesthetic appeal and effective use of the cute mascot character Fidget which save the game. At about 15 hours long, it doesn't overstay its welcome, and its price is quite reasonable as a piece of downloadable software. If the game has aesthetic appeal to you, it might be worth a buy, but if you're looking for great gameplay, it would be best to search elsewhere.

Although it has its flaws, and is still trying to find an equilibrium in some places, GalCivIII is a solid space 4x game. It's respectful of its roots (especially the
series) without slavish adherence to their methods; it also builds on the prior entires in the series, narratively and mechanically. You can see the family resemblance, but it can stand on its own. The addition of multiplayer is a huge bonus for me, and I don't believe it detracts meaningfully from the single-player story experience.
Overall, I'd rate it an 8/10. A good, solid 4x gaming experience; there's little that will rock your socks off, and the AI needs some more work, but you won't be disappointed with this game if you enjoyed the previous entries or similar games (MOO2, Space Empires, etc.) With time, the developers continue to smooth out the rough areas of the game, though sometimes I expected these things a lot sooner. For example, passwords for multiplayer games were only added in the most recent patch. It's truly great that the devs are making the game better with time, and their inexperience with MP games can be forgiven, but I can't help feeling that some of these bugs/missing features should've been present in the game at launch.
Also: Although the wiki is a very useful resource, it is WOEFULLY out of date. If you're gonna have an official wiki, give it some official love!

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a platformer/brawler made by Dean Dodrill. It features the protagonist, Dust, who wakes up with no recollection of his past and sets out looking for answers with the help of a talking sword and its batlike guardian.
Otherwise read on.
The first that must be said about Dust: An Elysian Tail is that the game is absolutely gorgeous. The game environmets range from lush forests to arctic peaks, all hand painted and all a treat to look at. Character models are a bit of a mixed bag. The hero. Dust, moves very smoothly both in and out of combat, but certain enemies and npcs have animations that one would expect from a flash game. Thankfully this is hardly noticeable while exploring and fighting enemies and doesn't detract from overall enjoyment.
What must be said second is that the combat is simply fun. It's fast, responsive, and has room for improvisation. You don't have many abilities and you unlock most of them in the first two chapters, but by keeping your move pool focused it makes it more enjoyable. There just isn't a useless ability, you'll use them all without even trying to. Combat in general is rather on the easy side unless you pick the hardest difficulty. Defeating enemies gives you materials, money and experience, which can be used to raise your stats via crafting, buying equipment or levelling up, respectively. Enemies respawn every time you enter an area, so if you are stuck on a hard fight, you can go back and grind a few levels or get some more healing items.
And what must be said third is that the story is ok. Just ok. The premise of an amnesiac hero has been done many times before, but the game manages to keep you interested as it slowly uncovers the facts. However, I found it a bit hard to be invested in fates of anyone but Dust and a few sidequest characters. They either aren't that much interesting, or their voice makes me cringe/chuckle. Yes, the voice acting can be at times very cheesy, especially in the final chapter, and you might recognize some voices from youtube shows. Despite all this, the voice acting works.
What does not work is the final chapter. Spoiler free.
Here I simply must be critical. In the final chapter difficulty does a rather sharp jump upwards and for all the wrong reasons. You fight enemies who have lots of invincibility frames, hit hard and block attacks seemingly at random. You also fight with a good number of npcs on your side so the combat suddenly resembles a mosh pit. It doesn't help that the environment, while still well painted, is much more boring than the rest of the game. This combined meant I opted to simply skip most of combat in the last chapter. Unfortunately the final boss fight was a culmination of disappointment.
Last chapter is rather short compared to others, but it does sour my final opinion a bit. There were apparently supposed to be several more chapters, but they were scrapped. The difficulty curve also goes up and down rather wildly and some platforming sections can get needlessly frustrating, but the controls are responsive enough to get you through, sooner or later.
So, if you can tolerate the subpar final bit of the game, you get a pretty enjoyable experience. The game has a few blemishes, but the degree of detail in other areas shows the care that was put into the game.
And in the end, that's what matters.

Brutally simple as it is, it is a great game. Little Inferno is a bit of a parody on consumer society and the entire product placement industry. You order products and you burn them, while corresponding via letters with different kinds of characters. It is much more interesting than it sounds, though. Almost every object you burn has its character and has its own weird physics and if you combine them properly, you get combo bonuses (in fact, you could say that that's your main in-game task). As the game itself states, mockingly self-conscious, there are no timers, level grinding and failures, mere incinerating with casual, but addictive, puzzle solving. In fact, if there was a genre called "sadistic pyro puzzle", this would be it.
Even though I got this from Humble Bundle, I would say that it is worth its standalone price.

Now that the game is in full release I feel it is appropriate to write a review for this.
You probably won't like the style of game if you're impatient or expecting Might and Magic 6 or newer tyle fantasy RPG games, or a fan of when ubisoft bought out the series in 2003 and started changing it. The game is still set in a part of Ashan, iirc about 10 years after Heroes 6. That being said though, there is very little story overlap that I've seen thus far (about 30-35% in) wich was a very common thing. They do make jabs at references to the older games in the series, like when you meet the governor's daughter, she wants to see the circus (M&M 6.)
The entire game is grid-based movement. Each square out of town is roughly 20-25 feet let's say. And you choose to move forward, backward, or left or right. Turning is a "Free action." After you move, any monsters in the vicinity will move. Then you move. Then they move. Combat is turn based as it was back in M&M1-5, as there's no option like there was in M&M6-9.
Character development is better than in M&M1-5, worse than 6-9. You pick a race, has two benefits particular to that race. Then you pick the "might", "magic", or "hybrid" path for that race. 4 races, 12 classes. 3 classes per race. Each class has one promotion quest, i.e. crusader turns into a paladin, a blade dancer turns into a war dancer.
While there is almost no relation to the previous games, as was the case with Might and Magic 9, there is a storyline in the game that I've enjoyed so far. Premise is, you're raiders. Adventurers. Call them what you will. At the end of your training, your mentor dies but tells you to bring his ashes home to Karthal. You get to the peninsula, and your adventure starts, as you free the area from all the baddies and monsters and ghosts. Pretty stereotypical of both the fantasy RPG genre as a whole, and of M&M series games. Just lacking (thus far) the sci-fi element that was throughout Might and Magic 1-8.
Graphics may seem old to some people, some Pre-release folks were complaining about it. Truthfully? I'm okay with less-intensive graphics. It doesn't detract from the gameplay at all, and they were on par with the graphics present in Heroes 5 in my opinion. My rig isn't exactly new, just gave it a new video card about two years ago, (Radeon HD 6350 iirc), and everything on ultimate and the game looks wonderful. Not Crysis wonderful, but wonderful nonetheless.
My recommendation? Try it out! It's a step back from the modern fantasy games out there. Something happened when 3D0 went under and this iconic series and style just about vanished overnight in 2003. This series has been going on now for 28 years and it's still good.

Stellaris is a 4x/Grand Strategy game from Paradox.  Fans of other Paradox titles such as Crusader Kings II or Europa Unversalis IV will enjoy this game.  While not perfect I find this game to be rock solid so far. I haven't run into many bugs and none of them have been game killers.  Ethos and traits give a large variation to the races you can create, which supports a large number of personal playstyles.  Everything from ruthless space slavers bent on galatic conquest to alien space hippys can be created.
There isn't really anything in the game I dislike, it's more that I hope Paradox improves on in follow up DLC's. The areas I find a little lacking is Diplomacy/Trade. Both are lumped into one window and are simple. Its not bad just simple. The other aspect which I think needs improvement is the limit on managable planets. Your can manage 5 planets before penalties kick in. Now you can run a few overr that limit and its not a big deal but I can already see that when I'm deeper into the game splitting my planets into various sectors could become a pita. The game is highly moddable so there is already a mod getting rid of the limit and allowing sectors as you wish.
All in all this is a rock solid game and given Paradox's habit of improving their games with DLC's gives me a positive outlook on Stellaris going forward. I would recommend this game to any strategy fan.

It's a great game that mixes two genres quite organically. Get it if you own a gamepad, otherwise the controls feel a bit clumsy on PC.
Vostok Inc. is a peculiar mix between an incremental game (think realm grinder) and shoot-em-up. In this game, you fly your ship and try to establish an intergalactic corporation. You go from planet to planet, build buildings and fight enemies while in space.
The freshness of the idea contributes to an engaging gameplay: you can spend your money on making your ship stronger or build your colonies. You get money by killing enemies, but the planetary bases give much more resources, and you can’t both at the beginning. This creates an interesting balancing/optimization choices for the player. Go for the first, and have a strong ship, but not enough passive income. Go for the second, and be richer, but have harder time surviving enemy encounters.
Speaking of enemy encounters: they are pretty straightforward. If you go through the space, you meet various enemies (depending on the galaxy you are in). They will chase you and shoot at you, and if you die: you must get to your base in an escape pod or you end up losing money / middle managers that improve your production output by a percentage. The battle controls are similar to other twin-stick shooter games: one stick to move, another to shoot. The player can have up to four weapons that can be switched between each other. The weapon system is different from the other games of shoot-em-up genre: your ships has three weapon slots. There are three possible weapons: beam, bullet, rocket. By combining those weapons, you get a new weapon type.
The shooting actually feels great: the bullet collisions are clearly visible and understandable, the enemies explode in a spectacular way and your bullets make nice sounds. On the down side, most weapons feel redundant or unnecessary: I’ve progressed in the game by mostly using bullet weapons. Other ones just did not feel powerful or did not help to solve any specific problems with the enemies: you don’t need homing rockets if you can turn around at any point and shoot shotgun/minigun at upcoming enemies with much faster rate and damage per second. The most basic beam weapon also felt like the best one to fight the slowest bosses: one projectile hits the large bosses’ bounding box multiple times, accumulating your combo meter VERY quickly and allowing you to do huge damage, ensuring quick boss kills. Actually, it feels like a problem with most large projectiles / large enemies: your hits get counted multiple times, and so it’s really easy to get max combo on slower bosses or enemies, dealing tremendous amounts of damage.
The incremental part is well balanced and allows for the smooth progression: you won’t be a billionaire straight away, instead you’ll have to gradually work for it, meticulously building your bases and purchasing upgrades. This base building part provides a good relaxation from the space fighting. There are also minigames like racing and collecting managers in space. Managers enhance your production percentage and offer some more minigames that imitate retro-gaming systems. Overall, this salad of features is what keeps Vostok Incorporated interesting.
However, when you get 20+ planets, a problem appears which I love to call “Fallout 4” problem. If you remember Fallout
4 base building, you got your homebase first, then you could go and help bases all through the commonwealth and get more villages under your protection. However, once you got too many of them, it quickly started to become a chore going from one place to another, fixing and improving things. The same thing can be observed here: going between 4+ system and visiting multiple planets becomes a chore. It would help to have an ability to build bases on planets remotly, but alas, there’s no such thing.
Speaking about the cons, I must mention that the settings are very weak: no mouse support in the menus. No resolution / display selection. The game was clearly designed with consoles in mind. The gamepad controls are very convenient, but even keyboard key rebindings can’t save the UI from the lack of mouse support and awkward menu switching.
While its not perfect – it is an engaging attempt to make a fusion of two game genres that succeeded. Vostok Inc. brings the new mechanics to the table, combining it with nice aesthetics and polish. Get it if you have a gamepad.

Before I knew it, I was a quadrillionare in Vostok Inc. If only it were that easy in real life! Perhaps that is why I find this game extremely addicting and fun to play. Starting out trying to reach a million or even a billion dollars makes you want to push a little more and the next thing you know another 3 hours have passed.
You start off going planet-by-planet constructing different buildings to produce income. I found it extremely satisfying purchasing buildings and watching my income climb. The game pushed me to reach for the next planet to have enough money for my next building to unlock or to purchase weapon upgrades to defeat the bosses in each system.
The twin-stick shooting mechanics feels responsive with satisfying weapons, like laser or shotgun style projectiles. You'll be shooting down enemies while you explore the distinctive solar systems filled with asteroids and randomized executive astronauts needing rescue. The executives provide bonus cash, but the only gripe I had was they get dissatisfied too quickly, so keeping them happy with collectible items felt like a chore. It is optional, but it will double the time to increase your cash flow.
There is a lot to keep you busy here; mini-games to play, executives to keep happy, upgrades for your radar and ship, there are even races you can partake in. Vostok Inc. is an addictive and fun game to play where you either get rich or die trying.

Necropolis is the latest game from Harebrained Schemes and one that I've been looking forward to. The studio wanted to try its hand at combining the rogue-like and action RPG genre with a unique game. Now that Necropolis is out, unfortunately it misses the point of what makes both these games compelling.
The story of the game is that you are trapped in the Necropolis: A dimensional holding ground by a powerful being. In order to get out, you need to work your way down and hopefully find an exit without being killed.
To start with some good, the game looks great. While the art style may be minimalistic, it creates a stylized atmosphere for the game. The game's levels are procedurally generated with different enemy placements and types for each playthrough.
Combat is set up similar to the Souls games: Controlling left and right hand equipment while managing stamina. As you play, you'll find, buy or scavenge new gear to wear of escalating tiers of power. Similar to traditional rogue-likes, there are scrolls and potions that have their function shuffled with each new play. The only way to know what they do is to either use an identifying scroll or try them out.
Playing through the game, you'll find pillars that unlock new biomes and enemies for future plays. This is one of only two forms of progression in Necropolis; the other has to do with codexes.
Long-term progression in Necropolis on the player's side is built around acquiring codexes. The codexes provide passive bonuses and unlock new crafting recipes to use during a run. Getting them requires the player to earn tokens which are unlocked two ways.
The first is to complete randomly assigned quests from your strange host during a play. The second comes in when you die. All the gems earned during a run are added to a pool that unlocks tokens with the cost getting successively higher. As with any good rogue-like Necropolis wants you to keep replaying to unlock more challenges and content for later runs.
Unfortunately, it's the combination of mechanics and progression that hurt the game the most.
Mixing genres is never easy for game designers. Taking what works in multiple genres and combining them can leave you with a game that doesn't appeal to anyone. Necropolis suffers with major issues in both the ARPG and rogue-like side of things.
Starting with ARPG, the game's combat system is woefully behind other games on the market. There are annoying wind-ups for any attack, leaving combat unresponsive. Enemies will sometimes attack through your attacks or get stunned with no real indicator as to why.
The game's combat system becomes very one-note as you learn how the game works. Shield bashing is the best way to stun enemies and has little downside to use.
Meanwhile, charge attacks will lower your max stamina until you have a healing item with each use. This causes the player to not use them and is a good example of a hoarding mechanic.
It feels like the game was designed around multiplayer first with how wide swings are and the wind-up, with singleplayer as an afterthought. The problem is that if the base mechanics don't feel right, then that extends out to every part of the combat.
The game loves to spawn enemies behind the player and fill up rooms that were already cleared. When you combine this with room and hallway structures that look the same, it's very easy to get lost and frustrated. There are tons of weapons in the game, but nowhere near the same level of depth and feel that you get in a game like Dark Souls.
Because the base gameplay is so simple, it makes the runs feel very boring to play through again and again. The best way to see what I'm talking about is to watch videos of plays of Dark Souls or my video companion piece of Necropolis linked below. Not helping matters is the progression model which the developers really screwed up on.
Playing a rogue-like, each run has to be different enough to keep the player on their toes and make the game replayable. Necropolis simply doesn't have any worthwhile progression.
The codex concept is a good idea, but you can only equip one at a time. This is supposed to make you choose different play styles, but comes off as leaving you without a lot of options of progression. The different biomes don't really add up to unique challenges, once again, because of the lackluster base mechanics. Not helping matters are confusing descriptions of the codexes; leaving players unsure as to what they actually do and how they impact the game.
The developers missed the chance to really grow out each new play with new challenges, such as in Rogue Legacy or The Binding of Isaac. The point is the player unlocks new content that changes subsequent runs. The more you play the more variety you'll see.
There's just nothing of note that unlocks through progression that makes me want to keep playing. And the content that does get unlocked uses the same one-note combat system.
Necropolis has some good ideas to it, but it's missing the connective tissue that made games like Rogue Legacy and The Binding of Isaac work. The developers have listened to these complaints and will be updating the game over the weeks to come. Here's hoping that Necropolis will have a second life along the lines of Skyshine's Bedlam, and not sealed in a tomb.

I'll be up front here.  I'm probably going to be a weird review, because a lot of what everyone else dislikes about this game I tend to view as good things.
The first thing I'll mention is length.  This game is not long.  I beat the game in approximately five hours.  Now that you've heard that, don't despair because I have a radical new position on this!  Ready?  LENGTH DOES NOT EQUAL VALUE!  Simply because a game is shorter doesn't mean it was any less fun, or worth any less than it's price tag.  Did I have $30 worth of fun playing this?  Yes.  Absolutely I did.  In addition to my first point, my second is that with roguelike games, a short game is good.  Since you are more or less guaranteed to die, I would prefer to have a shorter goal.  If I die on the 5th floor, then I didn't lose a huge chunk of time and feel like my character is wasted.  I just casually shrug my shoulders, accept that s#!t happens and start a new character.
Combat is the next thing I'll discuss.  Learning the combat in this game is part of the challenge.  Learning when you should and shouldn't swing is important.  You also want to know when to fall back, use an item, or charge a strong attack.  The combat isn't clunky or ineffective, you just need to learn to adapt to its pacing.
The crafting system also works well, and provides you with enough crafting items that you can make enough healing to get you through the game.  This is also where some play style variety appears as you can craft armor potions, bombs, or invisibility potions depending on how you want to approach certain areas or groups of enemies.
The procedurally generated dungeon is a great touch as well since it will make it pretty much impossible to just speed run through the floors by running straight to the exit.  Now I will concede that the first few floors do lack a little in variety.  The further down you go the more drastically everything changes.  This make the bottom few floors much more interesting.
Now not everything in this game is perfect.  A wider variety of enemies could help this game.  You seem to fight the same few types a lot as you proceed through the dungeon.  It would also have been nicer to provide more weapons and armor, and maybe provide a way to craft those as well.  This would give the player a little more control over their character's build.  Sometimes the game also suffers from, "more enemies equals higher difficulty."  This can mean slogging through a hoard of enemies every now and then which can get a little tiresome.  I found that potions of invisiblity are good choices in these scenarios.
All in all this game hits the mark quite effectively, and the bonus of playing with your friends is just icing on the cake.  In my personal opinion, this game earns a solid 8/10.  There is room for improvement, but it is already a fantastic way to kill all of your free time.

So I originally bought this game back in 2011 when it came out. Suffered through the many patches and changes and even noticed the missions that were removed.  I recently bought it on steam(for those wanting to use a trainer I tried a fling 3.3 and it works currently) when it was on sale just to have a steam copy. I've completed it more times than I can remember and still think its an awesome game.
Tech side: Don't even begin to believe the scaled down recommended specs given. Here's a link to a detailed bench test from 2011-12 that will give you an idea of what this game really needs:
I've played this on many different system configurations and can tell you that if you want to max the game and card settings you will need some serious hardware. My current setup (2 gigabyte g1 970's in SLI, 4930 Hex Core see profile to see rest) has been tested w/ all game settings maxed(including ubersampling) and all Nvidia settings maxed. Here's the results:
2D 1080p avg 110-120fps
3D 1080p avg 40-55 fps
4k(3860x2160 for correct aspect ratio) 35-45 fps
Playing at 4k does look beautiful but the 3D is one of the best I have ever seen. In 3D there is so much depth and occasional pop that it really sets the bar for 3D gaming. There's still occasional ghosting but its pretty minor. I imagine a single GTX960-970 will give favorable 2D 1080P experience but you will need some kind of dual gpu if you want to max it all. It is a DX9  game but possibly one of the best looking ones when maxed although if you lower the gamma it still has a bit of a 'cartoon' look but there's still a lot of detail in most textures.
The game itself: It's not a true open world but each level or area is pretty expansive. It is a linear story but there are many, many choices to be made and some will impact immediately while other consequences only  occur later. I forget exactly how many different endings there are but I've experienced about 5 or 6. It can be a fun world to explore. This game does have many similarities to game of thrones so fans of those books/shows may enjoy it. And on that note, this is NOT a game for young children.
I totally recommend this game to anyone who likes RPG's, even more so if you want a great 3d experience or 4k. It's a game that technology is still catching up to and has considerable replay factors.
