What exactly is a game? A game in my eyes, and probably innumerable others is something that can be enjoyed for an extended amount of time. This could be board games, card games, or video games. Everyone has a favorite video game, and the one I just couldn’t put down for who knows how long was…
The Binding of Issac
This game isn’t one to be taken easily, seeing as time and time again you will end up dying to a room you just can’t escape, or a boss you don’t have the health and power to beat.
The game mechanics can be a bit sketchy at times. The achievements make up for it, however. You can pour hours into the game, and still not have all of the achievements. Even if you aren’t a completionist, the simple arcade-like style will draw you into the old days.
Remember those dungeon crawler style arcade games? The Binding of Issac is a complete reboot of this sort of style, with hundreds of power ups, room combinations, pills, and more. To be brief, the game mechanics allow you to get a multitude of upgrades such as: speed, health, power, familiars, one-room-use items, and more.
The expansion pack is also a must get if you have beaten the normal Binding of Issac. Wrath of the Lamb adds more new items, increases the retro feels, and introduces new bosses and alternate room versions. Say goodbye to the Basement, and hello to the cellar where spiders live.
The sounds of the game can be highly disturbing for people both young and old. I, however will let you be the own judge on whether you want to listen to the sound.
There is still SO much praise this game should receive, if it hasn’t already. The truth is that time and time again you may feel an urge to come back to the game just because of the overwhelming memories, and feelings and saps from the mind and body.
For all hardcore players, completionists, and arcade era players, this game is a must have.
If you enjoy this one, the reboot is coming out soon as well. Look for it on steam sometime this year.

Well when I did the "early access" I was thinking it was okay, but noting to get excited about. In fact I think for this game "early access" was more of a gimick then anything else. I kind of feel that the final release was going to be pretty much what they had in mind from the start, and that's not really a bad thing. It's a pretty enjoyable game over all.
While it does have a vintage Might and Magic look, only updated, I wouldn't call it a faithful recreation of the old classic M&M games. I think the thing I've noticed most is that your ability to roam the game world is constricted compared to M&M games. You could pretty much go anywhere, but you'd get your @ss handed to you real quick if you strayed into too high a level area. So far with this game I've found that higher level areas are locked untill you've done the required quest/s. I think this is a developer design choice so I don't see it changing all that much as I progress.
Other then that it's a pretty faithfull reproduction of the old grid and turn based combat RPG. It seems that the developers added a dash of Wizardy and AD&D to their formula and it makes for a pretty good and engrossing game. Battles can be pretty intense, but it's not a action game by any means, so If you love the more modern action RPGs you might be dissapointed. But if you've been wishing for a return to the PC RPGs of the golden age this will be right up your alley. Or if you've never played this style of RPG and wonder what the fuss about the "golden age of RPGs" is give it a spin. It's priced right for what it is and what you get, which can't always be said about a lot of the releases on the market.

So, I’m liking the game but I am unsure if it is my love for this style of game or the game itself I’m loving.  I can say I feel there were a few missed opportunities.  I’m a huge fan of CK2 and Imperium Galactica 2 (oh how I was hoping for a worthy successor).  I am enjoying the game thought so please don’t be discouraged.  Paradox has a record of improving games with mods/patches/DLC and stand by their titles.  So I’m not overly worried.
Stellaris offers what many of us have been missing in that it is real time 4x space strategy game.  Finally no more “end turn” right?  Freely customizable race, easy modding, and a nice arrangement of traits/characteristics allow for replay ability.  Keep an eye out for mods in workshop though as they will probably be able to take the vanilla game further in its current state.
Diplomacy could use some work.  Coming from an experience like CK2 where there is such a detailed level of advisors, intrigue, relationships, etc.… you will be underwhelmed by the diplomacy.  Like no joke, there’s not much to it…
Planets…  So I am not sure if I am for or against this rather dated style of planet/colony management.  It reminds me of Master of Orion where planets have tiles which can be modified to produce a resource based off the building.  It works for the game so I have no real complaints on it, just seems like an old mechanic that we have seen before.  Something I’m not too fond of is the planet control system and how your kind a forced to give up control of your systems to a governor after you a mass a few colonies.  I suppose if there was more interaction or even the feeling that I was handing over my territory to someone of value it wouldn’t be so bad.  However, it feels quite static.  Made me miss CK2 and long for those intriguing back stabbing plots to break away or declare independence from my rule.  There is little you can do to control how you want your sectors run and leaders again are quite static.  Not to mention limited in availability.  Don’t expect to have scientist, generals, admirals, and leaders everywhere or even in all the above areas.
So combat is indeed 4x, but doesn’t really feel like it.  More or less move one fleet onto an enemy fleet and they swarm around firing.  No direct player control.  Again, not a complaint, it works.  And the UI window on battles during and after offers more details to help redesign your ships versus CK2 UI.  Sadly I feel the 4x component is wasted in this though…
Overall the game is very vanilla, like not even vanilla bean, or vanilla with sprinkles….it’s just vanilla.  However, mods and time will tell if Paradox adds to it and brings us the enjoyment we have seen in other titles (CK2) (I mention CK2 because I’d so die happy for a CK2 in space type game).  I am enjoying it though and have already logged many hours since its release here.
I will leave you with this thought…  Recall back to the early days of CK2 and how it was at first launch, or even some other titles…  I’m just looking towards the future and ready to reach for my pocket book for the plethora of DLC to come.  :)

I can't recommend this experience to the average gamer. It's trippy, it's slick, and it's stylistic, sure. The premise and ambience are cool and the overall visual execution is pretty good. However, it's riddled with gameplay issues that ultimately bring the entire experience down.
Don't take it the wrong way, there is some fun to be had here. If you enjoy extremely fast-paced top-down violence with a degree of luck, then this might be your sort of thing. For most folks, this will likely end up being more of a headache to play.
While it visually nails a retro vibe, this can also be to its own detriment. For some players, you may experience motion sickness or headaches after small amounts of play. The text pops out, vibrates, and changes colors. The game world wobbles a bit and has a static/VHS filter over it. The extremely fast nature of the gameplay can become visually exhausting after a while. The music can become throbbing or annoying during certain sequences.
I wouldn't call this game difficult, but brutally random. The AI and hit detection specifically. The AI in this game seem to have some kind of random omniscence. You can attack an enemy head on, and sometimes they'll instantly kill you. At other times, they won't even react. This is compounded by the fact that there is no wind up or hit spark for any attacks made by enemies. They only need to touch you and you are dead. They also have super speed, meaning you'll have only fractions of a second to react most of the time.
Gun-toting enemies are especially egregious of this behavior. Sometimes you can sneak up on an gun armed opponent and K.O. them easily. At other times, they'll sense you immediately, do a 180 degree snap turn(like an aimbot), and kill you from several yards away. They'll even snipe you from outside your view. It's almost bizarre, as sometimes the AI purposely plays "poorly", as if to be a good sport about it. Occasionally, I'd encounter enemies who couldn't shoot straight, or had trouble turning. At other times, they'd resort to the same "snap and kill" behavior.
The big keyword here is "Sometimes", because that's pretty much this game in a nutshell. Sometimes the AI is brutally efficient to the point they might as well be cheating. At other times they are so clueless they won't hear gunshots even when you fire right next to them. Sometimes doors will cover you, and other times enemies will see you through them and shoot you. Sometimes you can fire a full-auto weapon and no enemies will come running, and other times the entire level will be alerted. Sometimes your weapon will hit the enemy, sometimes it misses entirely.
Which leads to the next point, the hit detection is very spotty. The weapon mechanics in this game are fun, but they also seem to not connect half the time. Melee weapons seem to hit in a cone in front of them, but if you are too close to your opponent, you'll do no damage. However, they can still hit within a certain distance. If you end up walking on top of your enemy before swinging or shooting(say, in a furious brawl with multiple opponents), too bad. They'll instant kill you and you'll be forced to restart.
I think it really all comes down to consistency. I'm fine with the idea of a super fast murder spree retro game, but only if the rules are internally consistant. A lot of my victories feel like luck, and a lot of my losses feel cheap.
I haven't played the second game, so hopefully these issues are ironed out. It's a solid concept, I just wish it was executed better.

*More than likely a ton of spoilers so you have been warned* Honestly playing this game the first time I enjoyed it. Its not the best game but its good. But as everyone else begins saying there are plenty of issues with it. First was that the combat is pretty friggin easy. The first time I played I got to floor six and only died because thats the floor I began playing with my friend and we did quite a bit of team damage to each other fighting the same horde of enemies. I mean that can be one way to make it harder is just get more people playing with you and everyone has to take the same group of enemies out, because team damage will be high most likely. Another thing is the enemies are hella easy. Anytime I was ever encountered by a single enemy I never was scared. No Gemeater, Skulltotemthing, elite hoardsman or clockwork knight had a chance if it was alone. Hell even in twos there wasnt much challenge. And groups of enemies just hit each other. The only creature I ever saw as a real problem was the Changling because of its high damage, quick attack speed, and when it would usually dodge the first attack. Thats a low tier killer right there but even then as I got to lower floors and better gear it was in the end EZPZ. The gear too is pretty lacking. I remember playing through with my friends I typically found everything I found in my first few plays through, Playing alone I found much more of the high tier weapons and armor I failed to find on any other floors but then i just couldnt die. Which brings me to the boss fight towards the end. That thing is super easy. His attack is really slow and it does do very high damage but they are easy to dodge and after taking a hit healing is still easy to do. And just one boss fight made me sad. In one of the pictures you see a kind of giant hydra head from this little well and I thought that fighting that as a boss would be amazing, but in the end you cant kill it and its not hard to avoid. More boss fights would be perfect, like one at every exit to the floor (and for those who dont know there are multiple exits). It would definitely be more enjoyable with AI kind of like the Changeling and if the enemies instead of just being more in number actually were harder to kill and smarter as the floors went on. The gear needs a definite boost, not to like damage or anything but there needs to be different things to find because i generally found all the same stuff in all my time playing (but this is on the lower tier floors so higher tier I am unaware of some extra looties i missed). And that boss is too EZPZ. Honestly im not a rougelike player so if anyone wants to combat any of this feel free too, but i enjoyed the game and it needs work. For $30 i dont recommend it but for less on a sale or something I do. And before anyone tries to tell me I havent played enough to see everything I still do play and I have beaten and gone back to floor 7 i believe. Oh and the vagueness of all of the things in game doesnt really bother me. I like experimenting to find out what those things do and some of the codexes are not as vague as you think. They give some little weird hint whilst trying to be funny but they do explain them partially. Like the Ogre Book of no fall makes it harder for you to get knocked down (im pretty sure). With the price i recommend you buy it on sale in its current state, and its not a bad game. My goal  is to beat it a second time with friends all in tow. The low tier gear is lacking and im not sure about the high tier because i did find a tier 3 wrist grenade launcher later but other than that not very much extra stuff. But I would say buy it on sale or just wait until more updates come out to buy it if its still $30.

The game has classic Roguelike difficulty but there isn't very much like a roguelike in the sense that the threats become more and more difficult to fight. Past level 5 or 6 ( OF NINE ) there isn't a single new monster that you fight that is of notable threat or against whom your approach differs. By this point you will have seen every enemy (save a single boss)
Additionally, the weapons are lacking in variety: although they come with many different designs there only really seem to be 5 or 6: shortsword/knife, longsword, greatsword, slightly bigger greatsword, big heavy mace, and spear/hafted weapon. Regardless of the design of the weapon you're carrying or the name it carries, it becomes painfully obvious where your weapons fall. It's especially telling when you pick up a scythe in a later part of the game and it handles like the greatsword.
The gameplay itself isn't too far off of dark souls with an additional change in that unless you have one specific codex you're going to be investing a lot of frames with any swing you make. The biggest change comes in the multiplayer: you better have a headset on and start calling out your targets in a fight, or else you're going to get clipped by your allies and die CONSTANTLY.
The most disappointing thing by far is that as you find higher tiers of armors you realize that enemies weren't "hard" or challengin, they just have the damage ramped up MASSIVELY as you meet the bigger enemies. Once you put on tier 3 or 4 armor, all of a sudden everyone is way less dangerous and you can take more than 3 hits.
Still, the game is a fun, if simplistic beat'em up that groups of people can massively enjoy. I've played the game all of 3 times (all coop) and completely thrashed it the third time with one friend.
The game doesn't *FEEL* like a 30 dollar game. It's easy to blast through, outside of the level designs (which get more creative than most people are willing to admit by level 7 or 8) everything repeats itself a lot, and there isn't as great a sense of discovery compared to a souls game, or even a roguelike. The character progression is a mere raising of HP and stamina (the only two stats the game has that are determined by your character and not your equipment) This means that although later levels get so large they have separate ways of going further down, you have little reason to explore everything (outside of wanting just enough gems to level up) heck, since the weapon variety and movesets are so limited, there's barely a reason for replayability once you beat it: you've probably wielded every weapon type and need to go through the relatively boring levels of 1-3 before you even attempt to get something new.
This recommendation comes with notable caveat: The game is definitely fun and worth playing, but only under one of two circumstances.
You either have at least one additional human to play alongside, or you got the game for 10 dollars less. And even then, you might feel cheated because that additional human either makes the game too easy or completely impossible to beat.

I'm going to be perfectly honest - This game just isn't worth it, and I got it for *free,* so that's saying something.

The levels were uninspired and boring beyond belief; and the minimalist set design is evocative of Minecraft, but it just falls flat. And after that, guess what? MORE linear hallways and floating fields! Sometimes there are white tunnels, too, but nobody cares about them.
All in all, don't.
Just please.... Don't.

This game feels completely genuine. This game conveys all the hope, despair and lots more that goes with

You could not describe what happens in your head during such events so accurate without living it.
At NO point did this game feel like emotional blackmail or manipulative.
This is an extremely painful and beautiful game. Prepare to be in pieces.
Well done developers and thank you for sharing.

After reading all the negative reviews comparing Armikrog to The Neverhood I can't help but wonder - when did you guys last play The Neverhood? Does Armikrog still have bugs? Yeah. But they are not game-breaking.
Was the voice-acting overhyped? Pretty much. But it does its job of conveying the story and shaping the characters.
Are the puzzles redundant and repetetive? Kind of. But The Neverhood had a memory game and a sliding puzzle. And don't even get me started on that corridor.
Armikrog is still an original, engaging and fun experience. It is not a second Neverhood, as it does some things differently, but, hey, who would want two identical games, right?

It's a lot more like The Neverhood than you know.
-----------------------------------------------------
If a person has downvoted the game for not being enough like The Neverhood, they probably hadn't played the game in a long time. Truth is, it follows a lot of the same beats. The puzzles are maddening. There's a lot of boring transition time. Notepads and basic doodling skills are required. The plot doesn't really make an appearance until the very end. All of these things make up Armikrog, too.
You can finish the game in just a few hours with a walkthrough. If you're playing it that way, it helps to think of Armikrog as less of a game and more of an interactive picturebook.
Despite a buggy release, it doesn't deserve nearly the amount of unfiltered hate it's been getting. The Neverhood wasn't exactly a Day One critical success either. It took a few years. That said, don't buy it on Steam. Get it on
instead. You get a DRM-free copy and extras like music and artwork. Burn it to disc or save it to a memory stick, then pull it out in twenty-five years. You'll be happy you did.

Nation Red is an 'arcadey' top-down zombie shooter.
Presentation; Story, well, there isn't any. Zombies are here, you shoot them. There are a handful of game modes, but they're all just small variations on shooting zombies. The UI is not great, but it doesn't get in the way too much, I do wish the camera control could be a bit smoother though.
Gameplay; The gameplay feels pretty good. Running around, dodging zombies, and shooting to clear a path in front of you. There is a learning curve in every single match as both the quantity and danger of the zombies increases over time. The game is replayable in the sense that you can try using different weapons and different perks, or a different strategy altogether; but you've pretty much seen all the game has to offer after only a few matches. I do wish the arenas were bigger and more interesting.
Visuals; The graphics are adequate, not great. You won't be looking too closely at the zombie textures while you're playing, but the special effects aren't particularly impressive either.
Sounds; The music and sound effects both feel repetitive; While the gameplay itself is repetitive, some variation in sound would have been nice. No voice acting.
In conclusion, not a bad game. I had fun playing it for a bit. After a few days I got tired of it, and I haven't been back since.

'Dust : An Elysian Tail' is the best game I have played so far.
That will be very difficult to write down something long and descriptive about what I think about this game. But I will try to.
Gameplay :
The whole game consists of exploring a huge world where every area has been made smartly. If you can't go somewhere, that means you are not ready for this. During this exploration, you will have to face many monsters , no, tons of them. But Dust is able to swing his sword quickly and deadly with your help. Smashing the buttons might not be the right thing to do.
When fighting, you can, as said above, swing your sword with a single finger for an attack up to a 4-hit combo. However,this is not the only thing you will do, as Dust will learn more skills and ways to fight. Magic, for sample, that require a combination of attacks to become deadly.
Every battle is fast and requires you to dodge a lot. Your life doesn't regenerate itself with time in any way, and you can't rent a room. You can only buy food that looks quite expensive, but it is not that much after you've learned how to dodge.
There is also an energy bar that depletes itself by dodging or using magic. Being empty, you can't dodge or throw magic missiles anymore. But you can wait for it to fill up, or if you can't, attack ennemies.
The more hits you do in a row, the more rewards you gain.
Graphics :
Everything seems to have been drawn. No 3D. Simple 2D graphics that are amazingly beautiful and amazing. Characters are very adorable (excepted the monsters. They had to choose) and the background is very pleasant to watch. WIll you as well stop in the middle of a stage to watch the landscape ?
Musics :
I don't think there is a lot to say. The musics in this game are amazing as well, according to me.
Story ;
I didn't complete the game already. But as far as I have been, I've truly enjoyed the story. I won't spoil ~
Dust : An Elysian Tail is a game for people who wants to destroy everything on their path, for the ones who are looking for challenges - there is an hardcore mode where ennemies kiil you with two or three hits - but also the ones who are looking for a great story in a great world. It costed me €2.49, and I think this game deserves to be discovered.

So first off, Necropolis is not the best at first impressions. When you start the game, all you will see in the first levels are skeletons. Once you encounter different enemy types, they are unlocked and can appear any time in your run.
Necropolis is a Dark-Souls-inspired rogue-like dungeon crawler game with a beautiful, simplistic low poly art-style. The game is great and it is very fun... if you don't mind vagueness and just want to loot things instead of story. The fighting is tough, but only because getting hit is unavoidable and there are hordes of enemies thrown at you. There is no real tutorial and you only get told the controls.
Necropolis has many secrets, and massive biomes to explore. Sometimes it can be a bit overwhelming and get dull when you're backtracking through a massive dark hallway with only triple-rats and pyramid spiders to slay for loot.
The crafting is a little clunky and the need to eat is sorta annoying, but the game has a lot of charm. The dialogue, told through captioned gibberish, is mocking and charming and the humorous descriptions on items are pretty well-thought, but lack any stats or real description.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who loves dungeon-crawling, looting gems, and having cool weapons and armor for cosmetic and very small unique perks. The devs, as I have heard, have a good track record and I hope they support the game with free updates.
Haven't tried co-op, but others say it is fun. But don't buy the game based on positive reviews or negative reviews, buy the game depending on if you like the genre.

So I've played this game solo and co-op for nearly 10 hours. I felt it's important to give a review after getting a solid chunk of gameplay in, so here goes...
Would I recommend this game? Yes, if you have disposable income and don't mind paying $30 for a dozen or so hours of co-op Rogue-lite fun. A gorgeous visual aesthetic, fun and charming monsters and character designs, intuitive and likable combat. This game is as many describe, Dark Souls-lite combined with the Rogue-lite formula: randomized dungeons, random enemies, RNG loot, permadeath and the ability to acquire permanent buffs that will help you in later runs. I had some fun playing the game solo (which is pretty hard as one mistake can land you back at square 1), and even more fun playing with a friend. It seems that even two people with moderate skill can beat all 8 floors  (and the final boss floor) without too much practice. We beat it the first try in about 4 hours.
Now the make-or-break feature of this game would be its Rogue-lite elements. That is where Necropolis differs from other games of its ilk (Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon, Rogue Legacy etc.).
Here are the main differences and unique design decisions that I noticed:
- Necropolis does NOT have randomly generated character builds for each playthrough (as in Rogue Legacy and traditional Rogue-likes), or preset characters/classes you can pick (as in Enter the Gungeon or Binding of Isaac). You get one starting build with cosmetic changes, that's it.
- Necropolis doesn't have crazy and overpowered RNG weapons or items, most of the weapons you pick up drops consistently from the creature that uses it. Other items and weapons may randomly drop from specific "loot goblin"-like creatures or chests, but I haven't run into a "Holy-S**t" item in the game yet. It's fairly paced and doesn't offer gigantic RNG bonuses like other Rogue-lite games do sometimes.
- Necropolis features full-on co-op for up to four equal players. This makes for a greatly varying difficulty, as solo can be pretty hard, but if you have a party of four to res, craft, defend and attack with, I'd assume the game would be pretty easy. Which leads me to the next point.
- Necropolis has no transparent difficulty setting that I can find, so if you beat it, there's no greater challenge to overcome other than beating it again. This might be disappointing to the hardcore player, as many Rogue-lites like Isaac, Legacy and Gungeon are incredibly hard to get to the very end of a game's run.
- Co-op has always-on friendly fire. I kill my teammates more than the monsters do.
- Necropolis has a lot of resource management. There are two types of currency, one for more temporary items, one for more permanent items, crafting materials, potions, scrolls, food, stamina, maximum stamina. All of these can be gained and depleted.
- The particular bugbear people might have with this game is Maximum Stamina drain. Blocking, ranged attacks, charged attacks and heavy attacks all drain your Maximum Stamina, eventually landing on its minimum value which lets you get about one quick off before depleting your stamina.
- Unlike most RPGs and some Rogue-lites, there are zero stats on items. You have to guess as to how effective something is or isn't. No damage numbers or specific effects are detailed in item descriptions, so that can be a point of contention for people. You only get an arbitrary "Tier" number for items to estimate its effectiveness.
- There is only one true boss in the game. Unlike most Rogue-lites, there isn't a boss at the end of each major level or section of the game, there is just one final boss, and its design could definitely be improved.
Despite all this, I had a lot of fun, and I like the interesting take on the formula. But I could see hardcore players being disappointed with possible replayability issues down the road, or of 4-player parties clearing the dungeon too easily. On the $30 price point, I'm not sure I'd recommend it to everyone as there are more replayable options for smaller prices, but if you want a unique take on the genre and don't flinch at spending $30 on a few 3-4 hour playthroughs with friends, I'd heartily recommend the game.
Let's hope the devs see the points that could be improved and come out with some content/tweak patches. Just adding in a couple modes that adjust the RNG would do wonders for this game.

Now I am going to sound like I am giving it a lot of hate, and I am, but I really do like this game and want to see it get better as time passes. I put a recommend for this game because I do think it is worth your time, and I do think that it is worth considering if you want to play something coop with a friend. However, there are many issues that I, as a budding game designer, have learned to never do in a video game.
One of those is continually spawning enemies behind you. This game does that, A LOT. And while I do not generally hate spawning enemies, in fact I don't usually mind them, this game takes it to the extremes. On the run I completed the game with, I got to the point where I would kill 9 or 10 enemies at once, only to have 9 or 10 spawn again immediately, I eventually had to run because I just couldn't kill them fast enough. This game takes that mechanic to a point where it stops being fun and starts being annoying. Another bad mechanic, and it is a good mechanic when done right, is lack of information. The game tells you nothing, it literally tells you nothing. I bought 3 codexes and I still have yet to understand what some of them actually do. The game is also very short, there are only 9 floors. I got to floor 4 my first run, floor 6 my second, and beat it my third. Besides the last few levels the areas barely varied. There were some areas that were swampy, some that were like a sewer but then they lead into areas that you spent the first 3 levels seeing and it just ruins the fun.
Besides those glaring issues that might turn some people off of the game, the game offers a souls-like experience without busting your balls. It is hard, but it is only hard because of the things I mentioned before. So in conclusion, I think the game is great and I want to see where it goes in the future, but there are many problems and I honestly probably won't play through it again until there is an update. So if you want to give it a shot, it is worth trying, if you want to wait for a sale; I wouldn't blame you at all. If you have a friend who has it, try it before you buy it.

Actually, although this is a very technical subject, the developer's commentary that comes with it, is more than worthwhile listening to. Especially the little Byzantine church, part of the monastery on top of the cliffs, still feels amazing and oozes atmosphere. Valve did a wonderful job with the lighting inside the church, even letting dimmed light through the stained-glass windows. At the same time, it also made me a bit sad, because, well, how long has it been since we got the latest Half-Life content? Oh well, who knows....

Oh boy.... this is tough to review.  Everyone is walking the tight-rope of "acceptability" on this due to the subject.  I think we need to take a moment to break this down by looking at a summary of the other reviews, with my thought on them sprinkled in.  At the end I will explain why I ended up paying money for this game.
From many of the reviews you will see that the game has a great style.  I completely agree with this as the art, the voice acting, the story are each superb in their delivery of an emotionally rife game experience.  They all add up and blend together to pull you in.
I have also seen that the basic mechanics can be difficult and do somewhat hamper the immersive aspect of the game.  Once again, I am in agreement with those points.  There were times where my attention was solely focused on trying to figure out just what the game was expecting me to do and it pulled me out of the moment.
As has been noted time and again, religious content is also highly visible and presented with a very specific perspective.  Being such a highly charged topic I will only say that you need to decide if you are willing to sit down and hear what the Green's think and feel about their faith and how that plays in their experience with Joel's fight with cancer.  For them it played a significant part and, as this is their story, it is present in the game.  You don't have to agree with or accept what they think, you just need to decide if you want to listen.  Enough said for now.
For my own overall opinion, the negative points were quite minor and once I was past them they were completely forgotten in light of the deep impact of this story.
TLDR: Now we come to why I bought, played, and reviewed the game and my recommendation and advice.
As a new "Dada", this one hit me right in the tear-box from the video, even before I bought it.  Deeply emotional, I had to consider hard if this was a journey I was willing to make and a subject matter I was willing to immerse myself in.  Ultimately, I bought it because I wanted to support the family.  I could have let it sit there but I played it because... I wanted to see if I could handle it.  I needed to know, on a deeply personal level, if I could be exposed to this sort of situation "first hand" and come out the other end intact.  When I finished I was mostly intact but never will I forget what I felt imagining that this was my child.  I will never be the same for witnessing this story in this way.  I look at my child and my time with them very differently now.
Buy it to support the family if that is something you are willing to do.  Buy it if you want to have a very poignant, narrative driven, game experience.  Buy it if you want support the Indie Dev world.  Whatever your reason, make sure that once you've bought it you take time to play through it with an open mind and heart.  If you play it while closed off to the emotions of others you will likely not have a worth-while time with this game.  If you are open, this very likely will change the way you interact with those you love.  At least for a good long while.

Saw a lot of negative reviews, so I felt I had to give it a positive review, as I've had an absolute blast with the game. However, this does come with a caveat; this game is way, way more fun played cooperatively. Approaching the game for a single player experience akin to a Souls game, you would instead get quite bored and frustrated; the art style is gorgeous but repetative, the combat is fun but simplistic, gear progression does happen but is random and unplannablem and death is permanent and often happens for stupid reasons. These all add up to an initially enjoyable but (combined with odds stacked thoroughly against you on levels 5+) ultimately frustrating, infuriating, repetative single player game.
Fortunately, I played it in multiplayer all the way, and that is where the game truly has a chance to shine. Not just because multiplayer is inherently more fun and makes any game better, but because this game actually really strongly benefits from it. The unreasonable odds on levels 5+ become much more manageable, and should someone go down, their is a brief window wherein they can be resurrected intact, and even if you fail they still respawn, albeit naked and with their progression reset, which is a threatening kick in the teeth but can be overcome once you grab a decent weapon. And even the randomness of gear becomes much more enjoyable; there's a competative element to it when there are more people facing the same dilemma, or alternitively you can trade items if you're a more helpful sort of person.
The game is still challenging in multiplayer, but it's also more approachable and more fun. And the art direction is absolutely gorgeous, the music is immersive, and the writing (such as it is) is genuinely amusing. You can also see quite clearly many things in the game that are intended to be expanded on; I sincerely hope the developers aren't put off by all the mixed reviews, as I've had a great time and would love to see the game continue to grow.

That Dragon, Cancer is an indie game created by Developer and Programmer Ryan Green and tells the tragic story of he and his wife’s (Amy Green) personal experience of having a son diagnosed with a very rare and very aggressive form of cancer. The Game goes into detail expressing the feelings of the Family when dealing with the disease and the struggles that both Joel and the Parents face.
With a story such as That Dragon, Cancer a question often asked is would the game would have benefited being a written story or a movie (granted the documentary for the making of the game is going to be released soon and will no doubt show more details regarding the story) rather than a game. I feel that the story of That Dragon, Cancer could not have been told in any other way that would have been more beneficial to the overall tale. This is because the game allows for the player to more deeply connect and empathize with the character’s as they go through their hardships struggling along with the parents of Joel their struggles become the player’s struggles. The struggles are represented through the game’s mechanics and the interactivity allows the player to more deeply connect and empathize with both the parents and Joel as the game dynamics detail what it was really like for them to go through it on a more interactive and close level.
This technique of using game mechanics to tell a story has been used before, most notably in Anna Anthropy’s Dys4ia where having her story detailed through the mechanics and rule set of a game gave allowed her to tell her story in a way which no other form of media had access to and overall helped her communicate her story in a more meaningful and interesting way. She used the game mechanics to demonstrate to the player how she felt in a way that words never could. That Dragon, Cancer has the same idea but instead of using abstract artistry and design it goes for a much more visceral and direct means of 87617161_green-familycommunicating its message. Visceral is the only way to describe the overwhelming sadness when playing this game as the horrific events come one after the other and give little time for the character’s or the player to have respite. However That Dragon, Cancer is not always sad which makes those sad moments even more so, An example of this is the section of the game where Joel is racing around on his toy car in the hospital, the game turns into a pseudo Mario cart type game. Joel races around on his little car picking up power ups, only these power ups are representative of things to do with chemotherapy. This constantly reminds you that all though the moment right now is joyful, there will be sad moments in the future.
Throughout the game a big emphasis is put on the parents faith. Both Ryan and Amy Green are christian in real life and as such this is shown in the game. During the story both Ryan and Amy have different spiritual experiences. Amy has faith that God will perform and miracle and save her son, she has doubts but thinks that by having doubts that God may not save her son that it lessens the chance of such miracle happening so throughout that-dragon-cancer-park-at-the-edge-of-the-world1the story the player sees that Amy is constantly shoving aside her doubts and trying her best to believe that God will save her son even until the very end. Ryan however has a much different experience, His experience is one of despair as he feels that God will not save his son as he is not ‘important’ enough in Gods eyes, Ryan feels that God does not have time to save his son and this makes him feel depressed and unworthy throughout the game. However Ryan still tries to maintain faith praying for god to cure his son. During the Game there is a section where the player is in a church and if they go up to the stand the room will go dark and some of the candles will light up, in the background both Ryan and Amy can be heard desperately praying for God to save their son, eventually the candles will go out however the player can light them again. This creates a constant struggle of the player trying to keep as many candles lit as possible even though it is impossible to have them all lit whilst Ryan and Amy are heard in the background desperately praying to try and save their son. This produces the feeling of panic and desperation within the player as they constantly attempt to keep the candles lit similar to how the parents felt at the time praying for their son. The player feels empathetic towards the parents as it feels like they went through those same feelings.
The saddest part for some player’s in That Dragon, Cancer isn’t specifically the games story or sections, a lot of player’s will find a way that this story relates to a personal experience that they had. Whether that be an experience with cancer or having a sick family member The game manages to bring out those same feelings that the player might of had when they went through that experience, amplifying its emotional effect on the player. This is one of the strongest yet saddest points about the story in That Dragon, Cancer is that the story is relatable. Many of the players will reach the card section of the game and see a card that reminds them of that experience they had, amplifying the effectiveness of the games story as if the players feels like they can relate to the game then they are much more likely to have an emotional reaction to the game as they would if it were in real life.
Overall That Dragon, Cancer is a game that hits the player right where it hurts. The games compelling and interesting yet depressing story draws the player in and outright punches them in the heart with its harrowing tale of a son with cancer.

Fairly poor 4x game.
Racial abilities have little impact because almost everything is based on %. For example, a basic factory building might be 40% production bonus and take a few turns to build, or can be bought with starting cash. The strongest racial production bonus is also of the same order (around 25% as I recall), but only for either ships or buildings. So its basically worthless.
Same exact issue with both space stations and planetary modifiers to production, science etc. All are % based, and largely meaningless compared to a few low-tier cheap building.
This problem is all over the place in the core mechanics. Overly simplistic to the point of hurting the simulation.
It very much feels like they have missed the point that fun games arent perfectly balanced. A lot of the most famous games of this genre were famous because they had unbalanced, and fun tricks the players could learn. Not that this game has perfect balance, but it sure seems to try to keep all choices when setting up a game as boring as possible, to ensure you cant do anything fun.
Oh, and lets not forget the nickel and diming they have fully embraced by cutting out content that was in the previous game, and adding it as DLC released a month after the game. Stardock used to be different in a good way. Mind you, I havnt played the games they made since galciv2, so maybe I just have rose-tinted glasses and high expectations.

When I first saw this game on steam, it definitely caught my attention. Just from the art style alone. I love how smoothe the animations are. It has the basic RPG elements to it as well; earn exp to gain levels, which come by quickly I might add, which I think is nice, constantly getting new equipment to make yourself stronger... all that jazz. You even have a little companion with you, Fidget, that helps you throughout the game, and it isn't useless, only a little annoying. It can cast spells which you can mix with your attack to make the spell more powerful.
The only complaint I have with this game is your have to learn the most basic of skills which don't come until later on in the game like sliding and even grabbing onto vines to climb to higher points. The grabbing vines skill, I thought, was a little ridiculous to learn because it's nothing special, you just learn to grab a vine and can climb them. But that being said, I guess they don't want you doing everything right off the bat, there is backtracking to get treasures that you couldn't get before and that is something I like.
Overall, I think this game is amazing and I highly recommend it for anyone who enjoys action-RPGs.

People used to cite Double Fine as an example of how Kickstarters can go very, very wrong...but I think Armikrog might be a new contender.
Firstly, it's not as good as The Neverhood. Yeah, of course it's a tough one to live up to, and it's not fair to compare the games like for like.... WRONG. If they raise money for this game on the back of "Hey! Remember Neverhood? We want to do more of that!" then they invite comparisons. And it fails miserably.
It's nice to have HD graphics, but in nearly every other situation this game falls flat on it's face. The music is forgettable. It's hard to believe it's actually the same composer as Neverhood. Here it's just generic background music that you'll start ignoring after about five minutes. The voice acting, despite getting some big names like Mike Nelson from MST3K is lazy. They sound like they can't be bothered and just want to get it over and done with so they can get their paycheques. Also... why do the characters talk with loads of reverb when they're outdoors? Seriously. They sound like they're in a stadium or something. And the sound in the cutscenes keeps going out of sync. Sometimes when the characters talk in the game itself, their lips don't move at all, like they recorded the lines later but couldn't afford to go back and animate them.
The puzzles mostly consist of "see something, go to a different room, duplicate what you saw". Yes, Neverhood had those puzzles too, but here they seem to make up most of the game. The rest mostly seem to consist of "find a lever, put it in the hole and pull it." How many times did we have to do that? Eight? Nine? And you have to do the same lullaby puzzle three times. The same door-opening puzzle FOUR times. And the game is short. Very, very short. The reptition of puzzles just feels padding in a desperate attempt to make it last more than an hour. That 2.4 hours on record? That's how long it took me to finish the entire game...including lunch.
It's also buggy, I can't speak for the Windows version, but the custom cursors are overlayed with the system cursor...the hotspots don't seem to line up well with the items, and it keeps crashing without errors for some reason. Sometimes when a character animation begins [such as picking up an item], they'll jump out of place across the room and snap back when the animation finishes. And there's lots and lots and lots of loading. Every time you leave the room, up to 15 seconds or so, even if you've already been there. After about an hour of gameplay the sound effects [such as footsteps] died on me completely, though dialogue and music continued. Subtitles came and went on a whim, sometimes without the dialogue to accompany them.
It's completely devoid of any wit or charm. It thinks it's funny, but I didn't even smile once. A wisecracking, sarcastic sidekick. Wow! How original! None of the characters are enjoyable or fun to be around, and the whole thing seems devoid of purpose. They also can't make up their minds whether the characters are silent or not. There's plenty of dialogue during the opening and in some of the cutscenes, but both characters fall strangely silent the rest of the time. Part of the appeal of this game is supposed to be the claymation, but a large percentage of the cutscenes, including most of the opening and the backstory videos are digitally animated... And where are the set-pieces such as the "Battle of Robot Bil" or "Pulling the Pin"? There's very little feel of progression, and you just end up wandering around looking for something to do.
And...what's the excuse for a complete lack of Steamworks integration? No achievements....no trading cards....no Steam Cloud saves, nothing. I'm not saying that these things are essential for a game, but it does suggest a lack of care and effort.
Yes, I was a kickstarter for this game. And I feel utterly cheated. There's the kernel of a good game in here, and there are some interesting ideas, but it feels like a total waste of time and money. What a shame.

Nation Red is an addictive 'twin stick' (or keyboard and mouse) shooter with a zombie aesthetic. However, as realistic as the weapons and characters may lead you to believe, you'll soon be summoning clones with shotguns, calling down orbital lasers and splitting the Earth in two with a wide variety of power ups and perks fuelled by your killing spree.
Nation Red has a wide variety of maps and modes for players to try, ranging from no-perks single player to a holdout mode with four players desperately defending an encampment of minigun weapon stations from an ever increasing horde. For what's more or less a one-man-band project, Nation Red has grown massively since its 2009 release and continues to do so even now, with new achievements, maps and perks being added at somewhat irregular, but extremely welcome, intervals.
Average Game Length? Depending on skill, games can range from a few minutes to over an hour.
A Bit Like? Crimsonland, Smash TV
Is It Fun? The perks make this game beyond entertaining, and four-player modes add a chaotic atmosphere like few others!
Worth The Price? £7.99 may seem a bit steep for those looking at the screenshots and video, however playing the game is completely different and provided you like other similar games, you will certainly get your money's worth.

Since this game title is my third most played game I figured I should do a review on this game sometime in the near future, so here's my review. I felt kind of jipped in some aspect of this game beings that the game was kind of push off the production line a little sooner then what it probably should've been. For example I'm in a game with music turned on and I'm talking to my friend over skype. Here's where the first problem happens. The first problem is that there is no volume control for this game so the audio tracks just over power my call and this is where the second problem occurs. The second problem occurs when I try to mute the audio for this game and try to continue playing the game, the audio track will still be going to matter what and that irritates me because if I have a good run going not only do I have to exit out of that run in order to get the changes to take affect but it still over powers my friends audio on my end making it hard for me to hear what he's saying which then almost ends in the two of us sounding like old people arguing. But all in all it's a great game and I hope that Rebirth will improve my feelings about this game, I hope that next time I'm giving The Binding of Isaac and 9.5/10 to a 10/10 but for now I'm giving it a 8/10. (Note: If you never played a Danganronpa game, I highly suggest you go to Trigger Happy Havoc and play it first before buying this game, as it requires some logic of the first in order for it to make sense.  It is best to go into this series blind, so get a friend and tell them this is the happiest game on earth and watch them doubt you after the prologue.)
Now on to my review:
This game is set on a tropical island.  The characters consist of students of Hope's Peak Academy, a school that only accepts the most talent filled people.  Each character has a talent that defines them.
Your job as the main character is to befriend everyone on the island as they enjoy the tropical environment.  You give gifts to your favorite characters and chat with them under the sun as you work labor under the authority of a magical rabbit.  After reaching the highest in your affinity with your character of choice, you get their underwear. (Because every main character of Danganronpa has to be shipped with every single classmate)
Oh, and apparently the world has gone to hell and meanwhile you're  trapped on a tropical island with a malevolent bear who likes to toy with people like marionettes so.... (If you're wondering about the bunny, she's still there.... as a punching bag)
The gameplay consists of investigating murders as Monokuma tempts your classmates to kill each other in order to escape the island.  After finding clues, you are then taken to the class trial, where you solve the mystery behind each murder.  You fire "truth" bullets at characters statements and use many other methods to paint your way to the truth.  There are other methods as well such as Logic Dive, where you ride a snowboard down Hajime's mind, Hangman's Gambit, which is traffic simulator, and finally pasting panels together to paint the entire story of the investigation. There's also a part in the game where you play a point and click trapped room puzzle (Could never figure out the code without a hint).
The environments are very colorful and diverse.  Each island has a theme, and every area on said island fits the style.  4th Island is probably my favorite for it's catchy and colorful vibes.
The characters are unique and charming with personality.  As you hang out with each of them, you learn about them and bond, and soon, you too shall have a collection of underwear to hang on your wall.  These are well-written characters, and it is well worth the time to read through their dialogue, as you can sort of relate to some of the characters.
The story is well-structured.  It starts out confusing, but trust me, it will make sense as you play through.  The game gives you hints to various scenes that will happen later on, but you probably won't catch them until your second playthrough.  For the game to make sense, multiple playthroughs are required.  Feel yourself drown in Despair again as your classmates die again.
Did I also mention that your favorite character dies?  Your favorite character always die... Always.
Do I have any gripes about this game? Yes I do, they are minor but...
I dislike Chapter 2 , more specifically the extra event.  It felt forced and took me out of the experience of the game for a bit.  Chapter 2 is ok, but I really hate "A Man's Nut"; it's the only time in the game where Hajime breaks character and it annoyed me.
There was a certain thing that happened in Chapter 3 that felt rushed and unfinished (those that played the game will probably know what I am talking about.)
There are some parts of the game that were translated incorrectly.  I mean, it's not that bad, it just annoys me a bit because I'm somewhat of a grammer nazi.

I've been reading some reviews on this game and they just seem silly to me, so I thought I might post one of my own.  First off, if you can't get past the Uplay don't even bother reading further.  I guess there is some issues if you have  32-bit OS as well...  I have a 64-bit OS so it isn't as issue for me.  You might want to check into that if do.
Ok, so I fell in love with Might and Magic since I played M&M II: Gates to another world on the Sega Genesis.  I've played III, IV, V and VI all through completion.  I love the series!  I've also played Heroes of M&M I-VI.  THEY ARE DIFFERENT GAMES!  I saw reviews of people complaning this is nothing like Heroes...well...yeah!  It is nothing like Duel of Champions either!  The only thing this game has in common with Heroes is story background and creatures.  Game style is completely different!  I also saw a number of people comparing this to Grimlock.  Sounds like they were expecting this to be Grimlock but with an outside world.  I wonder if this is because all the Diablo Clones out there...Anyways...  Well, this games is completely different again.  Only thing in common with Grimlock is a party of 4 and a grid movement system.  Party make up and battles are different.  There is a lot more stratagy and party balance needed here.  You can't just take for rogues and expect to shoot/kite everything.  There is no kiting.  Mobs will catch you and eat you if you're not prepared.  You will learn what kind of attacks they have and will have to plan on what you need to do to counter them to keep your team alive.   It is turn based, so you know when to expect the attack.  Your four go, then the monsters go, repeat...  You will have time to think, because you'll need it.  This game does have a lot of do and explore.  I did play the early access and am a ways into act 1 of the full release.  Things have gotten much better than early access!  So don't read too much into reviews before 01/21/2014....  The music...I don't really care about music...I play games to play them not listen to music...  The game play is fun, complex and challenging so far.    If played other M&M games (again not Heroes) then you should like this.  If you like Grimlock and are open to more strategy in fighting and with less puzzles and kiting, then you'll probably like this...
It this is a great game if you're not expecting it to be a clone of other games you've played....

Royal Bounty is probably a game that falls in between two reasonably well know game sagas gameplay-wise, one beign Heroes of Might and Magic, and the second one being King's Bounty. Why am I saying this? Well there are elements taken from here and there, such as the time (days, weeks, months) system, the recruitment system, and stuff like that.
Anyway, without further ado, here's a point by point review on the game:
The art style of the game is something that you will either love or might not really be fond of. A little trick I personally applied was downscaling my screen options to something like 1280x720, and everything became much neater, bigger, and overall better.
The gameplay mimics those of the previously mentioned game titles, but falls short in some aspects, such as not allowing the player to move a unit and with the remaining action points, attack. This is a bit of a let down, since in King's Bounty, kitting is such and important ability to use.
Here's where the game really feels a bit unpolished. The sound seems generic, the music is unimpressive... It's definitely a department which needs a bit of work.
Is it worth it? For it's cheap price tag, I would say it's worth a shot, especially if you're into this game genre. The developers keep updating the game every couple of weeks so these issues might get a deserved improvement. Something worth pointing out is that I feel the game is best suited for a smartphone device rather than a PC (As far as I'm aware, the game has support for most mobile devices).
Overall a nice game, with room for improvement.

I pre-ordered this game about a month ago.  I stumbled upon it when i was shifting through Bandai Namco's facebook page.  And I was completley hooked.  I do not regret at all for pre-ordering the game, and I don't believe that the money that I spent was wasted.  I like to think of it as a 20 dollar game, and 10 dollars for the official soundtrack.  But enough about how I got it, let's dive into the game itself.  I personally enjoy this game 100%.  I love the exploration aspect, the combat the scenery, everything.  I was able to complete the game on the day of the release after 3 deaths.  And I have continued to play the game over and over again.  The replay value for this game is astonishing.  Not only that but the community of the delvers is fantastic aswell.
I have played several runs with people that I have never seen before in my life, but they are cool and interesting people who's goal is similar to my own, beat the Necropolis and escape in one piece.  I love playing this game alone and with other people.  This game might not be for everyone, which is fine.  Every game is like that.  But don't let the people who give negative reviews keep you from trying out this game for yourself.  If you don't enjoy it then ask for a refund, end of story.  Just don't turn into the type of person who just straight up mocks this game for no apparent reason.
Again, I have found so much enjoyment in playing this game, and I feel that I will be playing this game more and more when the free DLC's and paid expansions get released.  If you are looking for a good challenge and a great community, this game is meant for you.
There is one more thing that I would like to mention about this game.  I have been reading through the other reviews, the good and the bad, and I have noticed that a few of the negative are saying how the weapons may seem special but have no special effects.  That is very much incorrect.  This game is all about experimentation, you have to test out each weapon to know what its worth is.  And from playing the game and testing the varying weapon types, there are very key differences.  In the game there are 4 main "elements" to the weapons.  The grine, fire, ice, and acid/poison.  (I am excluding the electric ones because I have yet to find a tier 4 electric weapon) You find these weapons littered in chests, or carried by specific monsters, and after testing these weapons on several different monster types, there are actual advantages for using different elements.
For different types of units, the different elements do more damage.  For example, the clockwork enemies are metal, it seems rather logical that acid/poison would do more damage, which it does indeed do.  From what I have found here is the counter list
Acid/Poison beats clockwork monsters
Fire beats grine enemies
Grine beats regular mobs (Hordmen)
Ice beats skeletons
After testing and retesting these there are positive side effects for the type of weapon that you choose for the certain type of mob that you are fighting.
Now just to clarify, I am not 100% sure on the ice and grine element counters yet.  But fire does do way more damage to grine units, and acid/poison does do way more damage to clockwork mobs.
And i may be very wrong about most or all of these counters, but I have at least put in the effort to find this out, which is the purpose of this game.
Just once more, this game is all about exploring and testing your environment, you have to figure things out for yourself.  So don't just read through the reviews and take a side of good or bad. You have to try the game out for youself in order to make that decision.

Alright well, I went into this game with pretty mid-level expectations, and it did not exceed them. I'm a big fan of rogue-lites and the Dark Souls series so I was naturally drawn to this game, which promised a somewhat similar experience.
Well, it is isn;t a complete mess like many people are making it out to be, but it definitely isn't worth the $30 price tag, unless you're really looking for something to spend money on.
The combat system, while definitely 'souls-like', lacks a lot of variety. Every weapon in the game is a one-handed, swinging weapon. The only variation comes in how "heavy" or "light" the weapon is. They don't have unique movesets (with a few exceptions), and they just do flat damage despite appearances that would lead you to believe there are additional effects (like poison dripping from the bl;ade, fire or ice, etc). There are a few different enemy types and they do have interesting variants the farther down into the tombs that you go, but none of them present any real challenge. The only time your life will feel threatened is when you get swarmed by a large group of high-level enemies, and that threat is completely nullified when you play in co-op, where the permadeath is basically a non-factor.
Visually the game has a nice aesthetic, similar in many ways to the Windwaker style of cell-shading, but the environments feel very empty. There are several zones like swamps, dungeons, sewers, and floating ruins, but they are all functionally the same, just different coats of paint and in some of them you'll find more of a particular enemy type.
As far as difficulty, as a Souls veteran, the game felt like it posed almost zero challenge, as I stated earlier. I pretty much cleared the entire game in one go, playing solo. I imagine that it would be even easier with coop, or using the codexes (which I didnt have becasue it was my first run). It felt a little underwhelming that it was both 1) only 8 levels of dungeons, and 2) so easy to beat that it didn't even require the use of the game's "carry over" progression system.
There are some positive points, like the interesting theme, the visuals (for the most part), and the general originality, but overall the game just feels like it didn't live up to its potential.
In conclusion, on paper, a Dark Souls/Roguelike hybrid sounds like a dream come true for fans of either genre, but Necropolis doesn't manage to deliver on its initial promise. If you want a polished, deep game with progression, challenge, and variety, then Necropolis is not for you. Especially for $30.

At my initial point of purchase Royal Bounty HD was in bad shape.
The developer has since fixed many issues and made many improvements turning it from a disappointment to a mildly entertaining adventure.
Royal Bounty HD has several similarities to HOMM and King's Bounty.
It focuses more specifically on a sprawling single player adventure, and even sports a creative story line.
I personally missed the strategic elements of building economics and resource management.
There is good content depth, but it misses the polish that makes similar games shine.
Pixel graphics are well done, and will be enjoyable for fans but possibly disappointing for others.
There are several balance and timing issues (especially later in the game) that may frustrate most players, but may also have been intended as a difficulty curve.
(some of these may have been addressed in subsequent patches)
Royal Bounty HD is a respectable, passionate effort not to be overlooked by fans of the genre, but unfortunately can't recommend it as a 'yes' instead of a 'no' for everyone.
Despite the praise above for what it has done well, it could have done specific things differently and better.
Note : This review has been re-written thanks to constructive feedback from BlakesSanctum.

A lot of the negative opinions about this game are from people who have played many of the games that this one is supposed to be based upon (Kings Bounty, Heroes of M&M).  I've never really played either of those games, so I was able to come to it with a fresh perspective, and I happen to enjoy it.  "It's supposed to be based off of "x", but it's not exactly the same.  Thumbs down!"  Who cares!  Enjoy and respect this game for what it is.
The advent of the "easy" mode is a huge plus, as it allows you to get a few playthroughs in to explore the world, and figure out which quests you need to tackle and in what order.  This seems like a game that would be very difficult to beat on the first play through, due to the increase in enemy armies over the passage of time.  With that said, it only adds to the value of the game, as you'll get in more play time to hone your strategy and approach to each play through until you know exactly where to go, and the best ways to get there and what units (and treasures) to pick up along the way.
A lot of the strategy required in this game falls outside of battle.  Do you spend the few extra turns to go get the those treasure chests guarded by those tough monsters?  Or skip them, and complete that quest that's been waiting for you to complete it?  Or take the time to do both, but in which order?
I'm enjoying the game right now, and feel like I'll get many more hours of enjoyment as I delve deeper into the world, and work on better paths to complete the quests.  At first, I didn't like the idea of feeling "rushed" to complete certain quests, but I'm beginning to like the idea of doing several play throughs to "perfect" my path.
I find myself wanting to restart a lot of the RPGs I play, because after getting a feel for them, I see how I could do the beginning levels more efficiently.  In quite a few of those RPGs though, I experience what I like to call "restart remorse", in that I spend so much time on my first play through, that to restart to get "a more perfect party", and it tends to bother me a bit when I do finally restart.
In Royal Bounty (though not a traditional RPG per say), you are rewarded when you restart, as you have more knowledge that ends up benefitting you tremendously when you do begin a new game.
This is game is well worth it's $5 price tag, and lends value for the price.  Give it a try, and enjoy it for what it is.

I'm going to start off by saying I genuinely enjoy this game. It's a solid game, but I can see why people wouldn't want to shell out $30 for it. As with any game, there are some really good aspects about the game, but there are also some not so good aspects about the game.
As far as good goes, the number one on my list is that it has an outstanding multiplayer. If you have any friends at all who play Necropolis, it makes the game exponentiallybetter. Not saying the game is bad single player, just better multiplayer. It also has great level design, specifically on the swamp, sewer, and cathedral (factory?) areas. I also personally love the comedy style of the game, but I (once again) can see why some people wouldn't. It's a dry comedy, with some wit (but not excessive amounts).
There are indeed negatives though, the first on my list being the loot system. Every enemy drops items, and it can be pretty overwhelming (I feel the same way about Borderlands, and the like). I have no problem with the weapons themselves, but the map is usually littered with them, most of which are comparative trash to my current weapon. Also, the basic dungeon level design is serviceable, but leaves something to be desired. Not bad, just could be better IMO. Pretty much the only other problem I have with it is the ending (but no spoilers here)!

Royal bounty is can be summed up as a Kings Bounty clone using a HOMAM 2 engine. While I got a sense of nostalgic playing this game (who didn’t love HOMAM 2), there is a big issue - this combination doesn’t quite work.
My main gripe with the game is how linear it is and how little replayability it has.
Looking at it from an RPG site: Currently you only have one character to choose from. While skills can be gained on level up (with some degree of random), the skills are not balanced and you will find out quickly which are must have skills and which are junk skills (to the point of spamming load/save to ensure you get what you want).
You’ll be spamming load heaps of times as you adventure around the map, as you have no idea if the critters you are about to fight will be a walk in the park or annihilate you on the first turn (NOTE: I think this has been addressed in the latest patch).
Little to no replayability – the game becomes quite linear later on – do one quest before you can finish the next. The units will become available to you in the same order. The spells you get will always be unlocked in the same order. This means you’ll always play the game the same way. Also due to the difficulty of the game (see the next point) there are only a handful of strategies (I can think of 2, so I’m being honest) that work, so you can’t really deviate your playstyle if you actually want to finish this game.
The game is hard. While difficulty levels have been introduced by the latest patch (yet to test). Monster/critter stacks grow with time. I won’t go into detail as to why this isn’t a good idea, as pretty much every other review touches upon it. But it does mean if you don’t play optimally, you can get suck and will need to restart. It also means its best to race through the game as quick as possible - kind of a contradiction in an RPG.

Through my hours of playing Gmod, I had a blast.  Playing this game years ago and finding a TTT server where I met a lot of the close friends I have now was a great moment for me.  Though that's only if you're lucky enough to find a community that made you want to be a part of it.  Finding a great community is just one aspect that can make this game great.  Whenever you're bored and don't know what to do, getting on Gmod can be a great choice because of all the different Gamemodes that exist or are being created still.  You've got the base Sandbox mode where you can go to mess around with the default tools or the models and other miscellaneous things you can have at default, or download multiple other objects, models, etc... off of the Steam Workshop to increase the levels of fun you can have with this game.  Other than Sandbox you can find the other multiple things like TTT(Trouble in Terrorist Town), Hide'n'Seek, Prop Hunt, etc... the list goes on and on for the multiple things that can be created onto Gmod.
Even though there are a good amount of things you can find good about this game, there are those downsides to it.  Often times on some servers; specifically on TTT; there can be issues with the hit registry which can cause you to miss headshots or other shots which of course will cause you to get a bit upset.  Then there's also the issue where you need a Source game to be able to textures (that or going to another site to download the textures) which honestly shouldn't be that big of a deal now of days, especially with the bundles going for a very cheap price now of days.  Other than those, when you go to join a server, it can take a very long time to get into a server if it's one that included a lot of add-ons.
All in all I would recommend the game for everyone to play just on the basis that it's a good game to meet friends in, play with your current friends or just to mess around in the sandbox mode solo.  Have a wonderful day.

I was a bit hesitant to buy this game since I thought it looked cheesy and without lasting appeal. I can happily say I was very wrong. Of all the various couch games I own, this is the game that all of my friends and family, from highly seasoned and competitive gamers to my girlfriend's parents, all consistently are enthusiastic to play. The game has quirky, hilarious weapons and game mechanics, which often end in you getting yourself killed in a hilarious fashion. Unlike other party games, though, there is little luck factor involved and a high skill ceiling.
The game is also well-polished, with tons of little bells and whistles that really set it apart from other indie games:
The steam workshop is integrated very well into the game. You can even play random maps without having to subscribe to them, and then you can subscribe to the ones you like real-time.
You can set custom icons for your controls that match a number of popular controllers. These icons will display in the warm-up rooms, so you won't need to explain the controls to your friends (they even had the buttons for my USB SNES controllers!)
There's some kind of way to customize the warm-up room with furniture, but I haven't been too interested in it.
Pros:
The netcode has a system of client-side hit registry, which means your friends on the other side of the world don't have a significant disadvantage.
Can mix local couch players with online players, so you could have 2 local players and fill in with online players (though only 1 player from each client connection can play)
Cons:
No real singleplayer to speak of. There's a challenge mode but it gets old pretty quick
The random map system is a good way to get replay value, but it needs more variation.

An honest, frank and emotional retelling of the thoughts and feelings of the time spent with their son. This incredibly personal tale is wrapped in a beautiful landscape of sound and colour that is unlike any other experience. Glimpses into the reality are scattered throughout the piece with the final credit reel having a profound impact. This game is tough, on many occasions it allows you to linger in drawings or cards, yet the emotional weight makes progression a necessity.
My whole life I wanted to play a game that was this deep and meaningful, yet when it was released, it has taken me 2 months to play the game due to the nature of its contents. The loss of a child outweighs any pride for the industry reaching a higher standard in narrative for me.
I cannot say I know Joel, Ryan or Amy any better from this experience nor understand the pressure, emotions or burden that had in the 4 years their son was alive; but in this journey they have provided us with an insight that will last with me forever.
I wish everyone involved the best going forward with their lives.

One of the best couch party style multiplayer games, up there with titles like Smash Bros and Mario Party.
With a combination of easy to pickup controls, and a surprisingly high skill ceiling, Duck game is perfect for all levels of skill. Coupled with many levels that often play out in different ways, lightning fast moment to moment gameplay that wastes minimal time with BS (such as loading), a large variety of weapons that each have their own nuances, and a huge amount of customizability from a level editor, custom sprites and mods, and you've got a quality game that (in my opinion) you almost have to try to not like. There's very little to hate here.
That's not to say the game can't be improved. The single player could be a bit more fleshed out, the netcode could seriously use some improvement (there have been way too many times where I've been shot, even though I've already dodged the bullet), and features such as tournament mode and spectator mode would be appreciated. The only real issue here from a design standpoint is the camera, as in many levels the camera can be so zoomed in that you see very well where you're going, requiring you to have prior knowledge of the level.
Aside from those few minor gripes, Duck Game is a game I honestly feel like I could reccomend to anyone. At $13, Duck Game is a steal.
