Long review incoming. I prefer my steam reviews to be indepth so if you want short and sweet, this isn't it.
This Dragon, Cancer is an interactive experience about two of the main developers (the Green family) losing their son, Joel, to cancer. The game is designed as a tribute to him.
I brought this game after the recent fiasco about how it never made a single cent in sales, but I had it on my radar for many years. I for one am someone who loves one time, amazing, well crafted narratives and as a game developer myself, I don't believe a game needs to have a complex narrative with branching story plot.
Sure you could argue the game would be better as a movie, but it's deliberately made as a game so that users can experience a part of what the Green's were going through and basically...the game is all about emotion and you projecting yourself onto the story arc.
The soundtrack for this game is amazing, I'm going to buy it ASAP because it's a really nicely done soundtrack, while the low poly art style works well both technically and as a way to project yourself into the arc, which it was intended to do.
The game definetly relies alot on emotion and if you don't have emotion then this game is not for you. I read as
, until it got so much for me that I started to break down.
The game also includes briefly other peoples cancer stories and having family members who died of cancer, this part really hits home for me...hard.
I'd recommend this game, however I do agree that the price tag is steep. But then I also believe it shouldn't be brought on sale, it should be brought at full price as I'd feel like I'd ripped off a charitable donation if I brought it on sale. I like the art style, narrative and the soundtrack and I doubt it could have achieved the same effect if done any other way  (say, as a movie).
It also hit home for me to many other aspects of my life, especially as my name is Joel, the same as one of the Green's sons. Not even just about cancer, but about loss, grief, hope, illnesses (including mental illnesses) and lots of other aspects.
I'd rate it an 8/10.

When I first heard about That Dragon, Cancer from my children, I couldn't understand what the appeal would be. It is a "game" about a child having and dying from cancer. But, they kept asking for it, so when it went on sale, I bought it. I decide I would check it out before telling them. Here is what I learned:
I cried through the whole thing. My husband has been battling stage IV lung cancer since 2012. I write about the journey our family has been on. You have to do something to sort out the emotions you are experiencing, and writing is my gift.
Game development is the gift that Eli's dad has. He has used his gift in an amazing way to share his family's experience with the world. This is an immersive experience, more than a game. It is so real and raw.
So why would someone want to "relive" the cancer experience through a game, or through any other format for that matter? Because in seeing other people's journies, you discover that you are not alone. One of the interesting things in That Dragon, Cancer, was the different ways that each parent coped. The struggles with faith, the reactions to events. It was beautiful to see that other people have the same questions when they face the Dragon. It is also inspiring to see them overcome.
I have been thinking a lot lately about the phrase, "Walk a mile in my shoes."  Until you do that, you really can't impose your value system on others. There has been criticism in some of the reviews about the amount of God and faith in the game. This bothers me because our society has made God and faith taboo. God is how this family overcame the pain of their son's cancer. God is how our family, and many other families, overcome this Dragon.
I would recommend this game highly. Have a box of Kleenex nearby, though. You will need it.

That Dragon, Cancer firstly is not a game, but an 'experience', having few instances with game mechanics, neither of which requires success to advance. Mostly one simply clicks on obvious clickable objects and watches plot unfurl. This is not a deal breaker for me, as I can move past game mechanics to story.  With a story though, the expectation is of a good story. This game fails to deliver in that regard, emotional on the surface, but not eliciting that emotion.
This failure is in many ways muddled by the nature of the subject matter, childhood cancer, which makes me want to instinctively like it because to not feels like an endorsement of cancer and an attack on the people who made this who experienced a definitively tragic event. However, this is another big problem in the creation of the story. This game was created by people with first hand experience in this regard, but they are also the characters in the game, and they have most clearly written themselves into the game in their best Sunday dress. As a result the game is something of a story retold by the people who experienced it, but viewed through their own distorted views of themselves. No one in this game has any sort of flaw whatsoever, and the closest attempts for the characters to have flaws are laughable, amounting to being despondent in a situation where there is no fault feeling as such. The whitewashing crushes the authenticity that could've existed, had this not been a memoir. The entirety of the narration lacked a human feel to it, and made me feel all the worse for not connecting to them as the main character is a cancer patient.
Another issue is that one of the central arcs of this game is of Christian responses to crisis. I am not religious, nor am I vehement against it. It feels as though I should at least not be against the theme, because to feel so feels like an aspersion on Christianity, but the theme was poorly thought out and written.  Occasionally, the use feels much like a sermon. I don't require characters to forsake their religion, and it is perfectly fine to be a useful coping mechanism, but it fails as a core game mechanic, serving mostly to deflect the very mortal concepts that would be the story's potential strength. It is alienating, and nothing inspiring came from it.
The artistic feel of the game is bland, and much in the game looked like painted wood with occasional real images jarringly inserted into this world. There are no faces in this game, which is understandable as it would be almost impossible to effectively communicate emotion with such faces, but it is symbolic of how this game fails to communicate emotion. The music in the game does not inspire or reinforce the emotions the game is trying to elicit, and is not noteworthy, which given the emotional nature of the game and that music can elicit, is a shame.
In the end my emotional response to this game was feeling bad that I didn't feel something from this game, but feeling like I shouldn't criticize it because of what it is. That is not indicative of a quality experience, and at a hefty price tag (15$ as of this writing), that is a very difficult sell, as this game is also quite short. If you think that this is perhaps because of some charitable donation from purchasing this game, then I would look harder, because I could find nothing indicating such a donation, which seems an oversight.

This is probably one of the most difficult reviews I had to write. It's very tough to say whether I recommend this game or not.
Let's start with the positive stuff. The style of the game is unmistakable. As soon as you dive in, the clay animation and the goofiness of the main character sends you right back to the good days of the developer's previous works. Now our character has a sidekick with whom it has extensive interaction throughout the game which seems a pretty good find to me.
The gameplay itself is also very familiar for the fans. Strange mechanisms, weird symbols, looking for the right tip - all of that is back. Some solutions will require working together with the sidekick which definitely brings something new into the game.
The backstory is there, and it is given in separate pieces, just like before. So you uncover all the details as you go. I think it was also a great decision to implement it as stories which language you do not yet understand, so at first you just try to guess what it tries to tell you by looking at the picture.
So why do I doubt whether I should be recommending the game? The main reason is probably that it is simply
. The gameplay time is surprisingly short. I spent about 5 hours in the game, even though I didn't rush anything and was trying to get into the game. That's simply too little. Some people suggested that this could be a demo, and I somewhat agree, it's does not feel like a full game.
The game offers little in terms of the game world as well. In Neverhood we used to have a fairly large world with many locations and free movement between them. In here we only get several locations which are all inside the same castle. We don't get to go outside, the only available mode of transportation is the electric cart.
Same thing can be said about the story. Characters other than the main one and his sidekick get very little development. So when I finished the game, I definitely felt hungry for much more.
Some people here also complained about bugs, but I can't say that's true for me. For the entirety of this game I don't remember being stuck because of the bugs even once. Probably it's because I played the game much later after the launch, but that doesn't change the fact: it's well made by now.
My verdict: yes, you should probably play it. Despite being short, it is well-made and pretty enjoyable. Get it on a sale, and you will have some good time on a weekend. Just one thing you have to keep in mind: don't expect the scale of Neverhood, or you will be very disappointed.

I've played a lot of games in the 18 years I've been alive and kicking, some good and some bad. But this game is without a doubt the absolute best I have ever played.
I already own the XBLA version of the game and when I get a PS4, I plan on buying it for that console. It's that good.
The story revolves around the mysterious warrior Dust and his (sometimes not so faithful) companion, Fidget the Nimbat who may I say, is the greatest companion I have ever seen with her 4th-wall breaking dialogue and the fact that she is amazingly well thought out and written (I mean really, she has a fear of heights yet she can fly. Genius). Anyways back to the story, Dust wakes up with amnesia (bit of a generic start off) and a sword is summoned to his side. The sword one of the legenday Blades Of Elysium and it's name is the Blade of Ahrah, it is also the only one that knows of him and his past so far. All of a sudden, FIdget appears and is apparently the swords guardian. She then decides to travel with Dust in his epic quest to discover his past, filled with hardship, laughs, sadness and mystery.
On to the side content; there are many side quests to go through each with their own differeing difficulty level (one in particuar has you collecting materials, some are rare, most aren't. This quest because of the rarer items had took me up until I nearly beat the bloody game to compete in some occasions) There is also a side quest which is unlockable from completing this other side quest and this second one is given to you by this boy called Corbin and he wants you to get a 1000 Hit Combo (easier than it sounds, just head to the Blackmoor Mountains and use the Dust Storm and Fidget Projectile combo attack in a corner with many enemies. Make sure it is on the games difficulty is on Easy and you have no Fidget augments active for a much easier time). Enough of side quests, now onto colletibles. There are (if I remember correctly) 12 cages scattered throughout the game and they contain many beings such as Super Meat Boy, The Kid (from Bastion) and the HyperDuck Sound Studios logo made real. These cages require 4 Keys to unlock and are usually quite difficult to get to.
Now for the story as a whole. The entire story from start to finish is like a really damn good Disney or Pixar film (which ever you prefer) but there are three things that makes it stand out from either of those... it's the delivery, writing and voice-acting. The story, whilst generic is delivered so well it sent chills down my spine and I genuinely felt involved in the games events. The writing will flood you with many different emotions such as sadness, anger, happiness and pity and it just doesn't stop with the twists to keep you intruiged. The voice-acting is flawless, not even IGN could fault it, this one part half-way through the game actually had me in tears (as did the ending) and I was actually frightened of Dust at the half-way point when he blames himself for the death of an innocent.
So yeah, generally a perfect game... I do not think there will be one to beat it in years to come. 7.8, not enough water................. I am SO sorry (couldn't resist)
In all seriousness I give it 100%, 5 Stars, 10/10 max whatever rating system you can find or think of (and this rating comes from a highly cynical 18 year old male)

After only three hours play time, I can honestly say Abzû is one of the most elegant games I've ever played. It simply provides a storied environment to explore while simultaneously avoiding complex interfacing and objective-based gameplay. Instead, it simply paces the player through a diverse arrangement of different ocean environments while relying on the artistry to tell the tale.
The artwork is nothing short of breath-taking. Each environment, scene, and creature display organic movement and appearance. Despite adhering to a confined world map, the game allows one to spend a great deal of time simply looking around the different areas without worrying about survival-driven gameplay or distracting side missions. Each location boasts endemic populations of sea life. They all contribute in small ways to the story of the game, and when examining each species and location closely, some sort of anthropological/prehistoric tidbit can be found. I absolutely love those little hints; they add a great deal of depth to an otherwise simple game.
The score for the game is equally beautiful. I don't often play games for their music, but the Abzû soundtrack is easily one of the best I've ever heard. It doesn't feature much percussion or overzealous dynamics. Rather, it follows a very Chakra-meditative stylization. I own the tracks of Final Fantasy VI, VII and XII, Kingdom Hearts, Diablo, Guilty Gear XX, and Red Dead Redemption, but I can honestly say I'd play this game just to sit and listen while the marine life simulates in the background. I will certainly obtain the soundtrack to this game in the near future.
Altogether, the game is unquestionably well-composed. It may not be particularly fascinating in terms of the small amount of content or, for that matter, the lack of replayability, but it provides a supple and leisurely flow, gorgeous visuals, and, most importantly, a touching story. There are only a handful of games I've ever played that offered this sort of enjoyment. The only major criticism I can think of is the game's short playtime. If the developers decided to go back and really flesh out a more deliberate and lengthy story, I would buy it in a heartbeat. At any rate, I consider Abzû an amazing work of art. Thanks Giant Squid Studios!

I cannot recommend this game if you've played any other game developed by Thatgamecompany. I know this isn't mainly developed by them, but they did have a hand in making this, and Giant Squid only has this on their track record. I bought it and played it going in with an open mind and ready to enjoy the experience as I had done before with so many similar games. I spent a few minutes getting used to the controls in the first area and it felt pretty nice. I continued on into the next area and properly began. Honestly, this opening was where i most enjoyed the game. I didn't know what to expect, and swimming and breaching the water was pretty fun on its own. Unfortunately, it only sets up what pretty much just happens for all of what i played. I played 80 minutes or so, but those 80 minutes were spent doing the same thing over and over. I get a little robot to open up the gate to the next area, I swim around with some great looking fish for a while, and then i move on and do the same thing. The sequences that break from this have almost zero interactivity to speak of, so i can't judge those as gameplay as much as I can judge them as missed opportunities. One could argue that I should have given the game more time, but the game is about two hours long in the entirety and with the pace I was playing at. Thatgamecompany excelled with Journey by having a short length game that is entertaining and beautiful the entire way through. Flow had gameplay that changed as it progressed so it worked with the very simple premise it had. ABZU has a wonderful presentation, but the gameplay doesn't have any substance or depth to speak of. It was boring to me, and boring is the worst thing a game can be.

A fantastic strategy title by all counts, merges 4X and Grand Strategy into a hybrid that has more character than a lot of games of either ilk. The UI is a joy, events and anomalies are fun to interact with, most actions can be done from the galaxy map (which can be set to give you all the info you need at a glance), graphics are clean and pleasing, alien portraits are weird and wonderful, the AI is a notch above that in similar titles, and there is just enough customization to give Stellaris legs for days.
That said, you can sort of feel the holes in the game. No robust trade system, no spying or subterfuge, combat is basically a numbers game (you have a bigger fleet = you win), and while the research system is unique, it feels somewhat 'thin' as far as upgrades go. All said, this is a Paradox title, and with such a successful launch, I am sure we will get plenty of DLC down the road.
For the price of admission, you really cannot go wrong if you are a strategy fan or a sci fi nerd. I bought the game the day pre-releases opened and was downloading it the second it was available. Pretty much have played every waking hour since. Hugely rewarding game and far more accessible than other Paradox titles. I'm impressed, and eager to see what they bring next, and what modders have planned, of course.
Sober Addendum to Review After 30+ Hours: While I am not changing my recommendation, I do think that Stellaris is a buy only if you understand that it is fun and unique, if somewhat broken right now. There are incomplete features, a boring and somewhat broken mid and end game, and while a great time at first, with enough play time you may start to see the cracks in the facade. I already see myself not playing as much until things like sectors, quest chains, warscore goals, and the mid/late game get some much needed attention. There is a great game somewhere in Stellaris, but that game could very well be months away and partially placed behind DLC pay walls.

What makes a role-playing game great? The role-playing, and the game. The Witcher 2 isn’t very good at either. What’s left is a poorly written teen-lit choose-your-own-adventure that assassinates all of the rules of good story telling and doesn’t get away with it.
Let’s start with the role-playing. Most role-playing games let you pick who you are. The Witcher 2 does not: you are one person. This can work – maybe role playing can mean playing some specific, interesting person. By those lights, playing Bruce Wayne in the Batman: Arkham games is role-playing. The comparison is apt: Geralt of Rivia is not an interesting character, and his alter-ego is a sub-plot. This humorless tough never met a turn of phrase or character arc. He’s just a sword-wielding inventory bot. He stands motionless, expressionless, occasionally punctuating his punch-less dialogue with an ill-timed wave of the hand, pound of the fist, or the unintentional comedy of walking in a small circle…in the middle of a conversation. The primary benefits of being Geralt are to be good at, well, everything but dialogue, and attractive to all females. He scores with such bracing lines as, “Oh…you know. Stuff.” This undoubtedly is the generic formula for y-chromosome wish fulfillment. What’s curious is how generic, and ultimately how uninteresting, it is to play that role. If forced to role-play someone else, it would be best to role-play someone with a personality, not a teenager in fantasy Eastern European Batman’s body who, the lore tells us, had his personality excised as a child.
As for the game, it’s not much better. In place of a numbers-based combat system, we endlessly click through more action-oriented combat whose challenge comes primarily from the design behind the numbers, not the enemy’s unique abilities. The net result is to waste the best part of being Geralt…being good at fighting…on rolling and diving around. When the witcher is good, it’s when it combines the potion-crafting, trapping, and a unique combat encounter. Being a monster hunter would lend itself to the game focusing its combat on boss battles. But this would break with CRPG tradition, which means we’re saddled with endless inventory management, fetching large volumes of store-brand digital loot to peddle to in-game money dispensers without the benefit of fast-traveling. The Witcher 2 is a game that is extraordinarily generous with one’s time. And of course slaughtering an ecosystem’s worth of generic monsters who materialize out of thin air.
And what of that fiction? What is supposed to have raised The Witcher 2 above its peers is its setting and its story. The Eastern European-infused setting would be interesting, if the game spent any time developing it. It’s more interested in talking about the racism of its setting at the expense of its broader world. We therefore keep having new kingdoms and kings foisted on us in each Act, introduced without any prior build-up and generally dispatched with similar disinterest.
The game instead wastes its time on loading us up with exposition at the expense of character and setting development. If anyone in this game has a personality, they certainly do not have a personality arc. The narrator’s voice sounds of someone found off the street. People die but, since we never grew to care for any of them there is no consequence to their death. It’s just some stuff that happened. And for the most part, it will happen in text. Breaking the only rule of script-writing, “Show me, don’t tell me,” almost everything happens in often atrocious in-game dialogue. The denouement of this design choice is that the “climax” is an overlong conversation with the antagonist in which he helpfully reiterates everything that just happened in the game from his perspective. It has all the narrative impact of a button click.
Which leaves us with the game’s selling point, the element of choice. Anytime you are fighting a boss, control will be taken out of your hands at the key moment, and the winner determined by a cut-scene. How awkward it was to have deftly defeated the game’s arch-antagonist in an Act 1 showdown, only to have the game take control and inform me through a cutscene and journal entry that, no, indeed he had easily defeated me. If this game is really about choice, why can’t my actions be a choice? Why can’t you show me that I can’t beat him instead of telling me? Why am I even here? If this is all just a series of cutscenes where I step in at a few junctures, why inflict so much wandering and inventory management on me inbetween. Why not have me press the critical “choice” buttons and play me the movie? I guess, because, as a movie this isn’t much of a game, and as a game, not much of a movie.

I give Crypt of The Necrodancer a 9/10.
Sick beats, dungeon dancefloors, and monsters at every turn. Crypt of The Necrodancer is a rogue/rhythm game that incorporates all of these to make for a pretty great game. Replay-ability value, sound, and visual effects is what drives this game and will continue to for a long time to come.
Brace Yourself Games’ Crypt of The Necrodancer centers on “Cadence” a girl who lost her mother to a plague that struck her village when she was young. Cadence’s father, devastated, dived into the depth of a crypt in search for a lost treasure that he believed would bring back the life of his wife and Cadence’s mother. Two years had passed since her father left to find the treasure; Cadence felt it was her duty now to find him. In her quest, she fell into the crypt where an evil Necrodancer took her heart and cursed it to move to the beat of the crypt forever. Cadence must now find her father and defeat the evil Necrodancer in order to lift the curse. This story line, while written well, interesting, and captivating at times, is just the cherry on top of this game’s gameplay, music, and visual effects.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rogue-rhythm dungeon crawler that consists of four zones, each with three randomly generated levels and a boss battle. You must complete all of these in order to set a checkpoint in the game and proceed onto the next zone. Each time you die you are reset to the beginning of the first level in the zone. Now, throughout the levels you will find and purchase upgrades like any fantasy dungeon crawler including health in the form of food, weapons, armor, spells, and enchanted items. Permanent and new upgrades are available for purchase, with diamonds that you have found in the crypt, in the lobby of the game, from characters you save from sick beat prison in zones you have completed. These permanent upgrades include the essentials like better armor, weapons, spells etc. However most of these purchased upgrades come in the form of chests that can be found within the crypt zones, excluding permanent upgrades like health, coin multipliers etc. These upgrades can be extremely helpful and can make all the difference in whether you complete a zone or rage out.
The game can become fairly difficult and kind of frustrating, especially when you’re first jumping into it. The rhythm aspect of the game and the way the almost “Zelda-esque” grid-style combat is set up, combined with the upgrade mechanics, provides a really fun challenge for players; punishing you by sending you back to the beginning of the randomly generated zone but rewarding you by letting you listen to the music again and again, as you will die a lot. I mean a lot. Although whenever you die you have the option to either: return to the lobby, to spend your hard earned diamonds, and maybe pick a new character; or do a quick restart where you would lose the diamonds you have found but jump right back into the zone. This quick restart feature, is convenient and allows you to get that salty runback when you need it most. Now when you get that really great zone run in and finish it off no problem, the feeling of reward just barely outweighs that of anger and vexation. I never found myself jumping for joy, more relieved that my anxiety of endless death was cured. However if you are a thrill seeker, or a madman and feel you want a bit of an extra challenge you can choose to not pick up weapons or health, and jump on floor tiles that will either speed up or slow down the tempo of the song, or even enter the deathless mode; where you must complete all four zones without dying once. And if you ever find yourself needing some help, the game supports local co-op play, which makes for a great “couch co-op” experience with a friend. Once you get the hang of the movement, and rhythm mechanics, you begin to notice and appreciate the crème-filling of the game, the music and visual effects.
It is hard for me to overstate how much I enjoyed what this game did with music. The soundtrack of the game itself is amazing and something I’ve found myself wanting to listen to outside of the game. However I did find myself getting rather upset playing through it the first time, dying then having to listen to the same song on the soundtrack over and over again from the beginning. I wish that this game had taken the same route as Hotline Miami, where once you die, and choose to do a quick restart, the song continues to play rather than starting it over from the beginning. So my recommendation if you want to stay sane, is either don’t die ever, or download some of the other soundtracks that have been released as DLC. If you decide to get the game on the recent port to PS4 these downloadable soundtracks are included with the game. But don’t let that be the deciding factor in whether you get the game on PC or PS4, as the PC version has easily my favorite feature of the game: MP3 Uploads. On the PC version you can upload any of your MP3 files, the game will analyze the tempo and allow you to play with your own music. This feature is not new to games, but feels brand new and refreshing when defeating giant dancing monsters to your favorite song or even playing through the whole game to a favorite album.
And I know some of you may have just a laptop with no gaming potential, and may fear that you will never get to play this game. Well you’re wrong. The simplistic 2D, top down, 16-bit art style of the game allows for optimal performance on any platform, not to mention it looks great. But while it may have good looks, the 16-bit art style has been used quite a lot in the past few years and has somewhat lost its luster of being a “new-retro game”, and the nostalgia factor just isn’t there anymore. That being said, the use of contrasting color in this 16-bit world creates a beautiful aesthetic. The zones are almost exclusively darker toned color palettes to set the scene of being in an underground crypt, but each monster when illuminated by your small torch brings vibrancy and brightness to the world. Not only this but when you kill a monster, your coin multiplier begins, and any time your coin multiplier is active, the crypt floor turns into an ever changing disco dancefloor. So while the art style maybe a bit over played, Crypt of The Necrodancer finds a way to make it fun.
This game may seem small when compared to some triple-a games of course but even with a $15 price point, it is packed full of content, allowing for hours upon hours of fun. Not to mention all of the variable features such as choosing a different character with different beginning perks, health, and weapons; adds a great variety of gameplay. And when paired with the different modes and soundtracks brings an astounding amount of replay-ability to the game. Music and games belong together, and Crypt of The Necrodancer is all around a fantastic game that will keep me coming back anytime I hear a new song or a new album that has me craving for some dancing monster dungeons.
I give Crypt of The Necrodancer a 9/10.

I am a huge srpg fan. Great or terrible, I'll give a game a fair spin. That being said, I don't understand what was going through the developer's mind when they created this game.
Royal Bounty honestly feels like a Heros of Might and Magic 2 senario that we've been duped into paying 5 bucks for. This game uses the same or extremely similar engine and you control one hero. While this engine marginally works for an explorative rpg, it was really designed to be resource management and tile strategy. This becomes apparent as the leveling up of your hero does practically nil. On top of that, the units do not level up. So fighting in a way only atrophies your army. Unless you are playing perfect (not just great) even minor losses will stack up.
The Ai is ok but nothing incredible. The fights are won or lost right off the bat. It's practically all about who has the bigger army. I suppose you could carry rogues with you the entire game and just scout what the fights are before hand. Fun. Alternatively, you can just mindlessly wonder your hero around for days, months, years just letting him passively collect income. You will earn approximately one unit a turn/day. Then your army will be able to storm through a couple fights before getting chiseled down and needing to repeat the cycle. I say this because the fights carelessly and randomly alternate between maybe half a dozen peons to literally hundreds of enemies comparable to your few elite soldiers.
The still screen artwork is actually really nice, as is the card artwork. The first introductory jailbreak scenario works. It is only maybe 15 minutes and one fight long, but this is the format the rest of the game should have followed by railroading the player and providing armies rather than making you brute force the system. I don't know if the story progresses into something memorable as I only have five hours of game time logged. It's pretty forgettable as of yet. Another huge test of your patience is the movement of your hero. He will stop REPEATEDLY. You will click for him to move and this will queue up movement footprints. Then you need to order him to move again by clicking again or pressing space. The problem with this movement check is the hero will stop again midmovement for day changes or text pop-ups. Sometimes he will stop for no reason at all. When you click again for him to move there is a long pause and you will not know if the computer is processing the move or if you will be waiting for eternity for the character to move. Repeat this process one million times.
So only go for this game if you want a really campy walk through a Heros 2 scenario.
Edit:
I put a great deal more time into this game since my initial review. I don't know that the game works perfectly as an open campain, but the developers have been putting big things in the works. After some grinding I was able to get a pretty serious playthrough of this game, albeit hammering a pretty serious exploit.
It still stands that I love the artwork. The controls are a pinch clunky. I hope they chisel an inventive game out of this old style engine.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is definitely one of the most unique roguelike games I’ve ever played, with the added bonus of actually resembling rogue instead of using roguelike as another term for “permadeath without saves”.  You play a family of musicians (or a motley crew of side-characters) determined to unlock the mystery of the magical lute and defeat the Necrodancer, a cursed necromantic bard.
True to its name, you “dance” around each level by moving in tune to the rhythm meter at the bottom of the screen. Each level has its own tune and rhythm and the game steadily increases the pace as you progress. Keeping in tune with the music while vanquishing enemies will net you a higher multiplier which increases the amount of gold you find, in addition to enhancing certain special items found throughout the crypt. Failing to keep to the beat will cause your multiplier to go down and may also prevent you from moving. Since the monsters in the game also move to the beat, they will eventually close in on you to attack and you cannot stand still to “pause” the action (unless you’re playing the bard character).
I found the soundtrack for CotN to be excellent and very diverse. Each level’s song fits its theme pretty well and there are a few tracks that are instantly catchy. The shopkeeper in each level will also sing along with the music, giving a clue to his location, and all of the monsters are either music-themed or have a name alluding to some musical term or instrument, adding an extra layer of detail to this thoroughly polished game.
There really aren’t any faults with this game that would prevent any fan of rogues from picking it up (playing as Aria is extremely hard though) and, even if you’re not normally into games in this genre, the learning curve is very fair. This game is worth picking up even at its original cost, though if you can catch it at the average sale price of $5 it’s quite a steal!

The Witcher is a dark, gritty, and mature RPG. It is probably one of the most grounded, and interesting RPG I've ever played. The Witcher itself is based on its famous novels written by Andrzej Sapkowski. Geralt of Rivia, The White Wolf, is a monster hunter for pay. Throughout Geralt's journey through Temeria for work, he is conflicted with political issues that arise after the events at Vizimia; this takes place during the Witcher 1. The Witcher 2 has a though provoking story that requires your attention. Books you pick up, as well as notes should be read. The combat in the Witcher 2 is probably its weakest aspect. It is, however, much better than the combat system introduced in the Witcher 1. In the Witcher 2, you are required to roll around during almost any combat situation. This effectively makes signs, or any other defensive abilties obselete.
The Witcher 2 requries a necessary playthrough as its story, characters, and universe are provoking. Even if the Witcher's combat system is medicore at best, it won't stop you from enjoying the numerous other aspects that the Witcher does correctly.

I love the production value of this game. The artwork, the cutscenes, the music, and the overall mechanics are definitely well-made. I also very much appreciate the fact that there is a calibration tool built into the game to account for any latency created by your hardware.
That being said, I caution people who are considering buying this game that it is very much a grind. The game centers around pattern recognition, but the worlds are randomly generated and enemies tend to cluster around you and confuse you (in more ways than one.)
You have to grind diamonds to upgrade your characters and forge better weapons, but you have to spend diamonds you find immediately after exiting a stage; they don't accumulate like they would in a normal RPG. This prevents you from cheesing the game, and in my opinion, is grinding done right.
However, later legs of the story limit you to certain weapons and penalize you for missing beats, which I feel should just be for an uber-masochistic sort of achievement and NOT part of the main game. The 19 game hours I've logged so far actually represent about a month and a half of playing this game. I don't have a lot of free time, and I can't dedicate myself to a game like this for hours on end just trying to finish the last leg of the story with a one-hit-kill no-missed-beats run for 4 zones straight.
I've reached the end of my patience with this game, but I would not at all call it bad. It's a fantastic game. Just too much of a grind and a multitasking nightmare for me to finish.

It is times like this that I wish that Steam had a maybe thumb for their reviews. The game is by no means a bad game, and there are certain people I would recommend it to. So lemme start off with the things that drew me to it in the first place and what I did like about the game.
First off, the aesthetic is just plain beautiful. It is almost like an impressionist painting, just the way no colors are blended and the people within are close approximations of humans. It is a great game to look at no doubt. The voice acting is top notch, due in large part that the voices are given by the family that had to endure this tragedy. The fact that this family just lost their young son to cancer and were then able to create nearly every facet of the game on their own truly is a feat not many could pull off. I love narrative driven "walking simulators" so when a new one with a unique look, superb acting, and a real world story of loss came on my radar, I was very intrigued.
This leads to the reason I am thumbing it down. I was on board with the tragic elements that were unfolding, when suddenly that was all undermined with a literal deus ex machina entering the story. We all process grief in different ways, so while I respect the Green family's turn to God, I couldn't help but feel completely disconnected from the game. I am not a religious person at all, but even looking at this story objectively, they were clearly going for an emotional aspect. If you then swoop in and remind the player that "Hey, its cool guys, we believe in God and this is God's plan for our kid to die," then you rob everyone of the emotional attachment they had. For me the tragedy moved to the Green's themselves, I couldn't help but think these poor people really follow a system in which they think a child's slow and painful death is a gift.
Okay, that sounded harsh perhaps, and I did say I would recommend it to a certain person. I would recommend it to the Christian casual gamer. This game could be a stepping stone for some to experience games with a rich story. And I would recommend it to those who perhaps could overlook the religious aspects as I guess a sort of anthropologic study of those who use faith to help cope with truly saddening events.  Numinous Games has proven they have the chops to design beautiful games and act the hell out of a story. I just hope the next game they produce is one I can connect to.

THE BAD:
As a few others have already touched on, about half way through, this game HEAVILY touches on the idea of religion and God. As someone who doesn't necessarily believe in this faith, it makes it extremely hard to continue with the story.
The voice acting is relatively bad and downright awful at points. There are a few times where the narration gets so over done you can actually hear the *crackle* of the recording microphone. In a game/story so heavily focused on narration you think this would be better done.
The controls are clunky and annoying. You shouldn't have to click on the screen five times just to walk in the same direction another five feet.
The price. This has been mentioned in pretty much any negative review about this game. Since I dropped $15 on this game, I'd expect that there would be some warning about the religious overtones. The description simply suggests that the game explores themes of faith, but it doesn't talk about the fact that a rather large part of the dialogue becomes about religion and God.
THE GOOD:
Honestly? Not a lot. I really wanted to love this game. To me, this game was very personal. When I was fourteen my father passed away from colon cancer. As someone who has watched a family member suffer, endure, and then become the victim of such a horrible disease, I expected this story to be very relatable. When you make a game/story about a touchy subject, such as cancer, you really need to make sure you do it justice.
That being said, there are parts of this game/story that are truly beautiful. Some of the metaphors are spot on when it comes to what the family's of cancer patients are feeling. The story also tries it's best to replicate what cancer patients are feeling as they go through the game. This gets to be an even touchier subject. How can you make a game/story off of the assumptions of how a cancer patient is feeling? Did I really have to be forced to listen to the main narrator sing "God loves Joel" for a good five minutes? What is the point?
For a game that is supposed to be focused on family, cancer, and the entire journey it is EXTREMELY focused on religion. Seriously, I honestly can NOT stress this enough. This game is 100% biased and 100% a religious story. The bible is quoted numerous times and there was one part where the word 'God' is said around fifteen times in the same paragraph.
My regret? Not reading the reviews before I bought this game, story, whatever you want to call it. I really wish I could go back in time and get my 1.6 hours back. I get that it's supposed to be a personal story, but if you're going to make a religious game and not warn your buyers....well, that's kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥move.

This is an incomplete game! I have been a huge fan of this series. I purchased the original on the day of its release (and wound up buying it twice more packaged with other games). GalCiv2 was amazing on many levels. Along comes Galactic Civilizations III. I waited to write this review until after the 1.4 mega update in the hopes they would fix the issues. I can't possibly list all of the flaws in this game, but here are some of the most annoying that fans of the previous games will be pulling their hair out over (I'm not talking about the wheel thing; that's just a matter of preference and I understand why some people hate the change, but it doesn't make the game unplayable like these do):
1) NO CIVILIZATION MANAGER
This is the most glaring thing to disappear from the game. It would be fine if they had replaced it with SOMETHING! But no, they didn't. For those who don't know, this handy tool in GC2 gave you a quick overview of your empire. You could easily see which starbases needed upgrades, which colonies had empty tiles and defenses, and much, much more. It was absolutely ESSENTIAL to managing a large empire. Now we have nothing and the only way to find out this information is to manually cycle through all of your bases and colonies one by one. I can not possibly express enough how aggravating this is on a large map.
2) Disappearing Notifications
Many notifications will disappear before you can read or respond to them. They also don't appear in the notifications tab so you can't go back and read them.
3) Can't Request Custom Constructors
Don't bother creating your own constructors (even though creating custom ships is one of the best parts of GC games) since you won't be able to call them for upgrading your starbases! If you use custom constructors, you will have to manually send each one to the base you want it to upgrade and keep track of how many you have sent to each base (or use rally points for every single starbase).
3) No Search Function!!!
One of the most useful features of GalCiv2 was the search option, especially on large maps. Now you can't search for anything. Not even your own resources!
4) Must Manually Search Map For EVERYTHING
Somewhat related to the above issue, this goes beyond the missing search function. You may as well not bother with sensors in this game, because you are going to have visually search the map for things like untapped resources, even ones sitting right next to your colonies. To be fair, I always felt GC2 could have made it easier for you to locate resources (at least those in sensor range), but I never spent 20 minutes just trying to find an Econ resource (or relic as GC3 calls them). You also must manually search for uncolonized planets, and colonies owned by other civilizations. Information that is vital for expansion and during wartime. Why bother having sensors at all?!?!?
5) No Espionage
Espionage has been a part of international politics throughout history. It was also part of GC1 and GC2. But apparently all the species of the galaxy have decided they don't need to know anything about their neighbors. Why is this important? It is VITAL! Especially on the harder difficulty levels. Knowing which defenses and offenses to specialize in could make the difference between winning and losing to a superior opponent in the previous games. Now you have to manually send ships into their territory (thankfully they have added stealth technologies to the tech tree) and scan their fleets to learn this information.
These and hundreds of similar little oversights make the game feel like it is still in pre-alpha stage.
The graphics are decent. That's about all I can say good about this game. I wasted my money and my years of devotion to Stardock are officially over.
Update: I just noticed that less than an hour ago a dev posted the schedule for future patches, claiming that in about a year most of the bugs should be fixed. So two years after the game is released they CLAIM they will have the major bugs worked out! That alone should tell you how low the level of quality control was with this release. is an intimately authentic experience beyond comparison, although the player's appreciation of its 2 hour journey may be dependent on their own life experience. I am usually not easily sensitive and yet this game had me teary-eyed for the better half of its short narrative.
To say it is a tragedy is an understatement, though its flawlessly dosed raw emotion is exactly its most alluring distinction. That Dragon, Cancer is as poignant as can be, without the overdone drama one could expect, and is a profoundly human yet distressing interactive tale.
Splendid art direction perfectly alternates between genuine memories and surreal moments, all rendered in stylish and colorful low-poly scenes, with minimal animation. I especially appreciated the subtle décor changes as the player pans the view. Outstanding audio envelops every scene interspersed with real recorded sound bytes. There is never any sense of urgency as the player takes time to fully evoke each moment.
As a game, and from a purely objective point of view, That Dragon, Cancer fails on many accounts, but that is completely beyond the point of what it aims to be. Crude controls and clunky interactions moderately damper the exploration. Moving about from point to point limits any sense of freedom. Mini games are few and deliberately executed clumsily.
This game regrettably suffers from its eventual surrender to religious beliefs. This was perhaps inevitable considering the Green family's Christian background but it was never essential to the intended communication. A neutral and measured spiritual position would have been more admirable.
At the risk of sounding condescending or inconsiderate, I must mention Amy's voice grew a bit grating at times, as was her over-reliance on faith. I found it much easier to relate to Ryan's more down to earth rationale and calm demeanor. One must never lose sight that these are real people, and as such I can only have the utmost respect for their determination.
Despite the game's obvious but forgivable imperfections, it delivers a unique and sincere passage that can only be experienced to be properly understood and deeply felt. That it managed to produce such emotion in me is a testament to its powerful integrity. It projected me into a highly emotional state I did not suspect possible from this medium. Every human being should play this, and be moved by it.

I can forgive that it's short due to budget, or that it's buggy, or that the variety of music lacks, or even that there is zero story. But I really, really can't forgive that they cheaped way out on visuals and feeling.
On itself it might have been fine, but sadly we were promised a game in the spirit of the Neverhood, which this so obviously is not. But even as a basic adventure time game it's pretty 'meh'.
The entire game is in the trailer (which is heartbreakingly deceiving).
At the start I felt excited to exlpore this new world. Sadly after literally 1 minute of intro, you'll be stuck with approx. 2 hours of walking around in half-animated, barely filled 1-colour rooms with no dialogue.  That's the game. Walking from the same room to the same room to do the exact same puzzles.
On top of that it seems that the only reason the main character(s) can talk is so they wouldn't have to animate their emotions. The characters have close to no personal traits (yet clayman did, without talking. Funny huh?), and the 'world' feel frustratingly small.
Do you remember those "oh wow!" "haha" "that's cool!" feelings with the Neverhood? Or how sad you felt for robot bill? Or how well written the story on those tapes was? The excitement of finding a new one? You will find none of that in this game.
I did still, in all fairness, enjoy the claymation and the art style a lot (although this is hard to find, considering 3/4 is regular animation or random plastic props). I read the bad reviews and I still bought it, and I don't regret buying it (though the price should have been 10 dollars).
To summarise: this is a 2/3 hour game that feels like it takes wáy too long to complete. That says all in my opinion.

Armikrog starts with a bombastic, hyperactive animation, followed by a theme song similar to the ones from the ’80s and ’90s cartoons. Before you get a chance to come around after this epic blow to all your senses (or in my case, nostalgia) comes another amazing animation, this time in a stop-motion technique in the sumptuous claymation style from the rest of the game. The visual style is definitely the main selling point of this game, and a large number of models and locations were really made from plasticine/clay and other materials and later the photos were incorporated into scenes that we see in the final product. As a spiritual successor to the almost two decades old game, The Neverhood, Armikrog also places the player in a weird world full of mysteries that invite you to investigate. It’s a pity that the rest of the game’s quality does not follow up to the one it starts with.
Armikrog would have easily been discarded as an amateur half-product if it didn’t look so lovely and unusual. It’s a great shame that because of programmers’ and designers’ incompetence all this hard work is gone to waste, all those stunning landscapes and objects which someone’s been building for months and carefully animated picture by picture are now in the same boat with some of the most irritating puzzles I've seen in the last few years. Considering that it doesn’t take more than 3-4 hours to finish the game, the price of 25€ is an insult. Just like Broken Age before it, Armikrog is a million-worth Kickstarter project that fails to justify it’s pedigree and unsuccessfully relies on the good will and nostalgia of fans.

An action/platforming RPG in the vein of Castlevania, Dust drew me in, hook, line, and sinker.
The game puts you in the shoes of an anthropomorphic amnesiac called Dust, and teams him up with floating friend Fidget and wizened talking sword Ahrah. Together, the three of you travel the land of Falana, righting wrongs and uncovering the secrets of Dust's true identity. The plot walks a tight balancing act between family-friendly and dire darkness, and while it's successful overall, some characters (Fidget) do tend to add a somewhat childish, yet still charming flavor to the tale. Despite the world's somewhat medieval vibe, the dialogue is wholly modern, which is oddly jarring, but in a Disney-film-set-in-the-olden-days-but-everyone-talks-like-it's-1990 sort of way. The banter between the three leads is mostly fun, and goes a long way to establishing them as companions — and eventually, friends.
As I mentioned, the game unfolds much in the same way as the Symphony of the Night flavor of Castlevanias: explore a variety of locations in 2D space, gather new equipment and ability upgrades to slowly expand your movement possibilities, fight lots of enemies and bosses, help out others via side quests, and gather hidden treasure. While Dust only has access to his sword and several of Fidget's magical projectiles, the tight physics and the outstanding combat keep the game feeling exciting all the way through. Mixing and matching various attacks and combos is thrilling, and combined with the awesome animation, the battles are utterly chaotic and begin to seem like one epic, violent dance. The final level and battle of the game are an utter symphony of carnage. Fortunately, the controls are tight, and you're very much in control of every slash, smash, and dodge. Dust occasionally turns to face a target other than the one desired, but it doesn't happen nearly often enough to really bother me. Also, while the entire game felt very fair, there is one particular enemy late in the adventure that can break all of the established rules of battle. Parrying you while facing the opposite direction or knocked down to the ground and dodging into the background with far greater frequency than even the final boss, this enemy felt a little cheap — though this is admittedly a nitpick that only affects the final hour or two of the game.
Visually, Dust looks like what every Disney game from the 1990's aspired to be. The hand-drawn background art is gorgeous and diverse, and the character models are big, colorful, and move with a fluid grace that gives Rayman a run for his lums. There are numerous particle effects like rain, wind, snow, and ash, and tons of dramatic lighting and blur effects during combat. If 2D graphics were food, I would eat Dust all day.
The musical score is deep, emotional, and diverse, and lends a huge degree of weight to the various locations and scenes it underscores. There's plenty of audio feedback during combat and in menus too, and all of it lives up to the high-water mark set by the graphics and music. The voice acting is generally pretty good — Dust in particular gives a great performance — but a few here and there (Fidget) are a wee bit cutesy for my taste. Still, no character's voice is outright bad.
The PC version automatically detects your control setup and changes the menu layout to suit your choice of mouse and keyboard, keyboard, or gamepad. Keyboard/mouse combinations are certainly serviceable, but the best way to play is undoubtedly with a controller in your hands. There's also a nice selection of knobs and dials to prettify your visual experience if you've got the hardware for it. Considering all of that, Dust absolutely makes a great transition to PC.
The game has a set of four difficulty options, the usual suite of Steam achievements, and several challenge rooms for you to struggle with, as well. Playing on hardcore difficulty and completing 100% of the game took me in the neighborhood of 19 hours, so there's certainly plenty of game here for the price, too. Dust was undoubtedly a labor of love by its creator, and it shows. This game oozes craft, artistry, and love, and shows it off in every facet of its design. There's great gameplay, graphics, music, and heart here, and I have no reservations whatsoever in wholeheartedly recommending it to anyone that enjoys these kinds of games.

After spending a decent amount of hours in this game, I will definitely recommend it to anyone even remotely interested in grand strategy/science fiction games. Paradox has made another immersive, intrigruing and downright fun game to play with. Ironman mode is an option(one I would highly recommend, for immersions sake) and each game feels different and unique. I have not reached late game yet but I really enjoy the way this game is building up to it.
Pros
1. Management is as advanced as you want it to be. You can minmax down to specific scientists for specific research jobs, specific generals for specific fleet types, specific governors for specific colonies.
2. Combat is interesting and diverse. There are different weapon types, different modifications to these weapon types, and you can fully customize and design the ships in your fleet. It's like a simplified version of building ships in EVE online, where you want to design fleets that do one job and do it really well.
3. Diplomacy is a thing. You can be diplomatic and peace-loving, you can also be war-hungry and aggressive. You may want to tune your plan depending on the neighbours you end up discovering around you. If you end up with a religious zealot focused on dominion and destruction, it may not be the wisest move to set yourself up for a slow methodical start. Unless you make friends, that is.
Cons
I have yet to find any real cons. I was a little bummed out when my main leader died, but that's the price of mortality I guess. There are genetic research you can do to expend lifespans, and it wouldn't surprise me if there is some biotechnology research you can do as well. We shall see, this game is still an adventure I'm discovering.

The Witcher is a dark, gritty, and mature RPG. It is probably one of the most grounded, and interesting RPG I've ever played. The Witcher itself is based on its famous novels written by Andrzej Sapkowski. Geralt of Rivia, The White Wolf, is a monster hunter for pay. Throughout Geralt's journey through Temeria for work, he is conflicted with political issues that arise after the events at Vizimia; this takes place during the Witcher 1. Geralt is now faced with treason, and is set out on a journey to clear his name.
The Witcher 2 has a though provoking story that requires your attention. Books you pick up, as well as notes should be read. The books you find will tell you the history of the Witcher universe, and give you tips when fighting difficult opponents. You will also be making choices that actually do make a difference within the universe.
The combat in the Witcher 2 is probably its weakest aspect. It is, however, much better than the combat system introduced in the Witcher 1. In the Witcher 2, you are required to roll around during almost any combat situation. This effectively makes signs, or any other defensive abilties obselete.
The Witcher 2 requries a necessary playthrough as its story, characters, and universe are provoking. Even if the Witcher's combat system is medicore at best, it won't stop you from enjoying the numerous other aspects that the Witcher does correctly.

While the game seems to build an interesting world and the characters/voice actors add a great deal of flavour to sidequests, i have attempted to play this game twice now over the span of a year. In both cases, i ended up quitting due to frustration in how slow the movement is. It's not that the map is large, but your character's run speed is slow and the directions you can go are predetermined. You run through the same route, have to walk around low obstacles you should easily be able to jump or climb over, and each time you need to climb up or jump down you need to pause, let the game detect you're in front of an interactable object, and then let the animation play.
On top of that, the save system is barebones. Autosaves only occur rarely, so if you are moving around and there's a surprise ambush you seem to have no chance of winning, you have to run (slowly) the entire way back, following the identical path.
For those who are interested in slow gameplay and sightseeing, this is a great game. For me, though, the repetitive and slow nature of travel just isn't worth trudging through to get to the actual gameplay and story.

Take two of the absolute most opposite mechanical bases, rhythm games and Roguelikes, and mash it together.  What happened?  Possibly one of the most intriguing, entertaining, and downright addictive puzzle games ever made.  A rather interesting soundtrack drives the game well, as well as support for custom soundtracks as well, and reinforces the rhythm half of this game.  Being a Roguelike, a full clear of the game can happen inside of an hour or two, but why stop there?  A myriad of options and mutator modes keep the experience fresh along with a rather robust random generation engine behind it.  I have yet to get truly repetitive experiences, but it also seems to be its biggest flaw.  The randomization can completely stack the deck against you, creating some tough scenarios that usually end in a badly timed death.  That being said, the ultra-simple controls combined with the rhythm-based score mechanics creates one extremely charming ride.  Worth the price for a fan of anything close to this style of game.

Danganronpa 2 shares a lot of similarities to its prequel and I dare say, shouldn't be played before DR1. The grievances I have w/ the first game still stick, namely its unnecessary inclusion of trial minigames and dated look (though I still like the artstyle).
The killing game takes place in an island, which made it lost the claustrophobic feel I had w/ DR1. Being a sequel, DR2 also dumps a lot of information--especially towards the last two chapters--which might lose you had you not played DR1. The chemistry between the characters here are considerably less apparent than in the first killing game. So DR2 plays more with your brain than your heart, probably partly due to not having the novelty of the first game or having to continue a relatively complicated story.
That said, playing with your brain is definitely what its good at. The game is very, very creative and I loved all its cases, particularly the one in the Funhouse. It maintains a sense of mystery throughout and is constantly full of surprises, with a canon story that follows DR1 really, really well and wraps up satisfyingly towards the end. Just like the first game, I can safely say that this game is worth playing for its story alone.
DR2 is much larger in scale than DR1, is heavy on the exposition but makes a brilliant mystery game. The trials are still easy, but the story is still amazing. The last two chapters are a huge rollercoaster ride and there're a lot of references to the first game as well as cameos which got me by surprise <3.

Armikrog uses claymation with some small cartoon animations thrown in there. It’s important to note that the claymation has an incredibly raw look to it, which I assume is intentional, like old-school Wallace & Gromit or The Trap Door.
Unlike most point and click adventures, there’s no real inventory management as most items are more or less given to you upon completion of the puzzles, which are the meat of the adventure. And even better, they are all rather intuitive logic puzzles. When you put your mind to it, they are all possible to complete without trawling through google for walkthroughs.
The story itself is simple in construct and while you have to back-track every now and then, the back-trackings flows naturally and often requires to approach the same place from a different route. The characters lack a bit of personality, and as such, any real motivations behind their actions and the events that take place. But I didn’t find this too disconcerting as the main focus is the puzzles.
My only real criticism for the game is its steep price for a max of two hours (give or take) of gameplay. Even this criticism I’m reserved in making as I’m aware of the amount of time and effort that goes into making claymation films (I’ve watched those Wallace and Gromit behind-the-scenes films). Then again, this was a kickstarter with close to a million dollars invested into it.
Despite all this, still worth the play and an examplery point and click adventure.

Decent game that does what it intends, but alas is not able to achieve all that I would expect of a truly all-rounder universal "play your own race" Space-Strategy Game.  It's a good game, but it needs work to be truly great.
WHat this game needs:
1) The ability to actually Christen (name) your own ships - not just designate a design-model name or number:
Currently you cannot Christen your ships; you can design an "Orion-class batle-ship" that is called orion, but you cannot christen it the "SS George Washington."  This is sorely lacking.
2) The Designer should allow you to draw/model 3d shapes - currently you only have default blocks to work with.
3) There should be jump-nodes or wormholes to make the galaxy truly EPIC and far-reaching. It is too simple to just boil it down to "faster than light travel"
4) The Designer should allow one to use an existing model ship and just make it bigger in terms of capacity... currently it forces one to re-design an ENTIRE ship from scratch to achieve the desired capacity.
5) There should be a chance for you to create your own Inter-national Organizations insead of being forced to pick the default "United Planets".... this would mirror what real states are doing in our world today = e.g. China and Asian states creating the Asian Development bank as opposed to the WOrld Bank.
Good things about this game:
1) Races & planets can be named, which is excellent... pity you cannot christen ships.
2) Diplomacy & race AI is good/reasonable - but on occasion AI playes will turn on you occasionally for no good reason.
3) Research tech tree is comprehensive.
4) Galactic Management is easy to pick up.
I heartily recommend you to buy this ONLY once they FIX the designer & the allow christening of ships.

Cars 2 is a racing game in the bane of Mario Kart and Sonic & SEGA Racing. It ditches the realistic aspects of the first three games and the hub world, and replaces it with expanded gameplay and a streamlined race system. But, before the actual review, let me explain the negativity behind this port.
It turns out this game is a port of the downgraded Wii version. It is missing DLC content and characters from the other versions, such as Chick Hicks and other characters from the first movie. Not only that, but the graphics suffered a TON during the porting process. Textures are low quality, shaders are too bright, and the game looks like a bad mix between a cartoon and PS2 game. What bothers me the most is how Steam/Valve hasn't acted on this at all. This is false advertising and shows how low quality the port is. The first two games look better than this, for pete's sake!
The core gameplay remains identical to the console versions. Unlike the previous games, this game is loose in the controls department. The drift is more like other Kart Racers, and you have more control over your character. The game also introduces weapons into the mix in Battle Races and Arena modes. You have your basics (Missiles, Machine Guns, Oil Slicks, etc). and then you have the outragous weapons like energy balls and beams that blow your character off the map. One thing that does suck is that by default, weapons will ALWAYS shoot forwards since the Up Arrow key is used to accelerate. Thankfully you can rebind the controls as you see fit or use a gamepad.
The game follows a main campaign (C.H.R.O.M.E Missions) that you complete to unlock courses and modes to play in Arcade mode (which supports 4 players in the console releases, but only 2 here. It's also local players only.) The modes you play include Races, Battle Races, Arena (a wave-based enemy gauntlet ending with a boss battle), and other various modes with their own twists. In one race you could be collecting energy to prevent Professor Z's lazer from killing you, and in another you could be going around a track destorying as many Lemon Cars as possible before the time runs out.
While the game doesn't have Steam Achievements, it does have in-game ones that are Crests and Badges. You unlock more characters from doing these to use in both Story Mode and Arcade mode. Or, if you're feeling lazy, you can always use Cheat Codes in the options menu to unlock everything from the get-go.
If you have a Xbox 360/One or PS3, get this on there instead. You're getting the better experience and more content. However, if you're stuck on PC and can bear the game's appearence and are a fan of Kart Racers, this is a hidden gem I can't recommend enough. If you like the gameplay of this, I also suggest Cars 3: Driven to Win. It has the same gameplay and most of the same modes.

This game is not very good.  The number one thing I was interested in was the story.  The story is thin and boring.  It's not conveyed very well, and it's not that interesting. Also, there's a significant amount of back tracking, and that involves you getting in a trolley system thing and manually going backwards which is really boring.
When I played this game it was also pretty glitchy, though I don't know if they patched that.  Often the sound would unsynch from the game, or I would glitch through a door without solving the puzzle.
The graphics are ok but lame.  They're clay and I expected them to be more ornate, more complex, more beautiful even - I really expected the team to try to push the envelope on 'clay graphics' for lack of a better term.  They're the only ones doing it, so go big!  But they didn't.  They were pretty simple, very Neverhood looking - which I didn't think was that great either.
Finally, a moment of slight spoilers - there is a room with a LONG written story on the wall.  I have no idea what that was about because I couldn't force myself to read it.  However, it's poor form to shoehorn a major story element into a game via a short novel length chunk of text.  Show, don't tell!
So in short, meh graphics, bad story, boring gameplay, overall a let down.

Pros:

After spending a decent amount of hours in this game, I will definitely recommend it to anyone even remotely interested in grand strategy/science fiction games. Paradox has made another immersive, intrigruing and downright fun game to play with. Ironman mode is an option(one I would highly recommend, for immersions sake) and each game feels different and unique. I have not reached late game yet but I really enjoy the way this game is building up to it.
Pros
1. Management is as advanced as you want it to be. You can minmax down to specific scientists for specific research jobs, specific generals for specific fleet types, specific governors for specific colonies.
2. Combat is interesting and diverse. There are different weapon types, different modifications to these weapon types, and you can fully customize and design the ships in your fleet. It's like a simplified version of building ships in EVE online, where you want to design fleets that do one job and do it really well.
3. Diplomacy is a thing. You can be diplomatic and peace-loving, you can also be war-hungry and aggressive. You may want to tune your plan depending on the neighbours you end up discovering around you. If you end up with a religious zealot focused on dominion and destruction, it may not be the wisest move to set yourself up for a slow methodical start. Unless you make friends, that is.
Cons
I have yet to find any real cons. I was a little bummed out when my main leader died, but that's the price of mortality I guess. There are genetic research you can do to expend lifespans, and it wouldn't surprise me if there is some biotechnology research you can do as well. We shall see, this game is still an adventure I'm discovering.

I held off on buying The Witcher 2 for a long time. Wasn't really sure what to expect to be honest. On sale for 2.99, I just couldn't resist when I wanted something new to play. I couldn't have had a better surprise. Honestly The Witcher 2 met and exceeded every single one of my expectations.
First was the assumption that it would be a rather ugly game. The screenshots don't really do it favor, and after my graphics card reccomended max settings I found it rivals Shadow of Mordor.
Secondly I wasn't expecting a deep RPG another place I was pleasantly surprised. The Witcher 2 is hard for me to place genre wise, but it's in a way the epitome of a Western RPG. The best comparison's would be Dragon Age, Shadow of Mordor, Assassins Creed, Skyrim and Dark Souls. While we are on the subject of it's contemporaries, I felt the Witcher 2 had combat that surpassed all of these entries. The interplay between the various sword types and temporary oils, limited alchemical potions with dubious advantages and a hard limit on how much preparation you can do lends a strategic flair that lacks compared to the standard drink 20 potions/cast all your buff magics before a fight that other titles aspire to. I've also heard a lot of complaints about the difficulty of combat, and I can't really disagree, but I enjoy it. The Witcher 2 gives you free reign to save whenever and whereever as long as you're not in a fight, it takes seconds and it's strongly encouraged. The game can be very punishing before you start getting stronger armor's and weapons, the Prologue area features enemies that can kill you in 4-5 hits. That danger never really goes away, but again it makes every fight strategic. This isn't Skyrim where you know you should avoid the 10 foot tall giants, daedra lords and sabercats for the first 20 levels and you'll be fine. In The Witcher any group of mobs with more than 3 members has the potential to kill you and should be treated with respect.
The Witcher 2 does have areas it's lacking in, but really It's just ways they could improve an already phenomenal game. An Assassins Creed/Shadow of Mordor style free running system would fit perfectly in the hands of Geralt, I can just imagine scaling mountains, sneaking over castle walls and clambering through the trees like one of the elves. The ability to lock on or switch between targets in combat could have been useful, and some of the boss fights are incredibly hard.
All in all I feel a little let down by Projekt Red. This is a game that I should have been way more informed on, It's a game with the potential to create a legacy. It's a game I wouldn't have felt bad paying 60 dollars for. It's a game I had to buy for 2.99 off a steam sale in the hopes of finding a mildly enjoyable experience with the knowledge that well some people like it...
Game Quality 10/10
CD Projekt Red Marketing Team 2/10
Steam Marketing Team 11/10
