Since I did not touch the game until its full release, this review is based entirely on my first-hand experience with the game, written by someone who is unaware of what may or may not have been changed, addressed or promised during the early access.
GAME CHOICES & MECHANICS:
- The game offers four traditional fantasy races to choose from when making characters; humans, dwarves, elves and orcs, each race offering three specific starting classes to choose from, as well as a varying setup of skills.
- The skills are fairly familiar to M&M players, with a few new additions in X, like for example Primordial Magic, Arcane Discipline, and Warfare. Some notable skills have disappeared as well; as there is no Alchemy, Identify Item, Learning, Merchant or Repair Item skill, as well as a few other examples.
- Gameplay-wise it has some important changes from previous M&Ms. You follow a tile-style map when moving around! For those familiar with pen and paper Role Playing games such as Dungeons & Dragons, think of it as the 5x5 hex-grid system (which the M&M X map looks like).
- Combat is more strictly turn-based. This means a monster will have to wait for its turn before attacking you (or you it), as each of your characters in turn takes their actions. Explained more thoroughly in my personal opinion.
- The Night/Day cycle is much quicker, especially outside of towns.
- Levelling up skills and attributes and what improvements it will grant you is 'tooltiped' by mouse-over, and the different character panels are somewhat easier to use.
MY PERSONAL OPINION
The game looks good. It has that M&M feeling to it, in a modern sense where lighting effects and shades are more modern than in older versions, yet it's not meant to look "outright realistic", and both NPCs and world objects look the way they 'always have' in the series.
The new and more strict turn-based system of combat also has its advances, in that you can take your time to plan your next and most optimal move with each character. It also means you can plan ahead of the monster's next attack, and since you can rearrange the order of your character's easily, you can put your heavy cannons to go first, after which, depending on whether they dealt enough damage or finished something off, your supporters can cast the appropriate buffs before the next turn begins.
Then again, nothing prevented you from pausing the game to think ahead in previous versions, just saying.. Yes, the stricter turn-based system can sometimes slow the gameplay down. You can still hold down a button to have all your characters repeatedly fire their arrows at whatever you're fighting, but you cannot move while doing so. Even if you didn't have to move, if three of your characters are just firing arrows away with their mana emptied, but the fourth being the one doing something different, you will have to stop and click a different number (taskbar being the traditional 1-9) for that particular character.
Personally, I like the old style where you manually set a spell and a non-spell attack and just blasted away, even if that is a less cost-efficient approach. Back then everything happened simultaneously as well, both your attacks and the monsters', each with their own cooldowns. I have yet to notice my characters using anything powerful enough to make them "lose their next turn due to recharging", or anything similar.
Because of the tile-style movement, you are less likely of getting lost, you wont get stuck in the environment, and it's easier to figure out where to go in some cases. It does limit your movement somewhat, though, and calling this "an exciting open world" is a stretch. Yes, you can SEE the world, but the tiles will tell you where you can and cannot go. In other words, forget scaling up those hills in an angle to skip some travelling, or nudging your way down a tall mountain to get to the bottom quicker. No tile = not an option! (I wonder if a Fly spell exists in this game)
The plus side of the tile system is that travelling between key points takes (much) less time than before, and it certainly is a game focused around combat and action, rather than sightseeing and flower-picking (..fond memories of my alchemist scaling the M&M7 mountains to pick those rare flowers for potions.. anyway.)
When in combat, the tile-system to me is less enjoyable than the good old free movement. You are LOCKED in combat. I.e. if you want to move somewhere, you have to wait for your turn. You can move one tile, then whatever you are fighting will either attack, or move after you, and then you can move again. This means no party kiting and killing that tough giant with their crude bows.
CONCLUSION
Overall the game to me falls into the pitfall of so many other games these days. It's a good and tried-and-true model that instead of being kept that way is slimmed down to make for faster, easier (to me in most cases less enjoyable) gameplay. Instead of feeling like a mighty hero who comes up with clever schemes to defeat your mighty adversaries, I feel like I'm being stripped of some of my powers and choices by the game simply telling me "sorry, we can not let you do that".  No crafting potions? No repairing my own items?
Finding your way because of the tile-system is nice at times, but it also strips me of going exactly where I want to go. Yes, you can most times choose option a, b or c to do first, but even if you choose c, you usually have to come back and do a and b in any order after before moving on to d.
For example, in M&M 7 you could pretty much walk to the tougher zones in the game as soon as you got off the starting island, and although you pretty much couldn't kill anything there (crude bows kiting comes to mind along with a heartful chuckle, though), you could still try to roam around for chests, pick those before mentioned flowers, followed by running for your life to leave the place as you just noticed one of the giants had gotten on your trail.
I want to like M&M X more than I do (that said I do enjoy it, albeit mostly for nostalgic reasons). On the plus-side the nostalgia from playing an M&M game made me want to revisit M&M 7 again, a game which I can also play while I'm offline, or while the rest of the world is offline too, for that matter. As long as my computer has power at least.
If you're a hardcore M&M fan, I would still recommend picking it up for the nostalgia. It's not a "bad game", despite giving it some harsh critique, it's just a well-made game that doesn't appeal to me in the old-fashioned M&M way, with a few too many things changed or altered (the combat + tile-style being my main drawbacks here. Adding that I am well-aware this was never meant to be a "typical M&M clone"!) The fact M&M is one of my all-time favourite series also means I set the bar quite high, if it sounds like most of the review is negatively charged.
So..  Would I recommend this game? The short answer is, it depends who is asking.
To a seasoned M&M player; yes, but to someone not familiar with the M&M series; probably not, as the gameplay is rather outdated.
If you know very little about the M&M series, but like old-style type of games, I'd recommend passing on this one, and instead picking up Might&Magic VII: For Blood and Honor from GOG (for only 6$!), and, baring in mind old graphics are what they are, you will have a more fleshed out game with a lot more depth to it than this one.
However, if you're only in it for the turn-based combat that M&M X focuses on, pass - there are better and more modern turn-based games out there today. :)
..Then again, it could be I'm just a masochistic hero who enjoys the pain and suffering of spending twice as much time on travelling from point a to point b, only to realise I went into the wrong cave and suddenly faced monsters ten times my level...

After some installing issues and finishing the game, I can give a proper review.
Initially I had problems running the game after install; which I fixed by forcing Administrator Rights in Windows.  Before this, the game would crash with an error report every single time.  This took several hours of trial-and-error, during which I was not very happy.
Having not played any of the other series before this one, I can say that the combat style is turned based, similar to say... Final Fantasy 7 turned-based.  Navigation through the world is tile-based, which I didn't like or dislike; since the graphic scenery was consistently believable enough.  There are some load time issues while traversing the world and I was getting bad frame rates in some areas.  The graphics are mostly above-average but occasionally there are some very poorly textured objects.
I did not find any game-ending bugs but there were some plot-line bugs and companion NPC's  working incorrectly like the Negotiator NPC not giving the proper discount for goods.
Plot-wise & quest-wise, the game held my attention enough for me to complete it from start to end.  I took my time finishing the game and even restarted several times to test out new class combinations.  It honestly took me about a week to finish but- as I said- I was learning the game and restarting several times.  There is a hard starting condition where your party has practically nothing and needs everything to survive- new equipment, new spells, new general knowledge to learn about the surrounding area, and a tide of quests to complete.  This is the funnest part of the game for me, due to the difficulty.  About mid-game it becomes apparent that your characters have every inventory slot filled (some with uber-powerful relics), necessary spells purchased & learned, with skill trees grand-mastered--- and while I would have liked the enemies, especially the bosses, to scale they did not.  A lot of the boss fights towards end game were simply the same exact spell casting order that I used to kill the lesser enemies on the plains.  This is when the difficulty practically tapers off.  Towards the end-game I distinctly remember several boss battles where I stayed at range and casted the same 2 ranged spells by my mages; meanwhile the boss couldn't even out-damage the base-line regen spell cast at the start of battle.  The boss inevitably dies to simple attrition and I get an uber relic.  Battles like this are stress-free and the most relaxing battles ever fought, but the fun-factor suffers greatly.
After finishing the game I think the final score lies somewhere between around 80/100.  Due to bugs I might drop that score down a bit since there are a lot of bugs that need to be addressed.  Then again, the asking price is what makes the game worthwhile at a little over $20 so regardless a score of 80 feels justified.  It is a thumbs-up.

Dead Bits is a First Person Shooter game that takes place in a very Minecraft/Roblox-like world. But is it worth buying? Here are the pros and cons of this game.
PROS:
+The music is decent
+The enemies explode in a very satisfying way
+Guns have bottomless clips
+Challenging, but not impossible
CONS:
-Slippery controls
-Enemies have no AI besides to chase you
-No checkpoints
-The credits say "Game Desing" instead of "Game Design"
-The "Story", if you can call it that, doesn't make any sense
-Insta-Kill features that become abundant later on
-Easy to fall off of a stage
-Random slo-mo that is really wonky
Overall, Dead Bits is a game that isn't worth buying, unless you can get it for between 14-19 cents like I did as it takes about 90 minutes to complete, gets annoying, and has no story. The music is good, I guess. 4.5/10

Galciv2 was easily my favorite 4X game of all time. So, you can guess that I was pretty damn excited for Galciv3. When it was half off, there was no stopping me from getting this game.
All in all, I think Galciv3 is a worth successor to 2, which is really saying something. The ship building is great, the addition of carriers and fleet-boosting modules is terrific. The starbases and strategic resources are awesome, too. Planet planning has gotten more in-depth than before as well. I was worried this game would be simplified to meet the modern standard but I'm glad that wasn't the case.
With Galciv3, I've noticed 3 glaring issues:
The soundtracks: theres literally ONE soundtrack for the main galaxy screen. It gets very tiresome very fast. There were like 5 or so in galciv2, and they changed based on the situation (ie warfare music, early game music, late game music). In galciv2, each faction had their own soundtrack. Not the case anymore. I do hope more are added with future patching.
The AI and the dialogue: AI is decent overall, but they do some really strange stuff that makes no sense sometimes. But whats worse, the dialogue is even less diverse than the soundtracks, which is a huge step back from galciv2. Now, there isn't any faction specific dialogue, and most dialogue isnt even ideology-specific (evil races say the same things as good races in the same situations). Every time I played Galciv2, I'd find the AI saying something new that I've never seen them say. But right now, this game could use a lot more dialogue. It's such an easy thing to add in too, I really hope they diversify the AI musings a bit. Even if they just copied the text from the previous game, it would be something.
And finally, this freezing, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ The constant freezing is literally Hitler, pls fix. Sounds like its a problem for everyone, too.

I feel that any attempts to judge a artistically embellished autobiographic account as tragic as this tale would only be misinterpreted as malicious. However, I assure you that I am not coming from a place of ill-intent; I am merely being honest with my own personal experience.
That being said, this is a woefully earnest tale of faith, love, and loss. It presents these mournful concepts with symbolic, and sometimes straightforward minigames that will make you feel something bittersweet. The dialogue is beautifully poetic and somber, and the dramatic impact is futher reinforced by wonderful music and superb vocal performances.
However, although it feels pointless to gripe about the mechanical aspects of this title, I have to be honest; the interface is particularly clunky in its restrictive way of navigating the environments and story. I understand that it is a narrative experience more than a traditional game, but I felt that it should be addressed. I was genuniely engaged and wanted to see more, but more often than not, general navigation and interaction was a chore.
Also, as a warning to those with adverse reactions to the mere mention of religion, this title has prevalent and reoccuring themes of faith that may alienate some players. During these particular segments I personally found it difficult to empathize fully with the game, although I still wholeheartedly understood and sympathized.
In conclusion, "That Dragon, Cancer" is beautiful, but not for everyone. Althought I could not connect with it as much as I had hoped, I am genuinely glad that something like that exists in the medium, even if it wasn't particularly made for me. And them I remember: it wasn't made for me. It was made for Joel, the child who fought so hard and was loved so dearly.

I have been waiting for this game for around 5 months when I first heard about. It was suppose to be a Souls-like game, and I love Souls-Borne series. Closer to release it was clearer this was more a rogue-like. I enjoy certain of them like Enter the Gungeon, but never got into any of the Dungeon crawlers. Necropolis has a Dark Souls controller scheme (with the exception of there is no two-handing, so the Y button becomes interact, and the A-button becomes the jump button with a controller. It does have the terrible keyboard+mouse scheme that the Souls game have with holding shift at the same time you right or left click the mouse).  While the game has the slow style combat of the Souls game, it doesn't really have parring and ripost, or backstab, so it is kinda bare bones, and a lot more sluggish and with not so good animations. In the sense that it's a rogue-like, it is punishing, but pretty fair. But there are where the difference between Necropolis and Soul-series end.
I didn't really mind that, but in the nature of being a rogue-like the level design is kinda meh. But I still really enjoyed the game. The art style is pretty good, even thought it does seem like a game where the fully texture hasn't been loaded in. But it has an unique style, and I really like the enemy design. The music is really good and atmospheric. Parts of it reminded me of 80's electronic artists, even thought it goes into more typical fantasy music.
What the game is really lacking is in replayability. The replayability is really in you failing. I have played this for around 10 hours, and 10 deaths. My first life I died after 80 minutes in the 3 level, but my 5 next life I died on the first floor, as the game can quit punish you if you start to play as a standard hack and slash and doesn't watch your stamina. Plus the enemies can take a big share of your health until you have upgraded it. I didn't finish the game until my 10 life, and it took me around 5,5 hours, which think is longer then the avarage, as I have seen most streamers do it with a group in around 4 hours. I haven't played the game in a group, but I recommend people to first play it alone, to get the most value out of the game, as it seem to easy with a group and you will finish it on your first try. Die a few times, unlock some codex and have fun. After finishing I went pack to finally get to unlock a few codex. Unlocking codex seem to be the only reason to continue to play the game, as there is really no other unlockables except for a few color dyes. While the levels change every time, each floor has a few templates that are always been used, and the first levels are kinda boring in that sense.
For this game to get more replayability it needs unlockalbe characters. This game could be like Gauntlet, and a few cool characters and playstyle, but instead it keep to one standard character. Yes there are crossbow, a granade launcher like weapon, and several different melee weapons, But with the exception of attack speed and elemental damage there are not much variety. Different character, playstyles and more weapon would add to the longvity of the game.
The game could also really need a boss on every level. There are only one boss in the game, and he comes at the last level. He is the same everytime (as far as I know). Bosses would increase the difficulty a lot, and make the game more enjoyable.

Despite a rough release at launch, this has polished up into a great game.
It's unfortunate that so much negativity descended on this game due to a release that was late, buggy, and missing some features. You'll see a lot of negative reviews here with very short play times here, and they're justified. The initial release had broken music that didn't play most of the time, a static cursor that made it tough to tell what you could interact with, some game-breaking bugs, and other issues that added up to a game that was not as fun as it should be, Almost all of this has now been fixed in the months since launch, and while it could still stand to have a few options and more logical menu design, it's playable in all the important ways.
So let's back up and forget the messy launch and start over. Most of the interest in this game surrounds its connection to The Neverhood, a cult-classic from 1996. Indeed this is the work of the same key staff: Writer/artist Doug Tennapel, animator/designers Ed Schofield and Mike Dietz, and composer Terry S. Taylor. Although there's no connection to the story or characters of The Neverhood, it is in every other way a direct successor, with the same distinctive claymation style, same basic gameplay, and similarly weirdo soundtrack.
To that effect, Armikrog is a smashing success. The backgrounds and characters are more gorgeous than ever, now in glorious high-def and with lighting and shadow not possible in the original. The animation is even better, and it shows that the project leads are best known as animators. The soundtrack, while maybe not quite as memorable or plain-old weird as The Neverhood, is still pretty fantastic, blending eerie sci-fi theramins with Taylor's playful whimsy.
Game design also follows a lot of the same cues, for better or worse. It uses the same, simple one-click interface, and inventory puzzles are of the simple lock-and-key sort, and work automatically if you have the right item. There's also plenty of logic puzzles, which, like Neverhood, often fall into tropes like sliding tiles around, entering in codes, or putting things in sequence. They're not wildly original, but they're balanced well, forcing players to think but rarely escalating to the point of frustration, with the possible exception of a difficult puzzle at the very end of the game.
Most of the game's strengths and flaws are the same as its predecessor, so if you liked The Neverhood, it's easy to recommend Armikrog. The only caveat is that Armikrog is missing the one thing that made The Neverhood stand out most of all: It's originality. The Neverhood defied comparisons by being totally unlike anything before it, while Armikrog is, by very nature of what it is, planted squarely in its predecessor's shadow. It might be a new world and a new story, but almost everything about Armikrog is a call-back to The Neverhood in some way. For most of us, that's exactly why we want to play it, but it also can't quite have the same impact the second time around.

This game has gotten very mixed reception, and I can see why.  It's very much a sequel to the Neverhood in the thematic sense, like Phantasmagoria 2 or the Final Fantasy games as it uses many of the same themes and structure.  Like the Neverhood, it's claymation, the story never really goes much of anywhere until near the end, the backstory is told through animated line art, there's a giant wall of text with more optional backstory and lots of puzzles in a relatively small structure.  Thankfully there aren't many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t puzzles like in the Neverhood, but the tradeoff is they're mostly pretty easy.  I thought a few were clever though.  It's also shorter, but feels like it would have dragged on if it went on for too much longer.  The ending isn't the best, but that's just another comparison to the Neverhood.
Armikrog made me feel nostalgic.  It made me feel like I was in the 90s again, and that makes it special.  If you aren't the kind of person who likes 90s adventure games, then it will seem dated in many ways.  I give it a recommendation, but a careful one.

Having never played Neverhood I had no nostalgia walking into this. All I knew is that it was a point and click adventure puzzle game made in stop motion, and for what it was it was pretty great. I became aware of the game a few week before it was released on steam and it had my interest. After release I heard that the game suffered from bugs, and I held off buying for a month or so while the patches came in. So coming into this I had a bug free experience that didn't effect my opinion of the game.
Visuals:
The visuals are pretty damn nice looking and the stop motion animations are of some damn good quality. Nothing looks off other than a few minor parts of the game where the green screen effect wasn't 100% removed from the objects in the world, but honestly its so minor I noticed it only on 2 things.
Gameplay:
Pretty standard as far as a point and click goes, but they did manage to streamline the whole clicking aspect. By this I mean you have no accessable inventory to grab items from and try and use them on different things. If you have the right object you'll be able to interact with it and progress. This elminates the trouble of "use-everything-on-everything-until-something-happens" part of PnC games that eventually happens. This makes the game more puzzle focused in terms of problem solving and finding the right clues to the puzzle and working with the puzzle with the knowledge you have.
I will say however that one puzzle isn't very clear in what you are needing to do, and for some reason has the puzzle solution given after you've already cleared the puzzle. However the solution is visible in the room its in, just not very obvious.
All in all this was a prtty solid game for what it was, and for me it was 3.6 hours start to finish, but the price tag of 25$ is a bit much. I paided 15$ for the deluxe edition that comes with the sounds track and I feel that the 15-20$ range of the base game is a much better price for the amount of content in the game. So if my opinion is worth anything I say get this when you can on sale for a bit cheaper.

A fun little game with some amusing and interesting riffs on its gameplay aspects. It feels like something new as opposed to "just another Souls-like game". Simpler than souls, for sure, but Necropolis can rear its head and toss you around if you get complacent. The co-op is fun and the inclusion of friendly fire can turn a co-op game into an impromptu (likely accidental) battle of accidents and miscommunication. Some people might balk and say that the game is barebones, claiming there's not enough game for the price, but I think, for what it currently lacks, Necropolis has huge replay value and has plenty of content for 30 dollars. All in all, a solid game that I would highly recommend.
Edit as of 8/17/2016 and Update 1.04:
With the most recent update, enemy AI has changed a bit, providing a better fight for you, usually necessitating more restoratives, the recipes for which have also been tweaked. Crafting material drop rates have also been tweaked. Enemies won't endlessly charge into your weapon and will go out of their way to avoid your attacks or dodge more often. I'm using power attacks more often and getting hit much more often. I'm burning through restoratives much quicker, and with the changes to drop rates and recipes, my inventory is no longer always full of the best food, which is a change for the better, I think. All told, I still very much recommend this game. With more updates in the pipe, it's only getting better.

Take two of the absolute most opposite mechanical bases, rhythm games and Roguelikes, and mash it together.  What happened?  Possibly one of the most intriguing, entertaining, and downright addictive puzzle games ever made.  A rather interesting soundtrack drives the game well, as well as support for custom soundtracks as well, and reinforces the rhythm half of this game.  Being a Roguelike, a full clear of the game can happen inside of an hour or two, but why stop there?  A myriad of options and mutator modes keep the experience fresh along with a rather robust random generation engine behind it.  I have yet to get truly repetitive experiences, but it also seems to be its biggest flaw.  The randomization can completely stack the deck against you, creating some tough scenarios that usually end in a badly timed death.  That being said, the ultra-simple controls combined with the rhythm-based score mechanics creates one extremely charming ride.  Worth the price for a fan of anything close to this style of game.

A fantastic strategy title by all counts, merges 4X and Grand Strategy into a hybrid that has more character than a lot of games of either ilk. The UI is a joy, events and anomalies are fun to interact with, most actions can be done from the galaxy map (which can be set to give you all the info you need at a glance), graphics are clean and pleasing, alien portraits are weird and wonderful, the AI is a notch above that in similar titles, and there is just enough customization to give Stellaris legs for days.
That said, you can sort of feel the holes in the game. No robust trade system, no spying or subterfuge, combat is basically a numbers game (you have a bigger fleet = you win), and while the research system is unique, it feels somewhat 'thin' as far as upgrades go. All said, this is a Paradox title, and with such a successful launch, I am sure we will get plenty of DLC down the road.
For the price of admission, you really cannot go wrong if you are a strategy fan or a sci fi nerd. I bought the game the day pre-releases opened and was downloading it the second it was available. Pretty much have played every waking hour since. Hugely rewarding game and far more accessible than other Paradox titles. I'm impressed, and eager to see what they bring next, and what modders have planned, of course.
Sober Addendum to Review After 30+ Hours: While I am not changing my recommendation, I do think that Stellaris is a buy only if you understand that it is fun and unique, if somewhat broken right now. There are incomplete features, a boring and somewhat broken mid and end game, and while a great time at first, with enough play time you may start to see the cracks in the facade. I already see myself not playing as much until things like sectors, quest chains, warscore goals, and the mid/late game get some much needed attention. There is a great game somewhere in Stellaris, but that game could very well be months away and partially placed behind DLC pay walls.

If you don't have a good sense of rhythm (like me) don't expect to get very many achievements, but DO expect to have one hell of a time playing it with friends.
For everyone who thought Mario Kart ruined friendships: you have no idea.

I feel absolutely... creastfallen... after playing this game...
I had no idea what to expect when I got it, I just heard the game's an amazingly good one, and that it's a must play. I got myself excited. After playing though, I feel no sense of achievement and wow I'm just really sad.
I agree with everyone that's aesthetically, it's incredibly gorgeous and would make you feel good in one way or another; the music was also great, if a little lacking in build-up. The story is subtle and vague, the kind that's thought provoking. As art, it did a splendid job. As a game though, I just can't agree with it. I love playing games due to the elated feeling I get when achieving an objective I worked for, even if the work is purely experiencing a story. I didn't get that in ABZU. As I said, the story content is vague and subtle, and mix that with simple gameplay mechanics - could just not get into it. It's really short as well and there's no fullfilment in trying to collect the items in-game since it barely does anything to change the experience. The interaction with the fishes were... educational and yes they're nice to stare at, but I still hadn't gotten anything noteworthy out of it (e.g. I rode sharky for a while hoping he'd swim me to the next area but nope). I like my stimulations bit more interactive. It hadn't helped that the movements in water was so fluid, I mean, it was fun in the beginning, but it makes it less motivating to explore and dizzying near end (it made me appreciate gravity more than ever at least).
So yeah for short, imsorrybutitwasboring.
It's art, I agree with everyone on that, but games aren't just about the visuals or graphics, to me at least. It's good, but it's not that good.

Quite fun. The mechanic of moving to the beat is an interesting gimmick, although I can't seem to get the hang of it. Keep missing some beats (because the soundtrack is incredibly excellent? Heh... not really. Just great, but not superb kinda thing). The soundtrack changes every level you go on, meaning that the beats change pace level to level. This also provides a nice variety while playing - you move at a different beat every level, and combined with the randomly generated levels (can't memorise paths - they always change) provides enough entertainment for a few hours.
You can also change music tracks if you want, which I'll be doing soon. So if you for some reason get disappointed in the music, swap to your own. The provided soundtracks are nice, but sometimes the fast(ish) beats combined with the dungeon monster aspects results in missed beats and dead characters.
I do not have any significant flaws with this game - it provides what it says it will - a different approach to rogue-like dungeon exploring that is enjoyable and not buggy at all (I didn't encounter any bugs while playing). Got it on sale at 50% price or something, but even at full price it would be worth grabbing to play.

Let me get this straight, this game is by no means a bad game. It is very well developed, it has a kind community, and developers that listen. But, I just don't like the game. The following is subjective and is my opinion, don't listen to it if you think it will deter you in buying the game, because this review is not meant for that purpose.
To begin, when I first saw it in the store, I was to say the least, very intrigued. Steam, itself, has not had a well done rogue-like in a long time, if ever. So, when it came out, I immediately bought it with no hesitations. However, instead of rushing ahead, I should have really looked into the game more.
The Good:
1. Unlike many other rogue-likes, I found it very interesting and great to see that the main character was a women, it was very fresh to see.
2. Though 8-bit (16, I'm unsure) the animations for the character and the monsters are very fluid.
3. The story is very different and unique, many dungeons revolve around the slaying and murder, but this game deters from that fact.
The Bad.
1. The music. Yes, though it is the main aspect that sets it apart from other rogue-likes, it did nit appeal to me. Yes, this is subjective, but the music put me on edge; though not horrible, I didn't click with it.
2. From the music, I felt very, very rushed. Though interesting, the pace of the music was rushing me. In other rogue-likes, I like to sit and strategize quietly, not be rushed by the beat. Though you could turn it off, it effects your gameplay, because the music is what the beat is, and if you can't hear the music, you have to keep your eyes off your character and watch the heart. It just felt really awkward for me.
3. The controls, though adjustable, they are still very clunky.
Like I stated before, by no means is this game horrible, it is a very unique rogue-like that could appeal to many people, and it already has; but not me. Maybe, in the future I'll realize how stupid I am and will change my review and play it again, but not at this moment.

Sum it up:  If you are a die-hard old school MM fan, this is something that you long for.  If you are a RPG lover, stop by and look for a decent rpg, then you need to look for other better games.
I have played through the early access, and it was disappointing. I didn't make a comment because it was still beta phase. The full version has made tremendous improvments. For instance, the weapons won't break every second; you wouldn't fail to see your fingers at night due to poor lighting design. I see more barrels with more intereting content and better designed balance such as monster strength and potion pricing.
However, the core problems of the early access are not addressed.
First is no innovation at all. The game play and design is shockingly simplistic. You walk, see monsters, press 1144, then the monsters die. Class leveling is a straight one-way ticket. Monster fighting is the battle on who has more potions. This kind of game design maybe interesting 20 years ago. But to produce such a game at 21st century and charge people 25 dollars for it is simply not acceptable. There are some interesting puzzles, but not enough to make the game attractive.
Then here comes the cheapskate strategy of reduce, recycle and reuse. Ubisoft used this strategy on heroes VI, I still bear with it. However, what is this?  The monster appearance, NPCs, music and every other thing you see basically comes from dark messiah and heroesVI. Being of the same world Ashan, I guess some repetition is fine. But this games has gone too far. The worst part is these two games are of totally different age and types. Forcing elements of these two games into one feels like a big modded rpg from some random players community like WOG. Not to mention the texture and graphic is horrible. Some people say it doesn't work with 32bit OS, but my win8 64bit seems to have the same problem as well. In one word: they shouldn't charge 25USD just for a recycled product.
In conclusion, I am not against turn-based strategy games or rpg. But this game is nowhere on par with any decent modern day rpg. It is good for nostalgia. But if you are a real old school MMM fan you won't be bothered to read this review anyway. So I won't recommend to any general rpg players.

The second major issue with this game is the complete lack of random monsters, at least in the first several hours of play.  This puts what initially looks like an open world game on rails.   The is a major issue because of the XP and leveling system.  Your heroes need to hit certain benchmarks by certain points in the game  or you will be unable to progress beyind those points. I really like these guys' wargame collection, it's pretty good for a little thing of casual wargames and fairly entertaining. I would recommend you go pick that up and play it because it's good. This game is not. It's more or less mindless, because they've elected to move character and unit upgrades to a currency you accumulate by doing bland challenges in missions rather than things that are fun. Since you can continue a mission once you finish the objectives, you'll find yourself sitting in  an already complete level saving up cash so you do the bonus objective of buy a bunch of stuff you don't need, or whatever. That's an annoying game design decision! This achievement currency is annoying to get, which is a problem because you'll want a lot of it: heroes don't stay between missions unless you pay for it, and units can't be upgraded. They'll level up, sure, but there are lots of bonuses you can only obtain this way.
Basically, they took a very simple game series and added things which appear, on the surface, to add depth, but really just add more things that aren't fun to play with. It's an easy mistake to make when you're doing a sequel, and I wish the early access process would help change stuff to make the game better. Instead I'm faced with a situation where you can buy their previous, much better game at a cheaper price, and at that point it's a no-brainer on what you should do. If you want a fun, breezy, risk-type wargame with a historical theme pick up
. If you want something more complex, you're looking in the wrong place here.

I've played a fair amount of this now. I bought it way back in early access but I waited because I knew it would only get better and I didn't want to ruin my final experience with the game. It seems some people's experiences in early access weren't that great.
I am having quite a bit of fun with it. There's a fair amount of character customization that you can do at the beginning of the game though not quite as much as  the M&M6-8 games. Mainly because you pick 1 of 4 races and each race has 3 class option. Those classes are a little bit limited in their further skill customization but there's still a fair amount of diversity to be had in terms of skill choices. You're also limited to 2 voice choices and 2 male potraits as well as 2 female portraits. At first I thought that it was a bit weak but I figured it didn't really matter what they looked or sounded like.
As far as the gameplay goes I found a lot of things nostalgic. The sounds they used, the way you interact with buildings, and a few other things reminded me a lot of M&M6-8. The big difference being it's not free roam and it's on a grid but you know what, I'm fine with that. If it was free movement people would compare it to other open world games and that's not fair. It works fine that it's grid based and I didn't find it to hurt the experience at all. When you level up there's lots of customization to be had in terms of skill lines to put skill points into and stat points to distribute. There's also plenty of loot to plunder and equip even though it's kind of annoying how much +resistance gear there is. It feels like a cheap cop out way to avoid giving you a useful stat on the item. Every single green item has +resistance and you have to find a blue item to even get an item worth caring about as green items don't roll anything but +resistance which is all but pointless.
Overall I would recommend this game to fans of the series and you should realize this game is a bit different than the M&M6-8 games. That doesn't mean you should avoid it though as there's a lot of fun to be had. Even people who are new to the series. If you enjoy tactical RPG type games then you should enjoy this.

The game features a small number of scenarios (eight); while the missions have plentiful secondary objectives that add some replay value, the general plan in each is fairly scripted based on the fixed starting conditions. Most scenarios give a huge economic, territory, and military advantage to the opponent; there is no skirmish mode where each faction is given equal footing to begin with. The benefits for the AI cannot be adjusted, as there are no difficulty settings. The only resource in the game is silver, accumulated each turn by occupying provinces around the map and spent on new infantry, cavalry, and archery units. Heroes whom lead each army can only perform one action per turn (move, attack, or recruit), which adds some strategic choices to the game. While combat is completely automated, units can be placed in formations before the battle begins, which does make a difference in attack and defense attributes. Because of the low unit cap (only seven heroes are allowed, and each hero can only recruit a specific number of units), it can be impossible to quickly finish a scenario even after it’s clear you will be victorious. Strategy & Tactics: Dark Ages is an approachable turn-based strategy game hindered by its small assortment of unbalanced, tedious scenarios.

When I completed the game, I wasn't sure whether I should recommend it.
In the game, you have a fireplace where you can burn things. Burning the objects gets you money to buy more objects. You can combine the objects to get stamps and more money. You're also free to just throw things in the fireplace and burn them as you please.
My favorite was building scenes in the fireplace, such as setting up block cities and adding things to the scenes such as the pixel trees or the goo balls. In that way, it's more like a zen garden that you burn down when you're ready to make another scene.
The problem, I think, is the heavy-handed and too obvious 'lesson' the game carries. Because it's a commentary on gaming, it backs itself into a corner. They wanted to teach that you shouldn't slave away mindlessly at reptitive, thoughtless games that make you pay to continue. But in my opinion, they failed at the irony they were going for by having you play a game just like that and then having to escape from it. Let's be honest here, I'm sure a lot of gamers are tired of playing a game that tells them they shouldn't be playing a game, or that they are playing the wrong kind of game.
I found the second half of the game to be dry, slow moving, and not interesting or eye-opening. It felt tacked on. I nearly closed out because I was bored and saw right where the ending was headed.
Despite that, it's still a fun game to play around with. I would try the game out if it's on sale or in a bundle. The sandbox part of it is enough to make me go back in and build small scale scenes when I'm bored and taking a break from something.
I would say the game is appropriate for all ages, despite some slight dark themes. There was no swearing that I caught, and everything seemed appropriate probably for ages 10 and up. (Unless someone feels otherwise.)

I kickstarted this game as a fan of Doug TenNapel and a fan of alternative graphic styles, such as claymation, cell shading, etc. I always liked his alternative worlds and particularly liked EarthWorm Jim.
Overall, the game is difficult and incomplete; the menu system, lack of view-able inventory, lack of ability to see what is interact-able or not, makes you feel like you are playing a prototype or beta.
As other reviewers have written, some of the puzzles aren't really puzzles and some of the interactions are awkward.
For example: there's a button and you try and click on it nothing happens, no cursor change, nothing. Is this button something you can't interact with? A button that's locked for now to be unlocked later? Nope. You just need your dog to click it with his tail. Really? My dumb dog can press that button with his tail but I can't bend down and press it?
Making it so that both characters could press the button would have been more realistic and if there is a situation where one character has to press a button while the other manipulates something, let me figure out that by having the wrong person press it, seeing the change in the world and what needs to happen, and adjusting accordingly.
In the end, it feels like they massively underestimated the cost and time required to produce this game. I feel that they intended to release something much grander but ran out of time and money.
If you are an absolute claymation or point-and-click fan, pick it up when it is on sale. Otherwise, I don't recommend it.
One last comment: I didn't have any of the technical issues that some other users have reported, on the current version of the game.

All games do one of two things. They either cast you as yourself, free to be who you are, to pursue your own goals, to define your own role. Or they cast you as someone else, and ask you to take on their personality, their goals, their role.
If you expect the former, you'll be disappointed. This game is decidely about empathizing with someone else's situation, and trying to understand their struggle to deal with it.
At points you will be frustrated, at points you will be bored, at points you will be angry, and at points you will be sad. At points you'll feel the whole thing is futile - or even that it's broken. At points you'll wish it was just over. And then you'll wish it wasn't. And judging by some of the negative reviews, at points you might even feel offended. But if you've ever been face-to-face with terminal illness, all of these emotions will be familiar, and this game does an excellent job of exposing you to each in a short period of time.
If you're just looking for something that'll make you cry, read a sad book. This game is about a lot more.

I'm really torn about Armikrog.
Sure, it's very charming. The claymation style is beautiful, very well animated, it's really funny at times, and the plot is overall pretty good, with tons of story in the background to find (and by tons, I mean there's a wall - a literal wall - of exposition for you to read at your own devices).
But then, there's the bad. It's really bare bones. No interactions with the environment, no clever uses of items, no inventory at all... There is absolutely nothing to do besides the essential; it's too simplistic for its own good.  Also, it's surprisingly short. I just beat it in one sitting, and there's really nothing to do afterwards.
Also, the audio. Oh boy, it's a bit of a mess. The voice acting seems like it's missing some punch to it; the main character in particular seems like he's just uninterested in everything. And for some reason, his recordings in particular sound really low quality in relation to all other voices. The soundtrack is fantastic, but there are a few bugs that will make the whole game go silent.
But I'd still say to give it a go. It gets frustrating at times, for various reasons, but its charm is undeniable. Just make sure to get it at a discount, because it is NOT worth its full price.

Moar Content Pls.

1) The Neverhood, this is not. It wasn't meant to be, so get that expectation out of your head before playing. The story isn't nearly as thrilling; that beautiful minimalism is gone and replaced by a sort of hollow Saturday-morning-adventure feel. You learn to live with it.
2) There's a real lack of balance with puzzles. For the vast majority of the game, you're working room-to-room through fairly linear puzzles. Near the end, things become exceedingly abstract: the final puzzle, many people have chosen walkthroughs over the actual work of translating the runic shapes (best done by watching these special FMVs a second time after playing through the whole game, hunting down certain NPCs).
3) The game is SHORT. My logged time, just over 4 hours, is what it took me to clear this game. That's a first-time play, taking time to explore everything I could, even watching the special "backer room" area and reading the long wall-o-text (not nearly as long as the insane wall from Neverhood, but still long-ish). Short, short game.
4) Terry S. Taylor's music isn't nearly as stand-out in this game as it was in Neverhood, or even Skullmonkeys. There were a few catchy tracks, but he didn't go nutso-crazy like he used to. His backer-name track was probably his best.
5) For all my complaints, the claymation is SUPERB. This is one area where they really stayed true to the original design plans. The game is really worth it for the visuals alone.
6) Short-short game sets itself up for a possible sequel at the end. It's a sort of "well, more adventures time!" But because Tommynaut has two siblings, and you only meet one of them on Armikrog, the studio has room to do another game with the third of the "nauts" siblings, and maybe improve on their failings that time around. Only time will tell.
Conclusion:
I acknowledge the glut of point-and-click adventures coming down the Steam pipe these days. I think the low metacritic score for this game has to do with pedigree ("wasn't this supposed to be as good as The Neverhood?") as well as significant bugs that have since been patched (for the most part). It's not so bad a game as to deserve being "mixed" in the public eye, IMO. It makes me nervous that this reception will put an end to "Pencil Test Studios" before they really got started. And that would be a shame, because they could probably move on to bigger and better now that they're no longer "rusty" in game dev land.

A biased review from the guy who played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of The Neverhood and then some more:
It pains me immensely to not recommend this game. The promise was amazing: the team that made The Neverhood, including the composer, to make a brand new clay stop motion adventure. But the result is just not up to the hype.
The main problem is repetitiveness. They happened to make a set of puzzles and managed to reuse them 4 times over. I kid you not.
The story is quite lazy, unimaginative and, frankly, boring.
Sprites look quite lazy on top of the backgrounds, they don't feel like  they are out there in the real environment. Maybe that's the result of modern technologies making problems be more noticeable, I don't really know.
Music variety is lacking.
All the things I loved from The Neverhood, besides amusingly insane art style are just not there.
You could expect to see a fan of the old game disappointed with the new one not being the same thing over, but most of the issues still stand even without the comparison: technical issues, repetitiveness, boring and short story.
It's very sad, but I can't recommend Armikrog at its full price. Get it when it's on sale, or better yet get your hands on The Neverhood, it runs well via scummvm on any modern operating system and is far superior to this.
The story, the music and the actual gameplay still holds up to this day. Now go imagine FF 7, 8 and 9 made in a modern engine. Pants blown yet?

The Binding of Isaac is a top down shooter that features randomly generated dungeons, RPG elements, and is influenced by The Legend of Zelda. In Isaac, you start on one floor, and go from room to room clearing out enemies, all the while collecting items that can potentially bolster or weaken your stats (increased movement speed or health downgrades) for the boss room of that floor. You go down floors, clearing out rooms until you make it to Mom. Yeah, that's right Mom (the game is inspired by the biblical tale of the Binding of Isaac).
The Binding of Isaac has a lot of religious elements in it, combined with a grotesquely unique art style, and it all feels quite fresh and well executed. Isaac is an interesting shooter in that its roguelike dungeons insure that no two runs will ever be the same. Combine that with the almost unfair difficulty of enemies who shoot, stomp, ram, and do pretty much anything to make sure that you don't progress, and you've got one challenging game. However, the game's controls are very tight and whenever you die, you won't really feel mad at the game, but rather at yourself for not doing your best in a room.
The game features an excellent soundtrack composed by Danny Barankowsky, and has really memorable tunes that will stay with you long after you finish a run. My only major gripe with this game is that it is very prone to slow down as it is made in Flash and with hectic explosions and enemies all over the place that can ruin the flow of a run, though this isn't enough to detract from your appreciation of the game.
I actually intend to play this game for a while as I still have not yet unlocked all the items and seen all the endings, and the game just has that allure about it: with everything in the game pretty much being randomized, you can see a whole bunch of different runs with item combinations that could potentially make the game nigh-impossible to beat, or perhaps make the game too easy with an overpowered avatar crushing all opposition.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who's played Zelda, enjoys top down shooters, and/or anyone who likes roguelikes. A really fun yet unforgiving game with a standout visual style, great soundtrack, and an amazing replayability factor, I give the game a 9 out of 10.

Dust: And Elysian Tail is a completely overhyped game, a trait that sincerely baffles me. The game does look very nice, and the controls are mostly* precise, but combat is a bore. It's one of the most exploitable combat systems I have seen in a game, making dodging, counters, and strategy a waste of time. Magic spamming is all you need for every enemy and boss alike. And while you're in combat, you will most likely take damage. And here begins one of the most annoying aspects of the game: health items. They are scarecely found, expensive to buy, and aren't very effective. A fair amount of time is spent hauling yourself back to a save point to heal, or waiting for your auto heal equipment to do so, and it sooooo annoying.
The platforming can sometimes be really satisfying. I genuinely enjoy some of the mechanics, and they were implemented well the first time you find a puzzle. However, it gets repetetive fairly quickly as the difficulty of the platforming sections often relies on the fact that the controls are not quite responsive enough to make a section as easy as it should be. There's even a secret area that takes actual luck to get to. Oh my god, I hated that. In general, the plaftorming was so close to being genuinely good, but was either really easy or hard because of bs. And that was a bit of a letdown.
As an RPG, it's pretty basic. I don't really have much to say there.
Finding items from/bits of slain enemies and making equipment out of them sounds great! Monster hunter, anyone? But in reality, the game does a pretty poor effort at it. All of the important items that you need to make decent equipment is from enemies that are annoying to get to and kill, and most of the time the item you want won't drop, forcing you to leave and return to an area. Also, since getting health items is so expensive, you will most likely have already sold necessary items by the time you get a new equipment recipe. So you sell your items to get food, and then you have to use your food in order to grind enemies until they drop the items you sold. All the crafting is is grinding.
And lastly, the story, characters, and voice acting. Some people said it was great, but I could not stand it. The characters are straight up stereotypical RPG archetypes. The "gritty" voice acting of Dust is grating to listen to, the forced humor and shrill voice of Fidget (probably my least favorite character name ever) is cringeworthy, and the story is, again, a stereotype, lacking the originality that a game like this needs. The art style was spot on. The uninspired story does not particularly hold my attention, and I actually stopped watching cutscenes about two hours into the game. They're just cringey.
Overall, I have been pretty harsh on the game. The art style is fantastic, and the combat actually is quite enjoyable until the game makes spamming magic one of your only few viable options, and by far the most effective one. But I have been harsh for a reason, because SOOOO many people gave the game a great score that I feel it just doesn't deserve. There are many flaws that severely affect my experience with it and I still can't get over some of that voice acting.
Dust: An Elysian Tail gets a 6/10. Not terrible, but not good either. Annoying, mostly.

Let me get this straight, this game is by no means a bad game. It is very well developed, it has a kind community, and developers that listen. But, I just don't like the game. The following is subjective and is my opinion, don't listen to it if you think it will deter you in buying the game, because this review is not meant for that purpose.
To begin, when I first saw it in the store, I was to say the least, very intrigued. Steam, itself, has not had a well done rogue-like in a long time, if ever. So, when it came out, I immediately bought it with no hesitations. However, instead of rushing ahead, I should have really looked into the game more.
The Good:
1. Unlike many other rogue-likes, I found it very interesting and great to see that the main character was a women, it was very fresh to see.
2. Though 8-bit (16, I'm unsure) the animations for the character and the monsters are very fluid.
3. The story is very different and unique, many dungeons revolve around the slaying and murder, but this game deters from that fact.
The Bad.
1. The music. Yes, though it is the main aspect that sets it apart from other rogue-likes, it did nit appeal to me. Yes, this is subjective, but the music put me on edge; though not horrible, I didn't click with it.
2. From the music, I felt very, very rushed. Though interesting, the pace of the music was rushing me. In other rogue-likes, I like to sit and strategize quietly, not be rushed by the beat. Though you could turn it off, it effects your gameplay, because the music is what the beat is, and if you can't hear the music, you have to keep your eyes off your character and watch the heart. It just felt really awkward for me.
3. The controls, though adjustable, they are still very clunky.
Like I stated before, by no means is this game horrible, it is a very unique rogue-like that could appeal to many people, and it already has; but not me. Maybe, in the future I'll realize how stupid I am and will change my review and play it again, but not at this moment.

Well. What can I say? I built my first pc and was in-Steam-enated 9 months ago, and I think I've finally given birth to a writhing mess of a gamer. After trying plenty of games from a myriad of genres and developers, you start to develop a certain immunity to a lot of the crap that's out there. Crypt of the NecroDancer, however, stands amongst only a few games that NAIL IT. What is 'it'? Largely, I'm not sure. However, here are a few things that I think contribute to it's success.
Unique - How many rhythm based, dungeon crawlers are there?
Balanced - The feature that sets it apart (the rhythm aspect) isn't overplayed. It doesn't stifle the flow of the game, it repeatedly surprises me. Its symbiosis with diverse enemy movement patterns almost gives a feeling of playing chess, whilst remaining equally accessible and challenging. So cleverly done. Strong tones of puzzle-y-ness, but not in a mundane sense.
Unrestrictive - Another game that allows this type of freedom of choice, is Undertale. Do you play conventionally, or destroy everything you can, just to push the boundaries of the game and its consequences? It gives you a feeling of discovery, that repeatedly draws you back.
Character Development - The more you play, the better equipment and stats you have access to. Nothing new, I know. BUT, it's executed very well. Alongside this, you can unlock access to various characters, each with their own abilities. This makes the levels you just completed, almost completely different experiences.
Aesthetics and Audio - I love the retro styling, even though it's been done OVER and OVER again over the past few years. I personally enjoy that style and the game carries it off well. I LOVE the soundtrack, so far. I am admittedly biased, because these '8-bit' graphics and audio are something I personally have taste for. However, if you don't like manic, MegaDrive, music then fear not! You can implement your own mp3s into the game and play along to those!
Criticisms -

Part rhythm game, part dungeon crawler, Crypt of the NecroDancer is a well-excuted and original concept that marries its inspirations effectively without sacrificing too much from either genre. While it doesn't dig too deep into either genre's traits, if you enjoy rhythm games or dungeon crawlers you will find something to like here (if you can look past its flaws).
The meat of the gameplay revolves around spelunking through four zones of four stages each, with the first three having a small pool of possible bosses at the end. By keeping with the rhythm of the track and timing your actions to the beat, you are rewarded with a multiplier bonus that increases your gold pickups (and which later on enhances some equipment). While this is very important exploring the first two zones (especially as a new player because your loot pool will be low), zone 3 becomes extremely hectic with very aggressive monsters, lots of damage traps, and higher base gold pickups. The coin multiplier is useless except for gear once you reach Zone 4 because the gold pickups are so large that you can ignore it completely outside of combat. This seems to go against the design decision of adding rhythm elements and makes the game feel more like a barebones mobile-esque experience instead of DDR with swords. This might change with other characters (of which there are 10 to choose from), but the zones felt very similar in terms of game design when playing with Melody and Cadence for me.
Even though the game only has 16 (randomized) floors, you have a great deal of customization options from the level select hub. Different characters completely change how the game plays; a monk who dies from touching gold, a bard who ignores the rhythm and turns the game into a turn-based crawler, and a miner with infinite kickable bombs are some examples of how the gameplay can be radically modified. CotN is also completely playable with a dance pad because everything is controlled with the arrow keys! This alone gives it my "Best One-Handed Game" award for 2015. A level editor and a seeded All Zones Mode are also included for enthusiasts.
Overall, Crypt of the NecroDancer is a superbly unique experience that is cheap enough that anyone who has played DDR should dust off their dance pad for. While it isn't the deepest rogue-like or the hardest rhythm game, there is enough content included to sink your teeth into for at least a dozen hours.

Early Access Watcher Public Service Announcement
Game: Strategy & Tactics: Dark Ages
Update Version: v1.0 Patch #1
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Game Footage:
Strategy & Tactics: Dark Ages is a turn-based strategy title by the developers over at HeroCraft. HeroCraft are no stranger to the strategy genre, making several medieval and modern themed games over the past year. It has been over a month since the game released into Early Access and it has already seen some patchwork to fix some of the crippling launch issues. While the tactics are indeed present in the game, some key mechanics and technical issues make the experience feel more like a battle of attrition than coherent operation.
The presentation value is currently the game's strength from the dynamic maps to the small details that are scattered across each map. Smoke can be seen rising from certain buildings, birds flock over towns and clouds shade the countryside as they move across the board in a natural manner. The figurines used to represent armies also look great, but the real artistic prowess is shown in full force with the unit cards and commander portraits. The battle animations used for the combat recaps are also quite nice to look at, but the desire to watch these fights play out are diminished greatly by the outcome already being known before watching them. It all meshes well with the game's soundtrack, which fits the setting beautifully. The tracks vary from calming harp and flute melodies to the frantic beating of drums and the heroic blows of trumpets. It all melds together into a very pleasing aesthetic that carries the game's limited combat.
Dark Ages focuses on recruiting commanders, recruiting troops, taking territory and building up an unstoppable force to conquer unforeseen foes. It also bolster over 50 different unit types with their own interesting lore, plenty of historic commanders rewritten for this alternate medieval setting and a mercenary system that can help turn the tide when a surprise scenario appears during a mission. At present, Dark Ages has a total of six missions to undertake with the first one acting as a tutorial. Each mission has a couple of primary objectives required to complete the scenario, but there are also a slew of secondary objectives that can be attempted even if the primary objectives are met.
The purpose of these objectives is to acquire glory, which is spent on upgrading the attack and defense values of unit types in the Forge or for hiring legendary commanders that can be re-used in later missions. Unfortunately, the cost for doing both is subjectively high and the difficulty spikes for certain parts of the missions make it critical to replay the same mission ad nauseam for the glory needed to progress. This can be fixed later down the line as more missions are added to the game.
Combat is essentially a numbers game that incorporates statistical changes from terrain type, weather conditions, commander traits on both forces, individual troop bonuses and the effectiveness levels of the formations used. Once all of these modifiers are applied, both sides attack simultaneously using attack strength and defensive standings to determine the damage inflicted to the health of each unit. Morale also plays an important role by allowing an army to reduce their enemy squad's morale low enough to cause them to desert, which can compensate for some rather insane modifier totals that have left me facing an army to weak to kill me, but too defensive to take damage. Everything is calculated in a hands-free fashion, making the selection of a commander's formation and placement on the map the only player interaction in regards to combat. There are also special abilities that can be activated to help sway the calculations, but they require a foresight to a possible engagement to be of any use.
Aside from the upgrade concerns, the game has a few technical problems that range from the annoying to the absolutely frustrating. The camera has a bad habit of stopping periodically while scrolling across the map using the WASD and arrow keys. The mouse also feels incredibly sluggish while moving the cursor, which could be offset by a mouse sensitivity slider. Upon launching the game, there is a chance (averaging 50/50) the game will fall to start up and merely sit there with a partial black screen. Crashing also rears its' ugly head at some of the strangest moment, which is thankfully countered by the game's auto-save function that will save progress following a completed turn. The last major issue is more of an exploit, but I have discovered if a match should end in defeat, a player can return to the last turn and complete the match (if all primary objectives are met) and receive the same amount of glory points as the earlier defeat. This essentially makes it possible to earn twice the glory for one match.
Strategy & Tactics: Dark Ages has established a great foundation for the game's core mechanics and has out done itself visually. It is a beautiful looking game with some interesting ideas held back by a lack of mission availability and a difficulty spike that demands a heavy glory grind. If the idea of grinding the same scripted missions for glory doesn't worry, then the current build could be enough to provide some solid hours of strategic entertainment. With the technical issues and hands-free combat, however, it would probably be best to wait and see how the game evolves before throwing down the $10 entry fee.

The latest edition of Stardock's 4x turn-based strategy title range, this third title offers shiny new graphics, expansive maps, custom ship designs, and tech trees dependent on racial outlook.
Leaving the
aside entirely, please take discussions about it to other sites.
As advertised, 'linear' victory conditions are out of the picture, letting players really achieve the "4x" standard - Exploration, Expansion, Extortion, and Extermination all have "win" conditions, from following the ancient species to ascension to simply being the only species left standing.
Graphics are quite nice, with detail paid to not only planetary design but ship combat processing as well.
Gameplay can be tweaked to suit fast, short games or epic-scale conquest.
Ship designer allows for immense customization, allowing players to create hundreds of variants for their roles.
Modding support enables incredible levels of customization for your game.
Lack of finishing in the QA process makes this the buggiest game of the GC series.  Crashing to desktop should be expected, and numerous unpatched errors still remain since release.
AI is not great, even on higher difficulty settings.
Multiplayer matchmaking takes far higher data requirements than theoretically necessary, making unnecessary latency issues for players in a turn-based strategy game.
Sound is particularly buggy, and players can expect that after certain memory thresholds will fail to function any more at all.
A thorough bug fix analysis is needed to cover the issues that are produced.  If you suffer repeat issues, opt-in to the "beta" through Steam to help bypass certain cloud-related issues.
8/10.  A solid sci-fi 4x turn strategy title.  Despite issues, can be played quite well, and the ship builder allows for plenty of workshop content even if you're not much of a modder yourself.

Danganronpa 2 is a great sequel to the amazing Danganronpa 1. I even think it's better than DR1. I went into this game knowing nothing about the story, characters, ect and I loved every second of it. If you loved DR1, you'll love this. I guess this game is also pretty great as a standalone game. But, if you play this without playing DR1, you might get confused during the last chapter.
The story is almost the same as DR1's. You play as a boy named Hajime Hinata who gets enrolled into Hope's Peak Academy- a school for insanely talented teenagers. Soon after you get there, you and your classmates suddenly go on a "school trip" to a strange island. The school trip was meant to be happy and fun, but then Monokuma shows up and ruins everything. Like the first game, he makes all the students participate in a killing game where they must kill each other if they want to leave the island.
One thing I really liked about this game is that they improved the Class Trial mini-games and made them a bit harder. In fact, the Class Trials are just harder in general. I was actually caught off guard by how hard they were. I expected them to be just as easy (or maybe a LITTLE harder) as the ones in DR1, but the first trial in this game took me 3 hours to complete because I failed... a lot.
Not only that, but they also added 2 NEW mini-games called "Rebuttal Showdown" and "Logic Dive" and I think they're pretty fun- especially Logic Dive. At first I didn't like Rebuttal Showdown because I didn't understand it, but it didn't take me long to figure it out.
The only bad thing about the new Class Trials is "Improved Hangman's Gambit." They basically just took Hangman's Gambit from DR1 and made it harder, but also made it more annoying and not fun.
This game introduces a new colorful cast of characters. And honestly, I love the cast from this game more than DR1's characters. DR2's characters seem a lot more interesting. The new characters each have their own unique personalities and they all have pretty awesome character designs. The Japanese voice acting is also great! (I don't use dubs, so I can't really say if it's good or not.)
There's also a couple of new features in this game. For one: when you open your e-handbook there's now a "Pets" tab. Yes, you get to raise your own pet! You're supposed to give it gifts so you can raise its "hope" status and every once in a while you're supposed to check it and clean up its♥♥♥♥♥♥ The pet grows the more steps you take in the game. There's different pets you can raise (there's a guide on Steam that tells you how to get each pet) and if you raise it well, you'll get rewards! Most pets just give you some Monocoins and a couple of gifts but 2 of the pets will reward you with a skill that can be used in the Class Trials.
Another new feature is a mini-game that can be accessed from the main menu called "Magical Girl Monomi." Though, I believe you can't play it right away. I think you have to progress in the main game a bit first. But anyways, in the mini-game, you play as Monomi and you basically have to fight these robot things. I've seen people complain about this game a lot. Even though I only played it to unlock the related achievements, I still enjoyed it. I thought it was pretty fun.
And for those of you who have played Danganronpa 1 and are familiar with "School Mode", it returns in this game! Except it's called "Island Mode" instead. But it's basically the same exact thing. In Island Mode, Monomi wants you and your classmates to create things for her. Just like School Mode, Island Mode is an easy way to unlock the character's Free Time events so you can learn more about them.

Wow, talk about a gut punch.
That Dragon, Cancer takes you on a journey no one should have to endure, that of finding out your child has cancer, watching your child battle the pain of both their disease and it's cure for years, and then being left behind when your child can fight no more. The emotion of it didn't even really hit me until the end credits, where players are shown a slide show with photographs of Joel (the child this story is about) and it all became real. These weren't just polygons rendered on a screen, this was a real family, with real suffering.
The only downside to the experience for me, and this is most certainly a personal thing, was how heavy-handed the religious element was. I certainly have no problem with religion, although I don't practice any myself, but having every other monologue be about God's love, Jesus' strength, or readings from the Bible made this feel like less of a story about the tragedy of childhood cancer, and more like someone encouraging me to go back to church.
Overall, I enjoyed the experience. I think it took advantage of the power behind the interactive narrative, allowing players to control the pacing of the experience, and also choosing to let them investigate many small items (like the cards in the hospitol, the one to TotalBiscuit was my favorite) or to let them pass to continue with the story.

In a preview in June 2015, I wrote that this game has a very unique feel that’s bound to attract plenty of gamers, but wondered whether it would have any material to keep them interested and voiced concerns about it being a case of ‘style over substance’. I also stated: “If the developers now focus their efforts on developing the gameplay and establish Armikrog as a title in its own right away from The Neverhood, we could potentially have something quite lovely on our hands.”
Sadly it doesn’t feel as if this happened. Despite a few delays, the game feels as if it would have benefitted from even more time and budget to polish up the clay-work so the quality at the end was the same standard as the beginning – as well as more testing to iron out the silly bugs. The gameplay is oversimplified, the characters have limited personalities, the puzzles are repetitive and have no drive, and the world of Spiro 5 and its fortress are flat and empty.
It’s the waste of potential that spoils it the most and I can imagine many of the Kickstarter backers coming away disappointed. Perhaps the developers were relying on fans of The Neverhood and their collective nostalgia to see them through and make the release a success, but this isn’t the spiritual successor they’re looking for.

This is going to be an odd review, because it's as much a tale of a personal journey as it is a writeup about a game.
I've been lucky enough to follow along with That Dragon Cancer's development, chatting with the devs on a few occasions and getting to check out a few scenes in a demo. It disheartens me to see people who didn't like the game claiming it is an attempt to "cash in" on the grief of others due to it being a rather simple, breif venture, because I've seen firsthand just how emotionally engrossed the game's staff was in telling this story. If suffering is art, the very process of developing this game was an artform in and of itself.
When it got a release date, I was left unsure how to promote it to others. Saying it was a "game" I was "looking forward" to "playing" felt wrong. Actually, when the game finally released, I purchased it and spent several days staring at it in my Steam library, procrastinating on actually playing it, because I knew I would be doing so much more than just "playing a game." Rather, I would be taking a very personal journey that would both look into the soul of a single human being and encompass the voices of the many, many people - myself included - who have lost a loved one to cancer.
I got exactly what I expected.
pulls no punches and tells the developer's story with no cencorship or remorse. It's an incredibly difficult game to play, as well as a very rewarding one.
It's hard to say a ton about the gameplay itself, because everything is fairly simple and exists more to help convey the emotion of the story than be "fun" in and of itself. This game pushes the boundaries of the line between cinema and gaming and creates something very unique and very engrossing for its efforts.
If you're expecting a "fun game" you "look forward" to playing, you won't find it here. If you're expecting to be invited into someone else's soul and watch the sympathy game genre evolve before your eyes through a brilliant mix of sincerity and development skill, you've come to the right place.
