The Binding of Isaac is a top down shooter that features randomly generated dungeons, RPG elements, and is influenced by The Legend of Zelda. In Isaac, you start on one floor, and go from room to room clearing out enemies, all the while collecting items that can potentially bolster or weaken your stats (increased movement speed or health downgrades) for the boss room of that floor. You go down floors, clearing out rooms until you make it to Mom. Yeah, that's right Mom (the game is inspired by the biblical tale of the Binding of Isaac).
The Binding of Isaac has a lot of religious elements in it, combined with a grotesquely unique art style, and it all feels quite fresh and well executed. Isaac is an interesting shooter in that its roguelike dungeons insure that no two runs will ever be the same. Combine that with the almost unfair difficulty of enemies who shoot, stomp, ram, and do pretty much anything to make sure that you don't progress, and you've got one challenging game. However, the game's controls are very tight and whenever you die, you won't really feel mad at the game, but rather at yourself for not doing your best in a room.
The game features an excellent soundtrack composed by Danny Barankowsky, and has really memorable tunes that will stay with you long after you finish a run. My only major gripe with this game is that it is very prone to slow down as it is made in Flash and with hectic explosions and enemies all over the place that can ruin the flow of a run, though this isn't enough to detract from your appreciation of the game.
I actually intend to play this game for a while as I still have not yet unlocked all the items and seen all the endings, and the game just has that allure about it: with everything in the game pretty much being randomized, you can see a whole bunch of different runs with item combinations that could potentially make the game nigh-impossible to beat, or perhaps make the game too easy with an overpowered avatar crushing all opposition.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who's played Zelda, enjoys top down shooters, and/or anyone who likes roguelikes. A really fun yet unforgiving game with a standout visual style, great soundtrack, and an amazing replayability factor, I give the game a 9 out of 10.

This game was a definite impulse buy for me. I loved the look of it, and it sounded fun. And for the first hour, it was-- right up until I started to experience the game's version of difficulty. Which is primarily through its mechanics. The combat is simple enough. Light attack, heavy attack, block, shield bash, use item-- the basics. There are also ranged weapons that take the place of your shield-- I don't recommend them, as you'll be using block a lot.
This is actually quite fun, however the issue comes with the food mechanic. As you fight, your stamina drains-- good, fine, encourages caution-- only to (seemingly randomly) drop in max amount due to hunger/exhaustion. This is whatever in the first couple floors, but as you go down, your power doesn't seem to increase (your items get better, and there are random upgrades you can buy for exorbitant prices before each floor-- you don't know what you're getting). This means that on about floor 5-6 there were a bunch of giant golden gorilla monstrosities that would do incredible damage to me, soak up tons of hits, all while I struggled to run away and quaff food-- which became almost impossible due to another fun quirk. Enemies randomly spawn behind you, in areas you've cleared out. Frequently. As in, I found a room with about 5 vikings in it, ran out of stamina, ran out to go and eat food, and after about 20 seconds of running I ended up with an army of about 20 following me. That's where the game stopped being fun, when the game decided that difficulty was not through harder AI, but through sheer numbers, and unfair mechanics.
This game just isn't worth it for its large price tag. Maybe if you could get it half off, it would be worth it. Not now.

Back in 2005,I was handed a pirated game by my friend.
"You HAVE to play this!". Curious,I installed and played the game on my then-fossil PC and found myself lost into the game for weeks!For I discovered a new genre.RPG,as the cool kids used to say.
Cut forward to 9 years.RPG Scenario has completely changed with Bethesda and Bioware as the demigods of WRPG.Souls' franchise has been hailed as the masochist's paradise.CD Projekt Red is promising to deliver possibly the most epic game in terms of both scope and and scale.
Square's Final Fantasy is struggling to keep up with its contemporaries due to the recent games which have been a complete blunder and is on the very verge of downfall should the next game fail.
So how does a primitive game like Final Fantasy VII hold up today?
{TL;DR Version Down Below}
PRESENTATION:
Oh, Final Fantasy VII was a complete looker for a game to be released in 1997 and the first game in series to have 3D graphics.
Polygon textures, Pre-rendered cutscenes, Modelled character designs were the terms people heard for the first time.
Storyline is above average but its narrative and storytelling is ace! This game proved that Square Soft knew how to do story right.They do have a few plotholes, but they aren't enough to bring the whole experience down.
Sure the game itself looks supremely fossil for today's standards.But when a game has memorable characters with zero voice acting...yes,picture this.. Characters with no voice actors that were memorable!
So yes, Great characters, a plot that just oozes intrigue to be uncovered and soul-rending music, Final Fantasy VII represents all that which the recent games seem to be lacking.
GAMEPLAY:
Final Fantasy VII is am old school JRPG in every sense which boasts an open-world setting, turn-based combat and some annoying mini-games.But you'll be interested in the former two aspects. The character progression system requires you to be playing a lot of hours because once you hit Level20,you are going to need a LOT of XP points to progress.For that reason I found myself farming XP for hours,that can be frustrating for some. The game does get tough eventually so you'll need to keep your character's levels higher and equip them with better gear from time to time.
Turn-based combat is also very well implemented with "Materia System" which is incredibly deep and allows for some interesting mix-and-match combinations.The influence of its combat can be seen in recent games like South Park:The Stick of Truth and Child of Light.
It takes a while for the game to open up.By end of first 7 hours, you almost learn everything you should about the mechanics and systems.
Animations are still clunky and stick-like, meaning its still the unchanged PS1 version you're playing.While it does have Keyboard support, you'll still want to play using a gamepad.
The game can be completed within 40hours.Even more if you try to unlock all characters, learn all techniques and defeat the additional bosses. For most part, the game fulfills your needs for everything Role-playing.
{FOR TL;DR SPAMMERS}
PROS:
+Satisfying storyline and narrative
+Great characters
+Robust combat
+Reasonably challenging
+Sublime music and OST
+Features one of the best antagonists in video game culture
CONS:
-Graphics sure look outdated.
VERDICT:
An absolute piece of masterwork.Final Fantasy VII was an achievement in RPG genre when it released.
The later games in the series sure had upgraded visuals and graphics but none of them come close to this one when it came to capturing the very soul of what makes RPG an RPG, like VII did.
All said and considered,Final Fantasy VII is the best game in FF series and one of the best JRPG of all time.
If you are a self-proclaimed fanatic of this genre,then pick this one up whenever you can. You owe it to yourself.

is the spiritual successor to
, an adorable point-and-click adventure game from 1996 made entirely out of clay.
is made by much of the original
team, including lead designer Doug TenNapel and wacky musician Terry S. Taylor. It’s a lot like
, and if you haven’t played that, it’s similar in gameplay to
.
So there’s good and bad. The good is pretty much all of the game design, story, art and music. It’s fantastic. More on that in a bit.
The bad is mostly technical. As you will see from many of these Steam reviews, this game is buggy. Like, really buggy. Little bugs, big bugs. A missing animation here, a difficult-to-find click-spot there, a game-breaking save corrupting bug every once in awhile. Save often, with a new name every time, because you never know how far back you’ll have to load because your game is in an (accidentally) unwinnable state. The good news is that the team have patched the game four times in the past few months and fixed many of the bugs and issues. There are still some left, but they are working on it.
So, looking past that, what’s the game like? As with its predecessor,
is a claymation game, and that’s just cool. In 1996, the cost and difficulty of producing a clay game vs a 3D computer graphics game was probably about even. In 2015, the tools and technology for 3D are so advanced that it’s the obvious choice. The team absolutely chose the hard road here and it’s worth it --- the soul of this game is in the fact that everything is literally hand-crafted. It feels so unique. Unlike
, this game also uses bits of other materials like fake fur, paper, metal, and yes, an accordion.
So you basically control this clay guy called Tommynaut who looks suspiciously like Klaymen, and can switch between him and his blind talking dog, Beak Beak. Each character has his own unique abilities: Tommynaut can pick up and use items and complex interfaces, while Beak Beak can go through small holes to reach new locations. So you have to use both characters in tandem to solve puzzles. The most annoying part is having to switch to the other character for non-obvious reasons (most common: if there is a knee-height switch, it won’t even register as an object for Tommy; you have to switch to Beaky and have him press it). There is also a distinct lack of feedback when you try the wrong thing, or the right thing at the wrong time. The puzzles are pretty simple and intuitive, and mostly based around learning a strange alphabet of symbols. Have a pen and paper handy and write down any clues you find, and you should be fine.
The game is missing the first-person outdoor areas from
. You pretty much never go outside, but it does have the track/cart sections connecting the different buildings together.
It’s a little short --- took me about 5 hours. The characters are likeable. The story is simple but compelling and worth seeing through to the end. All up, this is an undervalued gem, that lives up to the original game, and that I would wholeheartedly recommend, save for the many UI and technical issues.

I played Dark Souls. I didn't like it. I liked the idea, but Dark Souls gave me too little information about my goal and was very complicated without the necessary info. I like knowing what I'm supposed to do.
I played Lords of the Fallen. It ticked enough of the Dark Souls boxes, but also gave me the little objective that I needed. 'Do this' it would say, and I would not know how or where, but that was enough for me to puzzle and find out. I really liked that. Too bad LotF was quite glitchy and buggy in the end.
Then there's Necropolis. Somewhat similar, somewhat different. I really like it. It's light hearted enough to keep me coming back for more. It's combat mechanics are fun and challenging, even though they're no where as deep and complicated as Dark Souls, they're still interesting.
The variety is good enough to still come across new rooms and enemies 10 hours into the game.
The penalty for dying is big enough to be on your toes and create a sense of fear, but it's not bad enough as to discourage experimenting and exploration.
For me, this game is the perfect blend of balanced risk/reward, challenge, mystery and humour.
Some people don't like this type of dry humour, but it often reminds me of late Sir Terry Pratchett.
Yes, there are bugs.
Yes, there are glitches.
Yes, the enemy variation, especially in the start, is very limited and you might end up fighting the same guys for hours before progressing far enough and unlocking enough of the hidden rooms and biomes to see new ones.
Yes, the game does have some issues when it comes to performance.
Yes, there is an issue with 'weird traps' that spawn enemies right on top/behind/around you, although one could argue that's part of the challenge in this game.
But even though there are annoyances in this game, it's nothing that can't be fixed with some patches and updates.
This game gets a definite thumbs up from me, although I do not recommend getting this for more than 20 euro/dollar. It definitely is worth 20, but not more. Get it when it's on sale, or have a friend from a country where it's cheaper buy it for you.

It is actually one of the worst games I have ever played, and easily the worst mystery/visual novel game I have ever played. I tried to like it, I wanted to like it. But I wasted my money on this 60 hour crap-fest. Just read the WIKI or watch the ending on youtube. Trust me.
:
- The way Mahiru says, "Jeez"
- Nagito mentions the Aussie pop duo, "The Veronicas". Remember them?
-Ibuki's hair
- The graphic update from the first game looks great (the animated backgrounds are a nice touch)
:
- Obnoxious characters
- Complete tonal shift [from the first game]. The setting and the topics it deals with are a goofy, cartoony mess that lacks depth.
- Contrived storyline [btw, these are the three most important fundamentals of any novel or work of fiction]
- Abysmal pacing [you will spend 30-40 hours before anything meaningful to the overall story takes place]
- Unclear game mechanics
- Anachronisms
- Nonsensical dialogue that is impossible to interpret at times
- Sugesstive "humor" that isn't particularly clever [it feels a bit like you're watching Beavis and Butthead. Characters will just start talking about their boobs♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥without any motivation and derail the conversation to no comedic effect]
- Murder trials that start out goofy and irrational, and progressively deteriorate to the point where jarring contradictions are completely overlooked and never explained [as if the developers just gave up and assumed that the player wouldn't notice or care]
- Verbiage, there is no need for about 2/3rds of the game's dialogue. The characters tend to talk cyclically.
- One of the worst endings that I have personally experienced. It provides resolutions to most of the story's conflict, but it ultimately leaves the player without fulfillment. You won't walk away from this game with a new perspective on life or anything like that. You'll just be happy that it's over.
That's about all I can say without spoiling anything. Overall,
. To the very end. When you have a crappy setting/theme, crappy characters, crappy dialogue, and a storyline that forces itself way too hard, you get a crappy novel. You get a crappy game.
3/10, it looks pretty and it is generally functional, but I would not recommend it.

From the same producers of the Neverhood and those who have worked on productions such as Wall-e, Alladin and Eathworm Jim and can be found here...
While their resume is truly impressive, unfortunately it serves to no credit of this production called 'Armikrog'. By no means is this a BAD production, but when you compare it to the truly magical masterpieces such as 'The Neverhood' this unfortunately just stands sluggishly in it's shadows.
Since the developers no longer own licensing rights to the Neverhood and a evergrowing cult fan base were constantly demanding a similar stimulating imaginitive claymation adventure, some of those responsible in the previous game went on to make this one in the hope that they could copy the magic of the first one. Here is where it fizzles out into a pile of playdoh.
I can't help but think that the developers cut some serious corners thinking that they would get away with it or that it would simply pay off. IT DIDN'T!
So what makes this one rather limp wristed in comparison to its predecessor? First of all there is a serious lack of facial expressive shennanigans on the characters, therefore the animations seem rather dull in comparison to the Neverhood. Isn't facial expressions what makes fast paced animations like Roger Rabbit so memorable? While we mention fast pace, there isn't a real lot of that. Most of the backgrounds seem rather the same. The modes of travel along the cliff scaling clay cart was tediously long.
The music was constantly cutting in and out at random moments, producing long moments of deadly silence. There seemed to be a real lack of a musical score. While there was some momentful songs in the game like 'I wrote a song with your name in it', they were very few and far between.
Several places you could not only make the sound glitch by clicking on cut animations more than once, but you could also click your character off the cliff in various places where you were not suppose to go making your character spasm violently like he has been possessed.
The puzzles seemed to very similar to one another and not as imaginitive or as respectfully designed as it was in the Neverhood. While they built a long elaborate story to go with this game, one that is comparable to the size of the Bible just like they did in the Neverhood, but because of the lack of connection that most people will have with both characters and the uninspiring backgrounds and creatures, not many will even bother to read it.
One of their biggest mistakes was taking out the 3D dimensional view which was in the Neverhood and which made you feel like you were part of the alien landscape exploring it.
In short all this production did for me is long even more for the magic of 'the Neverhood'. Unfortunately I have serious doubts if they will ever make it. Why? I liken it to the 'Flying High' movies produced by the Zucker brothers which everyone loves. When Zucker brothers split each one making their own production, each one tried to produce something of the same high calibre magic. Some were close, but ultimately they all failed. It seems the true magic of the production came from the whole spectacular group working together. Maybe thats going to be  the same case here. Certain creative people missing, and so this will never be of the same rich level of gaming treasure history.
Am I exagerating how great 'Neverhood' was? Well let me put it this way. If you still own 'the Neverhood' in it's original box you can now sell it for around $150.00. I very much doubt in 20 years you would even be able to buy lunch with what you sell Armikrog for...
Close guys, but no cigar...

Oh God WHY?
Cars 2 was one of my most favorite party games back when I owned an Xbox 360. It had 4 player split screen (for ALL MODES, even the campaign), slick racing, and tons of mechanics such as drifting, driving on 2 wheels, driving backwards, jumping, ramming, and boosting that gave the game a suprisingly high skill ceiling. The highlight of the game was disruptor, a 2v2 match where you had to plant a bomb in the opposing player's base. The only downside to the game was the lack of online multiplayer. Whenever I showed the game to friends who had never played it before, they were always surprised to see how much fun it was despite it being a movie tie in game. Avalanche Studios, the creator of this game, made a hidden gem.
This brings me to the review. When I started up Cars 2 on my PC, I was so excited to play it again. That is until I got in game. The sight of the game left me speechless and confused. Cars 2 looks HORRIBLE on PC. The textures on everything are super muddy and stretched out, the sound is equalized so poorly that it constantly cuts out into loud static, and many assets do not show up in game such as street lamps (you only see a string of lights shining on you from middair). I was appalled. The PC version of a game like this should look better or at least equal to the 8 year old console version. Instead, it looks like a game that came out on the PlayStation 2. In fact, it looks Identical to the Nintendo DS version of Cars 2.
This revelation led me to start researching what the hell happened. How could a PC port be botched so badly? Here's what I found: The Steam port of Cars 2 was not done by Avalanche, it was done by an obscure company named Gamestar. Gamestar is a CHINESE development company that was established in 2002 and is focused on outsourcing. It has a staff of people who used to work at the Ubisoft Shanghai division. In 2008, Disney acquired the studio and set it to work on porting their games.
Disney Interactive VP said during the acquisition, "Gamestar will play an important role in our global growth plans, providing a high quality talent pool for our expanding product portfolio. Our global expansion is aimed at achieving a new level of creative capacity, quality, and expertise in video game software development.”
I sincerely hope the VP chokes on his own horsesh** that he just spewed out of his mouth. Disney bought out this outsourcing company based in CHINA with the sole purpose to lower the cost of porting games. This resulted in this awful, awful port of an originally fantastic game on Steam.
Hear me out: I would have been fine with the downgraded graphics, bugs, and annoyances of the port because at its base, Cars 2 is still a very good game. That is until I found the straw that broke the camel's back. I fired up my 4 controllers and hooked them up to my pc ready to have some fun playing a 4 player race just like I did 5 years ago with the Xbox version. Then I saw it. The game only supports 2 player split screen.
THATS RIGHT, DISNEY AND GAMESTAR SCREWED UP THE PC PORT SO BADLY THAT IT REDUCED THE AMOUNT OF SPLITSCREEN PLAYERS FROM 4 TO 2.
This will be the first (and last) game that I refund on steam. I am so very sad to see what has happened to my favorite party racer. If anyone from Avalanche Studios is reading this, I'm so sorry. I can't imagine what it feels like to put your heart and soul into making a great game only to see it eviscerated by an incompetent outsourced chinese studio. But in the end, it's really Disney's fault. They are a company that seeks the highest possible profit margin, and they are willing to turn great games into abominations like this in order to achieve that.
I hope that this review dissuades anyone from buying this game. Avoid any game ported by Gamestar like the plague. There are better racers to choose from on Steam, and the console versions are still avaliable to play.
Rest in peace, Cars 2

This powerful game about the Holocaust stands out in part because of the unusual perspective. It's told through the eyes of the 9-year-old duck of the commandant at Auschwitz, a boy who has no clue as to what is going on around him. This perspective allows readers to feel a strong sense of foreboding, long before they know the extent of the terror surrounding Bruno's world. Gamers will be struck by the contrast between Bruno's normalcy and naivety, and the extreme horrors of the time.
Gamers will quickly relate to Bruno, who is uprooted from his home and moved somewhere "nasty and cold" where he has no friends; he is lonely, his sister bugs him, and adults treat him as if he's not there. He wants to study art and read fantasy books rather than history and geography. He wants to get outside and explore. At one point Bruno even covets the life of the duck on the other side of the fence because at least he has other boys with whom he can play.

I'm going to be objective (as humanly possible) with this review because I know a lot of people truly enjoyed Dust, which is great. As a huge indie game supporter, I am ecstatic to see games like Dust do so well. I'm not trying to hate on it, but I personally did not enjoy Dust. Let's take a look:
Pros:
+ The graphics are absolutely gorgeous. Easily one of the prettiest games I've ever played.
+ The controls are very tight and feel good. There is no slipping. Very important for this type of gameplay. Good job here.
+ I don't understand how a single person made this game. Major props because this game is very long compared to other titles which were made by one to two people.
Cons:
- It's really important to connect with the characters in order to enjoy your time in the game. Unfortunately, the main character in this game has zero personality and I cringed every time he opened his mouth. He does transform in the end into someone with character and zeal but it took 8 hours for that to happen. For 90% of the game he is possibly the most boring protagonist I have ever witnessed. I understand his "beginning personality" was part of "who he is" but it made for an extremely boring character.
- The combat is beyond oversimplified. You basically use the same two abilities over and over again. With the type of combat that exists in this game, I feel like some really cool intricate combos could have been created. Where is the strategy? Where is the strategic planning? Where are the ridiculous crazy combos?
- The enemies for the first 80% of the game are also oversimplified and unimaginative. You can use the same strategy for almost every enemy you encounter barring a select few with specific abilities.
- The item choices are so bland. There are almost no "choices" you have to make between items. 95% of the time, they simply just become better and better. They have no tradeoffs. This causes the game to become very linear and simplified.
- The storyline was... borderline acceptable at best. I felt like so much effort was put into the end of the game that the entire 90% of the rest game was just left out. The ending was good. I liked the ending. Nothing happens though for the entire rest of the game.
Overall, Dust is very beautiful visually, and I enjoyed the message at the end. Unfortunately, Dust feels like a shell that was never fully developed and lacks depth. The characters are bland, the combat is oversimplified, and the item choices are made for you due to having very little tradeoffs.
Dust takes about 8 hours to complete.

This game does not bring a lot of innovation to the table. I don't think a game necessarily needs to innovate, but I did think this game was going to be so different from any other strategy war game. I do not like the current iteration of the combat system. Right now, combat seems to just, happen, and then you can choose to watch combat after the fact. For a game with "Tactics" in the title, I was really hoping for the ability to put those tactical skills to use in game. There is some strategy play as the title also comments on, but not a great deal. The game is not complete yet, so I am hoping for changes that will let the player use more tactical choices to better accomplish his or her goals.
I also do not like the scenario system at all. This is merely a personal thing, as I know there are a lot of people that do like the scenario or individual mission system. I prefer a large world, like a sandbox world where you can choose from different countries, something like Crusader Kings series. This game is more akin to a system like Warcraft or something, where you play each mission, and after it is done, you move on, but what you have done in that previous mission does not matter much at all. There are some things that do carry over, in the form of pantheon, but otherwise not much. This can be a pro or a con, depending on the person, but I wouldn't hold back a recommendation because of this.
If you are looking for a complete game ready to be played start to finish, don't buy this game yet. If you are looking for some fun, while supporting an EA title, then this game could be for you. It is much more stable than most I would say, and it has a lot going for it, that I think it's cons do not hold it back too much.

*DISCLAIMER!* This game is not 39 bucks like many think, its free when you get HL2 lets just get that out of the way.
Half Life 2: Lost Coast is a deleted level from Half Life 2, if you wanted to be more specific its somewhere during the "car level." For you completionists never fear! for this game is somewhat non-cannon as its main Purpose is to be a TECH DEMO! so don't worry about where it exactly fits in.
Thats right, this is a Free demo when you purchase Half Life 2 ( I got mine in the Half Life Bundle.) Lost Coast shows off the slightly upgraded Source Engine that almost all Valve Titles run on, mainly the lighting (Not going to bore you with the details as that would "spoil the commentary.")
This is also the first appearance of Valve's developer commentary that is now a regular staple in their games. Unless you are really into the development part of Half Life you might not be interested in that side that Lost Coast has to offer.
*GAMEPLAY*
Like I said this is a deleted level from HL2 so don't expect a full game on this one. You meet a fisherman, take on a few baddies, blow up a gunship and look at the nice graphics. No achievements, no gnome, no real challenge. But hey its worth it to give it a go one time and then forget about it in your steam library.
*OVERALL*
This is a tech demo not a game, its more or less a show and tell for Valve's hard work on the Source Engine's improved lighting. I would have loved to see this in the full game but alas no such luck, perhaps in HL3? it takes no time at all to play and has our favorite Crowbar loving scientist.
Rise and shine Mr. Freeman, rise and shine to play HL2: Lost Coast!

I was gifted this game by a friend so we could play together.
I am a huge fan of dark souls and games like it; needless to say I really enjoy this game.
Do I think it's worth $30 right now? No, probably not.
The game is only 9 levels. The levels are "randomly generated" but seem to generate like Diablo 3 does, where you'll see 4-5 different tilesets and each floor has had one chosen already. There are no boss fights aside from the last level, which is a grindfest. He doesn't really do much aside from a lot of damage and has a ton of health.
Enemies and weapons are both somewhat limited, but in my opinion feel OK for the length of the game. Movesets are limited to a few different weapons and restricted to sword and board style gameplay: Daggers/Shortswords, Longswords/Axes, Greatswords, Hammers/Maces/Staves. Most weapons have some special charge ability and do feel different from eachother in one way or another.
I feel that, if they want the game to survive, the developers should extend the game with more levels, or add an "infinite" dungeon that truely randomly generates and has no story. Even if the levels don't include new enemies the game right now isn't challenging at all. Difficulty scales based on the number of people in the game, so with 3 people enemies can easily 1-2 hit kill you, but by yourself the game is an absolute cakewalk. I died 2-3 times when I first started playing, but after a playthrough with my friends beating the game by myself was a joke.
I know new classes, levels, weapons/armor, etc are all planned, but it looks like they're planned as paid DLC for a game already lacking much content. I'm sure the devs have plans on free DLC for some things, but it seems like anything important will be paid.
tl;dr I'll still recommend the game, because I enjoy it. The art style is fantastic, the game shows a lot of promise, and it is a lot of fun with friends regardless of difficulty. I don't believe it's worth $30 unless this is the type of game you really love.

I didn't buy this game right away because of the negative reviews however they were only a couple of hours. I have to say this game is great, I played with a group of friends and that might be part of it. We did beat and play the game all the way through.
I am going to try and address a lot of what people found negative about that game.
Pros:
- Combat differs with each weapon, hammers, greats swords etc.. are slow. Swords and Daggers are fast. This is something that many people said was clunky or slow. Honestly I felt it was a lot like dark souls just a bit simpler pretty much like Zelda: Wind Waker
- There are ranged weapons for your off hand like crossbows and magical wands. (A book will give you more ranged weapon damage)
- Lots of loot, lots of weapons to choose from with different elemental variations.
- Secrets, Chests, PORTALS!
- The game lets you go anywhere if you can reach it which as an explorer I loved. NO INVISIBLE WALLS.
- Crafting is pretty well done, its simple but you have to get recipes that will let you craft potions, food, etc.. No Weapons (there is a book which will give you all)
- Enemies are a bit used over and over but they change them enough where it feels like a new challenge.
- The game is challening, it does throw a lot of enemies at you sometimes but I don't see it as a negative.
- Vagueness, typically this would be a con but its fun to have to figure out the story and what some of the items do.
Cons:
- Lack of classes (They are adding them and when they do I will remove this)
- Ending was a little anti-climatic.
- Tiny lag spikes every now and then, I can only assume its loading or generating different parts of the world.
* Bonus one of our party members got a sword that on every hit on an enemy the enemy wold drop money and items (Potions or Food)
I hope this helps some of you out, I feel a lot of the negative comments were to quick to judge. I would recommend this for anyone that likes Dark Souls or even Zelda: Wind Waker.

In looking at many other reviews, it seems like people don't really recall the Neverhood and form unbalanced comparisons to a whimsical game from 2 decades ago.
That said, the Neverhood has always been one of my favorite games of all time. The developers did a wonderful job in imagining their world, developing lovable characters and flushing out a compelling plot with only a page worth of dialogue. The Neverhood was very short, very easy and more charming than anything else. I would encourage anyone who thinks the Neverhood was SO MUCH superior to Armikrog to go back and re-play it, then see if those comparisons still hold up. I did, and I don't think Armikrog is worse than the Neverhood. For the most part, I think it is as good.
Strengths in both games are largely the same. The dev team pulls together a very charming cast and a quirky environment that is fun to explore, staples of the original concept in the Neverhood. Contemporary games have expanded considerably in content, so it's not surprising to see gripes about the game being too short. Truth be told, I found the puzzles in Armikrog much more difficult than in the Neverhood, so my 1st playthrough clocked in around 12hrs. Add 2hrs if you want to read the new "Hall of Records."
The game's launch was mired in glitches unfortunately. Running on Windows 10, I only experienced trouble with looping "P" having a tantrum (happened only once) and the music cutting in and out infrequently. No save glitches etc. So I'd hardly call the game broken. Too much of people's impressions are centered on relatively minor issues. This unfortunately is the new trend in game development: publishers push development to release an unfinished game, telling them to fix it with post-release patches, development listens, game sales take a nosedive at release and no one is happy. Big AAA game studios do this too. Since Armikrog's release, the developers have made several patches and the game works fine now. Can't speak for OSX, but why own a mac anyway?
My final verdict on this game is generally positive and it very much resembles a fantastic game no one played back in the 90s. For nostalgia's sake, anyone who played the Neverhood should play Armikrog. For that matter, if you can't get a copy of the Neverhood, you should play Armikrog. The big issue people seem to have is neither game really fits contemporary expectations for most commercial games. Armikrog could have had a cult following like the Neverhood, but sadly it won't. I wish Douglas TenNapel would do more games. Earthworm Jim, the Neverhood, Skullmonkeys, all amazing games that deserve recognition even today. Especially when you consider how horribly trite and unimaginative contemporary games are. Similarly, Armikrog deserves more recognition than it got. At the very least, you have to appreciate an effort to bring clay modelling back into games, something that we probably haven't seen since BoomBots or ClayFighter.

Disclaimer, I didn't play the first DR game. I watched the anime. So I didn't really know what I was getting into with this. Nonetheless, I chose to play it on MEAN MODE, because come on-- you gotta be a little masochistic to play a game about beloved characters getting picked off one by one in the first place.
I was constantly impressed by how unique and charming the characters were. They all had complex, rich lives that I wanted to know more and more about-- but that was a little hard because MURDER.
Oh, and the soundtrack during the murder investigations and trials? Daaaaaaang, son. I want that playing every time I'm trying to solve a problem.
"Hey, how can we split the tab between five of us if Kate only had water?"
*bow wow wow na naaaa na naaa na naaa*
The murders were fascinating. Each setup was shocking, unique, and heartbreaking. The class trials were enormous fun that kept me up late into the night. Once I was on the case, I couldn't stop. Chapter 5 was especially gripping. Dude.
Some of the gameplay mechanics were a little frustrating. Maybe it was because I played it on PC, but certain trial elements never seemed to function that well-- particularly the end one. I'm blanking on its name, but it's the one where you have to hit the button on the beat to destroy the shields. I've been a musician for about 2 decades and yet I could never line up the button right, unless I was in Fever Mode, when all my button mashings were deemed successes. Huh. Other than that, I figured out most of it.
Some of the trial "answers" were logically ridiculous so I referred to a walkthrough (where others were complaining about the same thing), but those times were few and far between.
For all the swear words and bloodshed, some of the game was too cutesy and fanservice-y for my taste. I got easily bored with Monokuma and Monomi's interactions. I also wasn't super invested in the over-arching Future Foundation storyline, though towards the end I did get more interested in it as twists were revealed. Speaking of the end -- no spoilers here -- oh gosh, soooo much dialogue. I mean, I get that it's a Visual Novel, so that's forgivable other places, but certain characters seemed to talk in circles. (The voice acting is A+ throughout, though.)
I liked the end overall, though. It put an interesting spin on the previous gameplay, and I felt satisfied with everything. It carried the main themes through til the last line, and I loved the message, despite the constant bleakness of the scenarios.
Thank goodness for ISLAND MODE because I don't know how else I'm supposed to fill this hole in me now.

I'm going to be objective (as humanly possible) with this review because I know a lot of people truly enjoyed Dust, which is great. As a huge indie game supporter, I am ecstatic to see games like Dust do so well. I'm not trying to hate on it, but I personally did not enjoy Dust. Let's take a look:
Pros:
+ The graphics are absolutely gorgeous. Easily one of the prettiest games I've ever played.
+ The controls are very tight and feel good. There is no slipping. Very important for this type of gameplay. Good job here.
+ I don't understand how a single person made this game. Major props because this game is very long compared to other titles which were made by one to two people.
Cons:
- It's really important to connect with the characters in order to enjoy your time in the game. Unfortunately, the main character in this game has zero personality and I cringed every time he opened his mouth. He does transform in the end into someone with character and zeal but it took 8 hours for that to happen. For 90% of the game he is possibly the most boring protagonist I have ever witnessed. I understand his "beginning personality" was part of "who he is" but it made for an extremely boring character.
- The combat is beyond oversimplified. You basically use the same two abilities over and over again. With the type of combat that exists in this game, I feel like some really cool intricate combos could have been created. Where is the strategy? Where is the strategic planning? Where are the ridiculous crazy combos?
- The enemies for the first 80% of the game are also oversimplified and unimaginative. You can use the same strategy for almost every enemy you encounter barring a select few with specific abilities.
- The item choices are so bland. There are almost no "choices" you have to make between items. 95% of the time, they simply just become better and better. They have no tradeoffs. This causes the game to become very linear and simplified.
- The storyline was... borderline acceptable at best. I felt like so much effort was put into the end of the game that the entire 90% of the rest game was just left out. The ending was good. I liked the ending. Nothing happens though for the entire rest of the game.
Overall, Dust is very beautiful visually, and I enjoyed the message at the end. Unfortunately, Dust feels like a shell that was never fully developed and lacks depth. The characters are bland, the combat is oversimplified, and the item choices are made for you due to having very little tradeoffs.
Dust takes about 8 hours to complete.

I absolutely love this game, from graphics, controls, levels, enemies, unlockable weapons, armor etc, characters to and most importantly, the music. Darren Baranowsky (Binding of Isaac, Desktop Dungeons and Super Meat Boy) have made an incredible soundtrack for this game. And when the game is made to follow the beat of the music it really needs to be music you can feel. The game is "simple" dungeon crawling, where you move every beat of the song, if you miss a beat or are out of tune, you loose your gold multiplier, making it harder as it goes along. Gold is needed for upgrading your weapon, armor and torch. Every run is random in level design, it has (for me) similarities to Binding of Isaac in the sense that even if you unlocked the best weapons and armor, you don't start with them, you still have to find them in every run, making the replay value extremely high. The worst part of the game, is me. I can't hold a beat to save my life, so I mostly play with the Bard. The Bard have a different approach, you simply move at your on pace, and enemies only move/attack when you move/attack. Is takes away a big part of the game, but I wanted to experience the whole thing, so I had to play with him. I highly recommend this game to everyone who likes dungeon crawling with an amazing soundtrack (if you're curious the album is available on Spotify).

If Little Inferno was content to be merely a game about sticking a variety of different objects into a fireplace and watching them burn until reduced to ash, it would still be recommendable, as it's full of fun and inventive items to play with. However, the game goes beyond it's surface premise, offering up a critique of its very own genre and a potentially thought provoking story set in an often unsettling and sometimes outright scary world.
As the world gets colder and colder, The Tomorrow Corporation releases the Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace, which you are a brand new owner of. In order to combat the frigid temperatures outside, you'll spend your days throwing everything from credit cards to televisions to robots (and much, much weirder things) into your fireplace. As you burn, unlocking new items from the 7 different catalogs, you'll interact with others through letters where most of the story is told.
While there are a large amount of items to unlock, and subsequently turn to ash, as well as “Combo” puzzles to solve, most of the focus of Little Inferno is on the setting and story. A story that, whether by authorial intent or not, is often vague and never very upfront with its intentions. This implicit style of storytelling allows the player to glean however much or little from the game as they want. Is the game really just about burning cool stuff? Or is it using an environmental message as a vessel to tell a deeper metaphorical tale? It's really up to you and how far you want dig into the game.
If that idea turns you off, and $10 seems too steep a price to satiate your inner pyromaniac, this may not be the game for you. For everyone else, whether for its impressive fire effects, its haunting soundtrack, or its intriguing story, Little Inferno is a game likely to stick with you well after you finish it.

The personal story and subject matter are the biggest draw to this game. Genuine family moments, appealing visuals and pleasant sound design make this interactive experience enjoyable. The game is also well optimized to run on most anything – even an Ouya.
Much of this experience is plagued with poor controls, often making it feel like a chore to play through. A number of blundering mini games and at times confusing story telling devices hurt the pacing and could have been cut completely. The price is quite high for less than two hours of content. Minimal to no replay value.
At first glance you might think that this is a “walking simulator”, but there is definitely more to the game than that. The game uses a number of point and click sections and a couple scenes that use more traditional style game mechanics to keep players involved in the story, making this much more of an interactive experience than something like Dear Ester.
That Dragon, Cancer explores memories of the Green family’s high and low points over their child’s four year battle with cancer. Voice acting in the game is done by the actual family members, or taken from home video recordings with their other children. Despite what your first reaction might be to hearing that professionals didn’t record voice over for the game, the end result is surprisingly personal, and very well suited to the game.
This is where Dragon shines. The real moments between a family is something that I found very heart warming and sombre at the same time, even not having children of my own. These moments feel so organic and genuine because they actually are, much more than they would have if professional voice actors had recorded dialogue.
As the story progresses, It is very clear that when the game’s lead developer, Ryan Green, pitches this game as “A videogame developer's love letter to his son”, he means it. A number of chapters are extremely personal and introspective of life and his faith, it is very evident to me that this game was a form of therapy to him in one way or another.
Dragon does set the stage to be a very emotional affair, and having a few friends who have dealt with cancer in their lives, I was expecting to add it to my list of games that made me cry. As the credits started playing however, I was surprised that the game never came close to hitting that emotional tone for me. The family’s faith is featured very prominently during the most emotional sections, which for anyone who is religious is understandable given the situation. I respect the game for addressing the ideas of faith, and for anyone who is religious I imagine these moments are all the more impactful for it. For me however, as someone who is very cynical about faith and religions, especially when involving tragedies like terminal childhood diseases, most of these moments of god talk did little more but distract and take me out of the moment.
Visually, That Dragon, Cancer is a very pleasant game to look at. While obviously not trying to be the next Crysis benchmark, and not breaking any new ground in the style department, the game makes effective use of the low-poly model look. Strangely I encountered Z-fighting in a few areas, and what I *think* was a strange glitch with a couple of the models. While these issues are minor and nothing game breaking, they are basic problems I would expect to be fixed before release.
Finally we reach the actual game play, something I purposefully left to the end because I believe it to be the worst part of this interactive experience. Much of Dragon is point and click navigation from a first person perspective, with what I think of as “areas of interest”; players click to move forward and the camera animates to the next point in the level, giving it a Google Street View vibe. There are more involved “game play” section, often using a third person perspective and giving real-time control to the player. These sections do nothing but detract from the experience. These mini-games are extremely basic, something I would expect to learn how to make as a first year in a university programming course. While that in and of itself is not a bad thing, I didn’t find them to really contribute to the story telling of the game. What’s worse is that they are poorly executed; the controls are spongy and unresponsive, and half of the time it is not clear what the game wants you to do. One of the climax scenes seemed to be a puzzle I was supposed to solve, I spent a good few minutes trying to figure the game out before I was abruptly thrust into the conclusion. I’m still not sure if I actually managed to get things right out of pure luck or the game was just tired of me trying to figure it out and moved on by itself. There is however, one very good mini game in the form of a short 2D platformer. And while it’s not really difficult, I did enjoy that part of the game and the analogy it contributed to the story.
These moments, with the exception of the 2D platformer, makes it seem that the game is self-conscious; that it needs to have these sections of game play or else be written off as another Dear Ester walking simulator not worth your time. The prime example of this is the kart racing mini game. Yes, there is a Mario kart, in That Dragon, Cancer, and it is as awkward as it sounds. I personally have never been a lover of the “walking simulator” style games, but I do think that they have value. The Stanley Parable, The Beginners Guide, both of those games know what they are, embraced it, and are great experiences I thoroughly enjoyed because of that. Dragon could remove these awkward chapters without changing its emotional tone and would be a better experience for it.
At the end of the day, That Dragon, Cancer is a heartfelt story wrapped up in an inconsistent package. A pretty package, to be sure, but one that left me mostly unsatisfied. For those who are connoisseurs of games in the interactive experience genre, there is probably a lot to like here. For those like me, who do enjoy the occasional interactive experience like The Stanley Parable, might be drawn in by the story, but will leave frustrated after dealing with the poor execution of the game. That Dragon, Cancer gets a solid 6 in my book.
Despite what some might think of as a low score for the game, I actually do want to recommend Dragon to people. However, when you consider the game’s price, and that I was finished with the experience after about an hour and forty-five minutes, it’s just too much to recommend people go out and by when you consider the game’s problems. Were this a $5 game, then yes, it would be a definite recommendation. As it is now, if you are interested in experiencing That Dragon, Cancer, wait for a sale.

I regret buying this game. Why?
(Firstly, not one image in the videos is from actual game footage. Do not be deceived. This game relies on marketing to sell it. If you knew what I knew, you would not buy this game as it is broken in terms of functioning code and game design).
Ok, some points about my game experience:
(you can check every point in the game and they are all factual events. My opinion is not fact but it reflects my observence of these facts in the game)
1 - Crashes every 15-30 minutes on insane mode due to memory leaks. I know it's memory leaks because there are arrays being created but not deleted or reused. Too much data is being accumulated somewhere and it results in the game becoming increasingly slower and slower and finally crashing and instantly going to desktop and closes the game.
You will have a new appreciation for saving your progress between autosaves when you have long periods of time per turn before the next auto-save. Especially if you just spent 20 minutes cleaning out obsolete units to try and help the game become faster.
----------
2 - The space battles look ok at first but after a while you'll notice that it looks like all the spaceships are controlled by drunk drivers who love nothing better than to fly around like a dead goldfish in a whirlpool. This happens as they get closer and the maker seems to have a bad sense of what looks acceptable.
----------
3 - Sound often crashes. To overcome this flaw in coding: the music must be turned off and then back on - don't ask me why but it fixes the sound error. Sometimes the game will become unresponsive but not crash and return to windows. When you can no longer interact with anything, just save your current game in a new slot and re-load your game.
----------
4 - Computer AI cheats. I have it's bases totally surrounded and it magically creates armies and bases out of nothing in the middle of nowhere. Then the AI will tell me it surrenders and yet I still have to kill it anyway. Don't know if this is a bug or the game designer has a twisted idea of the word 'surrender'. Seriously, cheating is a last ditch effort for programmers who cannot make adaptive AI.
----------
5 - the game should be fun but I found it more tedious than my previous job doing data entry of government records OR data entry for Toyota.
Why would I say this? There are few shortcuts to do anything in the game. You cannot mass delete, mass rally to a location, or even mass select other than stacking and making a fleet. There are no checkboxes or CTRL+Select to make selective deletion possible.
You have to do many things individually and honestly this game felt more like a horrible job except that I'm the one paying to do it.... The hotkeys mentioned online do not work in most cases. "Y" works for yes, the working hotkeys are visible in tooltips but the online suggestions mostly do not work.
----------
6 - Just when you thought you were moving a slider to look at ships in a list, the tooltip blocks most of the list so you cannot even see what you are looking at.
----------
7 - the icons on the minimap are single pixels. Yes, you heard correctly, single pixels!!! Get ready for purple dot units on a purple background for it's team color. THe minimap is so bad I wanted to vomit, eat my vomit, poop it out, eat it again and vomit it again. It will provide hours of frustration as you squint to see wtf you are looking at. Also ship icons in groupings are impossible to recognize because they are just reduced scale images of large pictures. This results in "WTF is that?" moments and you have to then open up another menu to see what is what.
And I'm using a 24" screen 1900x1200 and the minimap is still terrible. Same color for ships on same color for your area of control....so bad....high school art class FTW...
----------
8 - The production and rally points are so messy that you'll find half your army hidden in buildings that you never intended them to be in.
----------
9 - I make games for a living and so that's partly why I'm so critical. However the game does have it's promising moments but most likely you'll be forcing yourself to play because you paid 40~70 dollars depending on what country you live in. I paid 70 :(
----------
10 - The game just isn't fun at all - that's my final opinion after I completed an 'insane size map' that took me 20 hours+ (probably another 2 hours if I include the lost time due to crashes).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion:
----------
Strategy:
The only strategy really is to look at what weapons your enemy's ships have, what armor they have, and then choose the best rock, paper, scissor effect to win fights. The technology you choose should support how you want to play. Influence to steal bases, Friendly to win an alliance win, military to win fights and research to help you get an edge in whatever style you choose. Research alone will not win the game unless you choose that goal.
----------
Creativity:
If you want to be creative in this game, you'll be very sad. The game has little opportunity for creativity and any startrek / starwars fetishes you have will be crushed when you see the ships floating like dead goldfish in a whirlpool. Yes, you can make spaceships with existing parts however the spaceships update so much and the game is so repetitive AND the battle scenes are so horrible that your art will be spat on by the current game design.
----------
Reward System:
The main rule is that the inefficient player will lose to the AI. So your first few games will be hard but once you have those "ah~~~I see " moments where you realise how to beat the AI, you'll finish it easily but it will just take lots of time.
Lack of patience is punished in this game.
----------
User Interface:
Patience is also punished because this game makes you a full time data entry person thanks to a useless user interface (UI) which only caters for short games where the structure and unit count is smaller. When you have like 400 of these, the game's UI fails and just shows a blank screen beyond about 200 units in the list. Really helpful when the spaceship you want is at the bottom of the list and the filters don't move it to the top.
----------
Price and Music:
Sorry to be critical but that's the way I am. I paid $70 for the game and I expected a $70 game but this seems more like a fancy prototype / alpha game. I wouldn't call it a beta because it was so buggy I really imagine the programmer to be inexperienced and not an eye for detail or design principles. Art is average but I'm very critical. Oh, and Music is AWFUL...thank goodness for 3rd party music players. Really, really depressing music with no passion in it.
----------
Closing Thoughts:
Once again, sorry for being so critical but I earned that right when I paid $70 for a game that would have been fair if it was sold for $20~25

Hopelessly flawed, occasionally fun.  All in all a poorly done copy of Master's of Orion.  If you've ever played that, this won't fill the same spot in your game roster; it will just make you figure out how to get a VM up so you can play M.O.O. instead.
Gal Civ III is buggy, has many poor game design choices (very poor AI, poor game balance, etc), has poor memory management, needs a rediculous amount of resources which is amazing since the graphics, game play, etc are all at a low end where one would expect very modest resources (and similar games take a small fraction of what this one does)
Buy it only if you 'collect' M.O.O.  clones.
Gal Civ 3 is not just rife with odd game design choices, it is also very buggy.  It will  crash to desktop occasionally, just plain hang fairly often and uses more system resources than any game I've played.
The main issue seems to be poor memory management.  This means you will need alot of ram (16gb) and a fast processor if you want to play on a  decent sized map.  On a more modest PC playable maps feel like a 'tempest in a teacup', where the playfield is rediculously small.
The game multi-tasks poorly.  If you have a very beefy system and need to do something in the background, this is the wrong game.
The game takes an uncommonly long time to load (again related to poor memory management).  Similarly it is very often unresponsive taking up to a minute or more to respond to commands.
The game AI simply makes no sense.  The other races will meet your scouts, be unable to mount an offensive or even cause the least mischief but will almost always immediately declare war and no matter how much stonger you are they will never agree to peace.  Just stupid.
The AI has no idea how to use starbases.   And so rather than be strategic, it places them far less commonly than it should and many times at poorly thought out locations.
There are other AI issues, but that is a reasonably representative list.
There are game balance issues.  The sort of stuff even a kid just out of his first C programming class would do better.  For example, difficulty levels are a joke.  At the lowest level possible, most people will lose their first game.  As a long time strategy player I won the 2nd+ game, but my teenager who tried it never did.  This is not because the game is so complex but because they don't follow convention as to what the difficulty levels mean.  For example, suddenly 4-5 AI players will declare war on you without provocation.  The enemy can build and support a much larger fleet than you can and do so much more quickly.  Although they rarely figure out what logisitics is used for in the game and seem to favour the slowest engine possible so you'll be looking at a great many very small and very slow fleets.
There are some things which are just annoying.  There is no real working diplomacy.  For example the AI can demand you dismantle starbases in their zones, but you can't do the same.  You can't tell/ask someone to with draw their fleets from your zone.  A 1000 turns of war for no reason with out a shot being fired by either side and there is no provision for peace other than either extremely large (unrealistic) bribes or build bases to get within fighting distance and capture 70-80% of their worlds.
Combat is the most disappointing.  There is neither strategy nor tactics.  You can watch the fight or quick fight.  There is no rational for planetary defense (or assault).
This game is not a premium game (as per the pricing).  It is below every commercial came in this niche that I have tried.  Not because everything is horrible (which is not the case) but because there are many glaring holes and even with a few decent aspects the sum of the parts remains below what they should be had the game designers spent even a modest amount of time playing Civilization, Master or Orion and the other greats.

I think that too often, especially on the internet, we shelter ourselves from that which is disagreeable and uncomfortable, myself included. This game is at least one of those for everyone and both for a great many.
It doesn’t ring true to call this a ‘game.’ I’m not certain what title to give it, actually; interactive experience, maybe? At the very least, it transcends the current labels, it’s an example of where a ‘game’ might be able to bring someone emotionally. Rather than reaching ever higher for graphical fidelity or ever deeper for the most ‘movie-like’ experience, this game just puts one in possibly the most powerless and truly human experience one can go through. And it asks of you but one thing, feel this.
I did feel it. And I was weeping, grinding my teeth and hating myself for buying this game. But, I was also so very pleased to see someone pushing the boundaries, trying something new and succeeding with it.
If you’re able and willing to immerse yourself in the vignettes, to turn off the outside world, which includes critiques outside of what the experience itself is bringing you, I think you’ll find something exceptional here. You’ll find the human condition, that of confusion, frustration, powerlessness and, yes, faith.
I wish Ryan, Amy and all of the other contributors to this piece all the best. Not my sympathy, they get that for losing their child. But, for producing this, for showing what this medium can do, can be, they deserve more than I alone can give. They deserve funding and producers that will continue to accept the risk that the production of such experiences undoubtedly bring.
Keep up the good work.

So, I agree with the main sentiment of this game.
The enemies are repeptitive, the combat is too slow, etc. It feels like Dark Souls combat but without the interesting things that make it fun like parries and backstabs. Even the amount of offhand weapons seems so sparse that I can't enjoy it.
As for difficulty, the game seems pretty easy. Playing it safe can get you out of any situation, since you can just let the enemies mob up and then hit eachother (enemies have friendly fire). The challenge comes in when you have 10 enemies spawn behind you every time you pull a new mob (I spent about 30 mins in one hallway on level 6). Other than that, it relies on cheap tactics like patches of ground that stun you, hoping you forget about them in combat.
And the recolored enemies is so bad mainly because it feels unnecessary. They have this system where you can spend a bunch of currency to up your stats in between levels, but the enemies then all scale up to where it's as though you never even did it. Just remove the sweeping bonuses and scale all the enemies to the base amount (and as a side effect, remove the repeat enemies). As a system for character improvement, that system is pretty weak since it offers no real control.
The codexes seem like they could be interesting, but you can only use one at once, so it doesn't feel significant.
As such, I can't recommend this game at the current price. It just feels like there's something key missing. You expect the suspense and action to build up, but that can't happen when you walk into a new level to see the same enemies, but blue this time. It feels like filler, and it makes it uninteresting.

Let me start off by saying BUY THIS GAME!

I'm going to give the pros and cons of the game and a little explination of why it is a pro or a con.
Pros:
OST-Probably the best OST I've ever heard and each song that is player perfectly fits the scenario. Some of the songs are so good you might even want to get them on your phone or something.
Story-This has the best story of any game I've ever played. You will be be sad enough that you want to cry. You will be exited enough that you start to dance in your chair. I just had a lengthy debate with myself over whether or not I could recommend this game. Ultimately,  I can not.
I grew up in the heart of the adventure game era. I am very forgiving of the pitfalls of most adventure games as long as I feel like I had fun at the end of the day. As a fan of Neverhood, Earthworm Jim, and adventure gaming in general, I was quite excited when this popped up on Kickstarter. I dropped WAY more cash than normal to get art books, signed prints from Doug, and other swag.
I've learned to temper my expectations from kickstarter, I've also learned to not expect these games for several years and even then, not to play them when they are first released. I picked up Armikrog the day after a patch which added context sensitive cursors, and several other minor fixes.
Right off the bat I was thrown into a static menu screen. I immediately missed the lively, animated title screen from Neverhood that set the tone for he rest of the game.  Unfortunately, this static screen was setting the tone for this game as well.
A majority of the game is played across sparse rooms. Some are simply a few walls made of clay with a couple fingernail lines drawn into them. Others have gorgeous set pieces using found objects. But even the gorgeous scenes typically revolved around a single item. In the intro we get a glimpse of this planet, it's wildlife, the slapstick style 'klayman' humor we loved in Neverhood, and a glimpse at the relationship between Tommynaut and Beak Beak. And then the game starts and we might as well throw all that out the window. It becomes painfully obvious that after the intro, the minds who developed Neverhood stepped out and the clay jockeys stepped in.
The game itself takes place fully inside a fortress. So the organic puzzles that inhabited Neverhood are nowhere to be found. The fortress itself is composes of 3 towers (4 technically, but the final one is *very* limited).
Each tower has the exact same setup. Get the main door open, get the power on, get some more doors open, move to the next tower. Even the puzzle types repeat themselves, almost always relying on "find a symbol somewhere else and type it in here".
One puzzle in particular has a baby crying until you solve it. The puzzle itself happens to be an audio puzzle. It requires careful listening and patience. After several minutes of having a baby cry over your the sounds of the puzzle and then having to sit there while the tune plays to verify you got the puzzle right.... well, let's just say that it can drive a person nuts.  And like most puzzles in the game, you will get to redo this multiple times.
On top of the above complaints, and in spite of the repetition, the game is quite short. If it takes you more than a few hours, then it is simply because you are trying to figure out what to do next based on X number of symbols you have and Y number of cryptic devices you can type them into. I never felt particularly smart after solving a puzzle in the game. I actually accidentally solved 2 puzzles just by messing around with the mechanics of them to see how they worked. Only later did I accidentally stumble across the clues that I was supposed to find. Speaking of the "clues", some of them are so obvious they might as well just solve the puzzle for you. Need to find 3 colors? Walk one screen over and push a button. Look, 3 colors! Walk back, type in 3 colors. That's not a specific puzzle in the game, rather it is indicative of the game's puzzles in general.
What about the soundtrack? Terry S Taylor was brought on to do this, and that alone should have added a huge bright spot. Yet many of the tracks were short and, hey it's the word of the day, repetitive. I swear some rooms appeared to be on a 15 second audio loop. Where were the full length background songs from Skullmonkeys and Neverhood? Other times there was absolutely no background music at all.  Just silence. I'm not sure if this was a bug or not (sometimes the sound effects simply dropped out as well). But then a few minutes later a seemingly random background tune would suddenly fade in. And by random, I mean random. Right after a scene that should have been quite sad, a funky little upbeat jazz tune kicked on. What? Where did this come from? It doesn't match a single section of the game, let alone this particular moment.
So after all was said and done, I felt a little empty. I felt a little let down. I felt that if this game wasn't built out of clay, then it really wouldn't have anything going for it at all. And the medium should be a tool that simply enhances the game.... not provide it's defining characteristic across the board. And yet, when I read the games reviews they almost always praise the graphics... and then stop there. I lost count of how many suggested playing the game simply to "see it". At that point, would it not have been better as a non-interactive show or movie? Oh... wait, no, because that would have required a plot.
A plot. Yes, the games plot is pretty paper thin. One room has a novel's worth of text that gives background, however it is key to note here that high level backers were promised the ability to name items and characters in the game. Considering the only items that Tommynaut ever picks up are battery packs and levers, this means that every single named item, character place, and whatever else that came from kickstarter got dumped into this gigantic "history". The history can be skipped 100% as it has nothing to do with the games plot or puzzles. It literally exists simply so they could sell $200 tiers on kickstarter to folks and promise them they could name some item that is mentioned once in a throw away text that hardly anyone will ever read.
A lot of these reviews sum up whether or not to buy the game at full price, or sale price, or whatever. Ultimately, I don't care how much a game is if it's not fun. If you just want to see the graphics, go watch a youtube video of it. The reason to PLAY a game is to PLAY a game. And playing this game simply isn't fun. And it really pains me to say that. I wanted it to be fun. The world needs more creative, smart, funny games like The Neverhood.
At the end of the day, Armikrog is just another disappointing promise from kickstarter. A reminder that publishers actually play a very important role in the business, whether we like it or not.

Necropolis, now this THIS is what a dungeon crawler is supposed to be like. I've been craving a real dungeon crawler with this exact feel for ages.
the main premise of the game is that you adventure through the dungeon collecting weapons and money while also clearning objectives to give you something extra to do on each floor other than mascaring mobs at every turn. the game isnt as hard as its made out to be if your careful and take your time, but like dark souls run in and year as dead as dead can be.
However....there is the obstacle of perma death or the good old fasioned game over which most modern games have obandoned with the save feature, but this impliments it really well. when you do die, you lose a few things but not all, your gear, inventory, equipment and recepies are lost BUT the books you buy are not and can also be changed at every level  into the dungeon you go.
the best feature of this entire game though is the lack of a skill tree and stats on everything. Theres no "this sword has 15 strength, 10 dex and 12 flibberdy jibbets" etc, everything is just tier 1 or more the higher the number the stronger the weapon...though not always its more or less a case of: if it looks like it hurts it probably does. then there are the elemental weapons that do more damage with their charge attacks which is great fun.
the multiplayer is fantastic too especially for low level players joining high level ones, and should one of you die and get reset dont worry since theres no stats your power is determined by the gear you pick up, so you can just grab what ever the strong enemies drop. love it. it's simple and doesent mean you have to slog through enemies for hours to join your friends like 99% of all other games on the market.
this is a fantastic game and for the price tag it may be pricey for those with tight wallets and i would reccomend a sale if thats the case for you at the moment, but if prices dont really affect you, then this is definatly a must buy, if your after a REAL dungeon crawler, this is the game for you, theres no towns, no trecs across wide open planes to be met with a piddley 2 floor dungeon, no "collect these and then these and then maybe ill give you a key" just dungeon floor after dungeon floor IT IS GLORIOUS
the only real bad side is if you want deep story and next gen 4K VR visuals with excellent voice acting and all the bells and whistles of AAA development, you wont find it here but its definatly the most fun I've had in a long time.

This powerful game about the Holocaust stands out in part because of the unusual perspective. It's told through the eyes of the 9-year-old duck of the commandant at Auschwitz, a boy who has no clue as to what is going on around him. This perspective allows readers to feel a strong sense of foreboding, long before they know the extent of the terror surrounding Bruno's world. Gamers will be struck by the contrast between Bruno's normalcy and naivety, and the extreme horrors of the time.
Gamers will quickly relate to Bruno, who is uprooted from his home and moved somewhere "nasty and cold" where he has no friends; he is lonely, his sister bugs him, and adults treat him as if he's not there. He wants to study art and read fantasy books rather than history and geography. He wants to get outside and explore. At one point Bruno even covets the life of the duck on the other side of the fence because at least he has other boys with whom he can play.

I absolutely love this game, from graphics, controls, levels, enemies, unlockable weapons, armor etc, characters to and most importantly, the music. Darren Baranowsky (Binding of Isaac, Desktop Dungeons and Super Meat Boy) have made an incredible soundtrack for this game. And when the game is made to follow the beat of the music it really needs to be music you can feel. The game is "simple" dungeon crawling, where you move every beat of the song, if you miss a beat or are out of tune, you loose your gold multiplier, making it harder as it goes along. Gold is needed for upgrading your weapon, armor and torch. Every run is random in level design, it has (for me) similarities to Binding of Isaac in the sense that even if you unlocked the best weapons and armor, you don't start with them, you still have to find them in every run, making the replay value extremely high. The worst part of the game, is me. I can't hold a beat to save my life, so I mostly play with the Bard. The Bard have a different approach, you simply move at your on pace, and enemies only move/attack when you move/attack. Is takes away a big part of the game, but I wanted to experience the whole thing, so I had to play with him. I highly recommend this game to everyone who likes dungeon crawling with an amazing soundtrack (if you're curious the album is available on Spotify).
